You can also add shared <code>knitr</code> options to a project-wide <code>_quarto.yml</code> file or a project-directory scoped <code>_metadata.yml</code> file.</p> <h5 id="jupyter-options">Jupyter Options</h5> <h6 id="expression-printing">Expression Printing</h6> <p>When multiple expressions are present in a code cell, by default, only the last top-level expression is captured in the rendered output. For example, consider the code cell:</p> <pre><code>```{python} "first" "last" ```</code></pre> <p>When rendered to HTML the output generated is:</p> <pre><code>'last'</code></pre> <p>This behavior corresponds to the <code>last_expr</code> setting for <a href="https://ipython.readthedocs.io/en/stable/config/options/terminal.html#configtrait-InteractiveShell.ast_node_interactivity">Jupyter shell interactivity</a>.</p> <p>You can control this behavior with the <code>ipynb-shell-interactivity</code> option. For example, to capture all top-level expressions set it to <code>all</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: All expressions format: html ipynb-shell-interactivity: all ---</code></pre> <p>Now the above code cell results in the output:</p> <pre><code>'first' 'last'</code></pre> <p>NoteAll Expressions are Printed in Dashboards</p> <p>For dashboards the default setting of <code>ipynb-shell-interactivity</code> is <code>all.</code></p> <h5 id="intermediates">Intermediates</h5> <p>On the way from markdown input to final output, there are some intermediate files that are created and automatically deleted at the end of rendering. You can use the following options to keep these intermediate files:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>keep-md</code></p> <p>Keep the markdown file generated by executing code.</p> <p><code>keep-ipynb</code></p> <p>Keep the notebook file generated from executing code (applicable only to markdown input files)</p> <p>For example, here we specify that we want to keep the jupyter intermediate file after rendering:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" execute: keep-ipynb: true jupyter: python3 ---</code></pre> <h5 id="fenced-echo">Fenced Echo</h5> <p>If you are writing a tutorial or documentation on using Quarto code blocks, you’ll likely want to include the fenced code delimiter (e.g. ```<code>{python}</code>) in your code output to emphasize that executable code requires that delimiter. You can do this using the <code>echo: fenced</code> option. For example, the following code block:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| echo: fenced 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Will be rendered as:</p> <pre><code>```{python} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>This is especially useful when you want to demonstrate the use of cell options. For example, here we demonstrate the use of the <code>output</code> and <code>code-overflow</code> options:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| echo: fenced #| output: false #| code-overflow: wrap 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>This code block appears in the rendered document as:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| output: false #| code-overflow: wrap 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Note that all YAML options will be included in the fenced code output except for <code>echo: fenced</code> (as that might be confusing to readers).</p> <p>This behavior can also be specified at the document level if you want all of your executable code blocks to include the fenced delimiter and YAML options:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: echo: fenced ---</code></pre> <h6 id="unexecuted-blocks">Unexecuted Blocks</h6> <p>Often you’ll want to include a fenced code block purely as documentation (not executable). You can do this by using two curly braces around the language (e.g. <code>python</code>, <code>r</code>, etc.) rather than one. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{{python}} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Will be output into the document as:</p> <pre><code>```{python} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>If you want to show an example with multiple code blocks and other markdown, just enclose the entire example in 4 backticks (e.g. ``````) and use the two curly brace syntax for code blocks within. For example:</p> <pre><code>```` --- title: "My document" --- Some markdown content. ```{{python}} 1 + 1 ``` Some additional markdown content. ````</code></pre> <h5 id="engine-binding">Engine Binding</h5> <p>Earlier we said that the engine used for computations was determined automatically. You may want to customize this—for example you may want to use the Jupyter <a href="https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel">R kernel</a> rather than Knitr, or you may want to use Knitr with Python code (via <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/">reticulate</a>).</p> <p>Here are the basic rules for automatic binding:</p> <p>Extension</p> <p>Engine Binding</p> <p>.qmd</p> <p>Use Knitr engine if an <code>{r}</code> code block is discovered within the file</p> <p>Use Jupyter engine if any other executable code block (e.g. <code>{python}</code>, <code>{julia}</code>, <code>{bash}</code>, etc.) is discovered within the file. The kernel used is determined based on the language of the first executable code block discovered.</p> <p>Use no engine if no executable code blocks are discovered.</p> <p>.ipynb</p> <p>Jupyter engine</p> <p>.Rmd</p> <p>Knitr engine</p> <p>.md</p> <p>No engine (note that if an <code>md</code> document does contain executable code blocks then an error will occur)</p> <p>NoteUsing python and r together</p> <p>If your quarto document includes both <code>{python}</code> and <code>{r}</code> code blocks, then quarto will automatically use Knitr engine and <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/">reticulate</a> R package to execute the python content.</p> <p>For <code>.qmd</code> files in particular, you can override the engine used via the <code>engine</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>engine: jupyter engine: knitr</code></pre> <p>You can also specify that no execution engine should be used via <code>engine: markdown</code>.</p> <p>The presence of the <code>knitr</code> or <code>jupyter</code> option will also override the default engine:</p> <pre><code>knitr: true jupyter: python3</code></pre> <p>Variations with additional engine-specific options also work to override the default engine:</p> <pre><code>knitr: opts_knit: verbose: true jupyter: kernelspec: display_name: Python 3 language: python name: python3</code></pre> <h5 id="shell-commands">Shell Commands</h5> <p>Using shell commands (from Bash, Zsh, etc.) within Quarto computational documents differs by engine. If you are using the Jupyter engine you can use <a href="https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/01.05-ipython-and-shell-commands.html">Jupyter shell magics</a>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Using Bash" engine: jupyter --- ```{python} !echo "foo" ```</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>!</code> preceding <code>echo</code> is what enables a Python cell to be able to execute a shell command.</p> <p>If you are using the Knitr engine you can use ```<code>{bash}</code> cells, for example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Using Bash" engine: knitr --- ```{bash} echo "foo" ```</code></pre> <p>Note that the Knitr engine also supports ```<code>{python}</code> cells, enabling the combination of R, Python, and Bash in the same document</p> <h5 id="conditional-execution-1">Conditional Execution</h5> <p>In some cases you want code execution itself — not just visibility of its output — to depend on the active output format. For example, when rendering to PDF you may want to skip a cell that loads an interactive HTML widget, rather than execute it and hide the result.</p> <p>Quarto exposes the current rendering context in the <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> environment variable. Cells can read this variable to detect the active format and branch accordingly. See Execution Context Information for the full JSON schema and examples in R, Python, and Julia.</p> <p>This complements format-based conditional content, which controls visibility of already-executed output. <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> lets you skip work, choose a different code path, or load a different library before any output is produced.</p> <h3 id="inline-code-1">Inline Code</h3> <h4 id="inline-code-2">Inline Code</h4> <h5 id="overview-31">Overview</h5> <p>Inline code allows you to execute code within markdown, e.g. to automatically use the most up-to-date computations in narrative. Quarto provides an inline code syntax that works across all three engines (Jupyter, Knitr and OJS).</p> <p>The syntax for inline code is similar to code blocks, except you use a single tick (```) rather than triple ticks (````<code>), and you can use it in the middle of markdown. For example, the following code stores the variable</code>radius` in a code block and then accesses it in a sentence using inline code:</p> <ul> <li><p>Jupyter</p></li> <li><p>Knitr</p></li> <li><p>OJS</p> <p><code>{python} radius = 5</code></p> <p>The radius of the circle is <code>{python} radius</code></p></li> </ul> <p>This syntax works for any Jupyter kernel—so for Julia you would write an inline expression as <code>{julia} radius</code>).</p> <pre><code>```{r} radius <- 5 ``` The radius of the circle is `{r} radius` ```{ojs} radius = 5 ``` The radius of the circle is `{ojs} radius`</code></pre> <p>The result of the code is this markdown output:</p> <pre><code>The radius of the circle is 5.</code></pre> <p>CautionKeep Inline Code Simple</p> <p>Inline expressions should be confined to simple values that you have pre-computed within normal code cells (rather than function calls that do non-trivial work). This is because the protocol used for inline expressions is not compatible with some Python libraries (especially those that use multi-threading or multi-processing).</p> <p>Quarto also supports the native syntaxes of Knitr and OJS. Read more below in Syntax Compatibility.</p> <p>ImportantInline Code Cannot be Used in YAML</p> <p>Inline expressions are not generally supported inside YAML strings, e.g. you cannot use inline code to generate the <code>title</code> document option, or a <code>fig-cap</code> code cell option.</p> <p>If you need to generate a dynamic caption, instead of using the <code>fig-cap</code> or <code>tbl-cap</code> code cell option, combine inline code with the Cross-Reference Div Syntax.</p> <h5 id="usage-in-notebooks">Usage in Notebooks</h5> <p>Inline expressions are always evaluated when rendering and previewing <code>.qmd</code> files. However, for notebooks you need to execute the notebook with Quarto to evaluate inline expressions (i.e. they won’t be evaluated within the JupyterLab, Positron, VS Code, or PyCharm notebook editor).</p> <p>You can work in your favorite notebook front-end without Quarto execution, then once you are ready to publish execute the notebook during rendering as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also turn on execution within the YAML options of a notebook. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Notebooks" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="markdown-output">Markdown Output</h5> <p>By default, the output of inline expressions is treated as ordinary text (i.e. markdown within it is not rendered). Any markdown-like syntax within the output of inline expressions will be automatically escaped. For example, the following inline expression:</p> <pre><code> `{python} '**not bold**'`</code></pre> <p>Will produce the following markdown:</p> <pre><code>\*\*not bold\*\*</code></pre> <p>To explicitly create markdown output, you’ll need to use a function specific to your engine:</p> <ul> <li><p>Jupyter</p></li> <li><p>Knitr</p></li> <li><p>OJS Use the <code>Markdown()</code> function from <code>IPython.display</code>:</p> <p><code>{python} from IPython.display import Markdown</code></p> <p>This is <code>{python} Markdown('**bold**')</code></p></li> </ul> <p>Use the <code>I()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>This is `{r} I("**bold**")`</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>md</code> function:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} text = md`This is **bold**` ``` `{ojs} text`</code></pre> <h5 id="escaping-1">Escaping</h5> <p>If you are writing documentation about inline expressions (as we are in this article!) then you may need to escape the syntax so that it doesn’t execute. You can do that in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li>Use a double-brace around the expression. For example: <code>{{python}} x</code></li> <li>Enclose the expression in an extra backtick. For example: ```{python} x``` Each of the expressions above will render (unevaluated) as <code>{python} x</code> within the output document.</li> </ul> <h5 id="engine-binding-1">Engine Binding</h5> <p>If you use inline expressions in a document that does not have any executable code blocks then you should explicitly set the <code>engine</code> document option to ensure that your expressions are evaluated (automatic engine binding works for blocks but not inlines). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" engine: jupyter --- `{python} "hello"`</code></pre> <h5 id="syntax-compatibility">Syntax Compatibility</h5> <p>To make it easier to learn and use expressions across engines, Quarto provides a single syntax that works for all engines. However, you can also use the native syntaxes of Knitr and Observable.</p> <h6 id="knitr">Knitr</h6> <p>The native Knitr syntax also uses single backticks (```) but doesn’t enclose <code>r</code> in curly braces. For example:</p> <pre><code>The radius of the circle is `r radius`.</code></pre> <p>The native Knitr inline syntax has a different default behavior for handling Markdown Output. Specifically, it treats all inline output as containing markdown. This means the above example is equivalent to:</p> <pre><code>The radius of the circle is `{r} I(radius)`.</code></pre> <h6 id="ojs">OJS</h6> <p>Natively, OJS uses the syntax <code>\${expr}</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>The radius of the circle is ${radius}</code></pre> <h3 id="parameters">Parameters</h3> <h4 id="parameters-1">Parameters</h4> <h5 id="overview-32">Overview</h5> <p>You may have a set of parameters that are used to create different variations of a document. For example:</p> <ul> <li>Showing results for a specific geographic location.</li> <li>Running a report that covers a specific time period.</li> <li>Running a single analysis multiple times for different assumptions. This article describes how to define and use computational parameters with Quarto.</li> </ul> <h5 id="definition">Definition</h5> <p>Adding parameter definitions to a document works differently depending on whether you are using the <a href="https://jupyter.org">Jupyter</a>, <a href="https://yihui.name/knitr">Knitr</a> or Julia engine.</p> <h6 id="jupyter">Jupyter</h6> <p>For Jupyter, Quarto uses the same syntax for defining parameters as <a href="https://papermill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage-parameterize.html">Papermill</a>. To parameterize a document, designate a cell with the tag <code>parameters</code> and provide appropriate default values:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| tags: [parameters] alpha = 0.1 ratio = 0.1 ```</code></pre> <p>The parameters are available in the top level environment:</p> <pre><code>```{python} alpha ```</code></pre> <p>When the document is executed with a set of new parameters a cell is injected which overrides these defaults as appropriate.</p> <h6 id="knitr-1">Knitr</h6> <p>For Knitr, the standard Knitr <code>params</code> YAML option is used to define parameters. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- params: alpha: 0.1 ratio: 0.1 ---</code></pre> <p>The parameters are available in the <code>params</code> list:</p> <pre><code>```{r} params$alpha ```</code></pre> <h6 id="julia">Julia</h6> <p>For the Julia engine, parameters are defined via the <code>params</code> YAML option.</p> <pre><code>--- engine: julia params: alpha: 0.1 ratio: 0.1 ---</code></pre> <p>Each key is evaluated as a constant and can be accessed under that name. Note that this means only keys that are valid Julia variable names are allowed. For example, <code>some_key</code> is valid while <code>some-key</code> isn’t, even though the latter is a valid YAML key.</p> <pre><code>```{julia} alpha ```</code></pre> <h5 id="rendering">Rendering</h5> <p>To render using different parameters you can pass them on the command line using the <code>-P</code> flag (this works for both <code>.ipynb</code> or <code>.qmd</code> files):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.ipynb -P alpha:0.2 -P ratio:0.3</code></pre> <p>Alternatively you can create a YAML file that defines the parameter values you want to render with, then call quarto render with the <code>--execute-params</code> flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --execute-params params.yml</code></pre> <h3 id="rendering-script-files">Rendering Script Files</h3> <h4 id="rendering-script-files-1">Rendering Script Files</h4> <h5 id="overview-33">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto supports rendering script files (e.g. <code>.py</code>, <code>.jl</code>, or <code>.r</code>) that are specially formatted as notebooks. The specific syntax for the format is different for the Jupyter and Knitr engines. The Jupyter engine can render Python, Julia, and R (using the <a href="https://irkernel.github.io">IRkernel</a>) scripts, whereas the Knitr engine only renders R scripts.</p> <p>On this page you can learn the syntax for Jupyter and Knitr notebook scripts, how to Render and Preview notebook scripts as well as using notebook Scripts in Projects.</p> <h5 id="syntax">Syntax</h5> <p>The syntax for delineating YAML, code and Markdown depends on whether you are rendering with the Jupyter or Knitr engine. For Python and Julia scripts use the Jupyter engine. For R scripts, you can use either the Jupyter or Knitr engine.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-1">Jupyter</h6> <p>Script rendering for Jupyter makes use of the <a href="https://jupytext.readthedocs.io/en/latest/formats-scripts.html">percent format</a> that is supported by several other tools including Spyder, VS Code, PyCharm, and Jupytext.</p> <p>In the percent format:</p> <ul> <li><p>Markdown cells are delimited by <code># %% [markdown]</code>, and can include content as single line comments (<code>#</code>) or multi-line strings (<code>"""</code>).</p></li> <li><p>Code cells are delimited by <code># %%</code>. There are also Quarto-specific additions:</p></li> <li><p>The script must start with a markdown cell that includes a YAML header block (including the usual <code>---</code> YAML delimiters).</p></li> <li><p>You can add code cell options in the usual way with <code>#|</code> comments. For example, here is a Python script that includes both markdown and code cells (you can click on the numbers on the right for further details):</p> <p>script.py</p> <p># %% <a href="#markdown">markdown</a> # — # title: Palmer Penguins # author: Norah Jones # date: 3/12/23 # —</p> <p># %% #| echo: false import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv(“palmer-penguins.csv”)</p> <p># %% <a href="#markdown">markdown</a> ““” ## Exploring the data</p> <p>See <span class="citation" data-cites="fig-bill-sizes">@fig-bill-sizes</span> for an exploration of bill sizes by species. ““”</p> <p># %% #| label: fig-bill-sizes #| fig-cap: Bill Sizes by Species</p> <p>import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns</p> <p>g = sns.FacetGrid(df, hue=“species”, height=3, aspect=3.5/1.5) g.map(plt.scatter, “bill_length_mm”, “bill_depth_mm”).add_legend()</p></li> </ul> <p>1</p> <p>Scripts rendered with Quarto must begin with a markdown cell containing the YAML header.</p> <p>2</p> <p>A code cell.</p> <p>3</p> <p>A markdown cell containing a multiline string (<code>"""</code>).</p> <p>4</p> <p>Code cell options specified with <code>#|</code> comments.</p> <p>5</p> <p>You can include blank lines within cells—cells continue until another cell is encountered.</p> <h6 id="generating-markdown">Generating Markdown</h6> <p>Jupyter scripts are especially convenient when most of your document consists of code that dynamically generates markdown. You can write markdown from Python using functions in the <code>IPython.display</code> module. For example:</p> <pre><code># %% #| echo: false radius = 10 from IPython.display import Markdown Markdown(f"The _radius_ of the circle is **{radius}**.")</code></pre> <p>Note that dynamically generated markdown will still be enclosed in the standard Quarto output divs. If you want to remove all of Quarto’s default output enclosures use the <code>output: asis</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code># %% #| echo: false #| output: asis radius = 10 from IPython.display import Markdown Markdown(f"The _radius_ of the circle is **{radius}**.")</code></pre> <h6 id="raw-cells">Raw Cells</h6> <p>You can include raw cells (e.g. HTML or LaTeX) within scripts using the <code># %% [raw]</code> cell delimiter along with a <code>format</code> attribute, for example:</p> <pre><code># %% [raw] format="html" """ <iframe width="560" height="315" src="[youtube.com](https://www.youtube.com/embed/lJIrF4YjHfQ?si=aP7PxA1Pz8IIoQUX)"></iframe> """</code></pre> <h6 id="knitr-2">Knitr</h6> <p>Script rendering for Knitr is based on the <code>knitr::spin()</code> feature and makes use of the same <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/spin.html">syntax rules</a>:</p> <ul> <li><p>Markdown content is included on lines starting with a special <code>#'</code> comment.</p></li> <li><p>Lines that don’t start with <code>#</code> are code. Code blocks are split when Markdown content occurs , e.g. use <code>#'</code> to create another code block. There are also Quarto-specific additions:</p></li> <li><p>The R script must start with YAML header block using the special <code>#'</code> comment.</p></li> <li><p>You can add code cell options in the usual way with <code>#|</code> comments. For example, here is an R script that includes both markdown and code cells (you can click on the numbers on the right for further details):</p> <p>script.R</p> <p>#’ — #’ title: Palmer Penguins #’ author: Norah Jones #’ date: 3/12/23 #’ format: html #’ —</p> <p>library(palmerpenguins)</p> <p>#’ ## Exploring the data #’ See <span class="citation" data-cites="fig-bill-sizes">@fig-bill-sizes</span> for an exploration of bill sizes by species.</p> <p>#| label: fig-bill-sizes #| fig-cap: Bill Sizes by Species #| warning: false library(ggplot2) ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, group = species)) + geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) + labs(title = “Penguin bill dimensions”, subtitle = “Bill length and depth for Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo Penguins at Palmer Station LTER”, x = “Bill length (mm)”, y = “Bill depth (mm)”, color = “Penguin species”, shape = “Penguin species”)</p></li> </ul> <p>1</p> <p>Scripts rendered with Quarto must begin with a YAML header using <code>#'</code> comments.</p> <p>2</p> <p>R code is the main content of the R script and is included without any delimitation.</p> <p>3</p> <p>Preface Markdown content with the <code>#'</code> comment.</p> <p>4</p> <p>Code cell options are specified with <code>#|</code> comments and apply to code below them.</p> <h5 id="render-and-preview">Render and Preview</h5> <p>You can render and preview notebook scripts just as you would a <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> file. For example, the following commands are all valid:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto render script.py $ quarto render script.jl $ quarto render script.R $ quarto preview script.py $ quarto preview script.jl $ quarto preview script.R</code></pre> <p>The script must begin with the appropriate syntax for the YAML block to be rendered with Quarto. Based on the syntax detected Quarto will render with the Jupyter or Knitr engine.</p> <p>The <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Quarto VS Code Extension</a> also implements support for rendering and previewing scripts.</p> <h5 id="scripts-in-projects">Scripts in Projects</h5> <p>Notebook scripts can also be included within projects (e.g. websites, blogs, etc.). Scripts within projects are only rendered by Quarto when they start with the appropriate syntax.</p> <p>If for some reason you need to ignore such a script, you can create an explict render list in <code>_quarto.yml</code> that excludes individual scripts as required, for example:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website render: - "*.{qmd,R,py}" - "!utils.py"</code></pre> <p>Note that this technique is documented for the sake of completeness—in practice you should almost never need to do this since scripts rarely begin with a YAML block unless you are authoring them specifically for report rendering.</p> <h3 id="using-julia">Using Julia</h3> <h4 id="using-julia-1">Using Julia</h4> <h4 id="overview-34">Overview</h4> <p>Quarto supports executable Julia code blocks within markdown. This allows you to create fully reproducible documents and reports—the Julia code required to produce your output is part of the document itself, and is automatically re-run whenever the document is rendered.</p> <p>Quarto has two available engines for executing Julia code, the newer <code>julia</code> engine is using the <a href="https://github.com/PumasAI/QuartoNotebookRunner.jl/">QuartoNotebookRunner.jl</a> package to render notebooks, the older <code>jupyter</code> engine is using the <a href="https://github.com/JuliaLang/IJulia.jl">IJulia</a> Jupyter kernel.</p> <p>This table lists some of the reasons why the <code>julia</code> engine was created:</p> <p>julia Engine</p> <p>jupyter Engine</p> <p>Execute Julia code blocks</p> <p>✅</p> <p>✅</p> <p>Keep sessions alive for fast reruns</p> <p>✅</p> <p>✅</p> <p>No Python installation required</p> <p>✅</p> <p>❌</p> <p>No global package installation needed</p> <p>✅</p> <p>❌</p> <p>Automatic integration with juliaup (no kernel installation)</p> <p>✅</p> <p>❌</p> <p>Python & R Codeblocks (via PythonCall.jl and RCall.jl)</p> <p>✅</p> <p>❌</p> <p>“Expandable cells” or programmatic document generation (via <a href="https://pumasai.github.io/QuartoTools.jl/stable/">QuartoTools.jl</a>)</p> <p>✅</p> <p>❌</p> <p>Note</p> <p>For most users, the <code>julia</code> engine should offer the best experience. However, for backwards compatibility the <code>jupyter</code> engine remains the default engine for Julia code. The <code>julia</code> engine has to be specifically enabled either in the frontmatter or the project file.</p> <p>Using either of the two engines will require manually installing Julia if you have not done so already. Installation via <code>juliaup</code> is recommended, for further information check the <a href="https://julialang.org/install/">official Julia website</a>.</p> <p>Now, we will cover the basics of creating and rendering documents with Julia code blocks.</p> <h5 id="code-blocks-1">Code Blocks</h5> <p>Code blocks that use braces around the language name (e.g. ```<code>{julia}</code>) are executable, and will be run by Quarto during render. Here is a simple example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Plots Demo" author: "Norah Jones" date: "5/22/2021" format: html: code-fold: true engine: julia --- ### Parametric Plots Plot function pair (x(u), y(u)). See @fig-parametric for an example. ```{julia} #| label: fig-parametric #| fig-cap: "Parametric Plots" using Plots plot(sin, x->sin(2x), 0, 2π, leg=false, fill=(0,:lavender)) ```</code></pre> <p>You’ll note that there are some special comments at the top of the code block. These are cell level options that make the figure cross-referenceable.</p> <p>This document would result in the following rendered output:</p> <p>You can produce a wide variety of output types from executable code blocks, including plots, tabular output from data frames, and plain text output (e.g. printing the results of statistical summaries).</p> <p>There are many options which control the behavior of code execution and output, you can read more about them in the article on Execution Options.</p> <p>In addition to code blocks which interrupt the flow of Markdown, you can also include code inline. Read more about inline code in the Inline Code article.</p> <h6 id="multiple-outputs-1">Multiple Outputs</h6> <p>By default Julia cells will automatically print the value of their last statement (as with the example above where the call to <code>plot()</code> resulted in plot output). If you want to display multiple plots (or other types of output) from a single cell you should call the <code>display()</code> function explicitly. For example, here we output two plots side-by-side with sub-captions:</p> <pre><code>```{julia} #| label: fig-plots #| fig-cap: "Multiple Plots" #| fig-subcap: #| - "Plot 1" #| - "Plot 2" #| layout-ncol: 2 using Plots display(plot(sin, x -> sin(2x), 0, 2)) display(plot(x -> sin(4x), y -> sin(5y), 0, 2)) ```</code></pre> <h5 id="rendering-1">Rendering</h5> <p>Quarto will automatically run computations in any markdown document that contains executable code blocks. For example, the example shown above might be rendered to various formats with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd # all formats quarto render document.qmd --to pdf quarto render document.qmd --to docx</code></pre> <p>The <code>render</code> command will render all formats listed in the document YAML. If no formats are specified, then it will render to HTML. You can also provide the <code>--to</code> argument to target a specific format.</p> <p>Quarto can also render any Jupyter notebook (.ipynb):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.ipynb</code></pre> <p>Note that the target file (in this case <code>document.qmd</code>) should always be the very first command line argument.</p> <p>Note that when rendering an .ipynb Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <h5 id="workflow-2">Workflow</h5> <p>You can author Quarto documents that include Julia code using any text or notebook editor. No matter what editing tool you use, you’ll always run <code>quarto preview</code> first to setup a live preview of changes in your document. Live preview is available for both HTML and PDF output. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # preview as html quarto preview document.qmd # preview as pdf quarto preview document.qmd --to pdf # preview a jupyter notebook quarto preview document.ipynb</code></pre> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="embed-notebooks">Embed Notebooks</h5> <p>In addition to including executable Julia code chunks in a Quarto document, you can also embed cells from an external Jupyter Notebook (<code>.ipynb</code>). See Embedding Jupyter Notebook Cells for more details.</p> <h5 id="positron">Positron</h5> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Quarto Extension</a> is bundled with <a href="https://positron.posit.co">Positron</a>, and provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files. The extension integrates directly with the <a href="https://www.julia-vscode.org/docs">Julia Extension</a> to provide code completion, cell execution and side-by-side preview of Quarto documents.</p> <p>The extension includes a Quarto: Preview command that can be accessed via the Command Palette, the keyboard shortcut , or a Preview button () in the editor toolbar. After rendering, a preview is displayed in the Viewer pane within Positron.</p> <p>You can read more about using Positron in Tools: Positron.</p> <p>You can also use the Positron notebook editor to create <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks that you will render with Quarto. The Jupyter Lab section discusses using notebooks with Quarto in the context of Jupyter Lab, but the same concepts apply to Positron.</p> <h5 id="vs-code">VS Code</h5> <p>The <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Quarto Extension</a> for VS Code provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files in VS Code. The extension integrates directly with the <a href="https://www.julia-vscode.org/docs">Julia Extension</a> to provide the following Julia-specific capabilities:</p> <ul> <li>Code completion</li> <li>Cell execution</li> <li>Contextual help You can install the VS Code extension by searching for ‘quarto’ in the extensions panel or from the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">extension marketplace</a>.</li> </ul> <p>You can also use the VS Code notebook editor to create Julia notebooks that you will render with Quarto. The next section discusses using notebooks with Quarto in the context of Jupyter Lab, but the same concepts apply to VS Code.</p> <h5 id="jupyter-lab">Jupyter Lab</h5> <p>We could convert the simple <code>document.qmd</code> we used as an example above to a Jupyter notebook using the <code>quarto convert</code> command. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto convert document.qmd</code></pre> <p>If we open this notebook in Jupyter Lab and execute the cells, here is what we see:</p> <p>Note that there are three different types of cell here:</p> <ul> <li><p>The YAML document options at the top are in a Raw cell.</p></li> <li><p>The heading and explanation are in a Markdown cell.</p></li> <li><p>The Julia code and its output are in a Code cell. When working in a Jupyter notebook, you can use <code>quarto preview</code> to provide a live preview of your rendered document:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto preview document.ipynb</p></li> </ul> <p>The preview will be updated every time you save the notebook in Jupyter Lab.</p> <h4 id="using-the-julia-engine">Using the <code>julia</code> engine</h4> <h5 id="installation">Installation</h5> <p>The <code>julia</code> engine uses the <a href="https://github.com/PumasAI/QuartoNotebookRunner.jl/">QuartoNotebookRunner.jl</a> package to render notebooks. When you first attempt to render a notebook with the <code>julia</code> engine, Quarto will automatically install this package into a private environment that is owned by Quarto. This means you don’t have to install anything in your global Julia environment for Quarto to work and Quarto will not interfere with any other Julia environments on your system. Quarto will use the <code>julia</code> binary on your PATH by default, but you can override this using the <code>QUARTO_JULIA</code> environment variable.</p> <p>NoteUsing custom versions of <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code></p> <p>In special circumstances, you may not want to use the specific <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> version that Quarto installs for you. For example, you might be developing <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> itself, or you need to use a fork or an unreleased version with a bugfix. In this case, set the environment variable <code>QUARTO_JULIA_PROJECT</code> to a directory of a julia environment that has <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> installed.</p> <p>As an example, you could install the main branch of <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> into the directory <code>/some/dir</code> by executing <code>]activate /some/dir</code> in a julia REPL followed by <code>]add QuartoNotebookRunner#main</code>. As long as there is no server currently running, running a command like <code>QUARTO_JULIA_PROJECT=/some/dir quarto render some_notebook.qmd</code> in your terminal will ensure the server process is started using the custom <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code>. You can also set <code>quarto</code>’s <code>--execute-debug</code> flag and check the output to verify that the custom environment is being used.</p> <h5 id="enabling-the-julia-engine">Enabling the <code>julia</code> engine</h5> <p>To use the <code>julia</code> engine, you have to specifically enable it. For that, you have two options.</p> <p>Either specify the engine in your frontmatter:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "A julia engine notebook" engine: julia --- ```{julia} 1 + 2 ```</code></pre> <p>Or, starting with Quarto 1.7, you can prioritize the julia engine project-wide by adding <code>julia</code> to the <code>engines</code> array in your project file, giving it priority over all unlisted engines (more under Engine prioritization). Note that the project file approach is the only option in order to use the <code>julia</code> engine with percent-script files.</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml engines: ['julia']</code></pre> <h5 id="rendering-notebooks">Rendering notebooks</h5> <p>Requesting the first render of a notebook which contains Julia code blocks and has the <code>julia</code> engine enabled will start a persistent server process that loads QuartoNotebookRunner.jl. This package is installed automatically in an environment private to Quarto.</p> <p>The server spins up a separate Julia worker process for each notebook you want to render. Every purple node in the following graph represents a separate Julia process which runs independently from each short-lived <code>quarto</code> process that communicates with the server.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR A[<b>quarto render ...</b>] <-.-> B[<b>Server Process</b><br/>QuartoNotebookRunner.jl] B < C[<b>Worker Process 1</b><br/>notebook_A.qmd] B < D[<b>Worker Process 2</b><br/>notebook_B.qmd] B < E[<b>Worker Process 3</b><br/>notebook_C.qmd] style A color:#333 style B fill:#cb9be0,color:#333 style C fill:#e7d0f2,color:#333 style D fill:#e7d0f2,color:#333 style E fill:#e7d0f2,color:#333</code></pre> <p>You can check the status of the server, request it to shut down, and more using the <code>call julia engine</code> commands. The server will stay alive for five minutes after the last worker process has exited, unless it’s closed manually. Changes to environment variables that influence the server process will only be picked up once the next new server process is started.</p> <h6 id="notebook-environments">Notebook environments</h6> <p>By default, QuartoNotebookRunner will use the <code>--project=@.</code> flag when starting a worker. This makes Julia search for an environment (a <code>Project.toml</code> or <code>JuliaProject.toml</code> file) starting in the directory where the quarto notebook is stored and walking up the directory tree from there.</p> <p>For example, for a file <code>/some/dir/notebook.qmd</code> it will look at <code>/some/dir/[Julia]Project.toml</code>, <code>/some/[Julia]Project.toml</code> and so on. You could use this behavior to let all notebooks in a quarto project share the same Julia environment, by placing it at the project’s top-level directory.</p> <p>If no environment has previously been set up in any of these directories, the worker process will start with an empty environment. This means that only Julia’s standard library packages will be available for use in the notebook.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Creating a separate environment for each notebook or each set of closely related notebooks is considered best practice. If too many different notebooks share the same environment (for example the main shared environment that Julia usually loads by default), you’re likely to break some of them unintentionally whenever you make a change to the environment.</p> <p>You can create a Julia environment in multiple ways, for more information have a look at the <a href="https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1/environments/">official documentation</a>. One simple option for adding packages to the default environment of a new quarto notebook is to add some <code>Pkg</code> installation commands to the notebook and run it once. Afterwards, those commands can be deleted and a <code>Project.toml</code> and <code>Manifest.toml</code> file representing the environment should be present in the notebook’s directory.</p> <pre><code>--- engine: julia --- ```{julia} using Pkg Pkg.add("DataFrames") ```</code></pre> <p>Another option is to start <code>julia</code> in a terminal which loads the REPL, and to press <code>]</code> to switch to the <code>Pkg</code> REPL mode. In this mode, you can first activate the desired environment by running <code>activate /some/dir</code> and then, for example, install the <code>DataFrames</code> package with the command <code>add DataFrames</code>.</p> <p>If you do not want to use the notebook’s directory as the environment, you may specify a different directory via the <code>--project</code> flag in the <code>exeflags</code> frontmatter setting:</p> <pre><code>--- engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["--project=/some/other/dir"] ---</code></pre> <h6 id="worker-process-reuse">Worker process reuse</h6> <p>An idle worker process will be kept alive for 5 minutes by default, this can be changed by passing the desired number of seconds to the <code>daemon</code> key:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "A julia notebook with ten minutes timeout" engine: julia execute: daemon: 600 ---</code></pre> <p>Each re-render of a notebook will reuse the worker process with all dependencies already loaded, which reduces latency. As far as technically possible, QuartoNotebookRunner.jl will release resources from previous runs to the garbage collector. In each run, the code is evaluated into a fresh module so you cannot run into conflicts with variables defined in previous runs. Note, however, that certain state changes like modifications to package runtime settings or the removal or addition of function methods will persist across runs. If necessary, you can use the <code>--execute-daemon-restart</code> flag to force a restart of a notebook’s worker process.</p> <p>You can also disable the daemon which will use a new process for each render (with higher latency due to package reloads):</p> <pre><code>execute: daemon: false</code></pre> <p>The server process itself will time out after five minutes if no more worker processes exist.</p> <h5 id="engine-options">Engine options</h5> <p>Engine options can be passed under the <code>julia</code> top-level key:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "A julia engine notebook" engine: julia julia: key: value ---</code></pre> <p>The currently available options are:</p> <ul> <li><code>exeflags</code>: An array of strings which are appended to the <code>julia</code> command that starts the worker process. For example, a notebook is run with <code>--project=@.</code> by default (the environment in the directory where the notebook is stored) but this could be overridden by setting <code>exeflags: ["--project=/some/directory/"]</code>.</li> <li><code>env</code>: An array of strings where each string specifies one environment variable that is passed to the worker process. For example, <code>env: ["SOMEVAR=SOMEVALUE"]</code>.</li> </ul> <h5 id="quarto-call-engine-julia-commands"><code>quarto call engine julia</code> commands</h5> <p>Starting with Quarto 1.7, The julia engine offers CLI commands for configuration and monitoring via the <code>quarto call engine julia</code> entrypoint.</p> <h6 id="status"><code>status</code></h6> <p>The <code>status</code> command prints out information about the currently running server process as well as potential worker processes. For example:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto call engine julia status QuartoNotebookRunner server status: started at: 9:44:31 (47 seconds ago) runner version: 0.15.0 environment: /Users/username/Library/Caches/quarto/julia/ pid: 42008 port: 8000 julia version: 1.11.4 timeout: 5 minutes workers active: 1 worker 1: path: /Users/username/notebook.qmd run started: 9:44:38 (40 seconds ago) run finished: - timeout: 5 minutes pid: 42026 exe: `julia` exeflags: ["--color=yes"] env: ["JULIA_PROJECT=@."]</code></pre> <h6 id="close"><code>close</code></h6> <p>The <code>close</code> command allows shutting down notebook worker processes. By default, only closing of idle worker processes is allowed. A worker process is idle when its <code>run finished</code> status is populated. In this case, we can call <code>close</code> on it:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto call engine julia status QuartoNotebookRunner server status: started at: 9:44:31 (5 minutes 41 seconds ago) runner version: 0.15.0 environment: /Users/username/Library/Caches/quarto/julia/ pid: 42008 port: 8000 julia version: 1.11.4 timeout: 5 minutes workers active: 1 worker 1: path: /Users/username/notebook.qmd run started: 9:44:38 (5 minutes 34 seconds ago) run finished: 9:46:21 (took 1 minute 43 seconds) timeout: 5 minutes (1 minute 9 seconds left) pid: 42026 exe: `julia` exeflags: ["--color=yes"] env: ["JULIA_PROJECT=@."] $ quarto call engine julia close /Users/username/notebook.qmd Worker closed successfully.</code></pre> <p>To force a busy worker to close, for example if it’s stuck in an endless loop or because a computation is taking too long, the <code>--force</code> flag can be added. Using this flag means losing all the work that the worker process has done so far. At the next run, the worker process will have to be started from scratch and all packages loaded again:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto call engine julia status QuartoNotebookRunner server status: started at: 11:2:40 (16 seconds ago) runner version: 0.15.0 environment: /Users/username/Library/Caches/quarto/julia/ pid: 50642 port: 8000 julia version: 1.11.4 timeout: 5 minutes workers active: 1 worker 1: path: /Users/username/notebook.qmd run started: 11:2:47 (9 seconds ago) run finished: - timeout: 5 minutes pid: 50650 exe: `julia` exeflags: ["--color=yes"] env: ["JULIA_PROJECT=@."] $ quarto call engine julia close /Users/username/notebook.qmd ERROR: Julia server returned error after receiving "close" command: Failed to close notebook: /Users/username/notebook.qmd The underlying Julia error was: Tried to close file "/Users/username/notebook.qmd" but the corresponding worker is busy. Stack trace: [omitted for brevity] $ quarto call engine julia close --force /Users/username/notebook.qmd Worker force-closed successfully. $ quarto call engine julia status QuartoNotebookRunner server status: started at: 11:2:40 (46 seconds ago) runner version: 0.15.0 environment: /Users/username/Library/Caches/quarto/julia/ pid: 50642 port: 8000 julia version: 1.11.4 timeout: 5 minutes (4 minutes 56 seconds left) workers active: 0</code></pre> <h6 id="stop"><code>stop</code></h6> <p>The <code>stop</code> command shuts down the server process gracefully. Note that you will get an error if any workers are currently busy:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto call engine julia status QuartoNotebookRunner server status: started at: 11:2:40 (3 minutes 43 seconds ago) runner version: 0.15.0 environment: /Users/username/Library/Caches/quarto/julia/ pid: 50642 port: 8000 julia version: 1.11.4 timeout: 5 minutes (1 minute 59 seconds left) workers active: 0 $ quarto call engine julia stop Server stopped. $ quarto call engine julia status Julia control server is not running.</code></pre> <h6 id="kill"><code>kill</code></h6> <p>The <code>kill</code> command shuts the server process down forcefully. This command is intended as a last resort when the server is in a bad state and unresponsive. Note that all worker processes will be killed as well, so you will lose all progress.</p> <h6 id="log"><code>log</code></h6> <p>The <code>log</code> command prints the output of the internal log file of the server process. If the server process fails to start or unexpectedly quits, this log file might contain useful information.</p> <h5 id="juliaup-integration"><code>juliaup</code> integration</h5> <p><a href="https://github.com/JuliaLang/juliaup"><code>juliaup</code></a> is the recommended way to install and manage Julia versions. The <code>julia</code> engine supports using <code>juliaup</code>’s <code>+</code> channel specifier to select the Julia version that a notebook uses. This allow users to run several notebooks concurrently with different Julia versions on the same machine without the need for customizing their <code>PATH</code> in any way.</p> <p>To use this feature, ensure that you have used <code>juliaup</code> to install the channels that you wish to use in your notebooks. Then add the channel specifier to the notebook frontmatter in the <code>julia.exeflags</code> option:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "A Julia 1.11 notebook" engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11"] --- ```{julia} VERSION ```</code></pre> <p><code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> currently supports running Julia versions from 1.6 onwards. Support for earlier versions is not planned.</p> <h5 id="revise.jl-integration">Revise.jl integration</h5> <p><a href="https://github.com/timholy/Revise.jl">Revise</a> allows for automatically updating function definitions in Julia sessions. It is an essential tool in the Julia ecosystem for any user that wishes to develop their own packages or large projects. The <code>julia</code> engine supports using <code>Revise</code> within notebook processes by simply importing the package into a cell at the start of a notebook. Once imported <code>Revise</code> will automatically update functions imported from locally developed packages in the same way as it behaves in a Julia REPL.</p> <p>Ensure that <code>Revise</code> is installed in the project environment that the notebook is using, since the global environment is not included in the load path provided to Julia, unlike the behaviour of a Julia REPL session.</p> <h5 id="caching">Caching</h5> <p>The engine has built-in support for caching notebook results. This feature is disabled by default but can be enabled by setting the <code>execute.cache</code> option to <code>true</code> in a notebook’s frontmatter:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "A caching example" engine: julia execute: cache: true --- ```{julia} rand() ```</code></pre> <p>Notebook caches are invalidated based on the following criteria:</p> <ul> <li><p>Using a different Julia version to run the notebook.</p></li> <li><p>Changes to the <code>Manifest.toml</code> of the environment the notebook is run in. Adding, removing, or changing package versions will invalidate the cache.</p></li> <li><p>Changing any contents in the notebook’s frontmatter.</p></li> <li><p>Changing any contents of any executable Julia cells, including cell options. Changes that do not invalidate a cache:</p></li> <li><p>Editing Markdown content outside of executable Julia cells. Caches are saved to file in a <code>.cache</code> directory alongside the notebook file. This directory is safe to remove if you want to invalidate all caches. The contents of the individual cache files is an internal implementation detail and should not be relied upon.</p></li> </ul> <p>These caches are safe to save in CI via such tools as GitHub Actions <code>action/cache</code> to help improve the render time of long-running notebooks that do not often change.</p> <h5 id="r-and-python-support">R and Python support</h5> <p><code>{r}</code> and <code>{python}</code> executable code blocks are supported in the <code>julia</code> engine via integrations with the <a href="https://github.com/JuliaInterop/RCall.jl">RCall</a> and <a href="https://github.com/JuliaPy/PythonCall.jl">PythonCall</a> packages respectively. Using this feature requires the notebook author to explicitly <code>import</code> those packages into their notebooks in a <code>{julia}</code> cell after which they can use <code>{r}</code> and <code>{python}</code> cells.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Multi-language notebooks" engine: julia --- ```{julia} import PythonCall import RCall ``` Create some data in Julia: ```{julia} data = sin.(0:0.1:4pi) ``` Then plot it in R by interpolating the `data` variable from Julia into `R` via the `$` syntax: ```{r} plot($data) ``` The same `$` syntax can be used to interpolate Julia variables into Python code as well: ```{python} len($data) ```</code></pre> <h5 id="engine-extensions">Engine “extensions”</h5> <p>The implementation of <code>QuartoNotebookRunner</code> allows for extending the behaviour of notebooks via external Julia packages.</p> <p>One example of this is the <a href="https://pumasai.github.io/QuartoTools.jl">QuartoTools.jl</a> package, which enables fine-grained function call caching, support for serializing data between notebook processes and normal <code>julia</code> processes, and “expandable” cell outputs that allow for programatic creating of cell inputs and outputs within notebooks. See the linked documentation for more thorough discussion of that package’s features.</p> <p>The same approach used by that package can be applied to other third-party packages that wish to extend the functionality of notebooks in other ways. Please direct questions and requests regarding this functionality to the <a href="https://github.com/PumasAI/QuartoNotebookRunner.jl">QuartoNotebookRunner</a> repository.</p> <h5 id="conditional-execution-2">Conditional Execution</h5> <p>To execute a cell only for certain output formats, read the <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> environment variable inside the cell. For example, you could execute code only if the target format is based on HTML (e.g. for <code>html</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, and <code>dashboard</code> formats):</p> <pre><code>```{julia} using JSON info = JSON.parsefile(ENV["QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO"]) is_html = info["format"]["identifier"]["base-format"] == "html" if is_html # HTML-only code, e.g. an interactive widget end ```</code></pre> <p>This pairs well with conditional content when both visibility and execution should depend on format. See Execution Context Information for the full JSON schema.</p> <h4 id="using-the-jupyter-engine">Using the <code>jupyter</code> engine</h4> <h5 id="installation-1">Installation</h5> <p>In order to render documents with embedded Julia code you’ll need to install the following components:</p> <ul> <li>IJulia</li> <li>Revise.jl</li> <li>Optionally, Jupyter Cache We’ll cover each of these in turn below.</li> </ul> <h6 id="ijulia">IJulia</h6> <p><a href="https://julialang.github.io/IJulia.jl/stable">IJulia</a> is a Julia-language execution kernel for Jupyter. You can install IJulia from within the Julia REPL as follows:</p> <pre><code>using Pkg Pkg.add("IJulia") using IJulia notebook()</code></pre> <p>The first time you run <code>notebook()</code>, it will prompt you for whether it should install Jupyter. Hit enter to have it use the <a href="https://github.com/Luthaf/Conda.jl">Conda.jl</a> package to install a minimal Python+Jupyter distribution (via <a href="https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/stable/user-guide/install/index.html">Miniconda</a>) that is private to Julia (not in your <code>PATH</code>). On Linux, it defaults to looking for <code>jupyter</code> in your <code>PATH</code> first, and only asks to installs the Conda Jupyter if that fails.</p> <p>If you choose not to use Conda.jl to install Python and Jupyter you will need to make sure that you have another installation of it on your system (see the section on Installing Jupyter if you need help with this).</p> <h6 id="revise.jl">Revise.jl</h6> <p>In addition to IJulia, you’ll want to install <a href="https://timholy.github.io/Revise.jl/stable">Revise.jl</a> and configure it for use with IJulia. Revise.jl is a library that helps you keep your Julia sessions running longer, reducing the need to restart when you make changes to code.</p> <p>Quarto maintains a persistent kernel daemon for each document to mitigate Jupyter start up time during iterative work. Revise.jl will make this persistent process robust in the face of package updates, git branch checkouts, etc. Install Revise.jl with:</p> <pre><code>using Pkg Pkg.add("Revise")</code></pre> <p>To configure Revise to launch automatically within IJulia, create a <code>.julia/config/startup_ijulia.jl</code> file with the contents:</p> <pre><code>try @eval using Revise catch e @warn "Revise init" exception=(e, catch_backtrace()) end</code></pre> <p>You can learn more about Revise.jl at <a href="https://timholy.github.io/Revise.jl/stable">timholy.github.io</a>.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-cache">Jupyter Cache</h6> <p><a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> enables you to cache all of the cell outputs for a notebook. If any of the cells in the notebook change then all of the cells will be re-executed.</p> <p>If you are using the integrated version of Jupyter installed by <code>IJulia.notebook()</code>, then you will need to add <code>jupyter-cache</code> to the Python environment managed by IJulia. You can do that as follows:</p> <pre><code>using Conda Conda.add("jupyter-cache")</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, if you are using Jupyter from within any other version of Python not managed by IJulia, see the instructions below on Installing Jupyter for details on installing <code>jupyter cache</code>,</p> <h5 id="caching-1">Caching</h5> <p><a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> enables you to cache all of the cell outputs for a notebook. If any of the cells in the notebook change then all of the cells will be re-executed.</p> <p>To use Jupyter Cache you’ll want to first install the <code>jupyter-cache</code> package:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>To enable the cache for a document, add the <code>cache</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: cache: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify caching at the project level. For example, within a project file:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website format: html: theme: united execute: cache: true</code></pre> <p>Note that changes within a document that aren’t within code cells (e.g. markdown narrative) do not invalidate the document cache. This makes caching a very convenient option when you are working exclusively on the prose part of a document.</p> <p>Jupyter Cache include a <code>jcache</code> command line utility that you can use to analyze and manage the notebook cache. See the <a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> documentation for additional details.</p> <h6 id="rendering-2">Rendering</h6> <p>You can use <code>quarto render</code> command line options to control caching behavior without changing the document’s code. Use options to force the use of caching on all chunks, disable the use of caching on all chunks (even if it’s specified in options), or to force a refresh of the cache even if it has not been invalidated:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # use a cache (even if not enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --cache # don't use a cache (even if enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --no-cache # use a cache and force a refresh quarto render example.qmd --cache-refresh</code></pre> <h6 id="alternatives">Alternatives</h6> <p>If you are using caching to mitigate long render-times, there are some alternatives you should consider alongside caching.</p> <h6 id="disabling-execution">Disabling Execution</h6> <p>If you are working exclusively with prose / markdown, you may want to disable execution entirely. Do this by specifying the <code>enabled: false</code> execute option For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: enabled: false ---</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring using Jupyter <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks (as opposed to plain-text <code>.qmd</code> files) then this is already the default behavior: no execution occurs when you call <code>quarto render</code> (rather, execution occurs as you work within the notebook).</p> <h6 id="freezing-execution">Freezing Execution</h6> <p>If you are working within a project and your main concern is the cumulative impact of rendering many documents at once, consider using the <code>freeze</code> option.</p> <p>You can use the <code>freeze</code> option to denote that computational documents should never be re-rendered during a global project render, or alternatively only be re-rendered when their source file changes:</p> <pre><code>execute: freeze: true # never re-render during project render execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>freeze</code> controls whether execution occurs during global project renders. If you do an incremental render of either a single document or a project sub-directory then code is always executed. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render single document (always executes code) quarto render document.qmd # render project subdirectory (always executes code) quarto render articles</code></pre> <p>Learn more about using <code>freeze</code> with projects in the article on managing project execution.</p> <h6 id="kernel-selection">Kernel Selection</h6> <p>You’ll note in our first example that we specified the use of the <code>julia-1.8</code> kernel explicitly in our document options (shortened for brevity):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "StatsPlots Demo" jupyter: julia-1.8 ---</code></pre> <p>If no <code>jupyter</code> kernel is explicitly specified, then Quarto will attempt to automatically discover a kernel on the system that supports Julia.</p> <p>You can discover the available Jupyter kernels on your system using the <code>quarto check</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto check jupyter</code></pre> <h5 id="kernel-daemon">Kernel Daemon</h5> <p>To mitigate the start-up time for the Jupyter kernel Quarto keeps a daemon with a running Jupyter kernel alive for each document. This enables subsequent renders to proceed immediately without having to wait for kernel start-up.</p> <p>The purpose of the daemon is to make render more responsive during interactive sessions. Accordingly, no daemon is created when documents are rendered without an active tty or when they are part of a batch rendering (e.g. in a Quarto Project).</p> <p>Note that Quarto does not use a daemon by default on Windows (as some Windows systems will not allow the socket connection required by the daemon).</p> <p>You can customize this behavior using the <code>daemon</code> execution option. Set it to <code>false</code> to prevent the use of a daemon, or set it to a value (in seconds) to determine the period after which the daemon will timeout (the default is 300 seconds). For example:</p> <pre><code>execute: daemon: false execute: daemon: 60</code></pre> <p>Note that if you want to use a daemon on Windows you need to enable it explicitly:</p> <pre><code>execute: daemon: true</code></pre> <h6 id="command-line">Command Line</h6> <p>You can also control use of the Jupyter daemon using the following command line options:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # use a daemon w/ default timeout (300 sec) quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon # use a daemon w/ an explicit timeout quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon 60 # prevent use of a daemon quarto render document.qmd --no-execute-daemon</code></pre> <p>You can also force an existing daemon to restart using the <code>--execute-daemon-restart</code> command line flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon-restart</code></pre> <p>This might be useful if you suspect that the re-use of notebook sessions is causing an error.</p> <p>Finally, you can print extended debugging information about daemon usage (startup, shutdown, connections, etc.) using the <code>--execute-debug</code> flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --execute-debug</code></pre> <h6 id="installing-jupyter">Installing Jupyter</h6> <p>You can rely on the minimal version of Python and Jupyter that is installed automatically by IJulia, or you can choose to install Python and Jupyter separately. If you need to install another version of Jupyter this section describes how.</p> <p>If you don’t yet have Python 3 on your system, we recommend you install a version using the standard installer from <a href="https://www.python.org/downloads/">python.org</a>.</p> <p>If you are in a fresh Python 3 environment, installing the <code>jupyter</code> package will provide everything required to execute Jupyter kernels with Quarto:</p> <p>Pkg. Manager</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Pip</p> <p>(Mac/Linux)</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter</code></pre> <p>Pip</p> <p>(Windows)</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter</code></pre> <p>Conda</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda install jupyter</code></pre> <p>You can verify that Quarto is configured correctly for Jupyter with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto check jupyter</code></pre> <p>Quarto will select a version of Python using the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html#python-launcher-for-windows">Python Launcher</a> on Windows or system <code>PATH</code> on MacOS and Linux. You can override the version of Python used by Quarto by setting the <code>QUARTO_PYTHON</code> environment variable.</p> <p>If you are using a virtual environment with your environment or project, see more at Virtual Environments.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-cache-1">Jupyter Cache</h6> <p><a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> enables you to cache all of the cell outputs for a notebook. If any of the cells in the notebook change then all of the cells will be re-executed.</p> <p>To use Jupyter Cache you’ll want to first install the <code>jupyter-cache</code> package:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>Conda</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>To enable the cache for a document, add the <code>cache</code> option. For example:</p> <h5 id="conditional-execution-3">Conditional Execution</h5> <p>To execute a cell only for certain output formats, read the <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> environment variable inside the cell. For example, you could execute code only if the target format is based on HTML (e.g. for <code>html</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, and <code>dashboard</code> formats):</p> <pre><code>```{julia} using JSON info = JSON.parsefile(ENV["QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO"]) is_html = info["format"]["identifier"]["base-format"] == "html" if is_html # HTML-only code, e.g. an interactive widget end ```</code></pre> <p>This pairs well with conditional content when both visibility and execution should depend on format. See Execution Context Information for the full JSON schema.</p> <h3 id="using-observable">Using Observable</h3> <h4 id="using-observable-1">Using Observable</h4> <h5 id="overview-35">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto includes native support for <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable JS</a>, a set of enhancements to vanilla JavaScript created by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Bostock">Mike Bostock</a> (also the author of <a href="https://d3js.org/">D3</a>). Observable JS is distinguished by its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/runtime">reactive runtime</a>, which is especially well suited for interactive data exploration and analysis.</p> <p>The creators of Observable JS (Observable, Inc.) run a hosted service at <a href="https://observablehq.com/">observablehq.com</a> where you can create and publish notebooks. Additionally, you can use Observable JS (“OJS”) in standalone documents and websites via its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq">core libraries</a>. Quarto uses these libraries along with a <a href="https://github.com/asg017/unofficial-observablehq-compiler/tree/beta">compiler</a> that is run at render time to enable the use of OJS within Quarto documents.</p> <p>OJS works in any Quarto document (plain markdown as well as Jupyter and Knitr documents). Just include your code in an <code>{ojs}</code> executable code block. The rest of this article explains the basics of using OJS with Quarto.</p> <h5 id="example-3">Example</h5> <p>We’ll start with a simple example based on Allison Horst’s <a href="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/">Palmer Penguins</a> dataset. Here we look at how penguin body mass varies across both sex and species (use the provided inputs to filter the dataset by bill length and island):</p> <pre><code>data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } )</code></pre> <p>Let’s take a look at the source code for this example. First we create an <code>{ojs}</code> cell that reads in some data from a CSV file (e.g., <a href="palmer-penguins.csv"><code>palmer-penguins.csv</code></a>) using a <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/file-attachments">FileAttachment</a>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) ```</code></pre> <p>The example above doesn’t plot all of the data but rather a filtered subset. To create our filter we’ll need some inputs, and we’ll want to be able to use the values of these inputs in our filtering function. To do this, we use the <code>viewof</code> keyword and with some standard <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/inputs">Inputs</a>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) ```</code></pre> <p>Now we write the filtering function that will transform the <code>data</code> read from the CSV using the values of <code>bill_length_min</code> and <code>island</code>.</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) ```</code></pre> <p>Here we see reactivity in action: we don’t need any special syntax to refer to the dynamic input values, they “just work”, and the filtering code is automatically re-run when the inputs change. This works in much the same way a spreadsheet works when you update a cell and other cells that refer to it are recalculated.</p> <p>Finally, we’ll plot the filtered data using <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot">Observable Plot</a> (an open-source JavaScript library for quick visualization of tabular data):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } ) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that as with our inputs, we refer to the <code>filtered</code> variable with no special syntax—the plotting code will be automatically re-run whenever <code>filtered</code> changes (which in turn is updated whenever an input changes).</p> <p>That covers a basic end-to-end use of OJS (see the Penguins examples for the full source code).</p> <p>If you take a look at the Penguins code, you’ll notice something curious: the inputs and plotting code are defined before the data processing code. This demonstrates a critical difference between OJS cell execution and traditional notebooks: cells do not need to be defined in any particular order.</p> <p>Because execution is fully reactive, the runtime will automatically execute cells in the correct order based on how they reference each other. This is more akin to a spreadsheet than a traditional notebook with linear cell execution.</p> <h5 id="libraries">Libraries</h5> <p>Our example above made use of several standard libraries, including:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib">Observable stdlib</a> — Core primitives for DOM manipulation, file handling, importing code, and much more.</li> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs">Observable Inputs</a> — Standard inputs controls including sliders, drop-downs, tables, check-boxes, etc.</li> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/plot">Observable Plot</a> — High level plotting library for exploratory data visualization. The libraries are somewhat special because they are automatically available within notebooks on <a href="https://observablehq.com">observablehq.com</a> as well as within <code>{ojs}</code> cells in Quarto documents.</li> </ul> <p>Using other JavaScript libraries is also straightforward, they just need to be explicitly imported. For example, here we import a some libraries using the <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#require">require</a> function (which in turn loads NPM modules from <a href="https://www.jsdelivr.com/">jsDelivr</a>):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require("d3@7") topojson = require("topojson") ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Libraries to learn more about using standard and third-party libraries.</p> <h5 id="data-sources">Data Sources</h5> <p>In our initial example we used a <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#file-attachments">FileAttachment</a> as our data source. File attachments support many formats including CSV, TSV, JSON, Arrow (uncompressed), and SQLite so are a convenient way to read a dataset that has already been prepared for analysis.</p> <p>Frequently, you’ll need pre-process your data in Python or R before it’s ready for visualization. Using Quarto, you can do this pre-processing during document render, and then make the results available to OJS.</p> <p>Use the <code>ojs_define()</code> function from Python or R to define variables that you want to use within JavaScript. For example, to reproduce the simple CSV read in Python you might do this:</p> <pre><code>```{python} import pandas as pd penguins = pd.read_csv("palmer-penguins.csv") ojs_define(data = penguins) ```</code></pre> <p>The call to <code>ojs_define(data = penguins)</code> says that we want to make a variable named <code>data</code> (with the value of the <code>penguins</code> data frame) available to OJS</p> <p>Depending on the visualization library you use, one additional step may be required to consume the data from JavaScript. In this case, the <code>Plot</code> function expects data by row rather than by column, so we <code>transpose()</code> it before filtering:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} filtered = transpose(data).filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Data Sources to learn more about the various ways to prepare and read data.</p> <h5 id="ojs-cells">OJS Cells</h5> <p>There are many options available to customize the behavior of <code>{ojs}</code> code cells, including showing, hiding, and collapsing code as well as controlling the visibility and layout of outputs.</p> <p>The most important cell option to be aware of is the <code>echo</code> option, which controls whether source code is displayed. You’ll have different preferences depending on whether you are embedding visualizations in an article or creating a notebook or full-on tutorial.</p> <p>Code in <code>{ojs}</code> cells is displayed by default. To prevent display of code for an entire document, set the <code>echo: false</code> option in YAML metadata:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" execute: echo: false ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this option on a per-cell basis. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: false data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) ```</code></pre> <p>To learn about all of the options available, see the article on OJS Cells.</p> <p>In addition to OJS cells which interupt the flow of markdown, you can also include code inline. Read more about inline code in the Inline Code article.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-1">Learning More</h5> <p>These articles go into more depth on using OJS in Quarto documents:</p> <ul> <li><p>Libraries covers using standard libraries and external JavaScript libraries.</p></li> <li><p>Data Sources outlines the various ways to read and pre-process data.</p></li> <li><p>OJS Cells goes into more depth on cell execution, output, and layout.</p></li> <li><p>Shiny Reactives describes how to integrate Shiny with OJS.</p></li> <li><p>Code Reuse delves into ways to re-use OJS code across multiple documents. If you want to learn more about the underlying mechanics of reactivity, check out these notebooks from <a href="https://observablehq.com/@mbostock">Mike Bostock</a>:</p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/five-minute-introduction">Five Minute Introduction</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable’s not JavaScript</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/introduction-to-views">Introduction to Views</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/how-observable-runs">How Observable Runs</a></p></li> </ul> <h3 id="using-python">Using Python</h3> <h4 id="using-python-1">Using Python</h4> <h5 id="overview-36">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto supports executable Python code blocks within markdown. This allows you to create fully reproducible documents and reports—the Python code required to produce your output is part of the document itself, and is automatically re-run whenever the document is rendered.</p> <p>If you have Python and the <code>jupyter</code> package installed then you have all you need to render documents that contain embedded Python code (if you don’t, we’ll cover this in the installation section below). Next, we’ll cover the basics of creating and rendering documents with Python code blocks.</p> <h6 id="code-blocks-2">Code Blocks</h6> <p>Code blocks that use braces around the language name (e.g. ```<code>{python}</code>) are executable, and will be run by Quarto during render. Here is a simple example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "matplotlib demo" format: html: code-fold: true jupyter: python3 --- For a demonstration of a line plot on a polar axis, see @fig-polar. ```{python} #| label: fig-polar #| fig-cap: "A line plot on a polar axis" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots( subplot_kw = {'projection': 'polar'} ) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>You’ll note that there are some special comments at the top of the code block. These are cell level options that make the figure cross-referenceable.</p> <p>This document would result in the following rendered output:</p> <p>You can produce a wide variety of output types from executable code blocks, including plots, tabular output from data frames, and plain text output (e.g. printing the results of statistical summaries).</p> <p>There are many options which control the behavior of code execution and output, you can read more about them in the article on Execution Options.</p> <p>In addition to code blocks which interrupt the flow of markdown, you can also include code inline.
