Read more about inline code in the Inline Code article.</p> <h6 id="rendering-3">Rendering</h6> <p>Quarto will automatically run computations in any markdown document that contains executable code blocks. For example, the example shown above might be rendered to various formats with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd # all formats quarto render document.qmd --to pdf quarto render document.qmd --to docx</code></pre> <p>The <code>render</code> command will render all formats listed in the document YAML. If no formats are specified, then it will render to HTML. You can also provide the <code>--to</code> argument to target a specific format.</p> <p>Quarto can also render any Jupyter notebook (.ipynb):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.ipynb</code></pre> <p>Note that the target file (in this case <code>document.qmd</code>) should always be the very first command line argument.</p> <p>Note that when rendering an .ipynb Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <h5 id="installation-2">Installation</h5> <p>If you already have Python 3 and Jupyter installed in your environment, then you should have everything required to render Jupyter notebooks with Python kernels.</p> <p>If you don’t yet have Python 3 on your system, we recommend you install a version using the standard installer from <a href="https://www.python.org/downloads/">python.org</a>.</p> <p>If you are in a fresh Python 3 environment, installing the <code>jupyter</code> package will provide everything required to execute Jupyter kernels with Quarto:</p> <p>Pkg. Manager</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Pip</p> <p>(Mac/Linux)</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter</code></pre> <p>Pip</p> <p>(Windows)</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter</code></pre> <p>Conda</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda install jupyter</code></pre> <p>You can verify that Quarto is configured correctly for Jupyter with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto check jupyter</code></pre> <p>Quarto will select a version of Python using the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html#python-launcher-for-windows">Python Launcher</a> on Windows or system <code>PATH</code> on MacOS and Linux. You can override the version of Python used by Quarto by setting the <code>QUARTO_PYTHON</code> environment variable.</p> <p>If you are using a virtual environment with your environment or project, see more at Virtual Environments.</p> <h5 id="workflow-3">Workflow</h5> <p>You can author Quarto documents that include Python code using any text or notebook editor. No matter what editing tool you use, you’ll always run <code>quarto preview</code> first to setup a live preview of changes in your document. Live preview is available for both HTML and PDF output. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # preview as html quarto preview document.qmd # preview as pdf quarto preview document.qmd --to pdf # preview a jupyter notebook quarto preview document.ipynb</code></pre> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="embed-notebooks-1">Embed Notebooks</h5> <p>In addition to including executable Python code chunks in a Quarto document, you can also embed cells from an external Jupyter Notebook (<code>.ipynb</code>). See Embedding Jupyter Notebook Cells for more details.</p> <h5 id="positron-1">Positron</h5> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Quarto Extension</a> is bundled with <a href="https://positron.posit.co">Positron</a>, and provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files. The extension integrates directly with Positron’s native Python support to provide code completion, cell execution and side-by-side preview of Quarto documents.</p> <p>The extension includes a Quarto: Preview command that can be accessed via the Command Palette, the keyboard shortcut , or a Preview button () in the editor toolbar. After rendering, a preview is displayed in the Viewer pane within Positron.</p> <p>You can read more about using Positron in Tools: Positron.</p> <p>You can also use the Positron notebook editor to create <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks that you will render with Quarto. The Jupyter Lab section discusses using notebooks with Quarto in the context of Jupyter Lab, but the same concepts apply to Positron.</p> <h5 id="vs-code-1">VS Code</h5> <p>The <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Quarto Extension</a> for VS Code provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files in VS Code. The extension integrates directly with the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.python">Python Extension</a> to provide the following Python-specific capabilities:</p> <ul> <li>Code completion</li> <li>Cell execution</li> <li>Contextual help You can install the VS Code extension by searching for ‘quarto’ in the extensions panel or from the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">extension marketplace</a>.</li> </ul> <p>You can also use the VS Code notebook editor to create Python notebooks that you will render with Quarto. The next section discusses using notebooks with Quarto in the context of Jupyter Lab, but the same concepts apply to VS Code.</p> <h5 id="jupyter-lab-1">Jupyter Lab</h5> <p>We could convert the simple <code>document.qmd</code> we used as an example above to a Jupyter notebook using the <code>quarto convert</code> command. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto convert document.qmd</code></pre> <p>If we open this notebook in Jupyter Lab and execute the cells, here is what we see:</p> <p>Note that there are three different types of cell here:</p> <ul> <li><p>The YAML document options at the top are in a Raw cell.</p></li> <li><p>The heading and explanation are in a Markdown cell.</p></li> <li><p>The Python code and its output are in a Code cell. When working in a Jupyter notebook, you can use <code>quarto preview</code> to provide a live preview of your rendered document:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto preview document.ipynb</p></li> </ul> <p>The preview will be updated every time you save the notebook in Jupyter Lab.</p> <h5 id="caching-2">Caching</h5> <p><a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> enables you to cache all of the cell outputs for a notebook. If any of the cells in the notebook change then all of the cells will be re-executed.</p> <p>To use Jupyter Cache you’ll want to first install the <code>jupyter-cache</code> package:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter-cache</code></pre> <p>To enable the cache for a document, add the <code>cache</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: cache: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify caching at the project level. For example, within a project file:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website format: html: theme: united execute: cache: true</code></pre> <p>Note that changes within a document that aren’t within code cells (e.g. markdown narrative) do not invalidate the document cache. This makes caching a very convenient option when you are working exclusively on the prose part of a document.</p> <p>Jupyter Cache include a <code>jcache</code> command line utility that you can use to analyze and manage the notebook cache. See the <a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> documentation for additional details.</p> <h6 id="rendering-4">Rendering</h6> <p>You can use <code>quarto render</code> command line options to control caching behavior without changing the document’s code. Use options to force the use of caching on all chunks, disable the use of caching on all chunks (even if it’s specified in options), or to force a refresh of the cache even if it has not been invalidated:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # use a cache (even if not enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --cache # don't use a cache (even if enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --no-cache # use a cache and force a refresh quarto render example.qmd --cache-refresh</code></pre> <h6 id="alternatives-1">Alternatives</h6> <p>If you are using caching to mitigate long render-times, there are some alternatives you should consider alongside caching.</p> <h6 id="disabling-execution-1">Disabling Execution</h6> <p>If you are working exclusively with prose / markdown, you may want to disable execution entirely. Do this by specifying the <code>enabled: false</code> execute option For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: enabled: false ---</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring using Jupyter <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks (as opposed to plain-text <code>.qmd</code> files) then this is already the default behavior: no execution occurs when you call <code>quarto render</code> (rather, execution occurs as you work within the notebook).</p> <h6 id="freezing-execution-1">Freezing Execution</h6> <p>If you are working within a project and your main concern is the cumulative impact of rendering many documents at once, consider using the <code>freeze</code> option.</p> <p>You can use the <code>freeze</code> option to denote that computational documents should never be re-rendered during a global project render, or alternatively only be re-rendered when their source file changes:</p> <pre><code>execute: freeze: true # never re-render during project render execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>freeze</code> controls whether execution occurs during global project renders. If you do an incremental render of either a single document or a project sub-directory then code is always executed. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render single document (always executes code) quarto render document.qmd # render project subdirectory (always executes code) quarto render articles</code></pre> <p>Learn more about using <code>freeze</code> with projects in the article on managing project execution.</p> <h5 id="kernel-selection-1">Kernel Selection</h5> <p>The Jupyter kernel used by Quarto is determined using the <code>jupyter</code> metadata option. For example, to use the <a href="https://github.com/jupyter-xeus/xeus-python">Xeus Python</a> kernel, do this:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" jupyter: xpython ---</code></pre> <p>Note that you can also provide a full <code>kernelspec</code>, for example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" jupyter: kernelspec: name: "xpython" language: "python" display_name: "Python 3.7 (XPython)" ---</code></pre> <p>If no Jupyter kernel is specified, then the kernel is determined by finding an available kernel that supports the language of the first executable code block found within the file (e.g. ```<code>{python}</code>).</p> <p>ImportantKernels from Conda</p> <p>If you are using a kernel that is contained within an external conda environment you need to take an extra step to make sure it is recognized by Quarto. Please follow the instructions here to make conda managed kernels available:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/Anaconda-Platform/nb_conda_kernels#use-with-nbconvert-voila-papermill">github.com</a></p> <p>Note that this step is not required if you are merely using conda with Quarto. It applies to using kernels other than the default Python kernel that happen to be installed within a conda environment separate from the one you are using.</p> <h5 id="kernel-daemon-1">Kernel Daemon</h5> <p>To mitigate the start-up time for the Jupyter kernel Quarto keeps a daemon with a running Jupyter kernel alive for each document. This enables subsequent renders to proceed immediately without having to wait for kernel start-up.</p> <p>The purpose of the daemon is to make render more responsive during interactive sessions. Accordingly, no daemon is created when documents are rendered without an active tty or when they are part of a batch rendering (e.g. in a Quarto Project).</p> <p>Note that Quarto does not use a daemon by default on Windows (as some Windows systems will not allow the socket connection required by the daemon).</p> <p>You can customize this behavior using the <code>daemon</code> execution option. Set it to <code>false</code> to prevent the use of a daemon, or set it to a value (in seconds) to determine the period after which the daemon will timeout (the default is 300 seconds). For example:</p> <pre><code>execute: daemon: false execute: daemon: 60</code></pre> <p>Note that if you want to use a daemon on Windows you need to enable it explicitly:</p> <pre><code>execute: daemon: true</code></pre> <h6 id="command-line-1">Command Line</h6> <p>You can also control use of the Jupyter daemon using the following command line options:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # use a daemon w/ default timeout (300 sec) quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon # use a daemon w/ an explicit timeout quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon 60 # prevent use of a daemon quarto render document.qmd --no-execute-daemon</code></pre> <p>You can also force an existing daemon to restart using the <code>--execute-daemon-restart</code> command line flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --execute-daemon-restart</code></pre> <p>This might be useful if you suspect that the re-use of notebook sessions is causing an error.</p> <p>Finally, you can print extended debugging information about daemon usage (startup, shutdown, connections, etc.) using the <code>--execute-debug</code> flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --execute-debug</code></pre> <h5 id="conditional-execution-4">Conditional Execution</h5> <p>To execute a cell only for certain output formats, read the <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> environment variable inside the cell. For example, you could execute code only if the target format is based on HTML (e.g. for <code>html</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, and <code>dashboard</code> formats):</p> <pre><code>```{python} import json import os with open(os.environ["QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO"]) as f: info = json.load(f) is_html = info["format"]["identifier"]["base-format"] == "html" if is_html: # HTML-only code, e.g. an interactive widget ... ```</code></pre> <p>This pairs well with conditional content when both visibility and execution should depend on format. See Execution Context Information for the full JSON schema.</p> <h3 id="using-r">Using R</h3> <h4 id="using-r-1">Using R</h4> <h5 id="overview-37">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto is a multi-language, next generation version of R Markdown from RStudio, with many new features and capabilities. Like R Markdown, Quarto uses <a href="https://yihui.org/knitr/">Knitr</a> to execute R code, and is therefore able to render most existing Rmd files without modification.</p> <p>We’ll start by covering the basics of Quarto, then delve into the differences between Quarto and R Markdown in the sections on Chunk Options and Output Formats below.</p> <h6 id="code-blocks-3">Code Blocks</h6> <p>Code blocks that use braces around the language name (e.g. ```<code>{r}</code>) are executable, and will be run by Quarto during render. Here is a simple example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "ggplot2 demo" author: "Norah Jones" date: "5/22/2021" format: html: code-fold: true --- ## Air Quality @fig-airquality further explores the impact of temperature on ozone level. ```{r} #| label: fig-airquality #| fig-cap: "Temperature and ozone level." #| warning: false library(ggplot2) ggplot(airquality, aes(Temp, Ozone)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess") ```</code></pre> <p>You’ll note that there are some special comments at the top of the code block. These are cell level options that make the figure cross-referenceable.</p> <p>This document results in the following rendered output:</p> <p>You can produce a wide variety of output types from executable code blocks, including plots, tabular output from data frames, and plain text output (e.g. printing the results of statistical summaries).</p> <p>There are many options which control the behavior of code execution and output, you can read more about them in the article on Execution Options.</p> <p>In addition to code blocks which interrupt the flow of markdown, you can also include code inline. Read more about inline code in the Inline Code article.</p> <h6 id="rendering-5">Rendering</h6> <p>When a Quarto document is rendered, R code blocks are automatically executed. You can render Quarto documents in a variety of ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>Using the Render button in RStudio:</p></li> <li><p>The Render button will render the first format listed in the document YAML. If no format is specified, then it will render to HTML.</p></li> <li><p>From the system shell using the <code>quarto render</code> command:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto render document.qmd # all formats quarto render document.qmd –to pdf quarto render document.qmd –to docx</p></li> <li><p>Note that the target file (in this case <code>document.qmd</code>) should always be the very first command line argument.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>render</code> command will render all formats listed in the document YAML. If no formats are specified, then it will render to HTML. You can also provide the <code>--to</code> argument to target a specific format.</p></li> <li><p>From the R console using the quarto R package:</p> <p>library(quarto) quarto_render(“document.qmd”) # all formats quarto_render(“document.qmd”, output_format = “pdf”)</p></li> <li><p>The function <code>quarto_render()</code> is a wrapper around <code>quarto render</code> and by default, will render all formats listed in the document YAML.</p></li> <li><p>Note that the Quarto R package is a convenience for command line rendering from R, and is not required for using Quarto with R.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="installation-3">Installation</h5> <p>To use Quarto with R, you should install the rmarkdown R package:</p> <pre><code>install.packages("rmarkdown")</code></pre> <p>Installation of the rmarkdown package will also install the knitr package so you will have everything required to render documents containing R code.</p> <p>Quarto will select a version of R by looking on the system <code>PATH</code>. In addition, on Windows when R is not found on the <code>PATH</code>, the registry will be scanned for the current R version. You can override the version of R used by Quarto by setting the <code>QUARTO_R</code> environment variable to the directory where the R binary <code>RScript</code> is.</p> <h5 id="rstudio">RStudio</h5> <p>RStudio v2022.07 and later includes support for editing and preview of Quarto documents (the documentation below assumes you are using this build or a later version).</p> <p>If you are using Quarto within RStudio it is strongly recommended that you use the <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">latest release</a> of RStudio.</p> <p>You can download RStudio from <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">posit.co</a>.</p> <h6 id="creating-documents">Creating Documents</h6> <p>Use the File : New File : Quarto Document… command to create new Quarto documents:</p> <h6 id="render-and-preview-1">Render and Preview</h6> <p>Use the Render button to preview documents as you edit them:</p> <p>If you prefer to automatically render whenever you save you can check the Render on Save option on the editor toolbar.</p> <p>The preview will appear alongside the editor:</p> <p>The preview will update whenever you re-render the document. Side-by-side preview works for both HTML and PDF output.</p> <h6 id="projects">Projects</h6> <p>If you want to create a new project for a Quarto document or set of documents, use the File : New Project… command, specify New Directory, then choose Quarto Project:</p> <p>You can use this UI to create both vanilla projects as well as websites and books. Options are also provided for creating a <a href="https://git-scm.com/">git</a> repository and initializing an <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/">renv</a> environment for the project.</p> <h5 id="positron-2">Positron</h5> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Quarto Extension</a> is bundled with <a href="https://positron.posit.co">Positron</a>, and provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files. The extension integrates directly with Positron’s native R support to provide code completion, cell execution and side-by-side preview of Quarto documents.</p> <p>The extension includes a Quarto: Preview command that can be accessed via the Command Palette, the keyboard shortcut , or a Preview button () in the editor toolbar. After rendering, a preview is displayed in the Viewer pane within Positron.</p> <p>You can read more about using Positron in Tools: Positron.</p> <h5 id="vs-code-2">VS Code</h5> <p>The <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Quarto Extension</a> for VS Code provides a variety of tools for working with <code>.qmd</code> files in VS Code. The extension integrates directly with the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=REditorSupport.r">R Extension</a> to provide the following R-specific capabilities:</p> <ul> <li>Code completion</li> <li>Cell execution</li> <li>Contextual help You can install the VS Code extension by searching for ‘quarto’ in the extensions panel or from the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">extension marketplace</a>.</li> </ul> <p>The VS Code extension includes a Quarto: Preview command that can be accessed via the Command Palette, the keyboard shortcut , or a Preview button () in the editor. After rendering, a preview is displayed in a pane within VS Code alongside your document.</p> <p>You can read more about using VS Code in Tools: VS Code.</p> <h5 id="emacs">Emacs</h5> <p>The <a href="https://melpa.org/#/quarto-mode">quarto-mode</a> MELPA package is an Emacs mode for editing Quarto documents. Install <code>quarto-mode</code> as follows:</p> <pre><code>M-x package-refresh-contents M-x package-install quarto-mode</code></pre> <p>If you have <a href="https://ess.r-project.org/">ESS</a>, <code>quarto-mode</code> will make use of it for executing R code.</p> <p>Use <code>M-x quarto-preview</code> to start a <code>quarto preview</code> server that watches quarto content for changes and automatically refreshes it. If the current buffer has an associated file that exists in a quarto project, the command will preview the entire project. Otherwise, it will preview the specific file.</p> <h5 id="chunk-options">Chunk Options</h5> <p>One important difference between R Markdown documents and Quarto documents is that in Quarto chunk options are typically included in special comments at the top of code chunks rather than within the line that begins the chunk. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| echo: false #| fig-cap: "Air Quality" library(ggplot2) ggplot(airquality, aes(Temp, Ozone)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) ```</code></pre> <p>Quarto uses this approach to both better accommodate longer options like <code>fig-cap</code>, <code>fig-subcap</code>, and <code>fig-alt</code> as well as to make it straightforward to edit chunk options within more structured editors that don’t have an easy way to edit chunk metadata (e.g. most traditional notebook UIs).</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Note that if you prefer it is still possible to include chunk options on the first line (e.g. ```<code>{r, echo = FALSE}</code>). That said, we recommend using the comment-based syntax to make documents more portable and consistent across execution engines.</p> <p>Chunk options included this way use YAML syntax rather than R syntax for consistency with options provided in YAML front matter. You can still however use R code for option values by prefacing them with <code>!expr</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste("Air", "Quality")'</code></pre> <p>Caution</p> <p>the <code>!expr</code> syntax is an example of a YAML “tag” literal, and it can be unintuitive. <code>!expr</code> needs to be followed by a single YAML “flow scalar”: see the <a href="https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#73-flow-scalar-styles">YAML spec</a> for details on how double-quoted, single-quoted, and unquoted strings work.</p> <h5 id="chunk-labels">Chunk Labels</h5> <p>You can set a label for a code chunk with the <code>label</code> option:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| label: convert airquality$TempC <- (5 / 9) * (airquality$Temp - 32) ```</code></pre> <p>Unless you want to specify a cross-reference avoid using the reserved cross-reference prefixes for chunk labels.</p> <h5 id="conditional-execution-5">Conditional Execution</h5> <p>To execute a cell only for certain output formats, read the <code>QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO</code> environment variable inside the cell. For example, you could execute code only if the target format is based on HTML (e.g. for <code>html</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, and <code>dashboard</code> formats):</p> <pre><code>```{r} info <- jsonlite::fromJSON(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO")) is_html <- info$format$identifier$`base-format` == "html" if (is_html) { # HTML-only code, e.g. an interactive widget } ```</code></pre> <p>This pairs well with conditional content when both visibility and execution should depend on format. See Execution Context Information for the full JSON schema.</p> <p>For R cells using the knitr engine, knitr’s <code>knitr::is_html_output()</code>, <code>knitr::is_latex_output()</code>, and <code>knitr::pandoc_to()</code> predicates are also available for the common format-detection cases. See the <a href="https://pkg.yihui.org/knitr/manual#sec:man-output_type">knitr manual</a>.</p> <h5 id="output-formats">Output Formats</h5> <p>Another difference between R Markdown and Quarto is related to output formats. Quarto includes many more built in output formats (and many more options for customizing each format). Quarto also has native features for special project types like Websites, Books, and Blogs (rather than relying on external packages).</p> <p>To use a format in Quarto you use the <code>format</code> key rather than the <code>output</code> key as you did in R Markdown. Here’s a comparison of equivalent format specifications:</p> <h6 id="r-markdown">R Markdown</h6> <pre><code>title: "My Document" output: html_document: toc: true number_sections: true css: styles.css</code></pre> <h6 id="quarto">Quarto</h6> <pre><code>title: "My Document" format: html: toc: true number-sections: true css: styles.css</code></pre> <p>One source of the difference in syntax is that Quarto is more closely aligned with <a href="https://pandoc.org">Pandoc</a> format names and options (thus the use of <code>-</code> as a word separator rather than <code>_</code>).</p> <p>See the listing of all supported formats along with their user guides and reference pages for more details.</p> <p>See the articles on creating Websites, Books, and Blogs for additional details on more advanced output formats.</p> <h5 id="data-frames">Data Frames</h5> <p>You can control how data frames are printed by default using the <code>df-print</code> document option. Available options include:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>default</code></p> <p>Use the default S3 method for the data frame.</p> <p><code>kable</code></p> <p>Markdown table using the <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/kable.html"><code>knitr::kable()</code></a> function.</p> <p><code>tibble</code></p> <p>Plain text table using the <a href="https://tibble.tidyverse.org/"><code>tibble</code></a> package.</p> <p><code>paged</code></p> <p>HTML table with paging for row and column overflow (implemented using <a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/rmarkdown/reference/paged_table.html"><code>rmarkdown::paged_table()</code></a>)</p> <p>For example, here we specify that we want <code>paged</code> printing for data frames:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Document" format: html: df-print: paged ---</code></pre> <h5 id="knitr-options-1">Knitr Options</h5> <p>If you are using the Knitr cell execution engine, you can specify default document-level <a href="https://yihui.org/knitr/options/">Knitr chunk options</a> in YAML. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html knitr: opts_chunk: collapse: true comment: "#>" R.options: knitr.graphics.auto_pdf: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can additionally specify global Knitr options using <code>opts_knit</code>.</p> <p>The <code>R.options</code> chunk option is a convenient way to define R options that are set temporarily via <a href="https://rdrr.io/r/base/options.html"><code>options()</code></a> before the code chunk execution, and immediately restored afterwards.</p> <p>In the example above, we establish default Knitr chunk options for a single document. You can also add shared <code>knitr</code> options to a project-wide <code>_quarto.yml</code> file or a project-directory scoped <code>_metadata.yml</code> file.</p> <h5 id="caching-3">Caching</h5> <p>The <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/cache.html">Knitr Cache</a> operates at the level of individual cells rather than the entire document. While this can be very convenient, it also introduced some special requirements around managing the dependencies between cells.</p> <p>You can enable the Knitr cache at the document or project level using standard YAML options:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: cache: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can also enable caching on a per-cell basis (in this you would not set the document level option):</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| cache: true summary(cars) ```</code></pre> <p>There are a variety of other cell-level options that affect Knitr caching behavior. You can learn about them in the Knitr cell options reference. Another excellent resource is Yihui Xie’s article on <a href="https://yihui.org/en/2018/06/cache-invalidation/">cache invalidation</a>.</p> <h6 id="rendering-6">Rendering</h6> <p>You can use <code>quarto render</code> command line options to control caching behavior without changing the document’s code. Use options to force the use of caching on all chunks, disable the use of caching on all chunks (even if it’s specified in options), or to force a refresh of the cache even if it has not been invalidated:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # use a cache (even if not enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --cache # don't use a cache (even if enabled in options) quarto render example.qmd --no-cache # use a cache and force a refresh quarto render example.qmd --cache-refresh</code></pre> <h6 id="alternatives-2">Alternatives</h6> <p>If you are using caching to mitigate long render-times, there are some alternatives you should consider alongside caching.</p> <h6 id="disabling-execution-2">Disabling Execution</h6> <p>If you are working exclusively with prose / markdown, you may want to disable execution entirely. Do this by specifying the <code>enabled: false</code> execute option For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html execute: enabled: false ---</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring using Jupyter <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks (as opposed to plain-text <code>.qmd</code> files) then this is already the default behavior: no execution occurs when you call <code>quarto render</code> (rather, execution occurs as you work within the notebook).</p> <h6 id="freezing-execution-2">Freezing Execution</h6> <p>If you are working within a project and your main concern is the cumulative impact of rendering many documents at once, consider using the <code>freeze</code> option.</p> <p>You can use the <code>freeze</code> option to denote that computational documents should never be re-rendered during a global project render, or alternatively only be re-rendered when their source file changes:</p> <pre><code>execute: freeze: true # never re-render during project render execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>freeze</code> controls whether execution occurs during global project renders. If you do an incremental render of either a single document or a project sub-directory then code is always executed. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render single document (always executes code) quarto render document.qmd # render project subdirectory (always executes code) quarto render articles</code></pre> <p>Learn more about using <code>freeze</code> with projects in the article on managing project execution.</p> <h2 id="dashboards">Dashboards</h2> <h3 id="dashboard-data-display">Dashboard Data Display</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-data-display-1">Dashboard Data Display</h4> <p>Dashboards are compositions of components used to provide navigation and present data. Below we’ll cover presenting data using plots, tables, and value boxes, as well how to include narrative content within dashboards.</p> <h5 id="plots">Plots</h5> <p>Plots are by far the most common content type displayed in dashboards. Both interactive JavaScript-based plots (e.g. <a href="https://altair-viz.github.io">Altair</a> and <a href="https://plotly.com/graphing-libraries/">Plotly</a>) and standard raster based plots (e.g. <a href="https://matplotlib.org">Matplotlib</a> or <a href="https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org">ggplot2</a>) are supported.</p> <p>Below we provide some language specific tips and techniques for including plots within dashboards.</p> <ul> <li>Python</li> <li>R</li> </ul> <h6 id="plotly">plotly</h6> <p><a href="https://plotly.com/python/">Plotly</a> is a popular Python package for JavaScript based plots, and works very well in dashboard layouts. Plotly is also noteworthy because it includes many interactive features while still not requiring a server. For example, this plot supports an animated display of values changing over time:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| title: GDP and Life Expectancy import plotly.express as px df = px.data.gapminder() px.scatter( df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", animation_frame="year", animation_group="country", size="pop", color="continent", hover_name="country", facet_col="continent", log_x=True, size_max=45, range_x=[100,100000], range_y=[25,90] ) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="altair">altair</h6> <p><a href="https://altair-viz.github.io">Altair</a> is a declarative statistical visualization library for Python based on Vega and Vega-Lite. Altair plots are JavaScript based so automatically resize themselves to fit their container within dashboards.</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| title: Iowa Electricity import altair as alt from vega_datasets import data source = data.iowa_electricity() alt.Chart(source).mark_area(opacity=0.3).encode( x="year:T", y=alt.Y("net_generation:Q").stack(None), color="source:N" ) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="matplotlib">matplotlib</h6> <p>If you are using traditional plotting libraries within static dashboards, you’ll need to pay a bit more attention to getting the size of plots right for the layout they’ll be viewed in. Note that this is not a concern for plots in interactive Shiny dashboards since all plot types are resized dynamically by Shiny.</p> <p>If you are using <a href="https://matplotlib.org">Matplotlib</a> (or libraries built on it like <a href="https://seaborn.pydata.org">Seaborn</a>) then you can set plot sizes using the <code>figure.figsize</code> global option (or alternatively per-figure if that’s more convenient):</p> <pre><code>```{python} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (12, 3) ```</code></pre> <p>In the case that your plots are laid out at a wider aspect ratio, setting this option can make a huge difference in terms of using available space. For example, the top plot in the stack below uses the default figure size of 8 x 5 and the bottom one uses the 12 x 3 ratio specified above:</p> <p>Note that the need to explicitly size plots is confined to traditional plotting libraries—if you use Plotly or another JavaScript based plotting system plots will automatically resize to fill their container.</p> <h6 id="htmlwidgets">htmlwidgets</h6> <p>The <a href="https://www.htmlwidgets.org/">htmlwidgets</a> framework provides high-level R bindings for JavaScript data visualization libraries. Some popular htmlwidgets include <a href="https://plot.ly/r/">Plotly</a>, <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/">Leaflet</a>, and <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/dygraphs">dygraphs</a>.</p> <p>You can use htmlwidgets just like you use normal R plots. For example, here is how we embed a Leaflet map:</p> <pre><code>```{r} library(leaflet) leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers(lng=174.768, lat=-36.852, popup="The birthplace of R") ```</code></pre> <p>There are dozens of packages on CRAN that provide htmlwidgets. You can find example uses of several of the more popular htmlwidgets in the htmlwidgets <a href="https://www.htmlwidgets.org/showcase_leaflet.html">showcase</a> and browse all available widgets in the <a href="https://gallery.htmlwidgets.org">gallery</a>.</p> <h6 id="r-graphics">R Graphics</h6> <p>You can use any chart created with standard R raster graphics (base, lattice, grid, etc.) within dashboards. When using standard R graphics with static dashboards, you’ll need to pay a bit more attention to getting the size of plots right for the layout they’ll be viewed in. Note that this is not a concern for plots in interactive Shiny dashboards since all plot types are resized dynamically by Shiny.</p> <p>The key to good sizing behavior in static dashboards is to define knitr <code>fig-width</code> and <code>fig-height</code> options that enable the plots to fit into their layout container as closely as possible.</p> <p>Here’s an example of a layout that includes 3 charts from R base graphics:</p> <pre><code>## Row {height="65%"} ```{r} #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 8 plot(cars) ``` ## Row {height="35%"} ```{r} #| fig-width: 5 #| fig-height: 4 plot(pressure) ``` ```{r} #| fig-width: 5 #| fig-height: 4 plot(airmiles) ```</code></pre> <p>We’ve specified an explicit <code>fig-height</code> and <code>fig-width</code> for each plot so that their rendered size fits their layout container as closely as possible. Note that the ideal values for these dimensions typically need to be determined by experimentation.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>For static dashboards, there are pros and cons to using JavaScript-based plots. While JavaScript-based plots handle resizing to fill their container better than static plots, they also embed the underlying data directly in the published page (one copy of the dataset per plot), which can lead to slower load times.</p> <p>For interactive Shiny dashboards, all plot types are sized dynamically, so resizing behavior is not a concern as it is with static dashboards.</p> <h5 id="tables-5">Tables</h5> <p>You can include data tables within dashboards in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>As a simple tabular display.</p></li> <li><p>As an interactive widget that includes sorting and filtering. Below we provide some language specific tips and techniques for including tables within dashboards.</p></li> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>R There are many Python packages available for producing tabular output. We’ll cover two of the more popular libraries (itables and tabulate) below.</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="itables">itables</h6> <p>The Python <a href="https://mwouts.github.io/itables/quick_start.html">itables</a> package supports creating interactive data tables from Pandas and Polars DataFrames that you can sort and filter.</p> <p>Use the <code>show()</code> method from <code>itables</code> to display an interactive table:</p> <pre><code>```{python} from itables import show show(penguins) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="options-35">Options</h6> <p>Note that a few <code>itables</code> options are set automatically within dashboards to ensure that they display well in cards of varying sizes. The option defaults are:</p> <pre><code>from itables import options options.dom = 'fiBrtlp' options.maxBytes = 1024 * 1024 options.language = dict(info = "Showing _TOTAL_ entries") options.classes = "display nowrap compact" options.paging = False options.searching = True options.ordering = True options.info = True options.lengthChange = False options.autoWidth = False options.responsive = True options.keys = True options.buttons = []</code></pre> <p>You can specify alternate options as you like to override these defaults. Options can be specified in the call to <code>show()</code> or globally as illustrated above. Here’s an example of specifying an option with <code>show()</code>:</p> <pre><code>show(penguins, searching = False, ordering = False)</code></pre> <p>You can find the reference for all of the DataTables options here: <a href="https://datatables.net/reference/option/">datatables.net</a>. All base options are available, as well as the options for the following extensions (which are automatically included by Quarto):</p> <ul> <li><p><a href="https://datatables.net/extensions/buttons/">datatables.net</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://datatables.net/extensions/keytable/">datatables.net</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://datatables.net/extensions/responsive/">datatables.net</a> For example, to enable the copy and export (excel/pdf) buttons in a call to <code>show()</code>:</p> <p>show(penguins, buttons = [‘copy’, ‘excel’, ‘pdf’])</p></li> </ul> <p>Or alternatively, to enable these buttons for all tables:</p> <pre><code>from itables import options options.buttons = ['copy', 'excel', 'pdf']</code></pre> <h6 id="downsampling">Downsampling</h6> <p>When a table is displayed, the table data is embedded in the dashboard output. To prevent dashboards from being too heavy to load for larger datasets, itables will display only a subset of the table—one that fits into <code>maxBytes</code> (1024kb by default).</p> <p>If you wish, you can increase the value of <code>maxBytes</code> or even deactivate the limit (with <code>maxBytes=0)</code>. For example, to set a limit of 200kb:</p> <pre><code>```{python} show(penguins, maxBytes = 200 * 1024) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="tabulate">tabulate</h6> <p>The Python <a href="https://github.com/astanin/python-tabulate">tabulate</a> package supports creating markdown tables from Pandas data frames, NumPy arrays, and many other data types. You can generate a markdown table from any Pandas data frame via the <code>to_markdown()</code> method (being sure to wrap it as <code>Markdown</code> output using IPython):</p> <pre><code>```{python} import pandas as pd from IPython.display import Markdown penguins = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv") Markdown(penguins.to_markdown(index=False)) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>index = False</code> parameter supresses the display of the row index. Here is a card containing output from <code>tabulate</code>:</p> <p>You can also import <code>tabulate</code> directly and pass in the object to print directly:</p> <pre><code>```{python} from tabulate import tabulate Markdown( tabulate(penguins, showindex=False, headers=penguins.columns) ) ```</code></pre> <p>There are many R packages available for producing tabular output. We’ll cover two of the more popular approaches (kable and DT) below.</p> <h6 id="kable">kable</h6> <p>Simple markdown tables are ideal for smaller numbers of records (i.e. 20-250 rows). Use the <code>knitr::kable()</code> function to output markdown tables:</p> <pre><code>```{r} knitr::kable(mtcars) ```</code></pre> <p>Simple markdown tables in dashboards automatically fill their container (scrolling horizontally and vertically as required).</p> <h6 id="dt">DT</h6> <p>The <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/DT/">DT</a> package (an interface to the DataTables JavaScript library) can display R matrices or data frames as interactive HTML tables that support filtering, pagination, and sorting.</p> <p>To include a DataTable you use the <code>DT::datatable</code> function:</p> <pre><code>```{r} library(DT) datatable(mtcars) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="options-36">Options</h6> <p>Note that a few <code>DT</code> options are set automatically within dashboards to ensure that they display well in cards of varying sizes. The option defaults are:</p> <pre><code>options(DT.options = list( bPaginate = FALSE, dom = "ifrt", language = list(info = "Showing _TOTAL_ entries") ))</code></pre> <p>You can specify alternate options as you like to override these defaults.</p> <h5 id="value-boxes">Value Boxes</h5> <p>Value boxes are a great way to prominently display simple values within a dashboard. For example, here is a dashboard row with three value boxes:</p> <p>Here is the code you might use to create these value boxes. Note that we use a mix of Python and R cells in this example to illustrate the syntax for each language. Note also that we assume the variables <code>articles</code>, <code>comments</code>, and <code>spam</code> are computed previously within the document.</p> <pre><code>## Row ```{python} #| content: valuebox #| title: "Articles per day" #| icon: pencil #| color: primary dict( value = articles ) ``` ```{python} #| content: valuebox #| title: "Comments per day" dict( icon = "chat", color = "primary", value = comments ) ``` ```{r} #| content: valuebox #| title: "Spam per day" list( icon = "trash", color = "danger", value = spam ) ```</code></pre> <p>You can choose between specifying value box options within YAML or within a <code>dict()</code> or <code>list()</code> (for Python and R, respectively) printed by the cell. The latter syntax is handy when you want the <code>icon</code> or <code>color</code> to be dynamic based on the value.</p> <h6 id="icon-and-color">Icon and Color</h6> <p>The <code>icon</code> used in value boxes can be any of the 2,000 available <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com">bootstrap icons</a>.</p> <p>The <code>color</code> can be any CSS color value, however there are some color aliases that are tuned specifically for dashboards that you might consider using by default:</p> <p>Color Alias</p> <p>Default Theme Color(s)</p> <p><code>primary</code></p> <p>Blue</p> <p><code>secondary</code></p> <p>Gray</p> <p><code>success</code></p> <p>Green</p> <p><code>info</code></p> <p>Bright Blue</p> <p><code>warning</code></p> <p>Yellow/Orange</p> <p><code>danger</code></p> <p>Red</p> <p><code>light</code></p> <p>Light Gray</p> <p><code>dark</code></p> <p>Black</p> <p>You can override these defaults by specifying value box Sass variables in a custom theme.</p> <p>While the aliases apply to all themes, the colors they correspond to vary.</p> <h6 id="shiny">Shiny</h6> <p>In a Shiny interactive dashboard you can have value boxes that update dynamically based on the state of the application. The details on how to do this are language-specific:</p> <ul> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>R Use the <code>ui.value_box()</code> function within a function decorated with <code>@render.ui</code>. For example:</p> <p><code>{python} from shiny.express import render, ui @render.ui def value(): return ui.value_box("Value", input.value())</code></p></li> </ul> <p>Use the <code>bslib::value_box()</code> function along with an optional icon drawn from the <code>bsicons</code> package. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} library(bslib) library(bsicons) value_box( title = "Value", value = textOutput("valuetext"), showcase = bs_icon("music-note-beamed") ) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="markdown-syntax-3">Markdown Syntax</h6> <p>You can also create value boxes using plain markdown, in which case you’ll typically include the value via an inline expression. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Row ::: {.valuebox icon="pencil" color="blue"} Articles per day `{python} articles` :::</code></pre> <h5 id="text-content">Text Content</h5> <p>While you often fill dashboard cards with plots and tables, you can also include arbitrary markdown content anywhere within a dashboard.</p> <h6 id="content-cards">Content Cards</h6> <p>Here is a dashboard where the last card in a column is plain markdown:</p> <p>To do this just include a <code>.card</code> div alongside the other cells:</p> <pre><code>## Column ```{python} #| title: Population px.area(df, x="year", y="pop", color="continent", line_group="country") ``` ```{python} #| title: Life Expectancy px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", color="continent", line_group="country") ``` ::: {.card} Gapminder combines data from multiple sources into unique coherent time-series that can’t be found elsewhere. Learn more about the Gampminder dataset at <[gapminder.org](https://www.gapminder.org/data/)>. :::</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring using a Jupyter Notebook then markdown cells automatically become <code>.card</code> divs (i.e. they don’t need the explicit <code>:::</code> div enclosure).</p> <h6 id="content-within-cells">Content within Cells</h6> <p>To include content alongside the ouptut of a cell, just enclose the both the cell and the content in a <code>.card</code> div. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.card title="Life Expectancy"} ```{python} px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", color="continent", line_group="country") ``` Gapminder combines data from multiple sources into unique coherent time-series that can’t be found elsewhere. Learn more about the Gampminder dataset at <[gapminder.org](https://www.gapminder.org/data/)>. :::</code></pre> <h6 id="leading-content">Leading Content</h6> <p>Content that is included at the very top of a dashboard (and not explicitly within a <code>.card</code> div) is considered leading content, and will be included as is with no card styling (e.g. with no border). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Dashboard" format: dashboard --- This content will appear above all of the other rows/columns, with no border. ## Row ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="dynamic-content">Dynamic Content</h6> <p>You can use inline expressions to make text content dynamic. For example, here we have a row with text content that makes use of Python expressions:</p> <pre><code>::: {.card} The sample size was `{python} sample`. The mean reported rating was `{python} rating`. :::</code></pre> <h5 id="cell-output">Cell Output</h5> <p>The output of each computational cell within your notebook or source document will be contained within a Card. Below we describe some special rules observed when creating cards.</p> <h6 id="dynamic-titles">Dynamic Titles</h6> <p>You can create a dynamic <code>title</code> by printing a <code>title=</code> expression as a cell’s first output (in contrast to including the <code>title</code> as a YAML cell option). For example:</p> <ul> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>R</p> <p>```{python} from ipyleaflet import Map, basemaps, basemap_to_tiles</p> <p>lat = 48 long = 350</p> <p>print(“title=”, f”World Map at {lat}, {long}“)</p> <p>Map(basemap=basemap_to_tiles(basemaps.OpenStreetMap.Mapnik), center=(lat, long), zoom=2) ```</p> <p>```{r} library(leaflet)</p> <p>lat <- 48 long <- 350</p> <p>cat(“title=”, “World Map at”, lat, long)</p> <p>leaflet() |> addTiles() |> setView(long, lat, zoom = 2) ```</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="excluded-cells">Excluded Cells</h6> <p>Cells that produce no output do not become cards (for example, cells used to import packages, load and filter data, etc). If a cell produces unexpected output that you want to exclude add the <code>output: false</code> option to the cell:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| output: false # (code that produces unexpected output) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="expression-printing-1">Expression Printing</h6> <p>By default, all output from top level expressions is displayed within dashboards. This means that multiple plots can easily be generated from a cell. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| title: "Tipping Behavior" px.box(df, x="sex", y="total_bill", color="smoker") px.violin(df, x="sex", y="total_bill", color="smoker") ```</code></pre> <p>This behavior corresponds to the <code>"all"</code> setting for <a href="https://ipython.readthedocs.io/en/stable/config/options/terminal.html#configtrait-InteractiveShell.ast_node_interactivity">Jupyter shell interactivity</a>. You can customize this behavior within Quarto using the <code>ipynb-shell-interactivity</code> option.</p> <h6 id="card-layout">Card Layout</h6> <p>If a cell produces multiple outputs you can use cell layout options to organize their display. For example, here we modify the example to display plots side-by-side using the <code>layout-ncol</code> option:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| title: "Tipping Behavior" #| layout-ncol: 2 px.box(df, x="sex", y="total_bill", color="smoker") px.violin(df, x="sex", y="total_bill", color="smoker") ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Figures for additional documentation on custom layouts.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-2">Learning More</h5> <p>Layout shows you how to control the navigation bar, and how to arrange your content across pages, rows, columns, tabsets, and cards.</p> <p>Inputs demonstrates various ways to layout inputs for interactive dashboards (sidebars, toolbars, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</p> <p>Examples provides a gallery of example dashboards you can use as inspiration for your own.</p> <p>Theming describes the various way to customize the fonts, colors, layout and other aspects of dashboard appearance.</p> <p>Parameters explains how to create dashboard variants by defining parameters and providing distinct values for them on the command line.</p> <p>Deployment covers how to deploy both static dashboards (which require only a web host, but not a server) and Shiny dashboards (which require a Shiny Server).</p> <p>Interactivity explores the various ways to create interactive dashboards that enable more flexible data exploration.</p> <h3 id="dashboard-deployment">Dashboard Deployment</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-deployment-1">Dashboard Deployment</h4> <h5 id="overview-38">Overview</h5> <p>There are a wide variety of ways to deploy dashboards created using Quarto. The mechanics of deployment are different depending on whether you are publishing a Static Dashboard (with no server dependencies) or a Shiny Dashboard. Both scenarios are covered in detail below.</p> <h5 id="static-dashboards">Static Dashboards</h5> <p>If you are deploying a static dashboard (i.e. not using Shiny for interactivity) then you can publish dashboards to any web server. Quarto includes a <code>quarto publish</code> command to make it easy to publish to a few popular services as well as automate publishing via Continuous Integration (CI).</p> <p>To get started, review the documentation for using one of the following publishing services:</p> <p>Destination</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Posit Connect Cloud</p> <p>Hosted publishing platform for sharing Quarto documents and websites. Use Posit Connect Cloud when you want a Posit-hosted service for publishing content without managing infrastructure.</p> <p>GitHub Pages</p> <p>Publish content based on source code managed within a GitHub repository. Use GitHub Pages when the source code for your document or site is hosted on GitHub.</p> <p>Posit Connect</p> <p>Publishing platform for secure sharing of data products within an organization. Use Posit Connect when you want to publish content to your organization-managed Connect server.</p> <p>Quarto Pub</p> <p>Publishing service for Quarto documents, websites, and books. Use Quarto Pub when you want a free, easy to use service for publicly available content.</p> <p>Netlify</p> <p>Professional web publishing platform. Use Netlify when you want support for custom domains, authentication, previewing branches, and other more advanced capabilities.</p> <p>Confluence</p> <p>Publishing platform for supporting team collaboration. Use Confluence to share documents in team Spaces.</p> <p>Hugging Face Spaces</p> <p>Publishing platform specializing in learning models and datasets. Use Hugging Face Spaces when you want to share Quarto documents together with associated machine learning models and/or datasets.</p> <p>Other Services</p> <p>Content rendered with Quarto uses standard formats (HTML, PDFs, MS Word, etc.) that can be published anywhere. Use this if none of the methods above meets your requirements.</p> <p>If you don’t know which to choose, try Posit Connect Cloud which is a free hosted service, or GitHub Pages if your source code is on GitHub. If you are publishing to a destination not listed above, choose Other Services.</p> <p>These articles cover both straightforward direct publishing as well as Continuous Integration (CI) publishing with GitHub Actions. If you want to publish using CI and aren’t using GitHub Actions, the article on Publishing with CI provides additional details and documentation.</p> <h5 id="shiny-dashboards">Shiny Dashboards</h5> <p>Dashboards that use Shiny for Python or Shiny for R are web applications that require a server for deployment (so they can’t just be deployed to a generic web host). Deployment options for Shiny applications include:</p> <ul> <li>Public hosting services like <a href="https://www.shinyapps.io">shinyapps.io</a> and <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-sdks-docker-shiny">Hugging Face</a>.</li> <li><a href="https://posit.co/products/open-source/shinyserver/">Shiny Server</a> (an open-source server developed by the Shiny team).</li> <li><a href="https://posit.co/products/enterprise/connect/">Posit Connect</a> (an on-premises commercial server product). Below we’ll cover some deployment basics for Python and R and provide links to additional documentation on using the various available methods.</li> </ul> <h6 id="shiny-for-python">Shiny for Python</h6> <p>Shiny interactive documents are normal Shiny applications that are created using <code>quarto render</code>. In fact, you don’t need Quarto at all to serve interactive documents, rather, you can just <code>shiny run</code> the application generated by <code>quarto render</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render example.qmd shiny run app.py</code></pre> <p>Your deployed application will consist of both the HTML document and <code>app.py</code> script generated by <code>quarto render</code>:</p> <pre><code>example.html example_files/ app.py</code></pre> <p>See the following documentation for information on deploying Shiny applications in various environments:</p> <p>Destination</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://docs.posit.co/shinyapps.io/getting-started.html#working-with-shiny-for-python">shinyapps.io</a></p> <p>Cloud hosting service</p> <p><a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-sdks-docker-shiny#shiny-for-python">Hugging Face</a></p> <p>Cloud hosting service</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#deploy-to-shiny-server-open-source">Shiny Server</a></p> <p>Open source application server</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#deploy-to-posit-connect-commercial">Posit Connect</a></p> <p>Commerical publishing platform</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#other-hosting-options">Other Services</a></p> <p>Custom server/hosting environment</p> <p>You can also deploy interactive Shiny documents in a serverless configuration (where Python runs in the browser via <a href="https://pyodide.org/">Pyodide</a>). The <a href="https://github.com/wch/retirement-simulation-dashboard">Retirement Simulation</a> is an example that demonstrates this workflow.</p> <h6 id="shiny-for-r">Shiny for R</h6> <p>Quarto Dashboards that use Shiny for R can be deployed using all of the tooling and services available for normal Shiny applications. Shiny for R dashboards are run using the <code>quarto serve</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto serve dashboard.qmd</code></pre> <p>The <code>quarto serve</code> command is supported natively by <a href="https://www.shinyapps.io">shinyapps.io</a>, <a href="https://posit.co/products/open-source/shinyserver/">Shiny Server</a> , and <a href="https://posit.co/products/enterprise/connect/">Posit Connect</a>. See the in-depth documentation on Shiny for R Deployment for details.</p> <h3 id="dashboard-input-layout">Dashboard Input Layout</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-input-layout-1">Dashboard Input Layout</h4> <h5 id="overview-39">Overview</h5> <p>There are several ways to layout inputs within interactive dashboards:</p> <ul> <li>Sidebars provide a collapsible vertical panel for inputs.</li> <li>Toolbars provide a horizontal panel for inputs.</li> <li>Card Inputs provide a panel for card-specific inputs. These techniques all create regions for inputs with a special background color to distinguish them from ordinary content. You can also locate inputs anywhere else you wish within a dashboard (i.e. in a standard card).</li> </ul> <h5 id="sidebars">Sidebars</h5> <p>Sidebars are a great place to group inputs for dashboards. To include a sidebar, add the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 2 heading. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Sidebar" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ## {.sidebar} ```{python} ``` ## Column ```{python} ``` ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>Here’s how a sidebar would appear (note there is a button in the top right that enables the user to optionally close the sidebar):</p> <h6 id="global-sidebar">Global Sidebar</h6> <p>If you have a dashboard with multiple pages, you may want the sidebar to be global (i.e. visible across all pages). To do this, add the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 1 heading:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Sidebar" format: dashboard --- # {.sidebar} Sidebar content # Plots ```{python} ``` # Data ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="inline-sidebar">Inline Sidebar</h6> <p>While sidebars are often laid out at the page level (i.e. spanning the dashboard from top to bottom) you can actually include them anywhere within a layout. For example, here we have a sidebar that is within a row (rather than spanning all rows):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ## Row ### {.sidebar} ```{python} ``` ### Column ```{python} ``` ## Row ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="location-and-size">Location and Size</h6> <p>Sidebars can be located on either the left or right side. Layout a sidebar on the right by including it after the column(s) it is adjacent to. You can also modify the size of sidebars using the <code>width</code> attribute. This example demonstrates both of these techniques:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Sidebar" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ## Column ```{python} ``` ```{python} ``` ## {.sidebar width="300px"} ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h5 id="toolbars">Toolbars</h5> <p>Toolbars are similar to sidebars, but provide a horizontal layout. Create a toolbar by adding the <code>.toolbar</code> class to a level 2 row heading. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Toolbar" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ## {.toolbar} ```{python} ``` ## Row ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="global-toolbar">Global Toolbar</h6> <p>If you have a dashboard with multiple pages, you may want the toolbar to be global (i.e. visible across all pages). To do this, add the <code>.toolbar</code> class to a level 1 heading:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Toolbar" format: dashboard server: shiny --- # {.toolbar} Toolbar content # Page 1 ```{python} ``` # Page 2 ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="inline-toolbar">Inline Toolbar</h6> <p>While toolbars are often laid out at the page level (i.e. spanning the dashboard from left to right) you can actually include them anywhere within a layout. For example, here we have a toolbar that is within a column (rather than spanning all columns):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard: orientation: columns server: shiny --- ## Column ### {.toolbar} ```{python} ``` ### Row ```{python} ``` ## Column ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="location">Location</h6> <p>Toolbars can be located on either the top or bottom of content. Layout a toolbar on the bottom by including it after the rows(s) it is adjacent to. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Penguin Bills" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ## Row ```{python} ``` ## {.toolbar} ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h5 id="card-inputs">Card Inputs</h5> <p>In some cases you may want to connect inputs more directly to a single output. You can do this using either a card toolbar or card sidebar.</p> <h6 id="card-toolbars">Card Toolbars</h6> <p>To add a toolbar to a card, define it immediately above or below the cell that generates the output. You can do this by either adding the <code>content: card-toolbar</code> option to a cell or by creating a div with the <code>.card-toolbar</code> class. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| content: card-toolbar ``` ```{python} #| title: Penguin Bills ```</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>title</code> attribute is optional for cells with toolbars (if there is no <code>title</code> then the inputs will be left rather than right aligned).</p> <h6 id="card-sidebars">Card Sidebars</h6> <p>To add a sidebar to a card, define it immediately to the left or the right of the cell that generates the output. You can do this either by adding the <code>content: card-sidebar</code> option to a cell or by creating a div with the <code>.card-sidebar</code> class. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| content: card-sidebar ``` ```{python} #| title: Penguin Bills ```</code></pre> <h3 id="dashboard-layout">Dashboard Layout</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-layout-1">Dashboard Layout</h4> <p>Dashboards are compositions of components used to provide navigation and present data. Below we’ll describe the components that are used to structure the navigation and layout of dashboards.</p> <h5 id="navigation">Navigation</h5> <p>All dashboards include a top-level navigation bar that provide a title and (optionally) a logo and author. Dashboards with multiple pages also contain a link to each page on the navigation bar:</p> <p>The <code>title</code> and <code>author</code> are specified as they are with normal documents. You can also include a <code>logo</code> and one or more <code>nav-buttons</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" author: "Cobblepot Analytics" format: dashboard: logo: images/penguins.png nav-buttons: [linkedin, twitter, github] ---</code></pre> <p>The following special aliases are recognized for navigation buttons: <code>linkedin</code>, <code>facebook</code>, <code>reddit</code>, <code>twitter</code>, and <code>github</code>. You can also create custom buttons as described in Nav Items. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: dashboard: nav-buttons: - reddit - icon: gitlab href: [gitlab.com](https://gitlab.com/)</code></pre> <h5 id="layout-1">Layout</h5> <p>Within a page, dashboard components are laid out using alternating sets of rows and columns. Rows and columns are in turn defined by markdown headings and computational cells. For example, here’s a simple layout with two rows, where the second row is split into two columns:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" author: "Cobblepot Analytics" format: dashboard --- ## Row {height=70%} ```{python} ``` ## Row {height=30%} ```{python} ``` ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>Here, level 2 markdown headings (e.g. <code>## Row {height=70%}</code>) define the contents of rows as well as their relative height. The ```<code>{python}</code> code cells in turn automatically create cards that are laid out in columns within the row.</p> <p>NoteHeading text isn’t required</p> <p>Although markdown headings are used to define the layout of rows and columns in Quarto dashboards, the heading text itself is discarded. We use the headings <code>Row</code> and <code>Column</code> in these docs to aid understanding of the layouts, but you can use more descriptive headings if they help you navigate your source code.</p> <h6 id="orientation">Orientation</h6> <p>By default, dashboard pages are laid out first by row, then by column. However, you can change this by specifying the <code>orientation: columns</code> document option:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Diamonds Explorer" format: dashboard: orientation: columns --- ## Column {width=60%} ```{python} ``` ## Column {width=40%} ```{python} ``` ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h6 id="fill-vs.-flow">Fill vs. Flow</h6> <p>Each row in your dashboard that is not given an explicit height will determine its size by either filling available space or by flowing to its natural height. Filling layout is generally the default, however for certain types of content (e.g. markdown text) flow layout is the default.</p> <p>If the default behavior isn’t what you want, you can explicitly specify filling or flowing behavior using the <code>.fill</code> and <code>.flow</code> classes applied to a row. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Row {.fill} ## Row {.flow}</code></pre> <h6 id="scrolling">Scrolling</h6> <p>By default, dashboard content fills all available space in the page. You can alternatively specify the <code>scrolling: true</code> option to layout content using its natural height and scroll to accommodate page overflow. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Scrolling" format: dashboard: scrolling: true --- ```{python} ``` ```{python} ``` ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>Because of its ability to scroll this layout could easily accommodate many more charts. While this is useful, you might also consider Pages and Tabsets (described in the next two sections) as alternate ways to present content within layouts that fill their page.</p> <h5 id="pages">Pages</h5> <p>The layout examples above demonstrated only single-page dashboards. To introduce multiple pages, use level 1 headings above the level 2 headings used to define rows and columns. The text of the level 1 headings will be used to link to the pages in the navigation bar. For example, here is a dashboard that splits content across two pages:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard --- # Bills ```{python} ``` # Flippers {orientation="columns" scrolling="true"} ## Column ```{python} ``` ```{python} ``` ## Column ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>Note that we can set a per-page orientation by adding an <code>orientation</code> attribute to the page heading (here <code>orientation="columns"</code> for the second page). In addition, you can control per-page scrolling behavior using a <code>scrolling</code> attribute on the page heading (shown using <code>scrolling="true"</code> for the second page above).</p> <h5 id="tabsets-1">Tabsets</h5> <p>Use tabsets to include multiple views of data or to include content of secondary importance without having it crowd the main display. Tabsets are created by adding the <code>.tabset</code> class to a row or column. For example, this layout displays the bottom row as a set of two tabs.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard --- ## Row ```{python} ``` ## Row {.tabset} ```{python} #| title: Chart 2 ``` ```{python} #| title: Chart 3 ```</code></pre> <p>You can include tabsets at arbitrarily deep levels. Here we include a tabset within a column of a top level row:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard --- ## Row {height=70%} ```{python} ``` ## Row {height=30%} ### Column {.tabset} ```{python} #| title: Chart 2 ``` ```{python} #| title: Chart 3 ``` ### Column ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>Each cell within the tabset column becomes a tab, and we provide navigational titles for our tabs by adding a <code>title</code> option to the cell used to produce each tab.</p> <p>You can also have tabs that contain only markdown. To do this use a <code>::: {.card}</code> div and include a <code>title</code> attribute for the tab:</p> <pre><code>::: {.card title="My Title"} Card text :::</code></pre> <p>In the examples above, each tab included a single card. If you want tabs to contain multiple cards, introduce another level of headings below the tabset row or column. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" format: dashboard --- ## Row {.tabset} ### Plots ```{python} ``` ```{python} ``` ### Data ```{python} ```</code></pre> <h5 id="cards">Cards</h5> <p>Cards are the fundamental unit of display within dashboards. Cards are created automatically for cells and markdown content that are within rows and columns. So for example, each of the Python cells here become cards:</p> <pre><code>## Column {width=40%} ```{python} ``` ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>You can also create cards that contain arbitrary markdown via a <code>.card</code> div. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Column {width=40%} ```{python} ``` ::: {.card} This text will be displayed within a card ::: ```{python} ```</code></pre> <p>To provide a title for a markdown card use the <code>title</code> attribute. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.card title="My Title"} This text will be displayed within a card :::</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring within a Jupyter Notebook then markdown cells automatically become <code>.card</code> divs.</p> <p>For additional details on how cells and their content are mapped to cards (e.g. excluding cells, cells with multiple outputs, etc.), see Cell Output.</p> <h6 id="display-options">Display Options</h6> <p>By default, cards are displayed with no title and a small bit of padding around the edges. Here is a card that displays a <a href="https://ipyleaflet.readthedocs.io">Leaflet</a> map:</p> <p>You can add a title to a card by including the <code>title</code> cell option. You can also customize the padding using the <code>padding</code> option. For example, here we add a title and remove the padding entirely:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| title: "World Map" #| padding: 0px from ipyleaflet import Map, basemaps, basemap_to_tiles Map(basemap=basemap_to_tiles(basemaps.OpenStreetMap.Mapnik), center=(48.204793, 350.121558), zoom=2) ```</code></pre> <p>You can create a dynamic <code>title</code> by printing a <code>title=</code> expression as a cell’s first output. For example:</p> <ul> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>R</p> <p>```{python} from ipyleaflet import Map, basemaps, basemap_to_tiles</p> <p>lat = 48 long = 350</p> <p>print(“title=”, f”World Map at {lat}, {long}“)</p> <p>Map(basemap=basemap_to_tiles(basemaps.OpenStreetMap.Mapnik), center=(lat, long), zoom=2) ```</p> <p>```{r} library(leaflet)</p> <p>lat <- 48 long <- 350</p> <p>cat(“title=”, “World Map at”, lat, long)</p> <p>leaflet() |> addTiles() |> setView(long, lat, zoom = 2) ```</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="expanding-cards">Expanding Cards</h6> <p>By default, you can zoom in on the content of cards using the expand button in the bottom right:</p> <p>If you don’t want cards to be expandable you can specify <code>expandable: false</code> (either at the document level or for individual cards).</p> <h6 id="card-fill-behavior">Card Fill Behavior</h6> <p>Quarto inspects card contents and generally choose a fill behavior that best matches the contents of the card (by default cards will fill their container, though in specific cases like simple markdown the card will choose a <code>flow</code> layout). You can explicit control the fill behavior of card using the <code>fill</code> attribute with the desired boolean value. For example <code>fill="false"</code> will cause the card’s height to match the size of the content (not filling).</p> <h5 id="learning-more-3">Learning More</h5> <p>Data Display shows you how to display data in your dashboard as plots, tables, value boxes, and text.</p> <p>Inputs demonstrates various ways to layout inputs for interactive dashboards (sidebars, toolbars, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</p> <p>Examples provides a gallery of example dashboards you can use as inspiration for your own.</p> <p>Theming describes the various way to customize the fonts, colors, layout and other aspects of dashboard appearance.</p> <p>Parameters explains how to create dashboard variants by defining parameters and providing distinct values for them on the command line.</p> <p>Deployment covers how to deploy both static dashboards (which require only a web host, but not a server) and Shiny dashboards (which require a Shiny Server).</p> <p>Interactivity explores the various ways to create interactive dashboards that enable more flexible data exploration.</p> <h3 id="dashboard-parameters">Dashboard Parameters</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-parameters-1">Dashboard Parameters</h4> <h5 id="overview-40">Overview</h5> <p>You may have a set of parameters that are used to create different variations of a dashboard. For example:</p> <ul> <li>Showing results for a specific geographic location.</li> <li>Running a report that covers a specific time period.</li> <li>Running a single analysis multiple times for different assumptions. This article describes how to define and use computational parameters with Quarto.</li> </ul> <h5 id="definition-1">Definition</h5> <p>Adding parameter definitions to a dashboard works differently depending on whether you are using the <a href="https://jupyter.org">Jupyter</a>, <a href="https://yihui.name/knitr">Knitr</a> or Julia engine.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-2">Jupyter</h6> <p>For Jupyter, Quarto uses the same syntax for defining parameters as <a href="https://papermill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage-parameterize.html">Papermill</a>. To parameterize a dashboard, designate a cell with the tag <code>parameters</code> and provide appropriate default values:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| tags: [parameters] alpha = 0.1 ratio = 0.1 ```</code></pre> <p>The parameters are available in the top level environment:</p> <pre><code>```{python} alpha ```</code></pre> <p>When the dashboard is executed with a set of new parameters a cell is injected which overrides these defaults as appropriate.</p> <h6 id="knitr-3">Knitr</h6> <p>For Knitr, the standard Knitr <code>params</code> YAML option is used to define parameters. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- params: alpha: 0.1 ratio: 0.1 ---</code></pre> <p>The parameters are available in the <code>params</code> list:</p> <pre><code>```{r} params$alpha ```</code></pre> <h6 id="julia-1">Julia</h6> <p>For the Julia engine, parameters are defined via the <code>params</code> YAML option.</p> <pre><code>--- engine: julia params: alpha: 0.1 ratio: 0.1 ---</code></pre> <p>Each key is evaluated as a constant and can be accessed under that name. Note that this means only keys that are valid Julia variable names are allowed.
