For example, <code>some_key</code> is valid while <code>some-key</code> isn’t, even though the latter is a valid YAML key.</p> <pre><code>```{julia} alpha ```</code></pre> <h5 id="rendering-7">Rendering</h5> <p>To render using different parameters you can pass them on the command line using the <code>-P</code> flag (this works for both <code>.ipynb</code> or <code>.qmd</code> files):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render dashboard.ipynb -P alpha:0.2 -P ratio:0.3</code></pre> <p>Alternatively you can create a YAML file that defines the parameter values you want to render with, then call quarto render with the <code>--execute-params</code> flag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render dashboard.qmd --execute-params params.yml</code></pre> <h3 id="dashboard-theming">Dashboard Theming</h3> <h4 id="dashboard-theming-1">Dashboard Theming</h4> <h5 id="overview-41">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto Dashboards use same Bootstrap 5 based theming system as regular HTML documents (so themes you have built for HTML websites can also be used with dashboards). Use the <code>theme</code> option to choose a theme:</p> <pre><code>theme: cosmo</code></pre> <p>Quarto includes 25 themes from the <a href="https://bootswatch.com/">Bootswatch</a> project (for example, the website uses the <a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a> theme). Available themes include:</p> <ul> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/default/">default</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cerulean/">cerulean</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cyborg/">cyborg</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/darkly/">darkly</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/flatly/">flatly</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/journal/">journal</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/litera/">litera</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lumen/">lumen</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lux/">lux</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/materia/">materia</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/minty/">minty</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/morph/">morph</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/pulse/">pulse</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/quartz/">quartz</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sandstone/">sandstone</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/simplex/">simplex</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sketchy/">sketchy</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/slate/">slate</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/solar/">solar</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/spacelab/">spacelab</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/superhero/">superhero</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/united/">united</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/vapor/">vapor</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/yeti/">yeti</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/zephyr/">zephyr</a> Use of any of these themes via the <code>theme</code> option. For example:</p> <p>format: dashboard: theme: united</p></li> </ul> <p>In the following sections we’ll describe how you can customize these themes or create your own new themes.</p> <h5 id="theme-options">Theme Options</h5> <p>You can do extensive customization of themes using <a href="https://sass-lang.com/">Sass</a>. Bootstrap defines over 1,400 Sass variables that control fonts, colors, padding, borders, and much more. You can see all of the variables here:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/blob/main/scss/_variables.scss">github.com</a></p> <p>Sass theme files can define both variables that globally set things like colors and fonts, as well as rules that define more fine grained behavior. To customize an existing Bootstrap theme with your own set of variables and/or rules, just provide the base theme and then your custom theme file(s):</p> <pre><code>theme: - cosmo - custom.scss</code></pre> <p>Your <code>custom.scss</code> file might look something like this:</p> <pre><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/ $h2-font-size: 1.6rem !default; $headings-font-weight: 500 !default; /*-- scss:rules --*/ h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { text-shadow: -1px -1px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, .3); }</code></pre> <p>Note that the variables section is denoted by the <code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/</code> comment and the rules section (where normal CSS rules go) is denoted by the <code>/*-- scss:rules --*/</code> comment.</p> <h5 id="custom-themes">Custom Themes</h5> <p>You can naturally also create an entirely custom theme and provide only that (in this case you will inherit from the default Bootstrap theme):</p> <pre><code>theme: custom.scss</code></pre> <p>For example, here are the theme files for the 25 built-in Bootswatch themes:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/html/bootstrap/themes">github.com</a></p> <p>You can read more about the custom theming design here.</p> <h5 id="sass-variables">Sass Variables</h5> <p>The following Sass Variables can be specified within SCSS files (note that these variables should always be prefixed with a <code>$</code> and are specified within theme files rather than within YAML options):</p> <h6 id="colors">Colors</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$body-bg</code></p> <p>The page background color.</p> <p><code>$body-color</code></p> <p>The page text color.</p> <p><code>$link-color</code></p> <p>The link color.</p> <p><code>$input-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for HTML inputs.</p> <p><code>$popover-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for popovers (for example, when a citation preview is shown).</p> <h6 id="fonts">Fonts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$font-family-sans-serif</code></p> <p>The sans-serif font family for the page.</p> <p><code>$font-family-monospace</code></p> <p>The monospace font family for the page.</p> <p><code>$font-size-root</code></p> <p>The base font size for the page.</p> <p><code>$toc-font-size</code></p> <p>The font size for the page TOC.</p> <p><code>$h1-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h2-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h3-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h4-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h5-font-size</code></p> <p>Font sizes for the specified headings.</p> <h6 id="code-blocks-4">Code Blocks</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left</code></p> <p>By default, Quarto does not display a left border on code blocks. Set this variable to a truthy value or a CSS color to enable the left border.</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left-style</code></p> <p>The style of the left border displayed on code blocks. Defaults to <code>solid</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left-size</code></p> <p>The thickness of the left border displayed on code blocks. Defaults to <code>3px</code>;</p> <p><code>$code-block-padding-left</code></p> <p>The amount of padding applied between the code and the border. Defaults to <code>0.6em</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg</code></p> <p>By default, Quarto sets a background on code blocks by adding transparency to the theme’s <code>progress-bg</code> color. Set this variable to truthy value or a CSS color.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg-padding</code></p> <p>The padding applied to the code block. Defaults to <code>0.4em</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg-alpha</code></p> <p>The amount to alter the transparency fo the <code>progress-bg</code> color. This is not used if an explicit background color is set. Defaults to <code>-0.35</code>.</p> <h6 id="code-annotation-2">Code Annotation</h6> <p>You can customize the colors used to highlight lines when code annotation is used:</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-annotation-higlight-color</code></p> <p>The color used as a border on highlighted lines.</p> <p><code>$code-annotation-higlight-bg</code></p> <p>The color used for the background of highlighted lines.</p> <h6 id="code-copy">Code Copy</h6> <p>You can also customize the colors of the button which appears for <code>code-copy: true</code> with the following variables:</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$btn-code-copy-color</code></p> <p>The color used for the copy button at the top right of code blocks.</p> <p><code>$btn-code-copy-color-active</code></p> <p>The hover color used for the copy button at the top right of code blocks.</p> <h6 id="inline-code-3">Inline Code</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-bg</code></p> <p>The background color of inline code. Defaults to a mix between the <code>body-bg</code> and <code>body-color</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-color</code></p> <p>The text color of inline code. Defaults to a generated contrasting color against the <code>code-bg</code>.</p> <h6 id="table-of-contents">Table of Contents</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$toc-color</code></p> <p>The color for table of contents text.</p> <p><code>$toc-font-size</code></p> <p>The font-size for table of contents text.</p> <p><code>$toc-active-border</code></p> <p>The left border color for the currently active table of contents item.</p> <p><code>$toc-inactive-border</code></p> <p>The left border colors for inactive table of contents items.</p> <h6 id="layout-2">Layout</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$content-padding-top</code></p> <p>Padding that should appear before the main content area (including the sidebar, content, and TOC.</p> <h6 id="navigation-1">Navigation</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$navbar-bg</code></p> <p>The background color of the navbar. Defaults to the theme’s <code>$primary</code> color.</p> <p><code>$navbar-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the navbar. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$navbar-hl</code></p> <p>The highlight color for links in the navbar. If not specified, the <code>$link-color</code> is used or a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for a sidebar. Defaults to <code>\$light</code> except when a navbar is present or when the style is <code>floating</code>. In that case it defaults to the <code>\$body-bg</code> color.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the sidebar. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-hl</code></p> <p>The highlight color for links in the sidebar. If not specified, the <code>$link-color</code> is used.</p> <p><code>$footer-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for the footer. Defaults to the <code>$body-bg</code> color.</p> <p><code>$footer-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the footer. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <h6 id="callouts-2">Callouts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$callout-border-width</code></p> <p>The left border width of callouts. Defaults to <code>5px</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-border-scale</code></p> <p>The border color of callouts computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>0%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-icon-scale</code></p> <p>The color of the callout icon computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>10%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-top</code></p> <p>The amount of top margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1.25rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-bottom</code></p> <p>The amount of bottom margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1.25rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-color-<type></code></p> <p>The colors for the various types of callouts. Defaults:</p> <p>type</p> <p>default</p> <p><code>note</code></p> <p><code>$blue</code></p> <p><code>tip</code></p> <p><code>$green</code></p> <p><code>caution</code></p> <p><code>$orange</code></p> <p><code>warning</code></p> <p><code>$yellow</code></p> <p><code>important</code></p> <p><code>$red</code></p> <h6 id="value-boxes-1">Value Boxes</h6> <p>Use the <code>$valuebox-bg-<type></code> variables to override the background color of value boxes that are set with <code>color: <type></code>.</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Type</p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-primary</code></p> <p><code>color: primary</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-secondary</code></p> <p><code>color: secondary</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-success</code></p> <p><code>color: success</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-info</code></p> <p><code>color: info</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-warning</code></p> <p><code>color: warning</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-danger</code></p> <p><code>color: danger</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-light</code></p> <p><code>color: light</code></p> <p><code>$valuebox-bg-dark</code></p> <p><code>color: dark</code></p> <h6 id="bootstrap-variables">Bootstrap Variables</h6> <p>In addition to the above Sass variables, Bootstrap itself supports hundreds of additional variables. You can <a href="https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.1/customize/sass/">learn more about Bootstrap’s use of Sass variables</a> or review the <a href="https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/blob/main/scss/_variables.scss">raw variables and their default values</a>.</p> <h3 id="dashboards-with-observable-js">Dashboards with Observable JS</h3> <h4 id="dashboards-with-observable-js-1">Dashboards with Observable JS</h4> <h5 id="introduction">Introduction</h5> <p>Quarto includes native support for <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable JS</a>, a set of enhancements to vanilla JavaScript created by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Bostock">Mike Bostock</a> (also the author of <a href="https://d3js.org/">D3</a>). Observable JS is distinguished by its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/runtime">reactive runtime</a>, which is especially well suited for interactive data exploration and analysis.</p> <p>The creators of Observable JS (Observable, Inc.) run a hosted service at <a href="https://observablehq.com/">observablehq.com</a> where you can create and publish notebooks. Additionally, you can use Observable JS (“OJS”) in standalone documents and websites via its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq">core libraries</a>. Quarto uses these libraries along with a <a href="https://github.com/asg017/unofficial-observablehq-compiler/tree/beta">compiler</a> that is run at render time to enable the use of OJS within Quarto documents.</p> <h5 id="walkthrough">Walkthrough</h5> <p>Quarto Dashboards are a great way to present interactive OJS visualizations. Below we’ll provide a complete example which will give you a high level view of the basics. If you want to learn more, please see the complete documentation on Using OJS with Quarto.</p> <p>This example covers many of the techniques you’ll use when creating dashboards with OJS, including reactive calculations and more advanced layout constructs like sidebars and tabsets. Here is the interactive document we’ll be building:</p> <p>The source code for this dashboard is below. Note that we add the</p> <p><code>//| output: false</code> option to the first cell: this is to designate the cell as having only intermediate computations (so it should not be turned into a card in the dashboard layout).</p> <p>Click on the numbers on the far right for additional explanation of syntax and mechanics)</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" author: "Cobblepot Analytics" format: dashboard --- ```{ojs} //| output: false data = FileAttachment("penguins.csv") .csv({ typed: true }) filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) ``` # {.sidebar} ![](images/penguins.png){width="80%"} ```{ojs} viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], label: "Islands:" } ) ``` # Plot ```{ojs} Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } ) ``` # Data ```{ojs} Inputs.table(filtered) ```</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>We set <code>output: false</code> to indicate that this cell includes only intermediate calculations and should not have its contents printed.</p> <p>2</p> <p>We read the raw penguins dataset from a CSV when the page loads.</p> <p>3</p> <p><code>filtered</code> is a value that is automatically recomputed when variables declared with <code>viewof</code> change (in this case <code>bill_length_min</code> and <code>islands</code>).</p> <p>4</p> <p>Create global sidebars by adding the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 1 heading. Sidebars can include code cells as well as images, narrative, and links.</p> <p>5</p> <p>Here we define our inputs using <code>viewof</code> so that the <code>filtered</code> dataset is automatically recomputed when they change.</p> <p>6</p> <p>Level 1 headings (here <code># Plots</code> and <code># Data</code>) create pages within the dashboard.</p> <p>7</p> <p>The plot is automatically redrawn whenever the <code>filtered</code> dataset changes.</p> <p>8</p> <p>The tabular data display is automatically refreshed whenever the <code>filtered</code> dataset changes.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-4">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about using OJS with Quarto, see the following articles:</p> <p>Input describes various ways to layout inputs (sidebars, input panels, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.).</p> <p>Using OJS provides an introduction and overview of other topics.</p> <p>OJS Libraries covers using standard libraries and external JavaScript libraries.</p> <p>OJS Data Sources outlines the various ways to read and pre-process data.</p> <p>OJS Cells goes into more depth on cell execution, output, and layout.</p> <p>OJS Code Reuse delves into ways to re-use OJS code across multiple documents.</p> <h3 id="dashboards-with-shiny-for-python">Dashboards with Shiny for Python</h3> <h4 id="dashboards-with-shiny-for-python-1">Dashboards with Shiny for Python</h4> <h5 id="introduction-1">Introduction</h5> <p>The <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/">Shiny</a> package provides an easy way to build web applications with Python. Quarto dashboards can include embedded Shiny components (e.g. a plot with sliders that control its inputs).</p> <p>This section assumes you have no experience with Shiny, and will teach you the basic concepts you need to get up and running with Shiny with Quarto.</p> <p>If you are using R rather than Python, see the documentation on using Shiny for R.</p> <p>NoteShiny Prerequisites</p> <p>In order to use Shiny within Quarto documents you will need the latest version of the <code>shiny</code> (>=0.9.0) and <code>shinywidgets</code> (>=0.3.1) packages. You can install the latest version of these with:</p> <pre><code>pip install --upgrade shiny shinywidgets</code></pre> <h5 id="hello-shiny">Hello, Shiny</h5> <p>We’ll start with a very simple dashboard that consists of a single plot and some inputs to drive its display:</p> <p>Here is the source code for this dashboard (click on the numbers on the far right for additional explanation):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Penguin Bills" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ```{python} import seaborn as sns penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins") ``` ## {.sidebar} ```{python} from shiny.express import render, ui ui.input_select("x", "Variable:", choices=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]) ui.input_select("dist", "Distribution:", choices=["hist", "kde"]) ui.input_checkbox("rug", "Show rug marks", value = False) ``` ## Column ```{python} @render.plot def displot(): sns.displot( data=penguins, hue="species", multiple="stack", x=input.x(), rug=input.rug(), kind=input.dist()) ```</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>The <code>server: shiny</code> option instructs Quarto to run a Shiny Server behind the document.</p> <p>2</p> <p>Create sidebars by adding the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 2 heading. Sidebars can include code cells as well as images, narrative, and links.</p> <p>3</p> <p>A series of Shiny input elements (interacting with them updates the <code>input</code> object)</p> <p>4</p> <p>The plot is rendered and updated according to the current <code>input</code> values.</p> <p>In this dashboard, you can choose different values from the select boxes on the left, and the plot will update to reflect your choices. You can also click the checkbox to show or hide rug marks. Let’s go through the construction of this Shiny-enabled dashboard one step at a time.</p> <h6 id="metadata">Metadata</h6> <p>The first thing to do is add <code>server: shiny</code> to the front matter. This tells Quarto that the document should be rendered as a Shiny dashboard (which requires a Python runtime whenever the dashboard is being viewed), rather than as a static HTML page. When you run <code>quarto preview <filename>.qmd</code> on a <code>server: shiny</code> document, Quarto will start and maintain a Shiny process for you and open the dashboard in your browser.</p> <h6 id="adding-input-controls">Adding Input Controls</h6> <p>Next, we use functions matching the pattern <code>ui.input_xxx</code> to create input controls. For example, <code>ui.input_select()</code> creates a select box, <code>ui.input_slider()</code> creates a slider, and so on. The values returned by these functions are then rendered into HTML and JavaScript by Quarto.</p> <p>This example only uses two types of inputs, but Shiny has many more. Use the <a href="https://jcheng.shinyapps.io/shiny-component-browser/">Shiny Component Browser</a> to see them all, along with code snippets you can copy and paste into your dashboard.</p> <p>The example above defined an input with the following code:</p> <pre><code>```{python} ui.input_select("x", label="Variable:", choices=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]) ```</code></pre> <p>Every input function takes an input ID as its first argument. An input ID is string that uniquely identifies this input; it must be a simple, syntactically valid Python variable name. We will use this ID to access the input’s value from other parts of the dashboard.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>Make sure each input ID in your Shiny dashboard is unique. If you use the same ID for two different inputs, Shiny will not be able to tell them apart, and your dashboard will not work correctly.</p> <p>The second argument for each input function is usually a human-readable string that will be displayed next to the input control. For example, the <code>ui.input_select()</code> function passes <code>"Variable:"</code>as the second argument, which is why the select box has the label “Variable:” next to it.</p> <h6 id="sidebars-and-toolbars">Sidebars and Toolbars</h6> <p>In many dashboards, it’s desirable to visually gather all of your input controls into a sidebar. You can do this by adding the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 2 heading, as we did in the example:</p> <pre><code>## {.sidebar} ```{python} ui.input_select("x", "Variable:", choices=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]) ui.input_select("dist", "Distribution:", choices=["hist", "kde"]) ui.input_checkbox("rug", "Show rug marks", value = False) ```</code></pre> <p>As an alternative to sidebars, you can also layout inputs horizontally, or even attach them directly to cards. See the article on Inputs for further details.</p> <h6 id="displaying-dynamic-output">Displaying Dynamic Output</h6> <p>In Shiny, dashboards can contain outputs—plots, tables, text, etc.—that dynamically update in response to user input.</p> <p>The example above defined a dynamic plot with the following code:</p> <pre><code>```{python} @render.plot def displot(): sns.displot( data=penguins, hue="species", multiple="stack", x=input.x(), rug=input.rug(), kind=input.dist()) ```</code></pre> <p>The function here is given the name <code>displot</code>. The body of the function is using typical Seaborn code to create the plot. And a <code>@render.plot</code> decorator is added to the function, to indicate to Shiny that this function should be used to create a plot. (If you haven’t seen decorators before, they’re a Python feature that allows you to add additional behavior to a function.)</p> <p>The <code>input.x()</code>, <code>input.rug()</code>. and <code>input.dist()</code> method calls are retrieving the values of the <code>x</code>, <code>rug</code>, and <code>dist</code> inputs created earlier in the dashboard.</p> <p>Note that our code never calls the <code>displot()</code> function! Just the act of defining the function, and decorating it with <code>@render.plot</code>, is enough to tell Shiny and Quarto to:</p> <ul> <li>Insert a plot into the dashboard at this location.</li> <li>Use the function body to create the plot.</li> <li>Automatically re-run the function body whenever the values of <code>input.x()</code>, <code>input.rug()</code>, or <code>input.dist()</code> change due to user interaction, and use the result to update the existing plot. This example only contains a single <code>@render.plot</code> output, but it’s possible for Shiny apps to contain multiple outputs, and outputs of different types, as you’ll see in the following example. Check out the <a href="https://jcheng.shinyapps.io/shiny-component-browser/#outputs">Shiny Component Browser</a> to see what types of outputs are available.</li> </ul> <h6 id="reactive-programming">Reactive Programming</h6> <p>In the previous section, we said that the <code>displot</code> function would re-run automatically whenever any of the inputs it referred to changed. Shiny is a reactive programming framework, meaning it takes care of tracking the relationships between inputs and outputs in your app. When an input changes, only outputs that are affected by that input are re-rendered. This is a powerful feature that makes it easy to create dashboards that respond to user input efficiently.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The <code>input</code> object is designed to be tracked by Shiny’s reactive framework,</p> <p>Shiny specifically tracks changes to reactivity-aware objects like the <code>input</code> object, not to just any arbitrary Python variable. You can’t just write <code>x = 100</code>, then use <code>x</code> from the <code>displot</code> function, and expect <code>displot</code> to automatically rerun whenever <code>x</code> changes.</p> <p>Similarly, Shiny will only automatically re-run functions that are reactivity-aware, like ones decorated with <code>@render.plot</code>. It will not help re-execute code at the top level of the document or code in regular Python functions.</p> <h5 id="additional-features">Additional Features</h5> <p>Next, we’ll explore a more in-depth example that covers more features, including factoring out setup code, reactive calculations, and more advanced layout constructs like pages. Here is the interactive document we’ll be building:</p> <p>Here is the source code for this dashboard. You can click on the numbers on the far right for additional explanation of syntax and mechanics, and we’ll also explain in more detail below.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Palmer Penguins" author: "Cobblepot Analytics" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ```{python} #| context: setup import seaborn as sns from shiny import reactive from shiny.express import render, ui penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins") ``` # {.sidebar} ![](images/penguins.png){width="80%"} ```{python} species = list(penguins["species"].value_counts().index) ui.input_checkbox_group( "species", "Species:", species, selected = species ) islands = list(penguins["island"].value_counts().index) ui.input_checkbox_group( "islands", "Islands:", islands, selected = islands ) @reactive.calc def filtered_penguins(): data = penguins[penguins["species"].isin(input.species())] data = data[data["island"].isin(input.islands())] return data ``` ```{python} ui.input_select("dist", "Distribution:", choices=["kde", "hist"]) ui.input_checkbox("rug", "Show rug marks", value = False) ``` [Learn more](https://pypi.org/project/palmerpenguins/) about the Palmer Penguins dataset. # Plots ```{python} @render.plot def depth(): return sns.displot( filtered_penguins(), x = "bill_depth_mm", hue = "species", kind = input.dist(), fill = True, rug=input.rug() ) ``` ```{python} @render.plot def length(): return sns.displot( filtered_penguins(), x = "bill_length_mm", hue = "species", kind = input.dist(), fill = True, rug=input.rug() ) ``` # Data ```{python} @render.data_frame def dataview(): return render.DataGrid(filtered_penguins()) ```</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>The <code>server: shiny</code> option instructs Quarto to run a Shiny Server behind the document.</p> <p>2</p> <p>The <code>context: setup</code> cell option indicates that this code cell should run when the application starts (as opposed to when each new client session starts). Expensive initialization code (e.g. loading data) should be placed in <code>context: setup</code>.</p> <p>3</p> <p>Create global sidebars by adding the <code>.sidebar</code> class to a level 1 heading. Sidebars can include code cells as well as images, narrative, and links.</p> <p>4</p> <p>These checkbox input groups have their contents dynamically driven from the available categories in the <code>species</code> and <code>islands</code> fields of the dataset.</p> <p>5</p> <p>When the user interacts with the checkbox groups this results in a different filtered view of the dataset. The <code>@reactive.calc</code> function recomputes the filtered dataset and makes it available as <code>filtered_penguins()</code>.</p> <p>6</p> <p>These inputs affect the display of plots but not the contents of the filtered dataset.</p> <p>7</p> <p>Level 1 headings (here <code># Plots</code> and <code># Data</code>) create pages within the dashboard.</p> <p>8</p> <p>Plots are rendered by referencing the filtered dataset (<code>filtered_penguins()</code> as well as the plot display oriented inputs (<code>input.dist()</code> and <code>input.rug()</code>). Plots are automatically re-rendered when the dataset or these inputs change.</p> <p>9</p> <p>The Data tab also references <code>filtered_penguins()</code> and is updated whenever the filtered data changes.</p> <h6 id="setup-cell">Setup Cell</h6> <p>In static Quarto documents, <code>{python}</code> code cells run only when the document is rendered, not when it is viewed. In <code>server: shiny</code> documents, <code>{python}</code> code cells are run both during render time and each time the dashboard is loaded in a browser. This is important because each visitor to the dashboard needs their own independent copies of inputs/outputs in memory, so that simultaneous users don’t interfere with each other.</p> <p>However, sometimes we have code that would be excessive to run for every user, and we only want the code to run once, when the document’s Shiny runtime process is starting up. For example, in the example above, we import packages and load data using <code>sns.load_dataset("penguins")</code>:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| context: setup import seaborn as sns from shiny import reactive from shiny.express import render, ui penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins") ```</code></pre> <p>We do this in a setup cell because it would be wasteful in terms of both time and memory to load the data once for each user, instead of once for the process.</p> <p>By simply adding <code>#| context: setup</code> to the code cell, we can tell Quarto to run the code only once, when the Shiny process starts up. Setup cells are a great way to factor out code that you want to run once, not on every page load. Variables you define in setup cells can be read by all other code cells in the document.</p> <h6 id="dashboard-pages">Dashboard Pages</h6> <p>At the top of this dashboard, you can see “Plots” and “Data” headings. These are called dashboard pages. Dashboard pages are a way to organize your dashboard into multiple pages, each with its own set of outputs. You can insert dashboard pages by adding level 1 headings to your Markdown. In this case, <code># Plots</code> and <code># Data</code>:</p> <pre><code># Plots # Data</code></pre> <h6 id="data-frame-outputs">Data Frame Outputs</h6> <p>On the Data page, there’s a dynamic data frame output. This is created by the following code:</p> <pre><code>```{python} @render.data_frame def dataview(): return render.DataGrid(filtered_penguins()) ```</code></pre> <p>In a <code>@render.data_frame</code> function, you can simply return a Pandas data frame, and Shiny will automatically render it as an interactive data grid. (The <code>filtered_penguins()</code> function is a reactive calculation that returns a data frame–we’ll explore that next.)</p> <p>You also have the option of wrapping the data frame object in a <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/render.DataGrid.html"><code>render.DataGrid</code></a> or <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/render.DataTable.html#shiny.render.DataTable"><code>render.DataTable</code></a> constructor; in this case, we’re using the former. This is not strictly necessary, but it allows you to set additional options on the data grid or table, such as filtering and selection.</p> <p>The only difference between <code>render.DataGrid</code> and <code>render.DataTable</code> is the appearance of the rendered table: <code>render.DataGrid</code> uses a more compact, spreadsheet-like appearance, while <code>render.DataTable</code> uses a more traditional table appearance.</p> <h6 id="reactive-calculations">Reactive Calculations</h6> <p>In this example, the user uses select boxes to filter a dataset, and the filtered dataset is displayed in three different dynamic outputs: two plots and a data frame. Remember that as inputs change, Shiny automatically re-executes functions decorated with <code>@render.plot</code> and <code>@render.data_frame</code> that are affected by those inputs. But where do we put the code that filters the dataset?</p> <p>The most obvious place would be to duplicate the code in each of the three rendering functions. But this is a bad idea, both because duplicate code is annoying to maintain, and because it would be inefficient to re-run the same filtering code three times just to get the exact same results. We could extract the duplicated code into a function, which would remove the maintenance problem, but it would not be any more efficient.</p> <p>Shiny has a solution: reactive calculations. A reactive calculation is a reactive-aware function that is re-executed whenever its inputs change, but whose return value is not rendered into the dashboard. Instead, the return value is cached, and can be accessed by rendering functions (or even by other reactive calculations). This allows us to place the filtering logic in a single reactive calculation, and then have the three rendering functions access the filtered dataset from the reactive calculation.</p> <p>To create a reactive calculation, we use the <code>@reactive.calc</code> decorator. The following code creates a reactive calculation called <code>filtered_penguins</code>:</p> <pre><code>```{python} @reactive.calc def filtered_penguins(): data = penguins[penguins["species"].isin(input.species())] data = data[data["island"].isin(input.islands())] return data ```</code></pre> <p>To read the value of a reactive calc, call it like a function. For example, the <code>depth</code> plot looks like this:</p> <pre><code>```{python} @render.plot def depth(): return sns.displot( filtered_penguins(), x = "bill_depth_mm", hue = "species", kind = input.dist(), fill = True, rug=input.rug() ) ```</code></pre> <p>Note the <code>filtered_penguins()</code> call. To reiterate, this call does not necessarily cause the <code>filtered_penguins</code> function to run. Instead, it usually returns the cached value of the function, which is automatically updated whenever the inputs it refers to change. And because the <code>depth</code> plot refers to the <code>filtered_penguins</code> calculation, it will be re-rendered whenever those inputs change.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-5">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about Shiny for Python interactive documents see the following articles:</p> <p><a href="https://jcheng.shinyapps.io/shiny-component-browser/#outputs">Component Browser</a> enumerates the available Shiny inputs and outputs, along with code snippets you can copy and paste into your dashboard.</p> <p>Input Layout describes various ways to layout Shiny inputs (sidebars, input panels, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</p> <p>Running Dashboards covers in more depth how to run Shiny dashboards both within VS Code, Positron, and at the command line, as well as how to deploy them to end users.</p> <p>Execution Contexts goes in depth on when different code cells run (e.g. rendering vs. serving).</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/">Shiny for Python</a> provides in-depth documentation on all of the available UI and ouput widgets, as well as conceptual discussions on how things work.</p> <h3 id="dashboards-with-shiny-for-r">Dashboards with Shiny for R</h3> <h4 id="dashboards-with-shiny-for-r-1">Dashboards with Shiny for R</h4> <h5 id="introduction-2">Introduction</h5> <p>The <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/shiny-basics/lesson1/index.html">Shiny</a> package provides an easy way to build web applications with R. Quarto dashboards can include embedded Shiny components (e.g. a plot with sliders that control its inputs).</p> <p>This section covers integrating Shiny with Quarto and assumes that you already have basic familiarity with Shiny. To learn more about Shiny please visit <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/shiny-basics/lesson1/index.html">shiny.posit.co</a>. If you are using Python rather than R, see the documentation on using Shiny for Python.</p> <h5 id="walkthrough-1">Walkthrough</h5> <p>Here we’ll explore an in-depth example that covers many of the techniques you’ll use when creating dashboards with Shiny, including factoring out setup code, reactive calculations, and more advanced layout constructs like sidebars and tabsets. Here is the interactive document we’ll be building:</p> <p>Here is the source code for this dashboard (click on the numbers on the far right for additional explanation of syntax and mechanics):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Diamonds Explorer" author: "Barkamian Analytics" format: dashboard server: shiny --- ```{r} #| context: setup library(ggplot2) dataset <- diamonds ``` # {.sidebar} ```{r} sliderInput('sampleSize', 'Sample Size', min=1, max=nrow(dataset), value=min(1000, nrow(dataset)), step=500, round=0) br() checkboxInput('jitter', 'Jitter') checkboxInput('smooth', 'Smooth') ``` ```{r} selectInput('x', 'X', names(dataset)) selectInput('y', 'Y', names(dataset), names(dataset)[[2]]) selectInput('color', 'Color', c('None', names(dataset))) ``` ```{r} selectInput('facet_row', 'Facet Row', c(None='.', names(diamonds[sapply(diamonds, is.factor)]))) selectInput('facet_col', 'Facet Column', c(None='.', names(diamonds[sapply(diamonds, is.factor)]))) ``` # Plot ```{r} plotOutput('plot') ``` # Data ```{r} tableOutput('data') ``` ```{r} #| context: server dataset <- reactive({ diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), input$sampleSize),] }) output$plot <- renderPlot({ p <- ggplot( dataset(), aes_string(x=input$x, y=input$y)) + geom_point() if (input$color != 'None') p <- p + aes_string(color=input$color) facets <- paste(input$facet_row, '~', input$facet_col) if (facets != '. ~ .') p <- p + facet_grid(facets) if (input$jitter) p <- p + geom_jitter() if (input$smooth) p <- p + geom_smooth() p }) output$data <- renderTable({ dataset() }) ```</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>The <code>server: shiny</code> option instructs Quarto to run a Shiny Server behind the document.</p> <p>2</p> <p>The <code>context: setup</code> cell option indicates that this code cell should run when the application starts (as opposed to when each new client session starts). Expensive initialization code (e.g. loading data) should be placed in <code>context: setup</code>.</p> <p>3</p> <p>Create global sidebars by adding the <code>.sidebar</code> class to level 1 headings. Sidebars can include code cells as well as images, narrative, and links.</p> <p>4</p> <p>These select inputs have their contents dynamically driven from the available columns in the dataset.</p> <p>5</p> <p>Level 1 headings (here <code># Plots</code> and <code># Data</code>) create pages within the dashboard.</p> <p>6</p> <p>Include server code (reactives that compute values or render output) in a cell with <code>context: server</code>.</p> <p>7</p> <p>The <code>dataset()</code> reactive will be called to re-sample the dataset every time the sample size changes.</p> <p>8</p> <p>The <code>renderPlot()</code> function regenerates the plot whenever the <code>dataset()</code> reactive or another input option changes.</p> <p>9</p> <p>The <code>renderTable()</code> function regenerates the table whenever the <code>dataset()</code> reactive changes.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-6">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about Shiny for R interactive documents see the following articles:</p> <p>Input Layout describes various ways to layout Shiny inputs (sidebars, input panels, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</p> <p>Running Documents covers how to run interactive documents both within RStudio and at the command line, as well as how to deploy them to end users.</p> <p>Execution Contexts goes in depth on when different code blocks (e.g. rendering vs. serving) run as well as how to cache expensive computations for more responsive documents.</p> <p>External Resources describes how to make sure that Shiny can locate resources (e.g. CSS, JS, images, etc.) that you include in your document.</p> <h3 id="execution-contexts-dashboards">Execution Contexts (Dashboards)</h3> <h4 id="execution-contexts">Execution Contexts</h4> <h5 id="overview-42">Overview</h5> <p>Shiny interactive documents contain both code that executes at render time as well as code that executes on the server in response to user actions and changes in input values. A solid understanding of these execution contexts is important both to have the right mental model during development as well as to optimize the performance of your document.</p> <h5 id="default-execution">Default Execution</h5> <p>By default, all of the Python code in your document is executed at two different times:</p> <ul> <li>When you render the document using <code>quarto render</code> or <code>quarto preview</code>; and</li> <li>Whenever a new user connects to the Shiny application generated from the document. If the render time of your document is short, this default execution pattern will likely serve you well and you don’t need to think further about optimizing execution contexts.</li> </ul> <h5 id="setup-context">Setup Context</h5> <p>Many documents include setup code that loads required packages and data. If this setup code takes longer than a couple of seconds, it may make sense to explicitly designate it as setup code using the <code>context: setup</code> cell option. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| context: setup import seaborn as sns penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins") ```</code></pre> <p>When you add <code>context: setup</code> to a cell, the code cell will be executed:</p> <ul> <li>When you render the document using <code>quarto render</code> or <code>quarto preview</code>; and</li> <li>At the startup of the Shiny application (this is in contrast to the default behavior which is to run the code whenever a new user connects to the application). Explicitly designating setup code using <code>context: setup</code> is likely the only thing you’ll need to do in terms of explicitly specifying execution contexts. Not only does <code>context: setup</code> address the most common performance issues, it also preserves simple and easy to reason about source code (all data and functions in the document are available at both render and serve time).</li> </ul> <h5 id="ui-context">UI Context</h5> <p>It’s possible that you have cells in your document that only contribute to the user interface and does not need to execute on the server. For example, this could be a static visualization that is never dynamically redrawn in response to changes in inputs.</p> <p>To designate a call as only contributing to the user interface, specify the <code>context: ui</code> cell option. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| context: ui # plot that isn't ever updated after initial rendering sns.lmplot( data=penguins, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species", height=5 ) ```</code></pre> <p>Cells with <code>context: ui</code> will only run during <code>quarto render</code>. Code and data created by this cell are not available when the application is served.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-7">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about Shiny for Python interactive documents see the following articles:</p> <ul> <li>Getting Started explains the basics of Shiny interactive documents.</li> <li><a href="https://jcheng.shinyapps.io/shiny-component-browser/#outputs">Component Browser</a> enumerates the available Shiny inputs and outputs, along with code snippets you can copy and paste into your dashboard.</li> <li>Input Layout describes various ways to layout inputs (sidebars, input panels, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.).</li> <li>Running Dashboards covers how to run interactive dashboards both within VS Code, Positron, and at the command line, as well as how to deploy them to end users.</li> <li><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/">Shiny for Python</a> provides in-depth documentation on all of the available UI and ouput widgets, as well as conceptual discussions on how things work.</li> </ul> <h3 id="interactive-dashboards">Interactive Dashboards</h3> <h4 id="interactive-dashboards-1">Interactive Dashboards</h4> <h5 id="overview-43">Overview</h5> <p>Adding interactivity to a dashboard helps users explore the concepts and data you are presenting more deeply. There are several ways to add interactive components to Quarto dashboards:</p> <ul> <li>Shiny for Python for dashboards that use Jupyter for computations (requires a server component for deployment).</li> <li>Shiny for R for dashboards that use Knitr for computations (requires a server component for deployment).</li> <li>Observable JS for client-side interactivity using the Observable dialect of JavaScript.</li> <li>Jupyter Widgets or htmlwidgets for client-side interactivity based on standard Python and R JavaScript widget frameworks. Using Shiny-based interactivity is generally much more flexible and capable than client-only interactivity, however requires a server for deployment.</li> </ul> <h5 id="input-layout">Input Layout</h5> <p>No matter which type of interactivity you choose, you’ll want to present user inputs in a clear, accessible fashion. While you can locate inputs anywhere within a dashboard, there are some special containers that are tuned for this purpose:</p> <ul> <li>Sidebars provide a collapsible, full height panel for inputs.</li> <li>Toolbars provide a full page width horizontal panel for inputs.</li> <li>Card Inputs are directly embedded in the cards either as a card toolbar or as a card sidebar. The article on Inputs covers these methods in depth along with tips on doing more sophisticated layout of groups of inputs.</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-dashboards">Quarto Dashboards</h3> <h4 id="quarto-dashboards-1">Quarto Dashboards</h4> <h5 id="overview-44">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto Dashboards make it easy to create interactive dashboards using Python, R, Julia, and Observable:</p> <ul> <li>Publish a group of related data visualizations as a dashboard. Use a wide variety of components including <a href="https://plotly.com/python/">Plotly</a>, <a href="https://ipyleaflet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Leaflet</a>, Jupyter Widgets, <a href="https://www.htmlwidgets.org/">htmlwidgets</a>; static graphics (Matplotlib, Seaborn, ggplot2, etc.); tabular data; value boxes; and text annotations.</li> <li>Flexible and easy to specify row and column-based Layouts. Components are intelligently re-sized to fill the browser and adapted for display on mobile devices.</li> <li>Author using any notebook editor (JupyterLab, etc.) or in plain text markdown with any text editor (VS Code, Positron, RStudio, Neovim, etc.)</li> <li>Dashboards can be deployed as static web pages (no special server required) or you can optionally integrate a backend Shiny Server for enhanced interactivity.</li> </ul> <h5 id="examples-19">Examples</h5> <p>You can create highly customized layouts and use a wide variety of dashboard themes as illustrated in these examples (click to see them in more detail):</p> <p>For live versions of these dashboards, source code, and additional examples see the dashboard section of the gallery.</p> <h5 id="walkthrough-2">Walkthrough</h5> <p>Here we’ll walk through a simple example to illustrate the basics. Then, we’ll provide detailed instructions on how to get started with building your own dashboards.</p> <p>This simple single-page Python dashboard uses interactive Plotly visualizations to explore development indicators in the <a href="http://www.gapminder.org/data/">Gapminder</a> dataset. The dashboard includes two rows, the second of which includes two columns:</p> <p>Dashboards consist of several components:</p> <ul> <li>Navigation Bar — Icon, title, and author along with links to sub-pages (if more than one page is defined).</li> <li>Pages, Rows, Columns, and Tabsets — Pages, rows and columns are defined using markdown headings (with optional attributes to control height, width, etc.). Tabsets can be used to further divide content within a row or column.</li> <li>Cards, Sidebars, and Toolbars — Cards are containers for plots, data display, and free form content. The content of cards typically maps to cells in your notebook or source document. Sidebars and toolbars are used to present inputs within interactive dashboards. Dashboards can be created either using Jupyter notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) or using plain text markdown (<code>.qmd</code>). Here is the code for the notebook version of the above example (click the image for a zoomed view):</li> </ul> <p>Here is the plain text <code>.qmd</code> version of the dashboard (click on the numbers on the far right for additional explanation of syntax and mechanics):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Development Indicators by Continent" author: "Gapminder Analytics Group" format: dashboard --- ```{python} import plotly.express as px df = px.data.gapminder() ``` ## Row {height=60%} ```{python} #| title: GDP and Life Expectancy px.scatter( df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", animation_frame="year", animation_group="country", size="pop", color="continent", hover_name="country", facet_col="continent", log_x=True, size_max=45, range_x=[100,100000], range_y=[25,90] ) ``` ## Row {height=40%} ```{python} #| title: Population px.area( df, x="year", y="pop", color="continent", line_group="country" ) ``` ```{python} #| title: Life Expectancy px.line( df, x="year", y="lifeExp", color="continent", line_group="country" ) ```</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>The document options define the <code>title</code> and <code>author</code> for the navigation bar as well as specifying the use of the <code>dashboard</code> format.</p> <p>2</p> <p>Rows and columns are defined using headings. In this example we define two rows and specify their relative sizes using the <code>height</code> option.</p> <p>3</p> <p>Computational cells become cards that live within rows or columns. Cards can have an optional title (which here we specify using the <code>title</code> option).</p> <p>4</p> <p>The second row includes two computational cells, which are automatically split into two side by side cards.</p> <h5 id="getting-started">Getting Started</h5> <h6 id="step-1-install-quarto">Step 1: Install Quarto</h6> <p>Dashboards are a feature in the Quarto v1.4. Before you get started, make sure you install the latest release version of Quarto.</p> <p><a href="_">_</a> Find your operating system in the table below</p> <h6 id="highlights">Highlights</h6> <p>Quarto 1.10 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li><p>New <code>quarto.language</code> Pandoc template-variable namespace, exposing Quarto’s resolved localized strings to custom templates and template partials:</p> <p><span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>c</em><em>r</em><em>o</em><em>s</em><em>s</em><em>r</em><em>e</em><em>f</em> − <em>f</em><em>i</em><em>g</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em></span> <span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>t</em><em>o</em><em>c</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em> − <em>d</em><em>o</em><em>c</em><em>u</em><em>m</em><em>e</em><em>n</em><em>t</em></span></p></li> </ul> <h6 id="release-notes">Release Notes</h6> <p>You can find release notes and installers for all platforms in the download page.</p> <h6 id="step-2-learn-the-basics">Step 2: Learn the Basics</h6> <p>Start by learning how to lay out your dashboard and populate it with content:</p> <p>Dashboard Layout shows you how to control the navigation bar, and how to arrange your content across pages, rows, columns, tabsets, and cards.</p> <p>Data Display shows you how to display data in your dashboard as plots, tables, value boxes, and text.</p> <h6 id="step-3-explore-further">Step 3: Explore Further</h6> <p>Once you’ve mastered the basics, check out these additional articles to learn more.</p> <p>Examples provides a gallery of example dashboards you can use as inspiration for your own.</p> <p>Inputs demonstrates various ways to layout inputs for interactive dashboards (sidebars, toolbars, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</p> <p>Theming describes the various way to customize the fonts, colors, layout and other aspects of dashboard appearance.</p> <p>Parameters explains how to create dashboard variants by defining parameters and providing distinct values for them on the command line.</p> <p>Deployment covers how to deploy both static dashboards (which require only a web host, but not a server) and Shiny dashboards (which require a Shiny Server).</p> <p>Interactivity explores the various ways to create interactive dashboards that enable more flexible data exploration.</p> <h5 id="external-servers">External servers</h5> <p>Quarto is designed to minimize external dependencies. However, on occasion, Quarto documents might need resources hosted in external servers. See our page on External Sources for a full list.</p> <h3 id="running-dashboards">Running Dashboards</h3> <h4 id="running-dashboards-1">Running Dashboards</h4> <h5 id="overview-45">Overview</h5> <p>There are a number of ways to run Shiny for Python interactive documents:</p> <ul> <li>Use the Quarto: Preview command within VS Code or Positron.</li> <li>Use the <code>quarto preview</code> command line interface with any editor.</li> <li>Deploy them to a server for use by a wider audience. We’ll cover all of these scenarios in depth here.</li> </ul> <p>NoteShiny Prerequisites</p> <p>In order to use Shiny within Quarto documents you will need the latest version of the <code>shiny</code> (>=0.9.0) and <code>shinywidgets</code> (>=0.3.1) packages. You can install the latest version of these with:</p> <pre><code>pip install --upgrade shiny shinywidgets</code></pre> <h5 id="vs-code-and-positron">VS Code and Positron</h5> <p>The Quarto Extension for VS Code and Positron (available on both <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">OpenVSX</a> and <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Microsoft’s marketplace</a>) provides integrated support for previewing Shiny interactive documents (just use the Quarto: Preview command as you normally would with a static document):</p> <h5 id="command-line-2">Command Line</h5> <p>If you are using another notebook or text editor, you can also preview Shiny interactive documents from the command line via <code>quarto preview</code>. This works the same for notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) and plain text markdown (<code>.qmd</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview example.ipynb quarto preview example.qmd</code></pre> <p>There are a number of options to the <code>preview</code> command to control the port and host of the document server as well as whether a browser is automatically opened for the running document. You can learn more about these options with <code>quarto preview help</code>.</p> <p>If you want to serve your document without the features of <code>quarto preview</code> (i.e. automatic re-rendering when the document changes) you can use the <code>quarto serve</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto serve example.qmd</code></pre> <h5 id="deployment">Deployment</h5> <p>Shiny interactive documents are normal Shiny applications that are created using <code>quarto render</code>. In fact, you don’t need Quarto at all to serve interactive documents, rather, you can just <code>shiny run</code> the application generated by <code>quarto render</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render example.qmd shiny run app.py</code></pre> <p>Your deployed application will consist of both the HTML document and <code>app.py</code> script generated by <code>quarto render</code>:</p> <pre><code>example.html example_files/ app.py</code></pre> <p>See the following documentation for information on deploying Shiny applications in various environments:</p> <p>Destination</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://docs.posit.co/shinyapps.io/getting-started.html#working-with-shiny-for-python">shinyapps.io</a></p> <p>Cloud hosting service</p> <p><a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-sdks-docker-shiny#shiny-for-python">Hugging Face</a></p> <p>Cloud hosting service</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#deploy-to-shiny-server-open-source">Shiny Server</a></p> <p>Open source application server</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#deploy-to-posit-connect-commercial">Posit Connect</a></p> <p>Commerical publishing platform</p> <p><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/deploy.html#other-hosting-options">Other Services</a></p> <p>Custom server/hosting environment</p> <p>You can also deploy interactive Shiny documents in a serverless configuration (where Python runs in the browser via <a href="https://pyodide.org/">Pyodide</a>). The <a href="https://github.com/wch/retirement-simulation-dashboard">Retirement Simulation</a> is an example that demonstrates this workflow.</p> <h5 id="debugging">Debugging</h5> <p>You can run an interactive debugging session for Shiny documents by debugging the generated <code>.py</code> application file (e.g. <code>hello-app.py</code>). Use the Debug Shiny App menu command at the top right of the editor to launch a debugging session:</p> <p>CautionImportant Note</p> <p>The file you are debugging (e.g. <code>hello-app.py</code>) is generated from your interactive document. You should therefore not edit this file directly (as it will be overwritten on the next render) but rather the source document from which it is generated (e.g. <code>hello.qmd</code>).</p> <h5 id="learning-more-8">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about Shiny for Python interactive documents see the following articles:</p> <ul> <li>Getting Started explains the basics of Shiny interactive documents.</li> <li><a href="https://jcheng.shinyapps.io/shiny-component-browser/#outputs">Component Browser</a> enumerates the available Shiny inputs and outputs, along with code snippets you can copy and paste into your dashboard.</li> <li>Input Layout describes various ways to layout Shiny inputs (sidebars, input panels, attaching inputs directly to cards, etc.)</li> <li>Execution Contexts goes in depth on when different code cells run (e.g. rendering vs. serving).</li> <li><a href="https://shiny.posit.co/py/">Shiny for Python</a> provides in-depth documentation on all of the available UI and ouput widgets, as well as conceptual discussions on how things work.</li> </ul> <h2 id="downloading-quarto">Downloading Quarto</h2> <h3 id="release-notes-1">1.1 Release Notes</h3> <h4 id="release-notes-2">1.1 Release Notes</h4> <h5 id="jupyter-3">Jupyter</h5> <ul> <li>Daemonize jupyter notebooks referenced within listings (e.g. in a blog)</li> <li>Refine over-detection of Jupyter within IDEs)</li> <li>Fix tinytex failure to install packages caused by invalid installation of tinytex on MacOS</li> </ul> <h5 id="jupyter-4">Jupyter</h5> <ul> <li>Always ignore .ipynb inputs when classic</li> <li>Prevent overwrite of source .ipynb when output format is ipynb</li> <li>Prefer kernel declared in YAML front matter when executing notebooks</li> <li>Fix v1.1 regression in handling of cell display_data w/ Juptyer widgets</li> <li>Allow jupyter kernel to be determined project-wide (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2853">#2853</a>)</li> <li>Ensure that Jupyter engine dependencies (widgets) appear after other dependencies (manage require/define conflicts)</li> </ul> <h5 id="knitr-5">Knitr</h5> <ul> <li>Support specification of <code>connection</code> option in cell yaml options.</li> </ul> <h5 id="ojs-2">OJS</h5> <ul> <li>support <code>revealjs</code> and <code>html</code> formats in <code>width</code> builtin, fallback gracefully otherwise (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2058">#2058</a>)</li> <li>Don’t emit <code>ojs_define</code> HTML in non-html formats (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2338">#2338</a>)</li> <li>Support jszip and exceljs (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/1981">#1981</a>)</li> <li>Improve error messages when cell options are specified with wrong comment syntax (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/1856">#1856</a>)</li> <li>Hide <code>code-fold</code> chrome when OJS code is hidden (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2134">#2134</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="extensions-1">Extensions</h5> <ul> <li>Preview live reload for changes to extension source files</li> <li>HTML dependencies may be provided by paths to files outside the extension directory</li> <li>HTML dependencies may now include <code>serviceworkers</code>, which are copied into the output directory.</li> <li>New <code>quarto.doc.attach_to_dependency</code> function to attach files to html dependencies (copies files into the lib dir for a named HTML dependency).</li> <li>New <code>quarto.version</code>, which provides the Quarto version</li> <li>New <code>quarto.project.profile</code> which provides the list of currently active profiles (or an empty table if none are active)</li> <li>New <code>quarto.project.directory</code> which provides the current project directory (if a project is active)</li> <li>New <code>quarto.project.output_directory</code> which provides the current project output directory (if a project is active)</li> <li>New <code>quarto.project.offset</code> which provides an offset from the current input document to the project directory.</li> <li>New <code>quarto.doc.input_file</code> which provides the path to the input document</li> <li>New <code>quarto.doc.output_file</code> which provides the path to the output file</li> <li>Ensure that <code>quarto.utils.dump</code> works with pandoc’s builtin global variables (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2254">#2254</a>)</li> <li>Provide a better error message for non-existent format resources (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2291">#2291</a>)</li> <li>Ability to specify a minimum quarto version via the <code>quarto-required</code> option.</li> <li>Extension may now contribute project types (project metadata which will be merged with a project when project of that type are rendered)</li> <li>Include Pandoc <code>logging</code> Lua module from <span class="citation" data-cites="wlupton">@wlupton</span></li> <li>Improve path resolution of extensions</li> <li>Add support for extensions that contribute revealjs-plugins</li> <li>Fix issue loading extensions when the organization name is the same as the extension identifier</li> <li>Fix issue preventing installation of archived extensions from an arbitrary url (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2419">#2419</a>)</li> <li>Support installation of extensions using Github archive urls</li> <li>Support installation of extensions from with subdirectories of a github repo</li> <li>Lua <code>require</code> can now find modules adjacent to the current script</li> <li>Use snake case for Quarto Lua API functions (match Pandoc API)</li> <li>Fix theorem captions when there’s no text (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2166">#2166</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2228">#2228</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="projects-1">Projects</h5> <ul> <li>Project configuration <code>profile</code> for varying configuration and output based on global <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> or <code>--profile</code> command-line option.</li> <li>Project level environment variables (including local overrides)</li> <li>Ensure that <code>execute-dir</code> is always resolved to an absolute path</li> </ul> <h5 id="html-format-1">HTML Format</h5> <ul> <li>Fix error when restoring preserved HTML in output files that use <code>output-file</code></li> <li>Properly maintain dark/light state when navigating between pages</li> <li>Fix <code>code-copy</code> button issue when <code>page-layout</code> is full with no visible <code>toc</code> (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2388">#2388</a>)</li> <li>Add support for scss variables to better control the table of contents appearance (<code>\$toc-color</code>,<code>\$toc-font-size</code>,<code>\$toc-active-border</code>,<code>\$toc-inactive-border</code>)</li> <li>Provide more explicit code-copy feedback using a tooltip</li> <li>Improve coloring of code copy button when using various <code>highlight-styles</code>.</li> <li>Support scss variables to customize the code copy button using <code>\$btn-code-copy-color</code>, <code>\$btn-code-copy-color-active</code></li> <li>Add support for <code>date-modified</code> in document metadata</li> <li>Wrap inline code elements if necessary</li> </ul> <h5 id="pdf-format-1">PDF Format</h5> <ul> <li>Provide a better error message for PDF output that produces an empty document</li> <li>Improved detection of LaTeX caption regions (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2295">#2295</a>)</li> <li>Handle LaTeX error messages with no file output more gracefully (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2183">#2183</a>)</li> <li>Support cross reference-able figures with callouts</li> <li>Allow cross references inside of a callout</li> <li>Improve margin layout support for <code>twoside</code>, <code>oneside</code>, and <code>twoside=semi</code> options of <code>scrbook</code></li> <li>Properly default <code>number-sections</code> on when the documentclass is <code>scrbook</code></li> </ul> <h5 id="docx-format-1">Docx Format</h5> <ul> <li>Properly scale callout icons using DPI</li> <li>Properly space a consecutive table and figure (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2493">#2493</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="revealjs-format-1">Revealjs Format</h5> <ul> <li>Update to Reveal v4.3.1 (+ commit e281b32) to fix presentation scaling/zoom issues.</li> <li>Improved title slide that uses normalized author and affiliation schema</li> <li>Introduce template partials for RevealJS. You may provide partials for <code>title-slide.html</code> or <code>toc-slide.html</code>.</li> <li>Ensure that <code>output-location</code> works properly in fenced divs</li> <li>Change SCSS so styles respond to both linkColor and link-color (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2820">#2820</a>)</li> <li>When mermaidjs diagrams exist, set viewdistance to cover entire slideshow (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2607">#2607</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="markdown-formats">Markdown Formats</h5> <ul> <li>Support code folding for markdown output when <code>raw_html</code> is supported.</li> <li><code>docusaurus-md</code> format for Docusaurus compatible markdown</li> <li><code>docusaurus</code> and <code>hugo</code> project types for render/preview within external static site generators</li> </ul> <h5 id="ipynb-format">Ipynb Format</h5> <ul> <li>Strip attributes from images when converting to <code>ipynb</code> (leaving the attributes caused problems w/ attachments in VS Code)</li> </ul> <h5 id="ast-formats">AST Formats</h5> <ul> <li>Remove intermediate metadata for AST formats (<code>native</code> and <code>json</code>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="google-scholar-1">Google Scholar</h5> <ul> <li>Properly read Google Scholar reference data from dynamically generated bibliography YML</li> </ul> <h5 id="crossrefs-1">Crossrefs</h5> <ul> <li>Fix problem with crossref indexing for listing code blocks</li> </ul> <h5 id="tables-7">Tables</h5> <ul> <li>Don’t require array brackets for <code>tbl-colwidths</code> specification</li> <li>Override standard GT style in multiple-column spanners (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/3038">#3038</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="authors-and-affiliations">Authors and Affiliations</h5> <ul> <li>Improve handling of empty authors</li> <li>Parse <code>author</code> and <code>institute</code> (often used for RevealJs and Beamer) into normalized author schema</li> </ul> <h5 id="websites-1">Websites</h5> <ul> <li>Properly allow <code>twitter-card</code> and <code>open-graph</code> to override the page description.</li> <li>Don’t discover resources within a site or book output directory</li> <li>Enable use of custom HTML formats for websites</li> <li>Automatically populate sidebar menu using <code>auto</code> option for contents</li> <li>Properly handle <code>margin-header</code> and <code>margin-footer</code> files</li> <li>Ensure that the <code>code-copy</code> button is functional even when margin content is present.</li> <li>Add support for open graph image sizes</li> <li>Fix issue preventing <code>twitter-card</code> <code>site</code> metadata from being emitted.</li> <li>Prevent website content from shifting when page first loads</li> <li>Improve animation smoothness when expanding navbar in mobile mode (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/1873">#1873</a>)</li> <li>Permit icons in top level navbar, if specified</li> <li>Fix incorrect computation of the next and previous buttons after the first separator</li> </ul> <h5 id="books-2">Books</h5> <ul> <li>Fix issue that caused incomplete search indexes for books</li> <li>Don’t display the book description in each chapter’s title block</li> <li>Book YAML now accepts fields from csl-item schema (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2148">#2148</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2398">#2398</a>)</li> <li>Book YAML now accepts date-format explicitly (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2148">#2148</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2398">#2398</a>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="preview-3">Preview</h5> <ul> <li>Restart Jupyter kernel daemon if preview server is restarted.</li> <li>Enable use of external preview servers for serving project output</li> <li>Add <code>--no-serve</code> command line parameter to prevent serving altogether</li> <li>Do not add trailing slash to VSCODE_PROXY_URI set by code-server</li> </ul> <h5 id="publishing-2">Publishing</h5> <ul> <li>Handle CNAME file for <code>gh-pages</code> either without or without protocol prefix (e.g. https://)</li> </ul> <h5 id="languages">Languages</h5> <ul> <li>Italian translation for Quarto UI text</li> <li>Polish translation for Quarto UI text</li> <li>Korean translation for Quarto UI text</li> </ul> <h5 id="listing-and-feeds">Listing and Feeds</h5> <ul> <li>Fix escaping issue in RSS feed fields</li> <li>Properly support <code>max-desc-length</code> to trim descriptions within listings</li> <li>Properly support exclude globs (like <code>!blog/index.qmd</code>) when resolve listing contents</li> </ul> <h5 id="bibliographies-and-citations">Bibliographies and Citations</h5> <ul> <li>Support formats <code>bibtex</code>, <code>biblatex</code>, and <code>csljson</code>. When rendered to one of these formats any citations within the document will be rendered as the specified bibliography format.</li> <li>Always add citeproc filter if <code>citeproc: true</code> is specified, even if there isn’t a bibliography or references in the document (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2294">#2294</a>)</li> <li>Don’t process citations twice when <code>citeproc</code> is specified (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2393">#2393</a>)</li> <li>Fix <code>citation-hover</code> for footnote style reference formats</li> </ul> <h5 id="tinytex">TinyTex</h5> <ul> <li><code>quarto install tinytex</code> will now install TinyTex even if a system installation of TeX is detected.</li> <li><code>quarto install tinytex</code> will no longer add TinyTex to the system path by default.</li> <li>When rendering PDFs, Quarto will prefer an existing installation of TinyTex over a system Tex installation</li> <li>To prevent Quarto from using an installation of TinyTex (if you’d prefer the system installation be used), set <code>latex-tinytex: false</code> in your project or document front matter.</li> <li>To install TinyTex system wide, using the <code>--update-path</code> flag when installing (this will add TinyTex to the system path)</li> </ul> <h5 id="video-shortcode">Video Shortcode</h5> <ul> <li>The video shortcode extension is now native to the Quarto CLI</li> <li>Reveal-JS Video Snippet backgrounds are now better supported. For common video snippets, like YouTube, you can specify them as <code>background-video</code> and quarto will ensure the correct embed URL is used and swap to <code>background-iframe</code> background if needed.</li> </ul> <h5 id="creating-artifacts">Creating Artifacts</h5> <ul> <li>Introduce a new <code>quarto create</code> command which will create projects or extensions</li> </ul> <h5 id="miscellaneous-1">Miscellaneous</h5> <ul> <li>Render: ability to set <code>enigne</code> and <code>jupyter</code> metadata values from the command line</li> <li>Render: ability to compose <code>--to all</code> with other formats (e.g. <code>--to all,json</code>)</li> <li>Don’t call Deno.realPathSync on Windows (avoid problems w/ UNC paths)</li> <li>Don’t include Unicode literals on messages on values of type object (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2191">#2191</a>)</li> <li>Upgrade esbuild to 0.15.6</li> <li>Implement –help option for quarto preview and quarto run</li> <li>Increase contrast for a11y-light theme to work with default code-block background (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2067">#2067</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2320">#2320</a>)</li> <li>New metadata field <code>quarto-required</code> to specify required versions of quarto in a document</li> <li>Provide href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2349">#2349</a>)</li> <li>Don’t use default width/height on mermaid diagrams when better information is available (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2434">#2434</a>)</li> <li>Forward <code>--log-level</code> to Pandoc via <code>--trace</code>, <code>--verbose</code>, and (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2499">#2499</a>)</li> <li>Only pass <code>pagetitle</code> metadata for HTML file output</li> <li>Provide non-HTML treatment for code block <code>filename</code></li> <li>prevent Chrome CRI race during initialization (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/2733">#2733</a>)</li> <li>Work around <code>mermaid-format: svg</code> diagram clipping (<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/1622">#1622</a>)</li> <li>Don’t use tree-sitter outside of interactive IDE contexts (<a
