second parameter, default <code>light</code>.</li> </ul> <h6 id="conditional-content-3">Conditional Content</h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12462">#4411</a>): Added support for new format and aliases in <code>when-format</code> and <code>unless-format</code>: <code>confluence</code>, <code>docusaurus</code> (and <code>docusaurus-md</code>), <code>email</code>, <code>dashboard</code>, <code>gfm</code>, <code>hugo</code> (and <code>hugo-md</code>).</li> </ul> <h6 id="quarto-lua-api">Quarto Lua API</h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12462">#4411</a>): <code>quarto.format.is_format</code> is now working as expected with support of more aliases: <code>confluence</code>, <code>docusaurus</code> (and <code>docusaurus-md</code>), <code>email</code>, <code>dashboard</code>, <code>gfm</code>, <code>hugo</code> (and <code>hugo-md</code>)</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12299">#12299</a>): <code>quarto.doc.pdf_engine()</code> now correctly returns the PDF engine used for the document. <code>quarto.doc.cite_method()</code> now returns <code>nil</code> if no citation method will be used (i.e. no references is the document set).</li> </ul> <h5 id="languages-4">Languages</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12366">#12366</a>): Added Bulgarian translation for Quarto UI text (credit: <span class="citation" data-cites="sakelariev">@sakelariev</span>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="quarto-publish"><code>quarto publish</code></h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/9929">#9929</a>): <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> will now clean previous worktree directory leftover from previous deploys.</li> </ul> <h5 id="other-fixes-and-improvements-3">Other Fixes and Improvements</h5> <ul> <li>A new folder <code>quarto-session-temp</code> can be created in <code>.quarto</code> to store temporary files created by Quarto during a rendering. Reminder: <code>.quarto</code> is for internal use of Quarto and should not be versioned (thus added to <code>.gitignore</code>).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/commit/fb38eb56c11e09f44cef58fd3b697ff24bb5a3f3">fb38eb5</a>) Use the <code>latest</code> parser for Acorn when analyzing JS code imported from OJS blocks.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/7260">#7260</a>): Add support for <code>active</code> class in tabsets so the <code>.active</code> tab shows up by default.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/7757">#7757</a>): Session temporary files are now cleaned up when the session ends abnormally (e.g. <code>Ctrl+C</code>) also on Windows.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/8613">#8613</a>): Fix <code>giscus</code> color on load to support dark mode (by <span class="citation" data-cites="kv9898">@kv9898</span>).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/9867">#9867</a>): Blank lines are now trimmed in Raw HTML Table blocks.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/10532">#10532</a>): Changed default of <code>--headless=old</code> to <code>--headless</code> as <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/removing-headless-old-from-chrome">Chrome 132 has removed old headless mode</a> and only support new mode. To use old mode, set <code>QUARTO_CHROMIUM</code> to a <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-headless-shell">new <code>chrome-headless-shell</code> binary</a> or to an older chrome version (between 128 and 132). Set <code>QUARTO_CHROMIUM_HEADLESS_MODE</code> to <code>old</code> to use old headless mode with that compatible version.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/10961">#10961</a>): Add more information on which Chrome Headless will be used in <code>quarto check install</code>. This is helpful to help debug mermaid issues.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11441">#11441</a>): Don’t add newlines around shortcodes during processing.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/11606">#11606</a>): Added a new <code>QUARTO_DOCUMENT_FILE</code> env var available to computation engine to the name of the file currently being rendered.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11643">#11643</a>): Improve highlighting of nested code block inside markdown code block, i.e. using ```<code>{python}</code> or ```<code>python</code> inside ````<code>markdown</code> fenced code block.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11788">#11788</a>): <code>quarto add</code> and <code>quarto remove</code> will return non-zero code when they fail.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/11803">#11803</a>): Added a new CLI command <code>quarto call</code>. First users of this interface are the new <code>quarto call engine julia ...</code> subcommands.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11951">#11951</a>): Raw LaTeX table without <code>tbl-</code> prefix label for using Quarto crossref are now correctly passed through unmodified.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11967">#11967</a>): Produce a better error message when YAML metadata with <code>!expr</code> tags are used outside of <code>knitr</code> code cells.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12117">#12117</a>): Color output to stdout and stderr is now correctly rendered for <code>html</code> format in the Jupyter and Julia engines. This change includes support for ANSI color codes in output.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12264">#12264</a>): Upgrade <code>dart-sass</code> to 1.85.1.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12238">#12238</a>): Do not truncate very long console errors (e.g. in Jupyter Notebook with backtrace).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12338">#12338</a>): Add an additional workaround for the SCSS parser used in color variable extraction.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12369">#12369</a>): <code>quarto preview</code> correctly throws a YAML validation error when a <code>format</code> key does not conform.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12459">#12459</a>): Add <code>.page-inset-*</code> classes to completions.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12492">#12492</a>): Improve shortcode extension template with new parameters and a link to docs.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12513">#12513</a>): Fix an issue with <code>quarto preview</code> when using DiagrammeR R package for Graphiz diagram.</li> </ul> <h3 id="release-notes-15">1.8 Release Notes</h3> <h4 id="release-notes-16">1.8 Release Notes</h4> <h4 id="v1.9-backports">v1.9 backports</h4> <h5 id="in-this-release-3">In this release</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13694">#13694</a>): Fix <code>notebook-view.url</code> being ignored - external notebook links now properly use specified URLs instead of local preview files.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13732">#13732</a>): Fix automatic font package installation for fonts with spaces in their names (e.g., “Noto Emoji”, “DejaVu Sans”). Font file search patterns now match both with and without spaces.</li> </ul> <h5 id="in-previous-releases-3">In previous releases</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13369">#13369</a>): Fix failure in theme compilation when <code>brand.color.primary</code> is specified for light or dark but not both.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13383">#13383</a>): Fix failure when combining <code>minimal: true</code> with brand.yml.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13396">#13396</a>): Fix <code>quarto publish connect</code> regression.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13418">#13418</a>): Resolve logo paths specified directly in <code>brand.logo.{size}</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13445">#13445</a>): Brand logo shortcode will not add <code>.light-content</code>, <code>.dark-content</code> classes when <code>light</code> or <code>dark</code> is specifically requested.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13046">#13046</a>): Use new url for multiplex socket.io server <a href="https://multiplex.up.railway.app/">multiplex.up.railway.app</a> as default for <code>format: revealjs</code> and <code>revealjs.multiplex: true</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13506">#13506</a>): Fix navbar active state detection when sidebar has no logo configured. Prevents empty logo links from interfering with navigation highlighting.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13616">#13616</a>): Fix fatal error when rendering manuscript projects with custom blocks like ConditionalBlock.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13625">#13625</a>): Fix Windows file locking error (os error 32) when rendering with <code>--output-dir</code> flag. Context cleanup now happens before removing the temporary <code>.quarto</code> directory, ensuring file handles are properly closed.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13633">#13633</a>): Fix detection and auto-installation of babel language packages from newer error format that doesn’t explicitly mention <code>.ldf</code> filename.</li> </ul> <h4 id="v1.8-changes">v1.8 changes</h4> <h5 id="regression-fixes-1">Regression fixes</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/6607">#6607</a>): Add missing beamer template update for beamer theme options: <code>colorthemeoptions</code>, <code>fontthemeoptions</code>, <code>innerthemeoptions</code> and <code>outerthemeoptions</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12625">#12625</a>): Fire resize event on window when light/dark toggle is clicked, to tell widgets to resize.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12657">#12657</a>): Load Giscus in generated script tag, to avoid wrong-theming in Chrome.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12780">#12780</a>): <code>keep-ipynb: true</code> now works again correctly and intermediate <code>.quarto_ipynb</code> is not removed.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13051">#13051</a>): Fixed support for captioned Markdown table inside Div syntax for crossref. This is special handling, but this could be output by function like <code>knitr::kable()</code> with old option support.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13441">#13441</a>): Catch <code>undefined</code> exceptions in Pandoc failure to avoid spurious error message.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13456">#13456</a>): Ensure that the <code>axe</code> YAML completion only appears in HTML formats.</li> </ul> <h5 id="backwards-compatibility-breaking-changes">Backwards-compatibility breaking changes</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13104">#13104</a>): Remove <code>posit-cloud</code> as <code>quarto publish</code> destination. See <a href="https://docs.posit.co/cloud/whats_new/#october-2024">docs.posit.co</a> for details.</li> </ul> <h5 id="dependencies-2">Dependencies</h5> <ul> <li>Update <code>bootstrap-icons</code> to version v1.13.1 from v1.11.1.</li> </ul> <h5 id="formats-1">Formats</h5> <h6 id="html-1"><code>html</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/678">#678</a>): a11y - Provide appropriate <code>aria-label</code> to search button.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/726">#726</a>): a11y - Provide <code>.screen-reader-only</code> callout type when callout text doesn’t naturally include the type.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/5538">#5538</a>): Fix code-copy button style so that scrolling behaves properly.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/5879">#5879</a>): Improve font rendering of <code>kbd</code> shortcode on macOS. <code>kbd</code> will now also be stricter in converting keyboard shortcuts to macOS icons.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/8568">#8568</a>) Default inline code background color to the code block background color if not specified; foreground color is <code>$pre-color</code> in dark mode and (remains) purple in light mode.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/10983">#10983</a>): Fix spacing inconsistency between paras and first section headings.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11982">#11982</a>): Ensure brand.yml logos are resolved correctly when document is in a subdirectory.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12259">#12259</a>): Fix conflict between <code>html-math-method: katex</code> and crossref popups (author: <span class="citation" data-cites="benkeks">@benkeks</span>).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12341">#12341</a>): Enable light and dark logos for html formats (sidebar, navbar, dashboard).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12501">#12501</a>): Enable <code>source: file</code> for <code>brand.yml</code> fonts in HTML.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12643">#12643</a>): Ensure brand.yml logos using urls are rendered correctly by passing them through when resolving brand <code>processedData</code>, and not processing them as paths.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12734">#12734</a>): <code>highlight-style</code> now correctly supports setting a different <code>light</code> and <code>dark</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12747">#12747</a>): Ensure <code>th</code> elements are properly restored when Quarto’s HTML table processing is happening.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12766">#12766</a>): Use consistent equation numbering display for <code>html-math-method</code> and <code>html-math-method.method</code> for MathJax and KaTeX (author: <span class="citation" data-cites="mcanouil">@mcanouil</span>)</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12797">#12797</a>): Allow light and dark brands to be specified in one file, by specializing colors with <code>light:</code> and <code>dark:</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12919">#12919</a>): Ensure <code>kbd</code> shortcode output has hover tooltip.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12981">#12981</a>): Brand should be applied in dark mode when dark mode is enabled by the theme, not the brand.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13004">#13004</a>): Brand logo shortcode automatically applies <code>.light-content</code> and <code>.dark-content</code> classes, inserts both light and dark logo if brand mode is not specified, and uses alt text from brand logo spec.</li> </ul> <h6 id="revealjs-2"><code>revealjs</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/10933">#10933</a>): Revealjs supports alt text on logo, as well as customization of light and dark logos at the document level, consistent with other formats.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12550">#12550</a>): Revealjs supports <code>brand-mode</code>, allowing to select either the light or the dark brand.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/12598">#12598</a>): Ensure <code>.fragment</code> on an image with caption applies to whole figure.</li> <li>(<a <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13031">#13031</a>): Add <code>.quarto_ipynb</code> files to <code>.gitignore</code> by default.</li> <li>(<a (<span class="citation" data-cites="mcanouil">@mcanouil</span>)</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13121">#13121</a>): Allow <code>contents</code> shortcode to find inline elements.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13216">#13216</a>): Properly disable <code>downlit</code> (<code>code-link</code>) and enable <code>code-annotations</code> when non-R code blocks are present.</li> </ul> <h5 id="quarto-internals">Quarto Internals</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13155">#13155</a>): Process <code>pandoc-reader-FORMAT</code> raw blocks through <code>pandoc.read(FORMAT)</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13255">#13255</a>): Move some Lua code to use Pandoc’s Lua API.</li> </ul> <h3 id="release-notes-17">1.9 Release Notes</h3> <h4 id="release-notes-18">1.9 Release Notes</h4> <h4 id="v1.10-backports">v1.10 backports</h4> <h5 id="in-this-release-4">In this release</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14304">#14304</a>): Fix <code>quarto install tinytex</code> silently ignoring extraction failures. When archive extraction fails (e.g., <code>.tar.xz</code> on a system without <code>xz-utils</code>), the installer now reports a clear error instead of proceeding and failing with a confusing <code>NotFound</code> message.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14367">#14367</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14534">#14534</a>): Fix Dart Sass invocation failing on Windows when the user profile path contains <code>&</code> (e.g., <code>C:\Users\Tom & Jerry\</code>) and on enterprise systems where Group Policy blocks <code>.bat</code> execution from <code>%TEMP%</code>. Quarto now invokes the bundled <code>dart.exe</code> with <code>sass.snapshot</code> directly, bypassing <code>sass.bat</code> and <code>cmd.exe</code> entirely.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14489">#14489</a>): Restore <code>--output-dir</code> support for <code>quarto preview</code> of single files when no <code>_quarto.yml</code> is present (e.g. R-package workspaces). Regression introduced in v1.9.18.</li> </ul> <h5 id="in-previous-releases-4">In previous releases</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14267">#14267</a>): Fix Windows paths with accented characters (e.g., <code>C:\Users\Sébastien\</code>) breaking dart-sass compilation.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14281">#14281</a>): Fix transient <code>.quarto_ipynb</code> files accumulating during <code>quarto preview</code> with Jupyter engine.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14298">#14298</a>): Fix <code>quarto preview</code> browse URL including output filename (e.g., <code>hello.html</code>) for single-file documents, breaking Posit Workbench proxied server access.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/rstudio/rstudio/issues/17333">rstudio/rstudio#17333</a>): Fix <code>quarto inspect</code> on standalone files emitting project metadata that breaks RStudio’s publishing wizard.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/14334">#14334</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/9710">#9710</a>): Add arm64 Linux support for <code>quarto install chrome-headless-shell</code> using Playwright CDN as download source. <code>quarto install chromium</code> and <code>quarto update chromium</code> now show a deprecation warning — use <code>chrome-headless-shell</code> instead, which always installs the latest stable Chrome (the legacy <code>chromium</code> installer pins an outdated Puppeteer revision that cannot receive security updates). <code>quarto check install</code> also warns when legacy Chromium is detected.</li> </ul> <h4 id="v1.9-changes">v1.9 changes</h4> <p>All changes included in 1.9:</p> <h5 id="shortcodes-4">Shortcodes</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13342">#13342</a>): Ensure that the <code>contents</code> shortcode works inside metadata.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13489">#13489</a>): Add <code>mode=plain</code> option to the <code>kbd</code> shortcode to render keyboard shortcuts exactly as written, without OS-specific symbol translation.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14061">#14061</a>): Fix <code>meta</code> shortcode not preserving line breaks in values. The shortcode now respects its usage context (block, inline, or text) and preserves paragraph breaks in block and code block contexts.</li> </ul> <h5 id="regression-fixes-2">Regression fixes</h5> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13396">#13396</a>): Fix <code>quarto publish connect</code> regression.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13441">#13441</a>): Catch <code>undefined</code> exceptions in Pandoc failure to avoid spurious error message.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13046">#13046</a>): Use new url for multiplex socket.io server <a href="https://multiplex.up.railway.app/">multiplex.up.railway.app</a> as default for <code>format: revealjs</code> and <code>revealjs.multiplex: true</code>.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13506">#13506</a>): Fix navbar active state detection when sidebar has no logo configured. Prevents empty logo links from interfering with navigation highlighting.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13616">#13616</a>): Fix fatal error when rendering manuscript projects with custom blocks like ConditionalBlock.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13625">#13625</a>): Fix Windows file locking error (os error 32) when rendering with <code>--output-dir</code> flag. Context cleanup now happens before removing the temporary <code>.quarto</code> directory, ensuring file handles are properly closed.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13633">#13633</a>): Fix detection and auto-installation of babel language packages from newer error format that doesn’t explicitly mention <code>.ldf</code> filename.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13694">#13694</a>): Fix <code>notebook-view.url</code> being ignored - external notebook links now properly use specified URLs instead of local preview files.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13732">#13732</a>): Fix automatic font package installation for fonts with spaces in their names (e.g., “Noto Emoji”, “DejaVu Sans”). Font file search patterns now match both with and without spaces.</li> </ul> <h5 id="dependencies-3">Dependencies</h5> <ul> <li>Update <code>pandoc</code> to 3.8.3 <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13925">#13925</a>): Pandoc 3.8.3 introduces <code>^[text]^</code> as inline footnote syntax. This conflicts with superscript containing a Span at the start (e.g., <code>^[text]{.class}^</code>) since the <code>^[</code> sequence now triggers footnote parsing. A workaround is to insert a zero-width space or other invisible character between <code>^</code> and <code>[</code>.</li> </ul></li> <li>Update <code>typst</code> to 0.14.2</li> <li>Update <code>esbuild</code> to 0.25.10</li> <li>Update <code>deno</code> to 2.4.5</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13601">#13601</a>): Update <code>mermaid</code> to 11.12.0 (author: <span class="citation" data-cites="multimeric">@multimeric</span>)</li> </ul> <h5 id="formats-2">Formats</h5> <h6 id="all-formats">All Formats</h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13878">#13878</a>): Add <code>syntax-highlighting</code> option replacing the deprecated <code>highlight-style</code> in Pandoc 3.8. It supports style names (e.g., <code>tango</code>, <code>github</code>), custom <code>.theme</code> files, <code>none</code> to disable highlighting, or <code>idiomatic</code> for native format highlighting. The <code>highlight-style</code> option remains supported but is deprecated.</li> </ul> <h6 id="gfm"><code>gfm</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13421">#13421</a>): Do not word-wrap titles in header.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13603">#13603</a>): Fix callouts with title but no body content causing fatal error when rendering to GitHub Flavored Markdown.</li> </ul> <h6 id="email"><code>email</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13882">#13882</a>): Add support for multiple email outputs when rendering to <code>format: email</code> for Posit Connect.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14021">#14021</a>): Add <code>email-version</code> hook to override detected Connect version when rendering emails for Posit Connect.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/14098">#14098</a>): Add support for dynamic email recipients computed via Python or R code.</li> </ul> <h6 id="html-2"><code>html</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/14072">#14072</a>): Add q syntax files</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/11929">#11929</a>): Import all <code>brand.typography.fonts</code> in CSS, whether or not fonts are referenced by typography elements.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13413">#13413</a>): Fix uncentered play button in <code>video</code> shortcodes from cross-reference divs. (author: <span class="citation" data-cites="bruvellu">@bruvellu</span>)</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13508">#13508</a>): Add <code>aria-label</code> support to <code>video</code> shortcode for improved accessibility.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13685">#13685</a>): Fix remote font URLs in brand extensions being incorrectly joined with the extension path, resulting in broken font imports.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13825">#13825</a>): Fix <code>column: margin</code> not working with <code>renderings: [light, dark]</code> option. Column classes are now preserved when applying theme classes to cell outputs.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13883">#13883</a>): Fix unequal top/bottom spacing in simple untitled callouts.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13900">#13900</a>): Warn when <code>renderings</code> cell option contains duplicate names. Previously, duplicate names like <code>[dark, light, dark, light]</code> would silently use only the last output for each name.</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/14065">#14065</a>): Fix <code>SCSSParsingError</code> when custom SCSS themes contain non-ASCII characters in selectors (e.g., <code>#présentation</code>).</li> </ul> <h6 id="typst-7"><code>typst</code></h6> <ul> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/12803">#12803</a>): Fix callout text being centered instead of left-aligned when callout has a cross-reference ID prefix (e.g., <code>#tip-abc</code>).</li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/pull/13249">#13249</a>): Update to Pandoc’s Typst template following Pandoc 3.8.3 and Typst 0.14.2 support: <ul> <li>Code syntax highlighting now uses Skylighting by default.</li> <li>New template variables <code>mathfont</code>, <code>codefont</code>, and <code>linestretch</code> for font and line spacing customization.</li> <li>New template variables <code>linkcolor</code>, <code>citecolor</code>, and <code>filecolor</code> for link color customization.</li> <li>New template variable <code>thanks</code> for title footnote acknowledgment.</li> <li>New template variable <code>abstract-title</code> for abstract header customization.</li> <li>PDF accessibility metadata: document title, author, and keywords are now set for PDF readers.</li> <li>Two-column layout now uses <code>set page(columns:)</code> instead of <code>columns()</code> function, fixing compatibility with landscape sections.</li> <li>Title block now properly spans both columns in multi-column layouts.</li> </ul></li> <li>(<a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/13362">#13362</a>): Remove unused <code>blockquote</code> definitions from template.</li> <li>(<a Quarto.</p> <p><a href="_">_</a> Find your operating system in the table below</p> <h5 id="highlights-4">Highlights</h5> <p>Quarto 1.10 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li><p>New <code>quarto.language</code> Pandoc template-variable namespace, exposing Quarto’s resolved localized strings to custom templates and template partials:</p> <p><span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>c</em><em>r</em><em>o</em><em>s</em><em>s</em><em>r</em><em>e</em><em>f</em> − <em>f</em><em>i</em><em>g</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em></span> inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>t</em><em>o</em><em>c</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em> − <em>d</em><em>o</em><em>c</em><em>u</em><em>m</em><em>e</em><em>n</em><em>t</em></span></p></li> </ul> <h5 id="release-notes-22">Release Notes</h5> <h3 id="tarball-installation-on-linux">Tarball Installation On Linux</h3> <h4 id="tarball-installation-on-linux-1">Tarball Installation On Linux</h4> <p><a href="_">_</a> Find your operating system in the table below</p> <p>You can install Quarto for a single user on Linux by using the Quarto tarball and following the below set of steps.</p> <ol type="1"> <li><p>Download the tarball</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>wget <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v%5Eversion%5E/quarto-%5Eversion%5E-linux-amd64.tar.gz">github.com</a></p></li> <li><p>Extract Files</p></li> </ol> <p>Extract the contents of the tarball to the location where you typically install software (e.g. <code>~/opt</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal mkdir ~/opt tar -C ~/opt -xvzf quarto-^version^-linux-amd64.tar.gz</code></pre> <ol start="3" type="1"> <li>Create a Symlink</li> </ol> <p>Create a symlink to <code>bin/quarto</code> in a folder that is in your path. If there is no such folder, you can create a folder such as <code>~/.local/bin</code> and place the symlink there. For example:</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal mkdir ~/.local/bin ln -s ~/opt/quarto-^version^/bin/quarto ~/.local/bin/quarto</code></pre> <ol start="4" type="1"> <li>Ensure Folder in on Path</li> </ol> <p>If you can run <code>quarto -v</code> at this point, jump ahead to the next step.</p> <p>Otherwise, ensure that the folder where you created a symlink is in the path. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal ( echo ""; echo 'export PATH=$PATH:~/.local/bin\n' ; echo "" ) >> ~/.profile source ~/.profile</code></pre> <ol start="5" type="1"> <li>Check The Installation</li> </ol> <p>Use <code>quarto check</code> to confirm that the installation is successful:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto check</code></pre> <h2 id="extensions-6">Extensions</h2> <h3 id="brand-extensions">Brand Extensions</h3> <h4 id="brand-extensions-1">Brand Extensions</h4> <p>Brand extensions are Quarto extensions that provide a brand.yml file and its assets.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-1">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple brand extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension brand</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the brand extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension brand ? Extension Name › my-brand</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>my-brand</code> and press Enter—the brand extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>? Extension Name › my-brand Creating extension at /{...}/my-brand: - Created _quarto.yml - Created README.md - Created _extensions/my-brand/brand.yml - Created _extensions/my-brand/_extension.yml - Created .gitignore - Created example.qmd ? Open With ❯ positron vscode rstudio (don't open)</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the brand project.</p> <h5 id="contents-of-brand-extensions">Contents of Brand Extensions</h5> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/my-brand/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/my-brand/_extension.yml title: My-brand author: Gordon Woodhull version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=99.9.0" contributes: metadata: project: brand: brand.yml _extensions/my-brand/brand.yml # minimal brand.yml enabling dark mode # replace with your brand colors, logos, and typography! color: background: light: "#fff" dark: "#000" foreground: light: "#000" dark: "#fff"</code></pre> <p>This uses light and dark colors to enable dark mode. If you preview the <code>example.qmd</code> provided in the root of your brand extension</p> <pre><code>quarto preview example.qmd</code></pre> <p>you should see the dark mode toggle in the upper right corner, and if you click it you’ll see white text on a black background.</p> <p>Note that this example, and brand extensions in general, require a <code>_quarto.yml</code> project to be present where they are installed. This is because the metadata will be merged via the <code>project</code> key.</p> <p>We’ve provided the most basic Quarto project for this example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: default</code></pre> <p>The example brand.yml is to demonstrate dark mode.</p> <h5 id="how-brand-extensions-work">How Brand Extensions Work</h5> <p>The path to the brand file will be resolved relative to the <code>_quarto.yml</code> project.</p> <p>In turn, any assets such as logos or fonts will be resolved relative to the brand file.</p> <p>This way, when the extension is installed in a Quarto project, all paths will eventually be resolved relative to the project.</p> <p>The brand is resolved via the <code>project.brand</code> key, which is why brand extensions require a <code>_quarto.yml</code> project in the place they are installed. The project can be any type. This limitation may be lifted in the future.</p> <h3 id="creating-extensions">Creating Extensions</h3> <h4 id="creating-extensions-1">Creating Extensions</h4> <h5 id="overview-46">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto Extensions are a powerful way to modify or extend the behavior of Quarto, and can be created and distributed by anyone. There are several types of extensions available:</p> <p>Extension</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Shortcodes</p> <p>Special markdown directives that generate various types of content. For example, you could create shortcodes to embed tweets or videos in a document.</p> <p>Filters</p> <p>A flexible and powerful tool for introducing new global behaviors and/or new markdown rendering behaviors. For example, you could create filters to implement output folding, an image carousel, or just about anything you can imagine!</p> <p>Journal Articles</p> <p>Enable authoring of professional Journal articles using markdown, and produce both LaTeX (PDF) and HTML versions of the articles.</p> <p>Custom Formats</p> <p>Create new output formats by bundling together document options, templates, style sheets, and other content.</p> <p>Revealjs Plugins</p> <p>Extend the capabilities of HTML presentations created with Revealjs.</p> <p>Project Types</p> <p>Create new project project types that bundle together standard content and options, or make it easy to create a website for a custom HTML format.</p> <p>Starter Templates</p> <p>Help users get started with new projects by providing a template and example content. Starter templates aren’t strictly extensions (i.e. they aren’t installed in the <code>_extensions</code> directory) but they are often used with custom formats and project types.</p> <p>Metadata</p> <p>Provide YAML configuration that can be merged into existing Quarto projects.</p> <p>Brand</p> <p>Distribute a brand.yml file and its assets.</p> <p>Engine</p> <p>Provide an execution engine for running code blocks and capturing their output in Quarto documents.</p> <h5 id="development">Development</h5> <p>Each type of extension has its own development requirements: in some cases an extension can be created with YAML metadata alone, however in many cases you’ll end up doing some custom scripting using Lua.</p> <p>These articles provide in-depth documentation on learning and using Lua for extension development:</p> <ul> <li>Lua Development helps you get started with Lua (the language used to create extensions)</li> <li>Lua API Documentation provides documentation on the Pandoc and Quarto Lua APIs used for creating extensions.</li> </ul> <h5 id="distribution">Distribution</h5> <p>There are two distinct ways to distribute extensions to end users:</p> <ul> <li>Publish your extension in a public GitHub repository.</li> <li>Bundle your extension into a <code>.zip</code> or <code>.tar.gz</code> archive. Distributing Extensions goes into more depth on how to package and distribute extensions, both on GitHub and using plain gzip archives.</li> </ul> <h5 id="examples-20">Examples</h5> <p>The documentation linked to above provides simple motivating examples for each type of extension. Once you understand these, check out the following for more sophisticated examples of each type of extension:</p> <p>The <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/">Quarto Extensions</a> GitHub organization provides a set of extensions developed by the core Quarto team. Many of these extensions implement frequently requested features, and all of them provide sound examples of how to implement extensions.</p> <p>The <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">Quarto Journals</a> GitHub organization contains a set of Journal Article formats developed by the core Quarto team or contributed by third parties.</p> <p>Finally, most published extensions are hosted on GitHub and therefore have source code available that you can learn from.</p> <h3 id="creating-filters">Creating Filters</h3> <h4 id="creating-filters-1">Creating Filters</h4> <h5 id="overview-47">Overview</h5> <p>If the base features of Pandoc and Quarto don’t do exactly what you need, you can very likely create a <a href="https://pandoc.org/filters.html">Pandoc Filter</a> that bridges the gap.</p> <p>Pandoc consists of a set of readers and writers. When converting a document from one format to another, text is parsed by a reader into pandoc’s intermediate representation of the document—an “abstract syntax tree” or AST—which is then converted by the writer into the target format. The pandoc AST format is defined in the module <a href="https://hackage.haskell.org/package/pandoc-types-1.22/docs/Text-Pandoc-Definition.html"><code>Text.Pandoc.Definition</code></a> in the pandoc-types package.</p> <p>A “filter” is a program that modifies the AST, between the reader and the writer.</p> <pre><code>INPUT --reader AST --filter AST --writer OUTPUT</code></pre> <p>Pandoc’s built-in citation processing is implemented as a filter, as are many of Quarto’s internal extensions (e.g. cross-references, figure layout, etc.).</p> <p>You can write Pandoc filters using Lua (via Pandoc’s built-in Lua interpreter) or using any other language using a JSON representation of the Pandoc AST piped to/from an external process. We strongly recommend using Lua Filters, which have the following advantages:</p> <ul> <li>No external dependencies</li> <li>High performance (no serialization or process execution overhead)</li> <li>Access to the <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#pandoc-module">Pandoc</a> and Quarto libraries of Lua helper functions.</li> </ul> <h5 id="activating-filters">Activating Filters</h5> <p>If you’ve developed a filter and want to use it within a document you need to add it to the list of <code>filters</code> for the document. For example, here we arrange for the <a href="https://github.com/pandoc/lua-filters/tree/master/lilypond">lilypond</a> music-engraving filter to run:</p> <pre><code>--- filters: - lilypond.lua ---</code></pre> <p>By default, user filters are run before Quarto’s built-in filters. For some filters you’ll want to modify this behavior. For example, here we arrange to run <code>lilypond</code> before Quarto’s filters and <code>fontawesome</code> after:</p> <pre><code>filters: - lilypond.lua - quarto - fontawesome</code></pre> <p>Beyond a running filters before or after Quarto’s filters, you can also precisely target the location in the AST processing. Read more in Targeting of AST Processing Phases.</p> <p>You’ll notice that one of the extensions (<code>lilypond.lua</code>) has a file extension and the other (<code>fontawesome</code>) does not. This difference stems from how the extensions are distributed: an extension distributed as a plain Lua file uses <code>.lua</code> whereas a filter distributed as a Quarto Extension does not. The next section explores how to create filters as extensions.</p> <h5 id="filter-extensions">Filter Extensions</h5> <h6 id="quick-start-2">Quick Start</h6> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple filter extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension filter</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the filter extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension filter ? Extension Name › fancy-header</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>fancy-header</code> and press Enter—the filter extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>Creating extension at /Users/jjallaire/quarto/dev/fancy-header: - Created README.md - Created _extensions/fancy-header/_extension.yml - Created _extensions/fancy-header/fancy-header.lua - Created .gitignore - Created example.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/fancy-header/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/fancy-header/_extension.yml title: Fancy-header author: J.J. Allaire version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=99.9.0" contributes: filters: - fancy-header.lua _extensions/fancy-header/fancy-header.lua -- Reformat all heading text function Header(el) el.content = pandoc.Emph(el.content) return el end</code></pre> <p>Finally, the <code>example.qmd</code> file includes code that exercises the extension. For example:</p> <pre><code>example.qmd --- title: "Fancy-header Example" filters: - fancy-header --- ## Heading This filter adds formatting to heading text.</code></pre> <p>Note that the value provided to <code>filters</code> in <code>example.qmd</code> should be the name of the extension (<code>fancy-header</code>), not the filename of the filter (<code>fancy-header.lua</code>). This allows you to bundle more than one filter in your extension:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/fancy-header/_extension.yml contributes: filters: - fancy-header.lua - make-fancier.lua</code></pre> <p>All of filters in your extension will be applied when a user uses your extension in their document.</p> <p>To develop your filter, render/preview <code>example.qmd</code>, and then make changes to <code>fancy-header.lua</code> (the preview will automatically refresh when you change <code>fancy-header.lua</code>).</p> <h6 id="development-1">Development</h6> <p>To learn more about developing filter extensions:</p> <ul> <li>If necessary, brush up on Lua Development (Lua is the language used to create filters).</li> <li>Review the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html">Writing Lua Filters</a>.</li> <li>Read the Lua API Reference, which describes the Lua extension API for Quarto. If you want to write a JSON filter, see the documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/filters.html">Writing JSON filters</a>.</li> </ul> <p>To create a new filter extension, use the <code>quarto create extension filter</code> command as described above.</p> <h6 id="distribution-1">Distribution</h6> <p>If your extension source code is located within a GitHub repository, then it can be added to a project by referencing the GitHub organization and repository name. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # target the current HEAD of the extension quarto add cooltools/output-folding # target a branch or tagged release of the extension quarto add cooltools/output-folding@v1.2 quarto add cooltools/output-folding@bugfix-22</code></pre> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h6 id="examples-21">Examples</h6> <p>You might also find it instructive to examine the source code of these filter extensions authored by the Quarto team:</p> <p>Extension name</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/latex-environment">latex-environment</a></p> <p>Quarto extension to output custom LaTeX environments.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/lightbox">lightbox</a></p> <p>Create lightbox treatments for images in your HTML documents.</p> <h3 id="creating-shortcodes">Creating Shortcodes</h3> <h4 id="creating-shortcodes-1">Creating Shortcodes</h4> <p>This article describes how to create your own shortcodes.</p> <h5 id="overview-48">Overview</h5> <p>Shortcodes are special markdown directives that generate various types of content. Quarto shortcodes are similar in form and function to <a href="https://gohugo.io/content-management/shortcodes/">Hugo shortcodes</a> and <a href="https://codex.wordpress.org/Shortcode">WordPress shortcodes</a>.</p> <p>For example, the following shortcode prints the <code>title</code> from document metadata:</p> <pre><code>{{< meta title >}}</code></pre> <h5 id="built-in-shortcodes-1">Built-in Shortcodes</h5> <p>Quarto supports several shortcodes natively:</p> <p>Shortcode</p> <p>Description</p> <p>version</p> <p>Print Quarto CLI version</p> <p>var</p> <p>Print value from <code>_variables.yml</code> file</p> <p>meta</p> <p>Print value from document metadata</p> <p>env</p> <p>Print system environment variable</p> <p>pagebreak</p> <p>Insert a native page-break</p> <p>kbd</p> <p>Describe keyboard shortcuts</p> <p>video</p> <p>Embed a video in a document</p> <p>include</p> <p>Include contents of another qmd</p> <p>embed</p> <p>Embed cells from a Jupyter Notebook</p> <p>placeholder</p> <p>Add placeholder images to your document</p> <p>lipsum</p> <p>Add placeholder text to your document</p> <p>contents</p> <p>Rearrange content in your document</p> <h5 id="quick-start-3">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple shortcode extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio, you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension shortcode</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the shortcode extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension shortcode ? Extension Name › shorty</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>shorty</code> and press Enter—the shortcode extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>Creating extension at /Users/jjallaire/extensions/shorty/shorty: - Created README.md - Created _extensions/shorty/shorty.lua - Created _extensions/shorty/_extension.yml - Created .gitignore - Created example.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio, a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/shorty/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/shorty/_extension.yml title: Shorty author: J.J. Allaire version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.222" contributes: shortcodes: - shorty.lua _extensions/shorty/shorty.lua return { ['shorty'] = function(args, kwargs, meta) return pandoc.Str("Hello from Shorty!") end }</code></pre> <p>Finally, the <code>example.qmd</code> file includes code that exercises the extension. For example:</p> <pre><code>example.qmd --- title: "Shorty Example" --- {{< shorty >}}</code></pre> <p>To develop your shortcode, render/preview <code>example.qmd</code>, and then make changes to <code>shorty.lua</code> (the preview will automatically refresh when you change <code>shorty.lua</code>).</p> <h5 id="development-2">Development</h5> <p>Shortcodes are created using Lua. If you aren’t familar with Lua (or with Pandoc filters), here are some resources to help you along:</p> <ul> <li>Lua Development (Lua is the language used to create shortcodes).</li> <li>Lua API Reference, which describes the Lua extension API for Quarto. Specifically, consider consulting the <code>quarto.shortcode.*</code> entry points. Shortcodes are implemented as Lua functions that take one or more arguments and return a Pandoc AST node (or list of nodes).</li> </ul> <p>Here’s the implementation of the <code>env</code> shortcode that is built in to Quarto:</p> <pre><code>env.lua function env(args) local var = pandoc.utils.stringify(args[1]) local value = os.getenv(var) if value ~= nil then return pandoc.Str(value) else return pandoc.Null() end end</code></pre> <p>Note that arguments to shortcodes are provided in <code>args</code> (a 1-dimensional array), and that each argument is a list of Pandoc inlines (i.e. markdown AST parsed from the text).</p> <p>We use the <code>pandoc.utils.stringify()</code> function to convert the inlines to an ordinary string, and then the <code>os.getenv()</code> function to get its value.</p> <p>You would use this shortcode as follows:</p> <pre><code>{{< env HOME >}}</code></pre> <h5 id="distribution-2">Distribution</h5> <p>If your extension source code is located within a GitHub repository, then it can be installed by referencing the GitHub organization and repository name. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # install the current HEAD of the extension quarto add cooltools/shorty # install a branch or tagged release of the extension quarto add cooltools/shorty@v1.2 quarto add cooltools/shorty@bugfix-22</code></pre> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h5 id="examples-22">Examples</h5> <p>You might find it instructive to examine the source code of these shortcode extensions authored by the Quarto team:</p> <p>Extension</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/fancy-text">fancy-text</a></p> <p>Output nicely formatted versions of fancy strings such as LaTeX and BibTeX in multiple formats.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/fontawesome">fontawesome</a></p> <p>Use Font Awesome icons in HTML and PDF documents.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/extensions/quarto/video">video</a></p> <p>Embed videos in HTML documents and Revealjs presentations.</p> <p>Some additional annotated examples are provided below.</p> <h6 id="raw-output-1">Raw Output</h6> <p>Shortcodes can tailor their output to the format being rendered to. This is often useful when you want to conditionally generate rich HTML output but still have the same document render properly to PDF or MS Word.</p> <p>The <code>pagebreak</code> shortcode generates “native” pagebreaks in a variety of formats. Here’s the implementation of <code>pagebreak</code>:</p> <pre><code>pagebreak.lua function pagebreak() local raw = { epub = '<p style="page-break-after: always;"> </p>', html = '<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>', latex = '\\newpage{}', ooxml = '<w:p><w:r><w:br w:type="page"/></w:r></w:p>', odt = '<text:p text:style-name="Pagebreak"/>', context = '\\page' } if quarto.doc.isFormat('docx') then return pandoc.RawBlock('openxml', raw.ooxml) elseif quarto.doc.isFormat('pdf') then return pandoc.RawBlock('tex', raw.latex) elseif quarto.doc.isFormat('odt') then return pandoc.RawBlock('opendocument', raw.odt) elseif quarto.doc.isFormat('epub') then return pandoc.RawBlock('html', raw.epub) elseif quarto.doc.isFormat('html') then return pandoc.RawBlock('html', raw.html) elseif quarto.doc.isFormat('context') then return pandoc.RawBlock('context', raw.context) else -- fall back to insert a form feed character return pandoc.Para{pandoc.Str '\f'} end end</code></pre> <p>We use the <code>pandoc.RawBlock()</code> function to output the appropriate raw content for the target format. Note that raw blocks are passed straight through to the output file and are not processed as markdown.</p> <p>You’d use this shortcode as follows:</p> <pre><code>{{< pagebreak >}}</code></pre> <h6 id="named-arguments">Named Arguments</h6> <p>The examples above use either a single argument (<code>env</code>) or no arguments at all (<code>pagebreak</code>). Here we demonstrate named argument handling by implementing a <code>git-rev</code> shortcode that prints the current git revision, providing a <code>short</code> option to determine whether a short or long SHA1 value is displayed:</p> <pre><code>git.lua -- run git and read its output function git(command) local p = io.popen("git " .. command) local output = p:read('*all') p:close() return output end -- return a table containing shortcode definitions -- defining shortcodes this way allows us to create helper -- functions that are not themselves considered shortcodes return { ["git-rev"] = function(args, kwargs) -- command line args local cmdArgs = "" local short = pandoc.utils.stringify(kwargs["short"]) if short == "true" then cmdArgs = cmdArgs .. "--short " end -- run the command local cmd = "rev-parse " .. cmdArgs .. "HEAD" local rev = git(cmd) -- return as string return pandoc.Str(rev) end }</code></pre> <p>There are some new things demonstrated here:</p> <ul> <li><p>Rather than defining our shortcode functions globally, we return a table with the shortcode definitions. This allows us to define helper functions that are not themselves registered as shortcodes. It also enables us to define a shortcode with a dash (<code>-</code>) in its name.</p></li> <li><p>There is a new argument to our shortcode handler: <code>kwargs</code>. This holds any named arguments to the shortcode. As with <code>args</code>, values in <code>kwargs</code> will always be a list of Pandoc inlines (allowing you to accept markdown as an argument). Since <code>short</code> is a simple boolean value we need to call <code>pandoc.utils.stringify()</code> to treat it as a string and then compare it to <code>"true"</code>. We’d use this shortcode as follows:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: “My Document”</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>{{< git-rev >}} {{< git-rev short=true >}}</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="metadata-options">Metadata Options</h6> <p>In some cases you may want to provide options that affect how your shortcode behaves. There is a third argument to shortcode handlers (<code>meta</code>) that provides access to document and/or project level metadata.</p> <p>Let’s implement a different version of the <code>git-rev</code> shortcode that emits the revision as a link to GitHub rather than plain text. To do this, we make use of <code>github.owner</code> and <code>github.repo</code> metadata values:</p> <pre><code>git.lua function git(command) local p = io.popen("git " .. command) local output = p:read('*all') p:close() return output end return { ["git-rev"] = function(args, kwargs, meta) -- run the command local rev = git("rev-parse HEAD") -- target repo local owner = pandoc.utils.stringify(meta["github.owner"]) local repo = pandoc.utils.stringify(meta["github.repo"]) local url = "[github.com](https://github.com/)" .. owner .. "/" .. repo .. "/" .. rev -- return as link return pandoc.Link(pandoc.Str(rev), url) end }</code></pre> <p>As with <code>args</code> and <code>kwargs</code>, <code>meta</code> values are always provided as a list of Pandoc inlines, so often need to be converted to string using <code>pandoc.utils.stringify()</code>.</p> <p>To use this shortcode in a document, we provide the GitHub info as document options, then include the shortcode where we want the link to be:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" github: owner: quarto-dev repo: quarto-cli --- {{< git-rev >}}</code></pre> <p>The shortcode registration and GitHub metadata could just as well been provided in a project-level <code>_quarto.yml</code> file or a directory-level <code>_metadata.yml</code> file.</p> <h5 id="raw-arguments">Raw Arguments</h5> <p>In Quarto >= 1.3, you can also access the raw stream of inlines passed to a shortcode by adding a <code>raw_args</code> parameter. For example:</p> <pre><code>function shorty(args, kwargs, meta, raw_args) -- ... end</code></pre> <h5 id="context-awareness">Context Awareness</h5> <p>In Quarto >= 1.5, you can access the context in which the shortcode was invoked as the fifth parameter of the function call. <code>context</code> is a string that will be one of <code>block</code>, <code>inline</code>, or <code>text</code>:</p> <ul> <li>if <code>context</code> is <code>block</code>, then the shortcode exists in a block by itself</li> <li>if <code>context</code> is <code>inline</code>, then the shortcode exists as one of many inline nodes</li> <li>if <code>context</code> is <code>text</code>, then the shortcode exists inside a text field of a Pandoc node. These can be: <ul> <li>the content of <code>CodeBlock</code> or <code>Code</code> elements</li> <li>the content of <code>RawBlock</code> or <code>RawInline</code> elements</li> <li>the content of attributes of Pandoc elements like <code>Div</code>, <code>Span</code>, etc.</li> <li>the URL of a <code>Link</code> element</li> <li>the source of an <code>Image</code> element</li> </ul> function shorty(args, kwargs, meta, raw_args, context) – … end</li> </ul> <h5 id="escaping-2">Escaping</h5> <p>If you are writing documentation about using variable shortcodes (for example, this article!) you might need to prevent them from being processed. You can do this in two ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>Escape the shortcode reference with extra braces like this:</p> <p>{{{< var version >}}}</p></li> <li><p>Add a <code>shortcodes=false</code> attribute to any code block you want to prevent processing of shortcodes within:</p> <pre data-shortcodes="false"><code>{{< var version >}}</code></pre></li> </ul> <h3 id="custom-formats">Custom Formats</h3> <h4 id="custom-formats-1">Custom Formats</h4> <h5 id="overview-49">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto format extensions enable you to add new formats to the built-in formats (e.g. <code>html</code>, <code>pdf</code>, <code>docx</code>) already available. Custom formats can provide default document options, style-sheets, header, footer, or logo elements, and even bundle other extensions like filters and shortcodes. They are a great way to provide a common baseline for authoring documents or presentations within an organization, for a particular type of project or analysis, or for a specific publication.</p> <p>You can specify a custom format beneath the <code>format</code> key just like a built-in format. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: acm-pdf: toc: true ---</code></pre> <p>Custom formats all derive from one of the base formats, and include that base format as a suffix. Formats can also provide multiple variations that derive from distinct base formats. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" toc: true format: acm-pdf: default acm-html: default ---</code></pre> <p>Note that we moved the <code>toc</code> option to the top level since it is shared between both of the formats.</p> <p>Custom formats can also be used with the <code>--to</code> argument to <code>quarto render</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --to acm-html</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are specifically interested in using or creating custom formats for journals and manuscripts, you may want to proceed instead to the documentation on Journal Articles.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-4">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple HTML-based format extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension format:html</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the format to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension format:html ? Extension Name › lexdoc</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>lexdoc</code> (a document format for a fictional company named LexCrop) and press Enter—the custom format extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>Creating extension at /Users/jjallaire/quarto/dev/lexdoc: - Created README.md - Created _extensions/lexdoc/custom.scss - Created _extensions/lexdoc/_extension.yml - Created template.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <p>Note that this example creates a format that is derivative of the Quarto base <code>html</code> format. You can similarly create formats that are derivative of <code>pdf</code>, <code>docx</code>, and <code>revealjs</code> as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create extension format:pdf quarto create extension format:docx quarto create extension format:revealjs</code></pre> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/lexdoc/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/lexdoc/_extension.yml title: Lexdoc author: J.J. Allaire version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.222" contributes: formats: html: toc: true theme: [yeti, custom.scss]</code></pre> <p>The custom HTML format defined here is very simple. It takes the base <code>html</code> format, turns on the table of contents by default, and sets the theme as <code>yeti</code> along with a <code>custom.scss</code> file for additional customizations:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/lexdoc/custom.scss /*-- scss:defaults --*/ /* TODO: Customize appearance with SCSS variables */ /* See [HTML theme](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html#theme-options) */ /*-- scss:rules --*/ /* TODO: Provide custom CSS rules */</code></pre> <p>Finally, the <code>template.qmd</code> provides a base example article for users of the format:</p> <pre><code>template.qmd --- title: "Lexdoc Example" format: lexdoc-html: default author: J.J. Allaire date: last-modified --- ## Introduction *TODO* Create an example file that demonstrates the formatting and features of your format. ## More Information You can learn more about controlling the appearance of HTML output here: <[quarto.org](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html)></code></pre> <p>To develop your format, render/preview <code>template.qmd</code>, and then make changes to the various files in the <code>_extensions</code> directory (the preview will automatically refresh when you change these files).</p> <h5 id="example-revealjs">Example: Revealjs</h5> <p>Next, we’ll walk through the creation of a custom format that extends the <code>revealjs</code> presentation format. Here is what the source code repository of the format extension might look like:</p> <pre><code>README.md LICENSE template.qmd _extensions/ lexconf/ _extension.yml theme.scss logo.png title.png</code></pre> <p>Note that the format suffix (<code>revealjs</code>) is excluded from the directory name (this is to account for the possibility of multiple formats e.g. <code>lexconf-revealjs</code>, <code>lexconf-pptx</code>, etc.)</p> <p>As with other types of extensions, the only thing strictly required is the <code>_extensions</code> directory (anything above that is for your own purposes and is ignored during format installation). Even so, it’s good practice to include a <code>README.md</code> and <code>LICENSE</code> file. The <code>template.qmd</code> file serves a couple of purposes:</p> <ul> <li><p>It can be rendered as you develop your format to ensure that things work as expected.</p></li> <li><p>It can serve as the basis for a format template (which helps users gets started with using your format). Here is what the contents of <code>_extension.yml</code> might look like:</p> <p>title: LexConf 2022 Presentation author: LexCorp version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: “>=1.2.0” contributes: formats: revealjs: theme: [default, theme.scss] logo: logo.png footer: | Copyright 2022 (c) LexCorp, Inc. title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: title.png data-background-size: contain preview-links: auto</p></li> </ul> <p>This format mostly provides organization-level content and theming. As mentioned above, formats can also include filters which allow for adding custom markdown constructs and rendering behavior.</p> <p>Here is what the contents of <code>template.qmd</code> might look like:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" subtitle: "LexConf 2022" author: "Your Name" date: today format: lexconf-revealjs --- # Overview</code></pre> <p>Extension repositories are structured in such a way that you can test your extension and the template by simply rendering the <code>template.qmd</code> file right in the root of your repository. The <code>template.qmd</code> will be able to load your extension just as it would when installed, so testing and iterating should be as simple as working within your extension directory until you’re satisfied (without the need to repeatedly install or update the extension in order to test it).</p> <h5 id="format-templates-1">Format Templates</h5> <p>Above we described including a <code>template.qmd</code> alongside your extension and then installing the template and format together with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use template <gh-organization>/<extension></code></pre> <p>The <code>template.qmd</code> should demonstrate the functionality of the format and serve as a sound starting point for the user. When the extension template is copied into the target directory, the <code>template.qmd</code> will automatically be renamed to match the name that the user provided for the directory.</p> <p>You can also include other files alongside <code>template.qmd</code> and they will be copied as well. Note that by default, Quarto will exclude common Github repository files when copying an extension template. This includes any file name or directory starting with a <code>.</code> (e.g. <code>.gitignore</code>), <code>README.md</code>, <code>LICENSE</code>, etc.. If you’d like, you can place a <code>.quartoignore</code> file in the root of your repository with each line of the file being a glob describing file(s) to ignore (using syntax like a <code>.gitignore</code> file).</p> <h5 id="distributing-formats">Distributing Formats</h5> <p>You can distribute format extensions in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>As a template that includes both the format in the <code>_extensions</code> directory and the <code>template.qmd</code> (which is automatically renamed to match the name of the enclosing directory).</p></li> <li><p>As a plain format with no template scaffolding (this is useful for adding the format to an existing document or project). If you have a GitHub repository containing the files enumerated above in the <code>lexconf</code> example, users could install your extension and associated template as follows (where <code>lexcorp</code> is the GitHub organization hosting the repo):</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto use template lexcorp/lexconf</p></li> </ul> <p>This is often the preferred way to get started with a format as it provides the user with a working document right out of the box. It’s also possible to install only the format if you are working with an existing project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add lexcorp/lexconf</code></pre> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h5 id="multiple-formats">Multiple Formats</h5> <p>A single format extension can support more than one output format. For example, an extension may target <code>html</code> and <code>pdf</code> output. To support multiple formats in your extension, you can add additional base formats to the <code>contributes / format</code> key like so:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: html: # html-specific options pdf: # pdf-specific options</code></pre> <h5 id="common-metadata">Common Metadata</h5> <p>If you have metadata that is common to any output format when your format extension is targeted, you can place that metadata under the <code>common</code> key. For example:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: common: filters: - filter.lua shortcodes: - quarto-ext/fancy-text html: # html-specifc pdf: # pdf-specifc</code></pre> <h5 id="format-resources">Format Resources</h5> <p>You can usually include other files and resources within a format extension by placing those files within the extension directory and using relative paths to reference them in your <code>_extension.yml</code> metadata file. These relative paths will be properly handled as your extension’s metadata is merged with the rendered document metadata.</p> <p>If there are resources that you need to have copied to the input directory as a part of rendering the document (for example, a <code>bst</code> file for LaTeX bibliographies or a logo or other file referenced from a LaTeX template), you can provide <code>format-resources</code>, which is a list of file paths1. Each of these files will be copied into the directory containing the input that is being rendered when the document is rendered. For example:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: pdf: format-resources: - plos2015.bst</code></pre> <h5 id="extension-embedding">Extension Embedding</h5> <p>In some cases format extensions will want to make use of other extensions. This is permitted, but adding extensions for use within a custom format must be done with a special command line flag to ensure they are embedded correctly.</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create extension format:pdf myformat cd myformat quarto add quarto-ext/fancy-text --embed myformat</code></pre> <p>For example, here we want to make the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/fancy-text">fancy-text</a> extension (which provides special formatting for the words () and BibTEX) available for users of the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/jss">jss</a> custom format:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-ext/fancy-text --embed jss</code></pre> <p>This will produce the following output:</p> <pre><code>Output quarto-journals/jss └── _extensions └── jss ├── _extensions │ └── quarto-ext │ └── fancy-text └── partials</code></pre> <p>This will add the <code>quarto-ext/fancy-text</code> extension into the <code>jss</code> extension in the <code>_extensions</code> folder. By embedding an extension you make it available without creating the potential for conflict with other versions of the extension that users might already have installed.</p> <h5 id="footnotes-5">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>This is most common in the the case of PDF based formats which have a secondary step of converting the LaTeX produced by Pandoc into a PDF. If there are files that are referenced indirectly by the LaTeX, they will need to be discoverable and should typically be copied into the same directory that contains the LaTeX input.↩︎</li> </ul> <h3 id="distributing-extensions">Distributing Extensions</h3> <h4 id="distributing-extensions-1">Distributing Extensions</h4> <h5 id="overview-50">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto extensions are directories that contain an <code>_extensions</code> sub-directory with one or more extensions. The files above the <code>_extensions</code> directory are not installed, so typically contain README and LICENSE files, examples, test cases, etc.</p> <p>There are two distinct ways to distribute extensions to end users:</p> <ul> <li>Publish your extension in a public GitHub repository.</li> <li>Bundle your extension into a <code>.zip</code> or <code>.tar.gz</code> archive. Each method has benefits and drawbacks that will be explored below. First we’ll cover the basic file structure and contents of an extension.</li> </ul> <h5 id="extension-contents">Extension Contents</h5> <p>Quarto Extensions are directories that contain an <code>_extensions</code> folder that contains one or more extension contributions. While the most common case is the distribution of a single extension, it is possible to create a single extension directory that includes multiple shortcodes, multiple filters, or a combination of both.</p> <p>Here is the contents of an extension named <code>my-filter</code>:</p> <pre><code>README.md LICENSE example.qmd _extensions/ my-filter/ _extension.yml my-filter.lua</code></pre> <p>Note that the only thing strictly required is the <code>_extensions</code> directory (anything above that is for your own purposes and is ignored during installation). Even so, it’s good practice to include a <code>README.md</code> and <code>LICENSE</code> file, and the <code>example.qmd</code> will be useful for developing your extension.</p> <h6 id="extension.yml">_extension.yml</h6> <p>Each extension is defined by its <code>_extension.yml</code> file which contains the metadata about the extension as well as the what items it contributes when used. For example, here is the <code>_extension.yml</code> for a filter extension:</p> <pre><code>title: My Filter author: Cooltools version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.0" contributes: filters: - my-filter.lua</code></pre> <p>Here are all of the fields that can be specified in the <code>_extension.yml</code> file:</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The extension’s name</p> <p><code>author</code></p> <p>The author of the extension</p> <p><code>version</code></p> <p>A semantic version number this release. When installing, updating, or releasing an extension, this version number will be used to present a summary of actions to the user.</p> <p><code>quarto-required</code></p> <p>A semantic version number indicating the minimum quarto version required to run this extension.</p> <p><code>contributes</code></p> <p>The items that this extension will contribute to the render. These are allowed subkeys:</p> <p><code>shortcodes</code></p> <p>A list of shortcode files that should be loaded when this extension is installed.</p> <p><code>filters</code></p> <p>A list of filters that should be loaded when this extension is included in the list of filters used to render a document or project. The order of the filters in this list will be preserved.</p> <p><code>formats</code></p> <p>A record containing the key value pairs of output formats and the metadata associated with that output format.</p> <p><code>project</code></p> <p>Information about a custom Quarto project type.</p> <p><code>revealjs-plugins</code></p> <p>Information about a RevealJS plugin.</p> <p><code>metadata</code></p> <p>Metadata to be merged into the Quarto project using the extension.</p> <p><code>brand</code></p> <p>Information about a brand extension.</p> <p><code>engine</code></p> <p>Information about a custom engine.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The <code>version</code> field is checked for conformity to <a href="https://semver.org/">semantic versioning</a>. For example, valid <code>version</code> values would be:</p> <ul> <li><p>1.0.0</p></li> <li><p>2.3.4-alpha</p></li> <li><p>1.2.3-beta+build567</p></li> <li><p>3.0.0-alpha.2</p></li> <li><p>4.2.1+build.987 Invalid <code>version</code> values would be:</p></li> <li><p>1.2 (missing patch version)</p></li> <li><p>1.2.3.4 (extra version segment)</p></li> <li><p>1.2.3-beta.5+build (missing build metadata identifier)</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="github-distribution">GitHub Distribution</h5> <p>Distributing extensions on GitHub has a number of benefits, including compact syntax (e.g. <code>quarto add org-name/extension</code>), the use of organizations as a “namespace” for managing name conflicts, and the ability to target specific releases or tags.</p> <p>For example, the extensions in the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/"><code>quarto-ext</code></a> GitHub organization can be added to a project with these commands:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-ext/lightbox quarto add quarto-ext/fontawesome</code></pre> <p>By default, extensions are added from the <code>HEAD</code> of the <code>main</code> branch of the repository. You can also target tags and/or branches in your repository by including an <code>@</code> after the repository name. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-ext/lightbox@v1.2 quarto add quarto-ext/lightbox@bugfix-22</code></pre> <p>Extensions added from GitHub have another special property: the GitHub organization can be used as a namespace qualifier to disambiguate extensions that have the same name. For example, if you have two different <code>lightbox</code> extensions in your project, you explicitly specify the <code>quarto-ext</code> one as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- filters: - quarto-ext/lightbox ---</code></pre> <p>You can also add an extension from a subdirectory of a GitHub repository. For example, here we install two different extensions from the <code>cooltools/icons</code> repository:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add cooltools/icons/fontawesome quarto add cooltools/icons/iconify</code></pre> <h5 id="archive-distribution">Archive Distribution</h5> <p>Distributing extensions as a <code>.zip</code> or <code>.tar.gz</code> archive has the benefit of not requiring public distribution. These extensions can also be added directly from non-GitHub version control services using the archive URLs normally provided for repositories.</p> <p>Note that unlike GitHub hosted extensions, extensions installed from archives do not have an organizational namespace (they all share a single namespace).</p> <h6 id="git-repositories">Git Repositories</h6> <p>To add an extension to a project from a GitLab repository you could do this:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add [gitlab.com](https://gitlab.com/cooltools/shorty/-/archive/main/shorty-main.zip)</code></pre> <p>You’ll note that the above URL references the <code>main</code> branch. You can similarly target any other branch, tag, or release.
