For example, to add an extension using the <code>v1.0</code> tag:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add [gitlab.com](https://gitlab.com/cooltools/shorty/-/archive/v1.0/shorty-main.zip)</code></pre> <p>If you are using BitBucket, Azure DevOps, or another Git hosting provider, consult the appropriate service documentation to learn how to form archive URLs for repositories.</p> <h6 id="archive-files">Archive Files</h6> <p>The above examples demonstrate adding an extension from a Git repository, you can also add an extension from an archive published to an ordinary web host. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add [cooltools.org](https://cooltools.org/quarto/shorty.zip)</code></pre> <p>Or alternatively from a local archive file or even ordinary uncompressed directory:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add ~/Downloads/shorty.zip quarto add /share/quarto/extensions/shorty</code></pre> <h3 id="engine-extensions-1">Engine Extensions</h3> <h4 id="engine-extensions-2">Engine Extensions</h4> <p>Engine extensions are Quarto extensions that provide an execution engine for running code blocks and capturing their output in Quarto documents.</p> <p>Important</p> <p>Currently there is one execution engine per Quarto document, so you can’t have some code blocks executed by an engine extension and other code blocks executed by e.g. <code>jupyter</code> or <code>knitr</code>.</p> <p>Engine extensions do not allow control over the cell language handlers for diagrams like <code>mermaid</code> and <code>dot</code>.</p> <p>This is likely to improve in the future.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-5">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a basic engine extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension engine</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the engine extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension engine ? Extension Name › my-language-engine ? Default cell language name (my-language-engine) › my-language</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an engine name and a cell language name for cells, e.g.</p> <pre><code>```{my-language} x = 42 ```</code></pre> <p>The language name will default to the engine name. Type each name and press Enter—the engine extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>? Extension Name › my-prerender-scripts Creating extension at /Users/gordon/src/my-language-engine: - Created example.qmd - Created README.md - Created _extensions/my-language-engine/_extension.yml - Created .gitignore - Created src/my-language-engine.ts ? Open With ❯ positron vscode rstudio (don't open)</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <h5 id="contents-of-engine-extensions">Contents of Engine Extensions</h5> <p>The <code>quarto create extension engine</code> command has created an <code>_extensions</code> directory, which is what gets installed for users of your extension, and a <code>src</code> directory containing the TypeScript source.</p> <p>The <code>_extensions/my-language-engine/</code> directory will contain a Quarto extension configuration like this:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/my-language-engine/_extension.yml title: My-language-engine author: Gordon Woodhull version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.9.0" contributes: engines: - path: my-language-engine.js</code></pre> <p>To generate the JavaScript bundle this points to, run</p> <pre><code>quarto call build-ts-extension</code></pre> <p>This builds the TypeScript source <code>src/my-language-engine.ts</code> against the types and import map distributed with Quarto, and outputs <code>_extensions/my-language-engine/my-language-engine.js</code>.</p> <h5 id="how-engine-extensions-work">How Engine Extensions Work</h5> <p>The <code>ExecutionEngineDiscovery</code> interface specifies</p> <ul> <li>an <code>init</code> method providing the Quarto API to the engine</li> <li>methods used in determining which engine to use</li> <li>a <code>launch</code> method which takes the <code>EngineProjectContext</code> and provides methods for executing cells and capturing output, and returns an <code>ExecutionEngineInstance</code>. The Quarto API is not documented yet. See the Typescript types in <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/packages/quarto-types">quarto-types</a></li> </ul> <p>The <code>ExecutionEngineInstance.execute</code> method processes the entire markdown of the document after includes and embeds, and before cell language handlers and Pandoc.</p> <p>For the languages that it claims, it should replace each code block with:</p> <ul> <li><p>If <code>options.format.execute.echo</code> is true, the same code block in non-executable syntax.</p></li> <li><p>E.g. if the input is</p> <p><code>{python}</code></p></li> <li><p>Then the output should be</p> <div class="sourceCode" id="cb909"><pre class="sourceCode python"><code class="sourceCode python"></code></pre></div></li> <li><p>adding other classes and attributes as appropriate.</p></li> <li><p>If <code>echo</code> is false, the code should not be output.</p></li> <li><p>Any outputs from executing the code block, depending on <code>options.format.execute.output</code> See Execution Options for more information on execution options.</p></li> </ul> <h3 id="lua-api-reference">Lua API Reference</h3> <h4 id="lua-api-reference-1">Lua API Reference</h4> <h5 id="overview-51">Overview</h5> <p>This article provides documentation on the standard APIs available when implementing Lua filters and shortcodes. There are three major sets of APIs available:</p> <ul> <li>Lua Base API—Base functions provided for string handling, pattern matching, table manipulation, and file input and output.</li> <li>Pandoc Lua API—Core API provided by Pandoc for filter development, and includes both core AST types (e.g. <code>pandoc.Div</code>, <code>pandoc.CodeBlock</code>, etc.) as well as a wide variety of helper functions for common tasks.</li> <li>Quarto Lua API—Additional functions used for debugging, format detection, encoding (e.g. JSON), and adding dependencies to documents (e.g. JavaScript libraries or LaTeX packages). To get started with programming in Lua and learn about some recommended tools and workflow, see the article on Lua Development.</li> </ul> <h5 id="lua-base-api">Lua Base API</h5> <p>The Lua standard library provides core functions for low-level string, math, table, and file operations. Here we provide links to a few of the more useful standard libaries (complete documentation can be found in the <a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/">Lua Reference Manual</a>).</p> <p>Library</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.4">string</a></p> <p>This library provides generic functions for string manipulation, such as finding and extracting substrings, and pattern matching.</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.5">utf8</a></p> <p>This library provides basic support for UTF-8 encoding.</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.6">table</a></p> <p>This library provides generic functions for table manipulation.</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.7">math</a></p> <p>This library provides basic mathematical functions.</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.8">io</a>, <a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.8">file</a></p> <p>The I/O library provides two different styles for file manipulation: one uses implicit file handles and the other explicit handles.</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#6.9">os</a></p> <p>Date/time, locales, environment variables, etc.</p> <h5 id="pandoc-lua-api">Pandoc Lua API</h5> <p>Complete documentation for the Pandoc Lua API can be found in the <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html">Lua Filters</a> article available on the Pandoc website. Here are the various components of the API along with links to their reference documentation:</p> <p>Lua Module</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc">pandoc</a> (ast)</p> <p>Constructors for document tree elements (e.g. <code>pandoc.Div()</code>, <code>pandoc.Strong()</code>, etc.) as well as core components (e.g. <code>pandoc.Attr()</code>)</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#helper-functions">pandoc</a> (functions)</p> <p>Functions to parse text in a given format, filter and modify a sub-tree, and run child processes.</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-text">pandoc.text</a></p> <p>UTF-8 aware text manipulation functions (e.g. <code>upper()</code>, <code>lower()</code>, etc.)</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.list">pandoc.List</a></p> <p>This module defines pandoc’s list type. It comes with useful methods and convenience function (e.g <code>find_if()</code>, <code>includes()</code>, <code>filter()</code>, <code>map()</code>, etc.)</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.utils">pandoc.utils</a></p> <p>Internal pandoc functions and utility functions (e.g. <code>blocks_to_inlines()</code>, <code>stringify()</code>, <code>citeproc()</code>, etc.)</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.path">pandoc.path</a></p> <p>Module for file path manipulations (e.g. <code>is_absolute()</code>, <code>is_relative()</code>, <code>join()</code>, etc.</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.system">pandoc.system</a></p> <p>Access to system information and functionality (e.g. <code>get_working_directory()</code>, <code>list_directory()</code>, etc.</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.mediabag">pandoc.mediabag</a></p> <p>Access to pandoc’s media storage. The “media bag” is used when pandoc is called with the <code>--extract-media</code> or (for HTML only) <code>--embed-resources</code> option.</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.template">pandoc.template</a></p> <p>Compile and access defualt pandoc templates (e.g. <code>compile()</code>)</p> <p><a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#module-pandoc.types">pandoc.types</a></p> <p>Constructors for types which are not part of the pandoc AST (e.g. <code>Version()</code>)</p> <h5 id="quarto-lua-api-1">Quarto Lua API</h5> <h6 id="utility-functions">Utility Functions</h6> <p>Various utility functions are provided:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.version</code></p> <p>Return the current Quarto version as a <code>pandoc.Version</code> object.</p> <p><code>quarto.log.output(obj)</code></p> <p>Dump a text representation of the passed object to stdout.</p> <p><code>quarto.utils.resolve_path(path)</code></p> <p>Compute the full path to a file that is installed alongside your extension’s Lua script. This is useful for internal resources that your filter needs but should not be visible to the user.</p> <p><code>quarto.utils.string_to_inlines(path, sep)</code></p> <p>Converts a string to a list of Pandoc Inlines, processing any Quarto custom syntax in the string.</p> <p><code>quarto.utils.string_to_blocks(path)</code></p> <p>Converts a string to a list of Pandoc Blocks, processing any Quarto custom syntax in the string.</p> <p>Quarto includes the <a href="https://github.com/wlupton/pandoc-lua-logging">pandoc-lua-logging</a> library, which should be used in preference to the dump function. For example, you can examine an element passed to a filter function as follows:</p> <pre><code>function Div(el) quarto.log.output(el) end</code></pre> <h6 id="require"><code>require()</code></h6> <p>In larger, more complex filters, it becomes useful to structure your Lua code in modules. Quarto overwrites the standard LUA <code>require()</code> to support the use of relative paths, so that small modules can be easily created and reused.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>filter.lua local utility = require('./utils') function Pandoc(doc) -- process end</code></pre> <p>Using relative paths makes it harder for multiple filters to accidentally create conflicting module names (as would eventually happen when using the standard Lua <code>require('utils')</code> syntax). It’s possible to refer to subdirectories and parent directories as well:</p> <pre><code>filter2.lua local parsing = require('./utils/parsing') function Pandoc(doc) -- process end utils/parsing.lua local utils = require("../utils") -- ...</code></pre> <h6 id="document-metadata">Document Metadata</h6> <p>Extensions may need to access the path for the input and output files. Quarto makes these variables available:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.input_file</code></p> <p>Full path to input file for the current render.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.output_file</code></p> <p>Full path to output file for the current render.</p> <h6 id="project-metadata">Project Metadata</h6> <p>Extensions may need to know about paths relevant to the project. Quarto makes these variables available:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.project.directory</code></p> <p>Full path to current project directory (<code>nil</code> if no project).</p> <p><code>quarto.project.output_directory</code></p> <p>Full path to current project output directory (<code>nil</code> if no project).</p> <p><code>quarto.project.offset</code></p> <p>Offset (relative path) from the directory of the current file to the root of the project (<code>nil</code> if no project).</p> <p><code>quarto.project.profile</code></p> <p>List of currently active project profiles.</p> <h6 id="format-detection">Format Detection</h6> <p>Extensions will often need to detect the current format to create custom content depending on the target output medium. The <code>quarto.doc.is_format()</code> function</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.is_format(name)</code></p> <p>Detect if the current format matches <code>name</code>.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.has_bootstrap()</code></p> <p>Query whether <a href="https://getbootstrap.com/">Bootstrap CSS</a> is available within the current document (it is by default for standard <code>html</code> documents but this may have been overridden by e.g. <code>theme: none</code>).</p> <p>The <code>name</code> parameter can match an exact Pandoc format name (e.g. <code>docx</code>, <code>latex</code>, etc. or can match based on an alias that groups commonly targeted formats together. The following values format aliases are handled specially by <code>quarto.doc.is_format()</code>:</p> <p>Alias</p> <p>Formats</p> <p><code>latex</code></p> <p><code>latex</code>, <code>pdf</code>, <code>beamer</code></p> <p><code>pdf</code></p> <p><code>latex</code>, <code>pdf</code>, <code>beamer</code></p> <p><code>epub</code></p> <p><code>epub*</code></p> <p><code>html</code></p> <p><code>html*</code>, <code>epub*</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, <code>dashboard</code>, <code>email</code></p> <p><code>html:js</code></p> <p><code>html*</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, <code>dashboard</code>, <code>email</code></p> <p><code>markdown</code></p> <p><code>markdown*</code>, <code>commonmark*</code>, <code>gfm</code>, <code>markua</code>, <code>hugo-md</code>, <code>docusaurus-md</code></p> <p><code>odt</code></p> <p><code>odt</code>, <code>opendocument</code></p> <p><code>hugo</code></p> <p><code>hugo-md</code></p> <p><code>docusaurus</code></p> <p><code>docusaurus-md</code></p> <p><code>asciidoc</code></p> <p><code>asciidoc</code>, <code>asciidoctor</code></p> <p>Note that the <code>html:js</code> alias indicates that the target format is capable of executing JavaScript (this maps to all HTML formats save for ePub).</p> <p>Other values supported are directly the name of the format, including Quarto’s specific formats like <code>dashboard</code>, <code>email</code>, or <code>confluence</code>.</p> <p>For example, here we check for PDF and HTML output:</p> <pre><code>if quarto.doc.is_format("pdf") then -- pdf specific output elseif quarto.doc.is_format("html") then -- html specific output else -- output for other formats end</code></pre> <p>For LaTeX output, you may need to additionally detect which citation utility and pdf engine are being used for the current render. You can use these functions to do that detection:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.cite_method()</code></p> <p>Returns a string (<code>citeproc</code>, <code>natbib</code>, or <code>biblatex</code>) indicating the cite method in use.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.pdf_engine()</code></p> <p>Returns a string (<code>pdflatex</code>, <code>xelatex</code>, <code>lualatex</code>, or <code>tectonic</code>) indicating the PDF engine being used to render the document.</p> <h6 id="includes-2">Includes</h6> <p>Sometimes extensions need to inject content into the target document. There are three locations that content can be included (pass one of these locations as the first argument of the include functions):</p> <p>Location</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>in-header</code></p> <p>In the header of the document (HTML <code><head></code> tag or LaTeX preamble)</p> <p><code>before-body</code></p> <p>Before the document body</p> <p><code>after-body</code></p> <p>After the document body</p> <p>Note that the included content should use the raw target format (e.g. HTML or LaTeX) rather than markdown. You can use these functions to include text or the contents of a file:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.include_text(location, text)</code></p> <p>Include text at the specified location (<code>in-header</code>, <code>before-body</code>, or <code>after-body</code>)</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.include_file(location, file)</code></p> <p>Include file at the specified location (<code>in-header</code>, <code>before-body</code>, or <code>after-body</code>). The path to the file should relative to the Lua script calling this function.</p> <p>For example the following code includes an HTML file after the body in the rendered document:</p> <pre><code>quarto.doc.include_file("after-body", "comments.html")</code></pre> <h6 id="dependencies-4">Dependencies</h6> <p>Extensions will sometimes want to add external dependencies (for example, a JavaScript library and related CSS, or the usage of a LaTeX package). This can be accomplished with the following functions:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.add_html_dependency(dep)</code></p> <p>Add an HTML dependency (additional resources and content) to a document. See docs on the HTML Dependencies below for additional details.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.attach_to_dependency(name, attach)</code></p> <p>Attach a file to an existing dependency. <code>attach</code> is a file path relative to the Lua filter or table with <code>path</code> and <code>name</code> for renaming the file as its copied.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.use_latex_package(pkg, opt)</code></p> <p>Adds a <code>\usepackage</code> statement to the LaTeX output (along an options string specified in <code>opt</code>)</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.add_format_resource(path)</code></p> <p>Add a format resource to the document. Format resources will be copied into the directory next to the rendered output. This is useful, for example, if your format references a <code>bst</code> or <code>cls</code> file which must be copied into the LaTeX output directory.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.add_resource(path)</code></p> <p>Add a resource file to the current render, copying that file to the same relative location in the output directory. Learn more about resource handling in Site Resources.</p> <p><code>quarto.doc.add_supporting(path)</code></p> <p>Add a supporting file to the current render, moving that file to the same relative location in the output directory. Supporting files can be cleaned up after rendering.</p> <p>For example, here we add a LaTeX package dependency:</p> <pre><code>quarto.doc.use_latex_package("gamebook")</code></pre> <h6 id="html-dependencies">HTML Dependencies</h6> <p>HTML Dependencies can bundle together JavaScript, CSS, and even arbitrary content to inject into the <code><head></code> of the document. These dependencies have a name and a version, which is used to ensure that the same dependency isn’t bundled into the document more than once.</p> <p>The <code>dep</code> object passed to <code>quarto.doc.add_html_dependency()</code> has the following fields:</p> <p>Field</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>name</code></p> <p>Unique name. Required.</p> <p><code>version</code></p> <p>Version number (as a string). Required.</p> <p><code>scripts</code></p> <p>List of scripts to include (paths can be absolute or relative to the Lua file calling the function). Scripts can be either a simple path or a script object.</p> <p><code>stylesheets</code></p> <p>List of CSS style-sheets to include (paths can be absolute or relative to the Lua file calling the function). Stylesheets can either be a simple path or a stylesheet object</p> <p><code>links</code></p> <p>List of link tags to add to the document. Each tag should be a table with <code>rel</code> and <code>href</code> (required) and optionally <code>type</code></p> <p><code>resources</code></p> <p>Additional files to copy to the input directory (each resource is an object with <code>name</code> (target file name in input directory) and <code>path</code> (source file name relative to Lua script).</p> <p><code>serviceworkers</code></p> <p>JavaScript serviceworker files that should be copied to the root output directory (can be a simple string file name or table with <code>path</code> and <code>name</code> for renaming the file as its copied).</p> <p><code>meta</code></p> <p>Table of optional <code>key = value</code> meta tags to insert into the document <code><head></code></p> <p><code>head</code></p> <p>Arbitrary string to include in document <code><head></code></p> <p>For example, here we add a dependency to a JavaScript library:</p> <pre><code>quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({ name = "glightbox", version = "3.2.0", scripts = {"glightbox.min.js"}, stylesheets = {"glightbox.min.css"} })</code></pre> <h6 id="script-object">Script Object</h6> <p>The easiest way to specify <code>scripts</code> is with simple paths. However, in some cases you may need to add attributes to the <code><script></code> tag or specify that the script should go after the body. In those cases pass a script object:</p> <p>Field</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>path</code></p> <p>Path to the script (relative to the calling Lua script)</p> <p><code>attribs</code></p> <p>Table with <code>key = value</code> attributes to add to the <code><script></code> tag</p> <p><code>afterBody</code></p> <p>Specify that the <code><script></code> tag should be inserted after the body</p> <p>For example, here update the previous example to add an <code>integrity</code> attribute to the script:</p> <pre><code>quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({ name = "glightbox", version = "3.2.0", scripts = { { path = "glightbox.min.js ", attribs = {integrity = "R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx"} } }, stylesheets = {"glightbox.min.css"} })</code></pre> <h6 id="stylesheet-object">Stylesheet Object</h6> <p>The easiest way to specify <code>stylesheets</code> is with simple paths. However, in some cases you may need to add attributes to the <code><link></code> tag generated for the stylesheet. In those cases pass a stylesheet object:</p> <p>Field</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>path</code></p> <p>Path to the stylesheet (relative to the calling Lua script)</p> <p><code>attribs</code></p> <p>Table with <code>key = value</code> attributes to add to the <code><link></code> tag</p> <p>For example, here we update the previous example to add an <code>integrity</code> attribute to the stylesheet:</p> <pre><code>quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({ name = "glightbox", version = "3.2.0", scripts = { { path = "glightbox.min.js ", attribs = {integrity = "R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx"} } }, stylesheets = { { path = "glightbox.min.css ", attribs = {integrity = "GYl1kPzQho1wx"} } } })</code></pre> <h6 id="custom-nodes-1">Custom Nodes</h6> <p>Quarto defines custom AST node types that you can create programmatically in Lua filters. For details on the node types themselves (fields available when processing nodes in filters), see Quarto AST: Custom Nodes.</p> <p>The constructors below accept the same fields as documented for each node type, with some additional flexibility:</p> <p>Constructor</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>tbl</code> fields</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>quarto.Callout(tbl)</code></p> <p>Creates a Callout.</p> <p>Required: <code>type</code></p> <p>Optional: <code>title</code>, <code>content</code>, <code>appearance</code>, <code>collapse</code>, <code>icon</code>, <code>attr</code></p> <p><code>title</code> and <code>content</code> accept strings. <code>attr</code> sets div attributes.</p> <p><code>quarto.Tabset(tbl)</code></p> <p>Creates a Tabset.</p> <p>Optional: <code>tabs</code>, <code>level</code>, <code>attr</code></p> <p>Use <code>quarto.Tab()</code> to create entries for <code>tabs</code>.</p> <p><code>quarto.Tab(tbl)</code></p> <p>Creates a Tab for use in a Tabset.</p> <p>Required: <code>title</code></p> <p>Optional: <code>content</code>, <code>active</code></p> <p><code>title</code> and <code>content</code> accept strings.</p> <p><code>quarto.ConditionalBlock(tbl)</code></p> <p>Creates a Conditional Block.</p> <p>Required: <code>node</code>, <code>behavior</code></p> <p>Optional: <code>condition</code></p> <p><code>quarto.FloatRefTarget(tbl)</code></p> <p>Creates a cross-referenceable float.</p> <p>Required: <code>type</code>, <code>content</code>, <code>identifier</code></p> <p>Optional: <code>caption_long</code>, <code>caption_short</code>, <code>classes</code>, <code>attributes</code>, <code>attr</code>, <code>parent_id</code></p> <p><code>attr</code> is an alternative to separate <code>identifier</code>, <code>classes</code>, <code>attributes</code> fields.</p> <h6 id="json-encoding">JSON Encoding</h6> <p>Quarto includes a copy of <a href="https://github.com/rxi/json.lua">json.lua</a>. a lightweight JSON library for Lua. You can access the JSON functions as follows:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.json.encode(input)</code></p> <p>Encode a Lua table into a JSON string.</p> <p><code>quarto.json.decode(str)</code></p> <p>Parse a JSON string into a Lua table.</p> <p>For example, here we encode and then decode a table:</p> <pre><code>local json = quarto.json.encode({foo = "bar"}) local obj = quarto.json.decode(json)</code></pre> <h6 id="base64-encoding">Base64 Encoding</h6> <p>Quarto includes a copy of <a href="https://github.com/iskolbin/lbase64">lbase64</a>, a pure Lua implementation of Base64 encoding. You can access the Base 64 encoding functions as follows:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.base64.encode(str)</code></p> <p>Encode a string into Base 64.</p> <p><code>quarto.base64.decode(b64str)</code></p> <p>Decode a Base 64 string.</p> <h6 id="paths">Paths</h6> <p>Quarto exposes paths to utilities that are likely to be useful to Lua extension and filter authors. Currently, only the ones below are supported:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.paths.rscript()</code></p> <p>Returns the path to <code>Rscript</code> that Quarto uses in the <code>knitr</code> engine and R files for <code>quarto run</code> scripts</p> <p><code>quarto.paths.tinytex_bin_dir()</code></p> <p>Returns the path to <code>TinyTeX</code> binaries directory (where <code>tlmgr</code>, <code>pdlatex</code> and others are). If Quarto did not install <code>TinyTeX</code> and does not found it, it will return <code>nil</code>. This means that PDF rendering by Quarto probably used tools found in PATH.</p> <p><code>quarto.paths.typst()</code></p> <p>Returns the path to <code>typst</code> used by Quarto.</p> <h6 id="shortcodes-5">Shortcodes</h6> <p>Quarto offers the following helper functions for shortcode developers, to be typically used in shortcode handlers. See the shortcode development documentation for more:</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.shortcode.read_arg(args, [n])</code></p> <p>Returns the <code>n</code>-th argument of the shortcode invocation</p> <p><code>quarto.shortcode.error_output(name, message_or_args, context)</code></p> <p>Creates output to be used by shortcodes to depict an execution error, consistently with how Quarto shows such outputs</p> <h6 id="metadata-access">Metadata Access</h6> <p>Quarto provides programmatic access to document and project metadata from Lua filters and scripts. This is useful when you need to access metadata values within filter logic rather than in shortcode contexts.</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.metadata.get(key)</code></p> <p>Return the value of a metadata entry as a <code>pandoc.MetaValue</code>, or <code>nil</code> if the key is missing. This is the Lua equivalent of the <code>{{< meta key >}}</code> shortcode.</p> <p>The <code>key</code> parameter can reference top-level metadata or use dot notation to access nested values. For example:</p> <pre><code>function Meta(meta) -- Get a simple metadata value local title = quarto.metadata.get("title") -- Check if a value exists before using it local customField = quarto.metadata.get("custom-field") if customField then -- Process the metadata value local value = pandoc.utils.stringify(customField) end return meta end</code></pre> <p>The function returns a <code>pandoc.MetaValue</code>, which may be a <code>MetaString</code>, <code>MetaInlines</code>, <code>MetaList</code>, <code>MetaMap</code>, or other <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#type-metavalue">Pandoc metadata types</a>. You can use <code>pandoc.utils.stringify()</code> to convert these to strings when needed:</p> <pre><code>function Pandoc(doc) -- Get metadata as MetaValue local metaValue = quarto.metadata.get("description") -- Convert to string for processing local description = pandoc.utils.stringify(metaValue) -- Handle complex metadata structures local keywords = quarto.metadata.get("keywords") if type(keywords) == "table" then -- Process as a list or map for k, v in pairs(keywords) do quarto.log.output(pandoc.utils.stringify(v)) end end return doc end</code></pre> <h6 id="variables-access">Variables Access</h6> <p>Quarto projects can define variables in <code>_variables.yml</code> files. These variables can be accessed programmatically from Lua using the <code>quarto.variables.get()</code> function.</p> <p>Function</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>quarto.variables.get(name)</code></p> <p>Return the value of a variable from <code>_variables.yml</code> as a string, or <code>nil</code> if the variable is not defined. This is the Lua equivalent of the <code>{{< var name >}}</code> shortcode.</p> <p>For example, if your <code>_variables.yml</code> contains:</p> <pre><code>site-url: [example.com](https://example.com) api-version: v2.1 feature-enabled: true</code></pre> <p>You can access these values in your Lua filter:</p> <pre><code>function Pandoc(doc) -- Get a variable value local siteUrl = quarto.variables.get("site-url") -- Use in conditional logic local apiVersion = quarto.variables.get("api-version") if apiVersion == "v2.1" then -- Add version-specific content end -- Check if a variable exists local featureFlag = quarto.variables.get("feature-enabled") if featureFlag then quarto.log.output("Feature flag: " .. featureFlag) end return doc end</code></pre> <p>Variables are always returned as strings (or <code>nil</code> if not found), so you may need to perform type conversions when working with numeric or boolean values:</p> <pre><code>function Pandoc(doc) -- Get a numeric variable local maxItems = quarto.variables.get("max-items") if maxItems then local count = tonumber(maxItems) if count and count > 10 then -- Process with numeric value end end -- Get a boolean variable local enabled = quarto.variables.get("feature-enabled") if enabled == "true" then -- Feature is enabled end return meta end</code></pre> <h3 id="lua-development">Lua Development</h3> <h4 id="lua-development-1">Lua Development</h4> <h5 id="overview-52">Overview</h5> <p>The programming language used to create filters and shortcodes is Lua, a lightweight, high-level scripting language. <a href="https://www.lua.org/">Lua</a> is the extension language for Pandoc (which includes an embedded Lua interpreter). This means that Quarto extensions have no additional runtime dependencies or requirements.</p> <p>This article will start by providing an orientation to learning Lua for those new to the language. Then, we’ll provide some tips for productive Lua development.</p> <p>See the Lua API Reference for additional details on the APIs available for developing extensions.</p> <h5 id="learning-lua">Learning Lua</h5> <p>Lua is a scripting language similar to Python, R, Julia, and JavaScript. If you are familiar with one or more of those languages you won’t have trouble picking up Lua.</p> <p>Here is a recommended approach for learning Lua for use with Quarto:</p> <ul> <li><p>Read <a href="https://learnxinyminutes.com/docs/lua/">Learn Lua in 15 Minutes</a> for a quick overview of the language and its syntax.</p></li> <li><p>Check out the first two sections of the <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html">Pandoc Lua Filters</a> documentation then skip ahead to the <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html#macro-substitution">Filter Examples</a> section to make things a bit more concrete.</p></li> <li><p>Once you have the basic idea of Lua and filters, get a more complete picture by skimming the full <a href="https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html">Pandoc Lua Filters</a> documentation. You won’t understand everything, but it’s a good orientation to all of the moving parts.</p></li> <li><p>Finally, check out the source code of the extensions published in the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext">Quarto Extensions</a> GitHub organization (these are extensions maintained by the Quarto core team). Once you are able to read and understand that code you are ready to start developing your own extensions! Some additional learning resources you might find useful include:</p></li> <li><p><a href="luarefv51.pdf">Lua Quick Reference</a>, a PDF with a compact summary of the language and base library.</p></li> <li><p><a href="https://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/8590379868/lua-pilindex-20">Programming in Lua</a>, a book by Roberto Ierusalimschy, the chief architect of the language.</p></li> <li><p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/">Lua Reference Manual</a>, a complete definition of the language and base library.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="development-tools">Development Tools</h5> <h6 id="quarto-preview">Quarto Preview</h6> <p>Quarto preview, <code>quarto preview</code>, is aware of Lua source files within extensions, and will automatically reload the preview whenever a Lua source file changes.</p> <p>This makes it very easy to incrementally develop and debug Lua code (especially when combined with the native format a described below). Live reloading for Lua files will work no matter what source code editor you are using (Positron, VS Code, RStudio, Neovim, etc.).</p> <h6 id="vs-code-positron">VS Code / Positron</h6> <p>While you can use any text editor along with <code>quarto preview</code> for developing Lua extensions, we strongly recommend that you consider using VS Code or Positron, as they provide a number of additional tools including:</p> <ul> <li>Code completion and type checking.</li> <li>Diagnostics for various common problems with code.</li> <li>The ability to add types to your own functions. Code completion covers the Lua base library as well as the Pandoc and Quarto Lua APIs, and also provides documentation on hover:</li> </ul> <p>Diagnostics check for many common errors including failing to check for <code>nil</code>, undefined global values, shadowing of local variables, unused functions, etc.</p> <h6 id="installation-5">Installation</h6> <p>To get started with using VS Code or Positron for Lua extension development, install the following software:</p> <ul> <li>Install the latest version (v1.2 or greater) of Quarto</li> <li>Install the latest version (v1.40.0 or greater) of the Quarto Extension (available on both <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">OpenVSX</a> and <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Microsoft’s marketplace</a>) .</li> <li>For Lua code intelligence, install the Lua LSP Extension (available on both <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/sumneko/lua">OpenVSX</a> and <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=sumneko.lua">Microsoft’s marketplace</a>). Once you’ve installed these components you should see the features described above appear automatically in your Quarto workspaces that include Lua code.</li> </ul> <p>There are many options available for configuring Lua completion and diagnostics. It’s also possible to provide type information for your own functions. See the section on Lua in Positron and VS Code below for details.</p> <h5 id="diagnostic-logging">Diagnostic Logging</h5> <p>Use the functions in the <code>quarto.log</code> module to add diagnostic logging to your extension. You can use both temporary logging calls to debug a particular problem as well as add logging calls that are always present but only activated when the <code>--trace</code> flag is passed to <code>quarto render</code> or <code>quarto preview</code>.</p> <p>The <code>quarto.log</code> module is based on the <a href="https://github.com/wlupton/pandoc-lua-logging">pandoc-lua-logging</a> project from <a href="https://github.com/wlupton"><span class="citation" data-cites="wlupton">@wlupton</span></a>. You’ll recognize the functions described below from that module (e.g. <code>logging.output()</code>, <code>logging.warning()</code>, etc). For documentation on using all of the logging functions see the project <a href="https://github.com/wlupton/pandoc-lua-logging">README</a> file.</p> <h6 id="quarto.log.output">quarto.log.output</h6> <p>To log any object (including Pandoc AST elements), use the <code>quarto.log.output()</code> function. For example, here we log the <code>Div</code> passed to us in our filter callback function as well as some diagnostic text:</p> <pre><code>filter.lua function Header(el) quarto.log.output("=== Handling Header ===") quarto.log.output(el) end</code></pre> <p>This is log output you’d see in the terminal when the filter is executed:</p> <pre><code>=== Handling Header === Header { attr: Attr { attributes: AttributeList {} classes: List {} identifier: "section-one" } content: Inlines { [1] Str "Section" [2] Space [3] Str "One" } level: 2 }</code></pre> <h6 id="quarto.log.warning">quarto.log.warning</h6> <p>Use the <code>quarto.log.warning()</code> function to output warnings that can be suppressed with the <code>--quiet</code> flag:</p> <pre><code>filter.lua function RawBlock(el) if el.format == "html" then quarto.log.warning("Raw HTML not supported") return pandoc.Null() end end</code></pre> <p>For example, the warning above will not appear for this call to <code>quarto render</code>:</p> <pre><code>quarto render document.qmd --quiet</code></pre> <h6 id="quarto.log.debug">quarto.log.debug</h6> <p>Use the <code>quarto.log.debug()</code> function to write output whenever the <code>--trace</code> flag is present:</p> <pre><code>filter.lua function Header(el) quarto.log.debug("Header: " .. el.identifier) end</code></pre> <p>For example, the debug message will appear for this call to <code>quarto preview</code>:</p> <pre><code>quarto preview document.qmd --trace</code></pre> <p>You can keep these calls in your filter since they won’t produce output unless <code>--trace</code> is specified.</p> <h5 id="native-format">Native Format</h5> <p>A great tool for understanding the behavior of a Lua filter or shortcode in more depth is to target the <code>native</code> format (as opposed to <code>html</code>, <code>pdf</code>, etc.). The <code>native</code> format will show you the raw contents of the Pandoc AST. For example, here’s a simple markdown document alongside its <code>native</code> output:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- format: native --- ## Heading Some text below Pandoc Meta { unMeta = fromList [] } [ Header 2 ( "heading" , [] , [] ) [ Str "Heading" ] , Para [ Str "Some" , Space , Str "text" , Space , Str "below" ] ]</code></pre> <p>Here we add a simple filter to the document that wraps all headers in <code>pandoc.Emph</code> (italics). You can see that the <code>Emph</code> AST element now wraps the heading text in the <code>native</code> output:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- format: native filters: [filter.lua] --- ## Heading Some text below filter.lua function Header(el) el.content = { pandoc.Emph(el.content) } return el end</code></pre> <p>Pandoc</p> <p>Meta</p> <p>{ unMeta = fromList [] }</p> <p>[ Header</p> <p>2</p> <p>( “heading” , [] , [] )</p> <p>[ Emph [ Str “Heading” ]</p> <p>]</p> <p>, Para</p> <p>[ Str “Some”</p> <p>, Space</p> <p>, Str “text”</p> <p>, Space</p> <p>, Str “below”</p> <p>]</p> <p>]</p> <h5 id="lua-in-positron-and-vs-code">Lua in Positron and VS Code</h5> <h6 id="type-hints">Type Hints</h6> <p>While Quarto provides type information for the Pandoc and Quarto Lua APIs, this doesn’t cover functions that you write within your own extensions. You can however add type information using <a href="https://luals.github.io/wiki/annotations">Annotations</a>. For example, here we indicate that a function takes a <code>string</code> and a <code>pandoc.List()</code> and returns either a <code>pandoc.List()</code> or <code>nil</code>:</p> <pre><code>---@param text string ---@param blocks pandoc.List ---@return pandoc.List|nil function check_for_text(text, blocks) -- implementation end</code></pre> <p>With these type declarations, any attempt to call the function without the correct types will result in a diagnostic message. Further, if a caller fails to check for <code>nil</code> before using the return value a diagnostic will also occur.</p> <p>You can learn more about all of the available type annotations in the <a href="https://luals.github.io/wiki/annotations">Annotations Reference</a> for the Lua Language Server.</p> <h6 id="settings">Settings</h6> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/sumneko/lua">Lua Language Server</a> extension includes a wide variety of options to customize its behavior (e.g. what diagnostics to show, which completions to offer, etc.).</p> <p>All of the available options are documented in the <a href="https://luals.github.io/wiki/settings/">Settings Reference</a> for the Lua Language Server.</p> <p>Quarto provides a default configuration file (<code>.luarc.json</code>) within the root of any workspace that includes Quarto Lua extensions. This file is necessary because it provides a reference to the Lua type definitions for Pandoc and Quarto within your currently installed version of Quarto. Without it, the Lua extension wouldn’t know anything about Quarto and would report errors for “unknown” Pandoc modules.</p> <p>If, for example, Quarto is installed at <code>/opt/quarto/</code>, the default contents of the configuration file will be:</p> <pre><code>.luarc.json { "Generator": ["Quarto"], "Lua.runtime.version": "Lua 5.3", "Lua.workspace.checkThirdParty": false, "Lua.workspace.library": ["/opt/quarto/share/lua-types"], "Lua.runtime.plugin": "/opt/quarto/share/lua-plugin/plugin.lua", "Lua.completion.showWord": "Disable", "Lua.completion.keywordSnippet": "Both", "Lua.diagnostics.disable": ["lowercase-global", "trailing-space"] }</code></pre> <p>The <code>.luarc.json</code> file will also be automatically added to <code>.gitignore</code> since it points to the absolute path of Quarto on the local system.</p> <p>You can change any of the settings within this file save for the <code>Lua.workspace.library</code> and <code>Lua.runtime.plugin</code> (these are automatically maintained by the Quarto extension based on where Quarto is installed). See the <a href="https://luals.github.io/wiki/settings/">Settings Reference</a> for all available settings.</p> <p>If you prefer to manage this file manually, simply remove the <code>Generator</code> key and Quarto will no longer update the <code>Lua.workspace.library</code> and <code>Lua.runtime.plugin</code> settings automatically.</p> <p>You can also globally disable the automatic creation of <code>.luarc.json</code> using the Quarto > Lua: Provide Types setting.</p> <h3 id="managing-extensions">Managing Extensions</h3> <h4 id="managing-extensions-1">Managing Extensions</h4> <h5 id="installation-6">Installation</h5> <p>If you want to use an extension within a document or project you need to add it to a project or directory. Rather than installing into a global library, Quarto extensions are stored locally, directly alongside the document or project they are used within. For example, if you have a project in a directory named <code>myblog</code>, you could add some extensions for use with that the project as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal cd myblog quarto add quarto-ext/fontawesome quarto add quarto-ext/video</code></pre> <p>This will result in an <code>_extensions</code> folder being created at the root of your project, and the <code>fontawesome</code> and <code>video</code> extensions being placed within it.</p> <p>Note that a project isn’t strictly required for using extensions—if you add extensions in a directory that isn’t a project then any document located directly alongside the <code>_extensions</code> folder can use the extensions.</p> <p>WarningExtension Trust</p> <p>Quarto extensions may execute code when documents are rendered. Therefore, if you do not trust the author of an extension, we recommend that you do not install or use the extension.</p> <h6 id="version-control">Version Control</h6> <p>If you are using version control you should check the <code>_extensions</code> directory in to your repo along with your other code. Extensions used by a document or project are treated as source code to ensure very long term reproducibility—your project doesn’t need to rely on the availability of an external package manager (or the maintenance of older extension versions) to successfully render now and far into the future.</p> <h5 id="repositories">Repositories</h5> <p>The extensions in the example above were prefixed with <code>quarto-ext</code> because they were distributed from the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/">quarto-ext</a> GitHub organization. Extensions can be similarly distributed from any GitHub organization. So for example the following might also be valid command to add extensions to a project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add cooltools/lightbox quarto add bigstateu/fancytweet</code></pre> <p>While it’s convenient to distribute extensions using GitHub, you can also bundle them into a <code>.zip</code> or <code>.tar.gz</code> archive and distribute them using a URL or a local file. See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h5 id="updating">Updating</h5> <p>You can list and update configured extensions for a given project with the following commands:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto list extensions quarto update quarto-ext/fontawesome</code></pre> <p>Note that when updating an extension you’ll be prompted to confirm the update based on the version you have and the version you are attempting to update to.</p> <h5 id="removing">Removing</h5> <p>Use this command to remove an extension from a project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto remove quarto-ext/fontawesome</code></pre> <p>If you run the <code>quarto remove extension</code> command with no <code>extension-id</code>, you will be presented with a list of extensions that are present and you may select which extensions to remove.</p> <h3 id="metadata-extensions">Metadata Extensions</h3> <h4 id="metadata-extensions-1">Metadata Extensions</h4> <p>Metadata extensions are Quarto extensions that provide metadata (YAML objects) that can be merged to existing Quarto configurations in a reusable manner.</p> <p>Important</p> <p>Currently, metadata extensions only merge project-level metadata. (If there is no project, a temporary default project is created in memory.)</p> <p>This limitation will be lifted in the future.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-6">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple metadata extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension metadata</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the metadata extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension metadata ? Extension Name › my-prerender-scripts</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>my-prerender-scripts</code> and press Enter—the metadata extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>? Extension Name › my-prerender-scripts Creating extension at /Users/cscheid/Desktop/my-prerender-scripts: - Created README.md - Created _extensions/my-prerender-scripts/_extension.yml - Created .gitignore ? Open With ❯ vscode rstudio (don't open)</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <h5 id="contents-of-metadata-extensions">Contents of Metadata Extensions</h5> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/my-prerender-scripts/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/my-prerender-scripts/_extension.yml title: My-prerender-scripts author: Carlos Scheidegger version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=99.9.0" contributes: metadata: project: # your per-project metadata goes here</code></pre> <h5 id="how-metadata-extensions-work">How Metadata Extensions Work</h5> <p>Under the <code>project</code> key, any YAML you add will be automatically merged to any project using this extension. This behaves differently from custom project extensions. Quarto projects using metadata extensions do not need to change their project types for the metadata to be merged.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>As noted above, metadata extensions only merge project-level metadata in the <code>project</code> key (empty if there is no project).</p> <p>This limitation will be lifted in the future.</p> <h3 id="notebook-filters">Notebook Filters</h3> <h4 id="notebook-filters-1">Notebook Filters</h4> <h5 id="overview-53">Overview</h5> <p>If you are rendering existing Jupyter notebooks that were not created with Quarto in mind, you may wish to do some pre-processing on the notebook prior to its conversion to markdown. This can be accomplished by specifying one or more <code>ipynb-filters</code>. These filters are passed the <a href="https://nbformat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format_description.html">JSON representation</a> of the notebook on <code>stdin</code> and should write a transformed JSON representation to <code>stdout</code>.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The purpose of notebook filters is to adapt existing <code>.ipynb</code> files for use with Quarto. Consequently, notebook filters are only run when the original input is an <code>.ipynb</code> file (they are not run for <code>.qmd</code> files).</p> <h5 id="example-4">Example</h5> <p>For example, this notebook filter uses the <a href="https://nbformat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html">nbformat</a> package to read a notebook, prepend a comment to the source of each code cell, and then write it back to <code>stdout</code>:</p> <pre><code>import sys import nbformat # read notebook from stdin nb = nbformat.reads(sys.stdin.read(), as_version = 4) # prepend a comment to the source of each cell for index, cell in enumerate(nb.cells): if cell.cell_type == 'code': cell.source = "# comment\n" + cell.source # write notebook to stdout nbformat.write(nb, sys.stdout)</code></pre> <p>You can arrange for this filter to be run using the <code>ipynb-filters</code> option (specified at either the document or project level):</p> <pre><code>--- ipynb-filters: - filter.py ---</code></pre> <p>Note that the current working directory for the filter will be set to the location of the input notebook.</p> <h3 id="project-types">Project Types</h3> <h4 id="project-types-1">Project Types</h4> <h5 id="overview-54">Overview</h5> <p>Custom project types provide the ability to tailor projects for a particular purpose. This could be used to create a project type that implements an organization-level standard for creating documentation or conducting analyses.</p> <p>For example, if you created a project type extension called <code>lexdocs</code>, it could be used with:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: lexdocs</code></pre> <p>This single line of configuration could provide:</p> <ul> <li><p>Navigational elements</p></li> <li><p>Headers and footers</p></li> <li><p>Document filters</p></li> <li><p>Graphical elements</p></li> <li><p>HTML options and styles If you additionally include some basic scaffolding as a Starter Template for using the project type, and host it within a GitHub repository, then users could get a new project up and running as simply as:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto use template lexcorp/lexdocs</p></li> </ul> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute project type extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h5 id="development-tools-1">Development Tools</h5> <p>If you are using custom project types within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio, only the very latest versions of these tools handle custom project types correctly:</p> <ul> <li>For the Quarto VS Code Extension, use <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">version 1.45</a> or greater.</li> <li>For RStudio, use <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">version 2022.12</a> or higher. Please be sure to update your version(s) of these tools before proceeding.</li> </ul> <h5 id="complete-example">Complete Example</h5> <p>In this section we’ll describe exactly what a project type extension should include by providing a complete example of the <code>lexdocs</code> project type alluded to above. Here are the files contained in our <code>lexdocs</code> project type:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml index.qmd team.qmd _extensions lexdocs/ _extension.yml lexcorp.png theme.scss filter.lua</code></pre> <p>Note that this repository provides both:</p> <ul> <li>The project type extension (contained in the <code>_extensions</code> directory).</li> <li>A starter template for using the project type (the <code>_quarto.yml</code>, <code>index.qmd</code>, and <code>team.qmd</code> files in the root of the repository).</li> </ul> <h6 id="project-type-extension">Project Type Extension</h6> <p>Let’s explore the code for the extension first. Here is the main <code>_extension.yml</code> file:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/lexdocs/_extension.yml title: Lexdocs Project author: Lexcorp, Inc. version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.0" contributes: project: project: type: website website: sidebar: contents: auto search: true style: docked background: light logo: lexcorp.png page-footer: | "Copyright 2022, Lexcorp, Inc." format: lexdocs-html formats: html: theme: [default, theme.scss] code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: true filters: - filter.lua</code></pre> <p>The <code>contributes</code> key includes a <code>project</code> entry, which in turn defines the default values for the <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file when this project type is used.</p> <p>Note that custom project types always need to inherit from one of the base project types built into Quarto (<code>default</code>, <code>website</code>, or <code>book</code>). Here we specify <code>project: type: website</code>.</p> <p>You’ll also note that we additionally define a <code>lexdocs-html</code> Custom Format within the extension (and then make that the default format for the project). This enables us to reference that format explicitly within documents (e.g. if you want to include a document that renders both <code>pdf</code> and <code>lexdocs-html</code> variations).</p> <p>There are three additional files referenced in the custom <code>project</code> definition in <code>_extension.yml</code>. We won’t show their source code, but here’s a rundown on the role they play:</p> <ul> <li><code>lexcorp.png</code> is a logo added to the <code>sidebar</code>.</li> <li><code>theme.scss</code> provides a custom theme for HTML output.</li> <li><code>filter.lua</code> provides some additional transformations required by the format.</li> </ul> <h6 id="starter-template">Starter Template</h6> <p>This repository also provides a starter template by including these files at the root of the repository:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>_quarto.yml</code> is the project configuration file</p></li> <li><p><code>index.qmd</code> is an empty default home page</p></li> <li><p><code>team.qmd</code> is a page where users of the project type are encouraged to list the team members who contributed. Here’s what <code>_quarto.yml</code> might look like:</p> <p>_quarto.yml</p> <p>project: title: “Docs Site” type: lexdocs</p> <p>format: lexdocs-html: toc: true</p></li> </ul> <p>Users of the template will naturally change the default <code>title</code>, and can add whatever other project-, website-, or format-level options they require (these options will be merged with the defaults provided by the extension).</p> <h5 id="markdown-publishing">Markdown Publishing</h5> <p>If you are using Quarto to produce markdown for another publishing system, you can use a project type extension to tailor the markdown output created by Quarto, as well as integrate with the native preview capabilities of the other system.</p> <p>Quarto includes a couple of built-in project-types for integrating with the Hugo and Docusaurus publishing systems. You can see the source code for these project types here:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/extensions/quarto/hugo/_extension.yml"><code>hugo</code></a> project type</li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/extensions/quarto/docusaurus/_extension.yml"><code>docusaurus</code></a> project type</li> </ul> <h6 id="hugo-example">Hugo Example</h6> <p>Here is the <code>_extension.yml</code> file for the Hugo project type (this demonstrates a few of the additional options you’d typically specify when creating a project type for markdown publishing, we’ll describe these options below):</p> <pre><code>_extension.yml title: Hugo author: RStudio, PBC organization: quarto contributes: project: project: type: default detect: - ["config.toml", "content"] - ["config/_default/config.toml", "content"] render: - "**/*.qmd" - "**/*.ipynb" preview: serve: cmd: "hugo serve --port {port} --bind {host} --navigateToChanged" env: HUGO_RELATIVEURLS: "true" ready: "Web Server is available at" format: hugo-md formats: md: variant: gfm+yaml_metadata_block+definition_lists prefer-html: true fig-format: retina fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 wrap: preserve</code></pre> <p>Let’s look specifically at some project options provided for Hugo that you may not have seen before:</p> <pre><code>project: type: default detect: - ["config.toml", "content"] - ["config/_default/config.toml", "content"] render: - "**/*.qmd" - "**/*.ipynb" preview: serve: cmd: "hugo serve --port {port} --bind {host} --navigateToChanged" env: HUGO_RELATIVEURLS: "true" ready: "Web Server is available at"</code></pre> <p>The <code>detect</code> option enables Quarto to automatically detect when to activate this project type based on the presence of one or more files.</p> <p>The <code>render</code> option indicates which files Quarto should render (note that by default Quarto will render <code>.md</code> files, but this would interfere with Hugo’s native rendering of <code>.md</code> files so we exclude them here).</p> <p>The <code>preview</code> option enables <code>quarto preview</code> to launch the native preview server for Hugo. The <code>cmd</code> indicates the shell command to use (with spots to interpolate the <code>{port}</code> and <code>{host</code>}); the <code>env</code> option specifies values for environment variables; and the <code>ready</code> option is a sequence of characters to look for to indicate that the preview server has started and is ready to handle requests.</p> <h6 id="markdown-formats-3">Markdown Formats</h6> <p>When creating a project type for a markdown publishing system you’ll always need to define a custom format along with it which defines what flavor of markdown to produce. In the case of Hugo we define the markdown flavor using the <code>variant</code> option:</p> <pre><code>formats: md: variant: gfm+yaml_metadata_block+definition_lists+smart</code></pre> <p>This results in GitHub Flavored Markdown w/ YAML metadata blocks (which Hugo requires for tags/categories/etc) in addition to support for definition lists and smart typography.</p> <p>Note that for some systems you’ll need to do more than just declare a variant. For example, in the case of Docusaurus we declare the variant as well as a Lua filter that deals with Docusaurus-specific constructs like MDX, Callouts, and Tabsets:</p> <pre><code>formats: md: variant: +yaml_metadata_block+pipe_tables+tex_math_dollars+header_attributes-all_symbols_escapable filters: - docusaurus.lua</code></pre> <p>A project type for any given markdown publishing system will have its own variant, and will often also require filters to deal with non-standard constructs and other vagaries of the target system.</p> <h3 id="quarto-extensions">Quarto Extensions</h3> <h4 id="quarto-extensions-1">Quarto Extensions</h4> <p>Extensions are a powerful way to modify and extend the behavior of Quarto. Below is a listing of available extensions (please <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/tree/main/docs/extensions/listings">let us know</a> if you have an extension you’d like to see added to the list).</p> <p>See the articles on Creating Extensions to learn how to develop your own extensions.</p> <h5 id="shortcodes-and-filters">Shortcodes and Filters</h5> <p>Name</p>
