href="https://github.com/coatless-quarto/toggle">toggle</a></p> <p>Toggle Code Output in Quarto HTML Documents</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/coatless/">James Joseph Balamuta</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/jfsalzmann/quarto-typst-equations">typst-equations</a></p> <p>Write equations in quarto math blocks using Typst Math syntax. Works for both Typst-PDF (raw) and HTML (via cached SVG rendering) output formats.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/jfsalzmann">Johann-Friedrich Salzmann</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/christopherkenny/typst-function">typst-function</a></p> <p>Output divs and spans as Typst functions.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/christopherkenny">Christopher T. Kenny</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/sverrirarnors/typst-math">typst-math</a></p> <p>Changes math block syntax from LaTeX to Typst math.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/sverrirarnors">Sverrir Arnórsson</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/mcanouil/quarto-typst-render">typst-render</a></p> <p>A Quarto filter that compiles Typst code blocks to images (PNG, SVG, or PDF) using the bundled Typst binary, making Typst usable across all output formats.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/mcanouil">Mickaël CANOUIL</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/dragonstyle/unsplash">unsplash</a></p> <p>Shortcode to use Unsplash images within documents.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/dragonstyle">dragonstyle</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/leovan/quarto-watermark">watermark</a></p> <p>A Quarto filter to add watermark for html and pdf format output.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/leovan">范叶亮 > Leo Van</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/coatless/quarto-webr">webr</a></p> <p>Embed <a href="https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/">WebR</a> in HTML documents to enable interactive R code cells without the need for an R server.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/coatless/">James Joseph Balamuta</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/andrewheiss/quarto-wordcount">wordcount</a></p> <p>Quarto extension for calculating accurate word counts</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/andrewheiss/">Andrew Heiss</a></p> <p>No matching items</p> <h3 id="revealjs-plugins">Revealjs Plugins</h3> <h4 id="revealjs-plugins-1">Revealjs Plugins</h4> <h5 id="overview-55">Overview</h5> <p>Revealjs plugins enable you to extend the capabilities of HTML presentations created with Revealjs. The Reveal Plugin API is very rich, and many of the built-in capabilities of Quarto Revealjs presentations are implemented as plugins, including <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/plugins/menu">Menu</a>, <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/plugins/chalkboard">Chalkboard</a>, and <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/plugins/pdfexport">PDF Export</a>.</p> <p>Here are some examples of Revealjs plugins packaged as Quarto extensions:</p> <p>Extension</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/pointer">Pointer</a></p> <p>Adds support for switching the cursor to a ‘pointer’ style element while presenting.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/attribution">Attribution</a></p> <p>Display attribution text along the right edge of slides.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-7">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple Revealjs plugin extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension revealjs-plugin</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the plugin extension to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension revealjs-plugin ? Extension Name › shuffler</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>shuffler</code> and press Enter—the Revealjs plugin extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>Creating extension at /Users/jjallaire/quarto/dev/shuffler: - Created README.md - Created _extensions/shuffler/_extension.yml - Created _extensions/shuffler/shuffler.css - Created _extensions/shuffler/shuffler.js - Created .gitignore - Created example.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/shuffler/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/shuffler/_extension.yml title: Shuffler author: J.J. Allaire version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.222" contributes: revealjs-plugins: - name: RevealShuffler script: - shuffler.js stylesheet: - shuffler.css _extensions/shuffler/shuffler.js window.RevealShuffler = function () { return { id: "RevealShuffler", init: function (deck) { // TODO: Implement your plugin functionality // Learn more at [revealjs.com](https://revealjs.com/creating-plugins/) // This example shuffles the deck when the 'T' key is pressed deck.addKeyBinding({ keyCode: 84, key: "T" }, () => { deck.shuffle(); }); }, }; };</code></pre> <p>There is also a <code>shuffler.css</code> file for providing any styles required by your plugin.</p> <p>Finally, the <code>example.qmd</code> file includes code that exercises the extension. For example:</p> <pre><code>example.qmd --- title: "Shuffler Example" format: revealjs: default revealjs-plugins: - shuffler --- ## Breakfast - Eat eggs - Drink coffee ## Dinner - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine</code></pre> <p>To develop your plugin, render/preview <code>example.qmd</code>, and then make changes to <code>shuffler.js</code> and <code>shuffler.css</code> (the preview will automatically refresh when you change these files).</p> <h5 id="installation-and-use">Installation and Use</h5> <p>If your extension source code it located within a GitHub repository, then it can be added by referencing the GitHub organization and repository name. For example, you can install the <code>attribution</code> extension with the following:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-ext/attribution</code></pre> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <p>Once an extension has been added, you can use the Reveal plugin by adding it to the <code>reveal-plugins</code> key. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Presentation" format: revealjs revealjs-plugins: - attribution ---</code></pre> <h5 id="plugin-packaging">Plugin Packaging</h5> <p>Note that the plugins listed above were not initially developed for use with Quarto. Rather, they were developed intially as native Revealjs plugins and then packaged as Quarto extensions.</p> <p>For example, you can find the original implementation of the attribution plugin here: <a href="https://github.com/rschmehl/reveal-plugins/tree/main/attribution">github.com</a>. The plugin is implemented with a JavaScript file and a CSS file. To make the plugin available as a Quarto extension, we package these files along with an <code>_extension.yml</code> config file that registers the plugin. Here are the files in the Quarto extension:</p> <pre><code>LICENSE README.md example.qmd _extensions/ attribution/ _extension.yml attribution.js attribution.css</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>LICENSE</code> and <code>README.md</code> are standard documentation files and the <code>example.qmd</code> is used for development and documentation of the extension. None of those files are actually installed by end users (rather only the contents of the <code>_extensions</code> directory is installed).</p> <p>You can see the full source code of the Quarto version here: <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/attribution">github.com</a> (we’ll also walk through the code in detail below).</p> <h5 id="plugin-development">Plugin Development</h5> <p>You can develop either entirely new Revealjs plugins from scratch or you can package existing Revealjs extensions as described above.</p> <p>Here is a list of existing 3rd party plugins for Revealjs that you might consider packaging as Quarto extensions: <a href="https://github.com/hakimel/reveal.js/wiki/Plugins,-Tools-and-Hardware">github.com</a>.</p> <p>If you want to develop new plugins, check out the Quarto Reveal extensions listed above as well as the code of other 3rd party Reveal Plugins. The following documentation on the Revealjs website provides additional important technical details:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://revealjs.com/api/">API Methods</a></li> <li><a href="https://revealjs.com/events/">Reveal Events</a></li> </ul> <h5 id="plugin-configuration">Plugin Configuration</h5> <p>Some Revealjs plugins make available various user options. If you are developing a plugin from scratch, you should use a distinct key for your plugin’s configuration. Users can use this key alongside other <code>revealjs</code> options. For example the <code>pointer</code> extension can be configured as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Example Presentation" format: revealjs: pointer: pointerSize: 18 color: '#32cd32' revealjs-plugins: - pointer ---</code></pre> <p>The extension accesses options using the <code>deck.getConfig()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>return { id: "pointer", init: (deck) => { const config = deck.getConfig(); const options = config.pointer || {}; // etc } }</code></pre> <p>Note that when packaging an existing Revealjs plugin, you can override its default configuration using the <code>config</code> key within your <code>_extension.yml</code> file. For example, these are the overrides provided by the <code>pointer</code> extension:</p> <pre><code>title: Pointer author: Charles Teague contributes: revealjs-plugins: - name: RevealPointer script: - pointer.js stylesheet: - pointer.css config: pointer: key: "q" color: "red" pointerSize: 16 alwaysVisible: false</code></pre> <h5 id="example-attribution">Example: Attribution</h5> <p>Here we’ll walk through the complete source code for the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/attribution/">attribution</a> extension. This extension enables you to display attribution text sideways along the right edge of Revealjs slides.</p> <p>Here are source files used to develop the extension:</p> <pre><code>LICENSE README.md example.qmd _extensions/ attribution/ _extension.yml attribution.js attribution.css</code></pre> <p>The <code>example.qmd</code> and documentation files are used for development of the extension only (it is not installed by end users). The other files provide extension registration (<code>_extension.yml</code>) and the actual implementation of the Revealjs plugin (<code>attribution.js</code> and <code>attribution.css</code>).</p> <p>The <code>example.qmd</code> is a simple one-slide presentation that includes an image along with a div with class <code>.attribution</code>:</p> <pre><code>example.qmd --- title: "Attribution Extension" format: revealjs revealjs-plugins: - attribution --- ## Forest Image ![](ingtotheforest.jpg) ::: {.attribution) Photo courtesy of [@ingtotheforest](https://unsplash.com/@ingtotheforest) :::</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>revealjs-plugins</code> key references the <code>attribution</code> extension, which will implemented in the <code>_extensions/attribution</code> directory.</p> <p>The <code>_extension.yml</code> file indicates that the extension is making available a Revealjs plugin along with the plugin name, script, and style-sheets (note that the plugin name is not arbitrary, it will be whatever name is used within the script that implements the plugin, in this case <code>RevealAttribution</code>):</p> <pre><code>_extensions/attribution/_extension.yml title: Attribution author: Roland Schmehl version: 0.1.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.0" contributes: revealjs-plugins: - name: RevealAttribution script: - attribution.js stylesheet: - attribution.css</code></pre> <p>The <code>attribution.js</code> file contains the implementation of the Plugin using the Revealjs Plugin API:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/attribution/attribution.js window.RevealAttribution = window.RevealAttribution || { id: 'RevealAttribution', init: function(deck) { initAttribution(deck); } }; const initAttribution = function(Reveal){ var ready = false; var resize = false; var scale = 1; window.addEventListener( 'ready', function( event ) { var content; // Remove configured margin of the presentation var attribution = document.getElementsByClassName("attribution"); var width = window.innerWidth; var configuredWidth = Reveal.getConfig().width; var configuredHeight = Reveal.getConfig().height; scale = 1/(1-Reveal.getConfig().margin); for (var i = 0; i < attribution.length; i++) { content = attribution[i].innerHTML; attribution[i].style.width = configuredWidth + "px"; attribution[i].style.height = configuredHeight + "px"; attribution[i].innerHTML = "<span class='content'>" + content + "</span>"; attribution[i].style.transform = 'translate( -50%, -50% ) scale( ' + scale*100 + '% ) rotate(-180deg)'; } // Scale with cover class to mimic backgroundSize cover resizeCover(); }); window.addEventListener( 'resize', resizeCover ); function resizeCover() { // Scale to mimic backgroundSize cover var attribution = document.getElementsByClassName("attribution"); var xScale = window.innerWidth / Reveal.getConfig().width; var yScale = window.innerHeight / Reveal.getConfig().height; var s = 1; if (xScale > yScale) { // The div fits perfectly in x axis, stretched in y s = xScale/yScale; } for (var i = 0; i < attribution.length; i++) { attribution[i].style.transform = 'translate( -50%, -50% ) scale( ' + s*scale*100 + '% ) rotate(-180deg)'; } } };</code></pre> <p>Finally, <code>attribution.css</code> includes the CSS that repositions and rotates the element with class <code>.attribution</code> on the far right side of the slide:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/attribution/attribution.css /* Attribution plugin: text along the right edge of the viewport */ .attribution{ position: absolute; top: 50%; bottom: auto; left: 50%; right: auto; font-size: 0.4em; pointer-events: none; text-align: center; writing-mode: vertical-lr; transform: translate( -50%, -50% ) scale( 100% ) rotate(-180deg); } /* Attribution plugin: activate pointer events for attribution text only */ .attribution .content{ pointer-events: auto; }</code></pre> <h3 id="starter-templates">Starter Templates</h3> <h4 id="starter-templates-1">Starter Templates</h4> <h5 id="overview-56">Overview</h5> <p>Starter templates provide a straightforward way for users to get started with new Quarto projects by providing example content and options. You might use starter templates to:</p> <ul> <li>Create a working initial document for Journal Articles or Custom Formats.</li> <li>Provide the initial content for a custom Project Type.</li> <li>Scaffold a standard form of data analysis project used by your organization. Starter templates are essentially just GitHub repositories that are copied to a new directory on the user’s system. As we’ll describe below in Extensions & Templates, often times the repository for a custom format is also used as a starter template.</li> </ul> <h5 id="creating-a-template">Creating a Template</h5> <p>To create a starter template, just create a GitHub repository that includes the files you want copied into projects created with the template. All of the files in the repository are copied except for:</p> <ul> <li>Hidden files (any file or directory name that starts with <code>.</code> (e.g. <code>.gitignore</code>).</li> <li>Common GitHub repository files like <code>README.md</code> and <code>LICENSE</code>.</li> <li>AI assistant configuration files (<code>CLAUDE.md</code>, <code>AGENTS.md</code>). If you’d like, you can also include a <code>.quartoignore</code> file in the root of your repository listing other files or directories you’d like to exclude. Each line of the file should be a glob describing file(s) to ignore (using syntax like a <code>.gitignore</code> file).</li> </ul> <h6 id="template.qmd">template.qmd</h6> <p>There is one special file you’ll typically want to include in templates that target creation of documents (as opposed to projects): <code>template.qmd</code>. There are two reasons to include a <code>template.qmd</code>:</p> <ul> <li>It provides an easy way to test that your template is working as expected.</li> <li>When the template is copied into the target directory, the <code>template.qmd</code> will automatically be renamed to match the name that the user provided for the directory. If you are creating a template that targets creation of a website or book, a <code>template.qmd</code> is generally not necessary (as the <code>index.qmd</code> file already serves this purpose).</li> </ul> <h5 id="using-a-template">Using a Template</h5> <p>Once you’ve created the template repository and pushed it to GitHub, it can be instantiated with the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use template cooltools/cool-project</code></pre> <p>This command copies the contents of the GitHub repository at <code>https://github.com/cooltools/cool-project</code> to the local system (excluding selected files as discussed above).</p> <p>If the command is run in an empty directory, the user will be prompted whether they’d like to use the existing directory or create a new directory. If the command is run in a directory which contains other files or directories, they’ll be prompted for the name of a directory to create.</p> <h5 id="extensions-templates">Extensions & Templates</h5> <p>When creating Journal Articles, Custom Formats, or Project Type extensions, we recommend that you additionally provide a starter template to make it easy for users to get started.</p> <p>This is generally as easy as adding a <code>template.qmd</code> file to your extension that demonstrates its use. With this configuration, users can either begin using your extension via the template or by a conventional <code>quarto install</code> of the extension.</p> <p>For example, consider the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/acm">ACM</a> Journal Article extension. The extension repository supports either getting started with a template:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use template quarto-journals/acm</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, you can add the format (without the template) into an existing project or directory:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-journals/acm</code></pre> <h2 id="frequently-asked-questions">Frequently asked questions</h2> <h3 id="faq-for-r-markdown-users">FAQ for R Markdown Users</h3> <h4 id="faq-for-r-markdown-users-1">FAQ for R Markdown Users</h4> <p>Answers to R Markdown users’ most frequently asked questions about Quarto.</p> <h5 id="what-can-i-use-quarto-for">What can I use Quarto for?</h5> <p>Quarto® is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system built on Pandoc. You can weave together narrative text and code to produce elegantly formatted output as documents, web pages, blog posts, books and more.</p> <h5 id="quarto-sounds-similar-to-r-markdown.-what-is-the-difference-and-why-create-a-new-project">Quarto sounds similar to R Markdown. What is the difference and why create a new project?</h5> <p>At its core, Quarto works the same way as R Markdown:</p> <p>The goal of Quarto is to make the process of creating and collaborating on scientific and technical documents dramatically better. Quarto combines the functionality of R Markdown, bookdown, distill, xaringian, etc into a single consistent system with “batteries included” that reflects everything we’ve learned from R Markdown over the past 10 years.</p> <p>The number of languages and runtimes used for scientific discourse is very broad (and the Jupyter ecosystem in particular is extraordinarily popular). Quarto is at its core multi-language and multi-engine (supporting Knitr, Jupyter, and Observable today and potentially other engines tomorrow).</p> <p>On the other hand, R Markdown is fundamentally tied to R which severely limits the number of practitioners it can benefit. Quarto is Posit’s attempt to bring R Markdown to everyone! Unlike R Markdown, Quarto doesn’t have a dependency or requirement for R. Quarto was developed to be multilingual, beginning with R, Python, Javascript, and Julia, with the idea that it will work even for languages that don’t yet exist.</p> <p>While it is a “new” system, it should also be noted that it is highly compatible with existing content: you can render most R Markdown documents and Jupyter notebooks unmodified with Quarto. The concept is to make a major, long term investment in reproducible research, while keeping it compatible with existing formats and adaptable to the various environments users work in.</p> <h5 id="is-r-markdown-going-away-will-my-r-markdown-documents-continue-to-work">Is R Markdown going away? Will my R Markdown documents continue to work?</h5> <p>R Markdown is not going away! R Markdown is used extensively and continues to work well. It will continue to be actively supported. We’re not leaving R Markdown, we’re expanding our scope. Over the years there have been many feature requests, and rather than implementing them all in R Markdown, for certain features we may refer you to Quarto. Everything that is currently in R Markdown will continue to work and be supported. There are no plans for deprecation.</p> <p>Read more about this in Yihui Xie’s blog post <a href="https://yihui.org/en/2022/04/quarto-r-markdown/">With Quarto Coming, is R Markdown Going Away? No.</a></p> <h5 id="should-i-switch-from-r-markdown-to-quarto">Should I switch from R Markdown to Quarto?</h5> <p>If you like using R Markdown, there’s no need to switch! R Markdown will continue to be supported and work as it always has been. You’re welcome to try Quarto if you like, but there’s no need to switch. Some new features may only exist in Quarto, so if you want to use those, then that’s where you would give those a try.</p> <p>We should emphasize that switching is not imperative. While we don’t plan on major feature initiatives in R Markdown and related packages, we are going to continue to maintain them (smaller improvements and bug fixes) for a long time to come. Furthermore, since Rmd files can in most cases be rendered without modification by Quarto, you can continue using R Markdown and the switching cost will still be minimal whenever you decide to do it.</p> <h5 id="i-use-x-bookdown-blogdown-etc..-what-is-the-quarto-equivalent">I use X (bookdown, blogdown, etc.). What is the Quarto equivalent?</h5> <p>Here are the Quarto equivalents for various packages and features of the R Markdown ecosystem (in some cases Quarto equivalents are not yet available but will be later this year):</p> <p>Feature</p> <p>R Markdown</p> <p>Quarto</p> <p>Basic Formats</p> <ul> <li><p><a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/rmarkdown/reference/html_document.html">html_document</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/rmarkdown/reference/pdf_document.html">pdf_document</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/rticles/">rticles</a></p> <p>Quarto Journal Articles</p> <p>Paged HTML</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/rstudio/pagedown">pagedown</a></p> <p>Planned</p> <p>Dashboards</p> <p><a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/flexdashboard/">flexdashboard</a></p> <p><a href="https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/">Quarto Dashboards</a></p> <p>Interactive Tutorials</p> <p><a href="https://pkgs.rstudio.com/learnr/">learnr</a></p> <p><a href="https://r-wasm.github.io/quarto-live/">Quarto Live</a> Extension</p> <h5 id="can-you-create-custom-formats-for-quarto-like-you-can-for-r-markdown">Can you create custom formats for Quarto like you can for R Markdown?</h5> <p>Quarto offers an Extension mechanism to add features to a format using Shortcodes or Filters but also create custom formats. A major difference with custom output format in R Markdown is that Quarto Extension does not use R but Lua, for example if you need to add some logic behind custom metadata fields. See Developing with Lua to get started if you need use it your extension. Some of the features from R Markdown custom formats like customizing knitting behavior can also now be done in YAML with execution options.</p> <p>As example of custom formats for Quarto, Journal Articles for Quarto are port of some custom output format inside the rticles R package. Extensions lives in <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">Quarto Journals</a> Github organization, and you can find information on how to customize templates and manage Authors for you format.</p> <p>If you are an advanced developer of R Markdown custom format, the Extension mechanism may still have limitation (like pre and post processor). The Extension feature in Quarto will be improved over time - do not hesitate to share with us your use case or wished in our <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions">Discussion Board</a>.</p> <h5 id="when-would-be-a-good-time-to-start-new-projects-in-quarto-rather-than-r-markdown">When would be a good time to start new projects in Quarto rather than R Markdown?</h5> <p>Quarto v1.0 was <a href="https://www.rstudio.com/blog/announcing-quarto-a-new-scientific-and-technical-publishing-system/">announced at rstudio::conf(2022)</a>. This is the first stable release which is already an excellent foundation for starting new projects with Quarto or migrating existing R Markdown projects (if you are so inclined). If you start using Quarto, please do stay updated with latest release and changes as development is very active.</p> <h5 id="does-the-rstudio-ide-support-quarto">Does the RStudio IDE support Quarto?</h5> <p>Yes! You need to use RStudio v2022.07 or a later version, which includes support for editing and preview of Quarto documents.</p> <p>You can download the latest release of RStudio from <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">posit.co</a>.</p> <h5 id="does-posit-connect-support-quarto">Does Posit Connect support Quarto?</h5> <p>Yes! You can publish Quarto content to Posit Connect v2021.08.0 or later. Quarto has to be enabled as documented in the Posit Connect <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/admin/appendix/configuration/#Quarto">admin guide</a>. Connect’s user <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/quarto/">documentation</a> refers to Quarto.org docs on how to publish from the RStudio IDE. To publish Python-based Quarto content, you can use the <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/rsconnect-python/">rsconnect-python CLI</a> from various locations, including VSCode, JupyterLab or the terminal.</p> <h5 id="can-i-use-expr-or-r-syntax-in-yaml-options-and-headers-like-i-do-in-r-markdown">Can I use <code>!expr</code> or <code>!r</code> syntax in YAML options and headers like I do in R Markdown?</h5> <p>It depends on where you use them:</p> <ul> <li>Inside knitr cells for options using YAML syntax: Yes, <code>!expr</code> can be used as documented. However, <code>!r</code> cannot be used because it will fail Quarto’s YAML validation.</li> <li>Inside YAML blocks for Quarto document or project configurations: No, neither <code>!expr</code> nor <code>!r</code> is supported. Quarto differs from R Markdown because it doesn’t rely entirely on R for YAML processing. <code>!expr</code> is handled by the yaml R package, while <code>!r</code> is handled by knitr via <code>xfun::yaml_load()</code>. These are specific to R’s YAML parsing and are not supported in Quarto’s YAML metadata blocks. However, when using <code>engine: knitr</code> (the default for documents with R cells), YAML options inside knitr cells are parsed by knitr, allowing the use of <code>!expr</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Lastly, note that Quarto’s YAML validation supports <code>!expr</code> but not <code>!r</code>. If you’re a <code>!r</code> user, switch to <code>!expr</code> for compatibility.</p> <h3 id="frequently-asked-questions-1">Frequently Asked Questions</h3> <h4 id="frequently-asked-questions-2">Frequently Asked Questions</h4> <p>If you are an R Markdown user wondering about the relationship between Quarto and R Markdown, see also our FAQ for R Markdown Users.</p> <h5 id="general">General</h5> <h6 id="what-can-i-use-quarto-for-1">What can I use Quarto for?</h6> <p>Quarto® is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system built on Pandoc. You can weave together narrative text and code to produce elegantly formatted output as documents, web pages, blog posts, books and more.</p> <h6 id="how-do-i-install-quarto">How do I install Quarto?</h6> <p>Visit the Quarto.org - Get Started page, which provides installation instructions for Windows, Mac OS, and Linux.</p> <h6 id="what-output-formats-can-quarto-create">What output formats can Quarto create?</h6> <p>There are many output formats available in Quarto. This includes all of the built in Pandoc formats (e.g. HTML, PDF, MS Word, Revealjs, ePub, etc.) as well as various ways to publish multiple documents (websites, blogs, and books). Learn more at Quarto Formats.</p> <h6 id="what-editing-tools-can-i-use-with-quarto">What editing tools can I use with Quarto?</h6> <p>You can use a wide variety of tools with Quarto. We have provided documentation for writing and editing Quarto documents in VSCode, JupyterLab, RStudio IDE, or any text editor. Visit the Get Started with Quarto page to install, and then choose your tool for a brief introductory guide.</p> <h6 id="can-i-use-jupyter-notebooks-with-quarto">Can I use Jupyter notebooks with Quarto?</h6> <p>Yes! Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks and you can use Jupyter, JupyterLab or any other .ipynb notebook editor with Quarto. You can render existing .ipynb notebooks as-is with Quarto, but adding Quarto-specific output options or a YAML header can enhance the output. Visit theJupyterLab page for more information.</p> <h6 id="what-programming-languages-are-supported-in-quarto">What programming languages are supported in Quarto?</h6> <p>The principal languages supported by Quarto are Python, R, Julia, and Observable JavaScript. Integration with Jupyter also enables the use of many other languages.</p> <p>Each Quarto document can be optionally processed by a computational engine (the engine can be manually specified or automatically detected based on the code chunks within). Current engines include Knitr (which is also used by R Markdown and supports <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/other-languages.html">a variety of languages</a> including R, Python, and Julia, etc.) and Jupyter (which supports many languages including Python, Julia, and R). See the documentation on Engine Binding for additional details.</p> <h6 id="what-human-languages-are-supported-in-quarto">What human languages are supported in Quarto?</h6> <p>You can write your Quarto documentation in your human language of choice. The <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#language-variables">lang</a> document option is used to identify the main language of the document using IETF language tags (following the <a href="https://tools.ietf.org/html/bcp47">BCP 47 standard</a>), such as en or en-GB.</p> <h6 id="where-can-i-report-bugs-or-request-features">Where can I report bugs or request features?</h6> <p>Thanks for finding something and sharing with us! You can file an issue in the Quarto repository <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues">github.com</a>.</p> <h6 id="where-can-i-ask-questions-and-discuss-using-quarto-with-others">Where can I ask questions and discuss using Quarto with others?</h6> <p>The best place to ask questions and see what questions other people have is in Quarto discussions (https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions).</p> <h5 id="development-and-maintenance">Development and Maintenance</h5> <h6 id="how-can-i-upgrade-dependencies">How can I upgrade dependencies?</h6> <p>Generally, you cannot. Quarto produces output tailored to its downstream dependencies (Pandoc, <code>typst</code>, etc), and uses features that depend on specific upstream dependencies (Deno). Our installers bundle all required dependencies to eliminate version mismatch risks, and we strongly recommend that third-party packagers follow the same policy.</p> <h6 id="how-often-are-dependencies-updated">How often are dependencies updated?</h6> <p>Ideally, we update dependencies exactly once every stable release (1.2, 1.3, etc). We reserve the right to change the cadence as necessary for our development.</p> <h6 id="what-are-quartos-dependencies">What are Quarto’s dependencies?</h6> <p>Quarto’s dependencies include:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://pandoc.org">Pandoc</a></li> <li><a href="https://typst.app">Typst</a></li> <li><a href="https://deno.com">Deno</a></li> <li><a href="https://mermaid.js.org">Mermaid</a></li> <li><a href="https://esbuild.github.io/">esbuild</a></li> <li><a href="https://sass-lang.com/dart-sass/">Dart Sass</a> See the open source license page for a fuller list of bundled components and their licenses.</li> </ul> <h5 id="licensing">Licensing</h5> <h6 id="is-quarto-free-to-use">Is Quarto free to use?</h6> <p>Yes! Quarto is open source. Quarto version 1.3 (and earlier) is licensed under the <a href="https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/gpl-2.0.en.html">GNU GPL v2</a>. Quarto version 1.4 is licensed under the <a href="https://opensource.org/license/mit/">MIT License</a>.</p> <h6 id="can-i-use-quarto-to-develop-proprietary-content">Can I use Quarto to develop proprietary content?</h6> <p>Yes! The copyright on Quarto does not cover the original content that you generate using Quarto. Using Quarto to create original content does not place any restrictions, legally, on the license that you choose for the original content that you create, nor does it “reach through” to affect software that you might be writing documentation for with Quarto.</p> <h6 id="but-doesnt-the-gpl-cover-exported-html-documents-when-they-include-styles-or-functionalities-from-quarto">But doesn’t the GPL cover exported HTML documents when they include styles or functionalities from Quarto?</h6> <p>It covers the styles or functionalities themselves. It does not cover your original content because your original content is not a derivative work of the Quarto styles or functionalities.</p> <h6 id="how-can-i-share-documents-and-have-people-comment-on-them">How can I share documents and have people comment on them?</h6> <p>You can publish Quarto content to various locations. See the user guides for publishing for details on using Quarto Pub, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Posit Connect, and other services with Quarto. Once documents are published you can use <a href="https://web.hypothes.is/">hypothes.is</a>, <a href="https://utteranc.es/">Utterances</a>, or <a href="https://giscus.app/">Giscus</a> for commenting. Learn more in the documentation on commenting.</p> <h6 id="can-i-do-collaborative-editing-with-quarto">Can I do collaborative editing with Quarto?</h6> <p>There is not yet anything specific for collaborative editing in Quarto. You can collaborate on .qmd files in the same way you currently do for any text or code files.</p> <p>Posit Workbench allows for <a href="https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/articles/211659737-Sharing-Projects-in-RStudio-Workbench-RStudio-Server-Pro">Project Sharing</a> for interactive editing and collaboration on the same document.</p> <h6 id="where-can-i-publish-quarto-websites">Where can I publish Quarto websites?</h6> <p>There are a wide variety of ways to publish Quarto websites. Website content is by default written to the <code>\_site</code> sub-directory (you can customize this using the output-dir option). Publishing is simply a matter of copying the output directory to a web server or web hosting service.</p> <p>The publishing documentation describes several convenient options for Quarto website deployment including Posit Connect, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase, Site44, and Amazon S3. We’ll mostly defer to the documentation provided by those various services, but will note any Quarto website specific configuration required.</p> <h5 id="quarto-posit">Quarto + Posit</h5> <h6 id="does-posit-connect-support-quarto-1">Does Posit Connect support Quarto?</h6> <p>Yes! You can publish Quarto content to Posit Connect v2021.08.0 or later. Quarto has to be enabled as documented in the Posit Connect <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/admin/appendix/configuration/#Quarto">admin guide</a>. Connect’s user <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/quarto/">documentation</a> refers to Quarto.org docs on how to publish from the RStudio IDE. To publish Python-based Quarto content, you can use the <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/rsconnect-python/">rsconnect-python CLI</a> from various locations, including VSCode, JupyterLab or the terminal.</p> <h5 id="meta-2">Meta</h5> <h6 id="who-are-the-developers-of-quarto">Who are the developers of Quarto?</h6> <p>Development of Quarto is sponsored by <a href="https://www.posit.co/">Posit, PBC</a>. The same core team works on both Quarto and R Markdown:</p> <ul> <li>Carlos Scheidegger (<a href="https://github.com/cscheid"><span class="citation" data-cites="cscheid">@cscheid</span></a>)</li> <li>Gordon Woodhull (<a href="https://github.com/gordonwoodhull"><span class="citation" data-cites="gordonwoodhull">@gordonwoodhull</span></a>)</li> <li>Christophe Dervieux (<a href="https://github.com/cderv"><span class="citation" data-cites="cderv">@cderv</span></a>)</li> <li>Charles Teague (<a href="https://github.com/dragonstyle"><span class="citation" data-cites="dragonstyle">@dragonstyle</span></a>)</li> <li>J.J. Allaire (<a href="https://github.com/jjallaire/"><span class="citation" data-cites="jjallaire">@jjallaire</span></a>)</li> <li>Yihui Xie (<a href="https://github.com/yihui"><span class="citation" data-cites="yihui">@yihui</span></a>) Here is the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/graphs/contributors">full contributors list</a>. Quarto is open source and we welcome contributions in our github repository as well! <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli">github.com</a>.</li> </ul> <h6 id="why-the-name-quarto">Why the name Quarto?</h6> <p>We wanted to use a name that had meaning in the history of publishing and landed on Quarto, which is the format of a book or pamphlet produced from full sheets printed with eight pages of text, four to a side, then folded twice to produce four leaves. The earliest known European printed book is a Quarto, the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibyllenbuch_fragment">Sibyllenbuch</a>, believed to have been printed by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg">Johannes Gutenberg</a> in 1452–53.</p> <h2 id="getting-started-1">Getting started</h2> <h3 id="get-started">Get Started</h3> <h4 id="get-started-1">Get Started</h4> <p>Install Quarto, then check out the tutorials to learn the basics.</p> <h5 id="step-1">Step 1</h5> <h6 id="install-quarto">Install Quarto</h6> <p><a href="_">_</a> Find your operating system in the table below</p> <h6 id="highlights-5">Highlights</h6> <p>Quarto 1.10 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li><p>New <code>quarto.language</code> Pandoc template-variable namespace, exposing Quarto’s resolved localized strings to custom templates and template partials:</p> <p><span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>c</em><em>r</em><em>o</em><em>s</em><em>s</em><em>r</em><em>e</em><em>f</em> − <em>f</em><em>i</em><em>g</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em></span> <span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>t</em><em>o</em><em>c</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em> − <em>d</em><em>o</em><em>c</em><em>u</em><em>m</em><em>e</em><em>n</em><em>t</em></span></p></li> </ul> <h6 id="release-notes-23">Release Notes</h6> <h5 id="step-2">Step 2</h5> <h6 id="choose-your-tool">Choose your tool</h6> <h6 id="and-get-started">and get started</h6> <p><a href="hello/positron.html">Positron</a></p> <p><a href="hello/vscode.html">VS Code</a></p> <p><a href="hello/jupyter.html">Jupyter</a></p> <p><a href="hello/rstudio.html">RStudio</a></p> <p><a href="hello/neovim.html">Neovim</a></p> <p><a href="hello/text-editor.html">Text Editor</a></p> <h3 id="tutorial-authoring">Tutorial: Authoring</h3> <h4 id="tutorial-authoring-1">Tutorial: Authoring</h4> <h5 id="choose-your-tool-1">Choose your tool</h5> <h5 id="overview-57">Overview</h5> <p>In this tutorial we’ll show you how to author Quarto documents in RStudio. In particular, we’ll discuss the various document formats you can produce with the same source code and show you how to add components like table of contents, equations, citations, etc. The visual markdown editor in RStudio makes many of these tasks easier so we’ll highlight its use in this tutorial, but note that it’s possible to accomplish these tasks in the source editor as well.</p> <p>If you would like to follow along step-by-step in your own environment, install the <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">latest release</a> of RStudio.</p> <h5 id="output-formats-1">Output Formats</h5> <p>Quarto supports rendering notebooks to dozens of different output formats. By default, the <code>html</code> format is used, but you can specify an alternate format (or formats) within document options.</p> <h6 id="format-options-1">Format Options</h6> <p>You can choose the format you want to render your Quarto document to at the time of creating your new document. To create a new document, go to File > New File > Quarto Document… Alternatively, use the command palette (accessible via Ctrl+Shift+P), search for Create a new Quarto document and hit return.</p> <p>In the Title field, give a title for your document (e.g. the screenshot below suggests “Housing Prices”) and add your name to the Author field. Next, you will select the output format for your document. By default, RStudio suggests using HTML as the output, let’s leave that default for now.</p> <p>A new document will be created with the following YAML.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" ---</code></pre> <p>Note that our format choice (HTML) is not even reflected in the YAML as it is the default output format for Quarto documents. However you can directly edit the YAML to change the output format, e.g. to PDF (<code>pdf</code>) or MS Word (<code>docx</code>). Add <code>format: pdf</code> to your document’s YAML as shown below.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" format: pdf ---</code></pre> <p>Unfortunately, this document has no content, so rendering it would not result in very interesting output. To make it a bit easier to demonstrate all the features we want to highlight in this tutorial, let’s close this empty document and start with one that has a little bit of content in it. If you would like to follow along step-by-step in your own environment, download the Quarto document (<code>.qmd</code>) below and open it in RStudio.</p> <p><a href="_authoring.qmd">Download authoring.qmd</a></p> <p>CautionLaTeX Required for <code>format: pdf</code></p> <p>In order to create PDFs you will need to install a recent distribution of <a href="https://www.latex-project.org/">LaTeX</a>. We recommend the use of TinyTeX (which is based on TexLive), which you can install with the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install tinytex</code></pre> <p>See the article on PDF Engines for details on using other LaTeX distributions and PDF compilation engines.</p> <p>Once you have LaTeX setup, click on Render (or use the keyboard shortcut ⇧⌘K). We recommend also checking the box for Render on Save for a live preview of your changes. As shown below, you should see the rendered PDF in the Viewer in RStudio.</p> <p>Next, let’s add an option to the YAML, e.g. to add line numbers to the code chunks (<code>code-line-numbers: true</code>). Add this option to your document’s YAML as shown below, paying attention to the indentation scheme. Under <code>format:</code> our format choice <code>pdf</code> is indented (with two spaces) and it’s followed by <code>:</code> to indicate that further options for that format will be specified. In the next line, further indented by two spaces, we add <code>code-line-numbers: true</code>.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" format: pdf: code-line-numbers: true ---</code></pre> <p>If you checked Render on Save earlier, just save the document after making this change for a live preview. Otherwise render the document to see your updates reflected, including a table of contents that looks like the following.</p> <p>An incredibly exciting format option that we won’t go into too much detail in this tutorial is <code>revealjs</code>. Yes, you can make presentations with Quarto as well! In fact, Quarto supports a variety of formats for creating presentations, including <code>revealjs</code> for HTML slides, <code>pptx</code> for PowerPoint, and <code>beamer</code> for LaTeX/PDF. The Presentations article gives a thorough walk through of creating slide decks with Quarto.</p> <h6 id="multiple-formats-1">Multiple Formats</h6> <p>Some documents you create will have only a single output format, however in many cases it will be desirable to support multiple formats. Let’s add the <code>html</code> and <code>docx</code> formats to our document and modify some options specific to each format.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" syntax-highlighting: pygments format: html: code-fold: true html-math-method: katex pdf: geometry: - top=30mm - left=30mm docx: default ---</code></pre> <p>There’s a lot to take in here! Let’s break it down a bit. The first two lines are generic document metadata that aren’t related to output formats at all.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" ---</code></pre> <p>The next line is a document format option that applies to all formats, which is why it is specified at the root level.</p> <pre><code>--- syntax-highlighting: pygments ---</code></pre> <p>Next, we have the <code>format</code> option, where we provide format-specific options.</p> <pre><code>--- format: html: code-fold: true html-math-method: katex pdf: geometry: - top=30mm - left=30mm docx: default ---</code></pre> <p>The <code>html</code> and <code>pdf</code> formats each provide an option or two. For example, for the HTML output we want the user to have control over whether to show or hide the code (<code>code-fold: true</code>) and use <code>katex</code> for math text. For PDF we define some margins. The <code>docx</code> format is a bit different—it specifies <code>docx: default</code>. This indicates that we just want to use all of the default options for the format.</p> <h5 id="rendering-8">Rendering</h5> <p>Clicking the Render button (or using the keyboard shortcut ⇧⌘K) in RStudio will render the document to the first format listed in the YAML.</p> <p>Note that the Render button also has a drop down menu that enables you to render to any of the formats listed in YAML front matter:</p> <p>If you would like to render to all formats, you can do so with the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-r">quarto</a> package, which provides an R interface to the Quarto CLI. For example, to render the current document, use <code>quarto::quarto_render()</code>. You can also specify the name of the document you want to render as well as the output format(s).</p> <pre><code>quarto::quarto_render( "authoring.qmd", output_format = c("pdf", "html", "docx") )</code></pre> <p>As a result, you will see three new files appear in your Files pane:</p> <ul> <li><code>authoring.docx</code></li> <li><code>authoring.html</code></li> <li><code>authoring.pdf</code></li> </ul> <h5 id="sections-1">Sections</h5> <p>You can use a table of contents and/or section numbering to make it easier for readers to navigate your document. Do this by adding the <code>toc</code> and/or <code>number-sections</code> options to document options. Note that these options are typically specified at the root level because they are shared across all formats.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Housing Prices" author: "Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel" toc: true number-sections: true syntax-highlighting: pygments format: html: code-fold: true html-math-method: katex pdf: geometry: - top=30mm - left=30mm docx: default ---</code></pre> <p>Here’s what this document looks like when rendered to HTML.</p> <p>There are lots of options available for controlling how the table of contents and section numbering behave. See the output format documentation (e.g. HTML, PDF, MS Word) for additional details.</p> <h5 id="equations-2">Equations</h5> <p>If you are using the visual editor mode, you can add LaTeX equations to Quarto documents in RStudio using the Insert Anything tool. You can access it with / at the beginning of an empty block or Cmd+/ anywhere else.</p> <p>Display equations (in a new line) are delimited with <code>\$\$…\$\$</code> while inline equations are delimited with <code>\$…\$</code>. Add the following as display math in the document.</p> <pre><code>price = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times area + \epsilon</code></pre> <p>RStudio displays a rendered version of the tutorial as you type it in the editor. See the documentation on markdown equations for additional details.</p> <h5 id="citations-2">Citations</h5> <p>The Insert Anything tool can also be used to insert citations to your document.</p> <p>In the next window you can insert a citation via from a variety of sources including your document bibliography, Zotero personal or group libraries, DOI (Document Object Identifier) references, and searches of <a href="https://www.crossref.org/">Crossref</a>, <a href="https://datacite.org/">DataCite</a>, or <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/">PubMed</a>. You can find out more about citations with the visual editor here.</p> <p>Select From DOI on the left and copy-and-paste the DOI <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97"><code>10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97</code></a> in the search bar and hit Search. Then, select the found reference, and Insert it into your document.</p> <p>If this is the first citation you are adding to your document, RStudio will automatically create a bibliography file for you. This file is called <code>references.bib</code> by default and RStudio will also add <code>bibliography: references.bib</code> to your document’s YAML metadata.</p> <p>Note that items within the bibliography are cited using the <code>@citeid</code> syntax. Add the following text to your document.</p> <pre><code>We're going to do this analysis using literate programming [@knuth1984].</code></pre> <p>References will be included at the end of the document, so we include a <code>## References</code> heading at the bottom of the notebook. You might also add <code>.unnumbered</code> class to this section by clicking on the three dots (…) to edit its attributes.</p> <p>Here is what this document looks like when rendered (with middle sections removed to highlight the relevant parts.</p> <p>The <code>@</code> citation syntax is very flexible and includes support for prefixes, suffixes, locators, and in-text citations. See the documentation on Citations to learn more.</p> <h5 id="cross-references-7">Cross References</h5> <p>Cross-references make it easier for readers to navigate your document by providing numbered references and hyperlinks to figures, tables, equations, and sections. Cross-reference-able entities generally require a label (unique identifier) and a caption.</p> <p>For example, to add a label to the equation inserted earlier, click on the three dots to edit its attributes and use the suggested format (starting with <code>#eq-</code>) to label the equation.</p> <p>Then, add a cross reference using the Insert Anything tool in the visual editor. You might add a sentence like <code>"We can fit a simple linear regression model of the form shown in"</code> to contextualize the cross reference and then add the reference to the end of that sentence.</p> <p>In the Insert Cross Reference menu, navigate to the desired cross reference entity on the left, and select the equation labeled earlier.</p> <p>Alternatively, start typing the label of the equation to be referenced in the visual editor, and the autofill tool will bring up the cross references to choose from.</p> <p>Below we illustrate cross-referencing various types of entities using fragments from the document you’ve been working with.</p> <pre><code>We present the results of exploratory data analysis in @sec-eda and the regression model in @sec-model. @fig-scatterplot displays the relationship between these two variables in a scatterplot. @tbl-stats displays basic summary statistics for these two variables. We can fit a simple linear regression model of the form shown in @eq-slr.</code></pre> <p>This examples include cross-referenced sections, figures, and equations. The table below summarizes how we express each of these.</p> <p>Entity</p> <p>Reference</p> <p>Label / Caption</p> <p>Section</p> <p><code>@sec-eda</code></p> <p>ID added to heading:</p> <pre><code># Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}</code></pre> <p>Figure</p> <p><code>@fig-scatterplot</code></p> <p>YAML options in code cell:</p> <pre><code>#| label: fig-scatterplot #| fig-cap: "Scatterplot of price vs. area of houses in Duke Forest"</code></pre> <p>Table</p> <p><code>@tbl-stats</code></p> <p>YAML options in code cell:</p> <pre><code>#| label: tbl-stats #| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics for price and area of houses in Duke Forest"</code></pre> <p>Equation</p> <p><code>@eq-slr</code></p> <p>At end of display equation:</p> <pre><code>$$ {#eq-slr}</code></pre> <p>See the article on Cross References to learn more, including how to customize caption and reference text (e.g. use “Fig.” rather than “Figure”).</p> <h5 id="callouts-3">Callouts</h5> <p>Callouts are an excellent way to draw extra attention to certain concepts, or to more clearly indicate that certain content is supplemental or applicable to only some scenarios.</p> <p>Callouts are markdown divs that have special callout attributes. We can insert a callout using the Insert Anything tool.</p> <p>In the subsequent dialogue you can select one of five types of callout (note, tip, important, caution, or warning), customize its appearance (default, simple, or minimal), and decide whether you want to show the icon.</p> <p>Then, try inserting the following text in the callout box.</p> <pre><code>This is a pretty incomplete analysis, but hopefully the document provides a good overview of some of the authoring features of Quarto!</code></pre> <p>Here is what a callout looks like in the visual editor.</p> <p>And here is the rendered callout in the output document.</p> <p>You can learn more about the different types of callouts and options for their appearance in the Callouts documentation.</p> <h5 id="article-layout-5">Article Layout</h5> <p>The body of Quarto articles have a default width of approximately 700 pixels. This width is chosen to <a href="https://medium.com/ben-shoemate/optimum-web-readability-max-and-min-width-for-page-text-dee9987a27a0">optimize readability</a>. This normally leaves some available space in the document margins and there are a few ways you can take advantage of this space.</p> <p>We can use the <code>column: page-right</code> cell option to indicate we would like our figure to occupy the full width of the screen, with some inset. Go ahead and add this chunk option to the chunk labeled <code>fig-histogram</code>.</p> <pre><code>#| label: fig-histogram #| fig-cap: "Histograms of individual variables" #| fig-subcap: #| - "Histogram of `price`s" #| - "Histogram of `area`s" #| layout-ncol: 2 #| column: page-right</code></pre> <p>Here is what the relevant section of the document looks like when rendered.</p> <p>You can locate citations, footnotes, and asides in the margin. You can also define custom column spans for figures, tables, or other content. See the documentation on Article Layout for additional details.</p> <h5 id="publishing-7">Publishing</h5> <p>Once your document is rendered to HTML, you can publish to <a href="https://rpubs.com/">RPubs</a> (a free service from RStudio for sharing documents on the web) simply by clicking the Publish button on the editor toolbar or preview window. Alternatively, you can use the <code>quarto::quarto_publish_doc()</code> function.</p> <pre><code>quarto::quarto_publish_doc( "authoring.qmd", server = "rpubs.com" )</code></pre> <p>Other possible publishing options include RStudio Connect and ShinyApps as well as GitHub Pages, Netlify, etc. The Publishing HTML article gives a much more detailed overview of your publishing options.</p> <p>If you followed along step-by-step with this tutorial, you should now have a Quarto document that implements everything we covered. Otherwise, you can download a completed version of <code>computations.qmd</code> below.</p> <p><a href="_authoring-complete.qmd">Download authoring-complete.qmd</a></p> <h5 id="learning-more-9">Learning More</h5> <p>You’ve now learned the basics of using Quarto! Once you feel comfortable creating and customizing documents here are a few more things to explore:</p> <ul> <li>Presentations — Author PowerPoint, Beamer, and Revealjs presentations using the same syntax you’ve learned for creating documents.</li> <li>Websites — Publish collections of documents as a website. Websites support multiple forms of navigation and full-text search.</li> <li>Blogs — Create a blog with an about page, flexible post listings, categories, RSS feeds, and over twenty themes.</li> <li>Books — Create books and manuscripts in print (PDF, MS Word) and online (HTML, ePub) formats.</li> <li>Interactivity — Include interactive components to help readers explore the concepts and data you are presenting more deeply.</li> </ul> <h3 id="tutorial-computations">Tutorial: Computations</h3> <h4 id="tutorial-computations-1">Tutorial: Computations</h4> <h5 id="choose-your-tool-2">Choose your tool</h5> <p>TipR or Python?</p> <p>You can work through this tutorial using R or Python code examples. Select your preferred language:</p> <ul> <li>R</li> <li>Python You’ve selected to see examples in R. You can toggle to Python whenever you like throughout the guide.</li> </ul> <p>You’ve selected to see examples in Python. You can toggle to R whenever you like throughout the guide.</p> <h5 id="overview-58">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto supports executable code cells within markdown. This allows you to create fully reproducible documents and reports—the code required to produce your output is part of the document itself, and is automatically re-run whenever the document is rendered.</p> <p>In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to author fully reproducible computational documents with Quarto in Positron.</p> <p>You’ll learn how to:</p> <ul> <li>Run code cells interactively in the Console</li> <li>Control code output, including hiding code</li> <li>Control figure output including captions and layout</li> <li>Add new code cells and get help with code cell options</li> <li>Use values from your code cells in markdown text</li> </ul> <h5 id="setup">Setup</h5> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>Be sure that you have installed the <code>rmarkdown</code> and <code>tidyverse</code> packages:</p> <p>install.packages(“rmarkdown”) install.packages(“tidyverse”)</p></li> <li><p>Download <code>computations.qmd</code> below and open it in Positron.</p></li> <li><p>Download computations.qmd</p></li> <li><p>Run the Quarto: Preview command, use the keyboard shortcut , or use the Preview button () in the editor toolbar, to render and preview the document.</p></li> <li><p>Install the <code>jupyter</code> and <code>plotnine</code> packages using your preferred method. For example, with <code>pip</code>:</p> <p>pip install jupyter plotnine</p></li> <li><p>Download <code>computations.qmd</code> below and open it in Positron.</p></li> <li><p>Download computations.qmd</p></li> <li><p>Run the Quarto: Preview command, use the keyboard shortcut , or use the Preview button () in the editor toolbar, to render and preview the document.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="cell-execution">Cell Execution</h5> <p>As you author a document you may want to execute one or more code cells without re-rendering the entire document. You can do this using the Run Cell button above the code cell. Click the button, run the command Quarto: Run Cell, or use the shortcut , to execute the current cell in the Console:</p> <ul> <li>R</li> <li>Python In addition to running a single code cell, there are a variety of other commands and keyboard shortcuts available:</li> </ul> <p>Quarto Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Run Cell</p> <p>Run Current Code</p> <p>Run Next Cell</p> <p>Run Previous Cell</p> <p>Run Cells Above</p> <p>Run Cells Below</p> <p>Run All Cells</p> <p>TipTracking down code problems</p> <p>A good approach to troubleshooting the code in your document is to restart your Console (), and Quarto: Run All Cells (). This emulates Quarto’s approach to executing the code in your document: starting a clean session and executing code cells from top to bottom.</p> <h5 id="cell-output-1">Cell Output</h5> <p>By default, the code and its output are displayed within the rendered document.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python However, for some documents, you may want to hide all of the code and just show the output. To do so, specify <code>echo: false</code> in document header.</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: Quarto Computations</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>echo: false</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> </ul> <p>Preview again to see your updates reflected. The result will look like the following.</p> <p>You might want to selectively enable code <code>echo</code> for some cells. To do this add the <code>echo: true</code> option to a code cell. Try this with the cell labelled <code>scatterplot</code>.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = cty, color = cyl)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) + scale_color_viridis_c() + theme_bw()</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true ( ggplot(mpg, aes(x=“hwy”, y=“cty”, color=“cyl”)) + geom_point(alpha=0.5, size=2) + scale_color_continuous() + theme_bw() )</p></li> </ul> <p>Preview the document again and note that the code is now included for the <code>scatterplot</code> cell.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python The <code>echo</code> option controls whether the source code itself is shown in the rendered document. Other options control the display of other aspects of code cells. Like <code>echo</code> they can be set in the document header or overridden in code cells:</p></li> <li><p><code>output</code>: show output of the code like figures, tables, text output, etc. (default <code>true</code>)</p></li> <li><p><code>warning</code>: show warnings produced by the code (default <code>true</code>)</p></li> <li><p><code>include</code>: show anything, a catch-all for the code itself, output, and warnings (default <code>true</code>)</p></li> <li><p><code>eval</code>: whether to execute the code or not (default <code>true</code>)</p></li> <li><p><code>error</code>: whether execution should continue after an error and the error should be displayed (default <code>false</code>) You can read more about these options in Execution options.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="code-appearance">Code Appearance</h5> <p>There are lots of other options to tweak the appearance of code in your document. For example, an alternative to showing or hiding code is to use code folding.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true #| code-fold: true ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = cty, color = cyl)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) + scale_color_viridis_c() + theme_bw()</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true #| code-fold: true ( ggplot(mpg, aes(x=“hwy”, y=“cty”, color=“cyl”)) + geom_point(alpha=0.5, size=2) + scale_color_continuous() + theme_bw() )</p></li> </ul> <p>Code cells in the rendered document are placed under a collapsed “Code” button, which readers can expand at their discretion.</p> <p>As another example, you can add line numbers to your code cells with the <code>code-line-numbers</code>:</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| code-line-numbers: true ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = cty, color = cyl)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) + scale_color_viridis_c() + theme_bw()</p> <p>#| label: scatterplot #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| code-line-numbers: true ( ggplot(mpg, aes(x=“hwy”, y=“cty”, color=“cyl”)) + geom_point(alpha=0.5, size=2) + scale_color_continuous() + theme_bw() )</p></li> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python The options available for code cells depend on the engine used to execute the code cells. You can read more about how Quarto chooses an engine in Engine Binding.</p></li> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python If you’ve been working through this tutorial with R, you have been using the <code>knitr</code> engine. See Knitr Cell Options documentation for the complete list of available code cell options.</p></li> </ul> <p>If you’ve been working through this tutorial with Python, you have been using the <code>jupyter</code> engine. See the Jupyter Cell Options documentation for the complete list of available code cell options.</p> <p>Many code cell options can also be set in the document header to apply the option to all code cells. For instance, you could fold all code cells in the document by adding the <code>code-fold</code> option to the document header:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Quarto Computations" format: html: code-fold: true ---</code></pre> <p>To understand which options can be set in the document header, look at the Reference for the format you are using. For instance, <code>code-fold</code> can be set in the document header because it is listed as an HTML format option. You’ll learn more about when to set document header options nested under a format versus at the top level in the next tutorial: Authoring.</p> <p>You can see examples of other options that control code appearance in the HTML format in the Guide page HTML Code Blocks.</p> <h5 id="figures-4">Figures</h5> <p>Figures produced by code cells are automatically included in the rendered output. Code cell options provide additional control over how figures are displayed.</p> <p>For example, update the code cell for the scatter plot by adding a caption with <code>fig-cap</code>, and improve accessibility by adding <a href="https://medium.com/nightingale/writing-alt-text-for-data-visualization-2a218ef43f81">alternative text</a> with <code>fig-alt</code>:</p> <pre><code>#| fig-cap: City and highway mileage for 38 popular models of cars. #| fig-alt: Scatterplot of city vs. highway mileage for cars, where points are colored by the number of cylinders. The plot displays a positive, linear, and strong relationship between city and highway mileage, and mileage increases as the number of cylinders decreases.</code></pre> <p>To cross-reference a figure replace the <code>label</code> with one that that starts with <code>fig-</code>:</p> <pre><code>#| label: fig-scatterplot</code></pre> <p>Then you can update the narrative to refer to the figure using its label:</p> <pre><code>@fig-scatterplot shows a positive, strong, and linear relationship between the city and highway mileage of these cars.</code></pre> <p>Preview the document to see the plot now has a caption and an automatically generated number, which is linked from the text.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python You can control the size of all the figures in the document by setting <code>fig-width</code> and <code>fig-height</code>, expressed in inches, in the document header:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: Quarto Computations</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>echo: false</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>fig-height: 3.5</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>fig-width: 6</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python To override the figure size for individual images, use the <code>fig-width</code> and <code>fig-height</code> options as code cell options:</p> <p>#| label: fig-scatterplot #| fig-width: 6 #| fig-height: 3.5 ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = cty, color = cyl)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) + scale_color_viridis_c() + theme_bw()</p></li> </ul> <p>To override the figure size for individual images, specify the plot size in your code. For example, in <code>plotnine</code> you can use <code>figure_size</code> argument to <code>theme()</code>:</p> <pre><code>( ggplot(mpg, aes(x="hwy", y="cty", color="cyl")) + geom_point(alpha=0.5, size=2) + scale_color_continuous() + theme_bw() + theme(figure_size=(6, 3.5)) )</code></pre> <p>Quarto provides additional flexibility for figures. You can:</p> <ul> <li>Produce figure panels with multiple figures, each with its subcaption. See the article Figure Layout for details.</li> <li>Allow figures to span the page or screen, or place them in the margin. See the documentation on Article Layout to learn more.</li> </ul> <h5 id="cell-workflow">Cell Workflow</h5> <p>You can add a new code cell by running the command Quarto: Insert Code Cell, using the keyboard shortcut , or using the Insert Code Cell button in the editor toolbar.</p> <p>Since <code>.qmd</code> documents are plain text, you can also create a new code cell by typing (or copying and pasting) the code cell syntax:</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>```{r}</p> <pre><code> ```{python} </code></pre></li> </ul> <p>Go ahead and add a new code cell to your document after the scatter plot cell.</p> <p>To get help with code cell options, start by writing the code cell option comment (<code>#|</code>), then hit to bring up a list of completions. Keep typing to filter the list, or use the arrow keys to navigate. When you find the option you want, hit to insert it into your code cell.</p> <ul> <li>R</li> <li>Python Practice this to add <code>echo: true</code> to your code cell, and <code>label: nobs</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Finally, add some code to the cell.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>nrow(mpg)</p> <p>len(mpg)</p></li> </ul> <p>Preview the document again to see the output of your code cell.</p> <p>This isn’t a very pretty way to display the number of observations. An alternative is to use inline code, which you’ll cover next.</p> <p>TipCode blocks</p> <p>Code cells using the ```<code>{language}</code> syntax are sometimes called executable code cells because they will be executed by the computational engine (e.g. <code>knitr</code> or <code>jupyter</code>).</p> <p>If you want to show code without it being processed by the computational engine, use a code block:</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <div class="sourceCode" id="cb995"><pre class="sourceCode r"><code class="sourceCode r"><span id="cb995-1"><a href="#cb995-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># Code goes here</span></span></code></pre></div> <div class="sourceCode" id="cb996"><pre class="sourceCode python"><code class="sourceCode python"><span id="cb996-1"><a href="#cb996-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># Code goes here</span></span></code></pre></div></li> </ul> <p>You can read more and see some syntax alternatives at Markdown Basics: Source Code.</p> <h5 id="inline-code-4">Inline Code</h5> <ul> <li>R</li> <li>Python To include executable expressions within markdown text, enclose the expression in <code>{r}</code>1.</li> </ul> <p>To include executable expressions within markdown, enclose the expression in <code>{python}</code>.</p> <p>For example, you can use inline code to state the number of observations in our data. Try adding the following markdown text to your Quarto document.</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p> <p>There are <code>{r} nrow(mpg)</code> observations in our data.</p> <p>There are <code>{python} len(mpg)</code> observations in our data.</p></li> </ul> <p>Save your document and preview the rendered output. The expression inside the backticks has been executed and the sentence includes the actual number of observations.</p> <p>There are 234 observations in our data.</p> <p>You could now delete the code cell that did the same computation, since the inline code expression has replaced it.</p> <p>If the expression you want to inline is more complex, involving many functions or a pipeline, we recommend including it in a code cell (with <code>echo: false</code>) and assigning the result to an object. Then, you can call that object in your inline code.</p> <p>For additional details on inline code expressions, visit the Inline Code documentation.</p> <h5 id="final-document">Final Document</h5> <p>If you followed along step-by-step with this tutorial, you should now have a Quarto document that implements everything we covered. Otherwise, you can download a completed version of <code>computations.qmd</code> below.</p> <ul> <li>R</li> <li>Python <a href="_positron/r/computations-complete.qmd">Download <code>computations-complete.qmd</code></a></li> </ul> <p><a href="_positron/python/%60computations-complete.qmd%60">Download computations-complete.qmd</a></p> <h5 id="next-up">Next Up</h5> <p>You’ve now covered the basics of customizing the behavior and output of executable code in Quarto documents.</p> <p>Next, check out the Authoring Tutorial to learn more about output formats and technical writing features like citations, crossrefs, and advanced layout.</p> <h5 id="footnotes-6">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>Quarto also supports the Knitr syntax <code>r</code>, read more in Inline Code.↩︎</li> </ul> <h3 id="tutorial-hello-quarto">Tutorial: Hello, Quarto</h3> <h4 id="tutorial-hello-quarto-1">Tutorial: Hello, Quarto</h4> <h5 id="choose-your-tool-3">Choose your tool</h5> <h5 id="overview-59">Overview</h5> <p>In this tutorial we’ll show you how to use Quarto with Neovim. While we cover the basics here, you will also want to review the article on Using Neovim with Quarto to learn more about installing, using, and customizing Neovim for Quarto.</p> <p>If you already have Neovim configured to your liking, you may only want to add the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-nvim">quarto-nvim</a> plugin and only refer to this guide for inspiration and seeing the possibilities. But if you are entirely new to Neovim or want to simply try out a configuration already set up for data science with Quarto, you should head over to this <a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/quarto-nvim-kickstarter">kickstarter configuration</a>. This is also what we will be using for this tutorial.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Neovim is a highly customizable editor. So much so that Neovim core member TJ Devries has recently coined the term Personal Development Environments (PDE)1 to separate the concept from Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) such as VS Code and RStudio.</p> <p>Out of the box neovim is fairly minimal. To work efficiently and get all the nice features, you have to configure it. You have to make it your own. If this approach sounds enticing to you, read on. Welcome to the rabbit hole. 🐰</p> <p>You can also watch <a href="https://youtu.be/3sj7clNowlA">this video</a> for a quick guide to getting started with the kickstarter configuration alongside this write-up.</p> <p>The Quarto Neovim plugin aims to not reinvent the wheel. Existing plugins in the Neovim ecosystem are leveraged to provide the full experience. Some of the features provided by <code>quarto-nvim</code> and enhanced by plugins found in the kickstarter configuration are:</p> <ul> <li>Preview for Quarto documents.</li> <li>Syntax highlighting for markdown and embedded languages</li> <li>Completion for embedded languages (e.g. Python, R, Julia, etc.)</li> <li>Commands and key-bindings for running cells and selected lines.</li> <li>Completion for bibliography references, file paths, LaTeX math symbols, emoji.</li> <li>Optional spellchecking and completion.</li> <li>Code snippets.</li> <li>Export of code chunks into standalone scripts. See the article on Using Neovim with Quarto for all of the details.</li> </ul> <h6 id="basic-workflow">Basic Workflow</h6> <p>Quarto <code>.qmd</code> files contain a combination of markdown and executable code cells. Here’s what it might look like in Neovim to edit and preview a <code>.qmd</code> file:</p> <p>The <code>.qmd</code> file you see on the left is rendered into the HTML document you see on the right side. This is the basic model for Quarto publishing—take a source document and render it to a variety of output formats, including HTML, PDF, MS Word, etc.</p> <p>The tutorials will make use of the <code>matplotlib</code> and <code>plotly</code> Python packages—the commands you can use to install them are given in the table below.</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Commands</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib plotly</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter matplotlib plotly</code></pre> <p>Note</p> <p>Note that while this tutorial uses Python, using Julia (via the <a href="https://julialang.github.io/IJulia.jl/stable/">IJulia</a> kernel) or using R (via the <a href="https://github.com/yihui/knitr">knitr package</a>), are also well supported. See the articles on Using Julia and Using R for additional details.</p> <h5 id="render-and-preview-2">Render and Preview</h5> <p>We’ll start out by rendering a simple example (<code>hello.qmd</code>) to a couple of formats. If you want to follow along step-by-step in your own environment, create a new file named <code>hello.qmd</code> and copy the following content into it.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Quarto Basics" format: html: code-fold: true jupyter: python3 --- For a demonstration of a line plot on a polar axis, see @fig-polar. ```{python} #| label: fig-polar #| fig-cap: "A line plot on a polar axis" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots( subplot_kw = {'projection': 'polar'} ) ax.plot(theta, r); ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]); ax.grid(True); plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>To render and preview, execute the QuartoPreview command by pressing <code>:</code> to enter command mode and typing the command (there is autocompletion if you press the tab key). In the kickstarter configuration, there are more shortcuts starting with space q (spacebar followed by q, in normal mode).</p> <h6 id="how-it-works-1">How it Works</h6> <p>When you render a <code>.qmd</code> file with Quarto, the executable code blocks are processed by Jupyter, and the resulting combination of code, markdown, and output is converted to plain markdown. Then, this markdown is processed by <a href="http://pandoc.org/">Pandoc</a>, which creates the finished format.</p> <h6 id="authoring-3">Authoring</h6> <p>Let’s try making a small change and then re-rendering:</p> <ul> <li><p>Change the line of code that defines <code>theta</code> as follows:</p> <p>theta = 4 * np.pi * r</p></li> <li><p>Save the file using either <code>:w</code> in normal mode or <code>ctrl-s</code> 2 The document is rendered, and the browser preview is updated.
