This is the basic workflow for authoring with Quarto.</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="running-cells">Running Cells</h6> <p>You don’t need to fully render documents in order to iterate on code cells. With the provided configuration we can open a terminal of our choosing using the leader key (<code><space></code>) followed by<code>c</code> (for code) and then <code>p</code> (for python) or <code>i</code> (for ipython).</p> <p>If you wait a little in between the key presses a small window pops up at the bottom of your screen to tell you about existing keybindings:</p> <p>We can navigate between the code and the terminal using <code>ctrl</code> plus vim direction keys and enter commands into the python REPL by going into insert mode in this terminal buffer.</p> <p>To send code to the python REPL from quarto we navigate to one of our code blocks and press <code><space><cr></code> (space bar followed by Enter). The plugin responsible for sending code to various places, <a href="https://github.com/jpalardy/vim-slime">vim-slime</a> will prompt us with the question which terminal to send the code to, pre filled with the latest terminal we created.</p> <p>If you want to use ctrl+Enter to send code just like in RStudio, you are going to have to tell your terminal emulator to send the correct key codes. For example, in the <a href="https://github.com/kovidgoyal/kitty">kitty</a> terminal the configuration looks as follows:</p> <pre><code>map ctrl+shift+enter no_op map shift+enter send_text all \x1b[13;2u map ctrl+enter send_text all \x1b[13;5u</code></pre> <p>This is what the kickstarter configuration has been tested with.</p> <p>There are few different types of content in <code>hello.qmd</code>, let’s work a bit with each type.</p> <h5 id="yaml-options">YAML Options</h5> <p>At the top of the file there is a YAML block with document level options.</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Quarto Basics" format: html: code-fold: true jupyter: python3 ---</code></pre> <p>Try changing the <code>code-fold</code> option to <code>false</code>:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-fold: false</code></pre> <p>Then re-render the document by saving it. You’ll notice that the code is now shown above the plot, where previously it was hidden with a Code button that could be used to show it.</p> <p>Narrative content is written using markdown. Here we specify a heading and a cross-reference to the figure created in the code cell below.</p> <pre><code>## Polar Axis For a demonstration of a line plot on a polar axis, see @fig-polar.</code></pre> <p>Try changing the heading and re-rendering—the preview will update with the new heading text.</p> <h5 id="code-cells">Code Cells</h5> <p>Code cells contain executable code to be run during render, with the output (and optionally the code) included in the rendered document.</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| label: fig-polar #| fig-cap: "A line plot on a polar axis" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots( subplot_kw = {'projection': 'polar'} ) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>You are likely familiar with the Matplotlib code given here. However, there are some less familiar components at the top of the code cell: <code>label</code> and <code>fig-cap</code> options. Cell options are written in YAML using a specially prefixed comment (<code>#|</code>).</p> <p>In this example, the cell options are used to make the figure cross-reference-able. Try changing the <code>fig-cap</code> and/or the code then re-rendering to see the updated preview.</p> <p>There are a wide variety of cell options that you can apply to tailor your output. We’ll delve into these options in the next tutorial.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>One particularly useful cell option for figures is <code>fig-alt</code>, which enables you to add alternative text to images for users with visual impairments. See Amy Cesal’s article on <a href="https://medium.com/nightingale/writing-alt-text-for-data-visualization-2a218ef43f81">Writing Alt Text for Data Visualization</a> to learn more.</p> <h5 id="next-up-1">Next Up</h5> <h5 id="next-up-2">Next Up</h5> <p>You now know the basics of creating and authoring Quarto documents. The following tutorials explore Quarto in more depth:</p> <ul> <li>Tutorial: Computations — Learn how to tailor the behavior and output of executable code blocks.</li> <li>Tutorial: Authoring — Learn more about output formats and technical writing features like citations, crossrefs, and advanced layout. See the article on Using Neovim with Quarto to learn more about installing, using, and customizing Neovim for Quarto.</li> </ul> <h5 id="footnotes-7">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>In <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QMVIJhC9Veg">this video</a>↩︎</li> <li>if you are using the kickstarter configuration – otherwise <code>ctrl-s</code> puts your terminal in a waiting mode until you press <code>ctrl+q</code>, which can be confusing↩︎</li> </ul> <h2 id="interactive-documents">Interactive documents</h2> <h3 id="arquero">Arquero</h3> <h4 id="arquero-1">Arquero</h4> <p>Simple demonstration of <a href="https://uwdata.github.io/arquero/">Arquero</a> using Allison Horst’s <a href="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/">Palmer Penguins</a> dataset.</p> <pre><code>import { aq, op } from '@uwdata/arquero' penguins = aq.loadCSV("palmer-penguins.csv") penguins.view() penguins .groupby('species') .filter(d => d.body_mass_g > 0) .rollup({ count: op.count(), avg_mass: op.average('body_mass_g') }) .view()</code></pre> <p>If you want to use inputs in an arquero query, you can use the <code>params</code> method of table. Below is a simple example of filtering a dataset by the values provided.</p> <pre><code>viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) penguins .params({ blm: bill_length_min, i: islands }) .filter((d, $) => op.includes($.i, d.island) && d.bill_length_mm > $.blm) .view()</code></pre> <h3 id="code-reuse">Code Reuse</h3> <h4 id="code-reuse-1">Code Reuse</h4> <p>As you build larger Quarto projects (like websites and books) that incorporate OJS, you’ll likely want to re-use code, data, and output across different pages.</p> <h5 id="modules">Modules</h5> <p>JavaScript modules are directly supported in Quarto’s OJS blocks. For example, if we have the following source file <code>square.js</code>:</p> <pre><code>export function square(x) { return x * x; }</code></pre> <p>Then you can import and use the <code>square()</code> function as follows:</p> <pre><code>import { square } from "./square.js" square(5)</code></pre> <h5 id="data">Data</h5> <p>You may be using Python or R to pre-process data that is then provided to OJS via the <code>ojs_define()</code> function (this is described in more depth in the Data Sources article). If you want to share data prepared in this fashion you can import it directly from another <code>.qmd</code>.</p> <p>For example, here we import the <code>co2data</code> that we read and pre-processed with dplyr in <code>data-sources.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>import { co2data } from "./data-sources.qmd"; Inputs.table(transpose(co2data))</code></pre> <h5 id="output-2">Output</h5> <p>You can import any reactive value from another <code>.qmd</code> file. Here, we’re reusing a chart directly from <code>data-sources.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>import { yearlyChart } from "./data-sources.qmd"; yearlyChart</code></pre> <h3 id="component-layout">Component Layout</h3> <h4 id="component-layout-1">Component Layout</h4> <h5 id="overview-60">Overview</h5> <p>When you introduce interactive components into a document you’ll want to be sure to lay them out in a fashion that optimizes for readability and navigation.</p> <p>There are of course a wide variety of ways you can incorporate interactivity spanning from visualizations embedded within a longer-form article all the way up to a more application/dashboard style layout. We’ll cover both of these layout scenarios below.</p> <p>We’ll use examples from both <a href="ojs/">Observable JS</a> and <a href="shiny/">Shiny</a> interactive documents—if you aren’t familiar with the code/syntax used for a given example just focus on the enclosing layout markup rather than the application code.</p> <h5 id="input-panel">Input Panel</h5> <p>If you have several inputs, you may want to group them inside an input panel (code block with option <code>panel: input</code> or div with class <code>.panel-input</code>). For example:</p> <p>The inputs are grouped in a panel and laid out in three columns by adding the <code>panel: input</code> and <code>layout-ncol: 3</code> options to the OJS code cell:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| panel: input //| layout-ncol: 3 viewof ch = checkbox({ title: "Passport color:", options: [ { value: "red", label: "Red" }, { value: "green", label: "Green" }, { value: "blue", label: "Blue" }, { value: "black", label: "Black" } ], value: ["red", "green", "blue", "black"], submit: false }) viewof type = radio({ title: "Representation:", options: [ { label: 'Passports', value: 'p' }, { label: 'Circles', value: 'c' } ], value: 'p' }) viewof k = slider({ title: "Symbol size:", min: 1, max: 10, value: 3, step: 1 }) ```</code></pre> <h5 id="tabset-panel">Tabset Panel</h5> <p>If you want to allow users to toggle between multiple visualizations, use a tabset (div with class <code>.panel-tabset</code>). Include a heading (e.g. <code>##</code>) for each tab in the tabset.</p> <p>For example, here are a plot and data each presented in their own tab:</p> <pre><code>data = FileAttachment("ojs/palmer-penguins.csv").csv({typed: true})</code></pre> <ul> <li><p>Plot</p></li> <li><p>Data</p> <p>Plot.rectY(data, Plot.stackY( Plot.binX( {y: “count”}, {x: “body_mass_g”, fill: “species”, thresholds: 20}) ) ).plot({ facet: { data, x: “sex” }, marks: [Plot.frame()] })</p> <p>Inputs.table(data)</p></li> </ul> <p>Here is the markup and code used to create the tabset:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset} ## Plot ```{ojs} Plot.rectY(data, Plot.stackY( Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20}) ) ).plot({ facet: { data, x: "sex" }, marks: [Plot.frame()] }) ``` ## Data ```{ojs} Inputs.table(filtered) ``` :::</code></pre> <h5 id="full-page-layout">Full Page Layout</h5> <p>By default Quarto documents center their content within the document viewport, and don’t exceed a maximum width of around 900 pixels. This behavior exists to optimize readability, but for an application layout you generally want to occupy the entire page.</p> <p>To do this, add the <code>page-layout: custom</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: page-layout: custom</code></pre> <p>Here’s an example of a Shiny application that occupies the full width of the browser:</p> <p>You’ll also note that the inputs are contained within a sidebar—the next section describes how to create sidebars.</p> <h5 id="sidebar-panel">Sidebar Panel</h5> <p>Sidebars are created using divs with class <code>.panel-sidebar</code>. You can do this using a markdown div container (as illustrated above for <code>.panel-input</code>), or, if the entire contents of your sidebar is created from a single code cell, by adding the <code>panel: sidebar</code> option to the cell.</p> <p>Sidebar panels should always have an adjacent panel with class <code>.panel-fill</code> or <code>.panel-center</code> which they will be laid out next to. The former (<code>.panel-fill</code>) will fill all available space, the latter (<code>.panel-center</code>) will leave some horizontal margin around its content.</p> <p>For example, here is the source code of the user-interface portion of the Shiny application displayed above:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Iris K-Means Clustering" format: html: page-layout: custom server: shiny --- ```{r} #| panel: sidebar vars <- setdiff(names(iris), "Species") selectInput('xcol', 'X Variable', vars) selectInput('ycol', 'Y Variable', vars, selected = vars[[2]]) numericInput('clusters', 'Cluster count', 3, min = 1, max = 9) ``` ```{r} #| panel: fill plotOutput('plot1') ```</code></pre> <p>The <code>panel: fill</code> option is added to the plot output chunk. You can alternately use <code>panel: center</code> if you want to leave some horizontal margin around the contents of the panel.</p> <p>Adding the <code>panel</code> option to a code chunk is shorthand for adding the CSS class to its containing div (i.e. it’s equivalent to surrounding the code chunk with a div with class e.g. <code>panel-fill</code>).</p> <p>Here’s an example of using a sidebar with OJS inputs:</p> <p>To do this you would use the following code:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| panel: sidebar viewof myage = { const myage = select({ title: "Quelle classe d'âge voulez-vous cartographier ?", options: ages, value: "80etplus" }); return myage; } viewof pctvax = slider({ title: '<br/>Objectif de vaccination', description: '200% signifie 2 doses par personnes pour tout le monde', min: 50, max: 200, value: 200, step: 10, format: v => v + "%" }) viewof overlay = radio({ title: "Écarter les cercles", options: [{ label: 'Oui', value: 'Y' }, { label: 'Non', value: 'N' }], value: 'N' }) viewof label = radio({ title: "Numéros des départements", options: [{ label: 'Afficher', value: 'Y' }, { label: 'Masquer', value: 'N' }], value: 'N' }) ``` ```{ojs} //| panel: fill (vaccine visualization code) ```</code></pre> <h5 id="panel-layout">Panel Layout</h5> <p>You can arrange multiple interactive components into a panel using the <code>layout</code> attribute of a containing div. For example, here we have a main visualization in the first row and two ancillary visualizations in the second row:</p> <p>As described in the article on Figures, you can arrange panels of figures in very flexible fashion using the <code>layout</code> attribute. For the example above we enclosed the three visualizations in the following div:</p> <pre><code>::: {layout="[ [1], [1,1] ]"} (outputs) :::</code></pre> <p>Note that you can apply the <code>layout</code> attribute to a div that is already a panel (e.g. <code>.panel-fill</code>) to specify layout for content adjacent to a sidebar. So the following markup is also valid:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-sidebar} (inputs) ::: ::: {.panel-fill layout="[ [1], [1,1] ]"} (outputs) :::</code></pre> <p>The <code>layout</code> attribute is an array of arrays, each of which defines a row of the layout. Above we indicate that we want the first row to encompass the first visualization, and then to split the next two equally over the second row.</p> <p>The values in rows don’t need to add up to anything in particular (they are relative within each row), so we could have just as well have specified different relative widths for the second row if that was better suited to presenting our data:</p> <pre><code>::: {layout="[ [1], [3,2] ]"} (outputs) :::</code></pre> <h3 id="data-sources-1">Data Sources</h3> <h4 id="data-sources-2">Data Sources</h4> <h5 id="overview-61">Overview</h5> <p>There are a wide variety of way to make data available to OJS:</p> <ul> <li>Read CSV, JSON, SQLite, and more using the <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#file-attachments">FileAttachments</a> API.</li> <li>Use the <code>ojs_define()</code> function to make data processed in Python or R available to <code>{ojs}</code> cells.</li> <li>Make calls to Web APIs for online services and data stores. We’ll explore all of these techniques below.</li> </ul> <h5 id="file-attachments">File Attachments</h5> <p>Use the <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#file-attachments">FileAttachment</a> function from the standard library to read data from a file. For example, here we read and plot a CSV of NOAA’s Monthly <a href="https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/data.html">CO2 concentration data</a> from Mauna Loa:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} data = { const co2data = await FileAttachment("co2_mm.csv") .csv({ typed: true } ); return co2data.map(d => { d["decimal date"] = Number(d["decimal date"]); d.average = Number(d.average); return d; }); } Plot.plot({ marks: [ Plot.line(data, { x: "decimal date", y: "average"}, { stroke: "black" } ) ] }) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that we specified the <code>typed: true</code> option to the <code>csv()</code> function. When this option is specified <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/d3-autotype">d3.autoType</a> is used to automatically detect numbers, dates, etc. and convert them to the correct JavaScript types. This is highly recommend when you know that your data is compatible with automatic type detection.</p> <p>Here are the methods available for structured data formats:</p> <p>Method</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_csv">csv</a></p> <p>Comma separated values</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_tsv">tsv</a></p> <p>Tab separated values</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_json">json</a></p> <p>JSON (JavaScript objects)</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_sqlite">sqlite</a></p> <p>SQLite database client</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib/blob/8d9f4d18df0b237a5e0870a6f39584048007aca7/src/fileAttachment.mjs#L59-L62">arrow</a></p> <p>Apache Arrow IPC file (uncompressed)</p> <p>There are also methods to get the raw data as a <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_blob">blob</a>, <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_text">text</a>, <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_image">image</a>, or <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#attachment_stream">stream</a>.</p> <p>Note that if you are using the <code>arrow()</code> method the Apache Arrow IPC file (Feather V2 file) should be written uncompressed. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} arrow::write_feather( mtcars, "data.arrow", compression = "uncompressed" ) ``` ```{ojs} data = FileAttachment("data.arrow").arrow() ```</code></pre> <h5 id="python-and-r">Python and R</h5> <p>The data you want to use with OJS might not always be available in raw form. Often you’ll need to read and preprocess the raw data using Python or R. You can perform this preprocessing during document render (in an <code>{r}</code> or <code>{python}</code> code cell) and then make it available to <code>{ojs}</code> cells via the <code>ojs_define()</code> function.</p> <p>Here’s an example. We’ll read the same data into R, do some grouping and summarization, then make it available to OJS using <code>ojs_define</code>:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| output: false library(readr) library(dplyr) co2 = read_csv("co2_mm.csv") %>% group_by(year) %>% summarize(max = max(average)) ojs_define(co2data = co2) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that we could have done the same thing using Python (the <code>ojs_define</code> function is available in any document that uses R or Python).</p> <p>Now we plot the data using <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/plot">Observable Plot</a>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} yearlyChart = Plot.plot({ marks: [ Plot.line(transpose(co2data), {x: "year", y: "max"}, { stroke: "black" } ) ]} ) ```</code></pre> <p>See the NOAA C02 example for the full source code.</p> <h6 id="transpose">Transpose</h6> <p>You’ll note one additional twist in the OJS code above: we call the <code>transpose</code> function on our <code>co2data</code> before plotting it. The <code>transpose</code> function is built in to Quarto’s OJS engine, and will convert column-oriented datasets (like the ones used in Python and R) into the row-oriented datasets used by many JavaScript plotting libraries (including <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/plot">Plot</a>).</p> <p>For example, the following JSON data emitted from R or Python:</p> <pre><code>{ "year": [1958, 1959, 1960], "max": [317.51, 318.29, 320.04] }</code></pre> <p>Is converted to the following via the call to <code>transpose</code>:</p> <pre><code>[ { "year": 1959, "max": 317.51 }, { "year": 1960, "max": 318.29 }, { "year": 1960, "max": 320.04 } ]</code></pre> <p>Check the documentation for whatever plotting library you are using from OJS to see whether a call to <code>transpose</code> is required.</p> <h5 id="web-apis">Web APIs</h5> <p>You can use the <a href="https://github.com/d3/d3-fetch/blob/v3.0.1/README.md#json"><code>d3.json()</code></a> function to read JSON data from web services and data sources. Here we query the GitHub API for data on contributions to the Python pandas package:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require('d3') contributors = await d3.json( "https://api.github.com/repos/pandas-dev/pandas/stats/contributors" ) commits = contributors.map(contributor => { const author = contributor.author; return { name: author.login, title: author.login, group: author.type, value: contributor.total } }) ```</code></pre> <p>View the data sorted by number of commits:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} Inputs.table(commits, { sort: "value", reverse: true }) ```</code></pre> <p>See the GitHub API example for the full source code.</p> <h3 id="execution-contexts-interactive-documents">Execution Contexts (Interactive documents)</h3> <h4 id="execution-contexts-1">Execution Contexts</h4> <h5 id="overview-62">Overview</h5> <p>Shiny interactive documents can contain both code that executes at render time as well as code that executes on the server in response to user actions and changes in input values. A solid understanding of these execution contexts is important both to have the right mental model during development as well as to optimize the performance of your document.</p> <h5 id="render-server-contexts">Render & Server Contexts</h5> <p>To break this down more clearly, let’s revisit the “Hello, Shiny” document we started with in the introduction to interactive documents:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Old Faithful" format: html server: shiny --- ```{r} sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:", min = 1, max = 50, value = 30) plotOutput("distPlot") ``` ```{r} #| context: server output$distPlot <- renderPlot({ x <- faithful[, 2] # Old Faithful Geyser data bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1) hist(x, breaks = bins, col = 'darkgray', border = 'white') }) ```</code></pre> <p>Here is how execution breaks down for this document:</p> <ul> <li>The first code chunk that contains the calls to <code>sliderInput()</code> and <code>plotOutput()</code> will execute when you render the document (e.g. <code>quarto render old-faithful.qmd</code>).</li> <li>The second code chunk with the <code>context: server</code> option will not execute at render time, but rather will execute only when the document is served. It’s critical to understand that the two chunks are run in completely separate R sessions. That means that you cannot access variables created in the first chunk within the second, and vice-versa. The is analogous to the <code>ui.R</code> and <code>server.R</code> scripts that compose most normal Shiny applications.</li> </ul> <p>Of course, it’s quite useful to be able to re-use code between contexts, and we’ll cover some ways to do this in the Sharing Code section below.</p> <p>In order to make the code of interactive documents straightforward to understand and work with, we strongly recommend that your server contexts (there can be more than one) be located at the bottom of the document. This makes the separate execution environments more clear in the flow of the document source code.</p> <h6 id="server.r">server.R</h6> <p>There is one other option if you prefer to have a stronger separation. You can restrict your <code>.qmd</code> file to only code that will execute at render time, and then split out the server code into a separate <code>server.R</code> file.</p> <p>Re-writing our example in this fashion would look like this:</p> <h6 id="old-faithful.qmd">old-faithful.qmd</h6> <pre><code>--- title: "Old Faithful" format: html server: shiny --- ```{r} sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:", min = 1, max = 50, value = 30) plotOutput("distPlot") ```</code></pre> <h6 id="server.r-1">server.R</h6> <pre><code>function(input, output, session) { output$distPlot <- renderPlot({ x <- faithful[, 2] # Old Faithful Geyser data bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1) hist(x, breaks = bins, col = 'darkgray', border = 'white') }) }</code></pre> <p>This is perhaps a bit less convenient but does align better with the traditional <code>ui.R</code> / <code>server.R</code> separation that exists in traditional Shiny applications.</p> <h5 id="sharing-code">Sharing Code</h5> <p>Sharing code between rendering contexts works a bit differently depending on if your code is in a single <code>.qmd</code> file or if it uses <code>server.R</code>. We’ll cover both scenarios below.</p> <h6 id="single-file">Single File</h6> <h6 id="context-setup">context: setup</h6> <p>To have code execute in both rendering and serving contexts, create a code chunk with <code>context: setup</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| context: setup #| include: false # load libraries library(dplyr) # load data dataset <- import_data("data.csv") dataset <- sample_n(dataset, 1000) ```</code></pre> <p>This code will execute at both render time as well as when the server is created for each new user session. Note that we also specify <code>include: false</code> to make sure that code, warnings, and output from the chunk are not included in the rendered document.</p> <h6 id="context-data">context: data</h6> <p>The loading and manipulation of data often dominates the startup time of Shiny applications. Since interactive documents are executed in two phases (the initial render and then the serving of the document to users) we can perform the expensive data manipulations during rendering and then simply load the data when starting up the application.</p> <p>You can define prerendered data by adding the <code>context: data</code> option to an R code chunk. The chunk will be executed during render and any R objects it creates will be saved to an .RData file, which will then be loaded during Shiny server startup. For example, we could take the setup chunk illustrated above and factor out the data loading into its own chunk:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| context: data #| include: false dataset <- import_data("data.csv") dataset <- sample_n(dataset, 1000) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that R objects created within a <code>context: data</code> chunk are available to both the UI rendering and server contexts.</p> <h6 id="knitr-cache">Knitr cache</h6> <p>You can further improve the performance of data rendering by adding the <code>cache: true</code> option to the data chunk. This will cause the code chunk to be re-executed only when required. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| context: data #| include: false #| cache: true #| cache.extra: !expr file.info("data.csv")$mtime dataset <- import_data("data.csv") dataset <- sample_n(dataset, 1000) ```</code></pre> <p>In this example the cache will be invalidated if either the R code in the chunk changes or the modification time of the “data.csv” file changes (this is accomplished using the <code>cache.extra</code> option).</p> <p>You can also invalidate an existing cache by removing the <code>_cache</code> directory alongside with your interactive document.</p> <h6 id="context-server-start">context: server-start</h6> <p>There is one additional execution context that enables you to share code and data across multiple user sessions. Chunks with <code>context: server-start</code> execute once when the Shiny document is first run and are not re-executed for each new user of the document. Using <code>context: server-start</code> is appropriate for several scenarios including:</p> <ul> <li><p>Establishing shared connections to remote servers (e.g. databases, Spark contexts, etc.).</p></li> <li><p>Creating reactive values intended to be shared across sessions (e.g. with <a href="http://shiny.rstudio.com/reference/shiny/latest/reactivePoll.html">reactivePoll</a> or <a href="http://shiny.rstudio.com/reference/shiny/latest/reactiveFileReader.html">reactiveFileReader</a>). For example:</p> <p>```{r} #| context: server-start</p> <p>library(DBI) db <- dbConnect(…) ```</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="multiple-files">Multiple Files</h6> <p>If your interactive document uses a <code>.qmd</code> file to define the user-interface and a <code>server.R</code> file for the server, you can put shared code in a file named <code>global.R</code>. Functions and variables defined within <code>global.R</code> will be available both during render as well as during execution of the server.</p> <p>In this scenario your interactive document consists of 3 source files:</p> <p>File</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>doc.qmd</code></p> <p>Markdown content as well as Shiny inputs and outputs (e.g. <code>sliderInput()</code>, <code>plotOutput()</code>, etc.)</p> <p><code>server.R</code></p> <p>Main server function with reactive expressions, assignments to outputs, etc.</p> <p><code>global.R</code></p> <p>Code shared between <code>doc.qmd</code> and <code>server.R</code>.</p> <h3 id="external-resources">External Resources</h3> <h4 id="external-resources-1">External Resources</h4> <h5 id="overview-63">Overview</h5> <p>There are two types of external resource file that might be referenced from within a Shiny interactive document:</p> <ul> <li>Files referenced from R code (e.g. R scripts, datasets, configuration files, etc.); and</li> <li>Static assets referenced from the web document (e.g. CSS style-sheets, images, etc.) Below we’ll describe how each of these resource types are handled within interactive documents.</li> </ul> <h5 id="code-resources">Code Resources</h5> <p>For files referenced from R code, you can reference anything located within the directory of (or sub-directories of) the main <code>.qmd</code> file. This is no different than with any other <code>.qmd</code> file or even R script.</p> <p>Similarly, files created by executing R code (e.g. figures generated from code chunks) are automatically located in the document <code>_files</code> directory alongside the HTML output file. No special handling is required for these files.</p> <h5 id="asset-resources">Asset Resources</h5> <p>Many interactive documents will consist of only the generated HTML and figures located in the <code>_files</code> directory. However, in some cases you may want to add static images, CSS files, or other assets to your document.</p> <p>In these cases, you need to be sure to locate the files within one of the following specially named sub-directories to ensure they can be located by the Shiny server:</p> <p>Directory</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>images/</code></p> <p>Image files (e.g. PNG, JPEG, etc.)</p> <p><code>css/</code></p> <p>CSS stylesheets</p> <p><code>js/</code></p> <p>JavaScript scripts</p> <p><code>www/</code></p> <p>Any other files (e.g. downloadable datasets)</p> <p>The reason that all files within the directory of the main <code>.qmd</code> can’t be referenced from within the web document is that many of these files are application source code and data, which may not be something you want to be downloadable by end users. By restricting the files which can be referenced to the above directories you can control which files are downloadable and which are not.</p> <h3 id="github-api">GitHub API</h3> <h4 id="github-api-1">GitHub API</h4> <ul> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Show All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Hide All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">View Source</a> Demonstration of using the <a href="https://developer.github.com/v3">GitHub API</a>.</li> </ul> <p>Code</p> <pre><code>viewof repo = Inputs.radio( [ "pandas-dev/pandas", "tidyverse/ggplot2", ], { label: "Repo:", value: "pandas-dev/pandas"} )</code></pre> <p>Code</p> <pre><code>import { chart } with { commits as data } from "@d3/d3-bubble-chart" chart</code></pre> <h5 id="data-1">Data</h5> <pre><code>d3 = require('d3') contributors = await d3.json( "[api.github.com](https://api.github.com/repos/)" + repo + "/stats/contributors" ) commits = contributors.map(contributor => { const author = contributor.author; return { name: author.login, title: author.login, group: author.type, value: contributor.total } }) Inputs.table(commits, { sort: "value", reverse: true })</code></pre> <h3 id="htmlwidgets-for-r">htmlwidgets for R</h3> <h4 id="htmlwidgets-for-r-1">htmlwidgets for R</h4> <h5 id="overview-64">Overview</h5> <p>The <a href="http://www.htmlwidgets.org">htmlwidgets</a> package enables you to use JavaScript visualization libraries like <a href="http://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/">Leaflet</a>, <a href="https://plot.ly/r/">Plotly</a>, <a href="http://rstudio.github.io/dygraphs/">dygraphs</a>, and <a href="https://bwlewis.github.io/rthreejs/">threejs</a> directly from R.</p> <p>If you are using the Knitr engine with Quarto this is a great way to incorporate interactivity without learning JavaScript or requiring a Shiny Server to view your document.</p> <h5 id="usage-3">Usage</h5> <p>Including htmlwidgets within a Quarto document is as easy as including an R plot. For example, here is how we embed a <a href="http://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/">Leaflet</a> map:</p> <pre><code>```{r} library(leaflet) leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% # Add default OpenStreetMap map tiles addMarkers(lng=174.768, lat=-36.852, popup="The birthplace of R") ``` Warning: package 'leaflet' was built under R version 4.1.2</code></pre> <h5 id="layout-3">Layout</h5> <p>You can also use <code>layout</code> options with htmlwidgets. For example, here we provide a custom <code>layout</code> to arrange three <a href="http://rstudio.github.io/dygraphs/">dygraph</a> time series plots:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| layout: [[1,1], [1]] library(dygraphs) dygraph(fdeaths, "Female Deaths") dygraph(mdeaths, "Male Deaths") dygraph(ldeaths, "All Deaths") ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Figures for additional documentation on custom layouts.</p> <p>To learn about available htmlwidgets see the <a href="http://www.htmlwidgets.org/showcase_leaflet.html">showcase page</a> and the <a href="http://gallery.htmlwidgets.org/">htmlwidget gallery</a>.</p> <h3 id="interactivity">Interactivity</h3> <h4 id="interactivity-1">Interactivity</h4> <h5 id="overview-65">Overview</h5> <p>Adding interactivity to an article is a great way to help readers explore the concepts and data you are presenting more deeply. There are three ways to add interactive components to Quarto documents:</p> <ul> <li>Create custom JavaScript visualizations using <a href="ojs/">Observable JS</a>.</li> <li>Use the <a href="shiny/">Shiny</a> R package to add interactivity to Knitr engine documents.</li> <li>Incorporate Jupyter Widgets or htmlwidgets (for the Jupyter and Knitr engines, respectively) into your document. Each of these techniques has distinct benefits and drawbacks in terms of expressiveness, ease of development, and deployment requirements. We’ll touch on these considerations briefly below, then provide links to more in depth documentation for learning more.</li> </ul> <h5 id="observable-js">Observable JS</h5> <p>Quarto includes native support for <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable JS</a>, a set of enhancements to vanilla JavaScript created by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Bostock">Mike Bostock</a> (also the author of <a href="https://d3js.org/">D3</a>). Observable JS is distinguished by its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/runtime">reactive runtime</a>, which is especially well suited for interactive data exploration and analysis.</p> <p>Here’s an example that provides slider inputs to condition the behavior of a visualization:</p> <pre><code>viewof talentWeight = Inputs.range([-2, 2], { value: 0.7, step: 0.01, label: "talent weight" }) viewof looksWeight = Inputs.range([-2, 2], { value: 0.7, step: 0.01, label: "looks weight" }) viewof minimum = Inputs.range([-2, 2], { value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "minimum fame" }) { const w = 400 const h = 400; const result = d3.create("svg").attr("width", w).attr("height", h); const margin = 20; const xScale = d3.scaleLinear().domain([-2, 2]).range([margin, w - margin]); const yScale = d3.scaleLinear().domain([-2, 2]).range([h - margin, margin]); const points = result .append("g") .selectAll("circle") .data(actors) .join(enter => { const sel = enter .append("circle") .attr("r", 3) .attr("cx", d => xScale(d.talent)) .attr("cy", d => yScale(d.looks)) .attr("fill", d3.lab(50, 40, 20)); return sel.filter(d => d.fame <= minimum) .attr("fill", "rgb(200, 200, 200)") .attr("r", 2); }); const linearRegression = regression.regressionLinear() .x(d => d.talent) .y(d => d.looks) .domain([-2, 2]); const chosenActors = actors .filter(d => d.fame > minimum); const line = result .append("g") .append("line") .attr("stroke", d3.lab(20, 40, 20)) .attr("stroke-width", 1.5) .datum(linearRegression(chosenActors)) .attr("x1", d => xScale(d[0][0])) .attr("x2", d => xScale(d[1][0])) .attr("y1", d => yScale(d[0][1])) .attr("y2", d => yScale(d[1][1])); const xAxis = d3.axisBottom(xScale).ticks(3); result.append("g") .attr("transform", `translate(0, ${yScale(0)})`) .call(xAxis); result.append("text") .attr("x", xScale(0.05)) .attr("y", yScale(2)) .text("Looks"); result.append("text") .attr("y", yScale(0.1)) .attr("x", xScale(-2)) .text("Talent"); const yAxis = d3.axisLeft(yScale).ticks(3); result.append("g") .attr("transform", `translate(${xScale(0)}, 0)`) .call(yAxis); return result.node(); } actors = transpose(points).map(v => ({ talent: v.x, looks: v.y, fame: v.x * talentWeight + v.y * looksWeight })); transpose = function(df) { const keys = Object.keys(df); return df[keys[0]] .map((v, i) => Object.fromEntries(keys.map(key => [key, df[key][i] || undefined]))) .filter(v => Object.values(v).every(e => e !== undefined)); } regression = require('d3-regression@1');</code></pre> <p>Observable JS uses some special keywords and a custom runtime to make JavaScript reactive. For example, the “minimum fame” slider in the example above was created with the following code:</p> <pre><code>viewof minimum = Inputs.range([-2, 2], { value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "minimum fame" })</code></pre> <p>It’s then referenced as a normal JavaScript variable in code that creates the plot:</p> <pre><code>sel.filter(d => d.fame <= minimum)</code></pre> <p>As the user interacts with the slider, the <code>minimum</code> value is updated and any code that references it is automatically re-executed.</p> <p>One benefit of using JavaScript for interactive documents is that all the logic and computation is performed on the client (so no server is required for deployment).</p> <p>To learn more see the articles on <a href="ojs/">Observable JS</a>.</p> <h5 id="shiny-2">Shiny</h5> <p>The Shiny package provides a flexible, easy to use framework for creating interactive web applications with R. Quarto in turn includes support for embedding Shiny components and applets into documents created with the Knitr engine.</p> <p>Here’s a live example of Shiny interactive components along with a brief explanation of the code required to create them:</p> <p>Shiny comes with a variety of built in input widgets. With minimal syntax it is possible to include widgets like the ones shown on the left in your apps:</p> <pre><code># Select type of trend to plot selectInput(inputId = "type", label = strong("Trend index"), choices = unique(trend_data$type), selected = "Travel")</code></pre> <p>Displaying outputs is equally hassle-free:</p> <pre><code>mainPanel( plotOutput(outputId = "lineplot", height = "300px"), )</code></pre> <p>Build your plots or tables as you normally would in R, and make them reactive with a call to the appropriate render function:</p> <pre><code>output$lineplot <- renderPlot({ plot(x = selected_trends()$date, y = selected_trends()$close, type = "l", xlab = "Date", ylab = "Trend index") })</code></pre> <p>Shiny makes it very straightforward to create interactive documents using only R. Unlike using JavaScript though, you will need to deploy documents that use Shiny to a server.</p> <p>To learn more see the articles on <a href="shiny/">Using Shiny with Quarto</a>.</p> <h5 id="widgets">Widgets</h5> <p><a href="https://jupyter.org/widgets">Jupyter Widgets</a> and <a href="https://www.htmlwidgets.org/">htmlwidgets</a> are great ways to incorporate interactivity into your documents if you don’t know JavaScript and prefer to work exclusively in Python or R. They also run entirely client-side so can be deployed within normal static HTML documents.</p> <p>For example, the following Python code is all that is required to embed a Leaflet map into a Jupyter engine document:</p> <pre><code>```{python} from ipyleaflet import Map, Marker, basemaps, basemap_to_tiles m = Map( basemap=basemap_to_tiles( basemaps.NASAGIBS.ModisTerraTrueColorCR, "2017-04-08" ), center=(52.204793, 360.121558), zoom=4 ) m.add_layer(Marker(location=(52.204793, 360.121558))) m ```</code></pre> <p>To learn more see these articles on using widgets with Quarto:</p> <ul> <li>Jupyter Widgets (Jupyter engine).</li> <li>htmlwidgets (Knitr engine).</li> </ul> <h5 id="layout-4">Layout</h5> <p>Once you’ve gotten familiar with using various interactive components see the article on Component Layout to learn how to:</p> <ul> <li>Group inputs into an input panel.</li> <li>Present multiple outputs in a tabset panel.</li> <li>Use a full page layout rather than the default article layout.</li> <li>Add a sidebar panel for inputs in a full page layout.</li> <li>Create custom panel layouts to arrange outputs into rows and columns.</li> </ul> <h5 id="observable-js-on-the-rstudio-ide">Observable JS on the RStudio IDE</h5> <p>Observable JS offers full access to <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/">NPM</a> libraries, and these tend to use JS features that require the Electron version of the RStudio IDE <a href="https://dailies.rstudio.com/">daily builds</a>. If you plan on using Observable JS in the RStudio IDE, we recommend the Electron daily builds.</p> <h3 id="jupyter-widgets">Jupyter Widgets</h3> <h4 id="jupyter-widgets-1">Jupyter Widgets</h4> <h5 id="overview-66">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://jupyter.org/widgets">Jupyter Widgets</a> enable you to use JavaScript visualization libraries like <a href="https://ipyleaflet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Leaflet</a>, <a href="https://plotly.com/python/">Plotly</a>, and <a href="https://pythreejs.readthedocs.io/">threejs</a> directly from Python.</p> <p>If you are using the Jupyter engine with Quarto this is a great way to incorporate interactivity without learning JavaScript.</p> <p>Note that while Quarto uses a Jupyter kernel during rendering, there is no Jupyter kernel once the site is published, so there is interactivity with JavaScript but not with Python.</p> <h5 id="leaflet-example">Leaflet Example</h5> <p>Including Jupyter Widgets within a Quarto document is as easy as including a plot. For example, here is how we embed a <a href="https://ipyleaflet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Leaflet</a> map:</p> <pre><code>from ipyleaflet import Map, Marker, basemaps, basemap_to_tiles m = Map( basemap=basemap_to_tiles( basemaps.NASAGIBS.ModisTerraTrueColorCR, "2017-04-08" ), center=(52.204793, 360.121558), zoom=4 ) m.add_layer(Marker(location=(52.204793, 360.121558))) m</code></pre> <p>To learn about available Jupyter Widgets visit <a href="https://jupyter.org/widgets">jupyter.org</a>.</p> <h5 id="plotly-1">Plotly</h5> <p>Plotly is an interactive graphics library that can also be used with the Jupyter engine. Here’s an example of using <a href="https://plotly.com/python/">Plotly</a>:</p> <pre><code>import plotly.express as px import plotly.io as pio df = px.data.iris() fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species", marginal_y="violin", marginal_x="box", trendline="ols", template="simple_white") fig.show()</code></pre> <p>Note</p> <p>If you are using Plotly within the VS Code Notebook Editor you will need to add a line of code to ensure that your plots can be seen both within VS Code and when rendered to HTML by Quarto. You can do this by configuring the Plotly <a href="https://plotly.com/python/renderers/#setting-the-default-renderer">default renderer</a> as follows:</p> <pre><code>```{python} import plotly.io as pio pio.renderers.default = "plotly_mimetype+notebook_connected" ```</code></pre> <p>This workaround is required because when running within VS Code, Plotly chooses a default rendering that can’t be easily exported to HTML (for more background, see this <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-jupyter/issues/6999">GitHub Issue</a> and related discussion). Note that this workaround is only required for the VS Code Notebook Editor (it is not required if you are using Jupyter Lab or if you are editing a plain-text <code>.qmd</code> file).</p> <h3 id="layout-5">Layout</h3> <h4 id="layout-6">Layout</h4> <p>You can control the layout of OJS content in a number of ways.</p> <h5 id="page-layout-full"><code>page-layout: full</code></h5> <p>This example uses <code>page-layout: full</code> to have its contents occupy the entire width of the page:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Layout" format: html: page-layout: full ---</code></pre> <p>Enclose the inputs in a sidebar panel and the outputs in a tabset panel (click the “Code” button at top right to see the full source code):</p> <pre><code>viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } )</code></pre> <ul> <li><p>Plot</p></li> <li><p>Data</p> <p>Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: “count”}, {x: “body_mass_g”, fill: “species”, thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: “sex”, y: “species”, marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } )</p> <p>Inputs.table(filtered)</p></li> </ul> <p>Read and filter the data based on the user’s inputs:</p> <pre><code>data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({typed: true}) filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); })</code></pre> <h5 id="width-and-layoutwidth-fine-grained-layout-tracking"><code>width</code> and <code>layoutWidth</code>: fine-grained layout tracking</h5> <p>Like ObservableHQ, <code>ojs</code> cells support the reactive <code>width</code> which tracks the <code>clientWidth</code> of the main HTML element.</p> <pre><code>width</code></pre> <p>In addition, if you need the widths of specific parts of the layout, use the CSS class <code>ojs-track-layout</code> in a div. Quarto’s OJS runtime tracks all such divs in <code>layoutWidth</code>. In this example, the tabset above has id <code>penguins-tabset</code>, and you can see its <code>clientWidth</code> reactively below. If this webpage is sufficiently wide, the sidebar will take up some of the space and the width of the resulting tabset will be smaller:</p> <pre><code>layoutWidth</code></pre> <h3 id="libraries-1">Libraries</h3> <h4 id="libraries-2">Libraries</h4> <h5 id="overview-67">Overview</h5> <p>There are three types of library you’ll generally use with OJS:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq">Observable core libraries</a> automatically available in every document.</li> <li>Third-party JavaScript libraries from <a href="https://docs.npmjs.com/about-packages-and-modules">npm</a> and <a href="https://observablehq.com">ObservableHQ</a>.</li> <li>Custom libraries you and/or your colleagues have created In this document we’ll provide a high-level overview of the core libraries and some examples of using third-party libraries (D3 and Arquero). Creating your own libraries is covered in the article on Code Reuse.</li> </ul> <h5 id="stdlib">Stdlib</h5> <p>The Observable standard library provides the core capabilities that underlie rendering content and loading code and data. Some particularly important components of the standard library include:</p> <p>Component</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#dom">DOM</a></p> <p>Dynamically creating DOM elements</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#file-attachments">FileAttachments</a></p> <p>Reading files in a variety of formats</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#require">require</a></p> <p>Importing third-party modules from NPM and GitHub</p> <p>You can find complete documentation for the standard library at <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib">github.com</a>.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Quarto always embeds a specific version of ObservableHQ’s runtime, which means that Quarto might be behind the very latest ObservableHQ version on their website. If you need to use the latest version of Plot (or other core libraries), you can use the <code>import</code> function to import the latest version directly from a CDN. For example:</p> <pre><code>Plot = import("[cdn.jsdelivr.net](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@observablehq/plot/+esm)")</code></pre> <h5 id="inputs">Inputs</h5> <p>The Observable inputs library provides widgets that can be bound to reactive expressions via the <code>viewof</code> keyword. Some particularly useful input include:</p> <p>Component</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs#Radio">Radio</a></p> <p>Choose from mutually exclusive set of options</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs#Checkbox">Checkbox</a></p> <p>Choose one or more options from a list</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs#Range">Range</a></p> <p>Slider for continuous numeric values</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs#Select">Select</a></p> <p>Drop down select box</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs#Table">Table</a></p> <p>Select one or more rows from a table</p> <p>You can find complete documentation for all of the inputs at <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs">github.com</a>.</p> <h5 id="plot">Plot</h5> <p>Observable Plot is a JavaScript library for exploratory data visualization. Plot is built upon a set of core concepts (<a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot-marks">Marks</a>, <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot-scales">Scales</a>, <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot-transforms">Transforms</a>, and <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot-facets">Facets</a>) that can be composed together to create custom visualizations.</p> <p>Here’s an example of a histogram of the weight of Olympic athletes created with Plot:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} athletes = FileAttachment("athletes.csv").csv({typed: true}) Plot.plot({ grid: true, facet: { data: athletes, y: "sex" }, marks: [ Plot.rectY( athletes, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "weight", fill: "sex"}) ), Plot.ruleY([0]) ] }) ```</code></pre> <p>You can find complete documentation for Observable plot <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/plot">github.com</a>.</p> <h5 id="d3">D3</h5> <p><a href="https://d3js.org/">D3.js</a> is a JavaScript library for manipulating documents based on data. D3 is capable of creating just about any interactive graphic you can imagine!</p> <p>Here’s a “zoomable sunburst” diagram (originally published at: <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-sunburst">observablehq.com</a>) created with D3. Only two layers of the hierarchy are shown at a time. Click a node to zoom in, or the center to zoom out.</p> <pre><code>sunburst = { const root = partition(flareData); root.each(d => d.current = d); const svg = d3.create("svg") .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, width]) .style("font", "15px sans-serif"); const g = svg.append("g") .attr("transform", `translate(${width / 2},${width / 2})`); const path = g.append("g") .selectAll("path") .data(root.descendants().slice(1)) .join("path") .attr("fill", d => { while (d.depth > 1) d = d.parent; return color(d.data.name); }) .attr("fill-opacity", d => arcVisible(d.current) ? (d.children ? 0.6 : 0.4) : 0) .attr("d", d => arc(d.current)); path.filter(d => d.children) .style("cursor", "pointer") .on("click", clicked); path.append("title") .text(d => `${d.ancestors().map(d => d.data.name).reverse().join("/")}\n${format(d.value)}`); const label = g.append("g") .attr("pointer-events", "none") .attr("text-anchor", "middle") .style("user-select", "none") .selectAll("text") .data(root.descendants().slice(1)) .join("text") .attr("dy", "0.35em") .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.current)) .attr("transform", d => labelTransform(d.current)) .text(d => d.data.name); const parent = g.append("circle") .datum(root) .attr("r", radius) .attr("fill", "none") .attr("pointer-events", "all") .on("click", clicked); function clicked(event, p) { parent.datum(p.parent || root); root.each(d => d.target = { x0: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x0 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI, x1: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x1 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI, y0: Math.max(0, d.y0 - p.depth), y1: Math.max(0, d.y1 - p.depth) }); const t = g.transition().duration(750); // Transition the data on all arcs, even the ones that aren’t visible, // so that if this transition is interrupted, entering arcs will start // the next transition from the desired position. path.transition(t) .tween("data", d => { const i = d3.interpolate(d.current, d.target); return t => d.current = i(t); }) .filter(function(d) { return +this.getAttribute("fill-opacity") || arcVisible(d.target); }) .attr("fill-opacity", d => arcVisible(d.target) ? (d.children ? 0.6 : 0.4) : 0) .attrTween("d", d => () => arc(d.current)); label.filter(function(d) { return +this.getAttribute("fill-opacity") || labelVisible(d.target); }).transition(t) .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.target)) .attrTween("transform", d => () => labelTransform(d.current)); } function arcVisible(d) { return d.y1 <= 3 && d.y0 >= 1 && d.x1 > d.x0; } function labelVisible(d) { return d.y1 <= 3 && d.y0 >= 1 && (d.y1 - d.y0) * (d.x1 - d.x0) > 0.03; } function labelTransform(d) { const x = (d.x0 + d.x1) / 2 * 180 / Math.PI; const y = (d.y0 + d.y1) / 2 * radius; return `rotate(${x - 90}) translate(${y},0) rotate(${x < 180 ? 0 : 180})`; } return svg.node(); }</code></pre> <p>To use D3 in an <code>{ojs}</code> cell, first import it using the <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#require">require</a> function (which loads modules hosted at <a href="https://www.jsdelivr.com/">jsDelivr</a>):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require("d3@7") ```</code></pre> <p>Then, use d3 as needed to create your visualization. For example, here are the first few lines of the cell that creates the visualization above:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} sunburst = { const root = partition(flareData); root.each(d => d.current = d); const svg = d3.create("svg") .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, width]) .style("font", "15px sans-serif"); // ...remainder of implementation return svg.node(); } ```</code></pre> <p>See the Sunburst example for the complete source code. To learn more about D3, visit <a href="https://d3js.org/">d3js.org</a>.</p> <h5 id="arquero-2">Arquero</h5> <p><a href="https://uwdata.github.io/arquero/">Arquero</a> is a JavaScript library for query processing and transformation of array-backed data tables. Following the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_algebra">relational algebra</a> and inspired by the design of <a href="https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/">dplyr</a>, Arquero provides a fluent API for manipulating column-oriented data frames.</p> <p>Here we’ll import Arquero (<code>aq</code>) and an alias to Arquero operations (<code>op</code>), read a dataset, then filter, aggregate, and view the data:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} import { aq, op } from '@uwdata/arquero' penguins = aq.loadCSV("palmer-penguins.csv") penguins .groupby('species') .filter(p => p.body_mass_g > 0) .rollup({ count: op.count(), avg_mass: op.average('body_mass_g') }) .view() ```</code></pre> <p>See the Arquero example for complete source code. To learn more about using Arquero, see the <a href="https://observablehq.com/@uwdata/introducing-arquero">Introducing Arquero</a> tutorial.</p> <h5 id="modules-1">Modules</h5> <h6 id="npm">NPM</h6> <p>The <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#require">require</a> function in the standard library can be used to import <a href="https://docs.npmjs.com/about-packages-and-modules">npm modules</a> (which are served from the <a href="https://www.jsdelivr.com/">jsDelivr</a> CDN):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require("d3") topojson = require("topojson") ```</code></pre> <p>Modules can optionally include an <code>@</code> sign with a version. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require("d3@7") ```</code></pre> <p>See the <a href="https://www.jsdelivr.com">jsDelivr documentation</a> for additional details. Note that the require function automatically prepends the prefix <code>https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/</code> when resolving imports, so where the jsDeliver documentation says to use this URL:</p> <pre><code>[cdn.jsdelivr.net](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/package@version/file)</code></pre> <p>You need only pass this to <code>require</code>:</p> <pre><code>package@version/file</code></pre> <h6 id="observablehq">ObservableHQ</h6> <p>Notebooks published on <a href="http://observablehq.com">observablehq.com</a> can also be compiled and downloaded as <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/downloading-and-embedding-notebooks#notebooks-as-es-modules">JavaScript modules</a>.</p> <p>While notebooks often have their own embedded dataset, you can actually replace this data with your own when you import them! Returning to the sunburst example from above, here we <code>import</code> a notebook and use the <code>with</code> keyword to provide our own value for <code>data</code>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} pdata = FileAttachment("population.json").json() import { chart } with { pdata as data } from "@d3/zoomable-sunburst" chart ```</code></pre> <p>One important restriction to be aware of is that not all notebooks published on ObservableHQ have an open-source license. Notebooks need to <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/licenses">explicitly tagged with a license</a> as an indication that it’s okay to use them outside of ObservableHQ.</p> <p>You can see the license for a notebook in its header area. For, example this notebook is tagged with the ISC license:</p> <p>You should check the license of ObservableHQ notebooks before you import them. See the documentation on <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/licenses">notebook licenses</a> for additional details on how to do this.</p> <h5 id="appendix-1">Appendix</h5> <pre><code>```{ojs} flareData = FileAttachment("examples/flare-2.json").json() ``` ```{ojs} partition = flareData => { const root = d3.hierarchy(flareData) .sum(d => d.value) .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value); return d3.partition() .size([2 * Math.PI, root.height + 1]) (root); } ``` ```{ojs} color = d3.scaleOrdinal(d3.quantize(d3.interpolateRainbow, flareData.children.length + 1)) ``` ```{ojs} format = d3.format(",d") ``` ```{ojs} width = 932 ``` ```{ojs} radius = width / 6 ``` ```{ojs} arc = d3.arc() .startAngle(d => d.x0) .endAngle(d => d.x1) .padAngle(d => Math.min((d.x1 - d.x0) / 2, 0.005)) .padRadius(radius * 1.5) .innerRadius(d => d.y0 * radius) .outerRadius(d => Math.max(d.y0 * radius, d.y1 * radius - 1)) ``` ```{ojs} d3 = require("d3@7") ```</code></pre> <h3 id="noaa-co2">NOAA CO2</h3> <h4 id="noaa-co2-1">NOAA CO2</h4> <p>Read and plot a CSV of NOAA’s Monthly <a href="https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/data.html">CO2 concentration data</a> from Mauna Loa:</p> <pre><code>data = { const co2data = await FileAttachment("co2_mm.csv") .csv({ typed: true }); return co2data.map(d => { d["decimal date"] = Number(d["decimal date"]); d.average = Number(d.average); return d; }); } Plot.plot({ marks: [ Plot.line(data, { x: "decimal date", y: "average"}, { stroke: "black" } ) ] })</code></pre> <p>Read the same data into R, do some grouping and summarization, then make it available using <code>ojs_define</code>:</p> <pre><code>library(readr) library(dplyr) co2 = read_csv("co2_mm.csv") %>% group_by(year) %>% summarize(max = max(average)) ojs_define(co2data = co2)</code></pre> <p>Now plot the summarized data:</p> <pre><code>Plot.plot({ marks: [ Plot.line(transpose(co2data), {x: "year", y: "max"}, { stroke: "black" } ) ]} )</code></pre> <h3 id="observable-js-1">Observable JS</h3> <h4 id="observable-js-2">Observable JS</h4> <h5 id="overview-68">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto includes native support for <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable JS</a>, a set of enhancements to vanilla JavaScript created by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Bostock">Mike Bostock</a> (also the author of <a href="https://d3js.org/">D3</a>). Observable JS is distinguished by its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/runtime">reactive runtime</a>, which is especially well suited for interactive data exploration and analysis.</p> <p>The creators of Observable JS (Observable, Inc.) run a hosted service at <a href="https://observablehq.com/">observablehq.com</a> where you can create and publish notebooks. Additionally, you can use Observable JS (“OJS”) in standalone documents and websites via its <a href="https://github.com/observablehq">core libraries</a>. Quarto uses these libraries along with a <a href="https://github.com/asg017/unofficial-observablehq-compiler/tree/beta">compiler</a> that is run at render time to enable the use of OJS within Quarto documents.</p> <p>OJS works in any Quarto document (plain markdown as well as Jupyter and Knitr documents). Just include your code in an <code>{ojs}</code> executable code block. The rest of this article explains the basics of using OJS with Quarto.</p> <h5 id="example-5">Example</h5> <p>We’ll start with a simple example based on Allison Horst’s <a href="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/">Palmer Penguins</a> dataset. Here we look at how penguin body mass varies across both sex and species (use the provided inputs to filter the dataset by bill length and island):</p> <pre><code>filtered = transpose(data).filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } )</code></pre> <p>Let’s take a look at the source code for this example. First we create an <code>{ojs}</code> cell that reads in some data from a CSV file using a <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/file-attachments">FileAttachment</a>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) ```</code></pre> <p>The example above doesn’t plot all of the data but rather a filtered subset. To create our filter we’ll need some inputs, and we’ll want to be able to use the values of these inputs in our filtering function. To do this, we use the <code>viewof</code> keyword and with some standard <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/inputs">Inputs</a>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) ```</code></pre> <p>Now we write the filtering function that will transform the <code>data</code> read from the CSV using the values of <code>bill_length_min</code> and <code>island</code>.</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) ```</code></pre> <p>Here we see reactivity in action: we don’t need any special syntax to refer to the dynamic input values, they “just work”, and the filtering code is automatically re-run when the inputs change. This works in much the same way a spreadsheet works when you update a cell and other cells that refer to it are recalculated.</p> <p>Finally, we’ll plot the filtered data using <a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot">Observable Plot</a> (an open-source JavaScript library for quick visualization of tabular data):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } ) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that as with our inputs, we refer to the <code>filtered</code> variable with no special syntax—the plotting code will be automatically re-run whenever <code>filtered</code> changes (which in turn is updated whenever an input changes).</p> <p>That covers a basic end-to-end use of OJS (see the Penguins examples for the full source code).</p> <p>If you take a look at the Penguins code, you’ll notice something curious: the inputs and plotting code are defined before the data processing code. This demonstrates a critical difference between OJS cell execution and traditional notebooks: cells do not need to be defined in any particular order.</p> <p>Because execution is fully reactive, the runtime will automatically execute cells in the correct order based on how they reference each other. This is more akin to a spreadsheet than a traditional notebook with linear cell execution.</p> <h5 id="libraries-3">Libraries</h5> <p>Our example above made use of several standard libraries, including:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib">Observable stdlib</a> — Core primitives for DOM manipulation, file handling, importing code, and much more.</li> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/inputs">Observable Inputs</a> — Standard inputs controls including sliders, drop-downs, tables, check-boxes, etc.</li> <li><a href="https://github.com/observablehq/plot">Observable Plot</a> — High level plotting library for exploratory data visualization. The libraries are somewhat special because they are automatically available within notebooks on <a href="https://observablehq.com">observablehq.com</a> as well as within <code>{ojs}</code> cells in Quarto documents.</li> </ul> <p>Using other JavaScript libraries is also straightforward, they just need to be explicitly imported. For example, here we import a some libraries using the <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#require">require</a> function (which in turn loads NPM modules from <a href="https://www.jsdelivr.com/">jsDelivr</a>):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} d3 = require("d3@7") topojson = require("topojson") ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Libraries to learn more about using standard and third-party libraries.</p> <h5 id="data-sources-3">Data Sources</h5> <p>In our initial example we used a <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/stdlib#file-attachments">FileAttachment</a> as our data source. File attachments support many formats including CSV, TSV, JSON, Arrow (uncompressed), and SQLite so are a convenient way to read a dataset that has already been prepared for analysis.</p> <p>Frequently though you’ll need to do some pre-processing of your data in Python or R before it’s ready for visualization. Within Quarto, you can do this pre-processing during document render then make the results available to OJS.</p> <p>Use the <code>ojs_define()</code> function from Python or R to define variables that you want to use within JavaScript. For example, to reproduce the simple CSV read in Python you might do this:</p> <pre><code>```{python} import pandas as pd penguins = pd.read_csv("palmer-penguins.csv") ojs_define(data = penguins) ```</code></pre> <p>The call to <code>ojs_define(data = penguins)</code> says that we want to make a variable named <code>data</code> (with the value of the <code>penguins</code> data frame) available to OJS</p> <p>Depending on the visualization library you use, one additional step may be required to consume the data from JavaScript. In this case, the <code>Plot</code> function expects data by row rather than by column, so we <code>transpose()</code> it before filtering:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} filtered = transpose(data).filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) ```</code></pre> <p>See the article on Data Sources to learn more about the various ways to prepare and read data.</p> <h5 id="ojs-cells-1">OJS Cells</h5> <p>There are many options available to customize the behavior of <code>{ojs}</code> code cells, including showing, hiding, and collapsing code as well as controlling the visibility and layout of outputs.</p> <p>The most important cell option to be aware of is the <code>echo</code> option, which controls whether source code is displayed. You’ll have different preferences depending on whether you are embedding visualizations in an article or creating a notebook or full-on tutorial.</p> <p>Code in <code>{ojs}</code> cells is displayed by default. To prevent display of code for an entire document, set the <code>echo: false</code> option in YAML metadata:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" execute: echo: false ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this option on a per-cell basis. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: false data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) ```</code></pre> <p>To learn about all of the options available, see the article on OJS Cells.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-10">Learning More</h5> <p>These articles go into more depth on using OJS in Quarto documents:</p> <ul> <li><p>Libraries covers using standard libraries and external JavaScript libraries.</p></li> <li><p>Data Sources outlines the various ways to read and pre-process data.</p></li> <li><p>OJS Cells goes into more depth on cell execution, output, and layout.</p></li> <li><p>Shiny Reactives describes how to integrate Shiny with OJS.</p></li> <li><p>Code Reuse delves into ways to re-use OJS code across multiple documents. If you want to learn more about the underlying mechanics of reactivity, check out these notebooks from <a href="https://observablehq.com/@mbostock">Mike Bostock</a>:</p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/five-minute-introduction">Five Minute Introduction</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/observables-not-javascript">Observable’s not JavaScript</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/introduction-to-views">Introduction to Views</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/how-observable-runs">How Observable Runs</a></p></li> </ul> <h3 id="ojs-cells-2">OJS Cells</h3> <h4 id="ojs-cells-3">OJS Cells</h4> <p>OJS code cells <code>{ojs}</code> behave a bit differently than cells in traditional notebooks, and have many options available to control their display and layout.</p> <h5 id="cell-execution-1">Cell Execution</h5> <p>A critical difference between OJS cell execution and traditional notebooks is that in OJS cells do not need to be defined in any particular order.</p> <p>Because execution is fully reactive, the runtime will automatically execute cells in the correct order based on how they reference each other. This is more akin to a spreadsheet than a traditional notebook with linear cell execution.</p> <p>For example, in this cell we reference a variable that is not yet defined (it’s defined immediately below):</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} x + 5 ``` ```{ojs} x = 10 ```</code></pre> <p>This code works because the Observable runtime automatically determines the correct order of execution for the cells.</p> <h5 id="cell-output-2">Cell Output</h5> <p>By default, OJS cells show their full source code and output within rendered documents. Depending on the type of document you are creating you might want to change this behavior either globally or for individual cells.</p> <h6 id="code-visibility">Code Visibility</h6> <p>The <code>echo</code> option controls whether cells display their source code. To prevent display of code for an entire document, set the <code>echo: false</code> option in YAML metadata:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" execute: echo: false ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this option on a per-cell basis. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: false data = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({ typed: true }) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="output-visibility">Output Visibility</h6> <p>OJS cell output is also displayed by default. You can change this at a global or (more likely) per-cell level using the <code>output</code> option. For example, here we disable output for a cell:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| output: false data ```</code></pre> <p>Note that cells which only carry assignments do not print their output by default. For example, this assignment won’t print anything:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: fenced dummy1 = "aHiddenAssignment" ```</code></pre> <p>If you want to print even the results of assignments, you can specify the <code>output: all</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: fenced //| output: all dummy2 = [{key: 1, value: [1, 2, [3, 4], dummy1]}] ```</code></pre> <p>If you click the inspector you’ll see it expand to reveal the data as JSON.</p> <h6 id="code-display">Code Display</h6> <p>We talked about showing and hiding source code above, but what about controlling exactly how it’s displayed?</p> <p>There are options available for customizing the appearance of code blocks (highlighting, background, border, etc.) as well as how horizontal overflow is handled. See the article on HTML Code Blocks for all of the details.</p> <p>One option we wanted to specifically highlight here is code folding, which enables you to collapse code but still provide an option for users to view it. This is especially handy for custom JavaScript visualizations as they often span dozens of lines of code.</p> <p>Add the <code>code-fold: true</code> option to a code cell to enable code folding (you can also enable this globally). For example, click the “Code” button to show the code block (note the <code>code-fold: true</code> option is specified)</p> <p>Code</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| code-fold: true pdata = FileAttachment("palmer-penguins.csv").csv({typed: true}) Plot.plot({ facet: { data: pdata, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), Plot.rectY(pdata, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", thresholds: 20, fill: "species"} ) ), Plot.tickX(pdata, Plot.groupZ( {x: "median"}, {x: "body_mass_g", z: d => d.sex + d.species, stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 2 } ) ) ] }) ```</code></pre> <h5 id="cell-layout">Cell Layout</h5> <p>There are additional <code>panel</code> and <code>layout</code> options which you can add to OJS cells to customize how their output is presented. Here’s a version of some of the previous examples we’ve used presented with a sidebar and tabset:</p> <pre><code>filtered = pdata.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island); }) viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } )</code></pre> <ul> <li><p>Plot</p></li> <li><p>Data</p> <p>Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: “count”}, {x: “body_mass_g”, fill: “species”, thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: “sex”, y: “species”, marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } )</p> <p>Inputs.table(filtered)</p></li> </ul> <p>We created this layout by first adding the <code>panel: sidebar</code> option to the cell with our inputs:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| panel: sidebar viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } ) ```</code></pre> <p>We then added a tabset (div of class <code>.panel-tabset</code>) with Plot and Data tabs (headings within the div define the tabs):</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset} ## Plot ```{ojs} Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } ) ``` ## Data ```{ojs} Inputs.table(filtered) ``` :::</code></pre> <p>See the Layout example for the full source code.</p> <p>Learn more in the article on Layout for interactive documents.</p> <h5 id="cell-figures">Cell Figures</h5> <p>OJS cells can also be rendered as numbered, cross-referenceable figures. To do this, add the <code>label</code> and <code>fig-cap</code> options to the cell. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| echo: fenced //| label: fig-penguin-body-mass //| fig-cap: "Penguin body mass by sex and species" Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: "count"}, {x: "body_mass_g", fill: "species", thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: "sex", y: "species", marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } ) ```</code></pre> <p>Figure 1: Penguin body mass by sex and species</p> <p>See Figure 1 for further illustration.</p> <p>To reference the figure use its label in a markdown cross reference:</p> <pre><code>See @fig-penguin-body-mass for further illustration.</code></pre> <h3 id="penguins">Penguins</h3> <h4 id="penguins-1">Penguins</h4> <p>A simple example based on Allison Horst’s <a href="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/">Palmer Penguins</a> dataset. Here we look at how penguin body mass varies across both sex and species (use the provided inputs to filter the dataset by bill length and island):</p> <pre><code>viewof bill_length_min = Inputs.range( [32, 50], {value: 35, step: 1, label: "Bill length (min):"} ) viewof islands = Inputs.checkbox( ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"], { value: ["Torgersen", "Biscoe"], label: "Islands:" } )</code></pre> <ul> <li><p>Plot</p></li> <li><p>Data</p> <p>Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX( {y: “count”}, {x: “body_mass_g”, fill: “species”, thresholds: 20} )) .plot({ facet: { data: filtered, x: “sex”, y: “species”, marginRight: 80 }, marks: [ Plot.frame(), ] } )</p> <p>Inputs.table(filtered)</p> <p>data = FileAttachment(“palmer-penguins.csv”).csv({ typed: true })</p> <p>filtered = data.filter(function(penguin) { return bill_length_min < penguin.bill_length_mm && islands.includes(penguin.island);
