})</p></li> </ul> <h3 id="population">Population</h3> <h4 id="population-1">Population</h4> <p>This example demonstrates importing a notebook from ObervableHQ and replacing its data with data of our own (the code and data for this example were originally published <a href="https://github.com/observablehq/examples/tree/main/custom-data">here</a>).</p> <p>First we read from a local JSON file into <code>population</code>:</p> <pre><code>population = FileAttachment("population.json").json()</code></pre> <p>Then we import from <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-sunburst">observablehq.com</a> and specify that we’d like to use <code>population</code> instead of the data built in to the notebook:</p> <pre><code>import { chart } with { population as data } from "@d3/zoomable-sunburst"</code></pre> <p>Finally, we display the chart:</p> <pre><code>chart</code></pre> <h3 id="running-documents">Running Documents</h3> <h4 id="running-documents-1">Running Documents</h4> <h5 id="overview-69">Overview</h5> <p>There are a number of ways to run Shiny interactive documents:</p> <ul> <li><p>Use Run Document within the RStudio IDE.</p></li> <li><p>Use the <code>quarto serve</code> command line interface.</p></li> <li><p>Deploy them to a server for use by a wider audience. We’ll cover all of these scenario in depth here. Note that in order to run interactive Shiny documents you will to install the very latest version of the rmarkdown package (v2.10) which you can install as follows:</p> <p>install.packages(“rmarkdown”)</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="rstudio-ide">RStudio IDE</h5> <p>While you are developing an interactive document it will likely be most convenient to run within RStudio.</p> <p>Note that you need RStudio v2022.07 or a later version in order to run Quarto interactive documents. You can download the latest release at <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">posit.co</a>.</p> <p>Click the Run Document button while editing a Shiny interactive document to render and view the document within the IDE:</p> <p>When you make changes, just click Run Document again to see them reflected in the document preview.</p> <p>Two options you may want to consider enabling are Run on Save and Preview in Viewer Pane (by default previews occur in an external window). You can access these options on the editor toolbar:</p> <h5 id="command-line-3">Command Line</h5> <p>You can also run Shiny interactive documents from the command line via <code>quarto serve</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto serve document.qmd</code></pre> <p>There are a number of options to the <code>serve</code> command to control the port and host of the document server as well as whether a browser is automatically opened for the running document. You can learn more about these options with <code>quarto serve help</code>.</p> <p>If you are within an R session you can also use the quarto R package to run a document:</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_serve("document.qmd")</code></pre> <h5 id="deployment-1">Deployment</h5> <h6 id="shinyapps">ShinyApps</h6> <p>You can publish Shiny interactive documents to the <a href="http://shinyapps.io/">ShinyApps</a> hosted service. To do this you should ensure that you have:</p> <ul> <li><p>An account on ShinyApps (use the <a href="http://shinyapps.io/">signup form</a> to create an account).</p></li> <li><p>The very latest versions of the rsconnect and quarto R packages. You can install them as follows:</p> <p>install.packages(“rsconnect”) install.packages(“quarto”)</p></li> </ul> <p>You can then deploy your interactive document using the <code>quarto_publish_app()</code> function of the quarto package. You can do this as follows (working from the directory that contains your document):</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_publish_app(server = "shinyapps.io")</code></pre> <p>If you are using RStudio you can also use the Publish button available when working with an interactive document:</p> <p>Note that you should always Run Document locally prior to publishing your document (as this will create the <code>.html</code> file that is served on ShinyApps.</p> <h6 id="hugging-face">Hugging Face</h6> <p>HuggingFace Spaces provides an SDK for deploying Shiny for R applications. Learn more about using HuggingFace with Shiny for R here: <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-sdks-docker-shiny#shiny-for-r">huggingface.co</a>.</p> <h6 id="posit-connect">Posit Connect</h6> <p><a href="https://www.rstudio.com/products/connect/">Posit Connect</a> is a server product from Posit for secure sharing of applications, reports, and plots. You can publish Shiny interactive documents to Posit Connect in much the same way as described above for ShinyApps.</p> <p>First, make sure you very latest development versions of the rsconnect and quarto R packages. You can install them as follows:</p> <pre><code>install.packages("rsconnect") install.packages("quarto")</code></pre> <p>Next, deploy your interactive document using the <code>quarto_publish_app()</code> function of the quarto package, providing the domain name or IP address of your Posit Connect installation via the <code>server</code> parameter. You can do this as follows (working from the directory that contains your document):</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_publish_app(server = "rsc.example.com")</code></pre> <p>If you are using RStudio you can also use the Publish button as described above in the ShinyApps documentation:</p> <p>As with ShinyApps, you should always Run Document locally prior to publishing your document (as this will create the <code>.html</code> file that is served by Posit Connect).</p> <h3 id="shiny-3">Shiny</h3> <h4 id="shiny-4">Shiny</h4> <h5 id="introduction-3">Introduction</h5> <p>If you are an R user, you may already be familiar with <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/">Shiny</a>, a package that makes it easy to build interactive web apps with R.</p> <p>When using the Knitr computation engine, Quarto documents can include embedded Shiny components (e.g. a plot with sliders that control its inputs) or even simple Shiny applications that include several components.</p> <p>This section covers integrating Shiny with Quarto and assumes that you already have basic familiarity with Shiny. To learn more about Shiny please visit <a href="https://shiny.posit.co/">shiny.posit.co</a>.</p> <p>In order to run the examples below you will need a recent version of the rmarkdown package, which you can install with:</p> <pre><code> install.packages("rmarkdown")</code></pre> <h5 id="hello-shiny-1">Hello, Shiny</h5> <p>For example, here’s a document that contains a plot of the “Old Faithful” dataset along with a slider to control the number of bins:</p> <p>Here’s the source code for this example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Old Faithful" format: html server: shiny --- ```{r} sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:", min = 1, max = 50, value = 30) plotOutput("distPlot") ``` ```{r} #| context: server output$distPlot <- renderPlot({ x <- faithful[, 2] # Old Faithful Geyser data bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1) hist(x, breaks = bins, col = 'darkgray', border = 'white') }) ```</code></pre> <p>There are two important differences between this document and a normal static document:</p> <ul> <li><p>The inclusion of <code>server: shiny</code> within the document’s options, which instructs Quarto to run a Shiny Server behind the document:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: “Old Faithful”</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>format: html</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>server: shiny</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> <li><p>The inclusion of <code>context: server</code> as an option in the second code chunk, which delineates this R code as running within the Shiny Server (this is the code you would typically put in <code>server.R</code>):</p> <p><code>{r} #| context: server</code></p></li> </ul> <p>We’ll cover running and deploying Quarto documents with Shiny components in the article on Running Documents. Before that though, let’s cover a more in-depth example.</p> <h5 id="custom-layout-1">Custom Layout</h5> <p>Here’s an example that includes multiple inputs as well as a more application like page layout with a sidebar:</p> <p>Here’s the source code for this example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Iris K-Means Clustering" format: html: page-layout: custom server: shiny --- ```{r} #| panel: sidebar vars <- setdiff(names(iris), "Species") selectInput('xcol', 'X Variable', vars) selectInput('ycol', 'Y Variable', vars, selected = vars[[2]]) numericInput('clusters', 'Cluster count', 3, min = 1, max = 9) ``` ```{r} #| panel: fill plotOutput('plot1') ``` ```{r} #| context: server selectedData <- reactive({ iris[, c(input$xcol, input$ycol)] }) clusters <- reactive({ kmeans(selectedData(), input$clusters) }) output$plot1 <- renderPlot({ palette(c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3", "#FF7F00", "#FFFF33", "#A65628", "#F781BF", "#999999")) par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 0, 1)) plot(selectedData(), col = clusters()$cluster, pch = 20, cex = 3) points(clusters()$centers, pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 4) }) ```</code></pre> <p>There are a few things worth noting in this example:</p> <ul> <li>The YAML front-matter includes the <code>page-layout: custom</code> option (to indicate we want our content to occupy the entire page rather than being centered with padding).</li> <li>We add <code>panel: sidebar</code> and <code>panel: fill</code> to the two code chunks that define the user-interface to specify that we want them laid out in special panel containers.</li> <li>We again use <code>context: server</code> on the last R code chunk to indicate that it contains the Shiny Server code.</li> </ul> <h6 id="page-layout">Page Layout</h6> <p>Some interactive documents you create will use narrative interspersed with Shiny components and some (like this example) will be full page applications. Some may even by hybrids—for example imagine a sidebar on the left containing inputs that control outputs interspersed with narrative in the main document body.</p> <p>See the article on Component Layout to learn more about the available tools for managing the layout of interactive documents.</p> <h5 id="examples-23">Examples</h5> <p>Here are some deployed examples of Quarto documents that use Shiny:</p> <p>Example</p> <p>Source</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/shiny-old-faithful/">Old Faithful</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0qnQ">Code</a></p> <p>Demonstrates incorporating an interactive plot into the main flow of a document.</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/shiny-k-means/">K-Means</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0qnj">Code</a></p> <p>Demonstrates using a more “application-like” page layout (sidebar and main panel)</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/shiny-diamonds/">Diamonds</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0qcR">Code</a></p> <p>Demonstrates an alternate way to layout inputs (at the bottom of the page in three columns).</p> <h5 id="learning-more-11">Learning More</h5> <p>To learn more about Shiny interactive documents see the following articles:</p> <ul> <li>Running Documents covers how to run interactive documents both within RStudio and at the command line, as well as how to deploy them to end users.</li> <li>Execution Contexts goes in depth on when different code blocks (e.g. rendering vs. serving) run as well as how to cache expensive computations for more responsive documents.</li> <li>External Resources describes how to make sure that Shiny can locate resources (e.g. CSS, JS, images, etc.) that you include in your document.</li> <li>Component Layout enumerates the various techniques you can use to layout interactive components within your documents. If you are using both JavaScript and Shiny to create interactive documents, you might also be interested in the article on using Shiny Reactives with OJS.</li> </ul> <h3 id="shiny-reactives">Shiny Reactives</h3> <h4 id="shiny-reactives-1">Shiny Reactives</h4> <h5 id="overview-70">Overview</h5> <p>Earlier we described how to use the <code>ojs_define()</code> function to make data from Python and R available in OJS cells. In this scenario, data pre-processing is done once during render time then all subsequent interactions are handled on the client.</p> <p>But what if you want to do data transformation dynamically in response to user inputs? This is also possible with <code>ojs_define()</code>, as it can be passed not just static values but also Shiny reactives (assuming it’s running inside a Shiny interactive document).</p> <h5 id="hello-shiny-2">Hello, Shiny</h5> <p>Here is the <a href="https://shiny.rstudio.com/gallery/kmeans-example.html">K-Means Clustering</a> example from the Shiny Gallery implemented with an OJS client and Shiny Server:</p> <p>You can see the document deployed at <a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/kmeans-shiny-ojs/">jjallaire.shinyapps.io</a>.</p> <h6 id="source-code-1">Source Code</h6> <p>Let’s take a look at the source code. On the client we have familiar looking OJS inputs and a plot laid out using <code>panel: sidebar</code> and <code>panel: fill</code>:</p> <pre><code>```{ojs} //| panel: sidebar vars = ["Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"] viewof xcol = Inputs.select(vars, {label: "X Variable"}) viewof ycol = Inputs.select(vars, {label: "Y Variable", value: vars[1]}) viewof count = Inputs.range([1, 9], {label: "Cluster Count", step: 1, value: 3}) ``` ```{ojs} //| panel: fill Plot.plot({ color: { type: "ordinal", scheme: "category10" }, marks: [ Plot.dot(transpose(selectedData), { x: xcol, y: ycol, fill: (d, i) => clusters.cluster[i], }), Plot.dot(clusters.centers, { x: d => d[0], y: d => d[1], r: 10, stroke: "black", fill: (d, i) => i + 1 }), ] }) ```</code></pre> <p>Note that the plotting code references the variables <code>selectedData</code> and <code>clusters</code>. These will be provided by reactive expressions within the Shiny server code. Note also that we use the <code>transpose()</code> function to reshape the data into the row-oriented format that the Plot library expects.</p> <p>Here is the server code:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| context: server selectedData <- reactive({ iris[, c(input$xcol, input$ycol)] }) clusters <- reactive({ kmeans(selectedData(), input$count) }) ojs_define(selectedData, clusters) ```</code></pre> <p>We designate this code as running on the server via the <code>context: server</code> option.</p> <p>Note that we reference several inputs that were defined by <code>viewof</code> expressions on the client (e.g. <code>input$xcol</code>). When these inputs change they will cause the appropriate server side reactives to re-execute.</p> <p>We create two reactive values (<code>selectedData</code> and <code>clusters</code>) and provide them to the client using <code>ojs_define()</code>. The plot will be automatically re-drawn on the client side when these values change.</p> <h5 id="examples-24">Examples</h5> <p>Here are some examples that demonstrate various ways to use OJS with Shiny:</p> <p>Example</p> <p>Source</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/kmeans-shiny-ojs/">K-Means</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0kPK">Code</a></p> <p>Simple example of binding OJS inputs to Shiny inputs and shiny reactives to OJS plots.</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/binning-shiny-ojs/">Binning</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0kPu">Code</a></p> <p>Demonstrates fast binning of a medium sized dataset (32mb) on the server.</p> <p><a href="https://jjallaire.shinyapps.io/data-shiny-ojs/">Data Binding</a></p> <p><a href="https://git.io/J0kPl">Code</a></p> <p>Demonstrates importing a notebook from <a href="https://observablehq.com">observablehq.com</a> and binding its data field to a Shiny reactive.</p> <h5 id="bindings">Bindings</h5> <h6 id="ojs-to-shiny">OJS to Shiny</h6> <p>In the example above we took advantage of the fact that by default OJS <code>viewof</code> expressions are automatically propagated to Shiny inputs (e.g <code>input$xcol</code>). This provides a reasonable separation of concerns, and prevents excess network traffic in the case that you have large OJS variables.</p> <p>However, if you want to use other OJS variables as Shiny inputs this is also possible using the <code>ojs-export</code> option. The default behavior maps to the following configuration:</p> <pre><code>--- server: type: shiny ojs-export: viewof ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify <code>ojs-export: all</code> to cause all OJS reactives to be bound to Shiny inputs:</p> <pre><code>--- server: type: shiny ojs-export: all ---</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, you can specify a list of OJS reactives by name (including using <code>~</code> to filter out reactives), and optionally combine this with the <code>viewof</code> and/or <code>all</code> options. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- server: type: shiny ojs-export: [all, ~large_dataset] ---</code></pre> <h6 id="shiny-to-ojs">Shiny to OJS</h6> <p>Less common but occasionally useful is the ability to bind Shiny inputs into OJS. By default no such bindings occur, however you can use the <code>ojs-import</code> option to opt-in for specific Shiny inputs. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- server: type: shiny ojs-import: [minimum, maximum] ---</code></pre> <h3 id="sunburst">Sunburst</h3> <h4 id="sunburst-1">Sunburst</h4> <ul> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Show All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Hide All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">View Source</a> Originally published at <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-sunburst">observablehq.com</a></li> </ul> <p>Author</p> <p>Mike Bostock</p> <p>Published</p> <p>April 30, 2018</p> <p>This variant of a <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/sunburst">sunburst diagram</a> shows only two layers of the hierarchy at a time. Click a node to zoom in, or the center to zoom out. Compare to an <a href="https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-icicle">icicle</a>.</p> <p>Code</p> <pre><code>sunburst = { const root = partition(flareData); root.each(d => d.current = d); const svg = d3.create("svg") .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, width]) .style("font", "15px sans-serif"); const g = svg.append("g") .attr("transform", `translate(${width / 2},${width / 2})`); const path = g.append("g") .selectAll("path") .data(root.descendants().slice(1)) .join("path") .attr("fill", d => { while (d.depth > 1) d = d.parent; return color(d.data.name); }) .attr("fill-opacity", d => arcVisible(d.current) ? (d.children ? 0.6 : 0.4) : 0) .attr("d", d => arc(d.current)); path.filter(d => d.children) .style("cursor", "pointer") .on("click", clicked); path.append("title") .text(d => `${d.ancestors().map(d => d.data.name).reverse().join("/")}\n${format(d.value)}`); const label = g.append("g") .attr("pointer-events", "none") .attr("text-anchor", "middle") .style("user-select", "none") .selectAll("text") .data(root.descendants().slice(1)) .join("text") .attr("dy", "0.35em") .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.current)) .attr("transform", d => labelTransform(d.current)) .text(d => d.data.name); const parent = g.append("circle") .datum(root) .attr("r", radius) .attr("fill", "none") .attr("pointer-events", "all") .on("click", clicked); function clicked(event, p) { parent.datum(p.parent || root); root.each(d => d.target = { x0: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x0 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI, x1: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x1 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI, y0: Math.max(0, d.y0 - p.depth), y1: Math.max(0, d.y1 - p.depth) }); const t = g.transition().duration(750); // Transition the data on all arcs, even the ones that aren’t visible, // so that if this transition is interrupted, entering arcs will start // the next transition from the desired position. path.transition(t) .tween("data", d => { const i = d3.interpolate(d.current, d.target); return t => d.current = i(t); }) .filter(function(d) { return +this.getAttribute("fill-opacity") || arcVisible(d.target); }) .attr("fill-opacity", d => arcVisible(d.target) ? (d.children ? 0.6 : 0.4) : 0) .attrTween("d", d => () => arc(d.current)); label.filter(function(d) { return +this.getAttribute("fill-opacity") || labelVisible(d.target); }).transition(t) .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.target)) .attrTween("transform", d => () => labelTransform(d.current)); } function arcVisible(d) { return d.y1 <= 3 && d.y0 >= 1 && d.x1 > d.x0; } function labelVisible(d) { return d.y1 <= 3 && d.y0 >= 1 && (d.y1 - d.y0) * (d.x1 - d.x0) > 0.03; } function labelTransform(d) { const x = (d.x0 + d.x1) / 2 * 180 / Math.PI; const y = (d.y0 + d.y1) / 2 * radius; return `rotate(${x - 90}) translate(${y},0) rotate(${x < 180 ? 0 : 180})`; } return svg.node(); } flareData = FileAttachment("flare-2.json").json() partition = flareData => { const root = d3.hierarchy(flareData) .sum(d => d.value) .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value); return d3.partition() .size([2 * Math.PI, root.height + 1]) (root); } color = d3.scaleOrdinal( d3.quantize(d3.interpolateRainbow, flareData.children.length + 1) ) format = d3.format(",d") width = 932 radius = width / 6 arc = d3.arc() .startAngle(d => d.x0) .endAngle(d => d.x1) .padAngle(d => Math.min((d.x1 - d.x0) / 2, 0.005)) .padRadius(radius * 1.5) .innerRadius(d => d.y0 * radius) .outerRadius(d => Math.max(d.y0 * radius, d.y1 * radius - 1))</code></pre> <h5 id="reuse">Reuse</h5> <p>ISC License</p> <h2 id="journals">Journals</h2> <h3 id="article-templates">Article Templates</h3> <h4 id="article-templates-1">Article Templates</h4> <h5 id="overview-71">Overview</h5> <p>Journal article formats often require fine grained control of generated output as well as the ability to use Journal-specific commands and directives. This can be achieved for Quarto formats by providing custom Pandoc templates (LaTeX and/or HTML). Often these templates are a mix of Journal-specific LaTeX and standard directives required by Pandoc. This article describes how to create custom Journal templates that behave well with Pandoc and produce high-fidelity publisher ready output.</p> <h5 id="templates">Templates</h5> <p>Quarto uses <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#templates">Pandoc templates</a> to generate the rendered output from a markdown file. A Pandoc template is a mix of format specific content and variables. The variables will be replaced with their values from a rendered document. For example, the most basic template looks like:</p> <pre><code>mytemplate.tex \documentclass{scrartcl} \begin{document} $body$ \end{document}</code></pre> <p>In the above template, the <code>\$body\$</code> variable will be replaced with the LaTeX that is generated from the body of the document. If the body text is <code>Hello **world**!</code> in Markdown, the value of <code>\$body\$</code> will be <code>Hello \textbf{world}!</code>.</p> <p>By providing your own custom template used when rendering, you have complete control of the final output. You can provide this custom template to be used when rendering like this:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: template: mytemplate.tex</code></pre> <p>For more complete information about template syntax, see <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#template-syntax">Template syntax</a>.</p> <h5 id="localized-strings">Localized Strings</h5> <p>Quarto exposes its resolved localized strings to your template under the <code>quarto.language</code> namespace. The values reflect the document’s <code>lang</code> (default <code>en</code>) and any <code>language</code> overrides. For example, the cross-reference figure title is available as <code>\$quarto.language.crossref-fig-title\$</code>, and the document table-of-contents title as <code>\$quarto.language.toc-title-document\$</code>.</p> <p>See Localized Strings in Templates for the resolution rules and the full list of available keys.</p> <h5 id="template-partials">Template Partials</h5> <p>Replacing an entire template gives you complete control of the rendered output, but many features of Pandoc and Quarto depend upon code and variables that appear in the built in templates. If you replace the entire template and omit these variables, features will not work properly.</p> <p>It’s therefore recommended that you take one of two approaches when authoring templates:</p> <ul> <li>Selectively replace partials that exist within the master LaTeX or HTML template.</li> <li>Replace the entire LaTeX or HTML template, but then include partials provided with Quarto to ensure that your template takes advantage of all Pandoc and Quarto features. Below we’ll cover both of these approaches. Note that after reviewing this documentation you may also want to check out the source code of formats published on <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a> for additional examples.</li> </ul> <h6 id="replacing-partials">Replacing Partials</h6> <p>For LaTeX / PDF and HTML output, Quarto provides built in templates that are composed of a set of ‘partial’ template files. For these formats, you may replace portions of Quarto’s built in template, allowing you to customize just a portion of the template without needing to replace the whole thing. A simple partial to provide custom handling of the document title in LaTeX looks like:</p> <pre><code>title.tex \title{$title$} \author{$for(author)$$author$$sep$ \and $endfor$} \date{$date$}</code></pre> <p>You provide this partial to Quarto like:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: template-partials: - title.tex</code></pre> <p>When Quarto renders a document with a partial, it will use the built in template but replace a portion of the template with the provided partial. In the above case, the LaTeX title will be replaced with the implementation provided as the partial, while the rest of the built in template will be used.</p> <p>The name of the partial file is important. You choose which portion of the template to replace by providing a partial with that name. Providing an empty file as a partial is a way to opt out of some features without modifying the whole main template.</p> <p>You can see the list of partials available for each format below: LaTeX Partials, Beamer Partials, Typst Partials, HTML Partials and Revealjs Partials.</p> <h6 id="including-partials">Including Partials</h6> <p>In addition to replacing built in partials with your own, you may also choose to use built in partials when composing your own template. This allows you to create a template that takes advantage of the capabilities and options provided by Quarto and Pandoc without copying and maintaining the entire template code. For example, you can use the <code>\$pandoc.tex()\$</code> partial to include pandoc configuration for text highlighting, tables, graphics, tight lists, citations, and header includes:</p> <pre><code>my-template.tex \documentclass{scrartcl} $pandoc.tex()$ \begin{document} $body$ \end{document}</code></pre> <p>This modular approach means that it is easier to implement templates that:</p> <ul> <li>Include required elements of Pandoc templates</li> <li>Support general Pandoc features and options</li> <li>Provide only the minimal LaTeX or HTML rather than being required to provide all of it</li> </ul> <h5 id="latex-partials">LaTeX Partials</h5> <p>Note</p> <p>For <code>format: beamer</code>, see Beamer Partials</p> <p>View the Quarto LaTeX template and partials <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/pdf/pandoc">source code here</a>.</p> <p>Starting with Quarto 1.7, which provides Pandoc 3.6.3, there are two sets of partials: those specific to Quarto and those inherited from Pandoc. The source directory contains:</p> <ul> <li>partials with <code>.latex</code> extension that are inherited from Pandoc,</li> <li>partials with <code>.tex</code> extension that are provided by Quarto directly for more granular customization. template.tex</li> </ul> <p>The core LaTeX template which includes the basic document skeleton plus the following partials. This can’t be replaced as a <code>template-partial</code>, instead use the <code>template</code> option to provide your own template.</p> <p>passoptions.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations using the <code>\PassOptionsToPackage</code> command to modify options for packages that may be used later in the template.</p> <p>doc-class.tex</p> <p>Contains the document class declaration and options. By default we provide an identical document class to Pandoc, which implements many features. If you override this (which will be common), you will need to either implement support for the document class options or be aware that those options (e.g. <code>font-size</code>, <code>paper-size</code>, <code>classoption</code>, etc…) will not be supported in your output.</p> <p>fonts.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations to load LaTeX packages useful for fonts</p> <p>font-settings.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations to configure font packages, depending on which packages and LaTeX engine are used.</p> <p>common.latex</p> <p>Contains mostly declarations related to Pandoc features for LaTeX (like <code>linestretch</code>, <code>indent</code>, <code>verbatim-in-note</code>, <code>listings</code>, …). Quarto modifies this template from Pandoc to use more specific partials by splitting content between <code>common.latex</code> and <code>pandoc.tex</code>. You can either replace this partial entirely or a more specific one from <code>pandoc.tex</code>. In general, the <code>common.latex</code> and <code>pandoc.tex</code> partials must always be included within your custom template.</p> <p>pandoc.tex</p> <p>This includes configuration for most Pandoc features like text highlighting, tables, graphics, tight lists, citations, and header includes. In general, this partial must always be included within your custom template. In some circumstances, you may know that certain capabilities will not be needed, so this partial is further composed of the following partials, which could be used if sensible:</p> <p>tables.tex</p> <p>Provides configuration for the output of tables, table captioning, and footnotes within tables.</p> <p>graphics.tex</p> <p>Provides image scaling and placement configuration.</p> <p>citations.tex</p> <p>When using CSL references, provides configuration and commands for outputting the bibliography.</p> <p>babel-lang.tex</p> <p>When <code>lang</code> option is used, provides configuration and command for babel support and other language related LaTeX configuration.</p> <p>tightlist.tex</p> <p>Provides the tight list command.</p> <p>biblio-config.tex</p> <p>Provides natbib or biblatex configurations. To opt-out of these configurations (e.g. for a custom format where a specific documentclass handles it already), rather than provide an empty partial, use <code>biblio-config: false</code> for your document configuration.</p> <p>after-header-includes.latex</p> <p>Contains what needs to be inserted after user specific header includes, like bookmark configuration.</p> <p>hypersetup.latex</p> <p>Contains the <code>\hypersetup</code> command configuration.</p> <p>before-title.tex</p> <p>Appears in the document premable just before the title block. By default, this partial is empty.</p> <p>title.tex</p> <p>Provides configuration of document metadata for writing the title block. Note that in addition to these templates and partials, Quarto will also make normalized authors and affiliations data available to the template, making is easy to write custom title blocks against a standard schema.</p> <p>before-body.tex</p> <p>Implements the frontmatter, title page, and abstract.</p> <p>toc.tex</p> <p>Creates the table of contents, list of figures, and list of tables.</p> <p>before-bib.tex</p> <p>Placed after the content of the document, but before the bibliography. By default contains nothing.</p> <p>biblio.tex</p> <p>Creates the bibliography using either natbib or biblatex if used.</p> <p>after-body.tex</p> <p>Provides a placeholder to attach content at the end of the body, right before <code>\end{document}</code></p> <p>A copy of some of Pandoc’s original files are also kept in Quarto’s source as a reference. These files are: <code>latex.template</code>, the main template used as <code>template.tex</code> containing all the partials; and <code>latex.common</code> the original version of <code>common.latex</code>, which is tweaked to support Quarto’s more specific partials.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/pdf/pandoc/template.tex">full source code</a> for the Quarto LaTeX template to see how these partials are invoked by default.</p> <h5 id="beamer-partials">Beamer Partials</h5> <p>Note</p> <p>New from Quarto 1.7: <code>format: beamer</code> now uses its own template and partials.</p> <p>View the Quarto Beamer template and partials <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/beamer/pandoc">source code here</a>.</p> <p>Starting with Quarto 1.7, which provides Pandoc 3.6.3, there are two sets of partials: those specific to Quarto and those inherited from Pandoc. The source directory contains:</p> <ul> <li>partials with <code>.latex</code> extension that are inherited from Pandoc,</li> <li>partials with <code>.tex</code> extension that are provided by Quarto directly for more granular customization. template.tex</li> </ul> <p>The core LaTeX template which includes the basic document skeleton plus the following partials. This can’t be replaced as a <code>template-partial</code>, instead use the <code>template</code> option to provide your own template.</p> <p>passoptions.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations using the <code>\PassOptionsToPackage</code> command to modify options for packages that may be used later in the template.</p> <p>doc-class.tex</p> <p>Contains the document class declaration and options. By default we provide an identical document class to Pandoc, which implements many features. If you override this (which will be common), you will need to either implement support for the document class options or be aware that those options (e.g. <code>font-size</code>, <code>paper-size</code>, <code>classoption</code>, etc…) will not be supported in your output.</p> <p>fonts.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations to load LaTeX packages useful for fonts</p> <p>font-settings.latex</p> <p>Contains declarations to configure font packages, depending on which packages and LaTeX engine are used.</p> <p>common.latex</p> <p>Contains mostly declarations related to Pandoc features for LaTeX (like <code>linestretch</code>, <code>indent</code>, <code>verbatim-in-note</code>, <code>listings</code>, …). Quarto modifies this template from Pandoc to use more specific partials by splitting content between <code>common.latex</code> and <code>pandoc.tex</code>. You can either replace this partial entirely or a more specific one from <code>pandoc.tex</code>. In general, the <code>common.latex</code> and <code>pandoc.tex</code> partials must always be included within your custom template.</p> <p>pandoc.tex</p> <p>This includes configuration for most Pandoc features like text highlighting, tables, graphics, tight lists, citations, and header includes. In general, this partial must always be included within your custom template. In some circumstances, you may know that certain capabilities will not be needed, so this partial is further composed of the following partials, which could be used if sensible:</p> <p>tables.tex</p> <p>Provides configuration for the output of tables, table captioning, and footnotes within tables.</p> <p>graphics.tex</p> <p>Provides image scaling and placement configuration.</p> <p>citations.tex</p> <p>When using CSL references, provides configuration and commands for outputting the bibliography.</p> <p>babel-lang.tex</p> <p>When <code>lang</code> option is used, provides configuration and command for babel support and other language related LaTeX configuration.</p> <p>tightlist.tex</p> <p>Provides the tight list command.</p> <p>biblio-config.tex</p> <p>Provides natbib or biblatex configurations. To opt-out of these configurations (e.g. for a custom format where a specific documentclass handles it already), rather than provide an empty partial, use <code>biblio-config: false</code> for your document configuration.</p> <p>after-header-includes.latex</p> <p>Contains what needs to be inserted after user specific header includes, like bookmark configuration.</p> <p>hypersetup.latex</p> <p>Contains the <code>\hypersetup</code> command configuration.</p> <p>before-title.tex</p> <p>Appears in the document premable just before the title block. By default, this partial is empty.</p> <p>title.tex</p> <p>Provides configuration of document metadata for writing the title block. Note that in addition to these templates and partials, Quarto will also make normalized authors and affiliations data available to the template, making is easy to write custom title blocks against a standard schema.</p> <p>before-body.tex</p> <p>Implements the frontmatter, title page, and abstract.</p> <p>toc.tex</p> <p>Creates the table of contents, list of figures, and list of tables.</p> <p>before-bib.tex</p> <p>Placed after the content of the document, but before the bibliography. By default contains nothing.</p> <p>biblio.tex</p> <p>Creates the bibliography using either natbib or biblatex if used.</p> <p>after-body.tex</p> <p>Provides a placeholder to attach content at the end of the body, right before <code>\end{document}</code></p> <p>A copy of some of Pandoc’s original files are also kept in Quarto’s source as a reference. These files are: <code>beamer.template</code>, the main template used as <code>template.tex</code> containing all the partials; and <code>latex.common</code> the original version of <code>common.latex</code>, which is tweaked to support Quarto’s more specific partials.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/beamer/pandoc/template.tex">full source code</a> for the Quarto Beamer template to see how these partials are invoked by default.</p> <h5 id="typst-partials">Typst Partials</h5> <p>View the Quarto Typst template and partials <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/typst/pandoc/quarto">source code here</a>.</p> <p>template.typ</p> <p>The core Typst template file which includes the basic document skeleton plus the following partials. This can’t be replaced as a <code>partial</code>, instead use the <code>template</code> option to provide your own template.</p> <p>definitions.typ</p> <p>Definitions for Pandoc and Quarto features like block quotes, callouts, subfloats etc. In general, this partial must always be included within your custom template.</p> <p>typst-template.typ</p> <p>The definition of the Typst template function that will be called on the entire document contents. In the default template this function is called <code>article()</code> and generates a title block and author list, followed by the document content, optionally laid out in columns.</p> <p>page.typ</p> <p>Sets properties of the page such as size, margin, numbering, and background logo.</p> <p>typst-show.typ</p> <p>A show rule for the entire document that captures document metadata and passes it to the function defined in <code>typst-template.typ</code>.</p> <p>notes.typ</p> <p>Creates footnotes.</p> <p>biblio.typ</p> <p>Creates the bibliography.</p> <h5 id="html-partials">HTML Partials</h5> <p>View the Quarto html template and partials <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/html/pandoc">source code here</a>. Note that <code>html.template</code> is a copy of the complete Pandoc template that the Quarto template and partials is based upon.</p> <p>Quarto’s HTML template is broken down into the following components:</p> <p>template.html</p> <p>The core HTML template which includes the basic document skeleton plus the following partials. This can’t be replaced as a <code>partial</code>, instead use the <code>template</code> option to provide your own template.</p> <p>metadata.html</p> <p>Populates basic document metadata into the HTML document head. More advanced metadata elements are not currently implemented within this template (e.g. social media, academic metadata) but are implemented as post processors.</p> <p>title-block.html</p> <p>Provides the title block for the document.</p> <p>toc.html</p> <p>Provide the table of contents target for the document</p> <h5 id="revealjs-partials">Revealjs Partials</h5> <p>View the Quarto Revealjs template and partials <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/pandoc">source code here</a>. Note that <code>revealjs.template</code> is a copy of the complete Pandoc template that the Quarto template and partials is based upon.</p> <p>template.html</p> <p>The core Revealjs templates which includes the basic presentation skeleton plus the following partials. This can’t be replaced as a <code>partial</code>, instead use the <code>template</code> option to provide your own template.</p> <p>title-slide.html</p> <p>HTML used for the presentation title slide. By default, Quarto uses a fancy <code>title-slide.html</code> partial that leverages Authors & Affiliations handling. Use the <code>title-slide.html</code> <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/pandoc/title-fancy/title-slide.html">source code</a> as a starter if you want to tweak this partial.</p> <p>toc-slide.html</p> <p>HTML used for the presentation table of contents.</p> <h3 id="authors-affiliations-1">Authors & Affiliations</h3> <h4 id="authors-affiliations-2">Authors & Affiliations</h4> <h5 id="overview-72">Overview</h5> <p>An important goal for Quarto is to make it possible to use the same source document to produce multiple output formats. One significant challenge to overcome is defining a consistent way to express author and affiliation metadata such that articles targeting multiple Journals do not require special tweaking of authors and affiliations for each publication.</p> <p>Quarto’s answer to this challenge is two-fold:</p> <ul> <li>Parse a variety of expressions of authors and affiliations into a standard schema.</li> <li>Provide de-normalized views of authors together with affiliations such that it is straightforward for template authors to create the LaTeX required by Journals. Below we’ll explore these facilities in more detail from the standpoint of template authors. To learn more about these facilities from the perspective of article writers, see Authors & Affiliations.</li> </ul> <p>Note</p> <p>Note that while there is a great deal of variety afforded in how authors and affiliations are specified, for a given Journal <code>template.qmd</code> you will likely have a preferred approach, and it’s good form to seed the template with an example of this approach.</p> <h5 id="author-metadata">Author Metadata</h5> <p>Quarto will look in the <code>author</code> or <code>authors</code> field for data that can be parsed into a normalized representation of authors. This can be as simple as a name of list of names:</p> <pre><code>author: - Norah Jones - Bill Gates</code></pre> <p>Or alternatively can be a complex data structure expressing a variety of properties and attributes of authors along with their affiliations:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Bill Gates orcid: 0000-0003-1689-0557 email: bill@gates.com affiliations: - name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation address: 440 5th Ave N city: Seattle state: WA postal-code: 98109-4631</code></pre> <p>For both of the above expressions, Quarto processes and normalizes the author and affiliation data into the keys described below.</p> <h6 id="author-1">author</h6> <p>The <code>author</code> metadata key receives a simple list of names that will render properly in most existing Pandoc templates not aware of the Quarto extended schema.</p> <h6 id="authors">authors</h6> <p>The <code>authors</code> metadata key contains the normalized author data structure. Affiliations are referenced (rather than placed inline), so this typically shouldn’t be used by templates to output author data. The order the authors appear in the metadata will be preserved.</p> <h6 id="affiliations">affiliations</h6> <p>The <code>affiliations</code> metadata key contains the normalized affiliation data structure. Ids are automatically assigned if not defined. Affiliations contain no reference to their authors, so are typically not used by templates to output affiliation data. The order the affiliations appear in the metadata will be preserved. Duplicate affiliations are removed.</p> <h6 id="by-author">by-author</h6> <p>The <code>by-author</code> metadata key contains a denormalized version of the author data organized in the original order of the authors. Rather than referencing affiliations, each author will have the full parsed contents of affiliations available in the affiliations subkey, making it easy for template authors to iterate through authors and then, within that, their affiliations. The order the authors appear in the metadata will be preserved.</p> <h6 id="by-affiliation">by-affiliation</h6> <p>The <code>by-affiliation</code> metadata key contains a denormalized version of affiliation data in the original order the affiliations appeared. Author data appears in order in the authors subkey, which contains the full parsed author data. This makes it easy for template authors to iterate over affiliations and the authors for each affiliation. The order the affiliations appear in the metadata will be preserved.</p> <h5 id="author-schema">Author Schema</h5> <p>The complete, normalized, author schema is as follows:</p> <pre><code>author: - id: string number: number name: given: string family: string literal: string dropping-particle: string non-dropping-particle: string url: string email: string phone: string fax: string degrees: # see schema below orcid: string note: string acknowledgements: string attributes: corresponding: boolean equal-contributor: boolean deceased: boolean roles: # see schema below metadata: object affiliations: # see schema below</code></pre> <h6 id="names">Names</h6> <p>Most often, users will write a single string for name, like:</p> <pre><code>author: Norah Jones</code></pre> <p>or perhaps like:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Norah Jones</code></pre> <p>Which will be parsed into:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: given: Norah family: Jones literal: Norah Jones</code></pre> <p>Quarto will parse names using BibTeX (a la <a href="https://github.com/openjournals/inara/blob/main/data/filters/normalize-author-names.lua">openjournals/inara</a>), supporting BibTeX’s parsing behavior for comma count, capitalization, and so on. When the name is unparseable by BibTeX, Quarto will attempt to parse names into given and family using spaces (everything after the last space is considered a family name), but to disambiguate, you may provide separate keys for the given name, family name and particle:</p> <pre><code>name: given: Norah family: Jones dropping-particle: von</code></pre> <h6 id="degrees-1">Degrees</h6> <p>Degrees or academic titles can specified with <code>degrees</code> and can be either of:</p> <ul> <li><p>A single string:</p> <p>author: degrees: PhD</p></li> <li><p>An array of strings:</p> <p>author: degrees: - PhD - MsSc</p></li> </ul> <p>It will always be normalized into an array of degrees.</p> <h6 id="attributes">Attributes</h6> <p>Recognized attribute keys that appear at the top level (for example, <code>corresponding</code>) will automatically be normalized under attributes. For example:</p> <pre><code>author: name: Norah Jones corresponding: true</code></pre> <p>would be normalized into:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: given: Norah family: Jones literal: Norah Jones attributes: corresponding: true</code></pre> <h6 id="roles">Roles</h6> <p>Author roles can be specified with either <code>role</code> or <code>roles</code> and can be any of:</p> <ul> <li><p>A single string:</p> <p>author: role: “Conceived and designed the study”</p></li> <li><p>An array of strings:</p> <p>author: role: - conceptualization - methodology</p></li> <li><p>An array of key-value pairs of the form <code>role: contribution</code>:</p> <p>author: role: - conceptualization: lead - methodology: supporting</p></li> </ul> <p>If a role matches one of the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/f65180a75e1cf2996328cd51cb4fd5d02d391511/src/resources/filters/modules/authors.lua#L119-L144">CRediT roles or their aliases</a>, the additional properties <code>vocab-identifier</code>, <code>vocab-term</code>, and <code>vocab-term-indentifier</code>, will be added to the role with the appropriate value from the CRediT specification.</p> <h6 id="arbitrary-metadata">Arbitrary Metadata</h6> <p>The normalized authors schema at the top level is a closed schema. Unrecognized keys that are passed in the root of authors will be normalized under the <code>metadata</code> key. For example:</p> <pre><code>author: name: Norah Jones corresponding: true custom-info: "custom value"</code></pre> <p>would be normalized into:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: given: Norah family: Jones literal: Norah Jones attributes: corresponding: true metadata: custom-info: "custom value"</code></pre> <p>Keys that are normalized into <code>metadata</code> should be considered potentially template specific and may not be present or depended upon when implementing a template.</p> <h5 id="affiliations-schema">Affiliations Schema</h5> <p>The complete, normalized affiliations schema is defined as:</p> <pre><code>affiliations: - id: string number: number name: string department: string group: string address: string city: string region: string country: string postal-code: string url: string</code></pre> <h6 id="parsing-notes">Parsing Notes</h6> <ul> <li>You may specify either state or region- either will be normalized into the region key.</li> <li>If you specify only a string for an affiliation, it will be used as the name of affiliation.</li> <li>You may omit an id and the id will be automatically generated (a simple counter based id will be used).</li> <li>The url field may also be populated by an <code>affiliation-url</code> key in the author, which preserves compatibility with Distill metadata for authors and affiliations.</li> </ul> <h5 id="combinations">Combinations</h5> <p>To combine the above schemas, users may specify author and affiliations in a number of different ways. Each will be normalized into the standard schema described above.</p> <h6 id="inline-affiliations">Inline Affiliations</h6> <p>You may write affiliations as simple string or complex affiliations inline. For example:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Norah Jones affiliations: - Carnegie Mellon University - University of Chicago</code></pre> <p>or</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Norah Jones affiliations: - name: Carnegie Mellon University city: Pittsburgh state: PA - name: University of Chicago city: Chicago state: IL</code></pre> <h6 id="reference-affiliations">Reference Affiliations</h6> <p>You may write out the affiliations into a separate key and only reference the affiliation in the author. For example:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Norah Jones affiliations: - ref: cmu - ref: chicago affiliations: - id: cmu name: Carnegie Mellon University city: Pittsburgh state: PA - id: chicago name: University of Chicago city: Chicago state: IL</code></pre> <h6 id="inline-references">Inline References</h6> <p>You may also assign ids to affiliations created in the author key and use those ids as references in other authors. For example:</p> <pre><code>author: - name: Norah Jones affiliations: - id: cmu name: Carnegie Mellon University city: Pittsburgh state: PA - id: chicago name: University of Chicago city: Chicago state: IL - name: John Hamm affiliations: - ref: cmu - name: University of California, San Diego city: San Diego state: CA</code></pre> <h3 id="journal-articles-1">Journal Articles</h3> <h4 id="journal-articles-2">Journal Articles</h4> <h5 id="overview-73">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto supports the creation of custom formats that extend base formats like <code>pdf</code>, <code>html</code>, and <code>docx</code>. The custom format system is very flexible, and has been designed to accommodate the creation of articles for publishing in professional Journals.</p> <p>A major focus is single-source publishing: the same Quarto document source should be capable of producing both HTML and LaTeX output, and should also be capable of creating the LaTeX required for submission to multiple Journals. Key capabilities that enable this include:</p> <ul> <li>The ability to flexibly adapt the native LaTeX templates provided by Journals for use with Pandoc.</li> <li>The use of spans and divs to apply formatting (which enables targeting by CSS for HTML output and LaTeX macros/environments for PDF output).</li> <li>A standardized schema for authors and affiliations so that you can express this data once and then have it automatically formatted according to the styles required for various Journals.</li> <li>The use of Citation Style Language (CSL) to automate the formatting of citations and bibliographies according to whatever style is required by various Journals.</li> </ul> <h5 id="journal-formats">Journal Formats</h5> <p>The Quarto team has developed several Journal formats and made them available within the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a> GitHub organization. These formats include:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/acm">ACM</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/acm/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/plos">PLOS</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/plos/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/jasa">ASA</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/jasa/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/elsevier">Elsevier</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/elsevier/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/biophysical-journal">Biophysical</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/biophysical-journal/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/acs">ACS</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/acs/">(preview)</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/jss">JSS</a> <a href="https://quarto-journals.github.io/jss/">(preview)</a> Many more formats will be added over time and we welcome proposals from the community for contributed formats (please post an issue at <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/article-format-template/issues">github.com</a> if you are interested in contributing a format).</li> </ul> <p>The <code>quarto use template</code> command can be used to create an article from one these formats. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use template quarto-journals/acm quarto use template quarto-journals/plos quarto use template quarto-journals/elsevier quarto use template quarto-journals/acs quarto use template quarto-journals/jss</code></pre> <p>Note that the above commands will create a brand new article with default contents. In some cases you may want to use a Journal format in an existing document or project without copying the entire template. In that case you can just add the format extension by itself. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-journals/acm quarto add quarto-journals/plos</code></pre> <p>Follow the links for any of the formats above to learn more about how to use them with your own articles.</p> <h5 id="creating-formats">Creating Formats</h5> <p>While the list of supported journals on <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a> will grow over time, it’s likely that many users will want to create their own Journal formats. Creating a new format typically involves:</p> <ul> <li>Adapting the LaTeX template typically provided by Journals for use with Quarto.</li> <li>Selecting the appropriate citation processing and style for use with the format.</li> <li>Creating a <code>template.qmd</code> that demonstrates using the format.</li> <li>Optionally, ensuring that both HTML and LaTeX articles are well supported. See the article on Journal Formats for additional details on creating your own formats.</li> </ul> <h3 id="journal-formats-1">Journal Formats</h3> <h4 id="journal-formats-2">Journal Formats</h4> <h5 id="overview-74">Overview</h5> <p>This article provides a guide to creating your own custom Journal formats. As a supplement to this guide we also recommend the following learning resources:</p> <ul> <li>The source code for the Journal article formats available from the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a> GitHub organization.</li> <li>The <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/article-format-template">GitHub template repository</a> for creating new Journal formats. The code in the template repository is heavily annotated so creating a new repository using this template and experimenting with it is an excellent way to learn. Journal custom formats can be used just like normal Quarto formats (e.g. <code>pdf</code> and <code>html</code>):</li> </ul> <p>You can specify a custom format beneath the <code>format</code> key just like a built-in format. For example:</p> <pre><code>---- title: "My Document" format: acm-pdf: toc: true ---</code></pre> <p>Custom formats all derive from one of the base formats, and include that base format as a suffix. Formats can also provide multiple variations that derive from distinct base formats. For example:</p> <pre><code>---- title: "My Document" toc: true format: acm-pdf: default acm-html: default ---</code></pre> <p>Note that we moved the <code>toc</code> option to the top level since it is shared between both of the formats.</p> <p>Custom formats can also be used with the <code>--to</code> argument to <code>quarto render</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --to acm-pdf</code></pre> <h5 id="quick-start-8">Quick Start</h5> <p>Here we’ll describe how to create a simple Journal article format extension. We’ll use the <code>quarto create</code> command to do this. If you are using VS Code, Positron, or RStudio you should execute <code>quarto create</code> within their respective integrated Terminal panes.</p> <p>To get started, execute <code>quarto create extension journal</code> within the parent directory where you’d like the format to be created:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension journal ? Extension Name › aps</code></pre> <p>As shown above, you’ll be prompted for an extension name. Type <code>aps</code> (an acronym for a fictional academic association) and press Enter—the Journal format extension is then created:</p> <pre><code>Creating extension at /Users/jjallaire/quarto/dev/aps: - Created README.md - Created template.qmd - Created _extensions/aps/aps.lua - Created _extensions/aps/styles.css - Created _extensions/aps/_extension.yml - Created _extensions/aps/header.tex - Created bibliography.bib</code></pre> <p>If you are running within VS Code, Positron, or RStudio a new window will open with the extension project.</p> <p>Here’s what the contents of the files in <code>_extensions/aps/</code> look like:</p> <pre><code>_extensions/aps/_extension.yml title: Aps author: J.J. Allaire version: 1.0.0 quarto-required: ">=1.2.222" contributes: formats: common: toc: true filters: - aps.lua pdf: include-in-header: header.tex html: css: styles.css</code></pre> <p>The main <code>_extension.yml</code> config file defines the output formats available for this Journal. Here we defined <code>pdf</code> and <code>html</code> formats, which will be available to Quarto documents as <code>aps-pdf</code> and <code>aps-html</code>, respectively.</p> <p>The config file also points to a number of other files that are used to customize the appearance of the Journal article:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>header.tex</code> — Custom LaTeX header directives</p></li> <li><p><code>styles.css</code> — Custom CSS for HTML output</p></li> <li><p><code>aps.lua</code> — Lua filter for various custom transformations Finally, the <code>template.qmd</code> provides a base example article for users of the format:</p> <p>template.qmd</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: Aps Template</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>format:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>aps-pdf:</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>keep-tex: true</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>aps-html: default</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>author:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- name: Sarah Malloc</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>affiliations:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- name: An Organization</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>department: The Department</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>address: 1 Main St</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>city: Boston</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>country: USA</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>postal-code: 02210-1022</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- A second affiliation</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0000</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>email: sm@example.org</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>url: <a href="https://example.org/">example.org</a></td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- name: Eliza Dealloc</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>affiliations:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- Another Affiliation</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>abstract: |</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>This document is a template demonstrating the Aps format.</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>keywords: [template, demo]</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>bibliography: bibliography.bib</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>## Introduction {#sec-intro}</p> <p><em>TODO</em> Create a template that demonstrates the appearance, formatting, layout, and functionality of your format. Learn more about journal formats at <<a href="https://quarto.org/docs/journals/">quarto.org</a>>.</p></li> </ul> <p>To develop your format, render/preview <code>template.qmd</code>, and then make changes to the various files in the <code>_extensions</code> directory (the preview will automatically refresh when you change these files).</p> <h5 id="example-acm-format">Example: ACM Format</h5> <p>The Quick Start above creates a very simple Journal article format. Here we’ll walk through some of the code for a more complex example, the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">ACM Format</a> available from <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a>.</p> <p>Before proceeding to the example we recommend you review these articles which cover some foundations that will be made use of in the example:</p> <ul> <li>Article Templates</li> <li>Authors & Affiliations</li> </ul> <h6 id="format-components">Format Components</h6> <p>Here is what the source code repository for the ACM extension looks like:</p> <pre><code>.gitignore .quartoignore LICENSE README.md bibliography.bib template.qmd _extensions/ acm/ _extension.yml acm_proc_article-sp.cls sensys-abstract.cls include-in-header.tex acm-sig-proceedings.csl partials/ doc-class.tex title.tex before-bib.tex</code></pre> <p>For the time being we’ll ignore all of the files above the <code>_extensions</code> directory (those files aren’t strictly part of the extension but rather provide documentation and a starter template—we’ll describe their usage below).</p> <ul> <li><p>The <code>_extensions</code> directory contains one or more extensions—in this case it contains the <code>acm</code> format extension.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>_extension.yml</code> file declares the format extension and provides default metadata and options for articles created for the format (we’ll do a deep dive into its contents below).</p></li> <li><p>The <code>acm_proc_article-sp.cls</code> and <code>sensys-abstract.cls</code> files are LaTeX class files used by the ACM.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>include-in-header.tex</code> file provides some standard content included in the preamble of ACM articles.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>acm-sig-proceedings.csl</code> is a Citation Style Language (CSL) file that enables rendering of citations and bibliographies according to the standards of the ACM.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>partials</code> directory contains some <code>.tex</code> files that override various parts of the standard Pandoc LaTeX template (see Article Templates to learn more about partials). Here’s what the contents of <code>_extension.yml</code> look like:</p> <p>title: ACM Journal Format author: Charles Teague version: 0.1.0 quarto-required: “>=1.2.0” contributes: format: common: csl: acm-sig-proceedings.csl number-sections: true pdf: shift-heading-level-by: -1 template-partials: - partials/before-bib.tex - partials/doc-class.tex - partials/title.tex include-in-header: - include-in-header.tex</p></li> </ul> <p>As you can see, many of the files located in the <code>_extensions/acm</code> folder are referenced here. Also note that while there are several options declared for the <code>pdf</code> format, there are also some options declared in <code>common</code>—these options will be applied to <code>pdf</code> and will also be applied to other format variants (e.g. HTML) when they are developed.</p> <h6 id="format-template">Format Template</h6> <p>Now let’s return to the files outside of the <code>_extensions</code> directory. The <code>LICENSE</code> and <code>README.md</code> files provide documentation that is good form to include in all extensions. The <code>.gitignore</code> files masks selected files out of version control. The remainder of the files provide a format template that make it easier for users to get started with your format.</p> <p>For any custom format that includes a <code>template.qmd</code>, users can get started with the format with a command like this:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use template quarto-journals/acm</code></pre> <p>The files included within the ACM template are:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>template.qmd</code> is a starter template for using the format. Here’s what the YAML document options for the template look like:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: Short Paper</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>author:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- name: Alice Anonymous</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>email: alice@example.com</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>affiliation: Some Institute of Technology</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>- name: Bob Security</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>email: bob@example.com</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>affiliation: Another University</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>abstract: |</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>This is the abstract.</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>It consists of two paragraphs.</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>format:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>acm-pdf:</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>keep-tex: true</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>bibliography: bibliography.bib</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> <li><p><code>bibliography.bib</code> is a sample bibliography referenced by <code>template.qmd</code> Note that the schema for author information used here is relatively straightforward. See the article on Authors & Affiliations to learn about more sophisticated schemas for author information.</p></li> </ul> <p>You can also include other files alongside <code>template.qmd</code> and they will be copied as well. Note that by default, Quarto will exclude common Github repository files when copying an extension template. This includes any file name or directory starting with a <code>.</code> (e.g. <code>.gitignore</code>), <code>README.md</code>, <code>LICENSE</code>, etc.. If you’d like, you can place a <code>.quartoignore</code> file in the root of your repository with each line of the file being a glob describing file(s) to ignore (using syntax like a <code>.gitignore</code> file).</p> <h5 id="distributing-formats-1">Distributing Formats</h5> <p>You can distribute format extensions in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>As a template that includes both the format in the <code>_extensions</code> directory and the <code>template.qmd</code> (which is automatically renamed to match the name of the enclosing directory).</p></li> <li><p>As a plain format with no template scaffolding (this is useful for adding the format to an existing document or project). If you have a GitHub repository containing the files enumerated above in the <code>acm</code> example, users could install your extension and associated template as follows (where <code>quarto-journals</code> is the GitHub organization hosting the repo):</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto use template quarto-journals/acm</p></li> </ul> <p>This is often the preferred way to get started with a format as it provides the user with a working document right out of the box. It’s also possible to install only the format if you are working with an existing project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-journals/acm</code></pre> <p>Note that it is possible to bundle and distribute extensions as simple gzip archives (as opposed to using a GitHub repository as described above). See the article on Distributing Extensions for additional details.</p> <h5 id="multiple-formats-2">Multiple Formats</h5> <p>A single format extension can support more than one output format. For example, an extension may target <code>html</code> and <code>pdf</code> output. To support multiple formats in your extension, you can add additional base formats to the <code>contributes / format</code> key like so:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: html: # html-specific options pdf: # pdf-specific options</code></pre> <h5 id="common-metadata-1">Common Metadata</h5> <p>If you have metadata that is common to any output format when your format extension is targeted, you can place that metadata under the <code>common</code> key. For example:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: common: filters: - filter.lua shortcodes: - quarto-ext/fancy-text html: # html-specifc pdf: # pdf-specifc</code></pre> <h5 id="format-resources-1">Format Resources</h5> <p>You can usually include other files and resources within a format extension by placing those files within the extension directory and using relative paths to reference them in your <code>_extension.yml</code> metadata file. These relative paths will be properly handled as your extension’s metadata is merged with the rendered document metadata.</p> <p>If there are resources that you need to have copied to the input directory as a part of rendering the document (for example, a <code>bst</code> file for LaTeX bibliographies or a logo or other file referenced from a LaTeX template), you can provide <code>format-resources</code>, which is a list of file paths1. Each of these files will be copied into the directory containing the input that is being rendered when the document is rendered. For example:</p> <pre><code>contributes: format: pdf: format-resources: - plos2015.bst</code></pre> <h5 id="extension-embedding-1">Extension Embedding</h5> <p>In some cases format extensions will want to make use of other extensions. This is permitted, but adding extensions for use within a custom format must be done with a special command line flag to ensure they are embedded correctly.</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create extension format:pdf myformat cd myformat quarto add quarto-ext/fancy-text --embed myformat</code></pre> <p>For example, here we want to make the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/fancy-text">fancy-text</a> extension (which provides special formatting for the words () and BibTEX) available for users of the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/jss">jss</a> custom format:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto add quarto-ext/fancy-text --embed jss</code></pre> <p>This will produce the following output:</p> <pre><code>Output quarto-journals/jss └── _extensions └── jss ├── _extensions │ └── quarto-ext │ └── fancy-text └── partials</code></pre> <p>This will add the <code>quarto-ext/fancy-text</code> extension into the <code>jss</code> extension in the <code>_extensions</code> folder. By embedding an extension you make it available without creating the potential for conflict with other versions of the extension that users might already have installed.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-12">Learning More</h5> <p>Here are some additional learning resources you may find valuable:</p> <ul> <li>The source code for the Journal article formats available from the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/">quarto-journals</a> GitHub organization.</li> <li>The <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/article-format-template">GitHub template repository</a> for creating new Journal formats. The code in the template repository is heavily annotated so creating a new repository using this template and experimenting with it is an excellent way to learn.</li> <li>In depth treatment of creating Article Templates for Journals (including how to use partials to compose templates)</li> <li>Review of the schema and options for expressing and rendering Authors & Affiliations.</li> </ul> <h5 id="footnotes-8">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>This is most common in the the case of PDF based formats which have a secondary step of converting the LaTeX produced by Pandoc into a PDF. If there are files that are referenced indirectly by the LaTeX, they will need to be discoverable and should typically be copied into the same directory that contains the LaTeX input.↩︎</li> </ul> <h2 id="manuscripts-1">Manuscripts</h2> <h3 id="authoring-manuscripts">Authoring Manuscripts</h3> <h4 id="authoring-manuscripts-1">Authoring Manuscripts</h4> <h5 id="overview-75">Overview</h5> <p>On this page, we’ll show you how to author an academic manuscript with Quarto in VS Code. You’ll learn how to:</p> <ul> <li>Preview your manuscript using VS Code.</li> <li>Add scholarly front matter to describe your article.</li> <li>Add figures, tables, cross references, and citations with Quarto-specific markdown.</li> <li>Include output from computations using inline code or embedded from external notebooks. The syntax you’ll learn will apply regardless of the tool you are using to edit notebooks. And although we’ll use Python code examples, you could use R or Julia instead.</li> </ul> <p>TipDo you mostly use <code>.ipynb</code>?</p> <p>As a VS Code user, we recommend writing your article in a <code>.qmd</code> file. However, if you currently use VS Code primarily to work with <code>.ipynb</code> files, you may find the Jupyter Lab tutorial more applicable. Install the Quarto extension for Jupyter Lab, then pick up the Jupyter Lab tutorial at Clone the Template Repository. You might also like read about using Quarto with VS Code’s Notebook Editor.</p> <h6 id="is-this-tutorial-for-me">Is this tutorial for me?</h6> <p>We will assume you:</p> <ul> <li>are comfortable using VS Code to open and edit files,</li> <li>have a GitHub account, and are comfortable cloning a repo to your computer,</li> <li>are comfortable navigating your file system, and executing commands in a Terminal.</li> </ul> <h5 id="setup-1">Setup</h5> <p>To follow along, you’ll need to install the VS Code Quarto extension, install some Python packages, and clone the template repository.</p> <p>ImportantInstall Quarto First</p> <p>If you haven’t already, make sure you’ve installed the latest release version of Quarto, as described in the Manuscript Overview.</p> <h6 id="install-the-quarto-vs-code-extension">Install the Quarto VS Code Extension</h6> <p>Install the Quarto extension from the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">VS Code Extension Marketplace</a> or the <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Open VSX Registry</a>.</p> <h6 id="install-python-packages">Install Python Packages</h6> <p>The template manuscript includes some executable Python code. To render Python code you’ll need <code>jupyter</code> along with the packages specific to this code, <code>pandas</code>, and <code>matplotlib</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, once you have the template repo below, you can use the file <code>requirements.txt</code> to get the packages you need.</p> <h6 id="clone-the-template-repository">Clone the Template Repository</h6> <p>To follow this tutorial you’ll need your own copy of the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/manuscript-template-vscode">template repository</a>, including all of its branches.</p> <ul> <li><p>Head to <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/manuscript-template-vscode/generate">GitHub to create a new repository from the template</a>.</p></li> <li><p>Provide a Repository Name and make sure you check Include all branches. Then Create repository from template.</p></li> <li><p>Once your repository is created, clone it to your local computer.</p></li> <li><p>You can do this any way you are comfortable, for instance in the Terminal, it might look like:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>git clone git@github.com:<username>/<repo-name>.git</p></li> <li><p>Where you use your own user name and repo name.</p></li> <li><p>You’ll be working inside this directory throughout the tutorial, so if you are ready to proceed, open the directory in VS Code. Template manuscript open in VS Code</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="project-files">Project Files</h5> <p>At its simplest, a Quarto manuscript project has two files:</p> <ul> <li>A notebook file where you write your article: <code>index.qmd</code>. This file contains: <ul> <li>document metadata, including article front matter (authors, affiliations, etc.) and Quarto options,</li> <li>the article body, written using special Quarto markdown syntax that allows you to add things like cross references and citations, and</li> <li>optionally, code, where you control if, or how, the code and its output appear in the article.</li> </ul></li> <li>A configuration file <code>_quarto.yml</code> that identifies the project as a Quarto manuscript and controls how your manuscript is put together. This particular manuscript project includes some other files and folders, you’ll learn about these files as you work through this tutorial.</li> </ul> <h5 id="workflow-4">Workflow</h5> <p>The basic workflow for writing a manuscript in Quarto is to make changes to your article content in <code>index.qmd</code>, preview the changes with Quarto, and repeat. Let’s try it out.</p> <p>Open <code>index.qmd</code>.</p> <p>Preview the manuscript by hitting the Preview button () located in the menu bar of the editor:</p> <p>You’ll see some output from Quarto in the Terminal and then a live preview will appear in a new Quarto Preview pane.</p> <p>You’ll dive into the details of this <code>index.qmd</code> next, but for now let’s make a change and see what happens.</p> <p>Find the line:</p> <pre><code>title: La Palma Earthquakes</code></pre> <p>Change the line to:</p> <pre><code>title: La Palma Earthquake Mechanisms</code></pre> <p>Save the notebook, hit Preview, and you’ll see the preview update.</p> <h5 id="visual-editor">Visual Editor</h5> <p>The VS Code visual editor provides a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WYSIWYM">WYSIWYM</a> editing interface for Quarto notebooks.
