Some tasks, like adding citations, or creating tables, are easier in the visual editor - we’ll point these out as we introduce them.</p> <p>Source Editor</p> <p>Visual Editor</p> <p>To toggle between source and visual editor modes, use the Editor menu and select “Edit in Visual Mode” or “Edit in Source Mode” mode, or use the keyboard shortcut .</p> <p>There are other ways to switch modes, read about them, and other features of the visual editor at Visual Editing in VS Code.</p> <p>You can switch between the source and visual editor at any time - the location of your cursor and undo/redo history is preserved.</p> <h5 id="notebook-structure">Notebook Structure</h5> <p>The file <code>index.qmd</code> is a Quarto markdown file. It contains three types of content:</p> <ul> <li>It starts with a YAML header that is used to set document metadata, including scholarly front matter. The YAML header starts and ends with a line of three dashes (<code>---</code>), and within these lines, content is parsed as YAML.</li> <li>It may include executable code chunks which start with three backticks followed by the code language in curly braces (e.g. ```<code>{r}</code> or ```<code>{python}</code>). These code chunks may include Quarto comments at the top which start with <code>#|</code>. These comments set Quarto options that control how the code and its output appear in the article.</li> <li>The rest of the document is interpreted as Quarto specific markdown, which allows you to include things like figures, tables, equations, cross references and citations. The rest of this page walks you through this article from top to bottom, introducing you to the Quarto features you’ll most likely need to write a scholarly article.</li> </ul> <h5 id="front-matter-2">Front Matter</h5> <p>The YAML header consists of key-value pairs set using the syntax <code>key: value</code>. The header is often extensive for articles because it is used to specify much of the scholarly front matter, like the authors and their affiliations, and the abstract.</p> <p>TipExpand to see full YAML header for <code>index.qmd</code></p> <pre><code>title: La Palma Earthquakes author: - name: Steve Purves orcid: 0000-0002-0760-5497 corresponding: true email: steve@curvenote.com roles: - Investigation - Project administration - Software - Visualization affiliations: - Curvenote - name: Rowan Cockett orcid: 0000-0002-7859-8394 corresponding: false roles: [] affiliations: - Curvenote keywords: - La Palma - Earthquakes abstract: | In September 2021, a significant jump in seismic activity on the island of La Palma (Canary Islands, Spain) signaled the start of a volcanic crisis that still continues at the time of writing. Earthquake data is continually collected and published by the Instituto Geográphico Nacional (IGN). ... plain-language-summary: | Earthquake data for the island of La Palma from the September 2021 eruption is found ... key-points: - A web scraping script was developed to pull data from the Instituto Geogràphico Nacional into a machine-readable form for analysis - Earthquake events on La Palma are consistent with the presence of both mantle and crustal reservoirs. date: last-modified bibliography: references.bib citation: container-title: Earth and Space Science number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>For example, at the top level the header in <code>index.qmd</code> sets the following keys: <code>title</code>, <code>author</code>, <code>keywords</code>, <code>abstract</code>, <code>plain-language-summary</code>, <code>key-points</code>, <code>date</code>, <code>bibliography</code>, <code>citation</code>, and <code>number-sections</code>.</p> <p>You’ve seen how editing the <code>title</code> key updated the title of the article on the manuscript webpage. The <code>title</code> key is also used by the PDF and Word formats, but not all of the keys are used in all formats.</p> <p>You can read more about setting the front matter for your article in Scholarly Front Matter.</p> <h5 id="markdown">Markdown</h5> <p>Markdown cells in the document will be processed by Quarto’s specific markdown syntax. Quarto’s markdown syntax is based on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#pandocs-markdown">Pandoc Markdown</a>, which in turn is based on John Gruber’s <a href="https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/">Markdown</a>.</p> <p>As an example, the markdown to create the heading for the article’s introduction is:</p> <pre><code>## Introduction</code></pre> <p>First-level headings are reserved for the article title, so you’ll use second-level and deeper headings to structure the sections in your article.</p> <p>If Markdown syntax is unfamiliar, you might want to read about Quarto Markdown Basics.</p> <h5 id="computations-6">Computations</h5> <p>TipPython Examples</p> <p>This section uses Python code examples, but Quarto also supports R, Julia and Observable.</p> <p>Your article can include executable code. By default, code itself will not display in the article, but any output including tables and figures will. When you include code in your article, you’ll also get an additional link to the “Article Notebook” under Notebooks on the manuscript webpage. This is a rendered version of your article notebook that includes the code.</p> <p>For example, <code>index.qmd</code>, includes:</p> <pre><code>```{python} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np eruptions = [1492, 1585, 1646, 1677, 1712, 1949, 1971, 2021] ```</code></pre> <p>This code doesn’t appear in the rendered article, but does in the “Article Notebook”.</p> <p>Rendered Article</p> <p>Article Notebook</p> <p>You can add Quarto options to code cells by adding a <code>#|</code> comment to the top, followed by the option in YAML syntax. For example, adding the <code>echo</code> option with the value <code>true</code> would look like this:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| echo: true import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np eruptions = [1492, 1585, 1646, 1677, 1712, 1949, 1971, 2021] ```</code></pre> <p>The <code>echo</code> option describes whether the code is included in the rendered article. If you make this change and save <code>index.qmd</code>, you’ll see this code now appears in the article.</p> <p>You can find a list of all the code cell options available on the Jupyter Code Cell reference page.</p> <p>The next code cell creates a figure:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| label: fig-timeline #| fig-cap: Timeline of recent earthquakes on La Palma #| fig-alt: An event plot of the years of the last 8 eruptions on La Palma. plt.figure(figsize=(6, 1)) plt.eventplot(eruptions, lineoffsets=0, linelengths=0.1, color='black') plt.gca().axes.get_yaxis().set_visible(False) plt.ylabel('') plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>The <code>label</code> option is used to add an identifier to code cell and its output, for example to allow cross referencing. The prefix <code>fig-</code> is required for figure cross references, but the suffix, in this case <code>timeline</code>, is up to you. You’ll learn more about Cross References below.</p> <p>The option <code>fig-cap</code> provides the caption text displayed below the figure in the manuscript, and <code>fig-alt</code> provides alt text for the figure, helping your manuscript webpage to meet accessibility guidelines.</p> <p>Computations are also a good way to include tables based on data. You can read more about doing this in the Quarto documentation on Tables from Computations.</p> <p>If you have code output you don’t want to include in your article you can use <code>output: false</code>. For example, you may have a value that is helpful for writing your content, but you don’t want it to appear in the article itself. The next code cell is an example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| output: false avg_years_between_eruptions = np.mean(np.diff(eruptions[:-1])) avg_years_between_eruptions ```</code></pre> <p>If you are viewing the rendered “Article Notebook”, you’ll see the value of <code>avg_years_between_eruptions</code> displayed below this code, but the value does not appear in the rendered article.</p> <p>If you’d like to exclude a cell and its output from both the article and the rendered notebook, you could use <code>include: false</code> instead:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| include: false avg_years_between_eruptions = np.mean(np.diff(eruptions[:-1])) avg_years_between_eruptions ```</code></pre> <p>You can use computed values directly in your article text using the syntax <code>{python} expr</code>. For example, consider this line in <code>index.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>Based on data up to and including 1971, eruptions on La Palma happen every `{python} f"{avg_years_between_eruptions:.1f}"` years on average.</code></pre> <p>When rendered, it displays as:</p> <p>Based on data up to and including 1971, eruptions on La Palma happen every 79.8 years on average.</p> <p>You can read more about using code inline at Inline Code.</p> <p>Rather than including computations directly in your article you can also embed outputs from other notebooks, read more below in Embedding Notebooks.</p> <h6 id="when-is-code-executed">When is code executed?</h6> <p>By default, Quarto will execute code in a <code>.qmd</code> notebook during the rendering process. This means, as you edit <code>index.qmd</code> you may notice messages that indicate code is being run.</p> <p>This manuscript template uses Quarto’s freeze feature, which allows us to avoid having to set up a computational environment on GitHub during the publishing process. Freeze saves the rendered versions of notebooks so that they are not re-rendered, and consequently, the code is not re-evaluated unless their source changes.</p> <p>You may not have noticed, but the first time you rendered the manuscript no code was evaluated. This was because the template repo included the <code>_freeze/</code> folder, and the contents of <code>index.qmd</code> had not changed since the freeze was generated. As you change <code>index.qmd</code>, code will be re-evaluated, and the contents of <code>_freeze/</code> will be updated. Remember when you come to publish, you’ll need to commit the changes in <code>_freeze/</code> as well.</p> <h5 id="citations-3">Citations</h5> <p>TipArticle Citation</p> <p>This section describes adding citations in the text of your article. The citation for your own article that is displayed at the bottom of the article webpage is controlled using Front Matter.</p> <p>To add citations you need a bibliography file, <code>.bib</code>, containing the citation data. You can specify this file in the document YAML with the <code>bibliography</code> option. For example, the citation data for <code>index.qmd</code> is stored in <code>references.bib</code>:</p> <pre><code>bibliography: references.bib</code></pre> <p>The file <code>references.bib</code> contains only one citation:</p> <pre><code>references.bib @article{marrero2019, author = {Marrero, Jos{\' e} and Garc{\' i}a, Alicia and Berrocoso, Manuel and Llinares, {\' A}ngeles and Rodr{\' i}guez-Losada, Antonio and Ortiz, R.}, journal = {Journal of Applied Volcanology}, year = {2019}, month = {7}, pages = {}, title = {Strategies for the development of volcanic hazard maps in monogenetic volcanic fields: the example of {La} {Palma} ({Canary} {Islands})}, volume = {8}, doi = {10.1186/s13617-019-0085-5}, }</code></pre> <p>To cite an article from the bibliography in your text, you use <code>@</code> followed by the citation identifier, e.g. <code>marrero2019</code>. For example, the article includes this line citing this reference:</p> <pre><code>Studies of the magma systems feeding the volcano, such as @marrero2019, have proposed ...</code></pre> <p>This renders as:</p> <p>Studies of the magma systems feeding the volcano, such as Marrero et al. (2019), have proposed …</p> <p>Hovering over the citation text reveals the full reference details. Clicking on the citation takes a reader to the reference in the References section at the end of the article:</p> <p>The above citation is an example where the author’s names are incorporated into the sentence itself. Another common style is to place the citation within parentheses, often at the end of a sentence. You can achieve this by enclosing the citation syntax in square brackets <code>[</code>. For example,</p> <pre><code>A prior study of the magma systems feeding the volcano proposed that there are two main magma reservoirs feeding the Cumbre Vieja volcano [@marrero2019].</code></pre> <p>This renders as:</p> <p>A prior study of the magma systems feeding the volcano proposed that there are two main magma reservoirs feeding the Cumbre Vieja volcano (Marrero et al. 2019).</p> <p>There are many other syntax variations to include page numbers, chapters, or exclude the author names. You can read more in the Citations documentation.</p> <p>The Visual Editor Insert -> Citation dialog has utilities for adding citations from their DOI, your Zotero library, and public databases like Crossref, PubMed and DataCite. This provides an easy way to build the bibliography file (<code>.bib</code>) and generate the markdown citation syntax.</p> <h5 id="cross-references-8">Cross References</h5> <p>Quarto can generate cross references that keep track of numbering and linking for you. The general syntax for a cross reference is an <code>@</code> followed by a label. For example, to reference the timeline figure, you could write:</p> <pre><code>@fig-timeline</code></pre> <p>When rendered, cross references include a word to indicate the type of object being referenced, like “Figure” or “Table”. So for instance, this line in <code>index.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>Eight eruptions have been recorded since the late 1400s (@fig-timeline).</code></pre> <p>Results in the text:</p> <p>Eight eruptions have been recorded since the late 1400s (Figure 1).</p> <p>Where “Figure 1” is also a link to the appropriate figure.</p> <p>The labels you add to elements must have the appropriate prefix to allow cross referencing:</p> <p>Element</p> <p>Label Prefix</p> <p>Rendered Cross Reference</p> <p>Figure</p> <p><code>fig-</code></p> <p>Figure 1</p> <p>Table</p> <p><code>tbl-</code></p> <p>Table 1</p> <p>Equation</p> <p><code>eq-</code></p> <p>Equation 1</p> <p>Section</p> <p><code>sec-</code></p> <p>Section 1</p> <p>You’ve already seen you can add a label to output generated by code using the <code>label</code> code chunk option. You’ll see how to add labels to non-code generated elements, like equations, tables, and static figures, as you learn about them below.</p> <p>To cross reference sections your document YAML header must also include:</p> <pre><code>number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>You can add a label to a section heading in curly braces after the heading, e.g:</p> <pre><code>## Data & Methods {#sec-data-methods}</code></pre> <p>You can then reference this section in the text, like:</p> <pre><code>Data and methods are discussed in @sec-data-methods.</code></pre> <p>Which will be rendered as:</p> <p>Data and methods are discussed in Section 2.</p> <p>You can read more about the types of objects that can be referenced, including code listings, and mathematical theorems, as well as some of the options to control how references appear in the Quarto Cross References documentation.</p> <p>In the Visual Editor, you can use Insert -> Cross Reference to get a dialog box with the available labels in your document and quickly generate the syntax needed for a cross reference.</p> <h5 id="equations-3">Equations</h5> <p>Quarto markdown can include equations specified in LaTeX notation. Use single dollar signs (<code>\$</code>) to add an equation inline or double dollar signs (<code>\$\$</code>) to add a display equation. Both of these are illustrated in the following paragraph in <code>index.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>Let $x$ denote the number of eruptions in a year. Then, $x$ can be modeled by a Poisson distribution $$ p(x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{x}}{x !} $$ {#eq-poisson} where $\lambda$ is the rate of eruptions per year. Using @eq-poisson, the probability of an eruption in the next $t$ years can be calculated.</code></pre> <p>Notice the display equation has a label added in curly braces after the closing <code>\$\$</code>. This allows it to be referenced using <code>@eq-poisson</code> in the text.</p> <p>When rendered, this displays as:</p> <p>Let (x) denote the number of eruptions in a year. Then, (x) can be modeled by a Poisson distribution [ p(x) = ] where () is the rate of eruptions per year. Using Equation 1, the probability of an eruption in the next (t) years can be calculated.</p> <h5 id="tables-8">Tables</h5> <p>Tables can be added inline with what is known as pipe syntax. As an example, in <code>index.qmd</code> a table of earthquakes is specified as:</p> <pre><code>| Name | Year | | -------------------- | ------ | | Current | 2021 | | Teneguía | 1971 | | Nambroque | 1949 | | El Charco | 1712 | | Volcán San Antonio | 1677 | | Volcán San Martin | 1646 | | Tajuya near El Paso | 1585 | | Montaña Quemada | 1492 | : Recent historic eruptions on La Palma {#tbl-history}</code></pre> <p>Columns are separated by pipes (<code>|</code>), and the dashes (<code>-</code>) in the second row separate the header row from the rest of the table. A caption can be provided with a line starting with <code>:</code>. A label that can be used for cross references is added at the end of the caption inside curly braces. Like figures, the label prefix <code>tbl-</code> is required for cross references, but the suffix is up to you.</p> <p>Inserting and editing tables using markdown syntax can be cumbersome. The Visual Editor provides tools for editing existing tables, and inserting new tables. Use the Table menu in the visual editor toolbar or right-click inside a table to bring up the options.</p> <p>You can learn more about tables in Quarto, including an alternative syntax known as grid tables, on the Tables page in the Quarto documentation.</p> <h5 id="static-figures">Static Figures</h5> <p>To include a figure from a file, the markdown syntax looks like:</p> <pre><code>![Caption](file_path_to_image)</code></pre> <p>For example, to include the <code>la-palma-map.png</code> image from the <code>images/</code> folder in the project, along with the caption “Map of La Palma”, you would write:</p> <pre><code>![Map of La Palma](images/la-palma-map.png)</code></pre> <p>TipImage File Location</p> <p>You don’t have to store your images in a folder called <code>images/</code>, although it is a common convention. Your images can be anywhere inside your manuscript project directory, just make sure you include the full path to the image, relative to the location of <code>index.qmd</code>.</p> <p>The actual markdown in <code>index.qmd</code> includes a further attribute, <code>#fig-map</code> inside curly braces following the image path to provide a label for cross references:</p> <pre><code>![Map of La Palma](images/la-palma-map.png){#fig-map}</code></pre> <p>Another attribute that you may wish to add is <code>fig-alt</code>, the alt text to be provided for the image. For example:</p> <pre><code>![Map of La Palma](images/la-palma-map.png){#fig-map fig-alt="A map of the Canary Islands. The second most west island, La Palma, is highlighted."}</code></pre> <p>You can read more about including figures in Quarto documents, including how to resize figures and arrange multiple figures, on the Quarto docs Figures page.</p> <h5 id="external-embeds">External Embeds</h5> <p>NoteEmbedding Quarto Notebooks</p> <p>This section covers embedding outputs from Quarto documents (<code>.qmd</code>). You can also embed outputs from Jupyter Notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>).</p> <p>An alternative to including computations directly in the article notebook is to embed output from other notebooks. This manuscript project includes the notebook <code>data-screening.qmd</code> in the <code>notebooks/</code> folder.</p> <p>To embed output from a notebook, you can use the <code>embed</code> shortcode. Quarto shortcodes are special markdown directives that generate content. The <code>embed</code> shortcode is used in main article file in the line:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd {{< embed notebooks/data-screening.qmd#fig-spatial-plot >}}</code></pre> <p>The double curly braces (<code>{{</code>) and angle brackets (<code><</code>) indicate this is a shortcode. The <code>embed</code> shortcode requires a path to a notebook chunk. In this case, it’s the file path to a source notebook, <code>data-screening.qmd</code>, followed by <code>#</code> and a chunk label. The chunk label is set using the Quarto chunk option <code>label</code> in <code>data-screening.qmd</code> notebook:</p> <pre><code>data-screening.qmd ```{python} #| label: fig-spatial-plot #| fig-cap: Locations of earthquakes on La Palma since 2017. #| fig-alt: A scatterplot of earthquake locations plotting latitude against longitude. from matplotlib import colormaps cmap = colormaps['viridis_r'] ax = df.plot.scatter(x="Longitude", y="Latitude", s=47-df["Depth(km)"], c=df["Magnitude"], figsize=(12,10), grid="on", cmap=cmap) colorbar = ax.collections[0].colorbar colorbar.set_label("Magnitude") plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Just like any figure, using a label starting with <code>fig-</code> allows it to be cross referenced in the text. Any other options, like the figure caption (<code>fig-cap</code>) and alt text (<code>fig-alt</code>), can also be set in the source notebook.</p> <p>Whenever you change the content of <code>data-screening.qmd</code>, including updating chunk options like the caption, it will be re-rendered. Consequently, the code in <code>data-screening.qmd</code> will also be re-run.</p> <p>For example, if you edit the caption to:</p> <pre><code>#| fig-cap: "Earthquakes on La Palma since 2017."</code></pre> <p>You’ll notice in the background <code>quarto preview</code> re-renders the file:</p> <pre><code>Terminal processing file: data-screening.qmd output file: data-screening.qmd Rendering output notebook [notebooks/data-screening.qmd] Rendering HTML preview [notebooks/data-screening.qmd]</code></pre> <p>And then the caption in the main article preview updates.</p> <h5 id="up-next">Up Next</h5> <p>You’ve now covered the main features of Quarto for authoring a manuscript. You’ve edited <code>index.qmd</code>, added resources like figures, notebooks or bibliographic data, and previewed the result.</p> <p>Once, you are happy with the changes you’ve made, you’ll need update your public manuscript webpage.</p> <p>Head on to Publishing to learn how to publish and share your manuscript with the world.</p> <h3 id="next-steps">Next Steps</h3> <h4 id="next-steps-1">Next Steps</h4> <h5 id="learning-more-13">Learning More</h5> <p>You’ve seen the manuscript workflow, and examples of syntax in a complete template. One way to start your own manuscript is to alter the contents of this template. Alternatively, you could start from scratch. Either way, here are some resources to help you with your next steps.</p> <h6 id="basics">Basics</h6> <p>Head to Manuscript Basics to:</p> <ul> <li>Learn how to turn a directory into a manuscript project by adding the <code>_quarto.yml</code> file</li> <li>Start a new project with a minimal template using the <code>quarto create</code> command</li> <li>Controlling manuscript settings in <code>_quarto.yml</code></li> <li>Add an output format for a specific journal</li> </ul> <h6 id="quarto-projects">Quarto Projects</h6> <p>Quarto manuscripts are a type of Quarto project, so anything you can do in a Quarto project applies to a manuscript. For instance, these pages in the Project documentation might be of interest:</p> <ul> <li>Managing Execution: techniques to avoid expensive computations on every render.</li> <li>Virtual Environments: capture your computational environment to facilitate reproducing your work.</li> </ul> <h6 id="publishing-8">Publishing</h6> <p>We set up the publishing workflow for the template repository, but you can publish your manuscript website any way you can publish a Quarto website. For example, if you need to set up the workflow to publish to GitHub pages yourself, head to Publishing to GitHub Pages.</p> <h3 id="publishing-quarto-manuscripts">Publishing Quarto Manuscripts</h3> <h4 id="publishing-quarto-manuscripts-1">Publishing Quarto Manuscripts</h4> <h5 id="overview-76">Overview</h5> <p>ImportantComplete the Authoring Tutorial First</p> <p>This page is a continuation of the <a href="authoring/">Authoring Manuscripts</a> tutorial. We’ll assume you’ve cloned the template repository, have made some changes, and are happy with the preview generated by Quarto.</p> <p>Publishing a Quarto manuscript is the process of taking the preview you’ve been viewing on your computer and making it available to anyone on the web.</p> <p>We’ve set up the template manuscript to include most of the scaffolding needed to publish your manuscript to your repository’s GitHub Pages site. Publishing your manuscript website is as simple as pushing your changes to your repo.</p> <p>Since a Quarto manuscript is a special type of Quarto website, you can publish it any way you can publish a Quarto website. If GitHub Pages doesn’t suit your needs you can learn about other options in Publishing.</p> <p>On this page, you’ll change one setting in your GitHub repo to authorize read and write permissions for GitHub Actions, then walk through the publishing process.</p> <h5 id="authorize-github-actions">Authorize GitHub Actions</h5> <p>The template manuscript is configured with a GitHub Action in <code>.github/workflows/publish.yml</code>. This action is triggered when there is a push to the main branch; it renders your manuscript and puts the manuscript website source on the <code>gh-pages</code> branch.</p> <p>To ensure the action has permission to write to the <code>gh-pages</code> branch, you’ll need to make one change to your repository settings. Go to your repository and navigate to: Settings > Actions > General > Workflow Permissions. Check the “Read and Write Permissions” box.</p> <p>CautionThis GitHub Action will not evaluate your code</p> <p>The GitHub Action in <code>.github/workflows/publish.yml</code> does not set up any computational environments (e.g. Python or R), so is unable to evaluate code.</p> <p>Jupyter notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) include their output and do not need any special treatment. However, if your manuscript includes Quarto files (<code>.qmd</code>), you must first render locally to update the saved computational outputs in the <code>_freeze</code> directory.</p> <p>If you instead want your GitHub Action to also evaluate code, read how to set it up in the Executing Code section on the Publishing to GitHub page.</p> <h5 id="push-to-publish">Push to Publish</h5> <p>Publishing this manuscript to GitHub Pages is as simple as committing and pushing your changes, however we advise a full render first. On the Terminal, in your manuscript directory, run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>ImportantThe Render button isn’t enough</p> <p>The Render button in RStudio runs the command <code>quarto preview</code>, not <code>quarto render</code>. You’ll need to explicitly run <code>quarto render</code> on the Terminal.</p> <p>Unlike <code>quarto preview</code> which generates outputs as needed, <code>quarto render</code> will generate all outputs (all the article formats and the manuscript website). It is also the command that will be run by the GitHub action, so verifying it locally first is a good way to avoid issues on GitHub.</p> <p>If the render runs without issue, stage your changes.</p> <p>CautionChecked your staged files</p> <p>We’ve added a few lines to <code>.gitignore</code> to ignore common files Quarto creates in the rendering process that don’t need to be checked into version control. This means the files to stage should be the notebooks, and possibly items in the <code>_freeze</code> directory.</p> <p>If you’ve added any files to the project that you don’t want to be pushed to GitHub, double-check you haven’t staged them for the commit.</p> <p>Commit and push your changes to GitHub.</p> <p>Once pushed, you should see the actions trigger in GitHub: “Quarto Publish” is the action we’ve added to render the site and push it to the <code>gh-pages</code> branch; “pages-build-deployment” is GitHub’s action to deploy the <code>gh-pages</code> branch to your GitHub Pages URL.</p> <p>Once both actions are complete, navigate to your repository’s GitHub Page.</p> <p>You can find your GitHub Pages website address in the Settings for your repository on GitHub under Pages.</p> <p>Your manuscript is now published!</p> <h5 id="what-next">What Next?</h5> <p>You’ve now been through the full workflow of a Quarto manuscript: authoring content, previewing the generated manuscript and publishing it to GitHub Pages. When you are ready to dive into more detail, we have some recommendations on Next Steps.</p> <h3 id="quarto-manuscripts">Quarto Manuscripts</h3> <h4 id="quarto-manuscripts-1">Quarto Manuscripts</h4> <h5 id="overview-77">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto manuscript projects provide a framework for writing and publishing scholarly articles. A Quarto manuscript lets you:</p> <ul> <li>Use one or more notebooks or <code>.qmd</code> documents as the source of content and computations, and then publish these computations alongside the manuscript, allowing readers to dive into your code.</li> <li>Produce manuscripts in multiple formats (including LaTeX or MS Word formats required by journals), and give readers easy access to all of the formats through a manuscript website. The output of a Quarto manuscript is a website (<a href="https://quarto-ext.github.io/manuscript-template-jupyter/">live example</a>). The article itself appears as the content of the website, and can include all the elements common to scholarly writing like figures, tables, equations, cross references and citations. The website also makes available other formats (e.g. PDF, Docx) as well as links to all of the computations used to create the article.</li> </ul> <p>Article Content</p> <p>Navigation</p> <p>On the right, you’ll see navigation: a table of contents for the article itself followed by links to Other Formats, Notebooks and Other Links.</p> <h6 id="other-formats">Other Formats</h6> <p>These links allow a reader to download alternative formats of your article. In this example, there is an MS Word version that may be useful for a reviewer to provide feedback and a PDF version that uses the American Geophysical Union’s (AGU) template. Additionally, there is a MECA archive, a zip file that is designed to capture your article and its supporting documents into a single file suitable for sending to a publisher.</p> <h6 id="notebooks">Notebooks</h6> <p>These are links to notebooks included in the manuscript. The “Article Notebook” is the notebook version of the article itself. In this example, “Data Screening” is a notebook from which a single cell is embedded in the article. Any other notebooks that are included in the project, even if they are not directly used in the article will also appear here.</p> <p>When a reader visits any of these notebook links, they are served an HTML version of the notebook, allowing them to view the code and output without leaving their browser. In addition, a link to download the source code of the notebook is also provided.</p> <p>HTML view of the Data Screening notebook</p> <h6 id="other-links">Other Links</h6> <p>Links that leave the manuscript webpage, for example to take a reader to the manuscript’s GitHub Repo.</p> <h5 id="get-started-2">Get Started</h5> <h6 id="install-quarto-1">Install Quarto</h6> <p>Manuscripts are a feature in the 1.4 release of Quarto. Before you get started, make sure you install the latest release version of Quarto.</p> <p><a href="_">_</a> Find your operating system in the table below</p> <h6 id="highlights-6">Highlights</h6> <p>Quarto 1.10 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li><p>New <code>quarto.language</code> Pandoc template-variable namespace, exposing Quarto’s resolved localized strings to custom templates and template partials:</p> <p><span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>c</em><em>r</em><em>o</em><em>s</em><em>s</em><em>r</em><em>e</em><em>f</em> − <em>f</em><em>i</em><em>g</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em></span> <span class="math inline"><em>q</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>r</em><em>t</em><em>o</em>.<em>l</em><em>a</em><em>n</em><em>g</em><em>u</em><em>a</em><em>g</em><em>e</em>.<em>t</em><em>o</em><em>c</em> − <em>t</em><em>i</em><em>t</em><em>l</em><em>e</em> − <em>d</em><em>o</em><em>c</em><em>u</em><em>m</em><em>e</em><em>n</em><em>t</em></span></p></li> </ul> <h6 id="release-notes-24">Release Notes</h6> <p>You can find release notes and installers for all platforms in the download page.</p> <h6 id="choose-your-tool-4">Choose Your Tool</h6> <p>You can author Quarto manuscripts in any tool or notebook editor. The tutorials below walk you through authoring Quarto manuscripts with a few common tools.</p> <p>Choose your tool to start learning:</p> <p><a href="authoring/jupyterlab.html">Jupyter</a></p> <p><a href="authoring/vscode.html">VS Code</a></p> <p><a href="authoring/rstudio.html">RStudio</a></p> <h3 id="using-manuscripts">Using Manuscripts</h3> <h4 id="using-manuscripts-1">Using Manuscripts</h4> <h5 id="overview-78">Overview</h5> <p>Manuscripts are a type of Quarto project that allow you to write scholarly articles where computational notebooks are both the source of the article, and part of the published record.</p> <p>If you are new to Quarto manuscripts, start with the Manuscript Tutorial.</p> <p>On this page, you can learn how to:</p> <ul> <li>Create a manuscript project</li> <li>Control the manuscript output with options in <code>_quarto.yml</code></li> <li>Add a journal template</li> </ul> <h5 id="creating-a-manuscript-project">Creating a Manuscript Project</h5> <p>To identify a project as a manuscript specify <code>type: manuscript</code> in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: manuscript</code></pre> <p>Then, author your article content in either a Jupyter Notebook called <code>index.ipynb</code> or a Quarto document called <code>index.qmd</code>.</p> <p>You can control many manuscript options with the <code>manuscript</code> key in your configuration file. For instance, you can specify a file other than <code>index.*</code> for your article source using the <code>article</code> key, e.g.:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: article: earthquakes.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you would rather start with some template content, you can create a new manuscript project from the command line with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project manuscript</code></pre> <h5 id="including-notebooks">Including Notebooks</h5> <p>Any notebook files (<code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code>) that are included in your project directory will become part of your manuscript. These notebooks will be rendered to an HTML notebook view, and will be linked from your manuscript webpage under “Notebooks”.</p> <h6 id="notebook-links">Notebook Links</h6> <p>The text for link under “Notebooks” will be the notebook <code>title</code> as set in its YAML metadata, or if that isn’t set, the first markdown heading in the notebook. If neither exist, the link text will be the notebook file name.</p> <p>You can also set the text using <code>notebooks</code>. Use <code>notebook</code> to specify the path to the notebook, and <code>title</code> to set the link text:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: notebooks: - notebook: notebooks/data-screening.ipynb title: Data Processing</code></pre> <h6 id="external-notebooks">External Notebooks</h6> <p>To provide links to notebooks that are hosted elsewhere, add the <code>url</code> option:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: notebooks: - notebook: index.ipynb title: Binder Jupyter Lab Demo url: [mybinder.org](http://mybinder.org/v2/gh/binder-examples/jupyterlab/master?urlpath=lab/tree/index.ipynb)</code></pre> <p>If you want Quarto to produce an HTML notebook view from your notebook source, but you would like to provide a specific version for download, add the <code>download-url</code> option:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: notebooks: - notebook: notebooks/data-screening.ipynb title: Data Processing download-url: notebooks/data-screening-raw.ipynb</code></pre> <h5 id="code-links">Code Links</h5> <p>Use <code>code-links</code> to add links that will appear on your manuscript webpage under the heading “Code Links”. For example, the following adds a link to a Python script:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: code-links: - text: Data Import Code icon: file-code href: data-import.py</code></pre> <p>You can provide the following options for items in <code>code-links</code>:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>text</code></p> <p>The text to be displayed for the link.</p> <p><code>href</code></p> <p>The URL for the link.</p> <p><code>icon</code></p> <p>The <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com/">bootstrap icon</a> for the link.</p> <p><code>rel</code></p> <p>The rel used in the <code>a</code> tag for this link.</p> <p><code>target</code></p> <p>The target used in the <code>a</code> tag for this link.</p> <h6 id="github-and-binder-links">GitHub and Binder Links</h6> <p>There are also two special values you can pass as items to <code>code-links</code>:</p> <p><code>repo</code></p> <p>Add a link to “GitHub Repo” under “Code Links” that points at the GitHub repository of your manuscript:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: code-links: repo</code></pre> <p>Quarto infers the URL for the link from the Git settings of your manuscript project. For <code>code-links: repo</code> to work, your manuscript project should be a Git repository, and have GitHub as the remote <code>origin</code>.</p> <p><code>binder</code></p> <p>Add a link to “Launch Binder” under “Code Links” if your manuscript is configured to Use Binder:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: code-links: binder</code></pre> <h5 id="including-other-resources">Including Other Resources</h5> <p>Quarto will attempt to include resources needed to render your notebooks to HTML on the manuscript website. However, you can also explicitly include resources using <code>resources</code>. For example, to include a data file you’ve put in <code>data/earthquakes.csv</code> you would specify:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: resources: - data/earthquakes.csv</code></pre> <p>This ensures readers can access your data at: <code>{manuscript-url}/data/earthquakes.csv</code>.</p> <h5 id="meca-bundle">MECA Bundle</h5> <p>One of the formats a manuscript project can produce is a Manuscript Exchange Common Approach (MECA) bundle. This bundle is a standardized way to transport your manuscript and its resources, including computational notebooks.</p> <p>A MECA bundle is produced if the <code>jats</code> format is listed as an output format for your article:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: default jats: default</code></pre> <p>Or, you can explicitly set <code>meca-bundle</code> to <code>true</code> in the <code>manuscript</code> options:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: meca-bundle: true</code></pre> <p>By default the MECA bundle is named after your article file, e.g. <code>index-meca.zip</code>, but you can also use <code>meca-bundle</code> to provide a file name:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: meca-bundle: "bundle.zip"</code></pre> <h5 id="manuscript-url">Manuscript URL</h5> <p>Links to your notebooks in non-HTML formats are constructed using the URL of your manuscript website. If your manuscript is published to GitHub Pages, Quarto will detect and set the URL for you. However, if you publish to a different host, or the automatic detection isn’t working, you can set the URL explicitly with <code>manuscript-url</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: manuscript-url: www.posit.co</code></pre> <h5 id="using-binder">Using Binder</h5> <p><a href="https://mybinder.org/">Binder</a> allows you to provide readers with a link that restores your computing environment so they can interact with your manuscript notebooks in a cloud computing environment.</p> <p>Quarto can help you configure your manuscript to use Binder. Read more at Using Binder.</p> <h5 id="customizing-pages">Customizing Pages</h5> <p>The article page and notebook views on your manuscript site are HTML pages, and can be customized using options for the <code>html</code> format. A full list of options is available at HTML Options.</p> <h6 id="theme">Theme</h6> <p>For example, you can change the visual styling of your page with the <code>theme</code> option by providing an existing theme name:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: theme: solar</code></pre> <p>You can read more at HTML Theming.</p> <h6 id="commenting">Commenting</h6> <p>Quarto also integrates with three tools to allow commenting on your manuscript site. To enable commenting, use the <code>comments</code> option to the <code>html</code> format. For example, to enable <a href="https://web.hypothes.is/">Hypothes.is</a> comments, you just need to add <code>hypothesis: true</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: comments: hypothesis: true</code></pre> <p>The other two tools available are <a href="https://utteranc.es/">Utterances</a> and <a href="https://giscus.app/">Giscus</a>. You can read about setting them up at HTML Basics: Commenting.</p> <h5 id="add-a-journal-template">Add a Journal Template</h5> <p>You can find a list of available journal formats on the Quarto Extensions: Journal Articles page. To use a journal format, e.g. the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-journals/acs#american-chemical-society-acs">acs</a> format, you’ll need to complete two steps:</p> <ul> <li><p>Install the appropriate journal format. You’ll most likely be installing in an existing project, so you’ll use the <code>quarto install extension</code> command, e.g.:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>quarto install extension quarto-journals/acs</p></li> <li><p>The extension identifier, <code>quarto-journals/acs</code>, is the GitHub user and repository for the extension. You’ll generally find this, and the exact installation command in the extension’s documentation.</p></li> <li><p>Add the <code>format</code> to your configuration file:</p> <p>_quarto.yml</p> <p>format: html: default docx: default jats: default acs-pdf: default</p></li> <li><p>The format will be the extension’s name (<code>acs</code>), followed by an existing Quarto format (<code>-pdf</code>).</p></li> </ul> <h2 id="output-formats-2">Output formats</h2> <h3 id="all-formats-1">All Formats</h3> <h4 id="all-formats-2">All Formats</h4> <h5 id="overview-79">Overview</h5> <p>Pandoc supports a huge array of output formats, all of which can be used with Quarto. To use any Pandoc format just use the <code>format</code> option or the <code>--to</code> command line option.</p> <p>For example, here’s some YAML that specifies the use of the <code>html</code> format as well as a couple of format options:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html: toc: true code-fold: true ---</code></pre> <p>Alternatively you can specify the use of a format on the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --to html</code></pre> <p>See below for a list of all output formats by type along with links to their reference documentation.</p> <h5 id="documents">Documents</h5> <p>HTML</p> <p>HTML is a markup language used for structuring and presenting content on the web.</p> <p>PDF</p> <p>PDF is a file format for creating print-ready paged documents.</p> <p>MS Word</p> <p>MS Word is the word processor included with Microsoft Office.</p> <p>OpenDocument</p> <p>ODT is an open standard file format for word processing documents.</p> <p>ePub</p> <p>ePub is an e-book file format that is supported by many e-readers.</p> <h5 id="presentations">Presentations</h5> <p>Revealjs</p> <p>Revealjs is an open source HTML presentation framework.</p> <p>PowerPoint</p> <p>PowerPoint is the presentation editing software included with Microsoft Office.</p> <p>Beamer</p> <p>Beamer is a LaTeX class for producing presentations and slides.</p> <h5 id="markdown-1">Markdown</h5> <p>GitHub</p> <p>GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) is the dialect of Markdown that is currently supported for user content on GitHub.</p> <p>CommonMark</p> <p>CommonMark is a strongly defined, highly compatible specification of Markdown.</p> <p>Hugo</p> <p>Hugo is an open-source static website generator.</p> <p>Docusaurus</p> <p>Docusaurus is an open-source markdown documentation system.</p> <p>Markua</p> <p>Markua is a markdown variant used by Leanpub.</p> <h5 id="wikis">Wikis</h5> <p>MediaWiki</p> <p>MediaWiki is the native document format of Wikipedia.</p> <p>DokuWiki</p> <p>DokuWiki is a simple to use and highly versatile open source wiki software that doesn’t require a database.</p> <p>ZimWiki</p> <p>Zim is a graphical text editor used to maintain a collection of wiki pages.</p> <p>Jira Wiki</p> <p>Jira Wiki is the native document format for the Jira issue tracking and project management system from Atlassian.</p> <p>XWiki</p> <p>XWiki is an open-source enterprise wiki system.</p> <h5 id="more-formats">More Formats</h5> <p>JATS</p> <p>JATS (Journal Article Tag Suite) is an XML format for marking up and exchanging journal content.</p> <p>Jupyter</p> <p>Jupyter Notebooks combine software code, computational output, explanatory text and multimedia resources in a single document.</p> <p>ConTeXt</p> <p>ConTeXt is a system for typesetting documents based on TEX and METAPOST.</p> <p>RTF</p> <p>The Rich Text Format (RTF) is a file format for cross-platform document interchange.</p> <p>reST</p> <p>reStructuredText is an easy-to-read, what-you-see-is-what-you-get plaintext markup syntax and parser system.</p> <p>AsciiDoc</p> <p>AsciiDoc is a text document format for writing documentation, articles, and books, ebooks, slideshows, web pages, man pages and blogs.</p> <p>Org-Mode</p> <p>Org-Mode is an Emacs major mode for keeping notes, authoring documents, creating computational notebooks, and more.</p> <p>Muse</p> <p>Emacs Muse is an authoring and publishing environment for Emacs.</p> <p>GNU Texinfo</p> <p>Texinfo is the official documentation format of the GNU project.</p> <p>Groff Man Page</p> <p>The Groff (GNU troff) man page document formats consists of plain text mixed with formatting commands that produce ASCII/UTF8 for display at the terminal.</p> <p>Groff Manuscript</p> <p>The Groff (GNU troff) manuscript format consists of plain text mixed with formatting commands that produces PostScript, PDF, or HTML.</p> <p>Haddock markup</p> <p>Haddock is a tool for automatically generating documentation from annotated Haskell source code.</p> <p>OPML</p> <p>OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language) is an XML format for outlines.</p> <p>Textile</p> <p>Textile is a simple text markup language that makes it easy to structure content for blogs, wikis, and documentation.</p> <p>DocBook</p> <p>DocBook is an XML schema particularly well suited to books and papers about computer hardware and software.</p> <p>InDesign</p> <p>ICML is an XML representation of an Adobe InDesign document.</p> <p>TEI Simple</p> <p>TEI Simple aims to define a new highly-constrained and prescriptive subset of the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) Guidelines suited to the representation of early modern and modern books.</p> <p>FictionBook</p> <p>FictionBook is an open XML-based e-book format.</p> <h3 id="custom-typst-formats">Custom Typst Formats</h3> <h4 id="custom-typst-formats-1">Custom Typst Formats</h4> <h5 id="overview-80">Overview</h5> <p>When you author a Typst document in Quarto, you’ll be using a Quarto format that is in turn based on a Typst template. The default template provides a basic article layout, but Typst provides an easy way to <a href="https://typst.app/docs/tutorial/making-a-template/">define your own templates</a> to produce highly customized documents.</p> <p>Typst templates can be packaged as custom formats for Quarto to allow them to be easily used and shared. On this page, learn about some custom Typst formats available from the Quarto team, as well as how to create your own.</p> <h5 id="custom-formats-2">Custom Formats</h5> <p>You can create highly customized output with Typst by defining a new format based on a custom Typst template. The Typst team has created several useful <a href="https://github.com/typst/templates">templates</a>, a few which have been adapted for use with Quarto as custom formats. These formats include:</p> <p>Format</p> <p>Usage</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/poster">Poster</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/poster</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/ieee">IEEE</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/ieee</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/ams">AMS</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/ams</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/letter">Letter</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/letter</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/fiction">Fiction</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/fiction</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/dept-news">Dept News</a></p> <p><code>quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/dept-news</code></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/orange-book">orange-book</a></p> <p>Bundled; default for book projects</p> <p>The source code for these formats is available at <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates">github.com</a> and <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/orange-book">github.com</a>.</p> <h5 id="create-a-format">Create a Format</h5> <p>To create a new custom Typst format (or package an existing Typst template for use with Quarto) use the <code>quarto create</code> command to get started:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto create extension format</code></pre> <p>Then, choose <code>typst</code> as the base format and provide a name for the extension (e.g. <code>letter</code>). A sample Typst format extension will be created based on the code used in the default template that ships with Quarto. It will include the following files which you can edit to implement your custom format:</p> <p>File</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>_extension.yml</code></p> <p>Basic extension metadata (name, author, description, etc.) and format definition.</p> <p><code>README.md</code></p> <p>Documentation on how to install and use the format.</p> <p><code>template.qmd</code></p> <p>A starter document that demonstrates the basics of the format.</p> <p><code>typst-template.typ</code></p> <p>The core Typst template function (documentation on creating Typst templates can be found here: <a href="https://typst.app/docs/tutorial/making-a-template/">typst.app</a>).</p> <p><code>typst-show.typ</code></p> <p>File that calls the template’s function (mapping Pandoc metadata to function arguments).</p> <p>Additional resources you might find useful when creating custom formats include:</p> <ul> <li>The official Typst tutorial on <a href="https://typst.app/docs/tutorial/making-a-template/">Making a Template</a></li> <li>List of third party templates from the <a href="https://github.com/qjcg/awesome-typst#templates--libraries">Awesome Typst</a> repo.</li> </ul> <h5 id="book-format-extensions">Book Format Extensions</h5> <p>A Typst book format extension includes template partials that configure the underlying Typst package, and a Lua filter that transforms Quarto’s book structure into package-specific commands. The core partials are:</p> <ul> <li><code>typst-show.typ</code> — imports the Typst package and applies its template with Quarto metadata</li> <li><code>numbering.typ</code> — defines chapter-based numbering for equations, figures, callouts, and theorems, with appendix-aware transitions</li> <li><code>page.typ</code> — configures page geometry The Lua filter uses <code>quarto.doc.file_metadata()</code> to detect book item types (parts, chapters, appendices) and emit the appropriate Typst code for each. Extensions can also integrate with the <a href="https://typst.app/universe/package/marginalia">marginalia</a> package for margin notes with recto/verso page awareness.</li> </ul> <p>The bundled <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/orange-book">orange-book extension</a> provides a complete example of this structure.</p> <h5 id="advanced-customization">Advanced Customization</h5> <p>Note</p> <p>This section covers advanced customization of Typst format output and can be safely ignored unless you have found the method of defining custom Typst formats described above too limited.</p> <p>Above we describe a method of creating a Typst format based on specifying two template partials (<code>typst-template.typ</code> and <code>typst-show.typ</code>). These partials customize components of the default Typst Pandoc template, but leave some of the core scaffolding including definitions required by Pandoc for its Typst output as well as handling of bibliographies and footnotes (this means that your own custom Typst formats do not need to explicitly handle them).</p> <p>If you would like to fully override the Pandoc template used for rendering Typst, use the <code>template</code> option in your custom format (rather than <code>template-partials</code>) and provide an alternate implementation of the default template. For example, your <code>_extensions.yml</code> might look like this:</p> <pre><code>_extensions.yml title: Typst Custom Format author: Jane Smith version: "0.2.0" quarto-required: ">=1.4.11" contributes: formats: typst: template: template.typ template-partials: - typst-template.typ - typst-show.typ</code></pre> <p>Use the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/typst/pandoc/quarto/template.typ">source code</a> of the default template as a starting point for your <code>template.typ</code>. Note that you can call all of the template partials provided by Quarto (e.g. <code>biblio.typ()</code> or <code>notes.typ()</code>) from within your custom template implementation.</p> <p>The <a href="https://github.com/quarto-ext/typst-templates/tree/main/ams">AMS</a> format provides an example of redefining the main template (in that case, it is to prevent automatic bibliography processing by Quarto in deference to the built-in handling of the Typst AMS template).</p> <h5 id="bundling-typst-packages">Bundling Typst Packages</h5> <p>If your custom format uses packages from the Typst preview namespace (e.g., <code>@preview/cetz</code>), you can bundle them with your extension for offline use. The <code>quarto call typst-gather</code> command scans your template files for <code>@preview</code> imports and downloads the packages.</p> <p>From your extension directory, run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto call typst-gather</code></pre> <p>The command auto-detects your <code>.typ</code> files from <code>_extension.yml</code> and downloads packages into your extension directory (e.g., <code>_extensions/myformat/typst/packages/</code>).</p> <p>For configuration options and advanced usage, see Gathering Typst Packages.</p> <h3 id="docusaurus">Docusaurus</h3> <h4 id="docusaurus-1">Docusaurus</h4> <h5 id="overview-81">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://docusaurus.io">Docusaurus</a> is a popular markdown documentation system. Pages in Docusaurus websites are typically written in plain markdown, so don’t have a straightforward way to automatically and reproducibly incorporate computational output.</p> <p>Using the Quarto <code>docusaurus-md</code> format, you can incorporate computational output (e.g. R or Python code that produces plots) into Docusaurus websites. This article explains how.</p> <p>It’s important to note that many of the Quarto features related to theming, page layout, and navigation are not applicable when you are using Quarto with Docusaurus. Docusaurus has its own theming system, syntax highlighting, table of contents, page layout, navigational menus, and full text search. You’ll use Quarto to execute code and generate markdown that is rendered within the Docusaurus HTML publishing framework rather than Quarto’s own.</p> <h5 id="workflow-5">Workflow</h5> <p>The basic concept of using Quarto with Docusaurus is that you take computational markdown documents (<code>.qmd</code>) or Jupyter notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) and use them to generate plain markdown files (<code>.md</code>) that are rendered to HTML by Docusaurus.</p> <p>index.qmd quarto => index.md docusaurus => index.html</p> <p>The <code>quarto render</code> and <code>quarto preview</code> commands are used to transform <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> files to Docusaurus compatible markdown (<code>.md</code>). The computational files are located in the same place you would also locate ordinary markdown files (e.g. the <code>blog</code> directory).</p> <p>After rendering, a plain <code>.md</code> file is written right alongside the computational document. This markdown file is then processed by Docusaurus.</p> <h6 id="live-preview">Live Preview</h6> <p>The <code>quarto preview</code> command will automatically recognize when it is run from a directory that contains a Docusaurus website:</p> <pre><code>Terminal cd my-docusaurus-website quarto preview</code></pre> <p>This will automatically run <code>docusaurus start</code> on your behalf to bring up a local preview server. In addition, it will monitor the filesystem for changes to <code>.qmd</code> and <code>.ipynb</code> inputs and automatically re-render them to Docusaurus compatible <code>.md</code> files when they change.</p> <p>Note that this also works for the integrated Preview command within the Quarto VS Code Extension in VS Code or Positron.</p> <h6 id="rendering-9">Rendering</h6> <p>If you are not previewing and want to render all of the Quarto documents (<code>.qmd</code>) and notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) in your site, call <code>quarto render</code> from the root directory of the site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal cd my-docusaurus-website quarto render</code></pre> <p>Typically you’ll want to do a <code>quarto render</code> at the site level before you build the site for publishing:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render && npm run build</code></pre> <p>You can also render individual documents or notebooks:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render blog/2022-07-26/hello-quarto/index.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you have computationally expensive documents you may want to consider using Quarto’s freeze feature to only re-execute code when your document source code changes.</p> <p>Note that if aren’t ever rendering at the project level and just have individual files that you want to render with Quarto, you should specify the <code>docusaurus-md</code> format as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Blog Post" format: docusaurus-md ---</code></pre> <h6 id="configuration">Configuration</h6> <p>While Quarto works well within a Docusaurus site that has no <code>_quarto.yml</code> project config file, you can add one if you want to customize the default behavior, add a bibliography, etc. For example, here is what a simple customized <code>_quarto.yml</code> file might look like:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: docusaurus format: docusaurus-md: code-fold: true execute: warning: false bibliography: references.bib</code></pre> <p>It’s important to note that if you do provide an explicit <code>_quarto.yml</code> file you need to explicitly specify the project type (<code>type: docusaurus</code>) as shown above.</p> <h6 id="external-directory">External Directory</h6> <p>You might decide that you prefer to keep all of your Quarto documents and/or notebooks in their own directory, separate from the Docusaurus website. In this configuration you would mirror the directory structure of your site in the Quarto directory, and then set the <code>output-dir</code> in the project file to point to the Docusaurus directory. For example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: docusaurus output-dir: ../docusaurus-site</code></pre> <h5 id="code-blocks-6">Code Blocks</h5> <p>Code blocks in Docusaurus are very similar to Quarto. One important thing to keep in mind is that the syntax highlighting theme comes from Docusaurus rather than Quarto. See the <a href="https://docusaurus.io/docs/markdown-features/code-blocks#theming">theming</a> documentation for additional details.</p> <p>If you use the <code>filename</code> attribute in Quarto, it will automatically become the code block <code>title</code> in Docusaurus:</p> <pre><code>```{.python filename="hello.py"} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Code folding is also automatically applied. So, for example the following executable code block:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| code-fold: true 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Is rendered as a collasable block in Docusaurus:</p> <h5 id="callouts-tabsets">Callouts & Tabsets</h5> <p>Like Quarto, Docusaurus includes support for Callouts and Tabsets. When including these components in a document, you should use the Quarto standard markdown syntax, which will be automatically translated to the appropriate Docusaurus constructs.</p> <p>For example, here is a Quarto callout:</p> <pre><code>::: {.callout-important} Note the Quarto callout syntax is used here. :::</code></pre> <p>Which renders in Docusaurus as:</p> <p>Here is a Quarto tabset:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset group="fruits"} ## Apple This is an apple 🍎 ## Orange This is an orange 🍊 ## Banana This is a banana 🍌 :::</code></pre> <p>Which renders in Docusaurus as:</p> <h5 id="html-and-mdx">HTML and MDX</h5> <p>Docusaurus websites use a flavor of markdown (<a href="https://mdxjs.com/">MDX</a>) that has some major differences from Pandoc (Quarto’s native markdown renderer), the biggest of which is that while Quarto allows embedding of HTML, MDX does not. Rather, MDX allows direct embedding of JavaScript code and React JSX components (which look like HTML but have some significant differences in behavior).</p> <p>Quarto’s support for Docusaurus accounts for these differences, and enables you to embed raw HTML as well as use MDX components and JavaScript when required.</p> <h6 id="html-blocks">HTML Blocks</h6> <p>Docusaurus websites don’t allow arbitrary HTML content. Rather, JSX is used to emit HTML tags. While these JSX tags look and act like HTML tags most of the time, there are some important caveats and constraints, most notably that the <code>class</code> attribute must be written as <code>className</code>, and <code>style</code> attributes need to be specified as JavaScript objects rather than CSS strings.</p> <p>If you need to include raw HTML that doesn’t conform to JSX, you should use a raw ```<code>{=html}</code> code block. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{=html} <p style="color: green;">Paragraph</p> ```</code></pre> <p>If you need to embed HTML code (e.g. a badge, video, or tweet) you should definitely use raw HTML blocks as shown above to avoid errors which will occur if JSX encounters tags it can’t parse.</p> <p>Note that HTML produced by computations (e.g. a Pandas data frame displayed in a notebook) often use raw HTML with <code>class</code> and/or <code>style</code> tags. This computational output is automatically included in a raw ```<code>{=html}</code> code block so that it renders correctly in Docusaurus.</p> <h6 id="mdx-blocks">MDX Blocks</h6> <p>You can also use MDX components and JavaScript within Quarto documents that target Docusaurus. To do this, enclose them in an ```<code>{=mdx}</code> raw code block. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{=mdx} export const Highlight = ({children, color}) => ( <span style={{ backgroundColor: color, borderRadius: '2px', color: '#fff', padding: '0.2rem', }}> {children} </span> ); <Highlight color="#25c2a0">Docusaurus GREEN</Highlight> and <Highlight color="#1877F2">Rams blue</Highlight> are my favorite colors. I can write **Markdown** alongside my _JSX_! ```</code></pre> <p>Which is rendered as follows:</p> <p>Note that ordinary markdown content can also be included in <code>mdx</code> blocks alonside JavaScript and React components.</p> <h5 id="latex-math">LaTeX Math</h5> <p>By default, Quarto renders LaTeX math within Docusaurus projects using <a href="https://github.com/KTHse/webtex">WebTeX</a>, a service that creates PNG images for publishing on the web given TeX expressions as input.</p> <p>WebTeX works for any web page that can display images, and requires no special JavaScript or CSS. Any inline or display equations contained within your document will be converted to an image URL that requests a rendered version of the equation. For example, the following markdown:</p> <pre><code>$x + 1$</code></pre> <p>Will be converted to:</p> <pre><code>![](https://latex.codecogs.com/svg.latex?x%20%2B%201)</code></pre> <p>Which renders as:</p> <h6 id="dark-mode">Dark Mode</h6> <p>SVG is used as the default rendering method because it has the best overall appearance. However, if your <code>docusaurus</code> document is being rendered on a dark background, you may want to switch to PNG with a dark background specified. You can do this as follows:</p> <pre><code>format: docusaurus: html-math-method: method: webtex url: [latex.codecogs.com](https://latex.codecogs.com/png.image?%5Cbg_black&space);</code></pre> <h6 id="katex">KaTeX</h6> <p>It is possible to configure Docusaurus to use KaTeX for math rendering. See the Docusaurus documentation on <a href="https://docusaurus.io/docs/markdown-features/math-equations">using KaTeX</a> to learn more about this option.</p> <p>Once you’ve confirmed that KaTeX is rendering equations correctly in your site, you should update your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file to specify that <code>katex</code> rather than <code>webtex</code> should be used for rendering equations:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: docusaurus-md: html-math-method: katex</code></pre> <h3 id="github-gfm">GitHub (GFM)</h3> <h4 id="github-gfm-1">GitHub (GFM)</h4> <h5 id="overview-82">Overview</h5> <p>While markdown is the input format for Quarto, it can also in some cases be an output format (for example, if you have a website or CMS that accepts markdown as input and want to incorporate computations from Python or R).</p> <p>This article covers using Quarto to generate <a href="https://github.github.com/gfm/">GitHub Flavored Markdown</a> (GFM). You might want to do this in order to:</p> <ul> <li>Generate a GitHub README.md from a Jupyter notebook</li> <li>Create pages for a GitHub wiki that include computations (e.g. plot output).</li> </ul> <h5 id="gfm-format-1">GFM Format</h5> <p>Use the <code>gfm</code> format to create GitHub Flavored Markdown from Quarto. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Project" format: gfm ---</code></pre> <p>See the GFM format reference for a complete list of all options available for GFM output.</p> <p>To create a <code>README.md</code> using Quarto, start with a notebook (.ipynb) or computational markdown file (.qmd) that has README as its file name stem, for example:</p> <pre><code>README.qmd --- title: "My Project" format: gfm jupyter: python3 --- This is a GitHub README that has content dynamically generated from Python: ```{python} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Render the README with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render README.qmd</code></pre> <p>Which will create <code>README.md</code> alongside your input file.</p> <h5 id="preview-mode">Preview Mode</h5> <p>When you <code>quarto preview</code> a GitHub Flavored Markdown document, by default an HTML preview that approximates the look of markdown rendered on GitHub is shown. If you’d prefer to see the raw generated markdown, use the <code>preview-mode: raw</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Project" format: gfm: preview-mode: raw ---</code></pre> <h5 id="webtex-math">WebTeX Math</h5> <p>The <code>gfm</code> format renders LaTeX equations using standard dollar-delimited inline (<code>\$...\$</code>) and display (<code>\$\$...\$\$</code>) syntax. However, if the web environment you are publishing into doesn’t support dollar-delimited math, you can alternatively use <a href="https://github.com/KTHse/webtex">WebTeX</a> to display math. This is done by setting the Pandoc <code>html-math-method</code> to <code>webtex</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: gfm: html-math-method: webtex</code></pre> <p>WebTeX works for any web page that can display images, and requires no special JavaScript or CSS. Any inline or display equations contained within your document will be converted to an image URL that requests a rendered version of the equation. For example, the following markdown:</p> <pre><code>$x + 1$</code></pre> <p>Will be converted to:</p> <pre><code>![](https://latex.codecogs.com/svg.latex?x%20%2B%201)</code></pre> <p>Which renders as:</p> <h6 id="dark-mode-1">Dark Mode</h6> <p>SVG is used as the default rendering method because it has the best overall appearance. However, if your <code>gfm</code> document is being rendered on a dark background, you may want to switch to PNG with a dark background specified. You can do this as follows:</p> <pre><code>format: gfm: html-math-method: method: webtex url: [latex.codecogs.com](https://latex.codecogs.com/png.image?%5Cbg_black&space);</code></pre> <h5 id="github-wikis">GitHub Wikis</h5> <p>If you want to use Quarto to incorporate computations into a GitHub wiki start by <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/adding-or-editing-wiki-pages#adding-or-editing-wiki-pages-locally">cloning the wiki for local editing</a>.</p> <p>Then, simply create a computational markdown file (.ipynb, .qmd) for each page in the wiki. You can render all of these files at once into their corresponding .md files using Quarto Projects. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>You don’t even strictly need a Quarto project file to do this as <code>quarto render</code> will render all input files in a directory by default if there is no project file.</p> <h3 id="html-accessibility-checks">HTML Accessibility Checks</h3> <h4 id="html-accessibility-checks-1">HTML Accessibility Checks</h4> <p>Quarto includes integrated support for <a href="https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core"><code>axe-core</code></a>, a broadly-supported, open source, industry standard tool for accessibility checks in HTML documents.</p> <h5 id="interactive-accessibility-checks">Interactive accessibility checks</h5> <p>To enable the simplest form of accessibility checks, add the <code>axe</code> YAML metadata configuration to HTML <code>format</code>s (<code>html</code>, <code>dashboard</code>, and <code>revealjs</code>):</p> <pre><code>format: html: axe: true</code></pre> <p>Render and open the document in a browser. Accessibility violations will be visible as console messages in your browser’s development tools.</p> <p>For example, this document contains a color contrast violation:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Testing Quarto's accessibility checker format: html: axe: true --- This violates contrast rules: [insufficient contrast.]{style="color: #eee"}. --- title: Testing Quarto's accessibility checker format: html: axe: true --- This violates contrast rules: [insufficient contrast.]{style="color: #111"}.</code></pre> <p>Previewing the rendered page and opening the browser’s developer tools shows the violation <code>axe-core</code> found:</p> <p>The rendered webpage with the developer tools console open</p> <p>The rendered webpage with the developer tools console open</p> <h6 id="output-location">Output location</h6> <p>Quarto supports three output formats for the accessibility checks, available through the <code>output</code> option.</p> <ul> <li><p><code>document</code>: embedded reports</p> <p>format: html: axe: output: document</p></li> <li><p>With this option, Quarto will generate a visible report of <code>axe-core</code> violations on the webpage itself. Each violation displays its WCAG conformance level (e.g., <code>WCAG 2.0 AA</code>), so best-practice findings are distinguishable from genuine WCAG failures. This is useful for visual inspection of a page. Note that with this setting, Quarto will always produce a report.</p></li> <li><p>If you wish to use this feature, we recommend adding it to a “debug” project profile to reduce the chance you will accidentally publish a website to production with these reports.</p></li> <li><p><code>json</code>: JSON-formatted console output</p> <p>format: html: axe: output: json</p></li> <li><p>This option is useful if you’re comfortable with browser automation tools such as <a href="https://pptr.dev/">Puppeteer</a> and <a href="https://playwright.dev/">Playwright</a>, since it produces output to the console in a format that can be easily consumed.</p></li> <li><p>Specifically, the JSON object produced is the result of running <code>axe-core</code>’s <code>run</code> method on the webpage. We defer to <code>axe-core</code>’s <a href="https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core">documentation for full information on that object</a>.</p></li> <li><p><code>console</code></p> <p>format: html: axe: output: console</p></li> <li><p>This option is equivalent to <code>axe: true</code>. For the example above, <code>output: document</code> places the report on the page itself:</p></li> </ul> <p>The rendered webpage with an accessibility violation warning</p> <p>The rendered webpage with an accessibility violation warning</p> <h6 id="checking-against-a-wcag-conformance-level">Checking against a WCAG conformance level</h6> <p>By default, <code>axe-core</code> runs its full default rule set, which combines rules for several WCAG versions and levels with axe’s own “best practice” rules. If you are working toward a specific WCAG conformance level, use the <code>standard</code> option to check only the rules for that level:</p> <pre><code>format: html: axe: standard: wcag21aa</code></pre> <p>The available values name a WCAG version followed by a level: <code>wcag2a</code>, <code>wcag2aa</code>, <code>wcag2aaa</code>, <code>wcag21a</code>, <code>wcag21aa</code>, <code>wcag21aaa</code>, <code>wcag22a</code>, <code>wcag22aa</code>, and <code>wcag22aaa</code>. Each standard is cumulative — it includes the rules for the lower levels and earlier versions it builds on. For example, <code>standard: wcag21aa</code> checks the rules for WCAG 2.0 A, 2.0 AA, 2.1 A, and 2.1 AA.</p> <p>For the full list of rules, grouped by these same WCAG versions and levels, see <code>axe-core</code>’s <a href="https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/doc/rule-descriptions.md">rule descriptions</a>.</p> <p>When you specify <code>standard</code> Axe’s best-practice rules are excluded. To check them alongside a standard, add <code>best-practice: true</code>:</p> <pre><code>format: html: axe: standard: wcag21aa best-practice: true</code></pre> <p>You can also exclude the best-practice rules without choosing a standard by setting <code>best-practice: false</code> on its own.</p> <h5 id="site-wide-accessibility-checks">Site-wide accessibility checks</h5> <p>The checks above are interactive: they require opening each page in a local preview and inspecting the results in the browser.</p> <p>In the future, we envision a mode where every page of a website can be checked at the time of <code>quarto render</code> or <code>quarto publish</code> in order to reduce the amount of required manual intervention.</p> <h3 id="html-basics">HTML Basics</h3> <h4 id="html-basics-1">HTML Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-83">Overview</h5> <p>Use the <code>html</code> format to create HTML output. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My document" format: html: toc: true html-math-method: katex css: styles.css ---</code></pre> <p>This example highlights a few of the options available for HTML output. This document covers these and other options in detail. See the HTML format reference for a complete list of all available options.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-1">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Use the <code>toc</code> option to include an automatically generated table of contents in the output document. Use the <code>toc-depth</code> option to specify the number of section levels to include in the table of contents. The default is 3 (which means that level-1, 2, and 3 headings will be listed in the contents). For example:</p> <pre><code>toc: true toc-depth: 2</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>toc-expand</code> option to specify how much of the table of contents to show initially (defaults to 1 with auto-expansion as the user scrolls). Use <code>true</code> to expand all or <code>false</code> to collapse all.</p> <pre><code>toc: true toc-expand: 2</code></pre> <p>You can customize the title used for the table of contents using the <code>toc-title</code> option:</p> <pre><code>toc-title: Contents</code></pre> <p>If you want to exclude a heading from the table of contents, add both the <code>.unnumbered</code> and <code>.unlisted</code> classes to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered .unlisted}</code></pre> <p>The HTML format by default floats the table of contents to the right. You can alternatively position it at the <code>left</code>, or in the <code>body</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: toc: true toc-location: left</code></pre> <p>If you would like to display a table of contents both in the body and floating left or right, you can specify <code>left-body</code> or <code>right-body</code> respectively.</p> <p>The floating table of contents can be used to navigate to sections of the document and also will automatically highlight the appropriate section as the user scrolls. The table of contents is responsive and will become hidden once the viewport becomes too narrow. See an example on the right of this page.</p> <p>Note that the <code>toc-location</code> option is not available when you disable the standard HTML theme (e.g. if you specify the <code>theme: none</code> or <code>theme: pandoc</code> option).</p> <h5 id="section-numbering">Section Numbering</h5> <p>Use the <code>number-sections</code> option to number section headings in the output document. For example:</p> <pre><code>number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>number-depth</code> option to specify the deepest level of heading to add numbers to (by default all headings are numbered). For example:</p> <pre><code>number-depth: 3</code></pre> <p>To exclude an individual heading from numbering, add the <code>.unnumbered</code> class to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered}</code></pre> <h5 id="code-links-and-other-links">Code Links and Other Links</h5> <p>Use <code>code-links</code> and <code>other-links</code> to add links that will appear in the page navigation under the headings “Code Links” and “Other Links” respectively.
