For example, consider the following document YAML header:</p> <pre><code>--- format: html: other-links: - text: NASA Open Data href: [data.nasa.gov](https://data.nasa.gov/) code-links: - text: Data Import Code icon: file-code href: data-import.py ---</code></pre> <p>When rendered this results in:</p> <p>You can provide the following options for items in <code>code-links</code> and <code>other-links</code>:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>text</code></p> <p>The text to be displayed for the link.</p> <p><code>href</code></p> <p>The URL for the link.</p> <p><code>icon</code></p> <p>The <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com/">bootstrap icon</a> for the link.</p> <p><code>rel</code></p> <p>The rel used in the <code>a</code> tag for this link.</p> <p><code>target</code></p> <p>The target used in the <code>a</code> tag for this link.</p> <h6 id="github-and-binder-links-1">GitHub and Binder Links</h6> <p>For projects there are also two special values you can pass as items to <code>code-links</code>:</p> <p><code>repo</code></p> <p>Add a link to “GitHub Repo” under “Code Links” that points at the GitHub repository of your project.</p> <p><code>binder</code></p> <p>Add a link to “Launch Binder” under “Code Links” if your project is configured to Use Binder.</p> <h5 id="css-styles">CSS Styles</h5> <p>To add a CSS stylesheet to your document, just provide the <code>css</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: css: styles.css</code></pre> <p>Using the <code>css</code> option works well for simple tweaks to document appearance. If you want to do more extensive customization see the documentation on HTML Themes.</p> <h5 id="latex-equations">LaTeX Equations</h5> <p>By default, LaTeX equations are rendered using <a href="https://www.mathjax.org/">MathJax</a>. Use the <code>html-math-method</code> option to choose another method. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: html-math-method: katex</code></pre> <p>You can also specify a <code>url</code> for the library to load for a given method:</p> <pre><code>html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "[cdn.jsdelivr.net](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js)"</code></pre> <p>Available math rendering methods include:</p> <p>Method</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>mathjax</code></p> <p>Use <a href="https://www.mathjax.org/">MathJax</a> to display embedded TeX math in HTML output. The default configuration for <a href="https://docs.mathjax.org/">MathJax</a> is <a href="https://docs.mathjax.org/en/latest/web/components/combined.html?highlight=tex-chtml-full.js#tex-chtml-full"><code>tex-chtml-full.js</code></a> which loads all <a href="https://docs.mathjax.org/en/latest/input/tex/extensions.html">MathJax’s extensions</a> except <code>colorv2</code> and <code>physics</code> (available using <code>\require{physics}</code>).</p> <p><code>katex</code></p> <p>Use <a href="https://github.com/Khan/KaTeX">KaTeX</a> to display embedded TeX math in HTML output.</p> <p><code>webtex</code></p> <p>Convert TeX formulas to <code><img></code> tags that link to an external script that converts formulas to images.</p> <p><code>gladtex</code></p> <p>Enclose TeX math in <code><eq></code> tags in HTML output. The resulting HTML can then be processed by <a href="https://humenda.github.io/GladTeX/">GladTeX</a> to produce images of the typeset formulas and an HTML file with links to these images.</p> <p><code>mathml</code></p> <p>Convert TeX math to <a href="https://www.w3.org/Math/">MathML</a>.</p> <p><code>plain</code></p> <p>No special processing (formulas are put inside a <code>span</code> with <code>class="math").</code></p> <p>Note that there is more detailed documentation on each of these options in the Pandoc <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#math-rendering-in-html">Math Rendering in HTML</a> documentation.</p> <h5 id="tabsets-2">Tabsets</h5> <p>You can use tabsets to present content that will vary in interest depending on the audience. For example, here we provide some example code in a variety of languages:</p> <ul> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>Java</p></li> <li><p>Julia</p> <p>fizz_buzz <- function(fbnums = 1:50) { output <- dplyr::case_when( fbnums %% 15 == 0 ~ “FizzBuzz”, fbnums %% 3 == 0 ~ “Fizz”, fbnums %% 5 == 0 ~ “Buzz”, TRUE ~ as.character(fbnums) ) print(output) }</p> <p>def fizz_buzz(num): if num % 15 == 0: print(“FizzBuzz”) elif num % 5 == 0: print(“Buzz”) elif num % 3 == 0: print(“Fizz”) else: print(num)</p> <p>public class FizzBuzz { public static void fizzBuzz(int num) { if (num % 15 == 0) { System.out.println(“FizzBuzz”); } else if (num % 5 == 0) { System.out.println(“Buzz”); } else if (num % 3 == 0) { System.out.println(“Fizz”); } else { System.out.println(num); } } }</p> <p>function FizzBuzz(num) if num % 15 == 0 println(“FizzBuzz”) elseif num % 5 == 0 println(“Buzz”) elseif num % 3 == 0 println(“Fizz”) else println(num) end end</p></li> </ul> <p>Create a tabset via a markdown div with the class name panel-tabset (e.g. <code>::: {.panel-tabset}</code>). Each top-level heading within the div creates a new tab. For example, here is the markdown used to implement the first two tabs displayed above:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ``` {.r} fizz_buzz <- function(fbnums = 1:50) { output <- dplyr::case_when( fbnums %% 15 == 0 ~ "FizzBuzz", fbnums %% 3 == 0 ~ "Fizz", fbnums %% 5 == 0 ~ "Buzz", TRUE ~ as.character(fbnums) ) print(output) } ``` ## Python ``` {.python} def fizz_buzz(num): if num % 15 == 0: print("FizzBuzz") elif num % 5 == 0: print("Buzz") elif num % 3 == 0: print("Fizz") else: print(num) ``` :::</code></pre> <h6 id="tabset-groups">Tabset Groups</h6> <p>If you have multiple tabsets that include the same tab names, you can define a tabset <code>group</code>. Tabs within a <code>group</code> are all switched together (so in the example above once a reader switches to R or Python in one tabset the others will follow along). For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R Tab content ## Python Tab content :::</code></pre> <h6 id="active-tabset">Active Tabset</h6> <p>By default the first tab in the tabset will be active when a page loads. To have a different tab active on page load, add the <code>.active</code> class to the tab heading. For example, here the “Python” tab will be active on page load:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset} ## R Tab content ## Python {.active} Tab content :::</code></pre> <h5 id="self-contained">Self Contained</h5> <p>HTML documents typically have a number of external dependencies (e.g. images, CSS style sheets, JavaScript, etc.). By default these dependencies are placed in a <code>_files</code> directory alongside your document. For example, if you render <code>report.qmd</code> to HTML:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render report.qmd --to html</code></pre> <p>Then the following output is produced:</p> <pre><code>report.html report_files/</code></pre> <p>You might alternatively want to create an entirely self-contained HTML document (with images, CSS style sheets, JavaScript, etc. embedded into the HTML file). You can do this by specifying the <code>embed-resources</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: html: embed-resources: true</code></pre> <p>This will produce a standalone HTML file with no external dependencies, using <code>data:</code> URIs to incorporate the contents of linked scripts, style sheets, images, and videos. The resulting file should be self contained, in the sense that it needs no external files and no net access to be displayed properly by a browser.</p> <h5 id="anchor-sections">Anchor Sections</h5> <p>Hover over a section title to see an anchor link. Enable/disable this behavior with:</p> <pre><code>format: html: anchor-sections: true</code></pre> <p>Anchor links are also automatically added to figures and tables that have a cross reference defined.</p> <h5 id="smooth-scrolling">Smooth Scrolling</h5> <p>Enable smooth scrolling within the page. By default, smooth scroll is not enabled. Enable/disable it with:</p> <pre><code>format: html: smooth-scroll: true</code></pre> <h5 id="external-links">External Links</h5> <p>By default external links (i.e. links that don’t target the current site) receive no special visual adornment or navigation treatment (the current page is navigated). You can use the following options to modify this behavior:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>link-external-icon</code></p> <p><code>true</code> to show an icon next to the link to indicate that it’s external (e.g., external).</p> <p><code>link-external-newwindow</code></p> <p><code>true</code> to open external links in a new browser window or tab (rather than navigating the current tab).</p> <p><code>link-external-filter</code></p> <p>A regular expression that can be used to determine whether a link is an internal link. For example</p> <p><code>^(?:http:|https:)\/\/www\.quarto\.org\/custom</code></p> <p>will treat links that start with <code>http://www.quarto.org/custom</code> or <code>https://www.quarto.org/custom</code> as internal links (and others will be considered external).</p> <p>External links are identified either using the <code>site-url</code> (if provided) or using the <code>window.host</code> if no <code>site-url</code> or <code>link-external-filter</code> is provided. For example, here we enable both options and a custom filter:</p> <pre><code>format: html: link-external-icon: true link-external-newwindow: true link-external-filter: '^(?:http:|https:)\/\/www\.quarto\.org\/custom'</code></pre> <p>You can also specify one or both of these behaviors for an individual link using the <code>.external</code> class and <code>target</code> attribute. For example:</p> <pre><code>[example](https://example.com){.external target="_blank"}</code></pre> <h5 id="reference-popups">Reference Popups</h5> <p>If you hover your mouse over the citation, footnote and cross-reference in this sentence you’ll see a popup displaying the reference contents:</p> <p>Hover over Xie (2015) to see a reference to the definitive book on knitr1. Listing 1 shows you how to disable hover behaviour.</p> <p>This behavior is enabled by default. You can disable it with the following options:</p> <p>Listing 1</p> <pre><code>format: html: citations-hover: false footnotes-hover: false crossrefs-hover: false</code></pre> <h5 id="commenting-1">Commenting</h5> <p>This page has commenting with <a href="https://web.hypothes.is/">Hypothes.is</a> enabled via the following YAML option:</p> <pre><code>comments: hypothesis: true</code></pre> <p>You can see the Hypothesis UI at the far right of the page. Rather than <code>true</code>, you can specify any of the available Hypothesis embedding options as a sub-key of <code>hypothesis</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>comments: hypothesis: theme: clean</code></pre> <p>You can enable <a href="https://utteranc.es/">Utterances</a> commenting using the <code>utterances</code> option. Here you need to specify at least the GitHub repo you want to use for storing comments:</p> <pre><code>comments: utterances: repo: quarto-dev/quarto-docs</code></pre> <p>You can also specify the other options documented here.</p> <p>You may also enable <a href="https://giscus.app">Giscus</a> for commenting using the <code>giscus</code> option. Giscus will store comments in the ‘Discussions’ of a Github repo.</p> <pre><code>comments: giscus: repo: quarto-dev/quarto-docs</code></pre> <p>Like utterances, you need to specify at least the Git repo you want to use for storing comments. In addition, the repo that you use must:</p> <ul> <li>Be public</li> <li>Have the Giscus app installed.</li> <li>Have discussion enabled Review the <a href="https://giscus.app">Giscus documentation</a> for instructions on setting up Giscus in your repository. Additional options are covered here.</li> </ul> <h6 id="disabling-comments">Disabling Comments</h6> <p>If you have comments enabled for an entire website or book, you can selectively disable comments for a single page by specifying <code>comments: false</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "Home Page" comments: false</code></pre> <h5 id="includes-3">Includes</h5> <p>If you want to include additional content in your document from another file, you can use the <code>include-in-*</code> options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>include-in-header</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the header. This can be used, for example, to include special CSS or JavaScript in HTML documents or to inject commands into the LaTeX preamble.</p> <p><code>include-before-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the beginning of the document body (e.g. after the <code><body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\begin{document}</code> command in LaTeX). This can be used to include navigation bars or banners in HTML documents.</p> <p><code>include-after-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the document body (before the <code></body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\end{document}</code> command in LaTeX).</p> <p>You can specify a single file or multiple files for each of these options directly, or use the <code>file:</code> subkey. To include raw content in the YAML header, use the <code>text</code> subkey. When using <code>text:</code>, add the <code>|</code> character after <code>text:</code> to indicate that the value is a multi-line string. If you omit <code>file:</code> or <code>text:</code>, Quarto assumes you are providing a file.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: include-in-header: - text: | <script src="[examples.org](https://examples.org/demo.js)"></script> - file: analytics.html - comments.html include-before-body: header.html</code></pre> <h5 id="minimal-html">Minimal HTML</h5> <p>The default Quarto HTML output format includes several features by default, including bootstrap themes, anchor sections, reference popups, tabsets, code block copying, and responsive figures. You can disable all of these built in features at once using the <code>minimal</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html: minimal: true ---</code></pre> <p>When specifying <code>minimal: true</code> you can still selectively re-enable features you do want, for example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: html: minimal: true code-copy: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="external-servers-1">External servers</h5> <p>Quarto is designed to minimize external dependencies. However, on occasion, Quarto documents might need resources hosted in external servers. See our page on External Sources for a full list.</p> <h5 id="references-4">References</h5> <p>Xie, Yihui. 2015. Dynamic Documents with R and Knitr. 2nd ed. Chapman; Hall/CRC. <a href="https://yihui.name/knitr/">yihui.name</a>.</p> <h5 id="footnotes-9">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>knitr is an R package for creating dynamic documents.↩︎</li> </ul> <h3 id="html-code-blocks">HTML Code Blocks</h3> <h4 id="html-code-blocks-1">HTML Code Blocks</h4> <ul> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Show All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">Hide All Code</a></li> <li><a href="javascript:void(0)">View Source</a></li> </ul> <h5 id="overview-84">Overview</h5> <p>There are wide variety of options available to customize the display of source code within HTML documents, including:</p> <ul> <li>Hiding some or all code that was executed by <a href="https://yihui.name/knitr">Knitr</a> or <a href="https://jupyter.org">Jupyter</a>.</li> <li>Code folding for executed code (hidden by default and expandable by readers).</li> <li>Handling code that overflows the available horizontal display space.</li> <li>View the source code of the markdown file used to generate the document.</li> <li>Syntax highlighting themes and other options to control the appearance of code.</li> <li>Copy to clipboard button for code blocks.</li> <li>Generating hyperlinks to online documentation for functions used within code blocks via the <a href="https://downlit.r-lib.org/">downlit</a> package (note that this option currently only works when using the Knitr engine). Details on using all of these options are provided below.</li> </ul> <h5 id="hiding-code">Hiding Code</h5> <p>For many documents you may want to hide all of the executable source code used to produce dynamic outputs. You can do this by specifying <code>echo: false</code> in the document <code>execute</code> options. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" execute: echo: false jupyter: python3 ---</code></pre> <p>Note that we can override this option on a per code-block basis. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| echo: true import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot([1,2,3,4]) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Code block options are included in a special comment at the top of the block (lines at the top prefaced with <code>#|</code> are considered options).</p> <h5 id="folding-code">Folding Code</h5> <p>Use the <code>code-fold</code> option to include code but have it hidden by default using the HTML <code><details></code> tag. For example, click the Code button to see the code that produced this plot.</p> <p>Code</p> <pre><code>library(ggplot2) dat <- data.frame(cond = rep(c("A", "B"), each=10), xvar = 1:20 + rnorm(20,sd=3), yvar = 1:20 + rnorm(20,sd=3)) ggplot(dat, aes(x=xvar, y=yvar)) + geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth()</code></pre> <p>Here we specify both <code>code-fold: true</code> as well as custom summary text (the default is just “Code” as shown above):</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-fold: true code-summary: "Show the code"</code></pre> <p>Valid values for <code>code-fold</code> include:</p> <p>Value</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>false</code></p> <p>No folding (default)</p> <p><code>true</code></p> <p>Fold code (initially hidden)</p> <p><code>show</code></p> <p>Fold code (initially shown)</p> <p>Use the <code>code-fold</code> and <code>code-summary</code> chunk attributes to control this on a chunk-by-chunk basis:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| code-fold: true #| code-summary: "Show the code" ```</code></pre> <h5 id="code-overflow">Code Overflow</h5> <p>In some cases the width of source code will overflow the available horizontal display space. By default, this will result in a horizontal scroll bar for the code block. However if you prefer not to have scrollbars you can have the longer lines wrap instead.</p> <p>To set the global default behavior use the <code>code-overflow</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-overflow: wrap</code></pre> <p>Valid values for <code>code-overflow</code> are:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>scroll</code></p> <p>Scroll code blocks that exceed available width (default, corresponds to <code>white-space: pre</code>).</p> <p><code>wrap</code></p> <p>Wrap lines of code that exceed available width (corresponds to <code>white-space: pre-wrap</code>).</p> <p>You can also override the global default on a per-code-block basis. For computational cells you do this with the <code>code-overflow</code> cell option:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| code-overflow: wrap # very long line of code.... ```</code></pre> <p>For a static code block, add the <code>.code-overflow-scroll</code> or <code>.code-overflow-wrap</code> CSS class:</p> <pre><code>```{.python .code-overflow-wrap} # very long line of code.... ```</code></pre> <p>Note that irrespective of these options, code will always wrap within printed HTML output (as it would otherwise be clipped off the edge of the page).</p> <h5 id="code-tools">Code Tools</h5> <p>You can include a Code menu in the header of your document that provides various tools for readers to interact with the source code. Specify <code>code-tools: true</code> to activate these tools:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-fold: true code-tools: true</code></pre> <p>If you have a document that includes folded code blocks then the Code menu will present options to show and hide the folded code as well as view the full source code of the document:</p> <p>This document specifies <code>code-tools: true</code> in its options so you should see the Code menu above next to the main header.</p> <p>You can control which of these options are made available as well as the “Code” caption text using sub-options of <code>code-tools</code>. For example, here we specify that we want only “View Source” (no toggling of code visibility) and no caption on the code menu:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-tools: source: true toggle: false caption: none</code></pre> <p>By default, the source code is embedded in the document and shown in a popup window like this:</p> <p>You can alternatively specify a URL for the value of <code>source</code>:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-tools: source: [github.com](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/blob/main/index.md)</code></pre> <p>If you are within a project and have specified a <code>repo-url</code> option then you can just use <code>repo</code> and the correct link to your source file will be generated:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-tools: source: repo</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>code-tools</code> option is not available when you disable the standard HTML theme (e.g. if you specify the <code>theme: none</code> option).</p> <h5 id="appearance-1">Appearance</h5> <p>By default code blocks are rendered with a left border whose color is derived from the current theme. You can customize code chunk appearance with some simple options that control the background color and left border. Options can either be booleans to enable or disable the treatment or can be legal CSS color strings (or they could even be SASS variable names!).</p> <p>Here is the default appearance for code blocks (<code>code-block-bg: true</code>):</p> <p>You can instead use a left border treatment using the <code>code-block-border-left</code> option:</p> <pre><code>code-block-border-left: true</code></pre> <p>You can combine a background and border treatment as well as customize the left border color:</p> <pre><code>code-block-bg: true code-block-border-left: "#31BAE9"</code></pre> <h5 id="code-filename">Code Filename</h5> <p>Use the <code>filename</code> attribute on code blocks If you are documenting the contents of a file and want to be especially clear about the name of the file the code is associated with.</p> <p>For example, the following code:</p> <pre><code>```{.python filename="matplotlib.py"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot([1,23,2,4]) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Results in this HTML output:</p> <pre><code>matplotlib.py import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot([1,23,2,4]) plt.show()</code></pre> <p>Non-HTML formats will still have the filename, but it will simply be shown in bold above the code block.</p> <h5 id="highlighting">Highlighting</h5> <p>Pandoc will automatically highlight syntax in <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#fenced-code-blocks">fenced code blocks</a> that are marked with a language name. For example:</p> <pre><code>```python 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Pandoc can provide syntax highlighting for over 140 different languages (see the output of <code>quarto pandoc --list-highlight-languages</code> for a list of all of them). If you want to provide the appearance of a highlighted code block for a language not supported, just use <code>default</code> as the language name.</p> <p>You can specify the code highlighting style using <code>syntax-highlighting</code> and specifying one of the supported themes. These themes are “adaptive”, which means they will automatically switch between a dark and light mode based upon the theme of the website. These are designed to work well with sites that include a dark and light mode.</p> <ul> <li><p>a11y</p></li> <li><p>arrow</p></li> <li><p>atom-one</p></li> <li><p>ayu</p></li> <li><p>breeze</p></li> <li><p>github</p></li> <li><p>gruvbox All of the standard Pandoc themes are also available:</p></li> <li><p>pygments</p></li> <li><p>tango</p></li> <li><p>espresso</p></li> <li><p>zenburn</p></li> <li><p>kate</p></li> <li><p>monochrome</p></li> <li><p>breezedark</p></li> <li><p>haddock As well as an additional set of extended themes, including:</p></li> <li><p>dracula</p></li> <li><p>monokai</p></li> <li><p>nord</p></li> <li><p>oblivion</p></li> <li><p>printing</p></li> <li><p>radical</p></li> <li><p>solarized</p></li> <li><p>vim-dark The <code>syntax-highlighting</code> option determines which theme is used. For example:</p> <p>syntax-highlighting: github</p></li> </ul> <p>Highlighting themes can provide either a single highlighting definition or two definitions, one optimized for a light colored background and another optimized for a dark color background. When available, Quarto will automatically select the appropriate style based upon the code chunk background color’s darkness. Users may always opt to specify the full name (e.g. <code>atom-one-dark</code>) to by pass this automatic behavior.</p> <p>By default, code is highlighted using the <code>arrow</code> theme, which is optimized for accessibility. We’ve additionally introduced the <code>arrow-dark</code> theme which is designed to provide accessible highlighting against dark backgrounds.</p> <p>Examples of the light and dark themes:</p> <h6 id="arrow-light">Arrow (light)</h6> <h6 id="arrow-dark">Arrow (dark)</h6> <h6 id="ayu-light">Ayu (light)</h6> <h6 id="ayu-dark">Ayu (dark)</h6> <h6 id="custom-highlighting">Custom Highlighting</h6> <p>In addition to the built in themes available for syntax highlighting, you can also specify your own syntax highlighting by providing the path to a valid theme file (which is based upon the KDE XML syntax highlighting descriptions). Highlighting is implemented using <a href="https://github.com/jgm/skylighting">skylighting</a>.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>--- syntax-highlighting: custom.theme ---</code></pre> <p>In addition, if you’d like to provide adaptive themes, you may also pass both a light and dark theme file:</p> <pre><code>--- syntax-highlighting: light: custom-light.theme dark: custom-dark.theme ---</code></pre> <p>Note that as with adaptive text higlighting themes, when you provide a dark and light <code>syntax-highlighting</code>, background colors specified in the themes will be ignored in favor of the overall theme specified background colors.</p> <h5 id="code-annotation-4">Code Annotation</h5> <p>You can add annotations to lines of code in code blocks and executable code cells. See Code Annotation for full details.</p> <h5 id="line-numbers">Line Numbers</h5> <p>If you want to display line numbers alongside the code block, add the <code>code-line-numbers</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-line-numbers: true</code></pre> <p>Here’s how a code block with line numbers would display:</p> <pre><code>import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot([1,23,2,4]) plt.show()</code></pre> <p>You can also enable line numbers for an individual code block using the <code>code-line-numbers</code> attribute. For example:</p> <pre><code>``` {.python code-line-numbers="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot([1,23,2,4]) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <h5 id="executable-blocks">Executable Blocks</h5> <p>The documentation on computations covers how to include executable code blocks (code which is actually executed, with its output being included in the rendered document). We won’t additionally cover that here, but we will talk about how to include code blocks that demonstrate executable syntax (e.g. for writing a tutorial).</p> <p>Often you’ll want to include a fenced code block purely as documentation (not executable). You can do this by using two curly braces around the language (e.g. <code>python</code>, <code>r</code>, etc.) rather than one. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{{python}} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Will be output into the document as:</p> <pre><code>```{python} 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>If you want to show an example with multiple code blocks and other markdown, just enclose the entire example in 4 backticks (e.g. ``````) and use the two curly brace syntax for code blocks within. For example:</p> <pre><code>```` --- title: "My document" --- Some markdown content. ```{{python}} 1 + 1 ``` Some additional markdown content. ````</code></pre> <h5 id="copy-button">Copy Button</h5> <p>Hover over the code block below and you will see a copy icon in the top-right corner:</p> <pre><code>library(dygraphs) dygraph(nhtemp, main = "New Haven Temperatures") %>% dyRangeSelector(dateWindow = c("1920-01-01", "1960-01-01"))</code></pre> <p>This behavior is enabled by default but you configure it using the <code>code-copy</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-copy: false</code></pre> <p>Valid values for <code>code-copy</code> include:</p> <p><code>hover</code></p> <p>Show button on hover (default)</p> <p><code>true</code></p> <p>Always show code copy button</p> <p><code>false</code></p> <p>Never show code copy button</p> <h5 id="code-linking">Code Linking</h5> <p>The <code>code-link</code> option enables hyper-linking of functions within code blocks to their online documentation:</p> <pre><code>format: html: code-link: true</code></pre> <p>Code linking is currently implemented only for the knitr engine (via the <a href="https://downlit.r-lib.org">downlit</a> package). A limitation of downlit currently prevents code linking if <code>code-line-numbers</code> and/or <code>code-annotations</code> are also <code>true</code>.</p> <h3 id="html-theming">HTML Theming</h3> <h4 id="html-theming-1">HTML Theming</h4> <h5 id="overview-85">Overview</h5> <p>HTML documents rendered with Quarto use Bootstrap 5 by default. This can be disabled or customized via the <code>theme</code> option:</p> <pre><code>theme: default # bootstrap 5 default theme: cosmo # cosmo bootswatch theme theme: pandoc # pandoc default html treatment theme: none # no theme css added to document</code></pre> <p>Quarto includes 25 themes from the <a href="https://bootswatch.com/">Bootswatch</a> project (for example, this website uses the <a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a> theme). Available themes include:</p> <ul> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/default/">default</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cerulean/">cerulean</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cyborg/">cyborg</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/darkly/">darkly</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/flatly/">flatly</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/journal/">journal</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/litera/">litera</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lumen/">lumen</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lux/">lux</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/materia/">materia</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/minty/">minty</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/morph/">morph</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/pulse/">pulse</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/quartz/">quartz</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sandstone/">sandstone</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/simplex/">simplex</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sketchy/">sketchy</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/slate/">slate</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/solar/">solar</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/spacelab/">spacelab</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/superhero/">superhero</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/united/">united</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/vapor/">vapor</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/yeti/">yeti</a></p></li> <li><p><a href="https://bootswatch.com/zephyr/">zephyr</a> Use of any of these themes via the <code>theme</code> option. For example:</p> <p>format: html: theme: united</p></li> </ul> <p>You can also customize these themes or create your own new themes. Learn how to do this below in Theme Options.</p> <h5 id="basic-options">Basic Options</h5> <p>If you are using a Bootstrap theme or the Pandoc theme, there are a set of options you can provide in document metadata to customize its appearance. These include:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>max-width</code></p> <p>The maximum width occupied by page content. Defaults to 1400px for bootstrap themes and 36em for the pandoc theme.</p> <p><code>mainfont</code></p> <p>Sets the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/font-family"><code>font-family</code></a> property for the document.</p> <p><code>fontsize</code></p> <p>Sets the base CSS <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/font-size"><code>font-size</code></a> for the document.</p> <p><code>fontcolor</code></p> <p>Sets the default text <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color"><code>color</code></a> for the document.</p> <p><code>linkcolor</code></p> <p>Sets the default text <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color"><code>color</code></a> for hyperlinks.</p> <p><code>monofont</code></p> <p>Sets the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/font-family"><code>font-family</code></a> property for <code><code></code> elements.</p> <p><code>monobackgroundcolor</code></p> <p>Sets the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/background-color"><code>background-color</code></a> property for <code><code></code> elements.</p> <p><code>linestretch</code></p> <p>Sets the CSS <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/line-height"><code>line-height</code></a> property (affects distance between lines of text, defaults to 1.5).</p> <p><code>backgroundcolor</code></p> <p>Sets the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/background-color"><code>background-color</code></a> for the document.</p> <p><code>margin-left</code>, <code>margin-right</code>, <code>margin-top</code>, <code>margin-bottom</code></p> <p>Sets the CSS <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/margin"><code>margin</code></a> properties for the document body.</p> <p>For example. here we set the font-size a bit larger and specify that we want a bit more space between lines of text:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Document" format: html: theme: cosmo fontsize: 1.1em linestretch: 1.7</code></pre> <h5 id="theme-options-1">Theme Options</h5> <p>You can do extensive customization of themes using <a href="https://sass-lang.com/">Sass</a>. Bootstrap defines over 1,400 Sass variables that control fonts, colors, padding, borders, and much more. You can see all of the variables here:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/blob/main/scss/_variables.scss">github.com</a></p> <p>Sass theme files can define both variables that globally set things like colors and fonts, as well as rules that define more fine grained behavior. To customize an existing Bootstrap theme with your own set of variables and/or rules, just provide the base theme and then your custom theme file(s):</p> <pre><code>theme: - cosmo - custom.scss</code></pre> <p>Your <code>custom.scss</code> file might look something like this:</p> <pre><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/ $h2-font-size: 1.6rem !default; $headings-font-weight: 500 !default; /*-- scss:rules --*/ h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { text-shadow: -1px -1px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, .3); }</code></pre> <p>Note that the variables section is denoted by the <code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/</code> comment and the rules section (where normal CSS rules go) is denoted by the <code>/*-- scss:rules --*/</code> comment.</p> <h5 id="custom-themes-1">Custom Themes</h5> <p>You can naturally also create an entirely custom theme and provide only that (in this case you will inherit from the default Bootstrap theme):</p> <pre><code>theme: custom.scss</code></pre> <p>For example, here are the theme files for the 25 built-in Bootswatch themes:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/html/bootstrap/themes">github.com</a></p> <p>You can read more about the custom theming design here.</p> <h5 id="dark-mode-2">Dark Mode</h5> <p>In addition to providing a single theme for your html output, you may also provide a light and dark theme. For example:</p> <pre><code>theme: light: flatly dark: darkly</code></pre> <p>Setting the above themes in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> results in both a dark and light version of your output being available. For example:</p> <h6 id="flatly-themed-output">Flatly Themed Output</h6> <h6 id="darkly-themed-output">Darkly Themed Output</h6> <p>When providing both a dark and light mode for your html output, Quarto will automatically create a toggle to allow your reader to select the desired dark or light appearance. The toggle will automatically appear in the top right corner of your html output. When possible, the toggle will use browser local storage to maintain the user’s preference across sessions.</p> <p>To honor the user’s operating system or browser preference for light or dark mode, specify <code>respect-user-color-scheme: true</code>:</p> <pre><code>format: html: respect-user-color-scheme: true</code></pre> <p>Otherwise, the order of light and dark elements in the theme or brand will determine the default appearance for your html output. For example, since the <code>light</code> option appears first in the first example, a reader will see the light appearance by default, if <code>respect-user-color-scheme</code> is not enabled.</p> <p>Quarto will automatically select the appropriate light or dark version of the text highlighter that you have specified when possible. For more information, see Code Highlighting.</p> <p>As of Quarto 1.7, <code>respect-user-color-scheme</code> requires JavaScript support: users with JavaScript disabled will see the author-preferred (first) brand or theme.</p> <h6 id="mode-specific-content">Mode-specific content</h6> <p>To display content only in light mode, use the <code>.light-content</code> CSS class; to display content only in dark mode, use the <code>.dark-content</code> class.</p> <p>Usually you should provide light and dark content in the same place and at the same size, so that page layout is unaffected when switching between modes.</p> <p>For example, the paragraph produced by the following code will contain different text in light and dark mode:</p> <pre><code>::: {.light-content} This text will be shown in light mode. ::: ::: {.dark-content} This text will be shown in dark mode. :::</code></pre> <p>This text will be shown in light mode.</p> <p>This text will be shown in dark mode.</p> <p>TipHow this works</p> <p>The document <code>body</code> element has the <code>.quarto-light</code> class when it is in light mode, and the <code>.quarto-dark</code> class when it is in dark mode.</p> <p>CSS rules hide all elements with the <code>.light-content</code> class when the body has <code>.quarto-dark</code>, and all elements with the <code>.dark-content</code> class when the body has <code>.quarto-light</code>.</p> <p>The cell renderings feature applies the <code>.light-content</code> and <code>.dark-content</code> CSS classes to computational output such as plots and tables.</p> <h6 id="customizing-themes">Customizing Themes</h6> <p>As when providing a single theme, you may provide a custom theme for dark and light mode, or a list of <code>scss</code> files to customize the light and dark appearance. This website, for example uses the following to use a light <code>cosmo</code> theme and then customizes the <code>cosmo</code> theme with additional Sass variables when in dark mode:</p> <pre><code>theme: light: [cosmo, theme.scss] dark: [cosmo, theme-dark.scss]</code></pre> <p>Below are some of the lines of <code>theme-dark.scss</code> which turn the light cosmo theme dark:</p> <pre><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/ // Base document colors $body-bg: #181818; $body-color: #ccc; $link-color: #75AADB; // Code blocks $code-block-bg-alpha: -.9;</code></pre> <p>For more information about available Sass variables, see HTML Customization Using Sass Variables.</p> <h5 id="sass-variables-1">Sass Variables</h5> <p>The following Sass Variables can be specified within SCSS files (note that these variables should always be prefixed with a <code>$</code> and are specified within theme files rather than within YAML options):</p> <h6 id="colors-1">Colors</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$body-bg</code></p> <p>The page background color.</p> <p><code>$body-color</code></p> <p>The page text color.</p> <p><code>$link-color</code></p> <p>The link color.</p> <p><code>$input-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for HTML inputs.</p> <p><code>$popover-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for popovers (for example, when a citation preview is shown).</p> <h6 id="fonts-1">Fonts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$font-family-sans-serif</code></p> <p>The sans-serif font family for the page.</p> <p><code>$font-family-monospace</code></p> <p>The monospace font family for the page.</p> <p><code>$font-size-root</code></p> <p>The base font size for the page.</p> <p><code>$toc-font-size</code></p> <p>The font size for the page TOC.</p> <p><code>$h1-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h2-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h3-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h4-font-size</code></p> <p><code>$h5-font-size</code></p> <p>Font sizes for the specified headings.</p> <h6 id="code-blocks-7">Code Blocks</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left</code></p> <p>By default, Quarto does not display a left border on code blocks. Set this variable to a truthy value or a CSS color to enable the left border.</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left-style</code></p> <p>The style of the left border displayed on code blocks. Defaults to <code>solid</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-left-size</code></p> <p>The thickness of the left border displayed on code blocks. Defaults to <code>3px</code>;</p> <p><code>$code-block-padding-left</code></p> <p>The amount of padding applied between the code and the border. Defaults to <code>0.6em</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg</code></p> <p>By default, Quarto sets a background on code blocks by adding transparency to the theme’s <code>progress-bg</code> color. Set this variable to truthy value or a CSS color.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg-padding</code></p> <p>The padding applied to the code block. Defaults to <code>0.4em</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg-alpha</code></p> <p>The amount to alter the transparency fo the <code>progress-bg</code> color. This is not used if an explicit background color is set. Defaults to <code>-0.35</code>.</p> <h6 id="code-annotation-5">Code Annotation</h6> <p>You can customize the colors used to highlight lines when code annotation is used:</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-annotation-higlight-color</code></p> <p>The color used as a border on highlighted lines.</p> <p><code>$code-annotation-higlight-bg</code></p> <p>The color used for the background of highlighted lines.</p> <h6 id="code-copy-1">Code Copy</h6> <p>You can also customize the colors of the button which appears for <code>code-copy: true</code> with the following variables:</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$btn-code-copy-color</code></p> <p>The color used for the copy button at the top right of code blocks.</p> <p><code>$btn-code-copy-color-active</code></p> <p>The hover color used for the copy button at the top right of code blocks.</p> <h6 id="inline-code-5">Inline Code</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$code-bg</code></p> <p>The background color of inline code. Defaults to a mix between the <code>body-bg</code> and <code>body-color</code>.</p> <p><code>$code-color</code></p> <p>The text color of inline code. Defaults to a generated contrasting color against the <code>code-bg</code>.</p> <h6 id="table-of-contents-2">Table of Contents</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$toc-color</code></p> <p>The color for table of contents text.</p> <p><code>$toc-font-size</code></p> <p>The font-size for table of contents text.</p> <p><code>$toc-active-border</code></p> <p>The left border color for the currently active table of contents item.</p> <p><code>$toc-inactive-border</code></p> <p>The left border colors for inactive table of contents items.</p> <h6 id="layout-7">Layout</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$content-padding-top</code></p> <p>Padding that should appear before the main content area (including the sidebar, content, and TOC.</p> <h6 id="navigation-2">Navigation</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$navbar-bg</code></p> <p>The background color of the navbar. Defaults to the theme’s <code>$primary</code> color.</p> <p><code>$navbar-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the navbar. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$navbar-hl</code></p> <p>The highlight color for links in the navbar. If not specified, the <code>$link-color</code> is used or a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for a sidebar. Defaults to <code>\$light</code> except when a navbar is present or when the style is <code>floating</code>. In that case it defaults to the <code>\$body-bg</code> color.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the sidebar. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <p><code>$sidebar-hl</code></p> <p>The highlight color for links in the sidebar. If not specified, the <code>$link-color</code> is used.</p> <p><code>$footer-bg</code></p> <p>The background color for the footer. Defaults to the <code>$body-bg</code> color.</p> <p><code>$footer-fg</code></p> <p>The color of foreground elements (text and navigation) on the footer. If not specified, a contrasting color is automatically computed.</p> <h6 id="callouts-4">Callouts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$callout-border-width</code></p> <p>The left border width of callouts. Defaults to <code>5px</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-border-scale</code></p> <p>The border color of callouts computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>0%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-icon-scale</code></p> <p>The color of the callout icon computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>10%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-top</code></p> <p>The amount of top margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1.25rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-bottom</code></p> <p>The amount of bottom margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1.25rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-color-<type></code></p> <p>The colors for the various types of callouts. Defaults:</p> <p>type</p> <p>default</p> <p><code>note</code></p> <p><code>$blue</code></p> <p><code>tip</code></p> <p><code>$green</code></p> <p><code>caution</code></p> <p><code>$orange</code></p> <p><code>warning</code></p> <p><code>$yellow</code></p> <p><code>important</code></p> <p><code>$red</code></p> <h6 id="bootstrap-variables-1">Bootstrap Variables</h6> <p>In addition to the above Sass variables, Bootstrap itself supports hundreds of additional variables. You can <a href="https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.1/customize/sass/">learn more about Bootstrap’s use of Sass variables</a> or review the <a href="https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/blob/main/scss/_variables.scss">raw variables and their default values</a>.</p> <h3 id="hugo">Hugo</h3> <h4 id="hugo-1">Hugo</h4> <h5 id="overview-86">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://gohugo.io/">Hugo</a> is a very popular open source website publishing system. Pages in Hugo websites are typically written in plain markdown, so don’t have a straightforward way to automatically and reproducibly incorporate computational output.</p> <p>Using the Quarto <code>hugo-md</code> format, you can incorporate computational output (e.g. R or Python code that produces plots) into Hugo websites. This article explains how.</p> <p>It’s important to note that many of the Quarto features related to theming, page layout, and navigation are not applicable when you are using Quarto with Hugo. Hugo has its own theming system, syntax highlighting, table of contents, page layout, navigational menus, and full text search. You’ll use Quarto to execute code and generate markdown that is rendered within the Hugo HTML publishing framework rather than Quarto’s own.</p> <h5 id="site-config">Site Config</h5> <p>There are a couple of changes you should make to your Hugo <code>config.toml</code> in preparation for using Quarto with Hugo. First, make sure that <code>.qmd</code> and <code>.ipynb</code> files and other source code or data files are not published as part of the site. For example:</p> <pre><code>ignoreFiles = [ "\\.qmd$", "\\.ipynb$", "\\.py$" ]</code></pre> <p>Next, configure Hugo’s markdown renderer to allow raw HTML (as many R and Python packages will produce computational output using raw HTML rather than markdown):</p> <pre><code>[markup.goldmark.renderer] unsafe= true</code></pre> <h5 id="creating-a-page">Creating a Page</h5> <p>Hugo articles and posts that use Quarto should live in their own directory (taking advantage of the Hugo <a href="https://gohugo.io/content-management/page-bundles/">Page Bundles</a> feature). This allows any content generated/referenced by the page (e.g. plot output) to live right alongside the markdown source.</p> <p>To add Quarto documents to a Hugo site:</p> <ul> <li><p>Create a directory within <code>content</code> that will hold your Quarto article.</p></li> <li><p>Add an <code>index.qmd</code> document to the directory. When rendered this will create an <code>index.md</code>, which in turn will ensure that Hugo treats it as a <a href="https://gohugo.io/content-management/page-bundles/">Page Bundle</a> (automatically copying images and other referenced resources to the publish directory).</p></li> <li><p>Add the requisite Hugo <a href="https://gohugo.io/content-management/front-matter/">front matter</a>, then also specify <code>format: hugo-md</code> and any other required Quarto options. For example, let’s say we wanted to create a new article named <code>hello-quarto</code> within the <code>content</code> directory. The filesystem would look like this:</p> <p>mysite/ content/ hello-quarto/ index.qmd</p></li> </ul> <p>Here’s what the source code of <code>index.qmd</code> might look like:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Hello, Quarto date: "2012-04-06" categories: - Matplotlib - Coordinates format: hugo-md jupyter: python3 --- ## Polar Axis For a demonstration of a line plot on a polar axis, see @fig-polar. ```{python} #| label: fig-polar #| fig-cap: "A line plot on a polar axis" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <h5 id="workflow-6">Workflow</h5> <p>The basic concept of using Quarto with Hugo is that you take computational markdown documents (<code>.qmd</code>) or Jupyter notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) and use them to generate plain markdown files (<code>.md</code>) that are rendered to HTML by Hugo.</p> <p>index.qmd quarto => index.md hugo => index.html</p> <p>The <code>quarto render</code> and <code>quarto preview</code> commands are used to transform <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> files to Hugo compatible markdown (<code>.md</code>). The computational files are located in the same place you would also locate ordinary markdown files (e.g. the <code>blog</code> directory).</p> <p>After rendering, a plain <code>.md</code> file is written right alongside the computational document. This markdown file is then processed by Hugo.</p> <h6 id="live-preview-1">Live Preview</h6> <p>The <code>quarto preview</code> command will automatically recognize when it is run from a directory that contains a Hugo website:</p> <pre><code>Terminal cd my-hugo-website quarto preview</code></pre> <p>This will automatically run <code>hugo serve</code> on your behalf to bring up a local preview server. In addition, it will monitor the filesystem for changes to <code>.qmd</code> and <code>.ipynb</code> inputs and automatically re-render them to Hugo compatible <code>.md</code> files when they change.</p> <p>Note that this also works for the integrated Preview command within the Quarto VS Code Extension in VS Code or Positron.</p> <h6 id="rendering-10">Rendering</h6> <p>If you are not previewing and want to render all of the Quarto documents (<code>.qmd</code>) and notebooks (<code>.ipynb</code>) in your site, call <code>quarto render</code> from the root directory of the site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal cd my-hugo-website quarto render</code></pre> <p>Typically you’ll want to do a <code>quarto render</code> at the site level before you build the site for publishing:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render && hugo</code></pre> <p>You can also render individual documents or notebooks:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render blog/2022-07-26/hello-quarto/index.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you have computationally expensive documents you may want to consider using Quarto’s freeze feature to only re-execute code when your document source code changes.</p> <p>Note that if aren’t ever rendering at the project level and just have individual files that you want to render with Quarto, you should specify the <code>hugo-md</code> format as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Blog Post" format: hugo-md ---</code></pre> <h6 id="configuration-1">Configuration</h6> <p>While Quarto works well within a Hugo site that has no <code>_quarto.yml</code> project config file, you can add one if you want to customize the default behavior, add a bibliography, etc. For example, here is what a simple customized <code>_quarto.yml</code> file might look like:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: hugo format: hugo-md: code-fold: true execute: warning: false bibliography: references.bib</code></pre> <p>It’s important to note that if you do provide an explicit <code>_quarto.yml</code> file you need to explicitly specify the project type (<code>type: hugo</code>) as shown above.</p> <h6 id="external-directory-1">External Directory</h6> <p>You might decide that you prefer to keep all of your Quarto documents and/or notebooks in their own directory, separate from the Hugo website. In this configuration you would mirror the directory structure of your site in the Quarto directory, and then set the <code>output-dir</code> in the project file to point to the Hugo directory. For example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: hugo output-dir: ../hugo-site</code></pre> <h5 id="shortcodes-6">Shortcodes</h5> <p>Note that Hugo <a href="https://gohugo.io/content-management/shortcodes/">shortcodes</a> and Quarto shortcodes share the same basic syntax (e.g. <code>{{< var foo >}}</code>). This is normally not a problem as shortcodes not recognized by Quarto are passed through unmodified to Hugo.</p> <p>However, in some cases the use of a Hugo shortcode throws off Pandoc markdown processing, and its necessary to “protect” the Hugo shortcode from processing by Pandoc. This can typically be handled by escaping the shortcode with an extra brace. For example:</p> <pre><code>{{{< ref "foo/index.md" >}}}</code></pre> <p>It’s possible that this won’t be enough if the presence of the shortcode changes how Pandoc processes the surrounding markdown (e.g. this is currently known to occur for links). In this case you need to use a markdown raw block around the entire construct. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{=markdown} [click here]({{< ref "foo/index.md" >}}) ```</code></pre> <p>Or for inline content, use a markdown raw inline:</p> <pre><code>For more info, `[click here]({{< ref "foo/index.md" >}})`{=markdown}</code></pre> <h5 id="webtex-math-1">WebTeX Math</h5> <p>The <code>hugo</code> format renders LaTeX equations using standard dollar-delimited inline (<code>\$...\$</code>) and display (<code>\$\$...\$\$</code>) syntax. However, if the web environment you are publishing into doesn’t support dollar-delimited math, you can alternatively use <a href="https://github.com/KTHse/webtex">WebTeX</a> to display math. This is done by setting the Pandoc <code>html-math-method</code> to <code>webtex</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: hugo: html-math-method: webtex</code></pre> <p>WebTeX works for any web page that can display images, and requires no special JavaScript or CSS. Any inline or display equations contained within your document will be converted to an image URL that requests a rendered version of the equation. For example, the following markdown:</p> <pre><code>$x + 1$</code></pre> <p>Will be converted to:</p> <pre><code>![](https://latex.codecogs.com/svg.latex?x%20%2B%201)</code></pre> <p>Which renders as:</p> <h6 id="dark-mode-3">Dark Mode</h6> <p>SVG is used as the default rendering method because it has the best overall appearance. However, if your <code>hugo</code> document is being rendered on a dark background, you may want to switch to PNG with a dark background specified. You can do this as follows:</p> <pre><code>format: hugo: html-math-method: method: webtex url: [latex.codecogs.com](https://latex.codecogs.com/png.image?%5Cbg_black&space);</code></pre> <h3 id="including-other-formats">Including Other Formats</h3> <h4 id="including-other-formats-1">Including Other Formats</h4> <h5 id="overview-87">Overview</h5> <p>HTML pages (either standalone or in a website) can automatically include links to other formats specified in the document front matter. For example, the following document front matter:</p> <pre><code>title: Sample Page author: Norah Jones date: last-modified toc: true format: html: default ipynb: default</code></pre> <p>Results in an HTML page that includes a link to the additional notebook format in the right margin below the table of contents:</p> <p>If a table of contents is enabled for the page, the additional formats will be automatically placed within the table of contents as a new section. If no table of contents is displayed, the additional formats will be displayed in the right margin at the top of the document.</p> <p>Links to additional formats are displayed by default, but you can control whether they are shown or even which specific formats are included with the <code>format-links</code> YAML option.</p> <p>NoteRendering All Formats in Standalone HTML Documents</p> <p>The Render button in RStudio, and the Preview button in Positron and VS Code, will not automatically render all formats if the document isn’t part of a Quarto website. To render all formats use <code>quarto render</code> on the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render multi-format.qmd</code></pre> <h5 id="rendering-formats-with-the-same-extension">Rendering Formats with the Same Extension</h5> <p>If your formats share a file extension, for example, both HTML pages and Revealjs presentations use <code>.html</code>, their outputs will overwrite each other. To include formats with the same extension, use <code>output-file</code> to distinguish one. For example, to include a link to a RevealJS presentation provide a distinct <code>output-file</code>:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd title: Sample Page format: html: default revealjs: output-file: document-revealjs.html</code></pre> <h5 id="specifying-formats-to-link">Specifying Formats to Link</h5> <p>You can provide an explicit list of formats to include in the Other Formats section by providing a list as the value for <code>format-links</code>. For example, this document front matter will result in only the link to the Jupyter notebook format, excluding the PDF format:</p> <pre><code>title: Sample Page author: Norah Jones date: last-modified toc: true format: html: default ipynb: default pdf: default format-links: [ipynb]</code></pre> <p>You can also customize the links by passing <code>format-links</code> an object with keys:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>format</code>, the format to be linked</p></li> <li><p><code>text</code>, the text to be displayed for the link</p></li> <li><p><code>icon</code>, the name of a <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com">Bootstrap icons</a> For example, here a link to the <code>typst</code> format is displayed as the text “PDF” along with a PDF file icon:</p> <p>title: Sample Page author: Norah Jones date: last-modified toc: true format: html: default typst: default format-links: - html - format: typst text: PDF icon: file-pdf</p></li> </ul> <p>You can also provide <code>format-links</code> items using the same options as <a href="html-basics.html#code-links-and-other-links">Code Links and Other Links</a>. For example, rather than another format, you could to add a link to an external URL:</p> <pre><code>format-links: - text: Other Link href: [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/) icon: hand-thumbs-up</code></pre> <h5 id="hiding-all-links">Hiding All Links</h5> <p>To prevent format links from being shown at all, specify <code>format-links: false</code> in your document front matter. For example this front matter will not display the Other Formats links:</p> <pre><code>title: Sample Page author: Norah Jones date: last-modified toc: true format: html: default ipynb: default format-links: false</code></pre> <h5 id="controlling-formats-at-a-project-level">Controlling Formats at a Project Level</h5> <p>In a Quarto Project, to control the formats and their behavior for a specific folder, provide the <code>format</code> and <code>format-links</code> options in a <code>_metadata.yml</code> file. Similarly, you can specify these options for an entire project by including them in the <code>_quarto.yml</code> project file. See Directory Metadata or Project Metadata for additional details.</p> <p>The <code>format</code> option isn’t merged like all other metadata across <code>_quarto.yml</code>, <code>_metadata.yml</code>, and the document YAML. If you have some formats specified at a project or directory level, you’ll also need to explicitly list them in the document YAML. For example, suppose you have HTML options set at the project level:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: toc: true</code></pre> <p>In order to get an HTML document with a link to the PDF format, you’ll need to list both formats in the YAML header:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd format: html: default pdf: default</code></pre> <h3 id="lightbox-figures-1">Lightbox Figures</h3> <h4 id="lightbox-figures-2">Lightbox Figures</h4> <h5 id="overview-88">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto uses the <a href="https://biati-digital.github.io/glightbox/">GLightbox javascript library</a> to add lightbox styling and behavior to images in your HTML documents. Lightbox images allow a reader to click to see a larger version of the image (including any caption).</p> <p>For example, the following images have lightbox treatment:</p> <p>Photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@hush52?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Hush Naidoo Jade Photography</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/white-flower-in-clear-glass-vase-SutAduhzdRQ?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Unsplash</a></p> <p>Photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@ale_s_bianchi?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Alessandro Bianchi</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/light-bulb-illustration-_kdTyfnUFAc?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Unsplash</a></p> <p>Photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@ajoshuamelo?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Joshua Melo</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/powered-on-edison-light-bulbs-peFHn8r4t1o?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash">Unsplash</a></p> <p>To enable lightbox treatment for all images in a document add <code>lightbox: true</code> in the YAML header:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Simple Lightbox Example lightbox: true --- ![A Lovely Image](mv-1.jpg)</code></pre> <h5 id="enabling-lightbox">Enabling Lightbox</h5> <p>You can enable lightbox either for all images within a document, or for only selected images within a document. To enable lightbox for all images within a document, use the following yaml:</p> <pre><code>--- lightbox: true ---</code></pre> <p>When lightbox is set to automatically select images, it will match any image used as a figure or which appears as a block (by itself within a paragraph). By default, images that appear inline with other content will not receive lightbox treatment.</p> <h6 id="applying-lightbox-to-specific-images">Applying Lightbox to Specific Images</h6> <p>You can select specific images to receive the lightbox treatment by applying the <code>lightbox</code> class on the images you’d like to receive the treatment. In this case, there is no need to include <code>lightbox</code> in the front matter, the use of the <code>lightbox</code> class will automatically enable lightbox. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Simple Lightbox Example --- ![A Lovely Image](mv-1.jpg){.lightbox} ![Another Lovely Image](mv-2.jpg)</code></pre> <p>will result in the first image receiving a lightbox treatment, while the second image will not.</p> <h5 id="disabling-lightbox-treatment">Disabling Lightbox Treatment</h5> <p>You can disable lightbox for the whole document using the following yaml:</p> <pre><code>--- lightbox: false ---</code></pre> <p>When lightbox is explicitly disabled, no images will receive the lightbox treatment, even if the image is marked with a <code>lightbox</code> class (as described above).</p> <h6 id="disabling-lightbox-for-specific-images">Disabling Lightbox for Specific Images</h6> <p>If automatic lightboxing of images is enabled, you can select specific images to not receive the treatment by marking them with a <code>nolightbox</code> class. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Simple Lightbox Example lightbox: auto --- ![A Lovely Image](mv-1.jpg) ![Another Lovely Image](mv-2.jpg){.nolightbox}</code></pre> <p>In this example, the first image will receive the lightbox treatment, while the second image will not.</p> <h5 id="galleries">Galleries</h5> <p>In addition to simply providing a lightbox treatment for individual images, you can also group images into a ‘gallery’. When the user activates the lightbox, they will be able to page through the images in the gallery without returning to the main document. To create galleries of images, apply a <code>group</code> attribute (with a name) to the images that you’d like to gather into a gallery. Images with the same group name will be placed together in a gallery when given a lightbox treatment.</p> <p>For example, the following three images will be treated as a gallery:</p> <pre><code>![A Lovely Image](mv-1.jpg){group="my-gallery"} ![Another Lovely Image](mv-2.jpg){group="my-gallery"} ![The Last Lovely Image](mv-3.jpg){group="my-gallery"}</code></pre> <h5 id="options-37">Options</h5> <p>Quarto supports a number of options to customize the lightbox behavior for a document. Options include:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>match</code></p> <p>Set this to <code>auto</code> if you’d like any image to be given lightbox treatment. If you omit this, only images with the class <code>lightbox</code> will be given the lightbox treatment.</p> <p><code>effect</code></p> <p>The effect that should be used when opening and closing the lightbox. One of <code>fade</code>, <code>zoom</code>, <code>none</code>. Defaults to <code>zoom</code>.</p> <p><code>desc-position</code></p> <p>The position of the title and description when displaying a lightbox. One of <code>top</code>, <code>bottom</code>, <code>left</code>, <code>right</code>. Defaults to <code>bottom</code>.</p> <p><code>loop</code></p> <p>Whether galleries should ‘loop’ to first image in the gallery if the user continues past the last image of the gallery. Boolean that defaults to <code>true</code>.</p> <p><code>css-class</code></p> <p>A class name to apply to the lightbox to allow css targeting. This will replace the lightbox class with your custom class name.</p> <p>A complete example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Complete Lightbox Example lightbox: match: auto effect: fade desc-position: right loop: false css-class: "my-css-class" ---</code></pre> <h5 id="per-image-attributes">Per Image Attributes</h5> <p>The following options may be specified as attributes on individual images to control the lightbox behavior:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>desc-position</code></p> <p>The position of the title and description when displaying a lightbox. One of <code>top</code>, <code>bottom</code>, <code>left</code>, <code>right</code>. Defaults to <code>bottom</code></p> <h5 id="using-lightbox-with-computational-cells">Using Lightbox with Computational Cells</h5> <p>The Quarto lightbox treatment will use figure information for computational outputs. For example, the following plot will receive a lightbox treatment and will include a properly prefixed caption when the user zooms into the plot.</p> <pre><code>--- lightbox: auto --- ```{r} #| label: fig-basic #| fig-cap: Simple demo R plot plot(1:10, rnorm(10)) ```</code></pre> <p>If your computational cell produces multiple subfigures, each of the subfigures will receive the lightbox treatment and when zoom, the user may page back and forth through the subfigures. For example, the following will produce a ‘gallery’ lightbox view which includes both of the subfigures, allowing the viewer to easily navigate between sub figures:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| label: fig-plots #| fig-cap: | #| The below demonstrates placing more than one image in a gallery. Note #| the usage of the `layout-ncol` which arranges the images on the page #| side by date. Adding the `group` attribute to the markdown images places #| the images in a gallery grouped together based upon the group name #| provided. #| fig-subcap: #| - "This is a caption for the first sub figure" #| - "This is a caption for the second sub figure" #| layout-ncol: 2 plot(ToothGrowth) plot(PlantGrowth) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="advanced-customization-in-computations">Advanced Customization In Computations</h6> <p>Options for lightbox can be passed using the code cell option <code>lightbox</code> like the following:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| fig-cap: Simple demo R plot #| lightbox: #| group: r-graph #| description: This is 1 to 10 plot plot(1:10, rnorm(10)) ```</code></pre> <p>It is possible to create several plots, and group them in a lightbox gallery. Use list in YAML for options when you have several plots, on per plot.</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| fig-cap: #| - Caption for first plot #| - Caption for second plot #| lightbox: #| group: cars #| description: #| - This is the decription for first graph #| - This is the decription for second graph plot(mtcars) plot(cars) ```</code></pre> <h3 id="more-about-quarto-themes">More About Quarto Themes</h3> <h4 id="more-about-quarto-themes-1">More About Quarto Themes</h4> <p>As a part of Quarto, we’ve developed a simple single file format that describes declarations, variables, and rules that should be layered into Scss files when compiling them into css. The basic structure of a theme file is:</p> <ul> <li><p>A single text file that contains valid Scss</p></li> <li><p>Special comments are used to denote regions of functions, defaults, mixins, and rules (region decorators).</p></li> <li><p>At least one of these region decorators must be present in order for the theme file to be valid.</p></li> <li><p>More than one of each type of region decorator are permitted. If more than one of any type is present, all regions of a given type will be merged into a single block of that type in the order in which they are encountered in the file.</p></li> <li><p>When compiling, the sections will be layered according to type, functions first, then variables, then mixins, then rules.</p></li> <li><p>The directory that contains your theme file will be added to the load path, allowing <code>@use</code> or <code>@import</code> statements to be resolved using the same directory that contains the theme file. Here is an example file:</p> <p>/<em>– scss:functions –</em>/ <span class="citation" data-cites="function">@function</span> colorToRGB (<span class="math inline">$color) { @return "rgb(" + red($</span>color) + “,” + green(<span class="math inline">$color) + ", " + blue($</span>color)+ “)”; }</p> <p>/<em>– scss:defaults –</em>/ $h2-font-size: 1.6rem !default; $headings-font-weight: 500 !default;</p> <p>/<em>– scss:rules –</em>/ h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { text-shadow: -1px -1px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, .3); }</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="bootswatch-sass-theme-files">Bootswatch Sass Theme Files</h5> <p>We’ve merged Bootswatch themes for Bootstrap 5 into this single file theme format in our repo here:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/html/bootstrap/themes">github.com</a></p> <p>From time to time, as the Bootswatch themes are updated, we will update these merged theme files.</p> <h5 id="bootstrap-bootswatch-layering">Bootstrap / Bootswatch Layering</h5> <p>When using the Quarto <code>html</code> and <code>dashboard</code> formats, we allow the user to specify theme information in the document front matter (or project YAML). The theme information consists of a list of one or more of</p> <ul> <li><p>A valid built in Bootswatch theme name</p></li> <li><p>A theme file (valid as described above). For example the following would use the cosmo Bootswatch theme and provide customization using the custom.scss file:</p> <p>theme: - cosmo - custom.scss</p></li> </ul> <p>When compiling the CSS for a Quarto website or HTML page, we merge any user provided theme file(s) or Bootswatch themes with the Bootstrap Scss in the following layers:</p> <pre><code>Uses Bootstrap Theme(s) /*-- scss:uses --*/ Functions Bootstrap Theme(s) /*-- scss:functions --*/ Variables Themes(s) /*-- scss:defaults --*/ Bootstrap Mixins Bootstrap Theme(s) /* -- scss:mixins --*/ Rules Bootstrap Theme(s) /*-- scss:rules --*/</code></pre> <p>We order the themes according to the order that they are specified in the YAML, maintaining the order for declarations and rules and reversing the order for variables (allowing the files specified later in the list to provide defaults variable values to the files specified earlier in the list). Layering of the example themes above would be as follows:</p> <pre><code>Uses Bootstrap cosmo /*-- scss:uses --*/ custom.scss /*-- scss:uses --*/ Functions Bootstrap cosmo /*-- scss:functions --*/ custom.scss /*-- scss:functions --*/ Variables custom.scss /*-- scss:defaults --*/ cosmo /*-- scss:defaults --*/ Bootstrap Mixins Bootstrap cosmo /* -- scss:mixins --*/ custom.scss /* -- scss:mixins --*/ Rules Bootstrap cosmo /*-- scss:rules --*/ custom.scss /*-- scss:rules --*/</code></pre> <h5 id="revealjs-layering"><code>revealjs</code> Layering</h5> <p>The same system applies for <code>revealjs</code> and its themes. <code>revealjs</code> themes shipped with Quarto do not have a uniform variable naming convention, and so different SCSS files are likely to be needed to make effective changes to different themes.</p> <p>Nevertheless, the following examples illustrate what’s possible:</p> <pre><code># In this configuration, `custom.scss` takes precedence format: revealjs: theme: - blood - custom.scss # In this configuration, the `blood` theme takes precedence format: revealjs: theme: - custom.scss - blood</code></pre> <h5 id="brand.yml-layering"><code>_brand.yml</code> Layering</h5> <p>Quarto supports <a href="https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/brand/defaults.html">brand.yml</a>, see the Brand guide for more details. By default, styling information in <code>_brand.yml</code> takes the lowest precedence. To change this, use the <code>"brand"</code> string in your theme configuration in YAML:</p> <pre><code># In this configuration, the `blood` theme takes precedence # over `custom.scss` *and* the information in `_brand.yml` format: revealjs: theme: - custom.scss - blood # In this configuration, the information in `_brand.yml` takes # precedence over the `blood` theme and `custom.scss`, in that # order format: revealjs: theme: - blood - custom.scss - brand</code></pre> <h3 id="page-layout-1">Page Layout</h3> <h4 id="page-layout-2">Page Layout</h4> <h5 id="overview-89">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto provides a default layout for HTML pages that should work well for many documents. However, if the default layout isn’t working for your content, you can adjust it.</p> <p>On this page, learn about:</p> <ul> <li>The three high level layout options for your pages in Page Layout.</li> <li>How to adjust the width of the individual layout components (sidebar, body, margins, and gutter) to fit your content in Grid Customization.</li> </ul> <h5 id="page-layout-3">Page Layout</h5> <p>By default Quarto HTML documents display content centered at a width optimized for readability (typically from 600px to 900px wide). While this is a sound default layout for traditional articles, for other types of pages (e.g. landing or index pages) you may want to use other layouts.</p> <p>The <code>page-layout</code> option can be use to control the layout used. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: html: page-layout: full</code></pre> <p>The various <code>page-layout</code> options are described below.</p> <h6 id="article">Article</h6> <pre><code>page-layout: article</code></pre> <p>Article layout provides a content area with a page based grid layout that provides margins, areas for sidebars, and a reading width optimized body region. The precise size of the document regions will vary slightly depending upon the sidebar (if present) and the presence or absence of margin or complex layout elements. To learn more, checkout the guide to Article Layout.</p> <h6 id="full">Full</h6> <pre><code>page-layout: full</code></pre> <p>Full layout uses the article grid system, but automatically expands the content area to use the sidebar and margin region if no content is placed within those regions. This is useful for layouts that don’t need to be constrained to reading width and that will benefit from additional horizontal space (e.g. landing or index pages)</p> <h6 id="custom">Custom</h6> <pre><code>page-layout: custom</code></pre> <p>Custom layout provides a simple HTML content container with no default grid system, padding, or margins. The default HTML framing provided will look like this:</p> <pre><code><div class="page-layout-custom"> body content here </div></code></pre> <p>In websites, custom layouts do not include navigation sidebars but do include the site navbar and footer.</p> <h6 id="css-grid">CSS Grid</h6> <p>If you are using <code>page-layout: custom</code>, you’ll likely want to utilize the <a href="https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.1/layout/css-grid/">Bootstrap CSS Grid</a> layout system (which is available by default in Quarto documents) for creating more sophisticated layouts.</p> <p>For example, here’s a simple 2-column grid:</p> <pre><code>::: {.grid} ::: {.g-col-4} This column takes 1/3 of the page ::: ::: {.g-col-8} This column takes 2/3 of the page ::: :::</code></pre> <p>Bootstrap’s CSS Grid system includes facilities for responsiveness, wrapping, nesting, and fine grained customization of column behavior.</p> <p>Note that this isn’t the traditional Bootstrap grid used in older versions of Bootstrap – rather, it’s a brand new layout system introduced in Bootstrap 5.1 based on the CSS Grid standard.
