Quarto uses this newer system because it has more sophisticated layout capabilities akin to what LaTeX offers for print documents.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.1/layout/css-grid/">Bootstrap CSS Grid</a> documentation for additionals details.</p> <h5 id="grid-customization">Grid Customization</h5> <p>You can control the width of the layout components in HTML documents with YAML options and SCSS. For example, if long entries in a sidebar are being wrapped, it may make sense to increase the width of sidebar:</p> <p>Default Layout</p> <p>Wider Sidebar</p> <p>This change can be made by adding the <code>grid</code> option to the <code>_quarto.yml</code> file, increasing the <code>sidebar-width</code> from its default of 250px:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: grid: sidebar-width: 350px</code></pre> <p>There are four variables to control the four components of the layout: the sidebar, the body, the margin, and the gutters.</p> <p>The rest of this section describes these components, and their default values, as well as how to customize them either with YAML or SCSS variables. You can also find Additional Examples of customization in action.</p> <p>NoteTypst Grid Options</p> <p>For Typst output, only <code>margin-width</code>, <code>body-width</code>, and <code>gutter-width</code> apply (there is no sidebar in PDF documents). Typst also provides a <code>margin-geometry</code> option for fine-grained control over margin placement. See Typst Basics - Article Layout for details.</p> <h6 id="html-page-layout">HTML Page Layout</h6> <p>Quarto HTML documents are arranged in a structure composed of a sidebar on the left, the body of the document, the margin of the document on the right, and the space between these elements, known as gutters. This is illustrated below:</p> <p>The width of these four components is controlled by four variables. These variables, along with their default values are:</p> <p>Default values for the width of layout components</p> <p>Element</p> <p>Size</p> <p><code>sidebar-width</code></p> <p>250px</p> <p><code>body-width</code></p> <p>800px</p> <p><code>margin-width</code></p> <p>250px</p> <p><code>gutter-width</code></p> <p>1.5em</p> <p>The values of these variables don’t directly specify the display width of the corresponding component, instead they specify a maximum base value. The maximum values are scaled to create minimum values, and together they are used to compute the size and position of each component across different layout types (fixed vs. floating), responsive sizes (large screen vs. mobile size), and page contents (margin vs. no margin content).</p> <h6 id="customizing-component-widths">Customizing Component Widths</h6> <p>You can control the component width variables using YAML or SCSS variables. To set these options in YAML, you may use the <code>grid</code> option :</p> <pre><code>format: html: grid: sidebar-width: 300px body-width: 900px margin-width: 300px gutter-width: 1.5rem</code></pre> <p>Similarly, in a custom theme <code>scss</code> file, you may set variables like:</p> <pre><code>// The left hand sidebar $grid-sidebar-width: 300px !default; // The main body $grid-body-width: 900px !default; // The right hand margin bar $grid-margin-width: 300px !default; // The gutter that appears between the above columns $grid-column-gutter-width: 1.5rem !default;</code></pre> <p><code>sidebar-width</code>, <code>body-width</code>, and <code>margin-width</code> should be specified in pixels (<code>px</code>) as the values will be used when computing other sizes. Requiring pixel sizing is a limitation of our approach to the Quarto’s layout, but also typically makes sense since the overall document width is usually tied to the browser size and responsive breakpoints rather than font size or other relative measures.</p> <p><code>gutter-width</code> may be specified in pixels or other units such as <code>em</code> or <code>rem</code> which are responsive to the document font size.</p> <h6 id="additional-examples">Additional Examples</h6> <p>Increasing the margin width may make sense on a website that has many figures or tables in the margin. For example, this YAML increases the <code>margin-width</code> by 200px over the default value:</p> <pre><code>format: html: grid: margin-width: 450px</code></pre> <p>Default Layout</p> <p>Wider Margin</p> <p>The effect of changing <code>margin-width</code> without changing <code>body-width</code> is to increase the overall page width (there is less white space on the far left and right of the page). Alternatively, to keep the overall page width the same <code>body-width</code> can be decreased by the same amount as <code>margin-width</code> increased:</p> <pre><code>format: html: grid: margin-width: 450px body-width: 600px</code></pre> <p>Default Layout</p> <p>Wider Margin, Narrower Body</p> <h3 id="pdf-basics">PDF Basics</h3> <h4 id="pdf-basics-1">PDF Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-90">Overview</h5> <p>Use the <code>pdf</code> format to create PDF output. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My document" format: pdf: toc: true number-sections: true colorlinks: true ---</code></pre> <p>This example highlights a few of the options available for PDF output. This article covers these and other options in detail. See the PDF format reference for a complete list of all available options.</p> <p>If you want to produce raw LaTeX output (a .tex file) rather than a PDF, all of the options documented here are still available (see the LaTeX Output section below for additional details).</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Note that while we will focus here exclusively on the use of LaTeX to create PDFs, Pandoc also has support for creating PDFs using ConTeXt, roff ms, or HTML (via wkhtmltopdf). See the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#creating-a-pdf">Creating a PDF</a> for additional details.</p> <h6 id="prerequisites">Prerequisites</h6> <p>In order to create PDFs you will need to install a recent distribution of TeX. We recommend the use of TinyTeX (which is based on TexLive), which you can install with the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install tinytex</code></pre> <p>See the article on PDF Engines for details on using other TeX distributions and PDF compilation engines.</p> <h5 id="document-class">Document Class</h5> <p>Quarto uses <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/koma-script">KOMA Script</a> document classes by default for PDF documents and books. KOMA-Script classes are drop-in replacements for the standard classes with an emphasis on typography and versatility.</p> <p>For PDF documents this results in the following Pandoc options set by default:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: documentclass: scrartcl papersize: letter</code></pre> <p>You can set <code>documentclass</code> to the standard <code>article</code>, <code>report</code> or <code>book</code> classes, to the KOMA Script equivalents <code>scrartcl</code>, <code>scrreprt</code>, and <code>scrbook</code> respectively, or to any other class made available by LaTeX packages you have installed.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Setting your <code>documentclass</code> to either <code>book</code> or <code>scrbook</code> will automatically handle many of the common needs for printing and binding PDFs into a physical book (i.e., chapters start on odd pages, alternating margin sizes, etc).</p> <p>See the Output Options section below for additional details on customizing LaTeX document options.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-3">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Use the <code>toc</code> option to include an automatically generated table of contents in the output document. Use the <code>toc-depth</code> option to specify the number of section levels to include in the table of contents. The default is 3 (which means that level-1, 2, and 3 headings will be listed in the contents). For example:</p> <pre><code>toc: true toc-depth: 2</code></pre> <p>You can customize the title used for the table of contents using the <code>toc-title</code> option:</p> <pre><code>toc-title: Contents</code></pre> <p>If you want to exclude a heading from the table of contents, add both the <code>.unnumbered</code> and <code>.unlisted</code> classes to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered .unlisted}</code></pre> <h5 id="section-numbering-1">Section Numbering</h5> <p>Use the <code>number-sections</code> option to number section headings in the output document. For example:</p> <pre><code>number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>number-depth</code> option to specify the deepest level of heading to add numbers to (by default all headings are numbered). For example:</p> <pre><code>number-depth: 3</code></pre> <p>To exclude an individual heading from numbering, add the <code>.unnumbered</code> class to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered}</code></pre> <h5 id="syntax-highlighting">Syntax Highlighting</h5> <p>Pandoc will automatically highlight syntax in <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#fenced-code-blocks">fenced code blocks</a> that are marked with a language name. For example:</p> <pre><code>```python 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Pandoc can provide syntax highlighting for over 140 different languages (see the output of <code>quarto pandoc --list-highlight-languages</code> for a list of all of them). If you want to provide the appearance of a highlighted code block for a language not supported, just use <code>default</code> as the language name.</p> <p>You can specify the code highlighting style using <code>syntax-highlighting</code> and specifying one of the supported themes. Supported themes include: a11y, arrow, pygments, tango, espresso, zenburn, kate, monochrome, breezedark, haddock, atom-one, ayu, breeze, dracula, github, gruvbox, monokai, nord, oblivion, printing, radical, solarized, and vim.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>syntax-highlighting: github</code></pre> <p>In addition to theme names, <code>syntax-highlighting</code> accepts two special values:</p> <ul> <li><code>none</code> — disables syntax highlighting entirely.</li> <li><code>idiomatic</code> — delegates highlighting to the output format’s native system instead of Pandoc’s built-in Skylighting engine. For LaTeX/PDF output, <code>syntax-highlighting: idiomatic</code> uses the LaTeX <code>listings</code> package for code highlighting instead of Pandoc’s default approach (which uses <code>fancyvrb</code> with <code>\Shaded</code>/<code>\Highlighting</code> environments). This may be preferred when working with LaTeX templates or publishers that expect <code>listings</code>-based code blocks.</li> </ul> <p>Highlighting themes can provide either a single highlighting definition or two definitions, one optimized for a light colored background and another optimized for a dark color background. When available, Quarto will automatically select the appropriate style based upon the code chunk background color’s darkness. You may always opt to specify the full name (e.g. <code>atom-one-dark</code>) to bypass this automatic behavior.</p> <p>By default, code is highlighted using the <code>arrow</code> theme, which is optimized for accessibility. Here are examples of the <code>arrow</code> light and dark themes:</p> <ul> <li>Light</li> <li>Dark</li> </ul> <h5 id="code-annotation-6">Code Annotation</h5> <p>You can add annotations to lines of code in code blocks and executable code cells. See Code Annotation for full details.</p> <h5 id="output-options-1">Output Options</h5> <p>There are numerous options available for customizing PDF output, including:</p> <ul> <li><p>Specifying document classes and their options</p></li> <li><p>Including lists of figures and tables</p></li> <li><p>Using the <code>geometry</code> and <code>hyperref</code> packages</p></li> <li><p>Numerous options for customizing fonts and colors. For example, here we use a few of these options:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: “My Document”</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>format:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>pdf:</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>documentclass: report</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>classoption: [twocolumn, landscape]</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>lof: true</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>lot: true</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>geometry:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- top=30mm</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>- left=20mm</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>- heightrounded</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>mainfont: Times New Roman</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>colorlinks: true</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> </ul> <p>See the Pandoc documentation on metadata <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#variables-for-latex">variables for LaTeX</a> for documentation on all available options.</p> <h5 id="pdf-accessibility-standards">PDF Accessibility & Standards</h5> <p>Create PDFs that work with screen readers and meet archival requirements using the <code>pdf-standard</code> option. This enables PDF/UA for accessibility, PDF/A for long-term archival, or explicit PDF version control.</p> <h6 id="basic-example">Basic Example</h6> <p>For an accessible PDF that works with screen readers:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Accessible Report" format: pdf: pdf-standard: ua-2 ---</code></pre> <h6 id="supported-standards">Supported Standards</h6> <p>You can specify one or more standards. Quarto checks that the standards are supported by your output format and infers a compatible PDF version (some standards have maximum version requirements).</p> <p>Standard</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>ua-2</code></p> <p>PDF/UA-2 for screen reader accessibility</p> <p><code>a-1b</code></p> <p>PDF/A-1 for long-term archival</p> <p><code>a-2a</code>, <code>a-2b</code>, <code>a-2u</code></p> <p>PDF/A-2 archival with newer features</p> <p><code>a-3a</code>, <code>a-3b</code>, <code>a-3u</code></p> <p>PDF/A-3 archival allowing embedded files</p> <p><code>a-4</code>, <code>a-4f</code></p> <p>PDF/A-4 (based on PDF 2.0)</p> <p><code>x-4</code>, <code>x-4p</code>, <code>x-5g</code>, <code>x-5n</code>, <code>x-5pg</code>, <code>x-6</code>, <code>x-6n</code>, <code>x-6p</code></p> <p>PDF/X for print production</p> <p><code>1.4</code>, <code>1.5</code>, <code>1.6</code>, <code>1.7</code>, <code>2.0</code></p> <p>Explicit PDF version</p> <p>WarningQuote numeric-only versions</p> <p>When specifying only a PDF version like <code>1.7</code> or <code>2.0</code>, use quotes so YAML treats it as a string: <code>pdf-standard: "1.7"</code>.</p> <h6 id="combining-standards">Combining Standards</h6> <p>It’s common to combine PDF/A (archival) with PDF/UA (accessibility) for documents that need both long-term preservation and screen reader support:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: pdf-standard: [a-4f, ua-2]</code></pre> <p>You can only specify one standard from each family (one PDF/A variant, one PDF/UA variant, etc.).</p> <h6 id="accessibility-requirements">Accessibility Requirements</h6> <p>Although Quarto can’t on its own guarantee accessibility requirements are met, many are satisfied through the Markdown structure of the document:</p> <ul> <li>Document metadata: YAML fields like <code>title</code>, <code>author</code>, <code>date</code>, and <code>lang</code> are propagated into the PDF document metadata, fulfilling metadata requirements for accessibility and archival standards.</li> <li>Document tagging: Markdown provides the semantic structure to fulfill tagging requirements. Pandoc enables PDF tagging for LaTeX when you specify a standard that requires it (PDF/UA standards and PDF/A “a” variants like <code>a-2a</code>).</li> <li>Alt text propagation: Alt text from <code>fig-alt</code> attributes is passed through to the PDF for screen readers. See Figures for details on specifying alt text. Use validation (described below) to identify accessibility issues in your documents that may require manual attention.</li> </ul> <h6 id="validation-with-verapdf">Validation with veraPDF</h6> <p>When <code>pdf-standard</code> is set, Quarto can validate your output against PDF/A and PDF/UA specifications using <a href="https://verapdf.org/">veraPDF</a>. Install it with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install verapdf</code></pre> <p>NoteJava required</p> <p>veraPDF requires a stable version of Java: 8, 11, 17, or 21.</p> <p>Alternatively, set the <code>QUARTO_VERAPDF</code> environment variable to your veraPDF command or path, or have veraPDF available in your .</p> <p>Once installed, validation runs automatically after rendering. Any compliance issues appear as warnings in your render output, helping you identify accessibility or archival problems in your documents.</p> <h5 id="fonts-2">Fonts</h5> <p>Using <code>lualatex</code>, the default engine, or the <code>xelatex</code> engine, you can specify fonts with the YAML options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Document Element</p> <p><code>sansfont</code></p> <p>Headings</p> <p><code>mainfont</code></p> <p>Main body text</p> <p><code>monofont</code></p> <p>Code</p> <p><code>mathfont</code></p> <p>Math</p> <p><code>CJKmainfont</code></p> <p>The CJK main font family</p> <p>Values for these options should be the family name of system installed fonts. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- format: pdf: mainfont: "Times New Roman" ---</code></pre> <p>Fonts are set using the <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/fontspec"><code>fontspec</code></a> package. You can set additional font features using the corresponding <code><fontoption>options</code> key. For example, you could set headings to the color <code>#39729E</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- format: pdf: sansfont: "Open Sans" sansfontoptions: - Color=39729E ---</code></pre> <h6 id="pdflatex"><code>pdflatex</code></h6> <p>If you use the <code>pdflatex</code> engine, use the <code>fontfamily</code> option to specify a font from the <a href="https://tug.org/FontCatalogue/">The LaTeX Font Catalogue</a>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: pdflatex fonts format: pdf: pdf-engine: pdflatex fontfamily: anttor ---</code></pre> <h5 id="unicode-characters">Unicode Characters</h5> <p>By default, Quarto uses the <code>lualatex</code> engine to produce PDFs from LaTeX. <code>lualatex</code> has native support for unicode characters, but it is possible some customization will be required in order to properly typeset specific unicode characters. In particular, it is important that you use a font that supports the characters that you are using in your document. To identify fonts on your system that support specific language characters, you can use the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal fc-list :lang=<lang> family</code></pre> <p>Where <code><lang></code> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_639_language_codes">ISO 639 language code</a>. For example, to see a list of fonts that support Japanese characters, use:</p> <pre><code>Terminal fc-list :lang=ja family</code></pre> <p>Select a font name from the list and use that as the document’s main font:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Unicode test format: pdf mainfont: "Hiragino Sans GB" --- ## Test Document 青黑體簡體中文,ヒラギノ角</code></pre> <p>Another common example of Unicode characters are documents that include Greek symbols:</p> <pre><code>greek.qmd --- format: pdf --- ## α ```r α <- 3 ``` α is a great constant. ```</code></pre> <p>Follow the same process as above to discover fonts that support Greek:</p> <pre><code>Terminal fc-list :lang=el family</code></pre> <p>Then set the appropriate font options:</p> <pre><code>greek.qmd --- format: pdf: mainfont: "EB Garamond" sansfont: "Open Sans" monofont: "Roboto Mono" ---</code></pre> <p>(These particular fonts are available from <a href="https://fonts.google.com">Google Fonts</a>.)</p> <p>With fonts with appropriate support, Greek symbols render correctly in headings, the main text and code cells:</p> <p>Greek symbols in a rendered PDF</p> <h2 id="svg-images">SVG Images</h2> <h3 id="using-rsvg-convert-to-convert-to-pdf">Using <code>rsvg-convert</code> to convert to PDF</h3> <p>Quarto supports rendering of PDF documents that include SVG files, automatically converting them to PDF images if <code>rsvg-convert</code> is available on the system path during rendering.</p> <p>You can learn more about installing <code>librsvg</code> (which provides <code>rsvg-convert</code>), see https://wiki.gnome.org/Projects/LibRsvg. To install on specific platforms:</p> <ul> <li><p>On MacOS, use Homebrew: <code>brew install librsvg</code></p></li> <li><p>On Linux, tarballs available at: https://download.gnome.org/sources/librsvg/</p></li> <li><p>On Windows, install using chocolatey: <code>choco install rsvg-convert</code> or using Scoop:</p> <p># scoop bucket add r-bucket https://github.com/cderv/r-bucket.git scoop install rsvg-convert</p></li> </ul> <h3 id="alternative-using-inkscape">Alternative: Using Inkscape</h3> <p>If you prefer to use Inkscape instead of <code>rsvg-convert</code>, you can disable the default conversion by setting <code>use-rsvg-convert: false</code>. This will use the <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/svg">SVG LaTeX package</a> to include the svg using <code>\includesvg{}</code> which uses Inkscape to convert to PDF. This requires some configuration to opt-in:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: use-rsvg-convert: false pdf-engine-opts: ["-shell-escape"]</code></pre> <p>Note that this configuration requires:</p> <ul> <li>Inkscape to be installed and available on your system PATH</li> <li>The <code>-shell-escape</code> option for your LaTeX engine to allow execution of external programs</li> <li>The SVG LaTeX package (automatically included by Quarto)</li> </ul> <h3 id="platform-considerations">Platform Considerations</h3> <p>The availability and ease of installation for SVG conversion tools varies by platform:</p> <ul> <li>Linux/macOS: <code>rsvg-convert</code> is typically available through package managers (<code>librsvg</code> package). This is the recommended approach for these platforms.</li> <li>Windows: Installing <code>rsvg-convert</code> is more challenging. While it can be installed via Scoop (as shown above), most Windows users should consider using PNG format for diagrams rather than SVG.</li> <li>Inkscape: Available cross-platform but requires the <code>-shell-escape</code> configuration. Consider using this only when you specifically need Inkscape’s rendering capabilities. For diagram formats, PNG is generally recommended for best compatibility and ease of use. See the Note 1 below for more details.</li> </ul> <p>Note 1: SVG Format for Diagrams</p> <p>When using Mermaid or Graphviz diagrams in PDF documents, the default PNG format is recommended. While SVG output is possible with <code>mermaid-format: svg</code>, it requires external tooling:</p> <ul> <li><code>rsvg-convert</code> (default) - See installation instructions above</li> <li>Inkscape (alternative) - Requires <code>use-rsvg-convert: false</code> and <code>-shell-escape</code> configuration SVG format may also have rendering issues such as text clipping in diagrams with multi-line labels. For most users, PNG format provides better compatibility and ease of use. See Diagrams for more information.</li> </ul> <h2 id="remote-images">Remote Images</h2> <p>You can reference remote images directly using URLs:</p> <pre><code>![Penguins](https://example.com/images/penguins.png)</code></pre> <p>Images are automatically downloaded during rendering and embedded in the PDF.</p> <h2 id="citations-4">Citations</h2> <p>When creating PDFs, you can choose to use either the default Pandoc <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#citations">citation handling</a> based on citeproc, or alternatively use <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/natbib">natbib</a> or <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/biblatex">BibLaTeX</a>. This can be controlled using the <code>cite-method</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: cite-method: biblatex</code></pre> <p>The default is to use <code>citeproc</code> (Pandoc’s built in citation processor).</p> <p>See the main article on using Citations with Quarto for additional details on citation syntax, available bibliography formats, etc.</p> <h3 id="options-38">Options</h3> <p>When using natbib or biblatex you can specify the following additional options to affect how bibliographies are rendered:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p>biblatexoptions</p> <p>List of options for biblatex</p> <p>natbiboptions</p> <p>List of options for natbib</p> <p>biblio-title</p> <p>Title for bibliography</p> <p>biblio-style</p> <p>Style for bibliography</p> <h2 id="raw-latex">Raw LaTeX</h2> <p>When creating a PDF document, Pandoc allows the use of <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#extension-raw_tex">raw LaTeX</a> directives intermixed with markdown. Although Pandoc allows LaTeX to appear unescaped in Markdown, we instead recommend to wrap the content in a raw block. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{=latex} \begin{tabular}{|l|l|}\hline Age & Frequency \\ \hline 18--25 & 15 \\ 26--35 & 33 \\ 36--45 & 22 \\ \hline \end{tabular} ```</code></pre> <p>Raw LaTeX can be specified as a block element (as shown above), or as an inline element, such as ``. Raw LaTeX commands will be preserved and passed unchanged to the LaTeX writer.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>While it’s very convenient to use raw LaTeX, raw LaTeX is ignored when rendering to other formats like HTML and MS Word. If you plan on rendering to other formats then the example above would be better written using native markdown tables.</p> <p>In some cases raw LaTeX will require additional LaTeX packages. The LaTeX Includes section below describes how to include <code>\usepackage</code> commands for these packages in your document.</p> <h2 id="latex-includes">LaTeX Includes</h2> <p>If you want to include additional content in your document from another file, you can use the <code>include-in-*</code> options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>include-in-header</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the header. This can be used, for example, to include special CSS or JavaScript in HTML documents or to inject commands into the LaTeX preamble.</p> <p><code>include-before-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the beginning of the document body (e.g. after the <code><body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\begin{document}</code> command in LaTeX). This can be used to include navigation bars or banners in HTML documents.</p> <p><code>include-after-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the document body (before the <code></body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\end{document}</code> command in LaTeX).</p> <p>You can specify a single file or multiple files for each of these options directly, or use the <code>file:</code> subkey. To include raw content in the YAML header, use the <code>text</code> subkey. When using <code>text:</code>, add the <code>|</code> character after <code>text:</code> to indicate that the value is a multi-line string. If you omit <code>file:</code> or <code>text:</code>, Quarto assumes you are providing a file.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>format: pdf: include-in-header: - text: | \usepackage{eplain} \usepackage{easy-todo} - file: packages.tex - macros.tex</code></pre> <p>Any packages specified using includes that you don’t already have installed locally will be installed by Quarto during the rendering of the document.</p> <h2 id="latex-output-1">LaTeX Output</h2> <p>If you want Quarto to produce a LaTeX file (<code>.tex</code>) rather than a PDF (for example, if you want to do your own processing of the PDF) there are two ways to accomplish this:</p> <ul> <li><p>Use the <code>latex</code> format rather than the <code>pdf</code> format. For example:</p> <p>format: latex: documentclass: report classoption: [twocolumn, landscape] lof: true lot: true</p></li> <li><p>Note that all of the PDF format options documented above will also work for the <code>latex</code> format.</p></li> <li><p>Use the <code>pdf</code> format along with the <code>keep-tex</code> option. For example:</p> <p>format: pdf: documentclass: report keep-tex: true</p></li> <li><p>This technique will produce a PDF file for preview, but will also create a <code>.tex</code> file alongside it that you can do subsequent processing on. Both techniques will also produce all LaTeX temporary files, including <code>.bbl</code> files and so on, that might be required by a publisher that wants LaTeX sources. ```</p></li> </ul> <h3 id="pdf-engines">PDF Engines</h3> <h4 id="pdf-engines-1">PDF Engines</h4> <h5 id="overview-91">Overview</h5> <p>Pandoc supports the use of a wide range of TeX distributions and PDF compilation engines including pdflatex, xelatex, lualatex, tectonic, and latexmk.</p> <p>While you can employ whatever toolchain you like for LaTeX compilation, we strongly recommend the use of <a href="https://yihui.org/tinytex/">TinyTeX</a>, which is a distribution of <a href="https://tug.org/texlive/">TeX Live</a> that provides a reasonably sized initial download (~100 MB) that includes the 200 or so most commonly used TeX packages for Pandoc documents.</p> <p>We also recommend the use of Quarto’s built in PDF compilation engine, which among other things performs automatic installation of any missing TeX packages.</p> <h5 id="installing-tex">Installing TeX</h5> <p>To install TinyTeX, use the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install tinytex</code></pre> <p>TinyTeX is not installed to the system <code>PATH</code> so will not affect other applications that use TeX. If you want to use TinyTeX with other applications, add the <code>--update-path</code> flag when installing (this will add TinyTex to the system path):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install tinytex --update-path</code></pre> <p>If you already have another installation of TeX that you prefer to use with Quarto, add the <code>latex-tinytex: false</code> in your project or document front matter to prevent Quarto from using its internal version.</p> <p>If you prefer TeX Live, you can find instructions for installing it here: <a href="https://tug.org/texlive/">tug.org</a>.</p> <p>Note that Quarto’s automatic installation of missing TeX packages will work for TinyTeX and TeX Live, but not for other TeX distributions (as it relies on TeX Live’s <a href="https://www.tug.org/texlive/tlmgr.html">tlmgr</a> command).</p> <h5 id="managing-tex">Managing TeX</h5> <p>In addition to installing TinyTeX, you may also update or remove the installation of TinyTex. To see the currently installed version of TinyTex, use the command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto list tools</code></pre> <p>which will provide a list of available tools, the installed versions, and the latest available version:</p> <pre><code>[✓] Inspecting tools Tool Status Installed Latest chrome-headless-shell Not installed --- 147.0.7727.56 chromium Not installed --- 869685 tinytex Up to date v2026.04 v2026.04 verapdf Not installed --- 1.28.2</code></pre> <p>To update to the latest version, use the command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto update tinytex</code></pre> <p>which will download and install the latest version of TinyTex (following the same behavior as described for installing TinyTex above).</p> <p>To remove TinyTex altogether, use the command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto uninstall tinytex</code></pre> <p>Tip</p> <p>Each year in April, TeXlive updates their remote package repository to the new year’s version of TeX. When this happens, previous year installations of TeX will not be able to download and install packages from the remote repository. When this happens, you may see an error like:</p> <p>Your TexLive version is not updated enough to connect to the remote repository and download packages. Please update your installation of TexLive or TinyTex.</p> <p>When this happens, you can use <code>quarto update tinytex</code> to download and install an updated version of tinytex.</p> <h5 id="quarto-pdf-engine">Quarto PDF Engine</h5> <p>Quarto’s built-in PDF compilation engine handles running LaTeX multiple times to resolve index and bibliography entries, and also performs automatic LaTeX package installation. This section describes customizing the built-in engine (see the Alternate PDF Engines section below for docs on using other engines).</p> <h6 id="pdf-compilation">PDF Compilation</h6> <p>The following options are available for customizing PDF compilation:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>latex-min-runs</code></p> <p>Number (minimum number of compilation passes)</p> <p><code>latex-max-runs</code></p> <p>Number (maximum number of compilation passes)</p> <p><code>latex-clean</code></p> <p>Boolean (clean intermediates after compilation, defaults to <code>true</code>)</p> <p><code>latex-output-dir</code></p> <p>String (output directory for intermediates and PDF)</p> <p><code>latex-makeindex</code></p> <p>String (program to use for <code>makeindex</code>)</p> <p><code>latex-makeindex-opts</code></p> <p>Array (options for <code>makeindex</code>program)</p> <h6 id="package-installation">Package Installation</h6> <p>The following options are available for customizing automatic package installation:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>latex-auto-install</code></p> <p>Boolean (enable/disable automatic package installation)</p> <p><code>latex-tlmgr-opts</code></p> <p>Array (options for <a href="https://www.tug.org/texlive/tlmgr.html">tlmgr</a>)</p> <h5 id="alternate-pdf-engines">Alternate PDF Engines</h5> <p>You can use the <code>pdf-engine</code> and <code>pdf-engine-opts</code> to control the PDF engine that Quarto uses to compile the LaTeX output into a PDF. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Document" pdf-engine: xelatex pdf-engine-opts: - '--no-shell-escape' - '--halt-on-error'</code></pre> <p>The above example will use the <code>xelatex</code> PDF engine with some specific options, rather than the default <code>lualatex</code>.</p> <h5 id="latexmk">Latexmk</h5> <p>Quarto includes a built-in Latexmk engine, which will run the <code>pdf-engine</code> more than once to generate your PDF (for example, if you are using cross references or a bibliography). In addition, this engine will detect and attempt to install missing packages, fonts, or commands if TeX Live is available.</p> <p>You can disable Quarto’s built-in Latexmk engine by setting the <code>latex-auto-mk</code> option to <code>false</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Document" latex-auto-mk: false</code></pre> <p>Engine options can still be set using <code>pdf-engine-opts</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>latex-auto-mk: false pdf-engine: latexmk pdf-engine-opts: - '-auxdir=custom-aux' - '-emulate-aux-dir'</code></pre> <p>The above example will use <code>latexmk</code> as a PDF engine and set some options to modify the directory name for auxiliary files.</p> <h3 id="publishing-html">Publishing HTML</h3> <h4 id="publishing-html-1">Publishing HTML</h4> <h5 id="overview-92">Overview</h5> <p>This article covers the various ways you can publish Quarto HTML documents, including publishing to a hosting service or sharing a standalone HTML file using E-mail, Dropbox, etc.</p> <p>Note that it’s also possible to publish collections of Quarto documents as a website. See the article on Publishing Basics for additional details.</p> <h5 id="publish-command">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command provides a straightforward way to publish documents to Quarto Pub, GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Posit Connect.</p> <p>For example, here are the commands to publish <code>document.qmd</code> to each of these services:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish quarto-pub document.qmd quarto publish gh-pages document.qmd quarto publish netlify document.qmd quarto publish connect document.qmd</code></pre> <p>For simple publishing of individual documents there’s not much more to learn than <code>quarto publish</code>.</p> <p>Here’s a brief overview of the various supported services and when they might be an appropriate choice:</p> <p>Destination</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Quarto Pub</p> <p>Publishing service for Quarto documents, websites, and books. Use Quarto Pub when you want a free, easy to use service for publicly available content.</p> <p>GitHub Pages</p> <p>Publish content based on source code managed within a GitHub repository. Use GitHub Pages when the source code for your document or site is hosted on GitHub.</p> <p>Posit Connect</p> <p>Publishing platform for secure sharing of data products within an organization. Use Posit Connect when you want to publish content within an organization rather than on the public internet.</p> <p>Netlify</p> <p>Professional web publishing platform. Use Netlify when you want support for custom domains, authentication, previewing branches, and other more advanced capabilities.</p> <p>Other Services</p> <p>Content rendered with Quarto uses standard formats (HTML, PDFs, MS Word, etc.) that can be published anywhere. Use this if one of the methods above don’t meet your requirements.</p> <p>Note that the documentation linked to above generally references publishing an entire project (website or book) but all of the commands work just the same if you publish an individual document or presentation as demonstrated above.</p> <h5 id="standalone-html">Standalone HTML</h5> <p>You can optionally render Quarto documents into self contained HTML, whereby all of the content required to render the article (images generated by plots, required CSS and JavaScript, etc.) are bundled into a single HTML file. Use the <code>embed-resources</code> option to do this:</p> <pre><code>format: html: embed-resources: true</code></pre> <p>Then, you can share this HTML file using the same means you use to share other document types like spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs (e.g by uploading it to Dropbox or any other file sharing service).</p> <p>Note that when using <code>embed-resources: true</code>, math libraries like <a href="https://www.mathjax.org/">MathJax</a> and <a href="https://katex.org/">KaTeX</a> are not embedded by default because they are quite large and often time consuming to download. If you do want to embed math libraries, add the <code>self-contained-math: true</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: html: embed-resources: true self-contained-math: true</code></pre> <h3 id="typst-basics">Typst Basics</h3> <h4 id="typst-basics-1">Typst Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-93">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://typst.app/">Typst</a> is a new open-source markup-based typesetting system that is designed to be as powerful as LaTeX while being much easier to learn and use. Typst creates beautiful PDF output with blazing fast render times.</p> <p>Use the <code>typst</code> format to create a PDF document via Typst. For example:</p> <pre><code>hello-typst.qmd --- title: "Hello Typst!" format: typst: toc: true section-numbering: 1.1.a columns: 2 ---</code></pre> <p>Rendering or previewing this document will invoke the Typst CLI to create <code>hello-typst.pdf</code>, a PDF file, from your markdown source file. Quarto includes the Typst CLI so no separate installation of Typst is required.</p> <p>The above example highlights a few of the options available for Typst output. This document covers these and other options in detail. See the Typst format reference for a complete list of all available options.</p> <p>One of the highlights of Typst is the ease of creating highly customized templates. For example, here are some Typst templates that you can use in Quarto as custom formats:</p> <p>IEEE</p> <p>Poster</p> <p>Letter</p> <p>Dept News</p> <p>Learn more about how to use them, and how to create your own in Custom Formats.</p> <p>Typst is also supported for book projects.</p> <h5 id="known-limitations">Known Limitations</h5> <p>Since Typst is under active development, there are still some limitations to Quarto’s Typst support:</p> <ul> <li>The default size of images may not reflect the behavior you are used to in other output formats. This is a problem that Typst, pandoc and Quarto are actively working to fix. In the meantime, you can manually specify image widths.</li> <li>Various other small things might not yet be implemented. Please <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/new/choose">let us know</a> if you see things that could use improvement!</li> </ul> <h5 id="page-layout-4">Page Layout</h5> <p>You can control the size of the page (<code>papersize</code>), the page margins (<code>margin</code>), the number of columns used for page content (<code>columns</code>), and the page numbering (<code>page-numbering</code>). For example, the following YAML modifies the first three options:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Page Layout format: typst: papersize: a5 margin: x: 1cm y: 1cm columns: 2 ---</code></pre> <p>The resulting layout is shown below alongside an example of the default layout:</p> <p>Customized Layout</p> <p>Default Layout</p> <p>You can read more about these page layout options in the sections below.</p> <h6 id="paper-size">Paper Size</h6> <p>The <code>papersize</code> option expects a string matching one of Typst’s supported <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/page/#parameters-paper">paper sizes</a>. The default template is equivalent to:</p> <pre><code>papersize: us-letter</code></pre> <h6 id="margins">Margins</h6> <p>The <code>margin</code> option expects one or more of the suboptions: <code>x</code>, <code>y</code>, <code>top</code>, <code>bottom</code>, <code>left</code> and <code>right</code>. The default template uses margins equivalent to:</p> <pre><code>margin: x: 1.25in y: 1.25in</code></pre> <p>This sets the margins in the horizontal direction (<code>x</code>), i.e. <code>left</code> and <code>right</code>, as well as the margins in the vertical direction (<code>y</code>), i.e. <code>top</code> and <code>bottom</code> to 1.25 inches.</p> <p>The values for the margins are specified using Typst’s <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/length/">length</a>, (e.g. <code>5cm</code>) or <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/relative/">relative length</a> (e.g. <code>10%</code>) types. You can specify a single margin:</p> <pre><code>margin: left: 1cm</code></pre> <p>Then, any unspecified margins will inherit from the default margins.</p> <h6 id="columns">Columns</h6> <p>The <code>columns</code> option expects a number - the number of columns your body content should have. The default template sets <code>columns</code> to <code>1</code>.</p> <h6 id="page-numbering">Page Numbering</h6> <p>The <code>page-numbering</code> option expects a string that describes a <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/model/numbering/">Typst numbering</a> pattern. For example, the default, <code>1</code>, numbers pages with arabic numerals, and <code>i</code> numbers pages with lower case roman numerals. To omit page numbers, set <code>page-numbering</code> to <code>false</code>:</p> <pre><code>page-numbering: false</code></pre> <h5 id="table-of-contents-4">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Use the <code>toc</code> option to include an automatically generated table of contents in the output document. Use the <code>toc-depth</code> option to specify the number of section levels to include in the table of contents. The default is 3 (which means that level-1, 2, and 3 headings will be listed in the contents). For example:</p> <pre><code>toc: true toc-depth: 2</code></pre> <p>You can customize the title used for the table of contents using the <code>toc-title</code> option:</p> <pre><code>toc-title: Contents</code></pre> <p>If you want to exclude a heading from the table of contents, add both the <code>.unnumbered</code> and <code>.unlisted</code> classes to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered .unlisted}</code></pre> <p>The <code>toc-indent</code> option controls how far entries are indented in the displayed table of contents. The default is equivalent to:</p> <pre><code>toc-indent: 1.5em</code></pre> <h5 id="section-numbering-2">Section Numbering</h5> <p>Use the <code>number-sections</code> option to number section headings in the output document. For example:</p> <pre><code>number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>number-depth</code> option to specify the deepest level of heading to add numbers to (by default all headings are numbered). For example:</p> <pre><code>number-depth: 3</code></pre> <p>To exclude an individual heading from numbering, add the <code>.unnumbered</code> class to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered}</code></pre> <p>You can also customize the display of the section numbers with the <code>section-numbering</code> YAML option. This option expects a string that describes the numbering schema. For example, the following schema describes numbering sections with numerals, subsection with uppercase letters, and subsubsections with lower case letters, using <code>.</code> as a separator:</p> <pre><code>--- section-numbering: 1.A.a ---</code></pre> <p>You can read more about specifying the numbering schema in the <a href="https://typst.app//docs/reference/model/numbering#parameters-numbering">Typst documentation for numbering</a>.</p> <h5 id="syntax-highlighting-1">Syntax Highlighting</h5> <p>Pandoc will automatically highlight syntax in <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#fenced-code-blocks">fenced code blocks</a> that are marked with a language name. For example:</p> <pre><code>```python 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Pandoc can provide syntax highlighting for over 140 different languages (see the output of <code>quarto pandoc --list-highlight-languages</code> for a list of all of them). If you want to provide the appearance of a highlighted code block for a language not supported, just use <code>default</code> as the language name.</p> <p>You can specify the code highlighting style using <code>syntax-highlighting</code> and specifying one of the supported themes. Supported themes include: a11y, arrow, pygments, tango, espresso, zenburn, kate, monochrome, breezedark, haddock, atom-one, ayu, breeze, dracula, github, gruvbox, monokai, nord, oblivion, printing, radical, solarized, and vim.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>syntax-highlighting: github</code></pre> <p>In addition to theme names, <code>syntax-highlighting</code> accepts two special values:</p> <ul> <li><code>none</code> — disables syntax highlighting entirely.</li> <li><code>idiomatic</code> — delegates highlighting to the output format’s native system instead of Pandoc’s built-in Skylighting engine. ImportantChanged Default for Typst</li> </ul> <p>Starting with Quarto 1.9, Typst output uses Pandoc’s Skylighting engine for syntax highlighting by default, with the same themes available as HTML and LaTeX. Previously, Typst used its own native code highlighting.</p> <p>To restore the previous behavior, set <code>syntax-highlighting: idiomatic</code>.</p> <p>For Typst, setting <code>syntax-highlighting: idiomatic</code> delegates highlighting to Typst’s built-in code highlighting. In this mode, Typst receives plain fenced code blocks and applies its <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/text/raw/#styling">own styling</a>. This may be preferred when using custom Typst templates that style code blocks.</p> <p>Highlighting themes can provide either a single highlighting definition or two definitions, one optimized for a light colored background and another optimized for a dark color background. When available, Quarto will automatically select the appropriate style based upon the code chunk background color’s darkness. You may always opt to specify the full name (e.g. <code>atom-one-dark</code>) to bypass this automatic behavior.</p> <p>By default, code is highlighted using the <code>arrow</code> theme, which is optimized for accessibility. Here are examples of the <code>arrow</code> light and dark themes:</p> <ul> <li>Light</li> <li>Dark</li> </ul> <h5 id="code-annotation-7">Code Annotation</h5> <p>You can add annotations to lines of code in code blocks and executable code cells. See Code Annotation for full details.</p> <h5 id="article-layout-6">Article Layout</h5> <p>Quarto’s Typst format supports Tufte-style article layouts with margin content, full-width figures, and sidenotes, via the <a href="https://typst.app/universe/package/marginalia">Marginalia</a> package. See Article Layout for the complete guide to column classes and margin content.</p> <h6 id="grid-customization-1">Grid Customization</h6> <p>You can customize the width of the margin and body columns using the <code>grid</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: typst: grid: margin-width: 2in body-width: 4in gutter-width: 0.25in</code></pre> <p>Grid options for Typst</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>margin-width</code></p> <p>Width of the margin note column</p> <p><code>body-width</code></p> <p>Width of the main text column</p> <p><code>gutter-width</code></p> <p>Gap between body text and margin</p> <p>Note: <code>sidebar-width</code> does not apply to Typst output (there is no sidebar in PDF documents).</p> <p>For HTML grid customization, see Page Layout - Grid Customization.</p> <h6 id="margin-geometry">Margin Geometry</h6> <p>For fine-grained control over margin layout, use the <code>margin-geometry</code> option. This directly configures the underlying <a href="https://typst.app/universe/package/marginalia">Marginalia</a> package.</p> <pre><code>format: typst: margin-geometry: outer: far: 5mm width: 2in separation: 0.25in inner: far: 5mm width: 0in separation: 0in clearance: 8pt</code></pre> <p>Margin geometry options</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>outer.far</code></p> <p>Distance from outer page edge to wideblock boundary</p> <p><code>outer.width</code></p> <p>Width of the outer margin note column</p> <p><code>outer.separation</code></p> <p>Gap between outer margin and body text</p> <p><code>inner.*</code></p> <p>Same options for inner margin (left side on recto pages)</p> <p><code>clearance</code></p> <p>Minimum vertical spacing between margin notes (default 12pt)</p> <p>Quarto computes margin geometry based on <code>papersize</code>, using proportions from <a href="https://typst.app/universe/package/marginalia">Marginalia’s</a> A4 example.</p> <h5 id="bibliography">Bibliography</h5> <p>Typst comes with its <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/model/bibliography/">own citation processing system for bibliographies</a> and using <code>format: typst</code> defaults to it.</p> <p>Use the <code>csl</code> option to specify a bibliography style for Typst’s citation processing. The value can be a path to a CSL file or one of <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/model/bibliography/#parameters-style">Typst’s built-in styles</a>:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- bibliography: refs.bib csl: my-style.csl --- document.qmd --- bibliography: refs.bib csl: apa ---</code></pre> <p>The <code>bibliographystyle</code> option is also supported and accepts the same values as <code>csl</code>.</p> <p>If you prefer to use Pandoc’s citation processing instead of Typst’s, set <code>citeproc: true</code> explicitly:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- citeproc: true bibliography: refs.bib csl: [zotero.org](https://www.zotero.org/styles/apa-with-abstract) ---</code></pre> <p>See Citation Style for more on specifying citation styles with Pandoc’s system.</p> <h5 id="typst-blocks">Typst Blocks</h5> <p>If you want to change the appearance of blocks using native <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/block/">Typst <code>#block()</code></a> calls, you can add the <code>.block</code> class to a Div and provide whatever arguments are appropriate. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.block fill="luma(230)" inset="8pt" radius="4pt"} This is a block with gray background and slightly rounded corners. :::</code></pre> <p>This gets compiled to</p> <pre><code>#block(fill:luma(230), inset:8pt, radius:4pt, [This is a block with gray background and slightly rounded corners.])</code></pre> <h5 id="theorems">Theorems</h5> <p>Quarto uses the <a href="https://typst.app/universe/package/theorion">theorion</a> package for theorems in Typst output. You can control the appearance of theorems, lemmas, proofs, and related blocks using the <code>theorem-appearance</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: typst: theorem-appearance: fancy</code></pre> <p>Appearance</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>simple</code></p> <p>Classic LaTeX-style theorems (default)</p> <p><code>fancy</code></p> <p>Colored boxes using brand colors</p> <p><code>clouds</code></p> <p>Rounded backgrounds</p> <p><code>rainbow</code></p> <p>Colored left border with colored title</p> <p>The <code>fancy</code> appearance integrates with <code>_brand.yml</code>, using your brand colors for theorem boxes.</p> <h5 id="raw-typst">Raw Typst</h5> <p>If you want to use raw <code>typst</code> markup, use a raw <code>typst</code> block. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{=typst} #set par(justify: true) == Background In the case of glaciers, fluid dynamics principles can be used to understand how the movement and behavior of the ice is influenced by factors such as temperature, pressure, and the presence of other fluids (such as water). ```</code></pre> <p>To learn more about <code>typst</code> markup, see the tutorial here: <a href="https://typst.app/docs/tutorial/">typst.app</a>.</p> <h5 id="typst-css-2">Typst CSS</h5> <p>To allow similar styling between HTML and Typst, Quarto will translate CSS properties into Typst properties.</p> <p>You can use CSS properties directly in your Quarto markup, and they will get translated to appropriate Typst elements and properties.</p> <p>For example, text-related properties <code>color</code>, <code>opacity</code>, and <code>background-color</code> can be applied to spans:</p> <pre><code>Here is a [span with a green background]{style="background-color:green"}.</code></pre> <p><code>font-family</code> and <code>font-size</code> can be applied to a div or table:</p> <pre><code>:::{style="font-family: helvetica"} This div is rendered in Helvetica. :::</code></pre> <p>See the Advanced documentation for supported elements and properties, and how to add more using Lua filters.</p> <p>You are most likely to encounter Typst CSS when using libraries that produce HTML tables. The translation of the CSS means your table in Typst should look similar to how it looks in HTML without any intervention on your part.</p> <p>For example, here is a temperature heatmap using <code>gt</code> in R, and <code>pandas</code> in Python.</p> <ul> <li><p>R - gt</p></li> <li><p>Python - Pandas</p> <p>```{r} library(gt) temps <- data.frame( year = c(1920:1924), Jan = c(40.6, 44.2, 37.5, 41.8, 39.3), Jun = c(58.5, 58.7, 57.8, 52.7, 57.7) ) temps |> gt() |> data_color( columns = c(-year), fn = scales::col_numeric( colorspace::diverge_hcl(n = 9, palette = “Green-Orange”), domain = c(35, 62)) )</p> <pre><code> ```{python} import pandas as pd import numpy as np temps = pd.DataFrame({ 'year': [*range(1920, 1925)], 'Jan': [40.6, 44.2, 37.5, 41.8, 39.3], 'Jun': [58.5, 58.7, 57.8, 52.7, 57.7] }).set_index('year') def make_pretty(styler): styler.background_gradient(axis=None, vmin=31, vmax=66, cmap="RdYlGn_r") return styler temps.style.pipe(make_pretty) </code></pre></li> </ul> <p>Note that <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/visualize/color/#predefined-colors">named Typst colors</a> will be preferred over <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/named-color">named CSS colors</a>. If you want exactly the same color in your HTML and Typst output, specify the color using <code>rgb()</code> or hexadecimal <code>#rrggbb</code> syntax.</p> <p>Typst does not support opacity as a filter, so opacity is simulated using the alpha channel of the color.</p> <h5 id="pdf-accessibility-standards-1">PDF Accessibility & Standards</h5> <p>Create PDFs that work with screen readers and meet archival requirements using the <code>pdf-standard</code> option. This enables PDF/UA for accessibility, PDF/A for long-term archival, or explicit PDF version control.</p> <h6 id="basic-example-1">Basic Example</h6> <p>For an accessible PDF that works with screen readers:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Accessible Report" format: typst: pdf-standard: ua-1 ---</code></pre> <h6 id="supported-standards-1">Supported Standards</h6> <p>You can specify one or more standards. Quarto checks that the standards are supported by your output format and infers a compatible PDF version (some standards have maximum version requirements).</p> <p>Standard</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>ua-1</code></p> <p>PDF/UA-1 for screen reader accessibility</p> <p><code>a-1a</code>, <code>a-1b</code></p> <p>PDF/A-1 for long-term archival</p> <p><code>a-2a</code>, <code>a-2b</code>, <code>a-2u</code></p> <p>PDF/A-2 archival with newer features</p> <p><code>a-3a</code>, <code>a-3b</code>, <code>a-3u</code></p> <p>PDF/A-3 archival allowing embedded files</p> <p><code>a-4</code>, <code>a-4e</code>, <code>a-4f</code></p> <p>PDF/A-4 (based on PDF 2.0)</p> <p><code>1.4</code>, <code>1.5</code>, <code>1.6</code>, <code>1.7</code>, <code>2.0</code></p> <p>Explicit PDF version</p> <p>WarningQuote numeric-only versions</p> <p>When specifying only a PDF version like <code>1.7</code> or <code>2.0</code>, use quotes so YAML treats it as a string: <code>pdf-standard: "1.7"</code>.</p> <h6 id="combining-standards-1">Combining Standards</h6> <p>It’s common to combine PDF/A (archival) with PDF/UA (accessibility) for documents that need both long-term preservation and screen reader support:</p> <pre><code>format: typst: pdf-standard: [a-2b, ua-1]</code></pre> <p>You can only specify one standard from each family (one PDF/A variant, one PDF/UA variant, etc.).</p> <h6 id="accessibility-requirements-1">Accessibility Requirements</h6> <p>Although Quarto can’t on its own guarantee accessibility requirements are met, many are satisfied through the Markdown structure of the document:</p> <ul> <li>Document metadata: YAML fields like <code>title</code>, <code>author</code>, <code>date</code>, and <code>lang</code> are propagated into the PDF document metadata, fulfilling metadata requirements for accessibility and archival standards.</li> <li>Document tagging: Markdown provides the semantic structure to fulfill tagging requirements. Typst always has PDF tagging enabled.</li> <li>Alt text propagation: Alt text from <code>fig-alt</code> attributes is passed through to the PDF for screen readers. See Figures for details on specifying alt text. Use validation (described below) to identify accessibility issues in your documents that may require manual attention.</li> </ul> <h6 id="validation-with-verapdf-1">Validation with veraPDF</h6> <p>When <code>pdf-standard</code> is set, Quarto can validate your output against PDF/A and PDF/UA specifications using <a href="https://verapdf.org/">veraPDF</a>. Install it with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto install verapdf</code></pre> <p>NoteJava required</p> <p>veraPDF requires a stable version of Java: 8, 11, 17, or 21.</p> <p>Alternatively, set the <code>QUARTO_VERAPDF</code> environment variable to your veraPDF command or path, or have veraPDF available in your .</p> <p>Once installed, validation runs automatically after rendering. Any compliance issues appear as warnings in your render output, helping you identify accessibility or archival problems in your documents.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>Typst also validates documents against the requested standard and will fail to produce a PDF if it detects non-compliance. Its validation is thorough but not as complete as veraPDF.</p> <h6 id="image-alt-text">Image Alt Text</h6> <p>Quarto passes alt text from markdown image <code>fig-alt</code> attributes to the <code>alt</code> parameter of Typst’s <code>image()</code> function, making images accessible to screen readers. See Figures for details on specifying alt text.</p> <h6 id="equation-alt-text">Equation Alt Text</h6> <p>Equations in Typst can include alternative text for screen readers. Alt text is supported for cross-referenced equations using the <code>alt</code> attribute in the equation label:</p> <pre><code>$$ E = mc^2 $$ {#eq-einstein alt="Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation"}</code></pre> <p>The <code>alt</code> attribute provides a plain-text description of the equation’s meaning, which assistive technologies can read aloud. Mathematical notation is often inaccessible to screen readers by default, making this particularly valuable.</p> <p>WarningNo alt text on inline equations</p> <p>It is not possible under Pandoc syntax to provide alt text for inline equations. Use a cross-referenced block/display equation for PDF accessibility in Typst.</p> <p>Best practices for equation alt text:</p> <ul> <li>Describe what the equation represents, not just the symbols.</li> <li>Use plain language that conveys the equation’s purpose.</li> <li>Keep descriptions concise but meaningful. Equation</li> </ul> <p>Alt Text</p> <p><code>E = mc^2</code></p> <p>“Einstein’s mass-energy equivalence equation”</p> <p><code>a^2 + b^2 = c^2</code></p> <p>“Pythagorean theorem relating sides of a right triangle”</p> <p><code>\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))]</code></p> <p>“Chain rule for derivatives”</p> <h5 id="typst-file-.typ">Typst File (<code>.typ</code>)</h5> <p>The rendering process produces a native Typst file (<code>.typ)</code> which is then compiled to PDF using the Typst CLI. This intermediate file is then automatically removed. If you want to preserve the <code>.typ</code> file, use the <code>keep-typ</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: typst: keep-typ: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can compile a <code>.typ</code> file to PDF directly using the <code>quarto typst compile</code> command in a terminal. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto typst compile article.typ</code></pre> <p>The <code>quarto typst</code> command uses the version of Typst built in to Quarto and supports all Typst CLI actions and flags. For example, to determine the version of Typst embedded in Quarto:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto typst --version</code></pre> <h5 id="fonts-support">Fonts Support</h5> <p>The main font used for the document can be specified with the <code>mainfont</code> YAML option. Typst will search by default in installed system fonts. You can set additional paths to search using <code>font-paths</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: typst: mainfont: "Agbalumo" font-paths: myfonts ---</code></pre> <p>This will search for a <code>*.ttf</code> or <code>*.otf</code> file matching the font name in the <code>./myfonts/</code> directory, in addition to searching in installed system fonts.</p> <p>The <code>TYPST_FONT_PATHS</code> environment variable is also taken into account for compatibility with Typst configuration, but setting <code>font-paths</code> will take precedence over any path set in the <code>TYPST_FONT_PATHS</code> environment variable.</p> <p>Set the base size of the font used in the document with <code>fontsize</code>. The size used in the default template is equivalent to:</p> <pre><code>--- fontsize: 11pt ---</code></pre> <h5 id="logo-position">Logo Position</h5> <p>If there is a logo from brand.yml or specified directly in the document, Quarto’s Typst implementation allows customization of the logo position in the document (or project):</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- format: typst: logo: width: 1in location: right-top padding-right: 0.5in padding-top: 0.25in alt: Alternate alternate text ---</code></pre> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>width</code></p> <p>Width in CSS units. Default <code>1.5in</code>.</p> <p><code>location</code></p> <p>Location on the page in <code>X-Y</code>, where <code>X</code> is <code>left</code>, <code>center</code>, or <code>right</code> and Y is <code>top</code>, <code>middle</code>, or <code>bottom</code>. Applied as Typst <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/align/"><code>align</code></a>.</p> <p><code>padding</code>, <code>padding-top</code>, <code>padding-right</code>, <code>padding-bottom</code>, <code>padding-left</code></p> <p>Amount of padding to add to each side of the logo, using CSS <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/padding"><code>padding</code></a> conventions. Padding options are applied in alphabetical order. Applied as Typst <a href="https://typst.app/docs/reference/layout/block/#parameters-inset"><code>block.inset</code></a>. Default <code>padding: 0.75in</code>.</p> <h5 id="image-formats">Image Formats</h5> <h6 id="static-images">Static Images</h6> <p>Typst natively supports SVG, PNG, JPG/JPEG, GIF, and PDF image formats for static image includes. For example, you can include a PDF figure directly:</p> <pre><code>![My figure](figure.pdf)</code></pre> <p>The default extension for extension-less image paths (e.g. <code>![](elephant)</code>) is <code>.svg</code>. To use a different extension, set <code>default-image-extension</code> as described in Multiformat Figures.</p> <h6 id="computation-figure-format">Computation Figure Format</h6> <p>Typst has great support for SVG graphics, so <code>format: typst</code> defaults to <code>fig-format: svg</code>. This configuration means executable code cells that produce images will produce <code>.svg</code> output.</p> <p>If you prefer to include raster graphics, set <code>fig-format</code> to another value, like for example:</p> <pre><code>format: typst: fig-format: png</code></pre> <p>See other figure options on the Typst reference page</p> <h5 id="includes-4">Includes</h5> <p>If you want to include additional content in your document from another file, you can use the <code>include-in-*</code> options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>include-in-header</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the header. This can be used, for example, to include special CSS or JavaScript in HTML documents or to inject commands into the LaTeX preamble.</p> <p><code>include-before-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the beginning of the document body (e.g. after the <code><body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\begin{document}</code> command in LaTeX). This can be used to include navigation bars or banners in HTML documents.</p> <p><code>include-after-body</code></p> <p>Include contents of file, verbatim, at the end of the document body (before the <code></body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\end{document}</code> command in LaTeX).</p> <p>You can specify a single file or multiple files for each of these options directly, or use the <code>file:</code> subkey. To include raw content in the YAML header, use the <code>text</code> subkey. When using <code>text:</code>, add the <code>|</code> character after <code>text:</code> to indicate that the value is a multi-line string. If you omit <code>file:</code> or <code>text:</code>, Quarto assumes you are providing a file.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>format: typst: include-before-body: - text: | #show heading: set text(navy)</code></pre> <h3 id="word-basics">Word Basics</h3> <h4 id="word-basics-1">Word Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-94">Overview</h5> <p>Use the <code>docx</code> format to create MS Word output. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" format: docx: toc: true number-sections: true syntax-highlighting: github ---</code></pre> <p>This example highlights a few of the options available for MS Word output. This document covers these and other options in detail. See the Word format reference for a complete list of all available options.</p> <p>To learn about creating custom templates for use with the <code>docx</code> format, see the article on Word Templates.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-5">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Use the <code>toc</code> option to include an automatically generated table of contents in the output document. Use the <code>toc-depth</code> option to specify the number of section levels to include in the table of contents. The default is 3 (which means that level-1, 2, and 3 headings will be listed in the contents). For example:</p> <pre><code>toc: true toc-depth: 2</code></pre> <p>You can customize the title used for the table of contents using the <code>toc-title</code> option:</p> <pre><code>toc-title: Contents</code></pre> <p>If you want to exclude a heading from the table of contents, add both the <code>.unnumbered</code> and <code>.unlisted</code> classes to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered .unlisted}</code></pre> <h5 id="section-numbering-3">Section Numbering</h5> <p>Use the <code>number-sections</code> option to number section headings in the output document. For example:</p> <pre><code>number-sections: true</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>number-depth</code> option to specify the deepest level of heading to add numbers to (by default all headings are numbered). For example:</p> <pre><code>number-depth: 3</code></pre> <p>To exclude an individual heading from numbering, add the <code>.unnumbered</code> class to it:</p> <pre><code>### More Options {.unnumbered}</code></pre> <h5 id="syntax-highlighting-2">Syntax Highlighting</h5> <p>Pandoc will automatically highlight syntax in <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#fenced-code-blocks">fenced code blocks</a> that are marked with a language name. For example:</p> <pre><code>```python 1 + 1 ```</code></pre> <p>Pandoc can provide syntax highlighting for over 140 different languages (see the output of <code>quarto pandoc --list-highlight-languages</code> for a list of all of them). If you want to provide the appearance of a highlighted code block for a language not supported, just use <code>default</code> as the language name.</p> <p>You can specify the code highlighting style using <code>syntax-highlighting</code> and specifying one of the supported themes. Supported themes include: a11y, arrow, pygments, tango, espresso, zenburn, kate, monochrome, breezedark, haddock, atom-one, ayu, breeze, dracula, github, gruvbox, monokai, nord, oblivion, printing, radical, solarized, and vim.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>syntax-highlighting: github</code></pre> <p>In addition to theme names, <code>syntax-highlighting</code> accepts two special values:</p> <ul> <li><code>none</code> — disables syntax highlighting entirely.</li> <li><code>idiomatic</code> — delegates highlighting to the output format’s native system instead of Pandoc’s built-in Skylighting engine. Highlighting themes can provide either a single highlighting definition or two definitions, one optimized for a light colored background and another optimized for a dark color background. When available, Quarto will automatically select the appropriate style based upon the code chunk background color’s darkness. You may always opt to specify the full name (e.g. <code>atom-one-dark</code>) to bypass this automatic behavior.</li> </ul> <p>By default, code is highlighted using the <code>arrow</code> theme, which is optimized for accessibility. Here are examples of the <code>arrow</code> light and dark themes:</p> <ul> <li>Light</li> <li>Dark</li> </ul> <h5 id="code-annotation-8">Code Annotation</h5> <p>You can add annotations to lines of code in code blocks and executable code cells. See Code Annotation for full details.</p> <h3 id="word-templates">Word Templates</h3> <h4 id="word-templates-1">Word Templates</h4> <h5 id="using-templates">Using Templates</h5> <p>If you want to customize the appearance of MS Word output, Pandoc supports a special type of template called a reference document. Here’s an example of specifying a custom reference document for <code>docx</code>:</p> <pre><code>format: docx: reference-doc: custom-reference-doc.docx</code></pre> <p>Reference documents include sample text that uses all of the output styles used by Pandoc.</p> <p>To use a reference doc template, just copy it to your document’s directory and reference it as shown above.</p> <h5 id="creating-templates">Creating Templates</h5> <p>To create a new reference doc based on the Pandoc default, execute the following command:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto pandoc -o custom-reference-doc.docx \ --print-default-data-file reference.docx</code></pre> <p>Then, open <code>custom-reference-doc.docx</code> in MS Word and modify styles as you wish:</p> <p>You can open the Styles pane from the HOME tab in the MS Word toolbar.</p> <p>When you move the cursor to a specific element in the document, an item in the styles list will be highlighted. If you want to modify the style of any type of element, you can click the drop-down menu on the highlighted item, and you will see a dialog box like this:</p> <p>After you finish modifying the styles, you can save the document and use it as the template for future Word documents.</p> <h5 id="applying-custom-styles">Applying Custom Styles</h5> <p>Pandoc provides default styles for elements like paragraphs or code blocks and default formatting for inline elements like bold. Custom styles can be defined using divs for blocks and spans for text, so a specific style is used instead of the default.</p> <p>Set the <code>custom-style</code> attribute with the name of the style defined in the default or user-provided reference document.</p> <p>For example, this applies a text style called <code>Emphasis</code> to the <code>Get out</code> text instead of the default style for text:</p> <pre><code>[Get out]{custom-style="Emphasis"}, he said.</code></pre> <p>This will apply the paragraph style called <code>Poetry</code> to the content inside the Div (<code>:::</code>):</p> <pre><code>Dickinson starts the poem simply: ::: {custom-style="Poetry"} | A Bird came down the Walk--- | He did not know I saw--- :::</code></pre> <p>If the <code>reference.docx</code> file does not already contain the styles, they will be added to the output file with standard text as their base style. If the styles are already defined, their definitions will not be modified.</p> <p>A possible workflow could be:</p> <ul> <li>Create a document setting <code>custom-style</code> for all the styles you need,</li> <li>Render this document so that the styles are created in the output document,</li> <li>Save this document as a reference document for future rendering This ensures that the names of the styles used in <code>custom-style</code> exactly match the names of the styles defined in the reference document.</li> </ul> <p>Overall, this mechanism allows for great customization by allowing authors to define new styles in the reference document. For advanced users, this could be coupled with filters to apply a <code>custom-style</code> attribute to a filtered set of elements in the document.</p> <h2 id="prerelease-features">Prerelease features</h2> <h3 id="ast-processing-changes-in-v1.4">AST processing changes in v1.4</h3> <h4 id="ast-processing-changes-in-v1.4-1">AST processing changes in v1.4</h4> <p>In Quarto v1.3, we added support for parsing HTML tables as native Pandoc elements, so that sophisticated table layouts are available in more formats. Quarto v1.4 extends this in a few ways.</p> <h5 id="finer-control-over-table-processing">Finer control over table processing</h5> <p>In v1.3, this HTML processing could be disabled only by specifying an option in the HTML table itself, using <code>quarto-disable-processing="true"</code>.</p> <p>In v1.4, this behavior can be controlled by document- and project-level metadata, using the <code>html-table-processing: none</code> YAML option:</p> <pre><code>--- html-table-processing: none --- No HTML tables in this document will be processed. ```{r} library(huxtable) # your huxtable tables won't be processed by quarto ```</code></pre> <p>In addition, you can disable the processing selectively in parts of the document, by surrounding the elements with a fenced div having the attribute <code>{html-table-processing="none"}</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- html-table-processing: none --- No HTML tables in this document will be processed. ::: {html-table-processing="none"} ```{r} library(huxtable) # your huxtable tables won't be processed by quarto because of # the surrounding div ``` ::: ```{r} library(gt) # your gt tables will be processed as in 1.3 ```</code></pre> <h5 id="include-quarto-markdown-in-latex-raw-blocks">Include Quarto markdown in LaTeX Raw Blocks</h5> <p>In Quarto v1.3, HTML rawblocks can contain the syntax <code><span data-qmd="<<markdown-content>>"/></code> of <code><span data-qmd-base64="<<base64-encoded-markdown-content>>"</code> to allow libraries that emit raw blocks to benefit from Quarto features such as crossref resolution and shortcodes.</p> <p>In Quarto v1.4, this feature is also available in LaTeX formats. If the syntax <code>\QuartoMarkdownBase64{<<base64-encoded-markdown-content>>}</code> is detected by Quarto, the contents will be decoded, processed in Quarto (including user filters), and then inserted back into the LaTeX raw block.</p> <p>This is useful for third-party libraries that seek to emit LaTeX content that nevertheless can have “quarto content”. Note that, unlike the HTML feature, Quarto currently only supports base-64 encoded content in LaTeX blocks.</p> <p>Note that, unlike the HTML table parsing feature, this LaTeX feature cannot currently be disabled. We expect this to not be necessary because <code>QuartoMarkdownBase64</code> is unlikely to conflict with existing LaTeX environments.</p> <h3 id="behind-the-scenes-changes-to-cross-references">Behind the Scenes Changes to Cross-References</h3> <h4 id="behind-the-scenes-changes-to-cross-references-1">Behind the Scenes Changes to Cross-References</h4> <h5 id="changes-in-html-output">Changes in HTML output</h5> <p>The changes to cross-references in Quarto 1.4 also introduce some changes to the underlying HTML output of figures and other cross-referencable elements. For most users, these changes will be invisible. However, if you are operating on Quarto HTML output, you may be impacted. In particular:</p> <ul> <li><p>The DOM structure for HTML figures used to be such that the following CSS selector would work:</p> <p>div#fig-elephant > figure > figcaption.figure-caption</p></li> <li><p>In Quarto v1.4, this is now</p> <p>div#fig-elephant > figure.quarto-float.quarto-float-fig > figcaption.quarto-float-caption.quarto-float-fig</p></li> <li><p>Here’s a minimal, full HTML output for a figure:</p> <div id="fig-1" class="quarto-figure quarto-figure-center anchored"> <pre><code><figure class="quarto-float quarto-float-fig figure"> <div aria-describedby="fig-1-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca"> <img src="./img/content.jpg"> </div> <figcaption id="fig-1-caption-0ceaefa1-69ba-4598-a22c-09a6ac19f8ca" class="quarto-float-caption quarto-float-fig"> Figure&nbsp;1: This is a caption. </figcaption> </figure></code></pre> </div></li> <li><p>Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>All cross-referenceable elements use the <code>figure</code> HTML element with class <code>quarto-float</code>.</li> <li>Different float types are differentiated by the CSS class <code>quarto-float-fig</code> (or <code>-tbl</code>, <code>-lst</code>, or the <code>ref_type</code> of custom cross-reference types) as well as the additional CSS class <code>figure</code>, <code>table</code>, etc. If the element is a subfloat, this will be <code>quarto-subfloat-fig</code>.</li> <li>Similarly, float captions use the <code>figcaption</code> element with class <code>quarto-float-caption</code> (or <code>quarto-subfloat-caption</code> if they’re a subfloat), and also have the <code>quarto-float-*</code> CSS classes.</li> </ul></li> <li><p>This setup lets all “floats” be uniformly targeted by a single CSS rule, as well as allowing specific float types and their captions be targeted by a single additional CSS selector.</p></li> <li><p>Images by themselves used to have a surrounding paragraph;
