they no longer do.</p></li> <li><p>Floats include an extra div for ARIA referencing, so that captions are referenced appropriately and uniformly. As a result, if a table appears inside a float, its caption will be hoisted to the figure node itself.</p></li> </ul> <h3 id="connect-email-generation">Connect Email Generation</h3> <h4 id="connect-email-generation-1">Connect Email Generation</h4> <h5 id="overview-95">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto v1.4 adds an email generation feature that can be used for HTML documents published in <a href="https://posit.co/products/enterprise/connect/">Posit Connect</a>. This feature extends the HTML output format and enables users to generate HTML and/or text emails that can be selectively delivered when the document is rendered in Connect.</p> <p>Read full documentation of the feature on the <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect/user/quarto/#email-customization">Posit Connect Documentation</a>.</p> <h3 id="custom-ast-nodes">Custom AST Nodes</h3> <h4 id="custom-ast-nodes-1">Custom AST Nodes</h4> <h5 id="overview-96">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto now supports custom AST nodes in Pandoc filters. This allows more flexibility in defining and using Lua filters.</p> <p>We will slowly roll out more extensive changes of the AST, but currently, the following objects are custom AST nodes:</p> <ul> <li>Callouts</li> <li>Tabsets</li> <li>Conditional Blocks</li> </ul> <h5 id="example-callouts">Example: Callouts</h5> <p>In previous versions of Quarto, callouts would be represented directly as a div with a class starting with <code>callout</code>, and the contents laid out in a particular way.</p> <p>While authoring documents, this syntax remains unchanged. But when processing the document, the callout divs are now represented as a custom AST node, which can be processed directly in Lua filters. In Quarto 1.3, callouts can be captured in Lua filters more directly. For example, here is a filter that forces every callout to be of type “caution”:</p> <pre><code>function Callout(callout) -- do something with the callout callout.type = "caution" -- note that custom AST nodes are passed by reference. You can -- return the value if you choose, but you do not need to. end</code></pre> <p>Finally, custom AST node constructors are available in the <code>quarto</code> object: <code>quarto.Callout</code>, <code>quarto.Tabset</code>, etc. See the pages above for details.</p> <h3 id="html-table-processing">HTML Table Processing</h3> <h4 id="html-table-processing-1">HTML Table Processing</h4> <h5 id="overview-97">Overview</h5> <p>In Quarto 1.3, we have made some changes to how tables are processed. Recent Pandoc versions have added support for parsing HTML tables into Pandoc’s native data structures (including features such as rowspans and colspans), and Quarto now leverages this to make it easier to produce properly formatted tables in more formats.</p> <h6 id="html-tables-are-now-processed-in-every-format">HTML tables are now processed in every format</h6> <p>Specifically, Quarto will now attempt to parse HTML tables in <code>RawBlock</code> nodes in <code>html</code> format and convert them to Markdown tables, regardless of output format (intentionally including non-HTML formats). As a result, you can now use HTML table syntax in your documents and they will be properly converted to Markdown tables for all formats, and libraries which emit computational tables in HTML format can work in other output formats. In addition, this will allow Lua filters to manipulate the content of tables specified in HTML format.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>If you’re a library author, we hope that you will consider emitting HTML tables in your output. This will allow your users to use the full power of Quarto’s table processing in all formats.</p> <p>With that said, it’s possible that our processing of HTML tables interferes with your library’s processing. If this is the case, you can disable Quarto’s processing of HTML tables by adding the following data attribute to your table:</p> <pre><code><table data-quarto-disable-processing="true"> ... </table></code></pre> <h6 id="bootstrap-classes-can-be-added-to-tables">Bootstrap classes can be added to tables</h6> <p>Bootstrap table classes given as attributes next to a table caption are now inserted into the <code><table></code> element. The classes permitted are those that apply expressly to the entire table, and these are: <code>"primary"</code>, <code>"secondary"</code>, <code>"success"</code>, <code>"danger"</code>, <code>"warning"</code>, <code>"info"</code>, <code>"light"</code>, <code>"dark"</code>, <code>"striped"</code>, <code>"hover"</code>, <code>"active"</code>, <code>"bordered"</code>, <code>"borderless"</code>, <code>"sm"</code>, <code>"responsive"</code>, <code>"responsive-sm"</code>, <code>"responsive-md"</code>, <code>"responsive-lg"</code>, <code>"responsive-xl"</code>, <code>"responsive-xxl"</code>. For example, the following Markdown table will be rendered with row stripes and the rows will also be highlighted on hover:</p> <pre><code>| fruit | price | |--------|--------| | apple | 2.05 | | pear | 1.37 | | orange | 3.09 | : Fruit prices {.striped .hover}</code></pre> <h6 id="embedded-markdown-content-can-be-specified">Embedded Markdown content can be specified</h6> <p>In addition, Quarto now supports the specification of embedded Markdown content in tables. This is done by providing a data attribute <code>qmd</code> or <code>qmd-base64</code> in an embedded <code>span</code> or <code>div</code> node. These nodes can appear anywhere that such content is allowed: table headers, footers, cells, captions, etc. For example, consider the following table:</p> <pre><code><table> <caption><span data-qmd="As described in @Lovelace1864, computers are great."></span></caption> <thead> <tr> <th><span data-qmd="_Header 1_"></span></th> <th><span data-qmd="_Header 2_"></span></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><span data-qmd=""></span></td> <td>Regular output</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></code></pre> <p>The <code>span</code> nodes with the <code>data-qmd</code> attribute will be processed as embedded Markdown content. This allows you to embed arbitrary Markdown content in your tables, including citations, videos, etc. One thing to keep in mind is that the content of <code>data-qmd</code> needs to be escaped properly. Authors of libraries which generate table outputs should consider using the <code>data-qmd-base64</code> attribute, which will be decoded and then processed by Quarto.</p> <h5 id="limitations-1">Limitations</h5> <p>Quarto doesn’t support processing of:</p> <ul> <li>nested <code><table></code> elements.</li> <li>invalid HTML tables. Make sure your emitted HTML <a href="https://validator.w3.org/">passes validation</a>.</li> </ul> <h3 id="lua-filter-changes">Lua filter changes</h3> <h4 id="lua-filter-changes-1">Lua filter changes</h4> <p>Quarto v1.4 includes the following new features for Lua filters:</p> <h5 id="support-for-crossreferenceable-elements-in-filters">Support for crossreferenceable elements in filters</h5> <p>Quarto v1.4 brings significant changes to the handling of figures, tables, listings, etc. These changes simplify the writing of Lua filters that targets those elements, but will generally require changes in existing.</p> <h6 id="the-floatreftarget-ast-node">The <code>FloatRefTarget</code> AST node</h6> <p>In v1.4, crossreferenceable elements all have a single generic type, <code>FloatRefTarget</code>. This element can be constructed explicitly in a Lua filter. It can also be used as the element to be processed in a Lua filter directly.</p> <pre><code>-- A filter targeting FloatRefTarget nodes return { FloatRefTarget = function(float) if float.caption_long then float.caption_long.content:insert(pandoc.Str("[This will appear at the beginning of every caption]")) return float end end }</code></pre> <p><code>FloatRefTarget</code> nodes have the following fields:</p> <ul> <li><code>type</code>: The type of element: <code>Figure</code>, <code>Table</code>, <code>Listing</code>, etc. Quarto v1.4 supports custom node types that can be declared at the document or project level.</li> <li><code>content</code>: The content of the Figure, Table, etc. Quarto v1.4 accepts any content in any <code>FloatRefTarget</code> type (so if your tables are better displayed as an image, you can use that.).</li> <li><code>caption_long</code>: The caption that appears in the main body of the document</li> <li><code>caption_short</code>: The caption that appears in the element collations (such as a list of tables, list of figures, etc.)</li> <li><code>identifier</code>, <code>attributes</code>, <code>classes</code>: these are analogous to <code>Attr</code> fields in Pandoc AST elements like spans and divs. <code>identifier</code>, in addition, needs to be the string that is used in a crossref (<code>fig-cars</code>, <code>tbl-votes</code>, <code>lst-query</code>, and so on).</li> <li><code>parent_id</code>: if a <code>FloatRefTarget</code> is a subfloat of a parent multiple-element float, then <code>parent_id</code> will hold the identifier of the parent float.</li> </ul> <h5 id="custom-formats-and-custom-renderers-1">Custom formats and Custom renderers</h5> <p>Quarto v1.4 adds support for extensible renderers of quarto AST nodes such as <code>FloatRefTarget</code>, <code>Callout</code>. In order to declare a custom renderer, add the following to a Lua filter:</p> <pre><code>local predicate = function(float) -- return true if this renderer should be used; -- typically, this will return true if the custom format is active. end local renderer = function(float) -- returns a plain Pandoc representation of the rendered figure. end quarto._quarto.ast.add_renderer( "FloatRefTarget", predicate, renderer)</code></pre> <h5 id="relative-paths-in-require-calls">Relative paths in <code>require()</code> calls</h5> <p>In larger, more complex filters, it becomes useful to structure your Lua code in modules. Quarto v1.4 supports the use of relative paths in <code>require()</code> calls so that small modules can be easily created and reused.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>filter.lua local utility = require('./utils') function Pandoc(doc) -- process end</code></pre> <p>Using relative paths this way in quarto makes it harder for multiple filters to accidentally create conflicting module names (as would eventually happen when using the standard Lua <code>require('utils')</code> syntax). It’s possible to refer to subdirectories and parent directories as well:</p> <pre><code>filter2.lua local parsing = require('./utils/parsing') function Pandoc(doc) -- process end utils/parsing.lua local utils = require("../utils") -- ...</code></pre> <h5 id="more-precise-targeting-of-ast-processing-phases">More precise targeting of AST processing phases</h5> <p>Before Quarto 1.4, Lua filters are either “pre” filters (the default setting), or “post” filters. Those filters are specified like this:</p> <pre><code># "pre" filters: filters: - pre_filter_1.lua - pre_filter_2.lua # ... # "post" filters: filters: - quarto - post_filter_1.lua - post_filter_2.lua # ...</code></pre> <p>This syntax continues to work in 1.4. In addition, it is now possible to specify more precisely the place where a specific filter will be inserted. Quarto’s AST processing phase is now split into three parts: <code>ast</code>, <code>quarto</code>, and <code>render</code>.</p> <ul> <li><p><code>ast</code>: normalizes the input syntax from Pandoc, recognizing constructs such as <code>Callout</code>, <code>FloatRefTarget</code>, and so on.</p></li> <li><p><code>quarto</code>: processes the normalized syntax, for example by resolving cross-references.</p></li> <li><p><code>render</code>: produces format-specific output from the processed input. In Quarto 1.4, Lua filters can be inserted before or after any of these stages:</p> <p>filters: - at: pre-ast path: filter1.lua - at: post-quarto path: filter2.lua - at: post-render path: filter3.lua</p></li> </ul> <p>Any of the stages can be prefixed by <code>pre-</code> or <code>post-</code>. In Quarto 1.4, <code>pre-quarto</code> and <code>post-ast</code> correspond to the same insertion location in the filter chain, as do <code>post-quarto</code> and <code>pre-render</code>. The “pre” and “post” filter syntax from Quarto 1.3 remains valid. “Pre” filters are injected at the <code>pre-quarto</code> entry point, and “post” filters are injected at the <code>post-render</code> entry point.</p> <p>The new syntax also supports JSON filters, as 1.3 filters do. Either use <code>type: json</code> explicitly, or use a path that doesn’t end in <code>.lua</code>. Conversely, <code>type: lua</code> will force the file to be treated as a Lua filter.</p> <h3 id="pdf-format-improvements">PDF Format Improvements</h3> <h4 id="pdf-format-improvements-1">PDF Format Improvements</h4> <p>NoteContent Moved</p> <p>The SVG and Remote Images content from this page has been migrated to the main documentation:</p> <ul> <li>SVG Images</li> <li>Remote Images This page is retained for historical reference.</li> </ul> <h5 id="svg-images-1">SVG Images</h5> <p>Starting in Quarto 1.3, we support rendering of PDF documents that include SVG files, automatically converting them to PDF images if <code>rsvg-convert</code> is available on the system path during rendering.</p> <p>You can learn more about installing <code>librsvg</code> (which provides <code>rsvg-convert</code>), see <a href="https://wiki.gnome.org/Projects/LibRsvg">wiki.gnome.org</a>. To install on specific platforms, follow the below instructions:</p> <ul> <li>On MacOS, you can use Homebrew (https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/librsvg) <code>brew install librsvg</code></li> <li>Tarballs for Linux are available here: <a href="https://download.gnome.org/sources/librsvg/">download.gnome.org</a></li> <li>On Windows, you can <a href="https://community.chocolatey.org/packages/rsvg-convert">install using chocolatey</a>: <code>choco install rsvg-convert</code></li> </ul> <h5 id="remote-images-1">Remote Images</h5> <p>Starting in Quarto 1.3, when rendering PDFs, Quarto will automatically fetch remote image references and properly embed them within the PDF.</p> <h5 id="filenames-with-modifiers">Filenames with Modifiers</h5> <p>In quarto 1.3, the default filename for PDF files includes variants and modifiers, and so the following YAML front matter will work:</p> <pre><code># example.qmd format: pdf+simple: default # generates example+simple.pdf pdf: default # generates example.pdf</code></pre> <h3 id="quarto-1.3-pre-release">Quarto 1.3 Pre-Release</h3> <h4 id="quarto-1.3-pre-release-1">Quarto 1.3 Pre-Release</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>Quarto 1.3 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li>Confluence Publishing—Publish quarto documents and projects to Confluence spaces.</li> <li>Multi-Format Publishing—Simple discovery of other formats for HTML documents.</li> <li>Jupyter Cell Embedding—Embed code and outputs from Jupyter Notebooks in Quarto documents.</li> <li>Article Grid Customization—Customize the widths within the article grid in HTML documents.</li> <li>Code Block Annotation—Use annotation to provide contextual comments to help readers understand code.</li> <li>Quarto Book AsciiDoc Support—Output Quarto books to AsciiDoc files</li> <li>Website Navigation Improvements—Improved navigation for Quarto websites.</li> <li>Mermaid Diagram Theming—Mermaid diagram’s appearance automatically matches your document’s theme (or customize it)</li> <li>PDF: SVG and Remote Images—Improved handling for SVG images and remote images in PDF documents.</li> <li><code>kbd</code> Shortcode—Show well formatted keyboard shortcuts in Quarto documents.</li> <li>Extensions: Quarto AST—Use custom AST nodes for Quarto types like Callout when writing extensions.</li> <li>Extensions: HTML Tables—HTML tables are now processed and accessible to Lua filters in all formats (not just HTML). See the Pre-Release Download Page for a complete list of all the changes and bug fixes.</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-1.4-pre-release">Quarto 1.4 Pre-Release</h3> <h4 id="quarto-1.4-pre-release-1">Quarto 1.4 Pre-Release</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>Quarto 1.4 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li>Quarto Manuscripts—A new project type for scholarly articles, where notebooks are both the source of the article, and part of the published record.</li> <li>Quarto Dashboards–A new format for creating interactive dashboards.</li> <li>Typst Format—Support for the <code>typst</code> output format. <a href="https://github.com/typst/typst">Typst</a> is a new open-source markup-based typesetting system that is designed to be as powerful as LaTeX while being much easier to learn and use.</li> <li>Cross-reference changes: <ul> <li>Adds a new Cross-Reference Div Syntax to more flexibly define cross-referenceable elements.</li> <li>Allows the definition of Custom Cross-Reference Types via document or project YAML.</li> <li>Adds <code>lst-label</code> and <code>lst-cap</code> code cell options to create Cross-referenceable Listings for Executable Code.</li> <li>Allows Cross-Referencing Callouts.</li> <li>Adds the prefixes <code>rem-</code> and <code>sol-</code> to cross-reference Remarks and Solutions in addition to the existing theorem types.</li> <li>Makes other behind the scenes changes.</li> </ul></li> <li>Shiny for Python—Support for using Shiny for Python within Quarto documents.</li> <li>Inline Execution for Jupyter—Support for executing inline expressions when using Jupyter kernels.</li> <li>Script Rendering <ul> <li>Jupyter—Support for rendering script files (e.g. <code>.py</code>, <code>.jl</code>, or <code>.r</code>) that are <a href="https://jupytext.readthedocs.io/en/latest/formats-scripts.html">specially formatted</a> as notebooks.</li> <li>Knitr—Support for rendering R script files (e.g. <code>.r</code> or <code>.R</code>) that are formatted for report using <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/spin.html"><code>knitr::spin()</code> syntax</a>.</li> </ul></li> <li>Easy Binder Configuration for Quarto Projects—Support for generating files required to deploy a Quarto project using Binder.</li> <li>Connect Email Generation—Extends the <code>html</code> output format so that HTML/text emails can be created and selectively delivered through Posit Connect.</li> <li>Publish to Posit Cloud—Adds <code>posit-cloud</code> as a venue for <code>quarto publish</code>.</li> <li>Lightbox Treatment for Images and Figures—Support for zooming into images and figures using a <code>lightbox</code>. Includes support for grouping multiple images into a gallery.</li> <li>Lua changes—Quarto v1.4 adds new features to writers of Lua filters.</li> <li>AST processing changes—Quarto v1.4 improves on the HTML table processing added in v1.3 and adds a way for LaTeX raw blocks to include Quarto-compatible markdown for processing. See the Pre-Release Download Page for a complete list of all the changes and bug fixes.</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-1.9-pre-release">Quarto 1.9 Pre-Release</h3> <h4 id="quarto-1.9-pre-release-1">Quarto 1.9 Pre-Release</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>Quarto 1.9 includes the following new features:</p> <ul> <li>Posit Connect Cloud Publishing: Publish documents and websites to Posit Connect Cloud using <code>quarto publish posit-connect-cloud</code>.</li> <li>Output for LLMs: Generate <code>llms.txt</code> and <code>.llms.md</code> files for websites, making your content more accessible to large language models and AI-powered tools.</li> <li><code>quarto use brand</code> command: Add or update brand assets from an external source.</li> <li>List Tables: Create complex tables with a list-like syntax. An easier-to-maintain alternative to grid tables, originally developed by Martin Fischer with contributions from Albert Krewinkel and William Lupton.</li> <li>PDF Accessibility: <ul> <li>PDF Standards and Accessibility for LaTeX and Typst: New <code>pdf-standard</code> option enables PDF/A archival formats and PDF/UA accessibility compliance. Use <code>quarto install verapdf</code> to automatically validate compliance.</li> <li>Image alt text for PDF accessibility: Alt text <code>fig-alt</code> attributes now passes through to PDF output for screen reader support in both LaTeX and Typst formats.</li> <li>Alt text for cross-referenced equations in Typst: Provide descriptive text for equations using the <code>alt</code> attribute.</li> </ul></li> <li>Improvements to Typst support: <ul> <li>Typst book projects: Book projects can now render to Typst via the bundled <code>orange-book</code> extension, providing chapter numbering, cross-references, and professional textbook styling.</li> <li>Support for Article layout: Place content in the margins, create full-width figures, or add side notes.</li> <li>New options: <ul> <li><code>mathfont</code>, <code>codefont</code>, <code>linestretch</code></li> <li><code>linkcolor</code>, <code>citecolor</code>, <code>filecolor</code></li> <li><code>thanks</code></li> <li><code>abstract-title</code></li> </ul></li> <li>Theorem styling: New <code>theorem-appearance</code> option with four styles: <code>simple</code> (classic LaTeX), <code>fancy</code> (colored boxes with brand colors), <code>clouds</code> (rounded backgrounds), or <code>rainbow</code> (colored borders and titles).</li> </ul></li> <li>Privacy-focused features for websites: <ul> <li>A privacy-first default for cookie consent: The default for cookie consent has changed to <code>type: express</code>, providing opt-in consent that blocks cookies until users explicitly agree. This privacy-conscious default is designed with modern privacy regulations in mind.</li> <li>Algolia Search Insights avoids cookies: Use Algolia Insights now uses persistent cookies only if <code>cookie-consent</code> is active, and the user has opted-in.</li> <li>Use Plausible Analytics: Add privacy-friendly Plausible Analytics to websites via the <code>plausible-analytics</code> configuration option.</li> </ul></li> <li>Search Result Highlighting: Improved highlighting of search terms on destination pages, with persistent marks, automatic tab activation for matches inside tabsets, and cross-element highlighting for multi-word searches.</li> <li><code>aria-label</code> for videos: Improve accessibility of embedded videos by providing custom descriptive labels for screen readers instead of the default “Video Player” label.</li> <li>New <code>syntax-highlighting</code> Option: Replaces the deprecated <code>highlight-style</code> (Pandoc 3.8). Supports style names, custom <code>.theme</code> files, <code>none</code>, or <code>idiomatic</code> for format-native highlighting.</li> <li>Metadata and brand extensions now work without a <code>_quarto.yml</code> project. A temporary default project is created in memory.</li> <li>Engine extensions allow replacement of the execution engine: <ul> <li>Julia is now a bundled extension instead of being built-in.</li> <li>quarto-marimo will soon change from a filter extension to an engine extension.</li> <li>New <code>quarto create extension engine</code> command.</li> <li>New <code>quarto call build-ts-extension</code> command.</li> <li>New Quarto API for engine extensions to use. (This is in flux and will not be documented for the next few releases, but there will be a dev blog post about it.) See the Pre-Release Download Page for a complete list of all the changes and bug fixes.</li> </ul></li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-callouts-custom-node-api">Quarto Callouts Custom Node API</h3> <h4 id="quarto-callouts-custom-node-api-1">Quarto Callouts Custom Node API</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>In Quarto 1.3, callouts are represented as a custom AST node. You can create callout AST nodes in Lua filters with the <code>quarto.Callout</code> constructor. The constructor takes a single parameter, a table with entries <code>type</code>, <code>title</code>, and <code>content</code>, as described below. In Lua filters, callouts are represented as a table with the following fields:</p> <ul> <li><code>type</code>: the type of callout: <code>note</code>, <code>caution</code>, <code>warning</code>, etc (optional in the constructor).</li> <li><code>title</code>: The callout title (if any) (optional in the constructor),</li> <li><code>icon</code>: the callout icon (or <code>false</code> if none) (optional in the constructor)</li> <li><code>appearance</code>: <code>"minimal"</code>, <code>"simple"</code>, or <code>"default"</code> (optional in the constructor)</li> <li><code>collapse</code>: whether to render the callout as collapsible (optional in the constructor, default <code>false</code>)</li> <li><code>content</code>: the content of the callout (a <code>pandoc.Blocks</code> object, or a plain list in the constructor)</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-conditional-blocks-custom-node-api">Quarto Conditional Blocks Custom Node API</h3> <h4 id="quarto-conditional-blocks-custom-node-api-1">Quarto Conditional Blocks Custom Node API</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>In Quarto 1.3, conditional blocks are represented as a custom AST node. You can create conditional block AST nodes in Lua filters with the <code>quarto.ConditionalBlock</code> constructor. The constructor takes a single parameter, a table with entries <code>node</code>, <code>behavior</code>, and <code>condition</code>, as described below. In Lua filters, conditional blocks are represented as a table with the following fields:</p> <ul> <li><code>node</code>: the div containing the content</li> <li><code>behavior</code>: either <code>content-visible</code> or <code>content-hidden</code></li> <li><code>condition</code>: a list of 2-element lists, such as <code>{ { "unless-format", "html" } }</code> (optional in the constructor, default value <code>{}</code>). The first element of each sublist must be one of <code>when-format</code>, <code>unless-format</code>, <code>when-profile</code>, and <code>unless-profile</code>. The second element is the relevant format or profile.</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-tabsets-custom-node-api">Quarto Tabsets Custom Node API</h3> <h4 id="quarto-tabsets-custom-node-api-1">Quarto Tabsets Custom Node API</h4> <p>Published</p> <p>September 25, 2026</p> <p>In Quarto 1.3, tabsets are represented as a custom AST node. You can create conditional blocks in Lua filters with the <code>quarto.Tabset</code> constructor, with parameters <code>tabs</code>, <code>level</code> and <code>attr</code> as described above. In addition, you can use <code>quarto.Tab</code> to create the tab objects for the <code>tabs</code> field. <code>quarto.Tab</code> is more lenient with parameter types, converting strings to <code>Blocks</code> and <code>Inlines</code> as needed. In Lua filters, tabsets are represented as a table with the following fields:</p> <ul> <li><code>tabs</code>: a table containing the content for each tab. Each entry is a table with two entries: <code>title</code> (a <code>pandoc.Inlines</code>) and <code>content</code> (a <code>pandoc.Blocks</code>) (optional in the contructor, default value <code>{}</code>)</li> <li><code>level</code>: the level of the tab headings to be used in rendering the tabset (optional in the constructor, default value <code>2</code>)</li> <li><code>attr</code>: the <code>Attr</code> object for the resulting tabset div (optional in the constructor)</li> </ul> <h3 id="responsive-website-navigation-improvements">Responsive Website Navigation Improvements</h3> <h4 id="responsive-website-navigation-improvements-1">Responsive Website Navigation Improvements</h4> <h5 id="navbar-tools">Navbar Tools</h5> <p>The navbar can now display a set of tools (e.g. social actions, GitHub view or edit actions, etc.), see Navbar Tools.</p> <h5 id="responsive-navbar">Responsive Navbar</h5> <p>We’ve updated the responsive behavior of the navbar to improve the usability of Quarto websites on mobile devices. Changes include:</p> <ul> <li>When the items in a navbar collapse into a menu, we’ve moved the ‘hamburger’ button which controls the menu to the right side of the navbar. This makes it easier to access the menu on mobile devices.</li> <li>When the items in a navbar collapse into a menu, we place the search icon on right side of the navbar (rather than placing in the collapsed menu). This makes search always available, even when on small screens.</li> </ul> <h5 id="responsive-sidebar">Responsive Sidebar</h5> <p>We’ve updated the responsive behavior of the sidebar to improve the usability of Quarto websites on mobile devices. Changes include:</p> <ul> <li>The collapsed sidebar now appears as a vertically smaller band which includes a ‘sidebar’ icon on the left side. Clicking this icon will expand the sidebar to full width. In addition, this collapsed view includes ‘breadcrumbs’ for the current page which allow simple navigation up the hierarchy.</li> <li>When revealed, the sidebar will now animate from the side of the screen.</li> </ul> <h2 id="presentations-1">Presentations</h2> <h3 id="advanced-reveal">Advanced Reveal</h3> <h4 id="advanced-reveal-1">Advanced Reveal</h4> <h5 id="title-slide">Title Slide</h5> <p>The main title slide is the first slide of the presentation, and its content is generated based on a variety document options (title, subtitle, date, author, institute, etc.).</p> <h6 id="custom-background">Custom Background</h6> <p>If you want to provide a custom background for the title slide, then do the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>Use the <code>title-slide-attributes</code> key to provide background options.</p></li> <li><p>Within this key, specify any of the supported slide background options, but with <code>data-</code> prepended to them. For example:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: My Slide Show</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>title-slide-attributes:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>data-background-image: /path/to/title_image.png</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>data-background-size: contain</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>data-background-opacity: “0.5”</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> </ul> <h6 id="custom-template">Custom Template</h6> <p>You can replace the default title slide entirely with your own template. To do this, specify a <code>title-slide.html</code> template partial. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: My Slide Show format: revealjs: template-partials: - title-slide.html</code></pre> <p>Quarto natively supports a title slide which improves the handling of authors and affiliations. While it is backward compatible with <code>author</code> and <code>institute</code>, we now recommend that you use standard author metadata. To provide your own partial for <code>title-slide.html</code>, you can start from the source code for this <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/pandoc/title-fancy/title-slide.html">fancier title slide template</a>. Customize this template as required, then save the results to <code>title-slide.html</code> alongside your presentation.</p> <p>If you prefer pandoc’s default title slide you can opt-in using <code>title-slide-style: pandoc</code> in your YAML — this uses this <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/pandoc/title-slide.html">simpler title slide template partial</a>. However, this simpler partial does not leverage our improved handling for Authors & Affiliations, so we recommend using the fancy one as a starter for custom title slides.</p> <h6 id="centering">Centering</h6> <p>By default, the title slide is centered while all slides are top aligned (i.e. <code>center: false</code>). You can prevent the title slide centering by setting <code>center-title-slide</code> options:</p> <pre><code>title: My Slide Show format: revealjs: center-title-slide: false</code></pre> <p>If <code>center: true</code> is set, <code>center-title-slide</code> will be ignored. There is currently no way to have content slide centered and title slides top aligned. For slide content centering, see Section 6.3.</p> <h5 id="slide-transitions">Slide Transitions</h5> <p>Reveal supports a number of animated transition effects for both slide changes and slide background changes. By default no transitions are used, however you can enable them either globally or per-slide using the options described below.</p> <p>Here are the available transition types:</p> <p>Transition</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>none</code></p> <p>No transition (switch instantly)</p> <p><code>fade</code></p> <p>Cross fade</p> <p><code>slide</code></p> <p>Slide horizontally</p> <p><code>convex</code></p> <p>Slide at a convex angle</p> <p><code>concave</code></p> <p>Slide at a concave angle</p> <p><code>zoom</code></p> <p>Scale the incoming slide so it grows in from the center of the screen.</p> <p>Here’s how you would set the global transition style for both slides and backgrounds:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: transition: slide background-transition: fade ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify the <code>transition-speed</code> as <code>default</code>, <code>fast</code>, or <code>slow</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: transition: slide transition-speed: fast ---</code></pre> <p>You can also specify the <code>transition</code> and/or <code>transition-speed</code> for an individual slide:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {transition="fade" transition-speed="fast"}</code></pre> <p>You can also specify separate in and out transitions, for example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {transition="fade-in slide-out"}</code></pre> <h5 id="slide-visibility">Slide Visibility</h5> <p>You can hide a slide by adding the <code>visibility="hidden"</code> attribute to the slide heading. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {visibility="hidden"}</code></pre> <h6 id="uncounted-slides">Uncounted Slides</h6> <p>When preparing a presentation it can sometimes be helpful to prepare optional slides that you may or may not have time to show. This is easily done by appending a few slides at the end of the presentation, however this means that the Reveal progress bar and slide numbering will hint that there are additional slides.</p> <p>To “hide” those slides from the numbering system you can use <code>visibility="uncounted"</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide 1 ## Slide 2 ## Slide 3 {visibility="uncounted"}</code></pre> <h5 id="presentation-size">Presentation Size</h5> <p>All presentations have a “normal” size, that is, the resolution at which they are authored. This default “normal” size is 1050 x 700, which is used to match as nearly as possible the aspect ratio of most laptops.</p> <p>Reveal will automatically scale presentations uniformly based on the normal size to ensure that everything fits on any given display or viewport without changing the aspect ratio or layout of your content.</p> <p>You can change the slide size, the margin around content, as well as set limits on content scaling using the following options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>width</code></p> <p>Normal width (defaults to 1050)</p> <p><code>height</code></p> <p>Normal height (defaults to 700)</p> <p><code>margin</code></p> <p>Factor of the display size that should remain empty around the content (defaults to 0.1)</p> <p><code>min-scale</code></p> <p>Smallest possible scale to apply to content (defaults to 0.2)</p> <p><code>max-scale</code></p> <p>Largest possible scale to apply to content (defaults to 2.0)</p> <h5 id="absolute-position">Absolute Position</h5> <p>The <code>absolute</code> class lets you position elements at arbitrary positions on a slide. These elements have CSS <code>position: absolute</code> and can be placed relative to the <code>top</code>, <code>left</code>, <code>bottom</code>, and/or <code>right</code> edges of the slide.</p> <p>For example, here we add the <code>.absolute</code> class to three images and give them each a distinct position on the slide (note that we use also <code>width</code> and <code>height</code> to control their dimensions):</p> <pre><code>![](kitten-350-300.jpeg){.absolute top=200 left=0 width="350" height="300" fig-alt="Grey kitten"} ![](kitten-450-250.jpeg){.absolute top=50 right=50 width="450" height="250" fig-alt="Tabby kitten"} ![](kitten-300-300.jpeg){.absolute bottom=20 right=100 width="300" height="300" fig-alt="Kitten in snow"}</code></pre> <p>The following attributes can be used with <code>absolute</code>. All of these values can be specified in CSS units (e.g. <code>px</code>, <code>em</code>, etc.). If a number with no units is specified (as in the above example) then pixels are assumed.</p> <p>Attribute</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>width</code></p> <p>Width of element</p> <p><code>height</code></p> <p>Height of element</p> <p><code>top</code></p> <p>Distance from top of slide</p> <p><code>left</code></p> <p>Distance from left of slide</p> <p><code>bottom</code></p> <p>Distance from bottom of slide</p> <p><code>right</code></p> <p>Distance from right of slide</p> <p>Note that default size of presentation slides is 1050 x 700. See Presentation Size for details on customizing this.</p> <h5 id="layout-helpers">Layout Helpers</h5> <p>Reveal provides some helper classes for controlling the layout of content.</p> <h6 id="stack-layout">Stack Layout</h6> <p>The <code>r-stack</code> layout class lets you center and place multiple elements on top of each other. This is intended to be used together with fragments to incrementally reveal elements.</p> <p>For example, here we create a div with the <code>.r-stack</code> class and then include 3 images (each of which uses <code>.fragment</code> so they display incrementally):</p> <pre><code>::: {.r-stack} ![](image1.png){.fragment width="450" height="300"} ![](image2.png){.fragment width="300" height="450"} ![](image3.png){.fragment width="400" height="400"} :::</code></pre> <h6 id="fit-text">Fit Text</h6> <p>The <code>r-fit-text</code> class makes text as large as possible without overflowing the slide. This is great when you want BIG text without having to manually find the right font size. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.r-fit-text} Big Text :::</code></pre> <h6 id="center">Center</h6> <p>The <code>center</code> class when applied to a slide, will vertically center the slide content by adding the appropriate spacing at the top of the slide. Vertical distances between elements will not be modified. For example:</p> <pre><code>## This will be centered {.center} This text is moved as well</code></pre> <p>For controlling title slide centering, see Section 1.3.</p> <h6 id="stretch">Stretch</h6> <p>The <code>r-stretch</code> layout helper lets you resize an element, like an image or video, to cover the remaining vertical space in a slide. For example, here the image will automatically be resized to fit space remaining outside of the slide title and text before and after it:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title Here is an image: ![](image.png){.r-stretch} Some text after the image.</code></pre> <p>For slides that contain only a single top-level image, the <code>.r-stretch</code> class is automatically applied to the image. You can disable this behavior by setting the <code>auto-stretch: false</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: auto-stretch: false</code></pre> <p>You can also disable auto-stretch for an individual slide by adding the <code>.nostretch</code> class:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {.nostretch}</code></pre> <p>Or apply <code>.nostretch</code> directly to an individual image:</p> <pre><code>![](image.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" width="800px"}</code></pre> <p><code>auto-stretch</code> will only apply to non-nested images, which means an image in a feature block (e.g fragments, layout panel, columns, … ) or a custom Div will be ignored. For custom Divs, you can opt-in to <code>auto-stretch</code> behavior by adding the class <code>.r-stretch</code> to the outer div.</p> <p>NoteLimitation: Auto-stretch and Scrollable</p> <p>When a slide is scrollable the image size calculations used by auto-stretch may not work well and images may not appear. Two solutions depending on your needs are:</p> <ul> <li>Disable auto-stretch at the presentation level, <code>auto-stretch: false</code>, and use <code>.r-stretch</code> on individual images only where needed.</li> <li>On slides that are scrollable, add the <code>.nostretch</code> class to disable auto-stretch on the slide.</li> </ul> <h5 id="auto-animate">Auto Animate</h5> <p>Revealjs can automatically animate elements across slides. All you need to do is add the <code>auto-animate</code> attribute to two adjacent slides and Auto-Animate will animate all matching elements between the two.</p> <p>Here’s a simple example to give you a better idea of how it can be used. Note that the slides don’t have titles in this example (rather just the <code>auto-animate</code> attribute) however they could also include a title.</p> <pre><code>## {auto-animate=true} ::: {style="margin-top: 100px;"} Animating content ::: ## {auto-animate=true} ::: {style="margin-top: 200px; font-size: 3em; color: red;"} Animating content :::</code></pre> <p>This example uses the <code>margin-top</code> property to move the element but internally Reveal will use a CSS transform to ensure smooth movement. This same approach to animation works with most animatable CSS properties meaning you can transition things like <code>position</code>, <code>font-size</code>, <code>line-height</code>, <code>color</code>, <code>background-color</code>, <code>padding</code> and <code>margin</code>.</p> <h6 id="code-animations">Code Animations</h6> <p>You can also animate between code blocks to show changes in code. For example:</p> <pre><code>## {auto-animate="true"} ```r # Fill in the spot we created for a plot output$phonePlot <- renderPlot({ # Render a barplot }) ``` ## {auto-animate=true} ```r # Fill in the spot we created for a plot output$phonePlot <- renderPlot({ # Render a barplot barplot(WorldPhones[,input$region]*1000, main=input$region, ylab="Number of Telephones", xlab="Year") }) ```</code></pre> <h6 id="movement-animations">Movement Animations</h6> <p>Animations are not limited to changes in style. Auto-Animate can also be used to automatically move elements into their new position as content is added, removed or rearranged on a slide. All without a single line of inline CSS. For example, here the delta between the content on two slides is implicitly animated:</p> <pre><code>## {auto-animate=true} Animation ## {auto-animate=true} Implicit Animation</code></pre> <h6 id="element-matching">Element Matching</h6> <p>When you navigate between two auto-animated slides we’ll do our best to automatically find matching elements in the two slides. For text, we consider it a match if both the text contents and node type are identical. For images, videos and iframes we compare the <code>src</code> attribute. We also take into account the order in which the element appears in the DOM.</p> <p>In situations where automatic matching is not feasible you can give the objects that you want to animate between a matching <code>data-id</code> attribute. We prioritize matching <code>data-id</code> values above our automatic matching.</p> <p>Here’s an example where we’ve given several blocks a matching ID since automatic matching has no content to go on. This example also makes use of some additional animation attributes (<code>auto-animate-easing</code> and <code>auto-animate-delay</code>), which we’ll describe in the next section.</p> <pre><code>## {auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"} ::: {.r-hstack} ::: {data-id="box1" auto-animate-delay="0" style="background: #2780e3; width: 200px; height: 150px; margin: 10px;"} ::: ::: {data-id="box2" auto-animate-delay="0.1" style="background: #3fb618; width: 200px; height: 150px; margin: 10px;"} ::: ::: {data-id="box3" auto-animate-delay="0.2" style="background: #e83e8c; width: 200px; height: 150px; margin: 10px;"} ::: ::: ## {auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"} ::: {.r-stack} ::: {data-id="box1" style="background: #2780e3; width: 350px; height: 350px; border-radius: 200px;"} ::: ::: {data-id="box2" style="background: #3fb618; width: 250px; height: 250px; border-radius: 200px;"} ::: ::: {data-id="box3" style="background: #e83e8c; width: 150px; height: 150px; border-radius: 200px;"} ::: :::</code></pre> <h6 id="animation-settings">Animation Settings</h6> <p>You can override specific animation settings such as easing and duration either for the whole presentation, per-slide or individually for each animated element. The following configuration attributes can be used to change the settings for a specific slide or element:</p> <p>Attribute</p> <p>Default</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>auto-animate-easing</code></p> <p>ease</p> <p>A CSS <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/easing-function">easing function</a>.</p> <p><code>auto-animate-unmatched</code></p> <p>true</p> <p>Determines whether elements with no matching auto-animate target should fade in. Set to <code>false</code> to make them appear instantly.</p> <p><code>auto-animate-duration</code></p> <p>1.0</p> <p>Animation duration in seconds.</p> <p><code>auto-animate-delay</code></p> <p>0</p> <p>Animation delay in seconds (can only be set for specific elements, not at the slide level).</p> <p><code>auto-animate-id</code></p> <p>absent</p> <p>An id tying auto-animate slides together.</p> <p><code>auto-animate-restart</code></p> <p>absent</p> <p>Breaks apart two adjacent auto-animate slides (even with the same id).</p> <p>You can override the global defaults for easing, unmatched, and duration as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Slide" format: revealjs: auto-animate-easing: ease-in-out auto-animate-unmatched: false auto-animate-duration: 0.8 ---</code></pre> <h5 id="fragments">Fragments</h5> <p>Fragments are used to highlight or incrementally reveal individual elements on a slide. Every element with the class <code>fragment</code> will be stepped through before moving on to the next slide.</p> <p>Note that fragments as discussed here are a relatively advanced form of incremental content display—see Incremental Lists for documentation on creating incremental bullet lists and inserting content pauses in slides.</p> <p>The default fragment style is to start out invisible and fade in. This style can be changed by appending a different class to the fragment. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.fragment} Fade in ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-out} Fade out ::: ::: {.fragment .highlight-red} Highlight red ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out} Fade in, then out ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-up} Slide up while fading in :::</code></pre> <h6 id="fragment-classes">Fragment Classes</h6> <p>Here are all of the available fragment classes:</p> <p>Name</p> <p>Effect</p> <p><code>fade-out</code></p> <p>Start visible, fade out</p> <p><code>fade-up</code></p> <p>Slide up while fading in</p> <p><code>fade-down</code></p> <p>Slide down while fading in</p> <p><code>fade-left</code></p> <p>Slide left while fading in</p> <p><code>fade-right</code></p> <p>Slide right while fading in</p> <p><code>fade-in-then-out</code></p> <p>Fades in, then out on the next step</p> <p><code>fade-in-then-semi-out</code></p> <p>Fades in, then out to 50% on the next step</p> <p><code>grow</code></p> <p>Scale up</p> <p><code>semi-fade-out</code></p> <p>Fade out to 50%</p> <p><code>shrink</code></p> <p>Scale down</p> <p><code>strike</code></p> <p>Strike through</p> <p><code>highlight-red</code></p> <p>Turn text red</p> <p><code>highlight-green</code></p> <p>Turn text green</p> <p><code>highlight-blue</code></p> <p>Turn text blue</p> <p><code>highlight-current-red</code></p> <p>Turn text red, then back to original on next step</p> <p><code>highlight-current-green</code></p> <p>Turn text green, then back to original on next step</p> <p><code>highlight-current-blue</code></p> <p>Turn text blue, then back to original on next step</p> <h6 id="nested-fragments">Nested Fragments</h6> <p>Multiple fragments can be applied to the same element sequentially by wrapping it. The following example will fade in the text on the first step, turn it red on the second and partially fade out on the third:</p> <pre><code>::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.fragment .highlight-red} ::: {.fragment .semi-fade-out} Fade in > Turn red > Semi fade out ::: ::: :::</code></pre> <h6 id="fragment-order">Fragment Order</h6> <p>By default fragments will be stepped through in the order that they appear in the DOM. This display order can be changed using the <code>fragment-index</code> attribute. Note that multiple elements can appear at the same index:</p> <pre><code>::: {.fragment fragment-index=3} Appears last ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=1} Appears first ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=2} Appears second :::</code></pre> <h6 id="custom-fragments">Custom Fragments</h6> <p>Custom effects can be created by specifying CSS styles for <code>.fragment.effectname</code> and <code>.fragment.effectname.visible</code>. The <code>visible</code> class is applied to each fragment as they are navigated through during the presentation. A <code>custom</code> class can be added to each fragment to tell reveal.js to avoid applying its default fade-in fragment styles.</p> <p>For example, the following defines a fragment style where elements are initially blurred but become focused when stepped through.</p> <pre><code>::: {.fragment .custom .blur} First item to be unblurred ::: ::: {.fragment .custom .blur} Second one to be revealed :::</code></pre> <p>with this CSS for the style associated with <code>blur</code> class.</p> <pre><code>.reveal .slides section .fragment.blur { filter: blur(5px); } .reveal .slides section .fragment.blur.visible { filter: none }</code></pre> <h5 id="parallax-background">Parallax Background</h5> <p>If you want to use a parallax scrolling background, add the <code>parallax-background-image</code> and <code>parallax-background-size</code> options. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: parallax-background-image: background.png parallax-background-size: "2100px 900px" parallax-background-horizontal: 200 parallax-background-vertical: 50 ---</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>parallax-background-horizontal</code> and <code>parallax-background-vertical</code> options are not required (the defaults shown above will be used if they are not specified).</p> <h5 id="vertical-slides">Vertical Slides</h5> <p>Reveal uses classic linear slide navigation by default. If you wish you can also configure slide navigation to nest multiple slides within a single top-level slide to create a vertical stack.</p> <p>Use the <code>navigation-mode</code> option to fine tune Reveal navigation behavior:</p> <p>Navigation Mode</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>linear</code></p> <p>Left/right arrows keys step through all slides (both horizontal and vertical).</p> <p><code>vertical</code></p> <p>Left/right arrow keys step between horizontal slides. Up/down arrow keys step between vertical slides. Space key steps through all slides (both horizontal and vertical).</p> <p><code>grid</code></p> <p>When enabled, stepping left/right from a vertical stack to an adjacent vertical stack will land you at the same vertical index.</p> <p>If you use <code>vertical</code> or <code>grid</code> navigation, you should structure your slides using level 1 headings for the horizontal axis and level 2 headings for the vertical axis. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: navigation-mode: vertical --- # Slide 1 ## Slide 1.1 ## Slide 1.2 # Slide 2 ## Slide 2.1 ## Slide 2.2</code></pre> <h6 id="slide-controls">Slide Controls</h6> <p>When you enable <code>vertical</code> or <code>grid</code> navigation, controls will appear to provide a visual cue to where you are in the presentation (e.g. if there are vertical slides below you’ll see a down control).</p> <p>By default these controls appear at the edges of the presentation, you can position them in the bottom right corner using the <code>controls-layout</code> option. You can also provide an extra visual cue to viewers that the controls are available using the <code>controls-tutorial</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: navigation-mode: vertical controls-layout: bottom-right controls-tutorial: true ---</code></pre> <p>Note that using <code>controls-layout: bottom-right</code> isn’t compatible with including a <code>logo</code> (as the logo appears in the bottom right corner as well).</p> <p>You can also disable the controls entirely with <code>controls: false</code>.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>While vertical slides do provide some additional flexibility over the traditional linear model, they are in practice very confusing for end users (mostly because they are so unexpected). Users will often skip the vertical content because they simply don’t know it’s there.</p> <p>If your content benefits from vertical orientation (e.g. you have optional drill-down content that you don’t want in the main flow of the presentation), you can by all means use the vertical mode. Just know that if you distribute your slides to users they will very likely not end up viewing any of the vertical content.</p> <h5 id="touch-navigation">Touch Navigation</h5> <p>You can swipe to navigate through a presentation on any touch-enabled device.</p> <p>If you wish to disable this you can set the <code>touch</code> option to <code>false</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: touch: false controls: true ---</code></pre> <p>Note that we also enable <code>controls</code> at the same time (as users on phones or tablets don’t have access to a keyboard).</p> <h5 id="reveal-plugins">Reveal Plugins</h5> <p>To use <a href="https://github.com/hakimel/reveal.js/wiki/Plugins,-Tools-and-Hardware">Revealjs plugins</a>, you need to package them into a directory with a config file (<code>plugin.yml</code>). The config file lets Quarto know how to inject the plugin into the presentation (e.g. what scripts and/or css files to include, what the default configuration should be, etc.).</p> <p>See the source code of the plugins that are built into Quarto Reveal for examples:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/plugins">github.com</a></p> <p>To use a plugin, just include a reference to its directory in the list of <code>revealjs-plugins</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: revealjs-plugins: - myplugin ---</code></pre> <p>Note that many of the most popular Reveal plugins are already included with the Quarto version of Reveal, so there is no need to include them separately. Built-in plugins include:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/reveal/multiplex">Multiplex</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/denehyg/reveal.js-menu">RevealMenu</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/rajgoel/reveal.js-plugins/tree/master/chalkboard">RevealChalkboard</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/McShelby/reveal-pdfexport">PdfExport</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="example-6">Example</h6> <p>Let’s show an example with the <a href="https://github.com/rajgoel/reveal.js-plugins/tree/master/fullscreen">fullscreen</a> plugin. Here are the steps to bundle this plugin to use within your Quarto HTML presentation:</p> <ul> <li><p>Create a folder with the name you want for the plugin, here we’ll call it <code>fullscreen</code>.</p></li> <li><p>Download the plugin files into the created folder. Here the plugin only have a JS file called <code>plugin.js</code> that you can find <a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajgoel/reveal.js-plugins/master/fullscreen/plugin.js">on the repo rajgoel/reveal.js-plugins</a>. You can keep the name or rename it, e.g <code>fullscreen.js</code>.</p></li> <li><p>In that folder add a <code>plugin.yml</code> file, as in <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/plugins">Quarto Reveal examples</a>.</p> <ul> <li><code>name</code> is a mandatory field which should be the name of the JS function the JS plugin is defining. Open the JS script you downloaded to look for it.</li> <li>Other fields are for the resources to be used. In our example, only a JS script so we’ll use <code>script</code></li> </ul></li> <li><p>Our <code>plugin.yml</code> would be:</p> <p>name: RevealFullscreen script: [fullscreen.js]</p></li> <li><p>Now add the plugin reference into your document YAML header, using the path of the folder your created:</p> <p>format: revealjs: revealjs-plugins: - fullscreen</p></li> <li><p>The custom plugin will be loaded in your presentation and you can use it. The plugin fullscreen documentation shows an example of adding a Map fullscreen in a slide by adding an attribute on the section, and using stretch on the content. This would translate to having this slide in the <code>.qmd</code> file:</p> <p>## {fullscreen=true}</p> <p><iframe class="stretch" data-src="[google.com](https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=!1m14!1m12!1m3!1d61206.89156051744!2d-151.77366863890407!3d-16.50433878928727!2m3!1f0!2f0!3f0!3m2!1i1024!2i768!4f13.1!5e0!3m2!1sen!2sde!4v1467468929561)"></iframe></p></li> </ul> <h5 id="learning-more-14">Learning More</h5> <p>See these articles lo learn more about using Reveal:</p> <ul> <li>Reveal Basics covers the basic mechanics of creating presentations.</li> <li>Presenting Slides describes slide navigation, printing to PDF, drawing on slides using a chalkboard, and creating multiplex presentations.</li> <li>Reveal Themes talks about using and customizing existing themes as well as creating brand new themes.</li> </ul> <h3 id="beamer-1">Beamer</h3> <h4 id="beamer-2">Beamer</h4> <h5 id="overview-98">Overview</h5> <p>You can create <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer">Beamer</a> (LaTeX/PDF) presentations using the <code>beamer</code> format. Beamer presentations support core presentation features like incremental content and 2-column layouts, and also provide facilities for customizing column layout, specifying frame attributes, and using Beamer themes.</p> <p>By default, the Beamer format has <code>echo: false</code> and <code>warning: false</code>. As a result, executable code cells in standard Beamer documents won’t show their source or warnings generated. As with other options, you can override this behavior in the document metadata or individually in each executable cell.</p> <p>See the Beamer format reference for a complete list of all options available for Beamer output.</p> <h5 id="creating-slides">Creating Slides</h5> <p>In markdown, slides are delineated using headings. For example, here is a simple slide show with two slides (each defined with a level 2 heading (<code>##</code>)):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: beamer --- ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>You can also divide slide shows into sections with title slides using a level 1 heading (<code>#</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: beamer --- # In the morning ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Breakfast - Eat eggs - Drink coffee # In the evening ## Dinner - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>Finally, you can also delineate slides using horizontal rules (for example, if you have a slide without a title):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: beamer --- - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed --- - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>The examples above all use level 2 headings for slides and level 1 headings for sections/title slides. You can customize this using the <code>slide-level</code> option (See the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#structuring-the-slide-show">structuring the slide show</a> for additional details).</p> <p>In Beamer, headings below <code>slide-level</code> will place content inside a <code>block</code> environment:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: beamer: slide-level: 2 --- ## Slide ### Simple block Content</code></pre> <p>Add the <code>.alert</code> or <code>.example</code> class to place content inside an <code>alertblock</code> or <code>exampleblock</code> environment respectively:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: beamer: slide-level: 2 --- ## Slide ### Alert block {.alert} Content ### Example block {.example} Content</code></pre> <h5 id="incremental-lists">Incremental Lists</h5> <p>By default number and bullet lists within slides are displayed all at once. You can override this globally using the <code>incremental</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Presentation" format: beamer: incremental: true</code></pre> <p>You can also explicitly make any list incremental or non-incremental by surrounding it in a div with an explicit class that determines the mode. To make a list incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.incremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>To make a list non-incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.nonincremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>You can also insert a pause within a slide (keeping the content after the pause hidden) by inserting three dots separated by spaces:</p> <pre><code>## Slide with a pause content before the pause . . . content after the pause</code></pre> <p>Note this only works below headings that are creating slides (see Creating slides).</p> <h5 id="multiple-columns">Multiple Columns</h5> <p>To put material in side by side columns, you can use a native div container with class <code>.columns</code>, containing two or more div containers with class <code>.column</code>and a <code>width</code> attribute:</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} contents... ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} contents... ::: ::::</code></pre> <p>The div containers with classes <code>columns</code> and <code>column</code> can optionally have an <code>align</code> attribute. The class <code>columns</code> can optionally have a <code>totalwidth</code> attribute or an <code>onlytextwidth</code> class.</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns align=center totalwidth=8em} ::: {.column width="40%"} contents... ::: ::: {.column width="60%" align=bottom} contents... ::: ::::</code></pre> <p>The <code>align</code> attributes on <code>columns</code> and <code>column</code> can be used with the values <code>top</code>, <code>top-baseline</code>, <code>center</code> and <code>bottom</code> to vertically align the columns. It defaults to <code>top</code> in <code>columns</code>.</p> <p>The <code>totalwidth</code> attribute limits the width of the columns to the given value.</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns align=top .onlytextwidth} ::: {.column width="40%" align=center} contents... ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} contents... ::: ::::</code></pre> <p>The class <code>onlytextwidth</code> sets the <code>totalwidth</code> to <code>\textwidth</code>.</p> <p>See Section 12.7 of the <a href="http://mirrors.ctan.org/macros/latex/contrib/beamer/doc/beameruserguide.pdf">Beamer User’s Guide</a> for more details.</p> <h6 id="panel-layout-1">Panel Layout</h6> <p>In addition to using the presentation-native <code>columns</code>/<code>column</code> syntax described above, you can also use Quarto’s panel layout features using divs with the <code>layout</code> class. Quarto will convert those to Beamer columns as if they were written with the above syntax.</p> <h5 id="beamer-options">Beamer Options</h5> <p>Set additional options to change the appearance of PDF slides using <code>beamer</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: beamer: aspectratio: 32 navigation: horizontal theme: AnnArbor colortheme: lily ---</code></pre> <p>The options available are:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>aspectratio</code></p> <p>Slide aspect ratio: <code>43</code> for 4:3 <a href="#default">default</a>, <code>169</code> for 16:9, <code>1610</code> for 16:10, <code>149</code> for 14:9, <code>141</code> for 1.41:1, <code>54</code> for 5:4, <code>32</code> for 3:2</p> <p><code>beamerarticle</code></p> <p>Produce an article from Beamer slides</p> <p><code>beameroption</code></p> <p>Extra beamer options provided to <code>\setbeameroption{}</code></p> <p><code>institute</code></p> <p>Author affiliations: can be a list when there are multiple authors</p> <p><code>logo</code></p> <p>Logo image for slides</p> <p><code>navigation</code></p> <p>Controls navigation symbols (default is <code>empty</code> for no navigation symbols; other valid values are <code>frame</code>, <code>vertical</code>, and <code>horizontal</code>)</p> <p><code>section-titles</code></p> <p>Enables “title pages” for new sections (default is true)</p> <p><code>theme, colortheme, fonttheme, innertheme, outertheme</code></p> <p>Beamer themes</p> <p><code>themeoptions</code></p> <p>Options for LaTeX beamer themes (a list)</p> <p><code>titlegraphic</code></p> <p>Image for title slide</p> <h5 id="frame-attributes">Frame Attributes</h5> <p>Sometimes it is necessary to add the LaTeX <code>[fragile]</code> option to a frame in beamer (for example, when using the <code>minted</code> environment). This can be forced by adding the <code>fragile</code> class to the heading introducing the slide:</p> <pre><code># Fragile slide {.fragile}</code></pre> <p>All of the other frame attributes described in Section 8.1 of the <a href="http://mirrors.ctan.org/macros/latex/contrib/beamer/doc/beameruserguide.pdf">Beamer User’s Guide</a> may also be used: <code>allowdisplaybreaks</code>, <code>allowframebreaks</code>, <code>b</code>, <code>c</code>, <code>t</code>, <code>environment</code>, <code>label</code>, <code>plain</code>, <code>shrink</code>, <code>standout</code>, <code>noframenumbering</code>.</p> <h5 id="background-images">Background Images</h5> <p>To provide a common background image for all slides in a Beamer presentation, use the <code>background-image</code> format option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- format: beamer: background-image: background.png ---</code></pre> <h3 id="powerpoint">PowerPoint</h3> <h4 id="powerpoint-1">PowerPoint</h4> <h5 id="overview-99">Overview</h5> <p>You can create <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_PowerPoint">PowerPoint</a> presentations using the <code>pptx</code> format. PowerPoint presentations support core presentation features like incremental bullets, 2-column layouts, and speaker notes, and can also be rendered using custom PowerPoint templates.</p> <p>See the PowerPoint format reference for a complete list of all options available for PowerPoint output.</p> <h5 id="creating-slides-1">Creating Slides</h5> <p>In markdown, slides are delineated using headings. For example, here is a simple slide show with two slides (each defined with a level 2 heading (<code>##</code>)):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: pptx --- ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>You can also divide slide shows into sections with title slides using a level 1 heading (<code>#</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: pptx --- # In the morning ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Breakfast - Eat eggs - Drink coffee # In the evening ## Dinner - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>Finally, you can also delineate slides using horizontal rules (for example, if you have a slide without a title):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: pptx --- - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed --- - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>The examples above all use level 2 headings for slides and level 1 headings for sections/title slides. You can customize this using the <code>slide-level</code> option (See the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#structuring-the-slide-show">structuring the slide show</a> for additional details).</p> <h5 id="incremental-lists-1">Incremental Lists</h5> <p>By default number and bullet lists within slides are displayed all at once. You can override this globally using the <code>incremental</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Presentation" format: pptx: incremental: true</code></pre> <p>You can also explicitly make any list incremental or non-incremental by surrounding it in a div with an explicit class that determines the mode. To make a list incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.incremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>To make a list non-incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.nonincremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <h5 id="multiple-columns-1">Multiple Columns</h5> <p>To put material in side by side columns, you can use a native div container with class <code>.columns</code>, containing two or more div containers with class <code>.column</code>:</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns} ::: {.column} contents... ::: ::: {.column} contents... ::: ::::</code></pre> <h5 id="speaker-notes">Speaker Notes</h5> <p>You can add speaker notes to a slide using a div with class <code>.notes</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide with speaker notes Slide content ::: {.notes} Speaker notes go here. :::</code></pre> <h5 id="powerpoint-templates">PowerPoint Templates</h5> <p>By default PowerPoint output uses a fairly plain looking template. You can customize what template is used via the <code>reference-doc</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: pptx: reference-doc: template.pptx ---</code></pre> <p>Nearly all templates included with recent versions of PowerPoint (either with <code>.pptx</code> or <code>.potx</code> extension) are known to work, as are most templates derived from these.</p> <p>The specific requirement is that the template should contain layouts with the following names (as seen within PowerPoint, click on <code>Layout</code> under the <code>Home</code> menu to check):</p> <ul> <li>Title Slide</li> <li>Title and Content</li> <li>Section Header</li> <li>Two Content</li> <li>Comparison</li> <li>Content with Caption</li> <li>Blank For each name, the first layout found with that name will be used. If no layout is found with one of the names, Pandoc will output a warning and use the layout with that name from the default <code>reference-doc</code> instead.</li> </ul> <h6 id="creating-a-template-1">Creating a Template</h6> <p>To create a template from scratch, start with the default PowerPoint template as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto pandoc -o template.pptx --print-default-data-file reference.pptx</code></pre> <p>Then edit the <code>template.pptx</code> file within PowerPoint as desired, and use it as the value for <code>reference-doc</code> (as shown above) when rendering your slides:</p> <h5 id="slide-layouts">Slide Layouts</h5> <p>When creating slides, the pptx writer chooses from a number of pre-defined layouts, based on the content of the slide:</p> <p>Title Slide</p> <p>This layout is used for the initial slide, which is generated and filled from the metadata fields <code>date</code>, <code>author</code>, and <code>title</code>, if they are present.</p> <p>Section Header</p> <p>This layout is used for what pandoc calls “title slides”, i.e. slides which start with a header which is above the slide level in the hierarchy.</p> <p>Two Content</p> <p>This layout is used for two-column slides, i.e. slides containing a div with class <code>columns</code> which contains at least two divs with class <code>column</code>.</p> <p>Comparison</p> <p>This layout is used instead of “Two Content” for any two-column slides in which at least one column contains text followed by non-text (e.g. an image or a table).</p> <p>Content with Caption</p> <p>This layout is used for any non-two-column slides which contain text followed by non-text (e.g. an image or a table).</p> <p>Blank</p> <p>This layout is used for any slides which only contain blank content, e.g. a slide containing only speaker notes, or a slide containing only a non-breaking space.</p> <p>Title and Content</p> <p>This layout is used for all slides which do not match the criteria for another layout.</p> <p>These layouts are chosen from the default <code>pptx</code> reference doc included with Pandoc, unless an alternative reference doc is specified using <code>reference-doc</code>.</p> <h5 id="background-images-1">Background Images</h5> <p>To provide a common background image for multiple slides in a PowerPoint presentation, include the background image within the relevant slide layouts of a custom PowerPoint template (see Creating a Template for details on creating templates).</p> <p>To add a background image to an individual slide, add the <code>background-image</code> attribute to the slide’s heading. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-image="background.png"}</code></pre> <p>Note that this also works even if you don’t have slide heading text. For example:</p> <pre><code>## {background-image="background.png"}</code></pre> <p>For background images, only the “stretch” mode is supported, and the background image is centred around the slide in the image’s larger axis, matching the observed default behaviour of PowerPoint.</p> <h3 id="presentations-2">Presentations</h3> <h4 id="presentations-3">Presentations</h4> <h5 id="overview-100">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto supports a variety of formats for creating presentations, including:</p> <ul> <li><code>revealjs</code> — reveal.js (HTML)</li> <li><code>pptx</code> — PowerPoint (MS Office)</li> <li><code>beamer</code> — Beamer (LaTeX/PDF) There are pros and cons to each of these formats. The most capable format by far is <code>revealjs</code>, so it is highly recommended unless you have specific Office or LaTeX output requirements. Note that <code>revealjs</code> presentations can be presented as HTML slides or can be printed to PDF for easier distribution.</li> </ul> <p>Below, we’ll describe the basic syntax for presentations that applies to all formats. See the format-specific articles for additional details on their native capabilities.</p> <h5 id="creating-slides-2">Creating Slides</h5> <p>In markdown, slides are delineated using headings. For example, here is a simple slide show with two slides (each defined with a level 2 heading (<code>##</code>)):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>You can also divide slide shows into sections with title slides using a level 1 heading (<code>#</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- # In the morning ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Breakfast - Eat eggs - Drink coffee # In the evening ## Dinner - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>Finally, you can also delineate slides using horizontal rules (for example, if you have a slide without a title):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed --- - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>The examples above all use level 2 headings for slides and level 1 headings for sections/title slides. You can customize this using the <code>slide-level</code> option (See the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#structuring-the-slide-show">structuring the slide show</a> for additional details).</p> <h5 id="incremental-lists-2">Incremental Lists</h5> <p>By default number and bullet lists within slides are displayed all at once. You can override this globally using the <code>incremental</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Presentation" format: revealjs: incremental: true</code></pre> <p>You can also explicitly make any list incremental or non-incremental by surrounding it in a div with an explicit class that determines the mode. To make a list incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.incremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>To make a list non-incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.nonincremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <h5 id="multiple-columns-2">Multiple Columns</h5> <p>To put material in side by side columns, you can use a native div container with class <code>.columns</code>, containing two or more div containers with class <code>.column</code>and a <code>width</code> attribute:</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} contents... ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} contents... ::: ::::</code></pre> <h5 id="learning-more-15">Learning More</h5> <p>See these format-specific articles for additional details on the additional capabilities of each format:</p> <ul> <li><code>revealjs</code> — reveal.js (HTML)</li> <li><code>pptx</code> — PowerPoint (MS Office)</li> <li><code>beamer</code> — Beamer (LaTeX/PDF)</li> </ul> <h3 id="presenting-slides">Presenting Slides</h3> <h4 id="presenting-slides-1">Presenting Slides</h4> <h5 id="overview-101">Overview</h5> <p>This article covers the mechanics of presenting slides with Reveal. Basic navigation is done using the following keyboard shortcuts:</p> <p>Action</p> <p>Keys</p> <p>Next slide</p> <p>→ SPACE N</p> <p>Previous slide</p> <p>← P</p> <p>Navigate without fragments</p> <p>Alt → Alt ←</p> <p>Jump to first/last slide</p> <p>Shift → Shift ←</p> <p>You will often want to enter fullscreen mode when presenting. You can do this by pressing the FF key.</p> <p>In addition to basic keyboard navigation, Reveal supports several more advanced capabilities, including:</p> <ul> <li>Navigation menu and overview mode</li> <li>Speaker view (w/ speaker notes,timer, and preview of upcoming slides)</li> <li>Printing to PDF and publishing as self contained HTML</li> <li>Drawing on top of slides & chalkboard/whiteboard mode</li> <li>Multiplex, which allows your audience to follow the slides of the presentation you are controlling on their own phone, tablet or laptop. These capabilities are described below.</li> </ul> <h5 id="navigation-menu">Navigation Menu</h5> <p>Quarto includes a built in version of the <a href="https://github.com/denehyg/reveal.js-menu">reveal.js-menu</a> plugin. You can access the navigation menu using the Slide menu button located in the bottom left corner of the presentation. Clicking the button opens a slide navigation menu that enables you to easily jump to any slide:</p> <p>You can also open the navigation menu by pressing the MM key.</p> <p>The navigation menu also includes a Tools pane that provides access to the various other navigation tools including Fullscreen, Speaker View, Overview Mode, and Print to PDF.</p> <p>Use the following options to customize the appearance and behavior of the menu:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>side</code></p> <p>Side of the presentation where the menu will be shown. <code>left</code> or <code>right</code> (defaults to <code>left</code>).</p> <p><code>width</code></p> <p>Width of the menu (<code>normal</code>, <code>wide</code>, <code>third</code>, <code>half</code>, <code>full</code>, or any valid css length value).
