Defaults to <code>normal</code></p> <p><code>numbers</code></p> <p>Add slide numbers to menu items.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: menu: side: right width: wide</code></pre> <p>You can hide the navigation menu by specifying the <code>menu: false</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: menu: false</code></pre> <p>Note that you can still open the menu using the MM key even if the button is hidden.</p> <h5 id="jump-to-slide">Jump To Slide</h5> <p>You can skip ahead to a specific slide using reveal.js’ jump-to-slide shortcut. Here’s how it works:</p> <ul> <li>Press GG to activate</li> <li>Type a slide number or an id</li> <li>Press Enter to confirm You can either enter - a numeric value to navigate to the desired slide number - a string, which will try to locate a slide with a matching id and navigate to it.</li> </ul> <p>This feature can be opt-out by setting <code>jump-to-slide: false</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: jump-to-slide: false</code></pre> <h5 id="overview-mode">Overview Mode</h5> <p>Overview mode provides an alternate view that shows you a thumbnail for each slide:</p> <p>You can enable Overview Mode by pressing the OO key.</p> <h5 id="scroll-view">Scroll View</h5> <p>Reveal presentations can be presented in <a href="https://revealjs.com/scroll-view/">Scroll View</a> with vertically scrolled navigation instead of Slides. This is a new view mode introduced in Revealjs 5. It is always available in presentations as an alternative view mode (like Print view), and it will be used as the default view on small screens (e.g. viewing a presentation on a mobile).</p> <p>Our demo presentation can be seen <a href="https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/demo/?view=scroll">in scroll view mode</a> and below</p> <h6 id="entering-scroll-view">Entering Scroll View</h6> <p>To enter Scroll View , do one the following:</p> <ul> <li>Toggle into Scroll View using the RR key</li> <li>Toggle into Scroll View using the Navigation Menu</li> <li>Toggle into Scroll View by adding <code>?view=scroll</code> to the url, e.g. <code>https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/demo/?view=scroll</code> You can easily toggle out of Scroll View by the same action.</li> </ul> <h6 id="default-view-mode">Default View Mode</h6> <p>Scroll View can be set as the default mode for the presentation using the <code>scroll-view</code> option:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: scroll-view: true</code></pre> <h6 id="scroll-view-options">Scroll View Options</h6> <p>Scroll View can be configured using the following options under <code>scroll-view</code>:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>progress</code></p> <p><code>auto</code>: Show the scrollbar while scrolling and hide while idle (default). Set to <code>true</code> to always show, <code>false</code> to always hide.</p> <p><code>snap</code></p> <p><code>mandatory</code>: When scrolling, it will automatically snap to the closest slide (default). Only snap when close to the top of a slide using <code>proximity</code>. Disable snapping altogether by setting to <code>false</code>.</p> <p><code>layout</code></p> <p><code>full</code>: Each slide will be sized to be as tall as the viewport (default). If you prefer a more dense layout with multiple slides visible in parallel, set to <code>compact</code>.</p> <p><code>activation-width</code></p> <p>Control scroll view activation width. The scroll view is automatically activated when the viewport reaches mobile widths. Set to <code>0</code> to disable automatic scroll view or to another value in pixels to automatically trigger on bigger or smaller widths.</p> <p><code>activate</code></p> <p>Activate scroll view by default for the presentation (default <code>false</code>). Otherwise, entering scroll view require a manual trigger (See Entering Scroll View). <code>scroll-view: true</code> is equivalent to</p> <pre><code>scroll-view: activate: true</code></pre> <p>For example, the following specifies that we want a compact layout, proximity snap mode, to always show the progress scrollbar, and to never automatically activate for small screens:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: scroll-view: layout: compact snap: proximity progress: true activation-width: 0 ---</code></pre> <h5 id="slide-zoom">Slide Zoom</h5> <p>Hold down the AltAlt key and click on any element to zoom towards it. Try zooming in on one of these images:</p> <p>AltAlt or CtrlCtrl click again to zoom back out.</p> <h5 id="speaker-view">Speaker View</h5> <p>The speaker view shows the current slide along with the upcoming slide, a timer, and any speaker notes associated with the current slide:</p> <p>You can enable Speaker View by pressing the SS key.</p> <p>You can add speaker notes to a slide using a div with class <code>.notes</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide with speaker notes Slide content ::: {.notes} Speaker notes go here. :::</code></pre> <h5 id="slide-numbers">Slide Numbers</h5> <p>You can add slide numbers to your presentation using the <code>slide-number</code> option. You can also control in which contexts slide numbers appear using the <code>show-slide-number</code> option. For example, here we configure slides numbers for printed output only:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: slide-number: true show-slide-number: print ---</code></pre> <p>In addition to a simple <code>true</code> or <code>false</code> value, the <code>slide-number</code> option can also specify a format. Available formats include:</p> <p>Value</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>c/t</code></p> <p>Slide number / total slides (default)</p> <p><code>c</code></p> <p>Slide number only</p> <p><code>h/v</code></p> <p>Horizontal / Vertical slide number</p> <p><code>h.v</code></p> <p>Horizontal . Vertical slide number</p> <p>See Vertical Slides for additional information on vertical slides.</p> <p>The <code>show-slide-number</code> option supports the following values:</p> <p>Value</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>all</code></p> <p>Show slide numbers in all contexts (default)</p> <p>Only show slide numbers when printing to PDF</p> <p><code>speaker</code></p> <p>Only show slide numbers in the speaker view</p> <h5 id="print-to-pdf">Print to PDF</h5> <p>Reveal presentations can be exported to PDF via a special print stylesheet.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Note: This feature has been confirmed to work in <a href="https://google.com/chrome">Google Chrome</a>, <a href="https://www.chromium.org/Home">Chromium</a> as well as in <a href="https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/">Firefox</a>.</p> <p>To Print to PDF, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Toggle into Print View using the EE key (or using the Navigation Menu)</li> <li>Open the in-browser print dialog Ctrl+PCtrl+P.</li> <li>Change the Destination setting to Save as PDF.</li> <li>Change the Layout to Landscape.</li> <li>Change the Margins to None.</li> <li>Enable the Background graphics option.</li> <li>Click Save 🎉 If you entered print mode in the same window, you can toggle out of Print View using the same EE key, or navigate back to last slide seen using usual back button in your browser.</li> </ul> <p>Here’s what the Chrome print dialog would look like with these settings enabled:</p> <h6 id="print-options">Print Options</h6> <p>There are a number of options that affected printed output that you may want to configure prior to printing:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>show-notes</code></p> <p>Include speaker notes (<code>true</code>, <code>false</code>, or <code>separate-page)</code></p> <p><code>slide-number</code></p> <p>Include slide numbers (<code>true</code> or <code>false</code>)</p> <p><code>pdf-max-pages-per-slide</code></p> <p>Slides that are too tall to fit within a single page will expand onto multiple pages. You can limit how many pages a slide may expand to using the <code>pdf-max-pages-per-slide</code> option.</p> <p><code>pdf-separate-fragments</code></p> <p>Slides with multiple fragments are printed on a single page by default. To create a page for each fragment set this option to <code>true</code>.</p> <p>For example, the following specifies that we want to print speaker notes on their own page and include slide numbers:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: show-notes: separate-page slide-number: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="preview-links">Preview Links</h5> <p>Reveal makes it easy to incorporate navigation to external websites into the flow of presentations using the <code>preview-links</code> option.</p> <p>When you click on a hyperlink with <code>preview-links: true</code>, the link will be navigated to in an iframe that overlays the slide. For example, here we’ve clicked on a <a href="https://matplotlib.org/">Matplotlib</a> link and the website opens on top of the slide (you’d click the close button at top right to hide it):</p> <p>Available values for <code>preview-link</code> include:</p> <p>Value</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>auto</code></p> <p>Preview links when presenting in full-screen mode (otherwise navigate to them normally)</p> <p><code>true</code></p> <p>Always preview links</p> <p><code>false</code></p> <p>Never preview links (the default)</p> <p>For example, here we set <code>preview-links</code> to <code>auto</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: preview-links: auto ---</code></pre> <p>You can also set this option on a per-link basis. These two links respectively enable and disable preview:</p> <pre><code>[Preview](https://example.com){preview-link="true"} [NoPreview](https://example.com){preview-link="false"}</code></pre> <p>Previewing website in HTML format will use an <code><iframe></code>, which not all websites will allow (e.g. they could set in their response header <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/X-Frame-Options"><code>X-Frame-Options</code> to <code>deny</code></a>, or <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors"><code>frame-ancestor</code> restriction in their <code>Content-Security-Policy</code></a>). If a website disallow <code>iframe</code> usage, the preview will not be working in the Quarto document output.</p> <h5 id="slide-tone">Slide Tone</h5> <p>Slide tone plays a subtle sound when you change slides. It was <a href="https://github.com/yihui/xaringan/issues/214">requested by a blind user</a> and enables presenters to hear an auditory signal of their progress through the slides. Enable slide tone with:</p> <pre><code>format: revealjs: slide-tone: true</code></pre> <p>The tones increase in pitch for each slide from a low C to a high C note. The tone pitch stays the same for incremental slides.</p> <p>The implementation of slide tone was adapted from the <a href="https://github.com/gadenbuie/xaringanExtra/blob/master/docs/slide-tone/libs/slide-tone/slide-tone.js">slide tone plugin</a> in xaringanExtra.</p> <h5 id="auto-slide">Auto-Slide</h5> <p>Presentations can be configured to step through slides automatically, without any user input. To enable this you will need to specify an interval for slide changes using the <code>auto-slide</code> option (the interval is provided in milliseconds). The <code>loop</code> option can additionally be specified to continue presenting in a loop once all the slides have been shown.</p> <p>For example, here we specify that we want to advance every 5 seconds and continue in a loop:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: auto-slide: 5000 loop: true ---</code></pre> <p>A play/pause control element will automatically appear for auto-sliding decks. Sliding is automatically paused if the user starts interacting with the deck. It’s also possible to pause or resume sliding by pressing AA on the keyboard.</p> <p>You can disable the auto-slide controls and prevent sliding from being paused by specifying <code>auto-slide-stoppable: false</code>.</p> <h6 id="slide-timing">Slide Timing</h6> <p>It’s also possible to override the slide duration for individual slides and fragments by using the <code>autoslide</code> attribute (this attribute also works on Fragments). For example, here we set the auto-slide value to 2 seconds:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {autoslide=2000}</code></pre> <h5 id="publishing-9">Publishing</h5> <p>There are two main ways to publish Reveal presentations:</p> <ul> <li><p>As a PDF file—see Print to PDF above for details on how to do this.</p></li> <li><p>As an HTML file. For HTML, it’s often most convenient to distribute the presentation as a single self contained file. To do this, specify the <code>embed-resources</code> option:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: “Presentation”</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>format:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>revealjs:</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>embed-resources: true</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> <li><p>All of the dependent images, CSS styles, and other assets will be contained within the HTML file created by Quarto.</p></li> <li><p>Note that specifying <code>embed-resources</code> can slow down rendering by a couple of seconds, so you may want to enable <code>embed-resources</code> only when you are ready to publish. Also note that Reveal plugin Chalkboard is not compatible with <code>embed-resources</code> — when Chalkboard plugin is enabled, specifying <code>embed-resources: true</code> will result an error. See the documentation on Publishing HTML for details on additional ways to publish Reveal presentations including GitHub Pages and Posit Connect.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="navigation-options">Navigation Options</h5> <p>There are several navigational cues provided as part of Reveal presentations and corresponding options that control them:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>controls</code></p> <p>Show arrow controls for navigating through slides (defaults to <code>auto</code>, which will show controls when vertical slides are present or when the deck is embedded in an iframe).</p> <p><code>progress</code></p> <p>Show a progress bar at the bottom (defaults to <code>true</code>).</p> <p><code>history</code></p> <p>Push slide changes to the browser history. Defaults to <code>true</code>, which means that the browser Forward/Back buttons can be used for slide navigation.</p> <p><code>hash-type</code></p> <p>Type of URL hash to use for slides. Defaults to <code>title</code> which is derived from the slide title. You can also specify <code>number</code>.</p> <p>For example, the following configuration hides the progress bar and specifies that we want to use browser history:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: progress: false history: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="chalkboard">Chalkboard</h5> <p>Quarto includes a built-in version of the <a href="https://github.com/rajgoel/reveal.js-plugins/tree/master/chalkboard">reveal.js-chalkboard</a> plugin. Specify the <code>chalkboard: true</code> option to enable the plugin, which enables you to draw on a notes canvas on top of your slides and/or open up an empty chalkboard within your presentation:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: chalkboard: true ---</code></pre> <p>Note that Reveal plugin Chalkboard is not compatible with <code>embed-resources</code> output — when Chalkboard plugin is enabled, specifying <code>embed-resources: true</code> will result an error.</p> <p>Here are what the notes canvas and chalkboard look like when activated:</p> <p>To toggle the notes canvas on and off use the Toggle Notes Canvas button or the CC key.</p> <p>To toggle the chalkboard on and off use the Toggle Chalkboard button or the BB key.</p> <p>Here are all of the keyboard shortcuts associated with the notes canvas and chalkboard:</p> <p>Action</p> <p>Key</p> <p>Toggle notes canvas</p> <p>CC</p> <p>Toggle chalkboard</p> <p>BB</p> <p>Reset all drawings</p> <p>BACKSPACEBACKSPACE</p> <p>Clear drawings on slide</p> <p>DELDEL</p> <p>Cycle colors forward</p> <p>XX</p> <p>Cycle colors backward</p> <p>YY</p> <p>Download drawings</p> <p>DD</p> <p>The following mouse and touch gestures can be used for interacting with drawings:</p> <ul> <li>Click on the buttons at the bottom left to toggle the notes canvas or chalkboard</li> <li>Click on the color picker at the left to change the color (the color picker is only visible if the notes canvas or chalkboard is active)</li> <li>Click on the up/down arrows on the right to switch among multiple chalkboard (the up/down arrows are only available for the chalkboard)</li> <li>Click the left mouse button and drag to write on notes canvas or chalkboard</li> <li>Click the right mouse button and drag to wipe away previous drawings</li> <li>Touch and move to write on notes canvas or chalkboard</li> <li>Touch and hold for half a second, then move to wipe away previous drawings</li> </ul> <h6 id="restoring-drawings">Restoring Drawings</h6> <p>The DD key downloads any active drawings into a JSON file. You can then restore these drawings when showing your presentation using the <code>src</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: chalkboard: src: drawings.json ---</code></pre> <h6 id="chalkboard-options">Chalkboard Options</h6> <p>The following options are available to customize the behavior and appearance of the chalkboard:</p> <h4 id="option">Option</h4> <p><code>theme</code></p> <h4 id="description-2">Description</h4> <p>Can be set to either <code>chalkboard</code> (default) or <code>whiteboard</code>.</p> <p><code>boardmarker-width</code></p> <p>The drawing width of the boardmarker; larger values draw thicker line. Defaults to <code>3</code>.</p> <p><code>chalk-width</code></p> <p>The drawing width of the chalk; larger values draw thicker lines. Defaults to <code>7</code>.</p> <p><code>chalk-effect</code></p> <p>A float in the range <code>[0.0, 1.0]</code>, the intensity of the chalk effect on the chalk board. Full effect (default) <code>1.0</code>, no effect <code>0.0</code>.</p> <p><code>src</code></p> <p>Optional file name for pre-recorded drawings (download drawings using the DD key).</p> <p><code>read-only</code></p> <p>Configuration option to prevent changes to existing drawings. <code>true</code>: no changes can be made, <code>false</code> (default): changes can be made.</p> <p><code>buttons</code></p> <p>Add chalkboard buttons at the bottom of the slide (defaults to <code>true</code>).</p> <p><code>transition</code></p> <p>Gives the duration (in milliseconds) of the transition for a slide change, so that the notes canvas is drawn after the transition is completed.</p> <p>For example, the following configuration specifies that we want to use the <code>whiteboard</code> theme with a (thicker) boardmarker width, and that we want to hide the chalkboard buttons at the bottom of each slide:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: chalkboard: theme: whiteboard boardmarker-width: 5 buttons: false ---</code></pre> <p>If you disable the chalkboard buttons globally you can selectively re-enable them for individual slides with the <code>chalkboard-buttons</code> attribute. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {chalkboard-buttons="true"}</code></pre> <p>You can also use <code>chalkboard-buttons="false"</code> to turn off the buttons for individual slides.</p> <h5 id="multiplex">Multiplex</h5> <p>Quarto includes a built-in version of the <a href="https://github.com/reveal/multiplex">Reveal Multiplex</a> plugin. The multiplex plugin allows your audience to follow the slides of the presentation you are controlling on their own phone, tablet or laptop. When you change slides in your master presentations everyone will follow and see the same content on their own device.</p> <p>Creating a Reveal presentation that supports multiplex is straightforward. Just specify the <code>multiplex: true</code> option as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: multiplex: true ---</code></pre> <p>Rendering the presentation will result in two HTML files being created by Quarto:</p> <p>File</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>presentation.html</code></p> <p>This is the file you should publish online and that your audience should view.</p> <p><code>presentation-speaker.html</code></p> <p>This is the file that you should present from . This file can remain on your computer and does not need to be published elsewhere.</p> <p>The two versions of the presentation will be synchronized such that when the speaker version switches slides the viewers also all switch to the same slide.</p> <h6 id="multiplex-server">Multiplex Server</h6> <p>Behind the scenes there is a multiplex server that is synchronizing slide events between the viewer and speaker versions of the presentation. Note that the this server does not actually see any of the slide content, it is only used to synchronize events.</p> <p>By default, a server created and hosted by the Revealjs team is used for this: <a href="https://multiplex.up.railway.app/">multiplex.up.railway.app</a>. This server is used by default when you specify <code>multiplex: true</code>.</p> <h6 id="running-your-own-server">Running your own server</h6> <p>If you want to run your own version of this server its source code is here: <a href="https://github.com/reveal/multiplex/blob/master/index.js">github.com</a>.</p> <p>You can then configure multiplex to use an alternate server as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: multiplex: url: '[myserver.example.com](https://myserver.example.com/) ---</code></pre> <p>Note that Quarto calls the multiplex server behind the scenes to provision a id and secret for your presentation. If you want to provision your own id and secret you can do so at <a href="https://multiplex.up.railway.app/">multiplex.up.railway.app</a> (or using your custom hosted server URL) and provide them explicitly in YAML:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: multiplex: id: '1ea875674b17ca76' secret: '13652805320794272084' ---</code></pre> <p>Note that the <code>secret</code> value will be included in only the speaker version of the presentation.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-16">Learning More</h5> <p>See these articles lo learn more about using Reveal:</p> <ul> <li>Reveal Basics covers the basic mechanics of creating presentations.</li> <li>Advanced Reveal delves into transitions, animations, advanced layout and positioning, and other options available for customizing presentations.</li> <li>Reveal Themes talks about using and customizing existing themes as well as creating brand new themes.</li> </ul> <h3 id="quarto-presentations">Quarto Presentations</h3> <p>1</p> <p>1</p> <p>4</p> <p>2</p> <h3 id="reveal-themes">Reveal Themes</h3> <h4 id="reveal-themes-1">Reveal Themes</h4> <h5 id="using-themes">Using Themes</h5> <p>There are 11 built-in themes provided for Reveal presentations (you can also create your own themes). The <code>default</code> and <code>dark</code> themes use fairly classic typography and color schemes and are a good place to start.</p> <p>The <code>default</code> theme is used automatically — use the <code>theme</code> option to switch to an alternate theme. For example</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: dark ---</code></pre> <p>Here is the full list of available themes:</p> <ul> <li><code>beige</code></li> <li><code>blood</code></li> <li><code>dark</code></li> <li><code>default</code></li> <li><code>dracula</code></li> <li><code>league</code></li> <li><code>moon</code></li> <li><code>night</code></li> <li><code>serif</code></li> <li><code>simple</code></li> <li><code>sky</code></li> <li><code>solarized</code></li> </ul> <h5 id="customizing-themes-1">Customizing Themes</h5> <p>You can customize the built-in themes by adding your own <a href="https://sass-lang.com/">Sass</a> theme file to the theme declaration. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: [default, custom.scss] ---</code></pre> <p>Here’s what the contents of <code>custom.scss</code> might look like:</p> <pre><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/ $body-bg: #191919; $body-color: #fff; $link-color: #42affa; /*-- scss:rules --*/ .reveal .slide blockquote { border-left: 3px solid $text-muted; padding-left: 0.5em; }</code></pre> <p>Theme files use <a href="https://sass-lang.com/">Sass</a> (a variant of CSS that supports variables and other extended features) and are divided into sections.</p> <ul> <li><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/</code> is used to define variables that affect fonts, colors, borders, etc. (note that variables start with a <code>$</code>)</li> <li><code>/*-- scss:rules --*/</code> is used to create CSS rules. Note that CSS rules that target Reveal content generally need to use the <code>.reveal .slide</code> prefix to successfully override the theme’s default styles. See the Sass Variables documentation for a list of what’s available to customize.</li> </ul> <h5 id="creating-themes">Creating Themes</h5> <p>Creating a new theme is just a matter of re-defining one or more of the default Sass variables (you don’t need to re-specify values that you don’t want to override) and adding any additional CSS rules you need to.</p> <p>See the Sass Variables documentation for a list of what can be customized within a theme.</p> <p>For example, here is the source code for the built in <code>serif</code> theme:</p> <pre><code>/*-- scss:defaults --*/ // fonts $font-family-sans-serif: "Palatino Linotype", "Book Antiqua", Palatino, FreeSerif, serif !default; // colors $body-bg: #f0f1eb !default; $body-color: #000 !default; $link-color: #51483d !default; $selection-bg: #26351c !default; // headings $presentation-heading-font: "Palatino Linotype", "Book Antiqua", Palatino, FreeSerif, serif !default; $presentation-heading-color: #383d3d !default; /*-- scss:rules --*/ .reveal a { line-height: 1.3em; }</code></pre> <p>In this theme file you’ll notice that the <code>!default</code> suffix is placed after variable definitions. This is to make sure that anyone using this theme can override the variable value (without that the value is defined as not overrideable).</p> <p>You can use a custom theme by just specifying it as the <code>theme</code> option (all theme files implicitly inherit from the <code>default</code> theme). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: mytheme.scss ---</code></pre> <p>Here is the source code for all of the built-in themes for inspiration and examples:</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/src/resources/formats/revealjs/themes">github.com</a></p> <h5 id="sass-variables-2">Sass Variables</h5> <p>Here’s a list of all Sass variables (and their default values) used by Reveal themes. Note that some variables are defined using other variables, and several of the color variables use the <code>lighten()</code> Sass function to create a lighter variant of another color.</p> <h6 id="colors-2">Colors</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$body-bg</code></p> <p>#fff</p> <p><code>$body-color</code></p> <p>#222</p> <p><code>$text-muted</code></p> <p>lighten($body-color, 50%)</p> <p><code>$link-color</code></p> <p>#2a76dd</p> <p><code>$link-color-hover</code></p> <p>lighten($link-color, 15%)</p> <p><code>$selection-bg</code></p> <p>lighten($link-color, 25%)</p> <p><code>$selection-color</code></p> <p>$body-bg</p> <p><code>$light-bg-text-color</code></p> <p>#222</p> <p><code>$light-bg-link-color</code></p> <p>#2a76dd</p> <p><code>$light-bg-code-color</code></p> <p>#4758ab</p> <p><code>$dark-bg-text-color</code></p> <p>#fff</p> <p><code>$dark-bg-link-color</code></p> <p>#42affa</p> <p><code>$dark-bg-code-color</code></p> <p>#ffa07a</p> <h6 id="fonts-3">Fonts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$font-family-sans-serif</code></p> <p>“Source Sans Pro”, Helvetica, sans-serif</p> <p><code>$font-family-monospace</code></p> <p>monospace</p> <p><code>$presentation-font-size-root</code></p> <p>40px</p> <p><code>$presentation-font-smaller</code></p> <p>0.7</p> <p><code>$presentation-line-height</code></p> <p>1.3</p> <h6 id="headings-1">Headings</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$presentation-h1-font-size</code></p> <p>2.5em</p> <p><code>$presentation-h2-font-size</code></p> <p>1.6em</p> <p><code>$presentation-h3-font-size</code></p> <p>1.3em</p> <p><code>$presentation-h4-font-size</code></p> <p>1em</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-font</code></p> <p>$font-family-sans-serif</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-color</code></p> <p>$body-color</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-line-height</code></p> <p>1.2</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-letter-spacing</code></p> <p>normal</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-text-transform</code></p> <p>none</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-text-shadow</code></p> <p>none</p> <p><code>$presentation-heading-font-weight</code></p> <p>600</p> <p><code>$presentation-h1-text-shadow</code></p> <p>none</p> <h6 id="code-blocks-8">Code Blocks</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$code-block-bg</code></p> <p>$body-bg</p> <p><code>$code-block-border-color</code></p> <p>lighten($body-color, 60%)</p> <p><code>$code-block-font-size</code></p> <p>0.55em</p> <h6 id="inline-code-6">Inline Code</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$code-color</code></p> <p>var(–quarto-hl-fu-color)</p> <p><code>$code-bg</code></p> <p>transparent</p> <h6 id="tabsets-3">Tabsets</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$tabset-border-color</code></p> <p>$code-block-border-color</p> <h6 id="layout-8">Layout</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Default</p> <p><code>$border-color</code></p> <p>lighten($body-color, 30%)</p> <p><code>$border-width</code></p> <p>1px</p> <p><code>$border-radius</code></p> <p>3px</p> <p><code>$presentation-block-margin</code></p> <p>12px</p> <p><code>$presentation-slide-text-align</code></p> <p>left</p> <p><code>$presentation-title-slide-text-align</code></p> <p>center</p> <h6 id="callouts-5">Callouts</h6> <p>Variable</p> <p>Notes</p> <p><code>$callout-border-width</code></p> <p>The left border width of callouts. Defaults to <code>0.3rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-border-scale</code></p> <p>The border color of callouts computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>0%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-icon-scale</code></p> <p>The color of the callout icon computed by shifting the callout color by this amount. Defaults to <code>10%</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-top</code></p> <p>The amount of top margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-margin-bottom</code></p> <p>The amount of bottom margin on the callout. Defaults to <code>1rem</code>.</p> <p><code>$callout-color-<type></code></p> <p>The colors for the various types of callouts. Defaults:</p> <p>type</p> <p>default</p> <p><code>note</code></p> <p><code>#0d6efd</code></p> <p><code>tip</code></p> <p><code>#198754</code></p> <p><code>caution</code></p> <p><code>#fd7e14</code></p> <p><code>warning</code></p> <p><code>#ffc107</code></p> <p><code>important</code></p> <p><code>#dc3545</code></p> <p>Note that style for callout is to have left border using type color, and header background to use a variation of this color.</p> <p>You’ll notice that some of the Sass variables use a <code>presentation-</code> prefix and some do not. The <code>presentation-</code> prefixed variables are specific to presentations, whereas the other variables are the same as ones used for standard Quarto HTML Themes.</p> <p>Since all Quarto themes use the same Sass format, you can use a single theme file for both HTML / website documents and presentations.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-17">Learning More</h5> <p>See these articles to learn more about using Reveal:</p> <ul> <li>Reveal Basics covers the basic mechanics of creating presentations.</li> <li>Presenting Slides describes slide navigation, printing to PDF, drawing on slides using a chalkboard, and creating multiplex presentations.</li> <li>Advanced Reveal delves into transitions, animations, advanced layout and positioning, and other options available for customizing presentations.</li> <li>More About Quarto Themes describes the layering system in more detail, including interactions with other SCSS files and <code>_brand.yml</code>.</li> </ul> <h3 id="revealjs-4">Revealjs</h3> <h4 id="revealjs-5">Revealjs</h4> <h5 id="overview-102">Overview</h5> <p>You can create <a href="https://revealjs.com/">Revealjs</a> presentations using the <code>revealjs</code> format. The best way to get a sense for the capabilities of Revealjs is this <a href="demo/">demo</a> presentation:</p> <p>If you prefer to view the demo in a standalone browser you can do that <a href="demo/">here</a>. Check out the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/blob/main/docs/presentations/revealjs/demo/index.qmd">source code</a> for the demo to see how the slides were created.</p> <p>See the Revealjs format reference for a comprehensive overview of all options supported for Revealjs output.</p> <h5 id="creating-slides-3">Creating Slides</h5> <p>In markdown, slides are delineated using headings. For example, here is a simple slide show with two slides (each defined with a level 2 heading (<code>##</code>):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>You can also divide slide shows into sections with title slides using a level 1 heading (<code>#</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- # In the morning ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Breakfast - Eat eggs - Drink coffee # In the evening ## Dinner - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>Finally, you can also delineate slides using horizontal rules (for example, if you have a slide without a title):</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Habits" author: "John Doe" format: revealjs --- - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed --- - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <p>The examples above all use level 2 headings for slides and level 1 headings for sections/title slides. You can customize this using the <code>slide-level</code> option (See the Pandoc documentation on <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#structuring-the-slide-show">structuring the slide show</a> for additional details.</p> <h6 id="title-slide-1">Title Slide</h6> <p>You’ll notice in the above examples that a title slide is automatically created based on the <code>title</code> and <code>author</code> provided in the document YAML options. However, sometimes you don’t want an explicit title slide (e.g. if your first slide consists entirely of a background image). It’s perfectly valid to create a presentation without a title slide, just exclude the <code>title</code> and <code>author</code> options:</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs --- ## Getting up - Turn off alarm - Get out of bed ## Going to sleep - Get in bed - Count sheep</code></pre> <h5 id="incremental-lists-3">Incremental Lists</h5> <p>By default number and bullet lists within slides are displayed all at once. You can override this globally using the <code>incremental</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Presentation" format: revealjs: incremental: true</code></pre> <p>You can also explicitly make any list incremental or non-incremental by surrounding it in a div with an explicit class that determines the mode. To make a list incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.incremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>To make a list non-incremental do this:</p> <pre><code>::: {.nonincremental} - Eat spaghetti - Drink wine :::</code></pre> <p>You can also insert a pause within a slide (keeping the content after the pause hidden) by inserting three dots separated by spaces:</p> <pre><code>## Slide with a pause content before the pause . . . content after the pause</code></pre> <p>Note this only works below headings that are creating slides (see Creating slides).</p> <h5 id="multiple-columns-3">Multiple Columns</h5> <p>To put material in side by side columns, you can use a native div container with class <code>.columns</code>, containing two or more div containers with class <code>.column</code> and a <code>width</code> attribute:</p> <pre><code>:::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} Left column ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} Right column ::: ::::</code></pre> <h5 id="content-overflow">Content Overflow</h5> <p>If you have a slide that has more content than can be displayed on a single frame there are two slide-level classes you can apply to mitigate this:</p> <ul> <li><p>Use the <code>.smaller</code> class to use a smaller typeface so that more text fits on the slide. For example:</p> <p>## Slide Title {.smaller}</p></li> <li><p>Use the <code>.scrollable</code> class to make off-slide content available by scrolling. For example:</p> <p>## Slide Title {.scrollable}</p></li> </ul> <p>Both of these options can also be applied globally to all slides as follows:</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: smaller: true scrollable: true ---</code></pre> <p>Please note that section title slides are centered by default which prevents them from being scrollable. If you want to make title slides scrollable, you need to make them non-centered.</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: scrollable: true center-title-slide: false ---</code></pre> <p>NoteLimitation: Auto-stretch and Scrollable</p> <p>When a slide is scrollable the image size calculations used by auto-stretch may not work well and images may not appear. Two solutions depending on your needs are:</p> <ul> <li>Disable auto-stretch at the presentation level, <code>auto-stretch: false</code>, and use <code>.r-stretch</code> on individual images only where needed.</li> <li>On slides that are scrollable, add the <code>.nostretch</code> class to disable auto-stretch on the slide.</li> </ul> <h5 id="speaker-notes-1">Speaker Notes</h5> <p>You can add speaker notes to a slide using a div with class <code>.notes</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide with speaker notes Slide content ::: {.notes} Speaker notes go here. :::</code></pre> <p>This is a Revealjs feature from <a href="https://revealjs.com/plugins/#built-in-plugins">built-in plugin</a> which brings limitation: the content cannot rely on external dependencies. For instance, if you want to include a mermaid diagram that typically needs mermaid.js, it will need to be embed as an SVG or PNG image.</p> <p>Press the S key (or use the Navigation Menu) to show the presentation speaker view:</p> <p>You’ll typically use this view on one screen (e.g. your laptop) while presenting the slides on another screen.</p> <h5 id="themes">Themes</h5> <p>There are 11 built-in themes provided for Reveal presentations (you can also create your own themes). The <code>default</code> and <code>dark</code> themes use fairly classic typography and color schemes and are a good place to start.</p> <p>The <code>default</code> theme is used automatically — use the <code>theme</code> option to switch to an alternate theme. For example</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: dark ---</code></pre> <p>Here is the full list of available themes:</p> <ul> <li><code>beige</code></li> <li><code>blood</code></li> <li><code>dark</code></li> <li><code>default</code></li> <li><code>dracula</code></li> <li><code>league</code></li> <li><code>moon</code></li> <li><code>night</code></li> <li><code>serif</code></li> <li><code>simple</code></li> <li><code>sky</code></li> <li><code>solarized</code> See the article on Reveal Themes for additional details on customizing themes and creating brand new themes of your own.</li> </ul> <h5 id="asides-footnotes">Asides & Footnotes</h5> <p>Asides contain content of more peripheral interest, and are displayed in a smaller, lighter font at the bottom of the slide. Creates asides using a div with the <code>aside</code> class. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title Slide content ::: aside Some additional commentary of more peripheral interest. :::</code></pre> <p>Footnotes have a similar visual treatment to asides, but include a footnote number. For example, here we use a footnote and an aside on a single slide:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title - Green ^[A footnote] - Brown - Purple ::: aside Some additional commentary of more peripheral interest. :::</code></pre> <p>Which looks like this when rendered:</p> <p>If you prefer that footnotes be included at the end of the document, specify the <code>reference-location: document</code> option:</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: reference-location: document ---</code></pre> <p>Note that when specifying this option footnotes can still be viewed while on the slide by hovering over the footnote number.</p> <h5 id="footer-logo">Footer & Logo</h5> <p>You can include footer text and a logo at the bottom of each slide using the <code>footer</code> and <code>logo</code> options. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: logo: path: logo.png alt: "Company logo" footer: "Footer text" ---</code></pre> <p>Using <code>{footer=false}</code> on a slide heading allows to remove the presentation footer for this slide.</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: footer: "Footer text" --- ## Slide with default footer Content ## No footer {footer=false} No footer is shown on this slide</code></pre> <p>You can also include a custom footer per-slide by adding a footer div at the bottom of the slide.</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title Slide content ::: footer Custom footer text :::</code></pre> <h5 id="code-blocks-9">Code Blocks</h5> <p>Most of the core capabilities of Quarto HTML Code Blocks are available for Reveal slides, including code folding, code copy, and the ability to pick a custom syntax highlighting theme.</p> <h6 id="syntax-highlighting-3">Syntax Highlighting</h6> <p>You can specify the code highlighting style using the <code>syntax-highlighting</code> option. If you choose a dark Reveal theme then the default Quarto dark syntax highlighting theme will be used. See HTML Code Blocks: Highlighting for the full list of available themes.</p> <p>Note</p> <p><code>syntax-highlighting: idiomatic</code> is not currently supported for RevealJS presentations. If specified, Quarto falls back to the default Skylighting highlighting with a warning.</p> <h6 id="line-highlighting">Line Highlighting</h6> <p>You may want to highlight specific lines of code output (or even highlight distinct lines over a progression of steps). You can do this using the <code>code-line-numbers</code> attribute of code blocks. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{.python code-line-numbers="6-8"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Note that you can also highlight disparate ranges of lines by separating them with a comma. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{.python code-line-numbers="7,9"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Finally, you can highlight different line ranges progressively by separating them with <code>|</code>. For example, here we start by showing all lines, then progress to highlighting line 6, and finally to highlighting line 9:</p> <pre><code>```{.python code-line-numbers="|6|9"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>You can use this same option within an executable code cell by using the <code>code-line-numbers</code> cell options:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| code-line-numbers: "|6|9" #| fig-alt: "Spiral polar plot" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <h6 id="code-block-height">Code Block Height</h6> <p>By default, code blocks are limited to a maximum height of 500px. Code that exceeds this height introduces a scrollbar. To avoid a scrollbar you can increase the maximum height with the <code>code-block-height</code> option:</p> <pre><code>--- format: revealjs: code-block-height: 650px ---</code></pre> <h5 id="executable-code">Executable Code</h5> <p>You can include the output of executable code blocks on slides just the same as with other Quarto documents. This works essentially the same for slides as it does for other formats, however there are a couple of special considerations for slides covered below.</p> <h6 id="figure-size">Figure Size</h6> <p>You will frequently need to customize the size of figures created for slides so that they either fill the entire slide or whatever region of the slide you need them to. Quarto provides some help here: for Python the figure sizes for <a href="https://matplotlib.org/">Matplotlib</a> and <a href="https://plotly.com/python/plotly-express/">Plotly Express</a> are set to fill the slide area below the title, and for R the Knitr figure width and height are similarly defaulted.</p> <p>Nevertheless, you will frequently need to change these defaults for a given figure. The details on how to do this vary by graphics library. Here’s an example of explicitly sizing an <a href="https://altair-viz.github.io/">Altair</a> plot:</p> <pre><code>alt.Chart(cars).mark_point().encode( x='Horsepower', y='Miles_per_Gallon', color='Origin', ).properties( width=700, height=300 ).interactive()</code></pre> <h6 id="code-echo-1">Code Echo</h6> <p>Unlike with ordinary documents, within Quarto presentations executable code blocks do not <code>echo</code> their source code by default (this is because often the code produces a figure that wants to occupy as much vertical space as possible). You can override this behavior using the <code>echo</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{python} #| echo: true #| fig-alt: "Spiral polar plot" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={"projection": "polar"}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <h6 id="output-location-1">Output Location</h6> <p>By default, output from executable code blocks is displayed immediately after the code. You can use the <code>output-location</code> option to modify this behavior as follows:</p> <p><code>fragment</code></p> <p>Display output as a Fragment (delay showing it until it is explicitly stepped through by advancing the slide).</p> <p><code>slide</code></p> <p>Display output on the subsequent slide.</p> <p><code>column</code></p> <p>Display output in a column adjacent to the code.</p> <p><code>column-fragment</code></p> <p>Display output in a column adjacent to the code and delay showing it until it is explicitly stepped through by advancing the slide.</p> <p>For example, here we display cell output on its own slide:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| echo: true #| output-location: slide library(ggplot2) ggplot(airquality, aes(Temp, Ozone)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess") ```</code></pre> <p>See the documentation on Execution Options for more details on the various other ways to customize output from code execution.</p> <h5 id="tabsets-4">Tabsets</h5> <p>You can add tabbed content to slides using the standard Quarto syntax for tabsets. For example:</p> <pre><code>::: {.panel-tabset} ### Tab A Content for `Tab A` ### Tab B Content for `Tab B` :::</code></pre> <p>Note that one significant disadvantage to tabsets is that only the first tab will be visible when printing to PDF.</p> <h5 id="slide-backgrounds">Slide Backgrounds</h5> <p>Slides are contained within a limited portion of the screen by default to allow them to fit any display and scale uniformly. You can apply full page backgrounds outside of the slide area by adding a <code>background</code> attribute to your slide headings. Five different types of backgrounds are supported: color, gradient, image, video and iframe.</p> <h6 id="color-background">Color Background</h6> <p>All CSS color formats are supported, including hex values, keywords, <code>rgba()</code> or <code>hsl()</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-color="aquamarine"}</code></pre> <p>Note that if the background color of your media differs from your presentation’s theme (e.g. a dark image when using a light theme) then you should also explicitly set the <code>background-color</code> so that text on top of the background appears in the correct color (e.g. light text on a dark background).</p> <h6 id="gradient-background">Gradient Background</h6> <p>All CSS gradient formats are supported, including <code>linear-gradient</code>, <code>radial-gradient</code> and <code>conic-gradient</code>.</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-gradient="linear-gradient(to bottom, #283b95, #17b2c3)"} ## Slide Title {background-gradient="radial-gradient(#283b95, #17b2c3)"}</code></pre> <h6 id="image-backgrounds">Image Backgrounds</h6> <p>By default, background images are resized to cover the full page. Available options:</p> <p>Attribute</p> <p>Default</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>background-image</code></p> <p>URL of the image to show. GIFs restart when the slide opens.</p> <p><code>background-size</code></p> <p>cover</p> <p>See <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/CSS/background-size">background-size</a> on MDN.</p> <p><code>background-position</code></p> <p>center</p> <p>See <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/CSS/background-position">background-position</a> on MDN.</p> <p><code>background-repeat</code></p> <p>no-repeat</p> <p>See <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/CSS/background-repeat">background-repeat</a> on MDN.</p> <p><code>background-opacity</code></p> <p>1</p> <p>Opacity of the background image on a 0-1 scale. 0 is transparent and 1 is fully opaque.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-color="black" background-image="[placekitten.com](https://placekitten.com/100/100)" background-size="100px" background-repeat="repeat"} This slide's background image will be sized to 100px and repeated.</code></pre> <p>Since this image has a dark background and our slides use the default (light) theme, we explicitly set the <code>background-color</code> to black so that text drawn on top of it is light.</p> <h6 id="video-backgrounds">Video Backgrounds</h6> <p>Automatically plays a full size video behind the slide.</p> <p>Attribute</p> <p>Default</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>background-video</code></p> <p>A single video source, or a comma separated list of video sources.</p> <p><code>background-video-loop</code></p> <p>false</p> <p>Flags if the video should play repeatedly.</p> <p><code>background-video-muted</code></p> <p>false</p> <p>Flags if the audio should be muted.</p> <p><code>background-size</code></p> <p>cover</p> <p>Use <code>cover</code> for full screen and some cropping or <code>contain</code> for letterboxing.</p> <p><code>background-opacity</code></p> <p>1</p> <p>Opacity of the background video on a 0-1 scale. 0 is transparent and 1 is fully opaque.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-video="video.mp4" background-video-loop="true" background-video-muted="true"} This slides's background video will play in a loop with audio muted.</code></pre> <h6 id="iframe-backgrounds">IFrame Backgrounds</h6> <p>Embeds a web page as a slide background that covers 100% of the reveal.js width and height. The iframe is in the background layer, behind your slides, and as such it’s not possible to interact with it by default. To make your background interactive, you can add the <code>background-interactive</code> attribute.</p> <p>Attribute</p> <p>Default</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>background-iframe</code></p> <p>URL of the iframe to load</p> <p><code>background-interactive</code></p> <p>false</p> <p>Include this attribute to make it possible to interact with the iframe contents. Enabling this will prevent interaction with the slide content.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>## Slide Title {background-iframe="[example.com](https://example.com)"}</code></pre> <h6 id="slide-backgrounds-without-a-title">Slide Backgrounds Without a Title</h6> <p>You can always omit the title text, and specify only the slide background information:</p> <pre><code>## {background-color="aquamarine"} (A slide with no title) ## {background-color="black" background-image="[placekitten.com](https://placekitten.com/100/100)" background-size="100px" background-repeat="repeat"} (Another slide with no title)</code></pre> <h6 id="main-title-slide-background">Main Title Slide Background</h6> <p>The main title slide is the first slide, which is generated via document YAML options. As a result, the methods described above won’t work for providing a background for the title slide. Rather, you need to do the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>Provide the title slide background options under <code>title-slide-attributes</code></p></li> <li><p>Prepend the background options with <code>data-</code> For example:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: My Slide Show</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>title-slide-attributes:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>data-background-image: /path/to/title_image.png</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>data-background-size: contain</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>data-background-opacity: “0.5”</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> </ul> <h5 id="external-servers-2">External servers</h5> <p>Quarto is designed to minimize external dependencies. However, on occasion, Quarto documents might need resources hosted in external servers. See our page on External Sources for a full list.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-18">Learning More</h5> <p>See these articles lo learn about more advanced capabilities of Reveal:</p> <ul> <li>Presenting Slides describes slide navigation, printing to PDF, drawing on slides using a chalkboard, and creating multiplex presentations.</li> <li>Advanced Reveal delves into transitions, animations, advanced layout and positioning, and other options available for customizing presentations.</li> <li>Reveal Themes talks about using and customizing existing themes as well as creating brand new themes.</li> </ul> <h2 id="projects-6">Projects</h2> <h3 id="managing-execution">Managing Execution</h3> <h4 id="managing-execution-1">Managing Execution</h4> <h5 id="overview-103">Overview</h5> <p>Rendering a list of input files has the potential to be quite time consuming depending on the computations required. There are a number of techniques you can use to minimize the time required to rebuild a site that has expensive computations.</p> <h5 id="incremental-render">Incremental Render</h5> <p>When working on a project you are typically iterating on a single document at a time. You can render a single file (or single directory or list of files) incrementally by specifying it on the command-line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render introduction.qmd quarto render subdir/</code></pre> <p>Even though you are rendering only part of the project, any associated project-handling code is still executed. So for example in a book project the entire book is still produced (using previously rendered versions of the other chapters).</p> <h5 id="freeze">Freeze</h5> <p>You can use the <code>freeze</code> option to denote that computational documents should never be re-rendered during a global project render, or alternatively only be re-rendered when their source file changes:</p> <pre><code>execute: freeze: true # never re-render during project render execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>freeze</code> controls whether execution occurs during global project renders. If you do an incremental render of either a single document or a project sub-directory then code is always executed. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render single document (always executes code) quarto render document.qmd # render project subdirectory (always executes code) quarto render articles</code></pre> <h6 id="using-freeze">Using Freeze</h6> <p>Freeze is generally used when you have either a large number of collaborators or many computational documents created over a longer period of time. In both cases it can be challenging to fully re-execute every document when you render the site. This could be because some documents have esoteric or environment-specific requirements (e.g. require access/authentication to a data source) or due to general fragility of dependencies over time. Using freeze ensures that you can always reproducibly render your site.</p> <p>The computational results of documents executed with <code>freeze</code> are stored in the <code>_freeze</code> directory, and re-used when needed to fulfill document renders. You should check the contents of <code>_freeze</code> into version control so that others rendering the project don’t need to reproduce your computational environment to render it in their environment.</p> <p>Note that you’ll still want to take care to fully re-render your project when things outside of source code change (e.g. input data). You can remove previously frozen output by deleting the <code>_freeze</code> folder at the root of your project.</p> <h6 id="virtual-environments">Virtual Environments</h6> <p>You can also combine <code>freeze</code> with the use of virtual environments to divide your project into sub-directories that each have their own set of dependencies. This allows multiple collaborators to use a set of localized dependencies for the documents they are responsible for, but at the same time still be able to render the entire project without requiring all of its dependencies.</p> <p>To learn how to create and use a virtual environment, see the full documentation on Virtual Environments</p> <p>Here’s an example workflow of using virtual environments with freeze:</p> <ul> <li><p>Include <code>freeze: true</code> in the project execution options:</p> <p>execute: freeze: true</p></li> <li><p>Create a sub-directory of documents (e.g. <code>research</code>), initialize and use a virtual environment within it:</p> <p>research/ document1.qmd document2.qmd env/ requirements.txt</p></li> <li><p>When working within this sub-directory, activate the virtual environment before rendering its documents. For example:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>cd research source env/bin/activate quarto render # render all files in subdir quarto render document1.qmd # render a single-file</p></li> </ul> <p>This sub-directory render won’t use the cached <code>freeze</code> results but instead will re-run all of the computations using the directory-specific virtual environment. You can of course also include sub-directories within this directory and their documents will also be rendered using the parent virtual environment.</p> <h5 id="cache">Cache</h5> <p>You can use the <code>cache</code> option to cache the results of computations (using the <a href="https://yihui.org/knitr/demo/cache/">knitr cache</a> for R documents, <a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> for Jupyter documents, or <code>engine: julia</code>’s built-in support):</p> <pre><code>execute: cache: true</code></pre> <p>Note that cache invalidation is triggered by changes in chunk source code (or other cache attributes you’ve defined). You may however need to manually refresh the cache if you know that some other input (or even time) has changed sufficiently to warrant an update. To do this, render either individual files or an entire project using the <code>--cache-refresh</code> option:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render mydoc.qmd --cache-refresh # single doc quarto render --cache-refresh # entire project</code></pre> <h5 id="notebooks-1">Notebooks</h5> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <h5 id="working-dir">Working Dir</h5> <p>By default, the working directory for rendering files within a project is the directory of the file itself. If you prefer to use the main project directory instead, you can add the <code>execute-dir: project</code> option to your config:</p> <pre><code>project: execute-dir: project</code></pre> <p>Note that from within your code you can always determine the location of the currently executing Quarto project using the <code>QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR</code> environment variable.</p> <h3 id="project-basics">Project Basics</h3> <h4 id="project-basics-1">Project Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-104">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto projects are directories that provide:</p> <ul> <li>A way to render all or some of the files in a directory with a single command (e.g. <code>quarto render myproject</code>).</li> <li>A way to share YAML configuration across multiple documents.</li> <li>The ability to redirect output artifacts to another directory.</li> <li>The ability to freeze rendered output (i.e. don’t re-execute documents unless they have changed). In addition, projects can have special “types” that introduce additional behavior (e.g. websites or books).</li> </ul> <p>Note</p> <p>If you are just getting started with Quarto and/or you don’t have previous experience with markdown publishing systems, you probably want to skip learning about projects for now. Once you are comfortable with the basics, come back to this article to learn more.</p> <h5 id="creating-projects">Creating Projects</h5> <p>Use the <code>quarto create project</code> command to create a new project, using the prompt.</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project Output ? Type ❯ default website blog manuscript book confluence</code></pre> <p>Or define the type and the project name as arguments.</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project <type> <name></code></pre> <h5 id="shared-metadata">Shared Metadata</h5> <p>One of the most important features of Quarto Projects is the ability to share YAML metadata options across multiple documents. Shared metadata can be defined at both the project and directory level.</p> <h6 id="project-metadata-1">Project Metadata</h6> <p>All Quarto projects include a <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file. Any document rendered within the project directory will automatically inherit the metadata defined at the project level. Here is an example of what the <code>_quarto.yml</code> file might look like:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: output-dir: _output toc: true number-sections: true bibliography: references.bib format: html: css: styles.css html-math-method: katex pdf: documentclass: report margin-left: 30mm margin-right: 30mm</code></pre> <p>Note that the project file contains both global options that apply to all formats (e.g. <code>toc</code> and <code>bibliography</code>) as well as format-specific options.</p> <p>You can further customize project metadata based on different project profiles (e.g. development vs. production or creating multiple versions of a book or website). See the article on Project Profiles for additional details.</p> <h6 id="directory-metadata">Directory Metadata</h6> <p>You can also define metadata that should be inherited by only files within a directory. To do this, add a <code>_metadata.yml</code> file to the directory where you want to share metadata. For example, the following <code>_metadata.yml</code> sets up default Revealjs options for a series of presentations and disables <code>search</code> for documents within the directory:</p> <pre><code>_metadata.yml format: revealjs: menu: false progress: false search: false</code></pre> <p>Options provided within these files use the same schema as <code>_quarto.yml</code> and are merged with any options you’ve already provided in <code>_quarto.yml</code>.</p> <h6 id="metadata-merging">Metadata Merging</h6> <p>Metadata defined within <code>_quarto.yml</code>, <code>_metadata.yml</code>, and document-level YAML options are merged together. Document level options take priority, followed by directory options and finally project-level options:</p> <p>File</p> <p>Role</p> <p><code>_quarto.yml</code></p> <p>Project level default options</p> <p><code>dir/_metadata.yml</code></p> <p>Directory level default options (overrides project)</p> <p><code>dir/document.qmd</code></p> <p>Document options (overrides directory and project)</p> <p>Note that when metadata is combined, objects and arrays are merged rather than simply overwriting each other. For example, here is how project and directory level options that affect output format and bibliographies would be merged:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: toc: true bibliography: - refs.bib dir/_metadata.yml format: html: code-fold: true bibliography: - proj.bib merged format: html: toc: true code-fold: true bibliography: - refs.bib - proj.bib</code></pre> <p>The one exception to metadata merging is <code>format</code>. If the document-level YAML defines a format, it must define the complete list of formats to be rendered.</p> <h6 id="metadata-includes">Metadata Includes</h6> <p>You might find it convenient to break your metadata into multiple files. You can do this using the <code>metadata-files</code> option. For example, here we include some website options with a separate <code>_website.yml</code> in the <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: website metadata-files: - _website.yml _website.yml website: navbar: background: primary left: - href: index.qmd text: Home - about.qmd</code></pre> <p>Files listed in <code>metadata-files</code> are merged with the parent file in the same fashion that project, directory, and document options are merged. This means that included files can both provide new options as well as combine with existing options.</p> <h6 id="local-config">Local Config</h6> <p>Sometimes its useful to define local changes to project configuration that are not checked in to version control. You can do this by creating a <code>_quarto.yml.local</code> config file. For example, here we specify that we want to use the execution cache when running locally:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml.local execute: cache: true</code></pre> <p>Note that Quarto automatically writes an entry to <code>.gitignore</code> to ensure that <code>.local</code> files are not committed (note that environment variables can also be defined in a similar <code>.local</code> file).</p> <h5 id="rendering-projects">Rendering Projects</h5> <p>You can render files within a project either one-by-one or all at once (in either case, shared project metadata will be used).</p> <p>To render all of the documents within a project, just use <code>quarto render</code> within the project directory (or target a specific directory with a command line argument):</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render project in current dir quarto render # render project in 'myproject' quarto render myproject</code></pre> <p>You can also render only the files within a sub-directory of a project. For example, if the current directory contains a project with sub-directories <code>tutorials</code>, <code>how-to</code>, and <code>articles</code>, you can render just the contents of <code>articles</code> as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render only documents in the 'articles' sub-directory quarto render articles</code></pre> <p>Note that when rendering a project, command line arguments you pass to <code>quarto render</code> will be used for each file in the project. For example, this command will render only the PDF format:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render --to pdf quarto render myproject --to pdf</code></pre> <p>If you are working with Quarto from R, you can also render a project from the R console using the quarto R package.</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_render()</code></pre> <h5 id="render-targets">Render Targets</h5> <p>By default, all valid Quarto input files (.qmd, .ipynb, .md, .Rmd) in the project directory will be rendered, save for ones with:</p> <ul> <li><p>A file or directory prefix of <code>.</code> (hidden files)</p></li> <li><p>A file or directory prefix of <code>_</code> (typically used for non top-level files, e.g. ones included in other files)</p></li> <li><p>Files named <code>README.md</code> or <code>README.qmd</code> (which are typically not actual render targets but rather informational content about the source code to be viewed in the version control web UI).</p></li> <li><p>AI assistant configuration files (<code>CLAUDE.md</code>, <code>AGENTS.md</code>) which provide instructions for AI coding assistants and are not intended as rendered content. If you don’t want to render all of the target documents in a project, or you wish to control the order of rendering more precisely, you can add a <code>project: render: [files]</code> entry to your project metadata. For example:</p> <p>project: render: - section1.qmd - section2.qmd</p></li> </ul> <p>Note that you can use wildcards when defining the <code>render</code> list. For example:</p> <pre><code>project: render: - section*.qmd</code></pre> <p>You can also use the prefix <code>!</code> to ignore some files or directories in the <code>render</code> list. Note that in that case you need to start by specifying everything you do want to render. For example:</p> <pre><code>project: render: - "*.qmd" - "!ignored.qmd" - "!ignored-dir/"</code></pre> <p>Note</p> <p>If the name of your output file needs to start with <code>.</code> or <code>_</code> (for instance <code>_index.md</code> for Hugo users), you must name the Quarto input file without the prefix (for instance <code>index.qmd</code>) and add an explicit <code>output-file</code> parameter in the YAML such as</p> <pre><code>--- output-file: _index.md ---</code></pre> <h6 id="engine-prioritization">Engine prioritization</h6> <p>Quarto supports different engines to execute code. Historically, the R, Python and Julia languages were only supported by one engine, each, so there was no need to choose an execution engine. With the addition of the native Julia engine, this changed.</p> <p>When determining which execution engine to use for a given notebook, Quarto checks the available engines in a predefined order, which means that the Jupyter engine is always preferred for Julia over the native engine.</p> <p>Starting with Quarto 1.7, instead of specifying <code>engine: julia</code> in the frontmatter of every notebook in a project, you can set a different prioritization order in your project file using the <code>engines</code> key.</p> <p>All the engines you list there will be checked first in the order you provide. The remaining engines will be checked by Quarto in the usual predefined order. To enable the native Julia engine project-wide, it is therefore enough to add this line to your project file:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml engines: ['julia']</code></pre> <h5 id="learning-more-19">Learning More</h5> <p>These articles provide additional documentation on more advanced features of Quarto projects:</p> <ul> <li>Managing Execution covers various techniques you can use to minimize the time required to rebuild a site that has expensive computations.</li> <li>Project Profiles describes how you can adapt both the options and content of your projects for different scenarios (e.g. development vs. production or creating multiple versions of a book or website).</li> <li>Environment Variables covers how to define environment variables that should be set whenever your project is rendered (including how to vary those variables by project profile and/or for use in local development).</li> <li>Project Scripts describes how to add periodic or pre/post render scripts to projects for special processing of input data and project outputs.</li> <li>Virtual Environments explores how to create project-specific package libraries, which helps with faithfully reproducing your environment over time as well as ensuring that upgrading a package in one project doesn’t break other projects.</li> </ul> <h3 id="project-environment-variables">Project Environment Variables</h3> <h4 id="project-environment-variables-1">Project Environment Variables</h4> <h5 id="overview-105">Overview</h5> <p>You may have one or more environment variables that you want to make sure are set whenever you render your project. For example, you might be using environment variables to:</p> <ul> <li>Provide the URL of a server to download data from.</li> <li>Set the address of a proxy server (e.g. <code>HTTP_PROXY</code>).</li> <li>Provide credentials for accessing a remote server (note that below we cover best practices for using credentials stored in environment variables).</li> <li>Tune the behavior of executable code (e.g. <code>OMP_NUM_THREADS</code>, <code>ARROW_IO_THREADS</code>, etc.)</li> <li>Provide options for language interpreters (e.g. <code>PYTHONINSPECT</code> or <code>TZDIR</code>).</li> <li>Determine which versions of Python and R are used (e.g. <code>QUARTO_PYTHON</code>, <code>QUARTO_R</code>, <code>PY_PYTHON</code>, or <code>RETICULATE_PYTHON</code>). TipLooking for a specific Quarto environment variable?</li> </ul> <p>See Quarto Environment Variables for a list of environment variables that Quarto reads and sets.</p> <p>Quarto projects can define a set of standard environment variables as well as vary which environment variables are defined based on the active project profile. It’s also possible to use environment variables that are defined only on the local system and not checked in to version control.</p> <h5 id="environment-file">Environment File</h5> <p>If you include an <code>_environment</code> file at the root level of your project alongside <code>_quarto.yml</code> the values defined within the file will be read and set into the environment when the project configuration is read. For example:</p> <pre><code>_environment HTTP_PROXY="[proxy.example.com](https://proxy.example.com/)" OMP_NUM_THREADS=4</code></pre> <p>These environment variables will be available both within Quarto’s execution context as well as in child processes (e.g. Jupyter kernels).</p> <p>Note that variables defined in environment files do not take precedence over definitions that already exist in the external environment. Rather, they provide defaults that will be applied when no external variable of the same name is already defined.</p> <p>You can include comments in environment files, as well as reference other environment variables. For example:</p> <pre><code>_environment # database server DATABASE_SERVER=[db.example.com](https://db.example.com) DATABASE_API=${DATABASE_SERVER}/api</code></pre> <p>When referencing another environment variable, it must either also be defined within the same file or already exist in the external environment. See the complete environment variable <a href="https://github.com/denoland/deno_std/tree/main/dotenv#parsing-rules">parsing rules</a> for additional details on the syntax of environment files.</p> <h5 id="profile-environments">Profile Environments</h5> <p>If you are using Project Profiles to adapt your projects for different scenarios, you can create a custom environment file that will be activated along with the profile. For example, if you have a profile named <code>production</code>, then the variables defined in <code>_environment-production</code> will be read and applied.</p> <p>Here, we customize the <code>OMP_NUM_THREADS</code> environment variable to use more cores when running in production:</p> <pre><code>_environment-production OMP_NUM_THREADS=16</code></pre> <p>Note that profile environments are merged with the default <code>_environment</code> so you need only define the variables that vary in your profile and can rely on the defaults for others.</p> <p>Important</p> <p>If you have secrets (e.g. access tokens) that you need to specify using environment variables you shouldn’t use profile environments (as they are often checked in to version control). We’ll cover the recommended technique for this in Managing Secrets below.</p> <h5 id="local-environment">Local Environment</h5> <p>When working on a project locally you may want to use different values for some environment variables. For example, you might want to add some variables that provide additional diagnostic output for Python execution.</p> <p>You can do this by creating an <code>_environment.local</code> file. The values in the local file will override those specified in the default file:</p> <pre><code>_environment.local PYTHONDEVMODE=1</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>_environment.local</code> is not intended to be checked in to version control. Rather, it’s designed for values that you want to activate only on your system. To facilitate this, Quarto automatically adds the following to your project <code>.gitignore</code> file:</p> <pre><code>.gitignore /_*.local</code></pre> <p>This is especially useful when your environment variables contain secrets, which we’ll explore in more depth in the following section.</p> <h5 id="managing-secrets">Managing Secrets</h5> <p>Frequently, credentials or authorization tokens are provided to code via environment variables. In many cases these credentials are required to render the project (for example, if the project is accessing data in a remote database or web service).</p> <p>It’s especially critical that these credentials are not checked in to version control. Typically, this is accomplished by a combination of:</p> <ul> <li><p>When running on a server or CI service, provide the environment variable as an encrypted secret. Details on how to do this vary between services (GitHub Actions has <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/encrypted-secrets">deployed secrets</a>, Posit Connect supports <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/content-settings/#content-vars">content variables</a>, etc.)</p></li> <li><p>For local development, define variables in the <code>_environment.local</code> file (and ignore this file in version control, as Quarto does by default). For example, here we specify AWS credentials in a local environment file:</p> <p>_environment.local</p> <p>AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI</p></li> </ul> <p>One problem this leaves is ensuring that these variables are always specified. The next section on required variables covers how to do this.</p> <h5 id="required-variables">Required Variables</h5> <p>If there are certain environment variables that need to be specified in order to render the project, you can create an <code>_environment.required</code> file.
