This file can be copied to <code>_environment.local</code> as a starting point for local authoring, and also serves as documentation for server environments regarding which variables need to be defined.</p> <p>Returning to the example of AWS credentials, this <code>_environment.required</code> file provides documentation that these credentials will be required to render the project:</p> <pre><code>_environment.required AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID= AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=</code></pre> <p>Then, the <code>.local</code> file (which again, is not checked in to version control) would be populated with the actual credentials:</p> <pre><code>_environment.local AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI</code></pre> <p>Further, any server environment that wants to render this project could validate that the required variables have been specified, and fail to run (with an appropriate error message) if they are not.</p> <h3 id="project-profiles">Project Profiles</h3> <h4 id="project-profiles-1">Project Profiles</h4> <h5 id="overview-106">Overview</h5> <p>Project profiles enable you to adapt the options, environment, and content of your projects for different scenarios. For example:</p> <ul> <li><p>You may want to have distinct execution behavior when running on a production server. For example, you may want to use <code>freeze</code> or <code>cache</code> when rendering locally but always execute all of the code when running on a CI server.</p></li> <li><p>You may want to provide distinct access credentials for databases or web services depending on the profile.</p></li> <li><p>You may want to create different versions of a book from the same source code (e.g. a basic and advanced version). When a project profile is activated a number of things occur:</p></li> <li><p>Profile specific <code>config</code> is merged with the top-level <code>_quarto.yml</code>.</p></li> <li><p>Profile specific environment variables are applied.</p></li> <li><p>Divs can use the <code>when-profile</code> attribute to target content specifically for that project.</p></li> <li><p>The <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> environment variable includes the profile name so that other code (e.g. Python or R code) can condition its behavior on the active profile.</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="examples-25">Examples</h6> <p>Here’s an example of a <code>_quarto.yml</code> file that is extended by a <code>production</code> configuration defined in <code>_quarto-production.yml</code>. When activated, the <code>production</code> profile overrides the default rendering execution behavior (disabling the use of <code>freeze</code>):</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: website execute: freeze: true _quarto-production.yml execute: freeze: false</code></pre> <p>When the <code>production</code> profile is active, its configuration will be merged over the default project config (in this case resulting in the use of the frozen computational results being disabled).</p> <p>Here’s an example of using the <code>when-profile</code> attribute to include content only when the <code>advanced</code> profile is active:</p> <pre><code>::: {.content-visible when-profile="advanced"} This content will only appear in the advanced version. :::</code></pre> <p>The next section covers how to activate profiles, then subsequent sections go into more depth on the various capabilities of profiles.</p> <h5 id="activating-profiles">Activating Profiles</h5> <p>One or more named profiles can be activated by using either the <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> environment variable or the <code>--profile</code> command line argument.</p> <p>Here we activate a profile using the <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> environment variable:</p> <pre><code>Terminal export QUARTO_PROFILE=production quarto render</code></pre> <p>Here we activate a profile by passing the <code>--profile</code> argument on the Quarto command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render --profile production</code></pre> <p>The use of the <code>--profile</code> command line argument entirely replaces any defined <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> within the environment.</p> <p>Note that more than one profile can be activated at once. For example, here we activate both the <code>production</code> and <code>advanced</code> profiles:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render --profile production,advanced</code></pre> <h5 id="profile-configuration">Profile Configuration</h5> <p>Define profile-specific configuration by adding an additional project file that includes the name of the profile (for example, <code>_quarto-advanced.yml</code> for the <code>advanced</code> profile). For example, here we customize the <code>title</code> and <code>output-dir</code> based on the currently active profile:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: title: "My Website" type: website _quarto-advanced.yml project: title: "My Website (Advanced)" output-dir: _site-advanced</code></pre> <p>Warning<code>metadata-files</code> are not resolved in profiles</p> <p>Instead of using <code>metadata-files</code> in a profile configuration, copy the contents of your metadata file directly into the profile configuration file.</p> <p>It’s important to note that multiple profiles can be active. So the following enables you to vary configuration based on both <code>advanced</code> and <code>production</code> profiles:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: title: "My Website" type: website execute: freeze: true _quarto-advanced.yml project: title: "My Website (Advanced)" output-dir: _site-advanced _quarto-production.yml execute: freeze: false</code></pre> <p>The <code>advanced</code> and <code>production</code> profiles would each be applied if you specify them both:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # multiple profiles in environment export QUARTO_PROFILE=advanced,production quarto render # multiple profiles on command line quarto render --profile advanced,production</code></pre> <p>When multiple profiles are active and their configurations contain the same scalar key, the first-listed profile takes priority. For example, with <code>--profile advanced,production</code>, the <code>advanced</code> profile’s values win any scalar conflicts. Arrays and objects follow standard metadata merging rules (arrays are union-concatenated, objects are deep-merged).</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>If a profile is specified but no corresponding <code>_quarto-{name}.yml</code> file exists, the profile is silently ignored with no warning or error. This can lead to unexpected behavior if you mistype a profile name.</p> <h5 id="profile-content">Profile Content</h5> <p>You can also specify that content within your project only be included when a certain profile is active. You do this using the <code>.content-visible</code> class along with the <code>when-profile</code> attribute to a div or span. For example, here we defined a div that is included only for the <code>advanced</code> profile:</p> <pre><code>::: {.content-visible when-profile="advanced"} This content will only appear in the advanced version. :::</code></pre> <p>You can also exclude content from a given profile using the <code>unless-profile</code> attribute. Here we include content only when the profile is not <code>advanced</code>:</p> <pre><code>::: {.content-visible unless-profile="advanced"} This content will appear in all versions save for advanced. :::</code></pre> <p>It might be more clear to re-write the above using <code>.content-hidden</code>:</p> <pre><code>::: {.content-hidden when-profile="advanced"} This content will be hidden in the advanced profile :::</code></pre> <h5 id="profile-groups">Profile Groups</h5> <p>Often times a set of profile names form a mutually exclusive group, and you want to make sure that at least one of the profiles is always active. For example, here we define distinct chapter lists for <code>basic</code> and <code>advanced</code> profiles, along with a profile <code>group</code> entry indicating that they form a group:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: book book: title: "My Book" author: "Norah Jones" profile: group: - [basic, advanced] _quarto-basic.yml book: chapters: - intro.qmd - using.qmd - summary.qmd _quarto-advanced.yml book: chapters: - intro.qmd - using.qmd - advanced.qmd - summary.qmd</code></pre> <p>You’ll note that the base options for <code>book</code> do not include a chapter list (as we rely on the profiles for distinct lists). This means that to successfully render the project, you always need to have a profile defined—this might be inconvenient especially for local authoring and preview.</p> <p>By specifying a <code>group</code> we indicate that one of the profiles must be defined, and that the first one listed should be used as the default when no others are present.</p> <h5 id="default-profile">Default Profile</h5> <p>When authoring a Quarto project that uses profiles you might want to change which profile(s) are rendered by default to try out different variations of the project.</p> <p>While you could certainly do this by defining environment variables in your shell, this isn’t particularly convenient when using the integrated render and preview functionality in Positron, VS Code, and RStudio.</p> <p>To define a default profile that is used when an explicit <code>QUARTO_PROFILE</code> or <code>--profile</code> CLI argument is not present, add a <code>default</code> option to the <code>profile</code> key. For example, here we indicate that <code>development</code> should be the active profile if not otherwise specified:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml profile: default: development</code></pre> <h3 id="project-scripts">Project Scripts</h3> <h4 id="project-scripts-1">Project Scripts</h4> <h5 id="overview-107">Overview</h5> <p>Many more complex projects have additional processing that needs to take place periodically (e.g. data import and preparation) or even before/after each render. Project scripts are a way to incorporate this processing into your workflow.</p> <h5 id="periodic-scripts">Periodic Scripts</h5> <p>You can use the <code>quarto run</code> command to run a TypeScript, R, Python, or Lua script. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto run import.py</code></pre> <p>Available script interpreters for <code>quarto run</code> include:</p> <p>Language</p> <p>Interpreter</p> <p>TypeScript</p> <p><a href="https://deno.land/">Deno</a> (embedded in Quarto)</p> <p>Python</p> <p>Python from <code>PATH</code> (or <a href="https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0397/">launcher</a> on Windows)</p> <p>R</p> <p>Rscript from <code>PATH</code></p> <p>Lua</p> <p><a href="https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/">Lua 5.3</a> (embedded in Pandoc)</p> <p>Using TypeScript or Lua enables you to create scripts with no additional installation requirements. On the other hand, if your project is already using Python or R then scripts in those languages might be more convenient.</p> <p>If you are using TypeScript, please be sure to consult the section below on Deno Scripts for additional details on the Deno standard library and importing external scripts.</p> <h5 id="pre-and-post-render">Pre and Post Render</h5> <p>You can arrange for one or more scripts to execute before and/or after each render using the <code>pre-render</code> and <code>post-render</code> project options. For example:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website pre-render: prepare.py post-render: - compress.ts - fix-links.py</code></pre> <p>Note that <code>pre-render</code> and <code>post-render</code> also support arbitrary shell commands. So you could for example use <code>make</code> to do data preparation this way:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website pre-render: make prepare</code></pre> <p>Pre and post render scripts are run with the main project directory.</p> <p>The following environment variables are passed to pre and post-render scripts (note that all paths are relative to the main project directory):</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_RENDER_ALL</code></p> <p>Set to “1” if this is a render of all files in the project (as opposed to an incremental render or a render for preview). This is unset if Quarto is not rendering all files.</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_OUTPUT_DIR</code></p> <p>Output directory</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_INPUT_FILES</code></p> <p>Newline separated list of all input files being rendered (passed only to <code>pre-render</code>)</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_OUTPUT_FILES</code></p> <p>Newline separated list of all output files rendered (passed only to <code>post-render</code>).</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_SCRIPT_PROGRESS</code></p> <p>Set to <code>"1"</code> when progress output can be shown (e.g. rendering multiple files), <code>"0"</code> otherwise.</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PROJECT_SCRIPT_QUIET</code></p> <p>Set to <code>"1"</code> when the <code>--quiet</code> flag is active, <code>"0"</code> otherwise.</p> <p>Scripts can use <code>QUARTO_PROJECT_SCRIPT_PROGRESS</code> and <code>QUARTO_PROJECT_SCRIPT_QUIET</code> to adapt their output, for example by suppressing progress indicators when running in quiet mode or when progress display is not available.</p> <p>The project metadata and render list will be re-computed after any pre-render scripts have executed, allowing them to modify this project data. For example, a pre-render script might generate additional <code>qmd</code> files or <code>ipynb</code> files that should be rendered.</p> <p>Note that pre-render scripts cannot modify the project directory, the output directory, or the project type. If a pre-render script modifies any of these values, an error will be returned and the render will fail.</p> <p>If you have a <code>pre-render</code> step that is expensive, you may want only run it when the entire project is being rendered. Here’s how you would do this in the various supported script languages:</p> <ul> <li><p>TypeScript</p></li> <li><p>Python</p></li> <li><p>R</p></li> <li><p>Lua</p> <p>if (!Deno.env.get(“QUARTO_PROJECT_RENDER_ALL”)) { Deno.exit(); }</p> <p>import os if not os.getenv(“QUARTO_PROJECT_RENDER_ALL”): exit()</p> <p>if (!nzchar(Sys.getenv(“QUARTO_PROJECT_RENDER_ALL”))) { quit() }</p> <p>if not os.getenv(“QUARTO_PROJECT_RENDER_ALL”) then os.exit(); end</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="advanced-large-input-and-output-file-lists">Advanced: large input and output file lists</h6> <p>In some execution environments, the maximum size of an environment might be limited. In this case, a pre- or post-render script invocation might fail when Quarto attempts to build the appropriate environment variables.</p> <p>In such scenarios, you can declare the environment variable <code>QUARTO_USE_FILE_FOR_PROJECT_INPUT_FILES</code> (respectively, <code>QUARTO_USE_FILE_FOR_PROJECT_OUTPUT_FILES</code>) to direct Quarto to use the declared file as the destination of the file list that would have been written in <code>QUARTO_PROJECT_INPUT_FILES</code> (respectively, <code>QUARTO_PROJECT_OUTPUT_FILES</code>).</p> <h5 id="deno-scripts">Deno Scripts</h5> <p>If you want to create project scripts with TypeScript, <code>quarto run</code> enables you to use the <a href="https://deno.land/">Deno</a> TypeScript interpreter bundled with Quarto. This interpreter also includes much of Deno’s <a href="https://docs.deno.com/runtime/manual/basics/standard_library">standard library</a>. For example, to use the Deno YAML parser you would do this:</p> <h6 id="quarto-1.6-breaking-changes">Quarto 1.6 breaking changes</h6> <p>Warning</p> <p>Quarto 1.6 includes updates to Deno and Deno’s standard library which forced us to make breaking changes to the import syntax. We apologize for the inconvenience.</p> <pre><code>import { parse } from "stdlib/yaml"; // Quarto 1.6 syntax import { parse } from "[deno.land](https://deno.land/std/yaml/mod.ts)"; // Quarto 1.5 and earlier syntax const config = parse(Deno.readTextFileSync("_quarto.yml"));</code></pre> <p>Although Deno hosts its standard library online, it’s important to note that in Quarto 1.5, the library is not downloaded from a remote server (in fact, importing from remote servers is disabled entirely in the Quarto Deno interpreter). Quarto 1.6 ships with a version of Deno that has an unfortunate interaction between its standard library and the feature that disables downloading the library from the remote servers. As a result, Quarto 1.6 might download some files (once, and then cache them) when the standard library is invoked. Future versions of Quarto will ship with Deno 2, which does not suffer from this issue.</p> <p>If you want to enforce the behavior from Quarto 1.5, you can set the environment variable <code>QUARTO_RUN_NO_NETWORK</code> to <code>true</code>. Note that this means that the imports from <code>stdlib/</code> will not work in general.</p> <p>You may come across example code that embeds versions directly in Deno library imports. For example:</p> <pre><code>import { format } from "[deno.land](https://deno.land/std@0.119.0/datetime/mod.ts)"; import { format } from "jsr:@std/datetime@^0.224.0"</code></pre> <p>These version-bound imports will not work with Quarto (as its local standard library cache is populated with unversioned URLs). The correct form of the above import is thus:</p> <pre><code>import { format } from "stdlib/datetime";</code></pre> <p>You may also see examples of Deno code that imports 3rd party libraries directly from URLs. As noted above, this functionality is generally not available in Quarto Deno scripts. Rather, you should download any external libraries you wish to use, include them with your project source code, and import them using relative file paths.</p> <h6 id="making-.ts-scripts-portable-across-multiple-versions-of-quarto">Making <code>.ts</code> scripts portable across multiple versions of Quarto</h6> <p>If you need your project or extension to both include TypeScript project scripts and work with Quarto 1.5 and 1.6, use the following technique:</p> <pre><code>const multiImport = async (...sources: string[]) => { for (const source of sources) { try { return await import(source); } catch (e) {} } } const { readLines } = await multiImport( "stdlib/io", // Quarto 1.6 syntax "[deno.land](https://deno.land/std/io/mod.ts)", // Quarto 1.5 syntax );</code></pre> <h3 id="using-binder-with-quarto">Using Binder With Quarto</h3> <h4 id="using-binder-with-quarto-1">Using Binder With Quarto</h4> <h5 id="overview-108">Overview</h5> <p>The <a href="https://mybinder.org/">Binder</a> project provides a stack of tools designed to make it easy to share computing environments. Binder makes it straightforward to provide users with a link that restores the computing environment, and allows them to interact with your project code.</p> <p>To use Binder with a Quarto project, you need to include a set of configuration files that describe your computational environment. Quarto can automatically create these files with the <code>quarto use binder</code> command. Run the command from within your Quarto project directory. The command will scan the project and determine the configuration files required to restore the environment. Commit the generated files to your project repository and your project is Binder-ready.</p> <p>Keep reading for a more detailed walkthrough of the process, or skip ahead to learn about specifying Dependencies, the specific Configuration Files that may be generated, or how to Add a Link to Binder in your document.</p> <h5 id="walkthrough-3">Walkthrough</h5> <p>Consider a Quarto project that contains <code>_quarto.yml</code> and the document <code>histogram.qmd</code> which contains R executable code cells:</p> <pre><code>histogram.qmd --- title: Histogram --- ```{r} hist(rnorm(100)) ```</code></pre> <p>To build an environment for this project, Binder needs to install Quarto and R, and should use the same Quarto and R versions as those used to build the project locally. A nice addition to the environment is an IDE that makes sense for the project content—with R code cells in a <code>.qmd</code> document RStudio would be a good choice.</p> <p>To have Quarto generate the files describing the requirements, within the project directory, run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto use binder</code></pre> <p>The command will first detect and report the project configuration:</p> <pre><code>[✓] Detected Project configuration: Quarto most recent prerelease JupyterLab default Engine knitr R 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) Editor rstudio No files which provide dependencies were discovered. If you continue, no dependencies will be restored when running this project with Binder. Learn more at: [quarto.org](https://www.quarto.org/docs/prerelease/1.4/binder.html#dependencies) ? Do you want to continue? (Y/n) ›</code></pre> <p>Quarto detects the versions of Quarto and R in use, that our Quarto document uses the Knitr engine, and chooses an appropriate editor for the project.</p> <p>Quarto will also detect files that describe R, Python or Julia dependencies - you can read more about these below in Dependencies. This project has none of these files, since the R code requires no additional packages.</p> <p>If you continue, Quarto will list the files it will create:</p> <pre><code>The following files will be written: ┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ postBuild │ Configures Quarto and supporting tools │ ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ apt.txt │ Installs Quarto required packages │ ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ runtime.txt │ Installs R and configures RStudio │ └─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┘ ? Continue? (Y/n) ›</code></pre> <p>After a final confirmation, Quarto will then write these files to the project:</p> <pre><code>Writing configuration files [✓] postBuild [✓] apt.txt [✓] runtime.txt</code></pre> <p>These configuration files need to be committed to the project repository, along with the project files.</p> <p>At <a href="https://mybinder.org/">mybinder.org</a> you provide a link to the project repository. Binder builds the computational environment from the configuration files, and provides you a link where users can interact with the contents of your repository in the computing environment it has built.</p> <p>You can try the Binder out for this project by following this Binder URL: <a href="https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/cwickham/binder-example/HEAD?urlpath=rstudio">mybinder.org</a></p> <p>The <code>?urlpath=rstudio</code> at the end of this link, means the link will open an RStudio session. The Binder environment can take a little while to start up, but once it does, you should be in an RStudio instance with the project open. Since the computational environment has been configured, you can render the project in the usual ways (via the RStudio interface, or with <code>quarto render</code> in the Terminal).</p> <p>Depending on the language and engine your project uses Quarto may generate files other than those shown for this project. You can read more about the files that <code>quarto use binder</code> might create below in Configuration Files.</p> <p>Most projects will have additional dependencies such as R, Python or Julia packages. As mentioned, Quarto can detect the common files that specify these dependencies. You can read more about these files next in Dependencies.</p> <h5 id="dependencies-5">Dependencies</h5> <p>When your project is restored to a new computational environment using Binder, any dependencies that the project has must also be restored. The <code>quarto use binder</code> command won’t detect computational dependencies from within your Quarto documents, but it will detect the files commonly used to describe them. The most common ways to describe them for the each environment are as follows:</p> <p>Language</p> <p>Environment</p> <p>File</p> <p>R</p> <p><a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html">renv</a></p> <p><code>renv.lock</code></p> <p>R</p> <p><a href="https://mybinder.readthedocs.io/en/latest/using/config_files.html#install-r-install-an-r-rstudio-environment">Binder R Config</a></p> <p><code>install.R</code></p> <p>Python</p> <p><a href="https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/stable/">Conda</a></p> <p><code>environment.yml</code></p> <p>Python</p> <p><a href="https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/user_guide/#requirements-files">Pip</a></p> <p><code>requirements.txt</code></p> <p>Julia</p> <p><a href="https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1/toml-files/">Pkg</a></p> <p><code>project.toml</code></p> <p>Often these files are created as the result of using a virtual environment. See Virtual Environments for more about using Quarto with virtual environments.</p> <h5 id="configuration-files">Configuration Files</h5> <p>The following files may be generated by the <code>quarto use binder</code> command. Note that the command will prompt before overwriting any user files that it didn’t generate or any files that have been modified since they were generated.</p> <p><code>postBuild</code></p> <p>The post build script runs code after restoring the environment. This script is generated with commands required to ensure the proper version of Quarto is present in the environment, install any required tools like TinyTeX or Chrome Headless Shell, and to configure VSCode and the Quarto extension for VSCode when applicable.</p> <p><code>apt.txt</code></p> <p>Provides a list of Debian packages to install with <code>apt-get</code>. This file is generated with all Quarto package dependencies.</p> <p><code>runtime.txt</code></p> <p>For R projects, this file will be generated with the appropriate R version, which is used to ensure that the same R version is present in the computational environment. This also will result in RStudio being configured and available when the computational environment is restored by a user.</p> <p><code>install.R</code></p> <p>For R projects, an <code>install.R</code> file will be generated to activate any <code>renv</code> environment that is present.</p> <p><code>.jupyter</code></p> <p>For projects using QMD files with the Jupyter engine, a <code>.jupyter</code> directory will be generated which will configure support for VSCode from within the JupyterLab environment.</p> <p>You can read more about how Binder uses these configuration files in the <a href="https://mybinder.readthedocs.io/en/latest/using/config_files.html#config-files">Binder documentation</a>.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>Files generated by the <code>quarto use binder</code> command should be committed into your repo so they are available when the repo is used by Binder to restore the computational environment.</p> <h5 id="add-a-link-to-binder">Add a Link to Binder</h5> <p>If your project is hosted on GitHub, you can add a link to the Binder for your project by adding <code>code-links: binder</code> to your document YAML:</p> <pre><code>histogram.qmd --- title: Histogram code-links: binder ---</code></pre> <p>When rendered you’ll see a “Launch Binder” link under Code Links:</p> <p>If you have a manuscript project, you can also use <code>code-links: binder</code> in your manuscript configuration to get a link on your manuscript webpage:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml manuscript: code-links: binder</code></pre> <h3 id="virtual-environments-1">Virtual Environments</h3> <h4 id="virtual-environments-2">Virtual Environments</h4> <p>Virtual environments provide a project-specific version of installed packages. This both helps you to faithfully reproduce your environment (e.g. if you are collaborating with a colleague or deploying to a server) as well as isolate the use of packages so that upgrading a package in one project doesn’t break other projects.</p> <p>There are several popular flavors of virtual environment, we will cover the following ones here:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">venv</a> (built into Python 3)</li> <li><a href="https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html">conda</a> (built into Anaconda/Miniconda)</li> <li><a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html">renv</a> (package for managing R environments) Below we’ll provide some example workflows for using these tools with Quarto. In these examples we’ll assume that you are already within a project directory that contains Quarto documents (so the virtual environment will be created as a sub-directory of the project).</li> </ul> <p>We’ll also cover using virtual environments with JupyterLab, RStudio, Positron and VS Code.</p> <p>Quarto can also detect the virtual environments discussed on this page to configure your project for Binder. Read more at Using Quarto with Binder.</p> <h5 id="using-venv">Using venv</h5> <p>Here we’ll provide a brief run through of creating a venv for a Quarto project. See the <a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">full documentation</a> on using virtual environments with Python for additional details.</p> <p>To create a new Python 3 virtual environment in the directory <code>env</code>:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m venv env</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m venv env</code></pre> <p>To use the environment you need to activate it. This differs slightly depending on which platform / shell you are using:</p> <p>Shell</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal source env/bin/activate</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(Command)</p> <pre><code>Terminal env\Scripts\activate.bat</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(PowerShell)</p> <pre><code>Terminal env\Scripts\Activate.ps1</code></pre> <p>NotePowerShell Note</p> <p>Note that you may receive an error about running scripts being disabled when activating within PowerShell. If you get this error then execute the following command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Scope CurrentUser</code></pre> <p>Once you’ve activated the environment, you need to ensure that you have the packages required to render your documents. This will typically encompass <code>jupyter</code> / <code>jupyterlab</code> plus whatever other packages are used in your Python code. Use <code>pip</code> to install packages into your environment. For example:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas</code></pre> <p>Assuming you installed all of the required packages (likely more than just <code>pandas</code> and <code>matplotlib</code>) you should now be able to <code>quarto render</code> documents within the directory.</p> <p>To deactivate an environment use the <code>deactivate</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal deactivate</code></pre> <h6 id="saving-environments">Saving Environments</h6> <p>To make your environment reproducible, you need to create a <code>requirements.txt</code> file that enumerates all of the packages in use. To do this use the <code>pip freeze</code> command:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip freeze > requirements.txt</code></pre> <p>You should generally check the <code>requirements.txt</code> file into version control.</p> <h6 id="restoring-environments">Restoring Environments</h6> <p>To reproduce the environment on another machine you create an empty environment, activate it, and then <code>pip install</code> using <code>requirements.txt</code>:</p> <p>First, follow the instructions above for creating and activating a virtual environment for your platform/shell.</p> <p>Then, install packages from <code>requirements.txt</code>:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m pip install -r requirements.txt</code></pre> <h5 id="using-conda">Using conda</h5> <p>This section will cover the basics of creating and using conda environments with Quarto projects. See this article on <a href="https://towardsdatascience.com/managing-project-specific-environments-with-conda-406365a539ab">managing project specific environments</a> with Conda for additional details.</p> <p>To create a new environment in the directory <code>env</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda create --prefix env python</code></pre> <p>If this is the first time you’ve used conda in your shell, you may need to execute one of the following commands before using other conda tools:</p> <p>Shell</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Newer Mac</p> <p>(Zsh)</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda init zsh</code></pre> <p>Linux / Older Mac</p> <p>(Bash)</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda init bash</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(Command)</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda init cmd.exe</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(PowerShell)</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda init powershell</code></pre> <p>You will likely need to exit and restart your terminal for <code>conda init</code> to be reflected in your session.</p> <p>To use the environment you need to activate it, which you do as follows:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda activate ./env</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda activate .\env</code></pre> <p>Once you’ve activated the environment, you need to ensure that you have the packages required to render your documents. This will typically encompass <code>jupyter</code> / <code>jupyterlab</code> plus whatever other packages are used in your Python code. Use <code>conda install</code> to install packages into your environment. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda install jupyter conda install pandas matplotlib</code></pre> <p>Assuming you installed all of the required packages (likely more than just <code>pandas</code> and <code>matplotlib</code>) you should now be able to <code>quarto render</code> documents within the directory.</p> <p>Use <code>conda deactivate</code> to exit an activated environment:</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda deactivate</code></pre> <h6 id="saving-environments-1">Saving Environments</h6> <p>To make your environment reproducible, you need to create a <code>environment.yml</code> file that enumerates all of the packages in use. Do this using the <code>conda env export</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda env export > environment.yml</code></pre> <p>You should generally check the <code>environment.yml</code> file into version control.</p> <h6 id="restoring-environments-1">Restoring Environments</h6> <p>To reproduce the environment on another machine you just pass the <code>environment.yml</code> file as an argument to <code>conda env create</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal conda env create --prefix env -f environment.yml</code></pre> <h6 id="more-information">More information</h6> <p>For more on conda’s <code>environment.yml</code>, see Conda’s <a href="https://conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html">Managing Environments</a> documentation.</p> <h5 id="using-renv">Using renv</h5> <p>The <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html">renv</a> package provides functionality similar to the venv and conda, but for R packages. To create a new renv environment, install the renv package from CRAN then call the <code>renv::init()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>install.packages("renv") renv::init()</code></pre> <p>As part of initialization, your <code>.Rprofile</code> file is modified to ensure that the renv is activated automatically at the start of each R session.</p> <p>If you plan on using both R and Python in your project, you can have renv automatically create and manage a Python virtual environment as follows:</p> <pre><code>renv::use_python()</code></pre> <p>To install R packages use the standard R <code>install.packages</code> function. You can also install GitHub packages using the <code>renv::install</code> function. For example:</p> <pre><code>install.packages("ggplot2") # install from CRAN renv::install("tidyverse/dplyr") # install from GitHub</code></pre> <p>To install Python packages just use <code>pip</code> as described above from the built-in RStudio terminal.</p> <h6 id="saving-environments-2">Saving Environments</h6> <p>To record the current versions of all R (and optionally Python) packages, use the <code>renv::snapshot()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>renv::snapshot()</code></pre> <p>This will record an <code>renv.lock</code> file for R packages and a <code>requirements.txt</code> file for Python packages). These files should be checked into version control.</p> <h6 id="restoring-environments-2">Restoring Environments</h6> <p>To reproduce the environment on another machine use the <code>renv::restore()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>renv::restore()</code></pre> <h5 id="jupyterlab">JupyterLab</h5> <p>To use Jupyter or JupyterLab within a Python virtual environment you just need to activate the environment and then launch the Jupyter front end. For example:</p> <p>Shell</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal source env/bin/activate python3 -m jupyter lab</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(Command)</p> <pre><code>Terminal env\Scripts\activate.bat py -m jupyter lab</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <p>(PowerShell)</p> <pre><code>Terminal env\Scripts\Activate.ps1 py -m jupyter lab</code></pre> <p>All of the Python packages installed within the <code>env</code> will be available in your Jupyter notebook session. The workflow is similar if you are using conda environments.</p> <h5 id="rstudio-1">RStudio</h5> <p>If you are using Quarto within RStudio it is strongly recommended that you use the <a href="https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/download/">current release</a> of RStudio from <a href="https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/download/">rstudio.com</a> (the documentation below assumes you are using this build).</p> <h6 id="renv">renv</h6> <p>If you are using renv, RStudio will automatically do the right thing in terms of binding Quarto to the R and/or Python packages in your project-local environments.</p> <p>If you need to install R packages, use <code>install.packages</code>; if you need to install Python packages, simply use <code>pip</code> or <code>conda</code> within the terminal as described above.</p> <h6 id="venv-condaenv">venv / condaenv</h6> <p>RStudio will automatically activate any venv or condaenv that it finds within a project directory. Just be sure to create an RStudio project within the same directory where you created your <code>env</code> and things will work as expected with no additional configuration.</p> <p>NoteUsing python and r together</p> <p>If your quarto document includes both <code>{python}</code> and <code>{r}</code> code blocks, then quarto will automatically use Knitr engine and <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/">reticulate</a> R package to execute the python content and may use a different version of python than is included in your environment. To direct RStudio to use a specific version of python, you can specify explicitly a path to an installed python version, e.g. by adding the following line to the <code>.Rprofile</code> file in your project directory:</p> <pre><code>Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "/path/to/your/env/bin/python")</code></pre> <p>More about Python Version Configuration for reticulate at <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/articles/versions.html">rstudio.github.io</a></p> <p>If you need to install Python packages, simply use <code>pip</code> or <code>conda</code> within the terminal as described above.</p> <h5 id="positron-3">Positron</h5> <h6 id="renv-1">renv</h6> <p>If you are using renv, Positron will automatically do the right thing in terms of binding Quarto to the R and/or Python packages in your project-local environments. If you need to install R packages, use <code>install.packages</code>; if you need to install Python packages, simply use <code>pip</code> or <code>conda</code> within the terminal as described above.</p> <h6 id="venv-condaenv-1">venv / condaenv</h6> <p>If you create a virtual environment with <code>venv</code> or <code>conda</code> as described above, Positron should automatically discover that environment when you open the parent folder. You can also explicitly select the environment by using the Interpreter: Select Interpreter Session command.</p> <p>If you have installed the Quarto executable in a conda environment rather than in a system-wide install, you need to launch Positron from a terminal with that conda environment activated in order for Positron to detect the conda installation of Quarto. The Quarto path setting in the Quarto extension does not work with Quarto installed in conda environments.</p> <h5 id="vs-code-3">VS Code</h5> <p>If you create a virtual environment with <code>venv</code> in the <code>env/</code> directory as described above, Visual Studio Code should automatically discover that environment when you load a workspace from the environment’s parent directory.</p> <p>Visual Studio Code will also automatically detect a conda environment, but you need to bind it to the current session with the Python: Select Interpreter command.</p> <p>If you have installed the Quarto executable in a conda environment rather than in a system-wide install, you need to launch VSCode from a terminal with that conda environment activated in order for VSCode to detect the conda installation of Quarto. The Quarto path setting in the Quarto VSCode extension does not work with Quarto installed in conda environments.</p> <p>You can read more about VS Code support for Python virtual environments here: <a href="https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/python/environments">code.visualstudio.com</a>.</p> <h2 id="publishing-10">Publishing</h2> <h3 id="confluence-1">Confluence</h3> <h4 id="confluence-2">Confluence</h4> <h5 id="overview-109">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence">Atlassian Confluence</a> is a publishing platform for supporting team collaboration. Confluence has a variety of hosting options which include both free and paid subscription plans.</p> <p>ImportantConfluence Cloud Only</p> <p>Publishing is currently limited to Confluence Cloud. We do not yet support publishing to Confluence Server or Confluence Data Center.</p> <p>Quarto provides support for publishing individual documents, as well as projects composed of multiple documents, into <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/confluence-cloud/docs/use-spaces-to-organize-your-work/">Confluence Spaces</a>.</p> <p>A Quarto Document</p> <p>Published to Confluence</p> <p>A Quarto Project</p> <p>Published to Confluence</p> <p>Managing Confluence content with Quarto allows you to author content in Markdown, manage that content with your usual version control tools like Git and GitHub, and leverage Quarto’s tools for including computational output.</p> <p>The next section, Confluence Publishing Basics, walks through the process of publishing a single page to Confluence, including how to set up your Confluence account in Quarto, and how to specify a destination for your document in your Confluence Space.</p> <p>Before you use Confluence Publishing for your own project you’ll want to read the remaining sections on this page:</p> <ul> <li>Publishing Projects describes how to publish a collection of documents, including how your project structure translates to the structure of pages in your Confluence Space.</li> <li>Publishing Workflow describes the model for making updates to Confluence pages published from Quarto, including the page permissions that are set when you publish from Quarto.</li> <li>Authoring for Confluence describes some of the differences between authoring for Confluence and authoring for a Quarto website.</li> <li>Publishing Settings covers how to manage your publishing settings. ImportantBe Careful with Sensitive or Confidential Content</li> </ul> <p>Publishing Quarto documents to a public Confluence space will make the content of those documents public. It is your responsibility to understand the permissions of your Confluence Space and verify your publishing destination to protect against any sensitive or confidential content from being made publicly available.</p> <h5 id="confluence-publishing-basics">Confluence Publishing Basics</h5> <p>To demonstrate the process of publishing to Confluence, we’ll take a single document, <a href="_confluence_examples/confluence-demo.qmd"><code>confluence-demo.qmd</code></a>, and publish it as a page to a Confluence space. Here’s the contents of <code>confluence-demo.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Confluence Demo format: confluence-html --- ## Overview Write your content in Quarto documents and publish to Confluence.</code></pre> <p>Notice that the format is set to <code>confluence-html</code> in the document YAML. This allows the local preview of the document to mimic the eventual appearance on Confluence. You can preview your document locally as you would any other Quarto document, by using the Render button in RStudio; the Preview button, or Quarto: Preview command in VS Code and Positron; or by using <code>quarto preview</code> from the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview confluence-demo.qmd</code></pre> <p>The result of previewing <code>confluence-demo.qmd</code> locally is shown below:</p> <p>The preview attempts to provide an accurate idea of how your content will look. However, some items in the preview are merely placeholders, like the publishing date, author, and read time in the header. When the document is published to Confluence, these items will be generated by Confluence.</p> <p>To publish a document to Confluence use <code>quarto publish confluence</code> followed by the file name:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish confluence confluence-demo.qmd</code></pre> <p>Unless you’ve published to Confluence before, you’ll be prompted to set up an account and select a destination for your page.</p> <h6 id="setting-up-your-account">Setting Up Your Account</h6> <p>When you publish to Confluence for the first time, you’ll be prompted to set up a Confluence account in Quarto. To prepare, log in to Confluence, and navigate to the space, or page within a space, which you wish to publish to.</p> <p>You’ll first be prompted for your Confluence Domain. This is the first part of the URL to the Confluence page you wish to publish to. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal ? Confluence Domain: › ❯ e.g. [mydomain.atlassian.net](https://mydomain.atlassian.net/)</code></pre> <p>Next, you’ll be asked to enter the Email Address for the account used in this Confluence Domain (if you are unsure, look at your account profile on Confluence):</p> <pre><code>Terminal ? Confluence Account Email: ›</code></pre> <p>Finally, you’ll be asked for an API Token:</p> <pre><code>Terminal ? Confluence API Token: › ❯ Create an API token at [id.atlassian.com](https://id.atlassian.com/manage/api-tokens)</code></pre> <p>Confluence API Tokens are specific to your account. You’ll need to <a href="https://id.atlassian.com/manage/api-tokens">create a token</a>, copy, and then paste it into this prompt. For more information on Access Tokens please see the <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-account/docs/manage-api-tokens-for-your-atlassian-account/">Confluence Documentation on API Tokens</a>.</p> <p>Quarto saves this account information (domain, email and token) so it can be used for future calls to <code>quarto publish confluence</code>. The final prompt will ask you to select a destination for your page.</p> <h6 id="selecting-a-destination">Selecting a Destination</h6> <p>Pages in Confluence are arranged in a hierarchy: every page has a parent. When you publish from Quarto to Confluence you’ll be asked to specify the parent for your page by providing its URL:</p> <pre><code>Terminal ? Space or Parent Page URL: › ❯ Browse in Confluence to the space or parent, then copy the URL</code></pre> <p>If you want your page to be at the top level of your space, specify the space itself, e.g.:</p> <pre><code>[domain.atlassian.net](https://domain.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ABBR)</code></pre> <p>Otherwise, specify the URL for the parent page, e.g.:</p> <pre><code>[domain.atlassian.net](https://domain.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ABBR/pages/123456)</code></pre> <p>Once the destination is specified, Quarto will render the page for publishing, publish it to Confluence, and open a browser to view the published page.</p> <p>An example of the published version of <code>confluence-demo.qmd</code> is shown below:</p> <p>In the sidebar navigation this page is listed at the top level under Pages because the destination was set to the space URL.</p> <h5 id="publishing-projects">Publishing Projects</h5> <p>To publish a collection of documents, organize your documents in a Quarto project, and use the <code>confluence</code> project type. Here’s a minimal <code>_quarto.yml</code> file for a Confluence project:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: confluence</code></pre> <p>Include this file in a project directory, then arrange your <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> documents into whatever hierarchy you want to use for publishing. For example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml index.qmd team.qmd projects/ planning.qmd retrospectives.qmd</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, to get started with a template project in a new directory, use <code>quarto create</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project confluence</code></pre> <p>As with documents, you can preview your project using the Render command in VS Code and RStudio, or by using <code>quarto preview</code> from the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview</code></pre> <p>The project preview produces an HTML website with navigation automatically added to the sidebar. This navigation is for convenience, the navigation for the published pages will be handled internally by Confluence.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>The project preview attempts to style your content as it will appear on Confluence, however, you may notice some differences in appearance.</p> <p>To publish your project run <code>quarto publish confluence</code> from your project folder:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish confluence</code></pre> <p>You’ll be walked through the same steps as publishing a single document, setting up an account, if needed, and selecting a destination for your project on Confluence, before publishing your project to Confluence.</p> <h6 id="project-structure">Project Structure</h6> <p>The hierarchy of documents inside folders in your project will be respected in the publishing process. Confluence’s concept of folders is that pages can have children, so your folders will be represented by pages in Confluence.</p> <p>When a project is published, a single page is created in Confluence to hold it. Documents at the top level of the project are published as pages nested under this project page. Folders inside the project are represented by a page, and any documents (or other folders) inside the folder are represented as pages nested under the folder page.</p> <p>As an example, consider the following project structure:</p> <pre><code>example-project/ ├── _quarto.yml ├── project-roadmap.qmd ├── reports-folder │ ├── 2023-01.qmd │ └── 2023-03.qmd └── team-members.qmd</code></pre> <p>The Confluence structure resulting from publishing this project to the top level of the space is shown below:</p> <p>The titles used in the Confluence sidebar navigation are taken from the page and project title, as specified in the document YAML and <code>_quarto.yml</code> respectively, and generated from the folder name for folders. Quarto may add some additional characters to meet the Confluences requirement that every page in a space has a unique name.</p> <h6 id="index.qmd"><code>index.qmd</code></h6> <p>Pages in Confluence that represent folders will have no content unless an <code>index.qmd</code> is found inside the folder. If an <code>index.qmd</code> file exists its content will populate the folder page. For example, consider the following <code>index.qmd</code>:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- title: Reports --- Monthly reports on project progress</code></pre> <p>Adding this to the folder <code>reports-folder</code> and re-publishing the site, changes the name of the page representing this folder to “Reports” and adds this contents to the page.</p> <h5 id="publishing-workflow">Publishing Workflow</h5> <p>In Confluence, many people are able to make direct edits to pages. However, managing your content from Quarto requires a shift in perspective: edits to pages are made only in the Quarto project, and only one account should publish those changes to Confluence.</p> <p>Publishing to Confluence is a one-way street: there is no way to bring back content edits from Confluence to your Quarto project. Edits that are made on Confluence will be overwritten next time the page is published from Quarto. Updating a page requires editing the document in Quarto, and rerunning:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish confluence</code></pre> <p>To help avoid a situation where someone inadvertently edits a page being managed in Quarto, the permissions for pages are set when you publish so everyone with access to the space can view the page, but only you, the publisher, can edit the page.</p> <p>Permission to edit the page includes publishing updates, so any updates to a page need to be published from the same account as the original publish.</p> <p>NotePublishing without Control over Permissions</p> <p>We attempt to detect if you are publishing to a destination where you do not have control over page permissions and you’ll receive a warning. You may proceed with the publish, but any page you publish can be both viewed and edited by anyone with access to the space.</p> <p>If you delete a page on Confluence, and republish it from Quarto, you’ll see the error:</p> <pre><code>ERROR: API Error: 404 - Not Found</code></pre> <p>This occurs because Quarto stores and reuses the location of your page on Confluence in <code>_publish.yml</code>. If the page is deleted on Confluence, this location will no longer exist. To solve the problem, delete the corresponding entry in <code>_publish.yml</code>, and publish again. You’ll then be prompted to set the destination. You can read more about <code>_publish.yml</code> in the Publishing Settings section.</p> <h5 id="authoring-4">Authoring</h5> <p>Authoring for Confluence is very similar to authoring HTML documents and Quarto webpages. However, you should be aware of some key limitations as well as some features specific to Confluence publishing.</p> <h6 id="content-limitations">Content Limitations</h6> <p>The <code>confluence-html</code> format supports nearly all of the standard Quarto markdown content types, including tables, callouts, and cross references.</p> <p>However, there is currently no support for Citations, Videos, Diagrams, Tabsets, or Equations. In the future, we may add these features if there is a Confluence equivalent that can support the functionality.</p> <h6 id="links">Links</h6> <p>When creating links between pages in your Confluence Project, you can provide the source file as the link target (rather than the path to the Confluence page). You can also add hash identifiers (<code>#</code>) to the source file if you want to link to a particular section in the document. For example:</p> <pre><code>[about](about.qmd) [about](about.qmd#section)</code></pre> <h6 id="raw-confluence-blocks">Raw Confluence Blocks</h6> <p>Raw Confluence blocks allow you to include content that should pass through Quarto unchanged and be interpreted directly by Confluence. For example, <a href="https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-storage-format-790796544.html">Confluence’s Storage Format</a> includes specific tags for a task list. To include a Confluence task list in your document, use these tags inside a raw Confluence block:</p> <pre><code>```{=confluence} <ac:task-list> <ac:task> <ac:task-status>incomplete</ac:task-status> <ac:task-body>task list item</ac:task-body> </ac:task> </ac:task-list> ```</code></pre> <p>When published to Confluence this results in the following list:</p> <h6 id="website-limitations">Website Limitations</h6> <p>Confluence projects are a special type of website that don’t support the traditional Website features like Listings, Themes and Navigation (as these things are taken care of internally by Confluence).</p> <h6 id="confluence-limitations">Confluence Limitations</h6> <p>As discussed in Publishing Workflow edits to page content made in Confluence are overwritten when content is published from Quarto. This is also the case for any inline comments made on Confluence. Page level emojis and page level comments are preserved across publishes.</p> <h5 id="publishing-settings">Publishing Settings</h5> <p>Once you have published to Confluence, you might be interested in understanding how to manage your publishing and account settings.</p> <h6 id="publish.yml">_publish.yml</h6> <p>The <code>_publish.yml</code> file is used to specify the publishing destination. This file is automatically created (or updated) whenever you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command, and is located within the project or document directory.</p> <p>The service, id, and URL of the published content is specified in <code>_publish.yml</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project confluence: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[myteam.atlassian.net](https://myteam.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TEAMSPACE/pages/123456/Plan)"</code></pre> <p>The next time you publish the same document or project, the <code>_publish.yml</code> file will be used to provide account and space information so that you are not prompted for this information again.</p> <p>If you have an existing Confluence Space that you want to publish to, you should manually create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that looks like the example above, but with the appropriate <code>id</code> and <code>url</code> values for your document.</p> <p>Account information is not stored in <code>_publish.yml</code>, so it is suitable for checking in to version control and being shared by multiple publishers.</p> <h6 id="account-management">Account Management</h6> <p>You can list and remove saved Confluence accounts using the <code>quarto publish accounts</code> command:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto publish accounts ? Manage Publishing Accounts ❯ ✔ Confluence: jj@posit.co ✔ Netlify: jj@posit.co ❯ Use the arrow keys and spacebar to specify accounts you would like to remove. Press Enter to confirm the list of accounts you wish to remain available.</code></pre> <h3 id="github-pages">GitHub Pages</h3> <h4 id="github-pages-1">GitHub Pages</h4> <h5 id="overview-110">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://pages.github.com/">GitHub Pages</a> is a website hosting service that enables you to publish content based on source code managed within a GitHub repository.</p> <p>There are three ways to publish Quarto websites and documents to GitHub Pages:</p> <ul> <li>Render sites on your local machine to the <code>docs</code> directory, check the rendered site into GitHub, and then configure your GitHub repo to publish from the <code>docs</code> directory.</li> <li>Use the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish content rendered on your local machine.</li> <li>Use a GitHub Action to automatically render your files (a single Quarto document or a Quarto project) and publish the resulting content whenever you push a source code change to your repository. We’ll cover each of these methods below, but first an important pre-requisite: you need to have a Git repository on your local machine that is synced to GitHub. The URL of the published website will be derived from the combination of your username and the repository name (e.g. <code>https://username.github.io/reponame/</code>).</li> </ul> <p>You can optionally configure a custom domain for a GitHub Pages site, but before exploring that, get your site up and running with the default domain.</p> <h5 id="render-to-docs">Render to <code>docs</code></h5> <p>The simplest way to publish using GitHub Pages is to render to the <code>docs</code> directory and then check that directory into your repository. If you prefer not to check rendered output into version control see the discussion of using Publish Command below.</p> <p>To get started, change your project configuration to use <code>docs</code> as the <code>output-dir</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: website output-dir: docs</code></pre> <p>Then, add a <code>.nojekyll</code> file to the root of your repository that tells GitHub Pages not to do additional processing of your published site using Jekyll (the GitHub default site generation tool):</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal touch .nojekyll</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal copy NUL .nojekyll</code></pre> <p>Now, render your site and push it to GitHub:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render git add docs git commit -m "Publish site to docs/" git push</code></pre> <p>Finally, configure your GitHub repository to publish from the <code>docs</code> directory of your <code>main</code> branch:</p> <p>Once you’ve made this configuration change GitHub will trigger a deployment of your website. Your site will also be updated whenever you commit and push to <code>main</code>.</p> <h5 id="publish-command-1">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command is an easy way to publish locally rendered documents and websites. Before attempting to use <code>quarto publish</code> (either locally or from a GitHub Action) you should be sure to configure Ignore Output as described below. See Source Branch for an overview of how the <code>gh-pages</code> branch is managed.</p> <h6 id="source-branch">Source Branch</h6> <p><code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> automatically creates a <code>gh-pages</code> branch (locally and on the remote) on its first run if one does not already exist. For most repositories — the typical <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/what-is-github-pages#types-of-github-pages-sites">project site</a> case where the URL is <code>https://<username>.github.io/<repo>/</code> — GitHub then detects the new branch and configures GitHub Pages to deploy from it automatically. No manual configuration under Settings : Pages is required.</p> <p><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/what-is-github-pages#types-of-github-pages-sites">User and organization sites</a> (served at <code>https://<username>.github.io/</code>) behave differently on the GitHub side: their <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/configuring-a-publishing-source-for-your-github-pages-site#publishing-from-a-branch">default publishing source is the <code>main</code> branch</a>, not <code>gh-pages</code>. After the first run of <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> you therefore need to switch the source branch to <code>gh-pages</code> manually under Settings : Pages for your repository:</p> <p>Quarto prints a notice with a direct link to this settings page when it detects this case. See the User Site section below for the complete setup.</p> <p>TipCreating a <code>gh-pages</code> branch manually</p> <p>You usually do not need to do this — <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> will create the branch on its first run. If you prefer to set it up yourself beforehand, first make sure you have committed all changes on your current working branch with <code>git status</code>, then run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal git checkout --orphan gh-pages # make sure all changes are committed before running this! git reset --hard git commit --allow-empty -m "Initialising gh-pages branch" git push origin gh-pages</code></pre> <p>Get back to your original repository branch with, for example, <code>git checkout main</code>.</p> <h6 id="ignoring-output">Ignoring Output</h6> <p>It’s important to note that you don’t need to check your <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory into version control (if you have done this in the past you know it makes for very messy diffs!). Before proceeding you should add the output directory of your project to <code>.gitignore</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>.gitignore /.quarto/ /_site/</code></pre> <p>If you’ve already checked these files into source control you may need to remove them explicitly:</p> <pre><code>Terminal git rm -r _site</code></pre> <h6 id="publishing-11">Publishing</h6> <p>Once you have updated your <code>.gitignore</code>, navigate to the directory where your project / git repository is located, make sure you are not on the <code>gh-pages</code> branch, and execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command for GitHub Pages:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish gh-pages</code></pre> <p>The publish command will confirm that you want to publish, render your content, copy the output to a special <code>gh-pages</code> branch, push that branch to GitHub, and then open a browser to view your site once it is deployed.</p> <h6 id="private-sites">Private Sites</h6> <p>If you are publishing to a private (i.e. password protected) website then the logic within <code>quarto publish</code>that waits for your site to be available before opening a browser won’t work correctly. In this case you should pass the <code>--no-browser</code> option to bypass this:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish gh-pages --no-browser</code></pre> <h6 id="documents-1">Documents</h6> <p>To publish a document rather than a website or book, provide the path to the document (note that you can publish only one document from a given GitHub repository):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish gh-pages document.qmd</code></pre> <h6 id="options-39">Options</h6> <p>Here are all of the available command line options for <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code>:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>--no-prompt</code></p> <p>Do not prompt to confirm publish actions.</p> <p><code>--no-browser</code></p> <p>Do not open a browser after publish.</p> <p><code>--no-render</code></p> <p>Do not re-render prior to publish</p> <h5 id="github-action">GitHub Action</h5> <p>Using the <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> command to publish locally rendered content is the most simple and straightforward way to publish. Another option is to use <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a> to render and publish your site (you might prefer this if you want execution and/or rendering to be automatically triggered from commits).</p> <p>There are a few different ways to approach rendering and publishing content. Below, we’ll provide a how-to guide for publishing with GitHub Actions. For more conceptual background on the various approaches, see the discussion on Rendering for CI.</p> <h6 id="freezing-computations">Freezing Computations</h6> <p>To make sure that R, Python, and Julia code is only executed locally, configure your project to use Quarto’s freeze feature by adding this to your <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml execute: freeze: auto</code></pre> <p>Now, fully re-render your site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a <code>_freeze</code> directory has been created at the top level of your project. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a <code>.qmd</code> file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in <code>_freeze</code>.</p> <p>Note that an alternative approach is to execute the code as part of the GitHub Action. For now we’ll keep things simpler by executing code locally and storing the computations by using freeze. Then, further below, we’ll cover Executing Code within a GitHub Action.</p> <h6 id="publish-action">Publish Action</h6> <p>Before configuring the publishing action, it’s important that you run <code>quarto publish gh-pages</code> locally, once. This will create the <code>_publish.yml</code> configuration required by the subsequent invocations of the GitHub Action. To do this, run the following from within your project:</p> <pre><code>quarto publish gh-pages</code></pre> <p>Once you’ve completed a local publish, add a <code>publish.yml</code> GitHub Action to your project by creating this YAML file and saving it to <code>.github/workflows/publish.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: write steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: gh-pages env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <p>This action will run whenever you push to the <code>main</code> branch of your repository. It will also run when you manually trigger the action from the Actions tab of your repository. The action will render your content and publish it to GitHub Pages, thus you need to ensure that GitHub Actions has permission to write to your repository. This is done by checking the Read and write permissions box under Workflow permissions in the Actions section of your repository Settings.</p> <p>Once you’ve done this, check all of the newly created files (including the <code>_freeze</code> directory) into your repository and then push to GitHub. A GitHub Pages site will be created for your repository, and every time you push a new change to the repository it will be automatically rebuilt to reflect the change. Consult the Pages section of your repository Settings to see what the URL and publish status for your site is.</p> <h6 id="executing-code">Executing Code</h6> <p>If you prefer, you can also configure a GitHub Action to execute R, Python, or Julia code as part of rendering. While this might reflexively seem like the best approach, consider the following requirements imposed when you execute code within a CI service like GitHub Actions:</p> <ul> <li>You need to reconstitute all of the dependencies (R, Python, or Julia plus the correct versions of required packages) in the CI environment.</li> <li>If your code requires any special permissions (e.g. database or network access) those permissions also need to be present on the CI server.</li> <li>Your project may contain documents that can no longer be easily executed (e.g. blog posts from several years ago that use older versions of packages). These documents may need to have <code>freeze</code> individually enabled for them to prevent execution on CI.</li> </ul> <h6 id="prerequisites-1">Prerequisites</h6> <p>The best way to ensure that your code can be executed within a GitHub Action is to use a virtual environment like <a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">venv</a> or <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html">renv</a> with your project (below we’ll provide example actions for each). If you aren’t familiar with using these tools check out the article on using Virtual Environments with Quarto to learn more.</p> <p>Once you’ve decided to execute code within your GitHub Action you can remove the <code>freeze: auto</code> described above from your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration. Note that if you want to use <code>freeze</code> selectively for some documents or directories that is still possible (for a directory, create a <code>_metadata.yml</code> file in the directory and specify your freeze configuration there—this is what Quarto does by default for the <code>posts</code> folder of blog projects).</p> <h6 id="example-jupyter-with-venv">Example: Jupyter with venv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs Python, Jupyter, and package dependencies from <code>requirements.txt</code>, then executes code and renders output to GitHub Pages:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: write steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install Python and Dependencies uses: actions/setup-python@v7 with: python-version: '3.14' cache: 'pip' - run: pip install jupyter - run: pip install -r requirements.txt - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: gh-pages env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h6 id="example-knitr-with-renv">Example: Knitr with renv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs R and package dependencies from <code>renv.lock</code>, then executes code and renders output to GitHub Pages:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: write steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: '4.6.1' - name: Install R Dependencies uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 with: cache-version: 1 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: gh-pages env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h6 id="additional-options">Additional Options</h6> <p>It’s possible to have a Quarto project in a larger GitHub repository, where the Quarto project does not reside at the top-level directory. In this case, add a <code>path</code> input to the invocation of the <code>publish</code> action. For example:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: gh-pages path: subdirectory-to-use env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <p>By default, <code>quarto publish</code> will re-render your project before publishing it. However, if you store the rendered output in version control, you don’t need the GitHub action to re-render the project. In that case, add the option <code>render: false</code> to the <code>publish</code> action:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: gh-pages render: false env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <p>See the full definition of the Quarto <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-actions/blob/main/publish/action.yml">publish action</a> to learn about other more advanced options.</p> <h5 id="custom-domain">Custom Domain</h5> <p>A custom domain allows you to use your own domain name instead of the default <code>username.github.io</code> domain for your GitHub Pages site. To use a custom domain you need to complete two steps:</p> <ul> <li>Add your domain to your GitHub repository settings</li> <li>Configure records with your DNS provider</li> </ul> <h6 id="add-your-domain-to-your-github-repository-settings">1. Add your domain to your GitHub repository settings</h6> <p>Add a <code>CNAME</code> file to your project root directory (i.e., alongside <code>_quarto.yml</code>) that contains your custom domain:</p> <pre><code>website/ ├── _site/ ├── _quarto.yml ├── CNAME ├── about.qmd └── index.qmd CNAME blog.example.com</code></pre> <p>Quarto will recognize the <code>CNAME</code> file as a site resource and will copy it your site output directory when you render.</p> <p>Re-render and publish your site to ensure <code>CNAME</code> is available to GitHub Pages.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The GitHub Pages documentation describes adding your domain to your repository in the Settings pane. However, this creates a <code>CNAME</code> file in the location of your rendered site, which will be overwritten whenever you render your site with Quarto.</p> <h6 id="configure-records-with-your-dns-provider">2. Configure records with your DNS provider</h6> <p>The records you need to configure with your DNS provider depend on whether you are using an apex domain (e.g., <code>example.com</code>) or a subdomain (e.g., <code>www.example.com</code> or <code>blog.example.com</code>).</p> <p>Apex domains require an <code>ALIAS</code>, <code>ANAME</code>, or <code>A</code> record, whereas subdomains require a <code>CNAME</code> record. Find the appropriate values from the <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site/managing-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site#dns-records-for-your-custom-domain">DNS records summary table in the GitHub Pages documentation</a>. For apex domains, pay particular attention to the DNS record values, you may need to overwrite addresses your DNS provider has added by default.</p> <h5 id="user-site">User Site</h5> <p>In addition to creating sites tied to various repositories, you can also create a user site that is served from your root user domain (e.g. <code>https://username.github.io</code>). This is an ideal place to publish a blog or personal home page. To create a user site:</p> <ul> <li>Create a Git repo with the name <code>username.github.io</code> (where “username” is your GitHub username) and sync it to your local machine.</li> <li>Set the Source branch for your user site to <code>gh-pages</code> as described in Source Branch.</li> </ul> <h3 id="hugging-face-spaces">Hugging Face Spaces</h3> <h4 id="hugging-face-spaces-1">Hugging Face Spaces</h4> <h5 id="overview-111">Overview</h5> <p>Hugging Face is a comprehensive platform that offers a wide array of machine learning models, particularly in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision. It is designed to facilitate the training, deployment, and use of open-access machine learning models, making it easier for developers and researchers to access state-of-the-art models.</p> <p>Hugging Face also provides application and static site hosting as part of its <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-overview">Spaces project</a>. You can use <a href="https://huggingface.co/spaces">Hugging Face Spaces</a> to render and host Quarto websites as a way to document and present your work.</p> <p>Quarto’s integration in Hugging Face Spaces happens through a <a href="https://www.docker.com/">Docker</a> image created by the Quarto team that Hugging Face has made easily available for authors as a template.</p> <p>To create and publish a Hugging Face Space using Quarto, you’ll start by creating a new space using Quarto’s Docker Template. Then you’ll edit or replace the example content with your own. Learn more about this process in Getting Started below.</p> <p>Whenever changes are committed to your Hugging Face Space, a new build is initiated which renders and serves your Quarto website. You can make and commit changes directly in the Hugging Face UI. However, previewing your changes via a build on Hugging Face is time-consuming, so for faster iteration we recommend working locally and using the <code>quarto publish huggingface</code> command.
