This workflow is described below in Publish Command.</p> <h5 id="getting-started-2">Getting Started</h5> <h6 id="create-a-new-space">Create a New Space</h6> <p>To get started you’ll create a new Hugging Face Space using the Quarto template.</p> <p>Visit <a href="https://huggingface.co/new-space?template=posit%2Fquarto-template">the Hugging Face Create a New Space webpage</a>.</p> <p>If you’re not logged in to Hugging Face, log in first:</p> <p>The UI for logging in to Hugging Face</p> <p>Start by choosing a name and license for your space:</p> <p>The UI for choosing name and license for your space</p> <p>If you followed the link above, you will see “Docker” selected for the Space SDK, and “Quarto” chosen as the Docker template. If not, select them as shown below:</p> <p>The UI for Hugging Face Spaces creation webpage</p> <p>Finally, choose the hardware that will be used to run your space, whether the space will be public or private, and click on “Create Space”:</p> <p>The UI for choosing hardware configuration and space visibility</p> <p>Hugging Face will then “Build” your space:</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>It can take a couple of minutes for the Space to deploy to Hugging Face after the Docker build process completes. To see your changes you will need to do two things:</p> <ul> <li>Wait for your space’s status to go from ‘Building’ to ‘Running’(this is visible in the status bar above the Space)</li> <li>Force-reload the web page by holding Shift and hitting the reload button in your browser. Build process for a new space based on the Quarto template</li> </ul> <p>You’ll know the space is finished building when you see the <code>Running</code> in the top bar.</p> <p>Hugging Face <code>Running</code> badge</p> <p>Once built, your Space will display the rendered example website (you may need to refresh the page in your browser for this to appear):</p> <p>A Quarto template website running in a Hugging Face Space</p> <h6 id="quartos-hugging-face-template">Quarto’s Hugging Face Template</h6> <p>You can click on the <code>Files</code> tab in the top right to look at the files which make up the template. Quarto’s Hugging Face template consists of files used to create an environment to build and render the Quarto website (<code>Dockerfile</code>and <code>requirements.txt</code>), and the website source itself in <code>src/</code>:</p> <ul> <li><code>Dockerfile</code>: This contains the system setup to build and serve the Quarto site on Hugging Face. You probably won’t need to change this file unless you need to add additional system dependencies or modify the Quarto version.</li> <li><code>requirements.txt</code>: This is where you should include any Python dependencies which you need for your website. These are installed when the Dockerfile builds.</li> <li>The <code>src</code> directory contains the source files for the Quarto website. You can include Jupyter notebooks or markdown (<code>.qmd</code> or <code>.md</code>) files.</li> <li><code>src/_quarto.yml</code> defines the navigation for your website. If you want to add new pages or reorganize the existing ones, you’ll need to change this file. You can edit these files directly in the Hugging Face UI but we reccommend cloning your space, and making and previewing changes locally, then using the publish command as described in the next section.</li> </ul> <h5 id="publish-command-2">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish huggingface</code> command facilitates a workflow where you make and preview edits locally before publishing to your Hugging Face space. Before using the command you’ll need to complete some Setup.</p> <h6 id="setup-2">Setup</h6> <p>To get set up to use <code>quarto publish huggingface</code> you should have already:</p> <ul> <li><p>Created a space using Quarto’s Docker Template as described above. Then complete the following steps, explained at length below:</p></li> <li><p>(Optional) Create an authorization token if you lack one</p></li> <li><p>Clone the repository locally</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="create-an-authorization-token">Create an authorization token</h6> <p>In order to publish the results to Hugging Face, <code>quarto publish</code> needs access to your credentials. If you haven’t created such an authorization token yet, visit <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security-tokens#how-to-manage-user-access-tokens">Hugging Face’s documentation on user access tokens</a> and follow the instructions to create a token with the <code>write</code> role. You’ll need this token the first time you run the publish command.</p> <h6 id="clone-the-repository-locally">Clone the repository locally</h6> <p>The URL for your space, as well as the URL to clone the repository, is <code>https://huggingface.co/spaces/<your-hugging-face-username>/<name-of-space></code>. Use your favorite <code>git</code> interface to clone the Hugging Face Space you’ve just created with the URL above. You can also find instructions in your space under ⋮ > Clone repository.</p> <h6 id="edit-and-preview">Edit and Preview</h6> <p>Once your repository is set up, use whichever text editor you prefer to make changes to your repository. Quarto’s Hugging Face template includes a Quarto website in the <code>src/</code> directory of the repository. For information on how to create websites with Quarto, see our documentation</p> <p>To preview your changes, from the root of your repository, run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview src</code></pre> <h6 id="publish-2">Publish</h6> <p>When you are happy with the results in the repository, run:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish huggingface</code></pre> <p>Quarto will stage, commit, and push all required changes to Hugging Face, as well as fetching remote content and merging it with your repository’s contents first. If the repository you’re working on hasn’t been configured to take in an explicit user name and authorization token, Quarto will prompt you for such information on the command line.</p> <p>On completion Quarto will open your space in your default browser.</p> <h5 id="publishing-an-existing-repository">Publishing an Existing Repository</h5> <p>The command <code>quarto publish huggingface</code> requires that the <code>origin</code> <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/getting-started-with-git/managing-remote-repositories">git remote</a> point to a <code>https://huggingface.co/spaces</code> URL. If you used the instructions above, this will happen automatically.</p> <p>If you are working from an existing repository already configured with a Quarto template pointing to the right URL, you can use <code>quarto publish huggingface</code> directly without needing to create or clone a new space.</p> <h3 id="netlify">Netlify</h3> <h4 id="netlify-1">Netlify</h4> <h5 id="overview-112">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://www.netlify.com/">Netlify</a> is a professional web publishing platform with support for many advanced features including custom domains, authentication, branch previews, and instant rollbacks. Netlify also has a free plan that is ideal for personal projects, hobby sites, or experiments.</p> <p>There are several ways to publish Quarto content to Netlify:</p> <ul> <li>Use the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish content rendered on your local machine.</li> <li>If you are using GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps, you can point Netlify at your site’s source code and have it deployed whenever your code changes.</li> <li>If you are using GitHub, you can use a GitHub Action to automatically render your project and publish the resulting content whenever your code changes.</li> <li>If you are using another Continuous Integration (CI) service, you can script the <code>quarto publish</code> command to render and publish content to Netlify. We’ll cover each of these methods below, starting with the most straightforward and then proceeding to more sophisticated scenarios.</li> </ul> <h5 id="publish-command-3">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command is the easiest way to publish locally rendered content. From the directory where your project is located, execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command for Netlify:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify</code></pre> <p>If you haven’t published to Netlify before, the publish command will prompt you to authenticate.</p> <p>After confirming that you want to publish, your content will be rendered and deployed, and then a browser opened to view your site.</p> <h6 id="publish.yml-1">_publish.yml</h6> <p>The <code>_publish.yml</code> file is used to specify the publishing destination. This file is automatically created (or updated) whenever you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command, and is located within the project or document directory.</p> <p>The service, id, and URL of the published content is specified in <code>_publish.yml</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project netlify: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app](https://tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app)"</code></pre> <p>If you have an existing Netlify site that you want to publish to, you should manually create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that looks like the example above, but with the appropriate <code>id</code> and <code>url</code> values for your site.</p> <p>Account information is not stored in <code>_publish.yml</code>, so it is suitable for checking in to version control and being shared by multiple publishers.</p> <h6 id="options-40">Options</h6> <p>You can customize the behavior of <code>quarto publish</code> by providing the following command line options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>--no-prompt</code></p> <p>Do not prompt to confirm publish actions.</p> <p><code>--no-browser</code></p> <p>Do not open a browser after publish.</p> <p><code>--no-render</code></p> <p>Do not re-render prior to publish</p> <p>To publish a document rather than a website or book, provide the path to the document:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify document.qmd</code></pre> <h6 id="domain-name">Domain Name</h6> <p>The domain name for your published site will by default use a random identifier (e.g. <code>mystifying-jepsen-fa4396.netlify.app</code>). You can pick a more descriptive sub-domain (still using <code>netlify.app</code> as the main domain) or if you own another domain, assign that one to the site. These options are available (respectively) from the Site settings and Domain settings panels:</p> <p>Within Site settings, click the Change site name button to specify a different sub-domain:</p> <p>If you own another domain that you want to use for your site, follow the directions in Domain settings.</p> <h5 id="publish-from-git-provider">Publish from Git Provider</h5> <p>Netlify has the ability to automatically deploy sites when changes are committed to Git repositories hosted on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. The most straightforward approach to this is to check your rendered site (i.e. the <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory) into version control and have Netlify deploy that. We’ll cover that scenario first and then explore using a Netlify Build Plugin to render the site on Netlify servers.</p> <h6 id="importing-a-project">Importing a Project</h6> <p>Start by going to the main Netlify page for your team, choosing Add new site, and then Import an existing project:</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to authenticate with your version control provider, select a repository, and then finally specify the configuration for publishing the site.</p> <h6 id="publishing-configuration">Publishing Configuration</h6> <p>The build settings for our project will have no Build command and will specify <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> (as appropriate) for the Publish directory:</p> <p>If you have your <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory checked into version control then everything is now configured and your site will be deployed to Netlify automatically whenever you commit to your repository.</p> <h6 id="rendering-on-netlify">Rendering on Netlify</h6> <p>If you prefer not to check your rendered site into version control, you can also use the Quarto <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/netlify-plugin-quarto">Netlify Build Plugin</a> to render on a Netlify build server (note that Netlify servers can only render markdown and cannot execute R, Python, or Julia code).</p> <h6 id="freezing-computations-1">Freezing Computations</h6> <p>To make sure that R, Python, and Julia code is only executed locally, configure your project to use Quarto’s freeze feature by adding this to your <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml execute: freeze: auto</code></pre> <p>Now, fully re-render your site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a <code>_freeze</code> directory has been created at the top level of your project. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a <code>.qmd</code> file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in <code>_freeze</code>.</p> <h6 id="ignoring-output-1">Ignoring Output</h6> <p>It’s important to note that you don’t need to check your <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory into version control (if you have done this in the past you know it makes for very messy diffs!). Before proceeding you should add the output directory of your project to <code>.gitignore</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>.gitignore /.quarto/ /_site/</code></pre> <p>If you’ve already checked these files into source control you may need to remove them explicitly:</p> <pre><code>Terminal git rm -r _site</code></pre> <h6 id="plugin-configuration-1">Plugin Configuration</h6> <p>To use the Quarto Netlify Build Plugin, add the following two files to your project:</p> <pre><code>netlify.toml [[plugins]] package = "@quarto/netlify-plugin-quarto" package.json { "dependencies": { "@quarto/netlify-plugin-quarto": "^0.0.5" } }</code></pre> <p>Now, commit and push your modified project (including <code>_freeze</code>, <code>netlify.toml</code>, and <code>package.json</code>). Assuming that you configured the project correctly in the previous step (i.e. Publish directory set to the <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory) then Netlify will begin rendering and publishing your site each time you push a new commit.</p> <h5 id="github-action-1">GitHub Action</h5> <p>Using the <code>quarto publish netlify</code> command to publish locally rendered content is the most simple and straightforward way to publish. Another option is to use <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a> to render and publish your site (you might prefer this if you want execution and/or rendering to be automatically triggered from commits).</p> <p>There are a few different ways to approach rendering and publishing content. Below, we’ll provide a how-to guide for publishing with GitHub Actions. For more conceptual background on the various approaches, see the discussion on Rendering for CI.</p> <h6 id="publish-record">Publish Record</h6> <p>Prior to attempting to publish with a GitHub Action, you should have completed at least one publish using the Publish Command (described immediately above). This publish will create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that records the publishing destination to be used by the GitHub Action. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project netlify: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app](https://tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app)"</code></pre> <p>You can also manually create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that looks like the example above, but with the appropriate <code>id</code> and <code>url</code> values for your site.</p> <p>Do not proceed to the next step(s) until you have a <code>_publish.yml</code> that indicates your publishing destination.</p> <h6 id="freezing-computations-2">Freezing Computations</h6> <p>To make sure that R, Python, and Julia code is only executed locally, configure your project to use Quarto’s freeze feature by adding this to your <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml execute: freeze: auto</code></pre> <p>Now, fully re-render your site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a <code>_freeze</code> directory has been created at the top level of your project. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a <code>.qmd</code> file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in <code>_freeze</code>.</p> <p>Note that an alternative approach is to execute the code as part of the GitHub Action. For now we’ll keep things simpler by executing code locally and storing the computations by using freeze. Then, further below, we’ll cover Executing Code within a GitHub Action.</p> <h6 id="publish-action-1">Publish Action</h6> <p>Add a <code>publish.yml</code> GitHub Action to your project by creating this YAML file and saving it to <code>.github/workflows/publish.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: netlify NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h6 id="netlify-credentials">Netlify Credentials</h6> <p>The final step is to configure your GitHub Action with the credentials required for publishing to Netlify. To do this you need to create a Netlify personal access token and then configure your GitHub action to be able to read it:</p> <ul> <li>If you don’t already have an access token, go to the Netlify <a href="https://app.netlify.com/user/applications">applications page</a>, and click on New Access Token to create a new personal access token. Give this token a memorable name, and copy the token to the clipboard.</li> <li>Add the Netlify personal access token to your repository’s action Secrets (accessible within repository Settings). You will see a New repository secret button at the top right:</li> <li>Click the button and add the personal access token from step 1 as a secret named <code>NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN</code>:</li> </ul> <h6 id="ignoring-output-2">Ignoring Output</h6> <p>It’s important to note that you don’t need to check your <code>_site</code> or <code>_book</code> directory into version control (if you have done this in the past you know it makes for very messy diffs!). Before proceeding you should add the output directory of your project to <code>.gitignore</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>.gitignore /.quarto/ /_site/</code></pre> <p>If you’ve already checked these files into source control you may need to remove them explicitly:</p> <pre><code>Terminal git rm -r _site</code></pre> <h6 id="commit-to-publish">Commit to Publish</h6> <p>Once you’ve specified your publishing action and Netlify credentials, and pushed your updated repository (including the <code>_freeze</code> directory) to GitHub, your action will run with this and subsequent commits, automatically rendering and publishing to Netlify.</p> <h6 id="executing-code-1">Executing Code</h6> <p>If you prefer, you can also configure a GitHub Action to execute R, Python, or Julia code as part of rendering. While this might reflexively seem like the best approach, consider the following requirements imposed when you execute code within a CI service like GitHub Actions:</p> <ul> <li>You need to reconstitute all of the dependencies (R, Python, or Julia plus the correct versions of required packages) in the CI environment.</li> <li>If your code requires any special permissions (e.g. database or network access) those permissions also need to be present on the CI server.</li> <li>Your project may contain documents that can no longer be easily executed (e.g. blog posts from several years ago that use older versions of packages). These documents may need to have <code>freeze</code> individually enabled for them to prevent execution on CI.</li> </ul> <h6 id="prerequisites-2">Prerequisites</h6> <p>The best way to ensure that your code can be executed within a GitHub Action is to use a virtual environment like <a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">venv</a> or <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html">renv</a> with your project (below we’ll provide example actions for each). If you aren’t familiar with using these tools check out the article on using Virtual Environments with Quarto to learn more.</p> <p>Once you’ve decided to execute code within your GitHub Action you can remove the <code>freeze: auto</code> described above from your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration. Note that if you want to use <code>freeze</code> selectively for some documents or directories that is still possible (for a directory, create a <code>_metadata.yml</code> file in the directory and specify your freeze configuration there—this is what Quarto does by default for the <code>posts</code> folder of blog projects).</p> <h6 id="example-jupyter-with-venv-1">Example: Jupyter with venv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs Python, Jupyter, and package dependencies from <code>requirements.txt</code>, then executes code and renders output to Netlify:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install Python and Dependencies uses: actions/setup-python@v7 with: python-version: '3.14' cache: 'pip' - run: pip install jupyter - run: pip install -r requirements.txt - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: netlify NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h6 id="example-knitr-with-renv-1">Example: Knitr with renv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs R and package dependencies from <code>renv.lock</code>, then executes code and renders output to Netlify:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: '4.6.1' - name: Install R Dependencies uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 with: cache-version: 1 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: netlify NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h6 id="additional-options-1">Additional Options</h6> <p>It’s possible to have a Quarto project in a larger GitHub repository, where the Quarto project does not reside at the top-level directory. In this case, add a <code>path</code> input to the invocation of the <code>publish</code> action. For example:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: netlify path: subdirectory-to-use NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <p>By default, <code>quarto publish</code> will re-render your project before publishing it. However, if you store the rendered output in version control, you don’t need the GitHub action to re-render the project. In that case, add the option <code>render: false</code> to the <code>publish</code> action:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: netlify render: false NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}</code></pre> <h5 id="continuous-integration">Continuous Integration</h5> <p>You can publish Quarto content to Netlify using any CI service by scripting the <code>quarto publish</code> command.</p> <p>For example, here is a shell script that publishes to Netlify based on the information in a <code>_publish.yml</code> file in the root of the project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # credentials from [app.netlify.com](https://app.netlify.com/user/applications) export NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN="45fd6ae56c" # publish to the netlify site id provided within _publish.yml quarto publish netlify</code></pre> <p>Here are the contents of <code>_publish.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>- source: project netlify: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app](https://tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app)"</code></pre> <p>Here is another variation that provides the publish target on the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify --id 5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001</code></pre> <p>See the article on Publishing with CI for additional details on the various approaches to rendering and publishing with Continuous Integration.</p> <h3 id="other-services">Other Services</h3> <h4 id="other-services-1">Other Services</h4> <h5 id="overview-113">Overview</h5> <p>There are a wide variety of ways to publish Quarto websites. Other articles cover publishing to Quarto Pub, GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Posit Connect. Below we’ll describe some general guidelines as well as offer some specific advice for Firebase, Site44, and Amazon S3. We’ll mostly defer to the documentation provided by the various services, but will note any Quarto website specific configuration required.</p> <p>The most important thing to understand is that website content is by default written to the <code>_site</code> sub-directory and book content to the <code>_book</code> directory (you can customize either using the <code>output-dir</code> option). Publishing is simply a matter of copying the output directory to a web server or web hosting service.</p> <h6 id="rendering-for-publish">Rendering for Publish</h6> <p>Prior to publishing you should always do a final render of your project:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>This is particularly important to remember because changes you make to shared site configuration (e.g. <code>_quarto.yml</code>) aren’t reflected across your entire site until your render the entire project. To ensure that your output is up to date before publishing you should always do a full <code>quarto render</code>.</p> <h5 id="firebase">Firebase</h5> <p>Google Firebase has a <a href="https://firebase.google.com/docs/hosting/quickstart">web hosting service</a> that enables easy deployment of websites using a set of command line tools.</p> <p>Firebase websites by default deploy content from the <code>public</code> directory of the Firebase project directory. This means that you should set the <code>output-dir</code> to <code>"public"</code> within <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>project: type: website output-dir: public</code></pre> <h5 id="site44">Site44</h5> <p><a href="https://www.site44.com/">Site44</a> is a service that allows you to publish websites from within Dropbox folders. Site44 creates a <code>Dropbox/Apps/site44</code> directory, and any folders within that directory are published as websites.</p> <p>The recommended workflow for deploying Quarto websites to Site44 is to develop your website in a separate project directory, and then, when it’s ready for final publishing, copy the contents of the <code>_site</code> directory to the folder for your website.</p> <h5 id="amazon-s3">Amazon S3</h5> <p>If you are a user of Amazon Web Services you can serve your website directly from Amazon S3. Note however that this option is a bit more technically involved than GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Site44. See the article on <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/WebsiteHosting.html">Hosting a Static Website on Amazon S3</a> for additional details.</p> <h5 id="other-hosts">Other Hosts</h5> <p>Any web server or web host can be used to deploy a Quarto website. Here’s a recent <a href="https://www.cnet.com/web-hosting/">CNET roundup</a> of other web hosts you could consider. You can also deploy a Quarto website on any internal (intranet) web server.</p> <p>You can also render and publish Quarto websites using a Continuous Integration (CI) service. See the articles on Publishing with CI for additional details.</p> <h3 id="posit-connect-1">Posit Connect</h3> <h4 id="posit-connect-2">Posit Connect</h4> <h5 id="overview-114">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://www.rstudio.com/products/connect/">Posit Connect</a> is a publishing platform for secure sharing of data products within an organization. Use Posit Connect when you want to publish content within an organization rather than on the public internet.</p> <p>There are several ways to publish Quarto content to Posit Connect:</p> <ul> <li>Use the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish static content rendered on your local machine.</li> <li>Use the <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/rsconnect-python/">rsconnect-python</a> Python package or <a href="https://quarto-dev.github.io/quarto-r/">quarto</a> R package to publish code for rendering on a Posit Connect server (e.g. for a scheduled report).</li> <li>Use Connect’s support for <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/git-backed/">Git backed content</a> to automatically re-publish content when code is checked in to a Git repository.</li> <li>Use a Continuous Integration (CI) service like <a href="https://www.jenkins.io/">Jenkins</a>, <a href="https://airflow.apache.org/">Airflow</a>, or <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a>, to render and publish to Connect. Each of these options is covered in detail below. If you are just getting started, we strongly recommend using the first approach (<code>quarto publish</code>). Then, as your needs evolve, you can consider other more sophisticated options.</li> </ul> <h5 id="publish-command-4">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command is the easiest way to publish locally rendered content. From the directory where your project is located, execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command for Connect:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish connect</code></pre> <p>If you haven’t previously published to Connect you’ll be prompted to enter your server’s URL:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto publish connect ? Server URL: ›</code></pre> <p>You’ll then need to provide a <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/api-keys/">Connect API Key</a>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto publish connect ? Server URL: › [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/) ? API Key: ›</code></pre> <p>After authenticating, your content will be rendered and published, and then a browser will open to view its admin page on Connect.</p> <p>A record of your previous publishes will be stored in a <code>_publish.yml</code> file within the project or document directory. This file stores the service, id, and URL of the published content. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project connect: - id: "3bb5f59f-524a-45a5-9508-77e29a1e8bf0" url: "[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/content/3bb5f59f-524a-45a5-9508-77e29a1e8bf0/)"</code></pre> <p>Account information is not stored in this file, so it is suitable for checking in to version control and being shared by multiple publishers.</p> <p>You can customize this behavior of <code>quarto publish</code> by providing the following command line options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>--no-prompt</code></p> <p>Do not prompt to confirm publish actions.</p> <p><code>--no-browser</code></p> <p>Do not open a browser after publish.</p> <p><code>--no-render</code></p> <p>Do not re-render prior to publish</p> <p>To publish a document rather than a website or book, provide the path to the document:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish connect document.qmd</code></pre> <h5 id="publishing-with-code">Publishing with Code</h5> <p>In the preceding example, we rendered content locally and then published it to Connect. In some cases, however, you may want to publish your source code to Connect and then have it rendered on the server (for example, to create a scheduled report that is updated with new data automatically).</p> <p>The tools for publishing code differ depending on whether you are using the Knitr (R) or Jupyter (Python) engine, so we’ll cover them separately below. Note that Quarto must be installed on the Connect server before you attempt to publish with code (this is typically done by an administrator, see the <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/resources/install-quarto/">Quarto Installation</a> documentation for additional details).</p> <h6 id="knitr-r">Knitr (R)</h6> <p>The <a href="https://quarto-dev.github.io/quarto-r/">quarto</a> R package includes a set of publishing functions that you can use for publishing Quarto projects with R code to Posit Connect. For example, here we publish a document and a website:</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_publish_doc( "document.qmd", server = "rsc.example.com", account = "njones", render = "server" ) quarto_publish_site( server = "rsc.example.com", account = "njones", render = "server" )</code></pre> <p>The <code>render = "server"</code> argument is what specifies that you want code rather than just content published.</p> <p>Note that once you’ve published for the first time you can update without providing the explicit arguments:</p> <pre><code>quarto_publish_site()</code></pre> <p>See the article on <a href="https://quarto-dev.github.io/quarto-r/articles/publishing.html">Quarto Publishing from R</a> for additional details on using these functions.</p> <h6 id="rstudio-ide-1">RStudio IDE</h6> <p>If you are using the RStudio IDE, there is also support for push-button publishing to Posit Connect. Use the publish button from the source editor or viewer pane to publish a document or a website:</p> <p>See the Connect documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/publishing/">Publishing from the RStudio IDE</a> for additional details.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-python">Jupyter (Python)</h6> <p>The <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/rsconnect-python/">rsconnect-python</a> Python package provides a command line interface (CLI) that you can use to publish Quarto documents and websites that use Jupyter to Posit Connect. To use the CLI:</p> <ul> <li><p>First, install the rsconnect-python package and configure a Posit Connect server for publishing: <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/connecting-cli/">docs.rstudio.com</a></p></li> <li><p>Then, use the <code>rsconnect deploy quarto</code> command from your project directory:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>rsconnect deploy quarto</p></li> </ul> <p>See the complete documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/publishing-cli-quarto/">Publishing Quarto Content</a> for additional details on using the CLI for publishing to Connect.</p> <h5 id="publishing-from-git">Publishing from Git</h5> <p>Content may be deployed to Posit Connect directly from a remote Git repository. Content will automatically fetch from the associated remote Git repository and re-deploy. This allows for integration with Git-centric workflows and continuous deployment automation.</p> <p>In order to deploy Git-backed content to Posit Connect you’ll follow a two step process:</p> <ul> <li>Create and commit a manifest file (this includes information on the R or Python dependencies required to render your content)</li> <li>Link Posit Connect to the Git repository Note that Quarto must be installed on the Connect server before you attempt to publish from Git (this is typically done by an administrator, see the <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/resources/install-quarto/">Quarto Installation</a> documentation for additional details).</li> </ul> <h6 id="creating-a-manifest">Creating a Manifest</h6> <p>Consult the Connect documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/git-backed/">Git Backed Content</a> for complete details on creating manifests and checking them in to your repository. To give you a general idea of how this works, here is some sample code that creates a manifest for Knitr and Jupyter projects:</p> <pre><code># write a manifest for a Knitr project install.packages("rsconnect") # if required rsconnect::writeManifest() Terminal # write a manifest for a Jupyter notebook pip install rsconnect-python # if required rsconnect write-manifest notebook MyNotebook.ipynb</code></pre> <p>See the documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/git-backed/">Git Backed Content</a> for complete details on creating manifests.</p> <h6 id="connecting-a-repository">Connecting a Repository</h6> <p>Connect users must have at least the <code>publisher</code> role in order to create new content from a Git repository.</p> <p>On the Content page, there is a button near the top labeled Publish. Clicking on this button will expand a menu which contains an item called “Import from Git”, which may be clicked to launch a new content wizard.</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to provide your repository URL, branch to publish from, and target directory to publish from (e.g., the one containing your <code>manifest.json</code>).</p> <p>See the documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/git-backed/">Git Backed Content</a> for complete details on connecting Git repositories to Connect.</p> <h5 id="continuous-integration-1">Continuous Integration</h5> <p>You can also deploy Quarto content using a Continuous Integration (CI) service like <a href="https://www.jenkins.io/">Jenkins</a>, <a href="https://airflow.apache.org/">Airflow</a>, or <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a>. In most cases, this will entail scripting the <code>quarto publish</code> command, however in the case of GitHub Actions, you can take advantage of the standard Quarto <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-actions/tree/main/publish">publish action</a>.</p> <p>When publishing to Connect from a CI service you’ll need to consider whether you want to execute your Python or R code directly on the CI server or whether you want to take advantage of previously frozen execution results. We’ll explore this possibility first and then proceed to the specifics of how to publish from CI.</p> <h6 id="freezing-computations-3">Freezing Computations</h6> <p>Depending on how complicated your run-time requirements (packages, database credentials, etc.) are, you might find it more convenient to restrict execution of Python and R code to local contexts that have the required software and credentials.</p> <p>To make sure that R, Python, and Julia code is only executed locally, configure your project to use Quarto’s freeze feature by adding this to your <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml execute: freeze: auto</code></pre> <p>Now, fully re-render your site:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render</code></pre> <p>If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a <code>_freeze</code> directory has been created at the top level of your project. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a <code>.qmd</code> file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in <code>_freeze</code>.</p> <p>If you’d rather have CI publishing execute all Python and R code contained in your project, you’ll need to ensure that the requisite version of these tools (and any required packages) are installed on the CI server. How to do this is outside the scope of this article—to learn more about saving and restoring dependencies, see the article on Virtual Environments.</p> <h6 id="publish-command-5">Publish Command</h6> <p>You can publish Quarto content to Connect using any CI service by scripting the <code>quarto publish</code> command. To do this, you’ll need to make sure that your Connect server address and credentials are available as environment variables on the CI server.</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>CONNECT_SERVER</code></p> <p>Address of Posit Connect server (e.g., <code>https://connect.example.com</code>).</p> <p><code>CONNECT_API_KEY</code></p> <p>Posit Connect <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/api-keys/">API Key</a></p> <p>You will furthermore need to specify the ID of the target content to update. This will most frequently be drawn from the <code>_publish.yml</code> file that is saved into your project directory during publishing. For example:</p> <pre><code>_publish.yml - source: project connect: - id: 4f2ffc46-24b0-4cc7-a854-c5eb671e0dd7 url: '[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/content/4f2ffc46-24b0-4cc7-a854-c5eb671e0dd7/)'</code></pre> <p>Assuming that you have a <code>_publish.yml</code> like the above, you can publish to Connect from CI with the following commands:</p> <pre><code>Terminal export CONNECT_SERVER=[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/) export CONNECT_API_KEY=7C0947A852D8 quarto publish connect</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, if you don’t have a <code>_publish.yml</code> file, you can specify the ID on the command line as follows:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish connect --id 4f2ffc46-24b0-4cc7-a854-c5eb671e0dd7</code></pre> <h6 id="github-actions">GitHub Actions</h6> <p>If your CI service is <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a> then you can take advantage of Quarto’s standard <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-actions/tree/main/publish">publish action</a> to automate deploying to Connect.</p> <h6 id="server-credentials">Server Credentials</h6> <p>Before creating the publish action, you need to ensure that your repository has the credentials required for publishing to Connect. You can do this as follows:</p> <ul> <li>If you don’t already have one, create a Posit Connect <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/api-keys/">API Key</a> from the requisite Connect server and then copy it to the clipboard.</li> <li>Add the Connect API Key to your repository’s action Secrets (accessible within repository Settings). You will see a New repository secret button at the top right:</li> <li>Click the button and add the API Key from step 1 as a secret named <code>CONNECT_API_KEY</code>:</li> </ul> <h6 id="publish-action-2">Publish Action</h6> <p>To setup your publish action, create a <code>.github/workflows/publish.yml</code> file in your repository. If you are Freezing Computations (i.e. not running Python or R code within your action), then the file would look something like this:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: connect CONNECT_SERVER: [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com) CONNECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CONNECT_API_KEY }}</code></pre> <p>Once you’ve pushed your updated repository (including the publish action and <code>_freeze</code> directory) to GitHub, your action will run with this and subsequent commits, automatically rendering and publishing to Connect.</p> <h6 id="executing-code-2">Executing Code</h6> <p>If you prefer, you can also configure GitHub Actions to execute Python or R code as part of rendering. While this might reflexively seem like the best approach, consider the following requirements imposed when you execute code within a CI service like GitHub Actions:</p> <ul> <li>You need to reconstitute all of the dependencies (R, Python, or Julia plus the correct versions of required packages) in the CI environment.</li> <li>If your code requires any special permissions (e.g. database or network access) those permissions also need to be present on the CI server.</li> <li>Your project may contain documents that can no longer be easily executed (e.g. blog posts from several years ago that use older versions of packages). These documents may need to have <code>freeze</code> individually enabled for them to prevent execution on CI.</li> </ul> <h6 id="prerequisites-3">Prerequisites</h6> <p>The best way to ensure that your code can be executed within a GitHub Action is to use a virtual environment like <a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">venv</a> or <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html">renv</a> with your project (below we’ll provide example actions for each). If you aren’t familiar with using these tools check out the article on using Virtual Environments with Quarto to learn more.</p> <p>Once you’ve decided to execute code within your GitHub Action you can remove the <code>freeze: auto</code> described above from your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration. Note that if you want to use <code>freeze</code> selectively for some documents or directories that is still possible (for a directory, create a <code>_metadata.yml</code> file in the directory and specify your freeze configuration there—this is what Quarto does by default for the <code>posts</code> folder of blog projects).</p> <h6 id="example-jupyter-with-venv-2">Example: Jupyter with venv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs Python, Jupyter, and package dependencies from <code>requirements.txt</code>, then executes code and renders output to Connect:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install Python and Dependencies uses: actions/setup-python@v7 with: python-version: '3.14' cache: 'pip' - run: pip install jupyter - run: pip install -r requirements.txt - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: connect CONNECT_SERVER: [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com) CONNECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CONNECT_API_KEY }}</code></pre> <h6 id="example-knitr-with-renv-2">Example: Knitr with renv</h6> <p>Here is a complete example of a GitHub Action that installs R and package dependencies from <code>renv.lock</code>, then executes code and renders output to Connect:</p> <pre><code>.github/workflows/publish.yml on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main name: Quarto Publish jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: '4.6.1' - name: Install R Dependencies uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 with: cache-version: 1 - name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: connect CONNECT_SERVER: [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com) CONNECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CONNECT_API_KEY }}</code></pre> <h6 id="additional-options-2">Additional Options</h6> <p>It’s possible to have a Quarto project in a larger GitHub repository, where the Quarto project does not reside at the top-level directory. In this case, add a <code>path</code> input to the invocation of the <code>publish</code> action. For example:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: connect path: subdirectory-to-use CONNECT_SERVER: [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com) CONNECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CONNECT_API_KEY }}</code></pre> <p>By default, <code>quarto publish</code> will re-render your project before publishing it. However, if you store the rendered output in version control, you don’t need the GitHub action to re-render the project. In that case, add the option <code>render: false</code> to the <code>publish</code> action:</p> <pre><code>- name: Render and Publish uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with: target: connect render: false CONNECT_SERVER: [connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com) CONNECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CONNECT_API_KEY }}</code></pre> <h3 id="posit-connect-cloud-1">Posit Connect Cloud</h3> <h4 id="posit-connect-cloud-2">Posit Connect Cloud</h4> <h5 id="overview-115">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://connect.posit.cloud">Posit Connect Cloud</a> is an online platform from Posit for deploying and sharing data applications and documents. Use Posit Connect Cloud when you want a hosted service for publishing Quarto documents and websites without managing your own infrastructure. Posit Connect Cloud includes a free tier that allows unlimited publishing of static documents.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Looking for self-hosted deployment within your organization? See Posit Connect.</p> <p>There are several ways to publish Quarto content to Posit Connect Cloud:</p> <ul> <li>Use the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish locally rendered static content.</li> <li>Publish source content from a <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/user/publish/github.html">GitHub repository</a>. The source is rendered by Posit Connect Cloud, and redeployed automatically when content is pushed to the repository.</li> <li>Publish source content from an <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/user/publish/ide.html">IDE</a> (Positron, VS Code, or RStudio).</li> <li>Script the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish from a Continuous Integration (CI) service. Each of these options is covered below. If you are just getting started, we recommend using the first approach, <code>quarto publish</code>.</li> </ul> <h5 id="publish-command-6">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command is the easiest way to publish locally rendered content. From the directory where your project is located, execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command for Posit Connect Cloud:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish posit-connect-cloud</code></pre> <p>If you haven’t published to Posit Connect Cloud before, the publish command will prompt you to authenticate.</p> <p>A browser will open to authenticate using your Posit account:</p> <pre><code>Terminal $ quarto publish posit-connect-cloud ? Authorize (Y/n) › ❯ In order to publish to Posit Connect Cloud you need to authorize your account. Please be sure you are logged into the correct Posit Connect Cloud account in your default web browser, then press Enter or 'Y' to authorize.</code></pre> <p>After confirming that you want to publish, your content will be rendered and deployed, and then a browser opened to view your site.</p> <h6 id="publish.yml-2">_publish.yml</h6> <p>The <code>_publish.yml</code> file is used to specify the publishing destination. This file is automatically created (or updated) whenever you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command, and is located within the project or document directory.</p> <p>The service, id, and URL of the published content is specified in <code>_publish.yml</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project posit-connect-cloud: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[connect.posit.cloud](https://connect.posit.cloud/content/5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001)"</code></pre> <p>If you have an existing Posit Connect Cloud site that you want to publish to, you should manually create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that looks like the example above, but with the appropriate <code>id</code> and <code>url</code> values for your site.</p> <p>Account information is not stored in <code>_publish.yml</code>, so it is suitable for checking in to version control and being shared by multiple publishers.</p> <h6 id="options-41">Options</h6> <p>You can customize the behavior of <code>quarto publish</code> by providing the following command line options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>--no-prompt</code></p> <p>Do not prompt to confirm publish actions.</p> <p><code>--no-browser</code></p> <p>Do not open a browser after publish.</p> <p><code>--no-render</code></p> <p>Do not re-render prior to publish</p> <p>To publish a document rather than a website or book, provide the path to the document:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish posit-connect-cloud document.qmd</code></pre> <h6 id="multiple-accounts">Multiple Accounts</h6> <p>If you have multiple Posit accounts, you’ll be prompted to choose which account to publish with. You can manage stored accounts using:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish accounts</code></pre> <h5 id="publish-from-github">Publish from GitHub</h5> <p>Posit Connect Cloud can publish directly from a GitHub repository. When you push changes to the connected branch, Posit Connect Cloud automatically re-renders and redeploys your content. This is ideal for scheduled reports and collaborative projects.</p> <p>See the Posit Connect Cloud documentation on <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/user/publish/github.html">Publishing from GitHub</a> for setup instructions and details.</p> <h5 id="publish-from-your-ide">Publish from your IDE</h5> <p>You can publish source content directly from your editor using:</p> <ul> <li>Posit Publisher — A VS Code / Positron extension for deploying content to Posit Connect Cloud. Pre-installed in Positron; available from the VS Code Marketplace for VS Code.</li> <li>rsconnect — The rsconnect R package can deploy R content programmatically from RStudio or any R session. See the Posit Connect Cloud documentation on <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/user/publish/ide.html">Publishing from an IDE</a> for setup instructions and details.</li> </ul> <h5 id="continuous-integration-2">Continuous Integration</h5> <p>You can publish to Posit Connect Cloud from a CI service by scripting the <code>quarto publish</code> command with environment variables for authentication. These tokens are generated during the interactive <code>quarto publish</code> flow and stored locally — use <code>quarto publish accounts</code> to view stored credentials.</p> <p>Variable</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN</code></p> <p>OAuth access token for authentication (required).</p> <p><code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_REFRESH_TOKEN</code></p> <p>OAuth refresh token (required).</p> <p><code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCOUNT_ID</code></p> <p>Account ID to publish with (required if you have multiple accounts).</p> <pre><code>Terminal export POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN="..." export POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_REFRESH_TOKEN="..." quarto publish posit-connect-cloud --no-prompt --no-browser</code></pre> <p>See the article on Publishing with CI for additional details on non-interactive use of <code>quarto publish</code>.</p> <h3 id="publishing-basics">Publishing Basics</h3> <h4 id="publishing-basics-1">Publishing Basics</h4> <h5 id="overview-116">Overview</h5> <p>There are a wide variety of ways to publish documents, presentations, and websites created using Quarto. Since content rendered with Quarto uses standard formats (HTML, PDFs, MS Word, etc.) it can be published anywhere. Additionally, there is a <code>quarto publish</code> command available for easy publishing to various popular services (GitHub, Netlify, Posit Connect, etc.) as well as various tools to make it easy to publish from a Continuous Integration (CI) system.</p> <h5 id="getting-started-3">Getting Started</h5> <p>To get started, review the documentation for using one of the following publishing services:</p> <p>Destination</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Posit Connect Cloud</p> <p>Hosted publishing platform for sharing Quarto documents and websites. Use Posit Connect Cloud when you want a Posit-hosted service for publishing content without managing infrastructure.</p> <p>GitHub Pages</p> <p>Publish content based on source code managed within a GitHub repository. Use GitHub Pages when the source code for your document or site is hosted on GitHub.</p> <p>Posit Connect</p> <p>Publishing platform for secure sharing of data products within an organization. Use Posit Connect when you want to publish content to your organization-managed Connect server.</p> <p>Quarto Pub</p> <p>Publishing service for Quarto documents, websites, and books. Use Quarto Pub when you want a free, easy to use service for publicly available content.</p> <p>Netlify</p> <p>Professional web publishing platform. Use Netlify when you want support for custom domains, authentication, previewing branches, and other more advanced capabilities.</p> <p>Confluence</p> <p>Publishing platform for supporting team collaboration. Use Confluence to share documents in team Spaces.</p> <p>Hugging Face Spaces</p> <p>Publishing platform specializing in learning models and datasets. Use Hugging Face Spaces when you want to share Quarto documents together with associated machine learning models and/or datasets.</p> <p>Other Services</p> <p>Content rendered with Quarto uses standard formats (HTML, PDFs, MS Word, etc.) that can be published anywhere. Use this if none of the methods above meets your requirements.</p> <p>If you don’t know which to choose, try Posit Connect Cloud which is a free hosted service, or GitHub Pages if your source code is on GitHub. If you are publishing to a destination not listed above, choose Other Services.</p> <p>These articles cover both straightforward direct publishing as well as Continuous Integration (CI) publishing with GitHub Actions. If you want to publish using CI and aren’t using GitHub Actions, the article on Publishing with CI provides additional details and documentation.</p> <h3 id="publishing-with-continuous-integration-ci">Publishing with Continuous Integration (CI)</h3> <h4 id="publishing-with-continuous-integration-ci-1">Publishing with Continuous Integration (CI)</h4> <h5 id="overview-117">Overview</h5> <p>Continuous Integration (CI) refers to the practice of automatically publishing content from code checked in to a version control system. While publishing using CI is a bit more involved to configure, it has several benefits, including:</p> <ul> <li>Content is automatically published whenever source code changes (you don’t need to remember to explicitly render).</li> <li>Rendering on another system ensures that your code is reproducible (but note that this can be double-edged sword if rendering has special requirements—see the discussion below on Rendering for CI).</li> <li>Not checking rendered output into version control makes diffs smaller and reduces merge conflicts. This article covers how to implement CI for Quarto using GitHub Actions (a service run by GitHub), ordinary shell commands (which can be made to work with any CI service), and with Posit Connect.</li> </ul> <h5 id="rendering-for-ci">Rendering for CI</h5> <p>Before you start using a CI server you’ll need to think about where you want executable code (e.g. R, Python, or Julia code) to run and where you want <code>quarto render</code> to run. You might reflexively assume that you’ll always want to run everything on the CI server, however doing so introduces a number of complexities:</p> <ul> <li><p>You need to make sure that the appropriate version of Quarto is available in the CI environment.</p></li> <li><p>You need to reconstitute all of the dependencies (required R, Python, or Julia packages) in the CI environment.</p></li> <li><p>If your code needed any special permissions (e.g. database or network access) those permissions need also be present on the CI server.</p></li> <li><p>Your project may contain documents that can no longer be easily executed (e.g. blog posts from several years ago that use older versions of packages). In light of the above, you can think about rendering as a continuum that extends from running everything (including <code>quarto render</code>) locally all the way up to running everything remotely on CI:</p></li> <li><p>Local Execution and Rendering — Run everything in your local environment and then check output (e.g. the <code>_site</code> directory) into version control. In this scenario the CI server is merely making sure that the checked in content is copied/deployed to the right place every time you commit. You might choose this approach to place minimal requirements on software that needs to be present on the CI server.</p></li> <li><p>Local Execution with CI Rendering — Execute R, Python, or Julia code locally and use Quarto’s ability to freeze computational output to save the results of computations into the <code>_freeze</code> directory. Render the site on the CI server (which will use the computations stored in <code>_freeze</code>). Use this approach when its difficult to arrange fully re-executing code on the CI server.</p></li> <li><p>CI Execution and Rendering — Execute all code and perform rendering on the CI server. While this is the gold standard of automation and reproducibility, it will require you to capture your R, Python, or Julia dependencies (e.g. in an <code>renv.lock</code> file or <code>requirements.txt</code> file) and arrange for them to be installed on the CI server. You will also need to make sure that permissions (e.g. database access) required by your code are available on the CI server. Below we’ll describe how to implement each of these strategies using GitHub Actions, ordinary Shell Commands (which you should be able to adapt to any CI environment), or Posit Connect.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="github-actions-1">GitHub Actions</h5> <p><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a> is a Continuous Integration service from GitHub, and an excellent choice if your source code is already managed it a GitHub repository. Quarto makes available a set of <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-actions">standard</a> GitHub Actions that make it easy to install Quarto and then render and publish content.</p> <p>Learn about using GitHub Actions with various publishing services here:</p> <ul> <li>Quarto Pub</li> <li>GitHub Pages</li> <li>Netlify If you want to use the standard Quarto actions as part of another workflow see the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-actions">GitHub Actions for Quarto</a> repository.</li> </ul> <h5 id="posit-connect-3">Posit Connect</h5> <p>If you are publishing a source code version of your content to Posit Connect it’s possible to configure Connect to retrieve the code from a Git repository and then render and execute on the Connect Server.</p> <p>To learn more about this, see the documentation on <a href="https://docs.rstudio.com/connect/user/git-backed/">Git Backed Content</a> for Posit Connect.</p> <h5 id="posit-connect-cloud-3">Posit Connect Cloud</h5> <p>Posit Connect Cloud can publish directly from a GitHub repository, automatically re-rendering and redeploying your content when you push changes. This is the recommended approach for continuous deployment to Posit Connect Cloud.</p> <p>See the Posit Connect Cloud documentation on <a href="https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/user/publish/github.html">Publishing from GitHub</a> for setup instructions. For other CI environments, you can use <code>quarto publish</code> with environment variables as described in the Shell Commands section below.</p> <h5 id="shell-commands-1">Shell Commands</h5> <p>This section covers using the <code>quarto publish</code> command on a server where no user interaction is possible. This involves the following steps:</p> <ul> <li><p>Rendering your content.</p></li> <li><p>Specifying where to publish (which service/server, publishing target id, etc.).</p></li> <li><p>Providing the appropriate publishing credentials. For example, here is a shell script that publishes to Netlify based on the information in a <code>_publish.yml</code> file in the root of the project:</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p># credentials from <a href="https://app.netlify.com/user/applications">app.netlify.com</a> export NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN=“45fd6ae56c”</p> <p># publish to the netlify site id provided within _publish.yml quarto publish netlify</p></li> </ul> <p>Here are the contents of <code>_publish.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>- source: project netlify: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app](https://tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app)"</code></pre> <p>Here is another variation that provides the publish target on the command line:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify --id 5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001</code></pre> <p>Below we’ll cover the various components of a publishing script as well as provide a few additional complete examples.</p> <h6 id="rendering-for-publish-1">Rendering for Publish</h6> <p>By default when you execute the publish command, your site or document will be automatically re-rendered:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish</code></pre> <p>This is generally recommended, as it ensures that you are publishing based on the very latest version of your source code.</p> <p>If you’d like to render separately (or not render at all) you can specify the <code>--no-render</code> option:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish --no-render</code></pre> <p>By default, the call to <code>quarto publish</code> will execute all R, Python, or Julia code contained in your project. This means that you need to ensure that the requisite version of these tools (and any required packages) are installed on the CI server. How to do this is outside the scope of this article—to learn more about saving and restoring dependencies, see the article on Virtual Environments.</p> <p>If you want to execute code locally then only do markdown rendering on CI, you can use Quarto’s freeze feature. For example, if you add this to your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file:</p> <pre><code>execute: freeze: true</code></pre> <p>Then when you render locally computations will run and their results saved in a <code>_freeze</code> folder at the root of your project. Then, when you run <code>quarto publish</code> or <code>quarto render</code> on the CI server these computations do not need to be re-run (only markdown rendering will occur on the server).</p> <h6 id="publishing-destination">Publishing Destination</h6> <p>There are two ways to specify publishing destinations for the <code>quarto publish</code> command:</p> <ul> <li><p>Via the contents of a <code>_publish.yml</code> file created from a previous publish.</p></li> <li><p>Using command line parameters (e.g. <code>--id</code> and <code>--server</code>). When you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command, a record of your publishing destination is written to a <code>_publish.yml</code> file alongside your source code. For example:</p> <ul> <li>source: project netlify: <ul> <li>id: “5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001” url: “<a href="https://tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app">tubular-unicorn-97bb3c.netlify.app</a>”</li> </ul></li> </ul></li> </ul> <p>You can check the <code>_publish.yml</code> file into source control so it is available when you publish from the CI server. If you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command with no arguments and the above <code>_publish.yml</code> is in the project directory, then the publish will target Netlify with the indicated <code>id</code>:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify</code></pre> <p>You can also specify a publishing destination via explicit command line arguments. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish netlify --id 5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001</code></pre> <p>If you have multiple publishing targets saved within <code>_publish.yml</code> then the <code>--id</code> option can be used to select from among them.</p> <h6 id="publishing-credentials">Publishing Credentials</h6> <p>You can specify publishing credentials either using environment variables or via command line parameters. The following environment variables are recognized for various services:</p> <p>Service</p> <p>Variables</p> <p>Quarto Pub</p> <p><code>QUARTO_PUB_AUTH_TOKEN</code></p> <p>Netlify</p> <p><code>NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN</code></p> <p>Posit Connect</p> <p><code>CONNECT_SERVER</code> and <code>CONNECT_API_KEY</code></p> <p>Confluence</p> <p><code>CONFLUENCE_AUTH_TOKEN</code>, <code>CONFLUENCE_USER_EMAIL</code>, and <code>CONFLUENCE_DOMAIN</code></p> <p>Posit Connect Cloud</p> <p><code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN</code>, <code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_REFRESH_TOKEN</code>, and <code>POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCOUNT_ID</code></p> <p>Set these environment variables within your script before calling <code>quarto publish</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal export NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN="45fd6ae56c" quarto publish netlify</code></pre> <p>Note that you can also specify the publishing target <code>--id</code> as a command line argument. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal export CONNECT_SERVER=[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/) export CONNECT_API_KEY=7C0947A852D8 quarto publish connect --id DDA36416-F950-4647-815C-01A24233E294</code></pre> <h6 id="complete-examples">Complete Examples</h6> <p>Here are a few complete examples that demonstrate various ways to write publishing shell scripts:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # publish (w/o rendering) to quarto pub based on _publish.yml export QUARTO_PUB_AUTH_TOKEN="45fd6ae56c" quarto publish quarto-pub --no-render Terminal # render and publish to netlify based on _publish.yml export NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN="45fd6ae56c" quarto publish netlify Terminal # publish (w/o rendering) to netlify with explicit id export NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN="45fd6ae56c" quarto publish netlify --id DDA36416-F950-4647-815C-01A24233E294 --no-render Terminal # publish (w/o rendering) to connect based on _publish.yml export CONNECT_SERVER=[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/) export CONNECT_API_KEY=7C0947A852D8 quarto publish connect --no-render Terminal # render and publish to connect with explicit id export CONNECT_SERVER=[connect.example.com](https://connect.example.com/) export CONNECT_API_KEY=7C0947A852D8 quarto publish connect --id DDA36416-F950-4647-815C-01A24233E294 Terminal # render and publish to Confluence based on _publish.yml export CONFLUENCE_AUTH_TOKEN=7C0947A852D8 export CONFLUENCE_USER_EMAIL=email@domain.com export CONFLUENCE_DOMAIN=[domain.atlassian.net](https://domain.atlassian.net/) quarto publish confluence --no-browser --no-prompt Terminal # render and publish to Posit Connect Cloud based on _publish.yml export POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN="..." export POSIT_CONNECT_CLOUD_REFRESH_TOKEN="..." quarto publish posit-connect-cloud --no-prompt --no-browser</code></pre> <h3 id="quarto-pub">Quarto Pub</h3> <h4 id="quarto-pub-1">Quarto Pub</h4> <h5 id="overview-118">Overview</h5> <p>Important</p> <p>Quarto Pub is being replaced by Posit Connect Cloud. New projects should use Posit Connect Cloud for publishing. Existing Quarto Pub sites will continue to work, but we recommend migrating to Posit Connect Cloud.</p> <p><a href="https://quartopub.com">Quarto Pub</a> is a free publishing service for static content created with Quarto. Quarto Pub is ideal for blogs, course or project websites, books, presentations, and personal hobby sites.</p> <p>It’s important to note that all documents and sites published to Quarto Pub are publicly visible. You should only publish content you wish to share publicly.</p> <p>There are two ways to publish content to Quarto Pub (both are covered in more detail below):</p> <ul> <li>Use the <code>quarto publish</code> command to publish content rendered on your local machine (this is the recommend approach when you are getting started).</li> <li>If you are using GitHub, you can use a GitHub Action to automatically render your project and publish the resulting content whenever your code changes. Before attempting your first publish, be sure that you have created a free <a href="https://quartopub.com">Quarto Pub</a> account.</li> </ul> <p>Note</p> <p>Quarto Pub sites are publicly visible, can be no larger than 100 MB and have a soft limit of 10 GB of bandwidth per month. If you want to authenticate users, host larger sites, or use a custom domain, consider using a professional web publishing service like Netlify instead.</p> <h5 id="publish-command-7">Publish Command</h5> <p>The <code>quarto publish</code> command is the easiest way to publish locally rendered content. From the directory where your project is located, execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command for Quarto Pub:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish quarto-pub</code></pre> <p>If you haven’t published to Quarto Pub before, the publish command will prompt you to authenticate.</p> <p>After confirming that you want to publish, your content will be rendered and deployed, and then a browser opened to view your site.</p> <h6 id="publish.yml-3">_publish.yml</h6> <p>The <code>_publish.yml</code> file is used to specify the publishing destination. This file is automatically created (or updated) whenever you execute the <code>quarto publish</code> command, and is located within the project or document directory.</p> <p>The service, id, and URL of the published content is specified in <code>_publish.yml</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>- source: project quarto-pub: - id: "5f3abafe-68f9-4c1d-835b-9d668b892001" url: "[njones.quarto.pub](https://njones.quarto.pub/blog)"</code></pre> <p>If you have an existing Quarto Pub site that you want to publish to, you should manually create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that looks like the example above, but with the appropriate <code>id</code> and <code>url</code> values for your site.</p> <p>Account information is not stored in <code>_publish.yml</code>, so it is suitable for checking in to version control and being shared by multiple publishers.</p> <h6 id="options-42">Options</h6> <p>You can customize the behavior of <code>quarto publish</code> by providing the following command line options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p><code>--no-prompt</code></p> <p>Do not prompt to confirm publish actions.</p> <p><code>--no-browser</code></p> <p>Do not open a browser after publish.</p> <p><code>--no-render</code></p> <p>Do not re-render prior to publish</p> <p>To publish a document rather than a website or book, provide the path to the document:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto publish quarto-pub document.qmd</code></pre> <h5 id="managing-sites">Managing Sites</h5> <p>If you want to change the “slug” (or URL path) of a published site or remove the site entirely, you can use the site management interface at <a href="https://quartopub.com">quartopub.com</a>, which will display a list of all of your published sites:</p> <p>Click on a site to navigate to an admin page that enables you to change the slug, make the site the default one for your account, or remove the site entirely:</p> <h5 id="user-default-site">User Default Site</h5> <p>In addition to publishing documents and sites to paths within your Quarto Pub sub-domain (e.g. <code>https://username.quarto.pub/mysite/)</code> you can also designate one of your sites as the default site that users see when they navigate to your main sub-domain (e.g. <code>https://username.quarto.pub</code>). This is an ideal place to publish a blog or personal home page.</p> <p>To promote one of your sites to the default site, go to your admin page at <a href="https://quartopub.com">quartopub.com</a>, navigate to the site you want to promote, check the Default Site option, then Save your modified options:</p> <h5 id="multiple-accounts-1">Multiple Accounts</h5> <p>If you have multiple Quarto Pub accounts it’s important to understand the relationship between the use of accounts in the CLI interface (<code>quarto publish</code>) and the use of accounts in your browser (for authenticating and managing sites).</p> <p>When using <code>quarto publish</code>, there are a couple of scenarios where a web browser is launched:</p> <ul> <li>When you need to authorize the Quarto CLI to access your account.</li> <li>After publishing to open the admin page for your published site. Before publishing with a Quarto Pub account from the CLI you should always be sure to log in to that account within your default web browser. This ensures that when the CLI launches the browser that it binds to the correct Quarto Pub account.</li> </ul> <h5 id="access-tokens">Access Tokens</h5> <p>When you publish to Quarto Pub using <code>quarto publish</code> an access token is used to grant permission for publishing to your account. If no access token is available for a publish operation then the Quarto CLI will automatically launch a browser to authorize one:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto publish quarto-pub ? Authorize (Y/n) › ❯ In order to publish to Quarto Pub you need to authorize your account. Please be sure you are logged into the correct Quarto Pub account in your default web browser, then press Enter or 'Y' to authorize.</code></pre> <p>Authorization will launch your default web browser to confirm that you want to allow publishing from Quarto CLI. An access token will be generated and saved locally by the Quarto CLI. You can list and remove saved accounts using the <code>quarto publish accounts</code> command:</p> <pre><code>$ quarto publish accounts ? Manage Publishing Accounts ❯ ✔ Quarto Pub: jj@rstudio.com ✔ Netlify: jj@rstudio.com ❯ Use the arrow keys and spacebar to specify accounts you would like to remove. Press Enter to confirm the list of accounts you wish to remain available.</code></pre> <p>You can also view (and revoke) access tokens from the admin interface at <a href="https://quartopub.com">quartopub.com</a>:</p> <p>Within this interface you’ll see any token you’ve created from the Quarto CLI. You may revoke this token if you no longer wish it to be active. Click the New Token button to create additional tokens that can be used for publishing non-interactively (e.g. from a CI service):</p> <p>Once you have an access token you can use it with <code>quarto publish</code> by defining the <code>QUARTO_PUB_AUTH_TOKEN</code> environment variable. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # token created at [quartopub.com](https://quartopub.com/profile/) export QUARTO_PUB_AUTH_TOKEN="qpa_k4yWKEmlu5wkvx173Ls" # publish to quarto-pub site specified within _publish.yml quarto publish quarto-pub</code></pre> <p>See the article on Publishing with CI for additional details on non-interactive use of <code>quarto publish</code>.</p> <h5 id="github-action-2">GitHub Action</h5> <p>Using the <code>quarto publish quarto-pub</code> command to publish locally rendered content is the most simple and straightforward way to publish. Another option is to use <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/actions">GitHub Actions</a> to render and publish your site (you might prefer this if you want execution and/or rendering to be automatically triggered from commits).</p> <p>There are a few different ways to approach rendering and publishing content. Below, we’ll provide a how-to guide for publishing with GitHub Actions. For more conceptual background on the various approaches, see the discussion on Rendering for CI.</p> <h6 id="publish-record-1">Publish Record</h6> <p>Prior to attempting to publish with a GitHub Action, you should have completed at least one publish using the Publish Command (described immediately above). This publish will create a <code>_publish.yml</code> file that records the publishing destination to be used by the GitHub Action.
