Exception: with a shift of -N, a level-N heading at the beginning of the document replaces the metadata title.</p> <h5 id="code-36">Code</h5> <p><code>code-annotations</code></p> <p>The style to use when displaying code annotations. Set this value to false to hide code annotations.</p> <h5 id="execution-36">Execution</h5> <p>Execution options should be specified within the <code>execute</code> key. For example:</p> <pre><code>execute: echo: false warning: false</code></pre> <p><code>eval</code></p> <p>Evaluate code cells (if <code>false</code> just echos the code into output).</p> <ul> <li><code>true</code> (default): evaluate code cell</li> <li><code>false</code>: don’t evaluate code cell</li> <li><code>[...]</code>: A list of positive or negative numbers to selectively include or exclude expressions (explicit inclusion/exclusion of expressions is available only when using the knitr engine) <code>echo</code></li> </ul> <p>Include cell source code in rendered output.</p> <ul> <li><code>true</code> (default in most formats): include source code in output</li> <li><code>false</code> (default in presentation formats like <code>beamer</code>, <code>revealjs</code>, and <code>pptx</code>): do not include source code in output</li> <li><code>fenced</code>: in addition to echoing, include the cell delimiter as part of the output.</li> <li><code>[...]</code>: A list of positive or negative line numbers to selectively include or exclude lines (explicit inclusion/excusion of lines is available only when using the knitr engine) <code>output</code></li> </ul> <p>Include the results of executing the code in the output. Possible values:</p> <ul> <li><code>true</code>: Include results.</li> <li><code>false</code>: Do not include results.</li> <li><code>asis</code>: Treat output as raw markdown with no enclosing containers. <code>warning</code></li> </ul> <p>Include warnings in rendered output.</p> <p><code>error</code></p> <p>Include errors in the output (note that this implies that errors executing code will not halt processing of the document).</p> <p><code>include</code></p> <p>Catch all for preventing any output (code or results) from being included in output.</p> <p><code>cache</code></p> <p>Cache results of computations (using the <a href="https://yihui.org/knitr/demo/cache/">knitr cache</a> for R documents, and <a href="https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Jupyter Cache</a> for Jupyter documents).</p> <p>Note that cache invalidation is triggered by changes in chunk source code (or other cache attributes you’ve defined).</p> <ul> <li><code>true</code>: Cache results</li> <li><code>false</code>: Do not cache results</li> <li><code>refresh</code>: Force a refresh of the cache even if has not been otherwise invalidated. <code>freeze</code></li> </ul> <p>Control the re-use of previous computational output when rendering.</p> <ul> <li><code>true</code>: Never recompute previously generated computational output during a global project render</li> <li><code>false</code> (default): Recompute previously generated computational output</li> <li><code>auto</code>: Re-compute previously generated computational output only in case their source file changes</li> </ul> <h5 id="figures-44">Figures</h5> <p><code>fig-width</code></p> <p>Default width for figures generated by Matplotlib or R graphics.</p> <p>Note that with the Jupyter engine, this option has no effect when provided at the cell level; it can only be provided with document or project metadata.</p> <p><code>fig-height</code></p> <p>Default height for figures generated by Matplotlib or R graphics.</p> <p>Note that with the Jupyter engine, this option has no effect when provided at the cell level; it can only be provided with document or project metadata.</p> <p><code>fig-format</code></p> <p>Default format for figures generated by Matplotlib or R graphics (<code>retina</code>, <code>png</code>, <code>jpeg</code>, <code>svg</code>, or <code>pdf</code>)</p> <p><code>fig-dpi</code></p> <p>Default DPI for figures generated by Matplotlib or R graphics.</p> <p>Note that with the Jupyter engine, this option has no effect when provided at the cell level; it can only be provided with document or project metadata.</p> <p><code>fig-asp</code></p> <p>The aspect ratio of the plot, i.e., the ratio of height/width. When <code>fig-asp</code> is specified, the height of a plot (the option <code>fig-height</code>) is calculated from <code>fig-width * fig-asp</code>.</p> <p>The <code>fig-asp</code> option is only available within the knitr engine.</p> <h5 id="tables-48">Tables</h5> <p><code>df-print</code></p> <p>Method used to print tables in Knitr engine documents:</p> <ul> <li><code>default</code>: Use the default S3 method for the data frame.</li> <li><code>kable</code>: Markdown table using the <code>knitr::kable()</code> function.</li> <li><code>tibble</code>: Plain text table using the <code>tibble</code> package.</li> <li><code>paged</code>: HTML table with paging for row and column overflow. The default printing method is <code>kable</code>.</li> </ul> <h5 id="references-41">References</h5> <p><code>bibliography</code></p> <p>Document bibliography (BibTeX or CSL). May be a single file or a list of files</p> <p><code>csl</code></p> <p>Citation Style Language file to use for formatting references.</p> <p><code>citeproc</code></p> <p>Turn on built-in citation processing. To use this feature, you will need to have a document containing citations and a source of bibliographic data: either an external bibliography file or a list of <code>references</code> in the document’s YAML metadata. You can optionally also include a <code>csl</code> citation style file.</p> <p><code>citation-abbreviations</code></p> <p>JSON file containing abbreviations of journals that should be used in formatted bibliographies when <code>form="short"</code> is specified. The format of the file can be illustrated with an example:</p> <pre><code>{ "default": { "container-title": { "Lloyd's Law Reports": "Lloyd's Rep", "Estates Gazette": "EG", "Scots Law Times": "SLT" } } }</code></pre> <h5 id="cross-references-45">Cross-References</h5> <p><code>crossref</code></p> <p>Configuration for cross-reference labels and prefixes. See <a href="https://quarto.org/docs/reference/metadata/crossref.html">Cross-Reference Options</a> for more details.</p> <h5 id="citation-38">Citation</h5> <p><code>citation</code></p> <p>Citation information for the document itself specified as <a href="https://docs.citationstyles.org/en/stable/specification.html">CSL</a> YAML in the document front matter.</p> <p>For more on supported options, see <a href="https://quarto.org/docs/reference/metadata/citation.html">Citation Metadata</a>.</p> <h5 id="language-36">Language</h5> <p><code>lang</code></p> <p>Identifies the main language of the document using IETF language tags (following the <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp47">BCP 47</a> standard), such as <code>en</code> or <code>en-GB</code>. The <a href="https://r12a.github.io/app-subtags/">Language subtag lookup</a> tool can look up or verify these tags.</p> <p>This affects most formats, and controls hyphenation in PDF output when using LaTeX (through <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/babel"><code>babel</code></a> and <a href="https://ctan.org/pkg/polyglossia"><code>polyglossia</code></a>) or ConTeXt.</p> <p><code>language</code></p> <p>YAML file containing custom language translations</p> <p><code>dir</code></p> <p>The base script direction for the document (<code>rtl</code> or <code>ltr</code>).</p> <p>For bidirectional documents, native pandoc <code>span</code>s and <code>div</code>s with the <code>dir</code> attribute can be used to override the base direction in some output formats. This may not always be necessary if the final renderer (e.g. the browser, when generating HTML) supports the [Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm].</p> <p>When using LaTeX for bidirectional documents, only the <code>xelatex</code> engine is fully supported (use <code>--pdf-engine=xelatex</code>).</p> <h5 id="includes-41">Includes</h5> <p><code>include-before-body</code></p> <p>Include contents at the beginning of the document body (e.g. after the <code><body></code> tag in HTML, or the <code>\begin{document}</code> command in LaTeX).</p> <p>A string value or an object with key “file” indicates a filename whose contents are to be included</p> <p>An object with key “text” indicates textual content to be included</p> <p><code>include-after-body</code></p> <p>Include content at the end of the document body immediately after the markdown content. While it will be included before the closing <code></body></code> tag in HTML and the <code>\end{document}</code> command in LaTeX, this option refers to the end of the markdown content.</p> <p>A string value or an object with key “file” indicates a filename whose contents are to be included</p> <p>An object with key “text” indicates textual content to be included</p> <p><code>include-in-header</code></p> <p>Include contents at the end of the header. This can be used, for example, to include special CSS or JavaScript in HTML documents.</p> <p>A string value or an object with key “file” indicates a filename whose contents are to be included</p> <p>An object with key “text” indicates textual content to be included</p> <p><code>metadata-files</code></p> <p>Read metadata from the supplied YAML (or JSON) files. This option can be used with every input format, but string scalars in the YAML file will always be parsed as Markdown. Generally, the input will be handled the same as in YAML metadata blocks. Values in files specified later in the list will be preferred over those specified earlier. Metadata values specified inside the document, or by using <code>-M</code>, overwrite values specified with this option.</p> <h5 id="rendering-47">Rendering</h5> <p><code>from</code></p> <p>Format to read from. Extensions can be individually enabled or disabled by appending +EXTENSION or -EXTENSION to the format name (e.g. markdown+emoji).</p> <p><code>output-file</code></p> <p>Output file to write to</p> <p><code>output-ext</code></p> <p>Extension to use for generated output file</p> <p><code>template</code></p> <p>Use the specified file as a custom template for the generated document.</p> <p><code>template-partials</code></p> <p>Include the specified files as partials accessible to the template for the generated content.</p> <p><code>filters</code></p> <p>Specify executables or Lua scripts to be used as a filter transforming the pandoc AST after the input is parsed and before the output is written.</p> <p><code>shortcodes</code></p> <p>Specify Lua scripts that implement shortcode handlers</p> <p><code>keep-md</code></p> <p>Keep the markdown file generated by executing code</p> <p><code>keep-ipynb</code></p> <p>Keep the notebook file generated from executing code.</p> <p><code>ipynb-filters</code></p> <p>Filters to pre-process ipynb files before rendering to markdown</p> <p><code>ipynb-shell-interactivity</code></p> <p>Specify which nodes should be run interactively (displaying output from expressions)</p> <p><code>plotly-connected</code></p> <p>If true, use the “notebook_connected” plotly renderer, which downloads its dependencies from a CDN and requires an internet connection to view.</p> <p><code>extract-media</code></p> <p>Extract images and other media contained in or linked from the source document to the path DIR, creating it if necessary, and adjust the images references in the document so they point to the extracted files. Media are downloaded, read from the file system, or extracted from a binary container (e.g. docx), as needed. The original file paths are used if they are relative paths not containing … Otherwise filenames are constructed from the SHA1 hash of the contents.</p> <p><code>resource-path</code></p> <p>List of paths to search for images and other resources.</p> <p><code>default-image-extension</code></p> <p>Specify a default extension to use when image paths/URLs have no extension. This allows you to use the same source for formats that require different kinds of images. Currently this option only affects the Markdown and LaTeX readers.</p> <p><code>abbreviations</code></p> <p>Specifies a custom abbreviations file, with abbreviations one to a line. This list is used when reading Markdown input: strings found in this list will be followed by a nonbreaking space, and the period will not produce sentence-ending space in formats like LaTeX. The strings may not contain spaces.</p> <p><code>dpi</code></p> <p>Specify the default dpi (dots per inch) value for conversion from pixels to inch/ centimeters and vice versa. (Technically, the correct term would be ppi: pixels per inch.) The default is <code>96</code>. When images contain information about dpi internally, the encoded value is used instead of the default specified by this option.</p> <p><code>html-table-processing</code></p> <p>If <code>none</code>, do not process tables in HTML input.</p> <h5 id="text-output-32">Text Output</h5> <p><code>wrap</code></p> <p>Determine how text is wrapped in the output (the source code, not the rendered version).</p> <ul> <li><code>auto</code> (default): Pandoc will attempt to wrap lines to the column width specified by <code>columns</code> (default 72).</li> <li><code>none</code>: Pandoc will not wrap lines at all.</li> <li><code>preserve</code>: Pandoc will attempt to preserve the wrapping from the source document. Where there are nonsemantic newlines in the source, there will be nonsemantic newlines in the output as well. <code>columns</code></li> </ul> <p>Specify length of lines in characters. This affects text wrapping in generated source code (see <code>wrap</code>). It also affects calculation of column widths for plain text tables.</p> <p>For <code>typst</code>, number of columns for body text.</p> <p><code>tab-stop</code></p> <p>Specify the number of spaces per tab (default is 4). Note that tabs within normal textual input are always converted to spaces. Tabs within code are also converted, however this can be disabled with <code>preserve-tabs: false</code>.</p> <p><code>preserve-tabs</code></p> <p>Preserve tabs within code instead of converting them to spaces. (By default, pandoc converts tabs to spaces before parsing its input.) Note that this will only affect tabs in literal code spans and code blocks. Tabs in regular text are always treated as spaces.</p> <p><code>eol</code></p> <p>Manually specify line endings:</p> <ul> <li><code>crlf</code>: Use Windows line endings</li> <li><code>lf</code>: Use macOS/Linux/UNIX line endings</li> <li><code>native</code> (default): Use line endings appropriate to the OS on which pandoc is being run).</li> </ul> <h2 id="tools-and-editors">Tools and editors</h2> <h3 id="jupyterlab-1">JupyterLab</h3> <h4 id="jupyterlab-2">JupyterLab</h4> <h5 id="overview-123">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks represented as plain text (.qmd) or as a normal notebook file (.ipynb). One benefit of using .ipynb is that you can use <a href="https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/">JupyterLab</a> as your editor.</p> <p>Here is the “Hello, Quarto” example from the homepage inside JupyterLab:</p> <p>If you look at the source code you’ll note that YAML options were provided both at the top of the document and within the code cell. We’ll describe working with YAML options in more detail below.</p> <h5 id="workflow-7">Workflow</h5> <p>The ideal workflow for authoring Quarto notebooks in JupyterLab is to run the <code>quarto preview</code> command from within a terminal:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview notebook.ipynb</code></pre> <p>The notebook will be rendered and a web browser with a “live preview” opened. Position this browser so that you can see it as you edit and save the notebook:</p> <p>Every time you save within JupyterLab the preview will be automatically updated. You can use <code>quarto preview</code> for both HTML and PDF output.</p> <p>In the screenshot above you’ll note that we ran <code>quarto preview</code> inside a JupyterLab terminal window—this is generally recommended so that you can see progress and error messages when renders occur.</p> <p>Preview uses the default format specified within the document—to use an alternate format pass the <code>--to</code> option to <code>quarto preview</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview notebook.ipynb --to pdf</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring a book or website you can also use <code>quarto preview</code> on the project directory, which will create a live preview for the entire project.</p> <h6 id="running-jupyterlab">Running JupyterLab</h6> <p>To run JupyterLab, invoke the <code>jupyter</code> module from within the shell where you are using Quarto:</p> <p>Platform</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Mac/Linux</p> <pre><code>Terminal python3 -m jupyter lab</code></pre> <p>Windows</p> <pre><code>Terminal py -m jupyter lab</code></pre> <h6 id="render-without-preview">Render without Preview</h6> <p>You can render a notebook (or group of notebooks) without previewing them using the <code>quarto render</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>--to</code> argument to render to a specific format:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --to docx</code></pre> <p>Note that the target file (in this case <code>notebook.ipynb</code>) should always be the very first command line argument.</p> <h6 id="jupyterlab-extension">JupyterLab Extension</h6> <p>The Quarto JuptyerLab extension enables JupyterLab Notebooks which use Quarto markdown to properly display the contents of the markdown cells. For example, when the Quarto JupyterLab extension is installed, your Notebook will show rendered previews of elements like Callouts, Divs, Mermaid charts, as well as other Quarto elements (including the document front matter as a title block).</p> <p>You can read more about installing the extension in the Quarto JupyterLab Extension documentation.</p> <h5 id="yaml-front-matter">YAML Front Matter</h5> <p>The first cell of your notebook should be a Raw cell that contains the document title, author, and any other options you need to specify. Note that you can switch the type of a cell to Raw using the notebook toolbar:</p> <p>In this example we specify that we want code to appear collapsed by default. There are YAML options to control many other aspects of document rendering. See the documentation on Authoring and Output Formats for additional details.</p> <h5 id="markdown-cells">Markdown Cells</h5> <p>Here’s the underlying code for the markdown cell:</p> <p>Note that a Quarto cross-reference (<code>@fig-polar</code>) is included in the markdown. Any valid Pandoc markdown syntax can be included in markdown cells.</p> <h5 id="output-options-2">Output Options</h5> <p>Quarto uses leading comments with a special prefix (<code>#|</code>) to denote cell options. Here we specify the <code>label</code> and <code>fig-cap</code> options so that the plot generated from the cell can be cross-referenced.</p> <p>Note that options must appear at the very beginning of the cell. As with document front-matter, option names/values use YAML syntax.</p> <p>There are many output options available, including options to optionally hide code, warnings, and/or output. See the documentation on Output Options for additional details.</p> <h5 id="cell-execution-2">Cell Execution</h5> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <p>There are many other execution options available (e.g. to control caching, optimizing kernel start-up time, etc.). Learn more about these options in Execution Options.</p> <h5 id="plain-text-editing">Plain Text Editing</h5> <p>It’s also possible to edit Jupyter notebooks in a plain-text markdown format. You might prefer this if there is more narrative than code in your notebook or if you want to use a file format that is more version control friendly.</p> <p>Here is the plain text markdown version of the notebook used in the previous examples:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Matplotlib Demo" author: "Norah Smith" date: "5/22/2021" format: html: code-fold: true jupyter: python3 --- ## Polar Axis For a demonstration of a line plot on a polar axis, see @fig-polar. ```{python} #| label: fig-polar #| fig-cap: "A line plot on a polar axis" import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01) theta = 2 * np.pi * r fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'}) ax.plot(theta, r) ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]) ax.grid(True) plt.show() ```</code></pre> <p>Note that we’ve added the <code>jupyter: python3</code> option to the YAML front matter to indicate which Jupyter kernel to render with. You would render this document with:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render basics-jupyter.qmd</code></pre> <p>Markdown files with embedded code chunks should use the file extension <code>.qmd</code>.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>If you are doing most of your work in .qmd files you should consider using RStudio, which includes full support for editing .qmd files that use Python and Jupyter (including code completion, cell-at-a-time execution, and side-by-side preview). See the article on using RStudio for additional details.</p> <h6 id="converting-notebooks">Converting Notebooks</h6> <p>You can convert between .ipynb and .qmd representations of a notebook using the <code>quarto convert</code> command. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto convert basics-jupyter.ipynb # converts to qmd quarto convert basics-jupyter.qmd # converts to ipynb</code></pre> <p>See <code>quarto convert help</code> for additional details on converting notebooks.</p> <h6 id="jupytext">Jupytext</h6> <p>You can use Jupytext to maintain parallel synchronized versions of <code>.qmd</code> and <code>.ipynb</code> files. Learn more about Jupytext at <a href="https://jupytext.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">jupytext.readthedocs.io</a>.</p> <h3 id="jupyterlab-extension-1">JupyterLab Extension</h3> <h4 id="jupyterlab-extension-2">JupyterLab Extension</h4> <h5 id="overview-124">Overview</h5> <p>The Quarto JuptyerLab extension enables JupyterLab Notebooks which use Quarto markdown to properly display the contents of the markdown cells. For example, when the Quarto JupyterLab extension is installed, your Notebook will show rendered previews of elements like Callouts, Divs, Mermaid charts, as well as other Quarto elements (including the document front matter as a title block).</p> <h5 id="installing-the-extension">Installing the Extension</h5> <p>Installation depends on which version of JupyterLab you have:</p> <ul> <li><p>JupyterLab 4</p></li> <li><p>JupyterLab 3 You can install the Quarto JupyterLab extension one of two ways:</p></li> <li><p>In the JupyterLab UI: Search for ‘Quarto’ in the Extension Manager and install the <code>jupyterlab-quarto</code> extension. You’ll be prompted to refresh the page when complete.</p></li> <li><p>Using <code>pip</code>:</p></li> <li><p>Platform</p></li> <li><p>Commands</p></li> <li><p>Mac/Linux</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>python3 -m pip install jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>Windows</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>py -m pip install jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> </ul> <p>You can install the Quarto JupyterLab extension one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>Using <code>pip</code>, you can install the <code>jupyterlab-quarto</code> by executing:</p></li> <li><p>Platform</p></li> <li><p>Commands</p></li> <li><p>Mac/Linux</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>python3 -m pip install jupyterlab-quarto==0.1.45</p></li> <li><p>Windows</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>py -m pip install jupyterlab-quarto==0.1.45</p></li> <li><p>This is the preferred way to install the JupyterLab Quarto extension as this takes advantage of traditional python packaging and doesn’t require a rebuild of JupyterLab to complete the installation.</p></li> <li><p>In the JupyterLab UI, you can install the Quarto extension directly using the Extension Manager by searching for ‘Quarto’ and installing the <code>@quarto/jupyterlab-quarto</code> extension. To complete the installation you need to rebuild JupyterLab (you should see a prompt to complete this once you’ve installed the Quarto extension).</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="using-the-extension">Using the Extension</h5> <p>The Quarto extension, once installed, will automatically render the contents of markdown cells within your notebook. Cells without Quarto specific markdown will render normally, while cells containing Quarto specific markdown will show a preview of the content in a more usable form.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The Quarto contents shown in your Notebooks will not match the rendered output precisely. For example, callouts shown in the Notebook don’t change their display based upon callout options you specify in your markdown.</p> <h5 id="disabling-the-extension">Disabling the Extension</h5> <ul> <li><p>If you installed the Quarto JupyterLab extension using <code>pip</code>, you can use the following commands to disable and enable the extension.</p></li> <li><p>To disable extension, use the following command:</p></li> <li><p>Platform</p></li> <li><p>Commands</p></li> <li><p>Mac/Linux</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>python3 -m jupyter labextension disable jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>Windows</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>py -m jupyter labextension disable jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>To enable the extension, use the following command:</p></li> <li><p>Platform</p></li> <li><p>Commands</p></li> <li><p>Mac/Linux</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>python3 -m jupyter labextension enable jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>Windows</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>py -m jupyter labextension enable jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>If you installed the Quarto JupyterLab extension using the JupyterLab Notebook Extension Manager, you can use the UI directly to disable and enable the extension.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="uninstalling-the-extension">Uninstalling the Extension</h5> <ul> <li><p>If you installed the extension using <code>pip</code>, you can uninstall the Quarto extension using <code>pip</code>, like so:</p></li> <li><p>Platform</p></li> <li><p>Commands</p></li> <li><p>Mac/Linux</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>python3 -m pip uninstall jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>Windows</p> <p>Terminal</p> <p>py -m pip uninstall jupyterlab-quarto</p></li> <li><p>If you installed the extension using the JupyterLab Notebook Extension Manager, use the Extension Manager to uninstall the extension. To complete the uninstallation you need to rebuild JupyterLab (you should see a prompt to complete this once you’ve uninstalled the Quarto extension).</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="reporting-issues">Reporting Issues</h5> <p>Please report issues with the Quarto JuptyerLab extension <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto/issues/new">here</a>.</p> <h3 id="neovim">Neovim</h3> <h4 id="neovim-1">Neovim</h4> <h5 id="overview-125">Overview</h5> <p>The Quarto Neovim plugin aims to not reinvent the wheel. Existing plugins in the Neovim ecosystem are leveraged to provide the full experience. Some of the features provided by <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-nvim">quarto-nvim</a> and enhanced by plugins found in the <a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/quarto-nvim-kickstarter">kickstarter configuration</a> are:</p> <ul> <li>Preview for Quarto documents.</li> <li>Syntax highlighting for markdown and embedded languages</li> <li>Completion for embedded languages (e.g. Python, R, Julia, etc.)</li> <li>Commands and key-bindings for running cells and selected lines.</li> <li>Completion for bibliography references, file paths, LaTeX math symbols, emoji.</li> <li>Optional spellchecking and completion.</li> <li>Code snippets.</li> <li>Export of code chunks into standalone scripts. More <a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/quarto-nvim-kickstarter#screenshots">screenshots</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="installation-7">Installation</h6> <p>Installation instructions for the quarto plugin and the kickstarter configuration can be found in the respective readme files of the repository:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-nvim">quarto-nvim</a></li> <li><a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/quarto-nvim-kickstarter">quarto-nvim-kickstarter</a></li> </ul> <h5 id="render-and-preview-3">Render and Preview</h5> <p>To render and preview, execute the QuartoPreview command by pressing <code>:</code> to enter command mode and typing the command (there is autocompletion if you press the tab key). In the kickstarter configuration, there are more shortcuts starting with space q (spacebar followed by q, in normal mode).</p> <p>After running the <code>QuartoPreview</code> command in Neovim, the preview will automatically update each time the buffer is saved.</p> <h5 id="running-code-cells">Running Code Cells</h5> <p>You don’t need to fully render documents in order to iterate on code cells. With the provided configuration we can open a terminal of our choosing using the leader key (<code><space></code>) followed by<code>c</code> (for code) and then <code>p</code> (for python) or <code>i</code> (for ipython).</p> <p>If you wait a little in between the key presses a small window pops up at the bottom of your screen to tell you about existing keybindings:</p> <p>We can navigate between the code and the terminal using <code>ctrl</code> plus vim direction keys and enter commands into the python REPL by going into insert mode in this terminal buffer.</p> <p>To send code to the python REPL from quarto we navigate to one of our code blocks and press <code><space><cr></code> (space bar followed by Enter). The plugin responsible for sending code to various places, <a href="https://github.com/jpalardy/vim-slime">vim-slime</a> will prompt us with the question which terminal to send the code to, pre filled with the latest terminal we created.</p> <p>If you want to use ctrl+Enter to send code just like in RStudio, you are going to have to tell your terminal emulator to send the correct key codes. For example, in the <a href="https://github.com/kovidgoyal/kitty">kitty</a> terminal the configuration looks as follows:</p> <pre><code>map ctrl+shift+enter no_op map shift+enter send_text all \x1b[13;2u map ctrl+enter send_text all \x1b[13;5u</code></pre> <p>This is what the kickstarter configuration has been tested with.</p> <p>Here are all of the commands and keyboard shortcuts available for executing cells:</p> <p>Quarto Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Create new terminal</p> <p>space c x</p> <p>where x is the starting letter of python, r, ipython, julia or bash</p> <p>Choose terminal</p> <p>space c c</p> <p>Show terminal id</p> <p>space c s</p> <p>Run Current Cell</p> <p>space Enter</p> <p>Run Current Cell</p> <p>ctrl Enter (insert or normal mode)1</p> <p>Run Selected Line(s)</p> <p>Enter (visual mode)</p> <p>Note that you can quickly insert a new code cell using the Alt+I and Alt+Shift+I keyboard shortcuts, the first being an R and the second being a python code chunk. Feel free to change this from the kickstarter configuration depending on your most-used language.</p> <h5 id="contextual-assistance">Contextual Assistance</h5> <p>In a code chunk you get autocompletion for the respective language. Use Tab and Shift+Tab to iterate through the suggestions.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The otter in the completion list means that the completion plugin <a href="https://github.com/hrsh7th/nvim-cmp">cmp</a> got its completion suggestions from the <a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/otter.nvim">otter.nvim</a> plugin, which keeps track of the code in your Quarto document behind the scenes by writing only the code parts to another (an otter) document.</p> <h5 id="code-snippets">Code Snippets</h5> <p>Code snippets are templates that make it easier to enter repeating code patterns (e.g. code blocks, callouts, divs, etc.). You will find them in the autocompletion list and can trigger them with enter. Sometimes they contain multiple places within the snippet where the cursor can jump to. Use ctrl+n to jump to the next site.</p> <p>For example, we might want to create a two column layout, so we type <code>col2</code> and accept the suggestion with Enter to get</p> <pre><code>::: {layout-ncol=2} :::</code></pre> <p>If you find other helpful snippets, feel free to add a pull request to extend the ones included in the kickstarter configuration <a href="https://github.com/jmbuhr/quarto-nvim-kickstarter/blob/main/snips/snippets/markdown.json">snippet list</a>.</p> <h5 id="document-navigation">Document Navigation</h5> <p>Vim is famously good at letting you navigate documents quickly. Here, we only have a look at some additional features provided by quarto-nvim. For the full range of options, refer to the documentation of vim/neovim and of the plugins included in the kickstarter configuration.</p> <ul> <li>Press space l o to toggle a section overview</li> <li>Navigate to the next code chunk with [c or the previous one with ]c</li> <li>Delete/Change/Yank the code of a chunk with dio/cio/yio</li> <li>Delete/Change/Yank a whole code chunk with its delimiters with dao/cao/yao Take a look at the files of the kickstarter configuration for more inspiration.</li> </ul> <h5 id="extending-quarto-lua-development-in-neovim">Extending Quarto: Lua Development in Neovim</h5> <p>Since Lua is already the language used to configure Neovim and the kickstarter configuration installs the Lua Language Server, code completion and diagnostics will be enabled for Quarto extension development.</p> <h5 id="footnotes-21">Footnotes</h5> <ul> <li>if your terminal emulator supports this, see Running Cells↩︎</li> </ul> <h3 id="positron-4">Positron</h3> <h4 id="positron-5">Positron</h4> <h5 id="overview-126">Overview</h5> <p><a href="https://positron.posit.co">Positron</a> bundles both the Quarto CLI and the VS Code Quarto extension so it comes ready to work with Quarto out-of-the-box.</p> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Quarto VS Code Extension</a> provides the support for Quarto in Positron, including:</p> <ul> <li>Integrated render and preview for Quarto documents.</li> <li>Syntax highlighting for markdown and embedded languages</li> <li>Completion and diagnostics for YAML options</li> <li>Completion for embedded languages (e.g. Python, R, Julia, etc.)</li> <li>Commands and key-bindings for running cells and selected lines.</li> <li>Live preview for LaTeX math as well as Mermaid and Graphviz diagrams The Quarto extension integrates directly with Positron’s native R and Python features. For example, here the Quarto extension runs a Python cell in the active Python Console and shows a preview of an included image.</li> </ul> <p>The Quarto extension also works well with other extensions bundled with Positron, like Jupyter extension, and those you might install separately, like the Julia extension.</p> <h5 id="positron-editors">Positron Editors</h5> <p>Depending on your preference and the task at hand, you can author documents for rendering by Quarto using three different editors within Positron:</p> <ul> <li>The source code editor for editing <code>.qmd</code> documents as text.</li> <li>The Visual Editor for WYSIWYG editing of <code>.qmd</code> documents.</li> <li>The Notebook Editor for editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks. We’ll cover the source code editor below, however you might also want to consult the documentation for the Visual Editor or Notebook Editor after you’ve become familiar with the basics.</li> </ul> <h5 id="render-and-preview-4">Render and Preview</h5> <p>The Quarto VS Code extension includes commands and keyboard shortcuts for rendering Quarto documents (both standalone and within websites or books). After rendering, <code>quarto preview</code> is used behind the scenes to provide a preview in the Viewer Pane within Positron alongside your document:</p> <p>To render and preview, execute the Quarto: Preview command. You can alternatively use the Ctrl+Shift+K keyboard shortcut, or the Preview button () at the top right of the editor:</p> <p>Note that on the Mac you should use <code>Cmd</code> rather than <code>Ctrl</code> as the prefix for all Quarto keyboard shortcuts.</p> <h6 id="other-formats-1">Other Formats</h6> <p>The Quarto: Preview command renders the default format of the currently active document. If you want to preview a different format, use the Quarto: Preview Format command:</p> <p>When you execute Preview Format, you’ll see a quick pick list of formats to choose from (any formats declared in the document as well as some standard formats like PDF and MS Word):</p> <p>After previewing a different format, the Quarto: Preview command and Ctrl+Shift+K keyboard shortcut will be automatically rebound to the newly selected format for the duration of the current preview. To switch back to previewing the original format, use Quarto: Preview Format command again.</p> <p>Embedded preview is currently supported for HTML and PDF based formats (including <code>revealjs</code> and <code>beamer</code> slideshows). However, for Word and other formats you need to use an appropriate external program to preview the output.</p> <h6 id="render-command">Render Command</h6> <p>The Quarto: Preview command is what you will most commonly use while authoring documents. If you have a single format (e.g. HTML or PDF) then previewing also renders your document so it’s ready for distribution once you are happy with the output. However, if you have multiple formats will need to explicitly render them (as preview only renders a single format at a time). You can do this with the Quarto: Render Document command:</p> <p>If you have multiple declared formats you can render all of them. You can also selectively render any of the declared formats or other standard formats like PDF and MS Word.</p> <h5 id="render-on-save">Render on Save</h5> <p>By default Quarto does not automatically render <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> files when you save them. This is because rendering might be very time consuming (e.g. it could include long running computations) and it’s good to have the option to save periodically without doing a full render.</p> <p>However, you can configure the Quarto extension to automatically render whenever you save. You can do this either within Positron settings or within the YAML options for your project or document. To configure the Positron setting, search for <code>quarto.render</code> in settings and you’ll find the Render on Save option:</p> <p>You might also want to control this behavior on a per-document or per-project basis. If you include the <code>editor: render-on-save</code> option in your document or project YAML it will supersede whatever your Positron setting is. For example:</p> <pre><code>editor: render-on-save: true</code></pre> <p>You can also enable this setting using the checkbox in the Editor toolbar:</p> <h5 id="external-preview">External Preview</h5> <p>If you prefer to use an external browser for preview (or have no preview triggered at all by rendering) you can use the Preview Type option to specify an alternate behavior:</p> <h5 id="code-cells-5">Code Cells</h5> <p>There are a variety of tools that make it easier to edit and execute code cells. Editing tools include syntax highlighting, code folding, code completion, and signature tips:</p> <p>For Python, R, and Julia cells, commands are available to execute the current cell, previous cells, or the currently selected line(s).</p> <p>Here are all of the commands and keyboard shortcuts available for executing cells:</p> <p>Quarto Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Run Current Cell</p> <p>⇧⌘ Enter</p> <p>Run Selected Line(s)</p> <p>⌘ Enter</p> <p>Run Next Cell</p> <p>⌥⌘ N</p> <p>Run Previous Cell</p> <p>⌥⌘ P</p> <p>Run All Cells</p> <p>⌥⌘ R</p> <p>Run Cells Above</p> <p>⇧⌥⌘ P</p> <p>Run Cells Below</p> <p>⇧⌥⌘ N</p> <p>You can quickly insert a new code cell using the Ctrl+Shift+I keyboard shortcut.</p> <p>Positron includes enhanced features for R and Python code cells (e.g. completion, code execution). To get enhanced features for Julia, install the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=julialang.language-julia">Julia Extension</a>.</p> <h6 id="execution-directory">Execution Directory</h6> <p>The execution directory for code cells in Positron depends on the language of the code cell:</p> <ul> <li>R and Python cells will be executed in the appropriate Console in Positron. The default execution directory for the Console is folder that was opened as the workspace.</li> <li>Julia cells require the Julia Extension which runs code within the working directory of the Julia session running in the Julia REPL terminal. You can change this directory manually using <code>cd()</code>.</li> </ul> <h5 id="contextual-assistance-1">Contextual Assistance</h5> <p>Positron provides code assistance for Python and R code cells in Quarto documents. This includes:</p> <ul> <li>Code completion for functions and arguments</li> <li>Help tooltips as you write, or hover over, functions</li> <li>Opening help in a dedicated Help pane when you hit F1F1 while the cursor is in a function. For example, below the help for the <code>np.arange</code> function is shown in the Help pane.</li> </ul> <p>For additional contextual assistance, execute the Quarto: Show Assist Panel command to show a panel in the sidebar that shows contextual assistance depending on the current cursor location:</p> <ul> <li>A realtime preview of equations is shown when editing LaTeX math</li> <li>Thumbnail previews are shown when your cursor is located on a markdown image. For example, below an image preview is shown automatically when the cursor is located in the image path in the markdown:</li> </ul> <h5 id="live-preview-2">Live Preview</h5> <p>While editing LaTeX math or Mermaid and Graphviz diagrams, click the Preview button above the code (or use the Ctrl+Shift+L keyboard shortcut) to open a live preview which will update automatically as you edit.</p> <p>Here we see a preview of the currently edited LaTeX equation displayed in the Quarto assist panel:</p> <p>Here we see a Graphviz diagram preview automatically updated as we edit:</p> <h5 id="yaml-intelligence">YAML Intelligence</h5> <p>YAML code completion is available for project files, YAML front matter, and executable cell options:</p> <p>If you have incorrect YAML it will also be highlighted when documents are saved:</p> <h5 id="code-snippets-1">Code Snippets</h5> <p>Code snippets are templates that make it easier to enter repeating code patterns (e.g. code blocks, callouts, divs, etc.). Execute the Insert Snippet command within a Quarto document to insert a markdown snippet:</p> <h6 id="intellisense">IntelliSense</h6> <p>Positron uses IntelliSense to suggest snippets or possible values for a specific function while typing. This is turned off by default for snippets, but not for values. To enable snippet suggestions in IntelliSense while typing or when selecting a text snippet and pressing <code>ctrl+space</code>, the setting <code>editor.snippetSuggestions</code> needs to be set to a value other than <code>none</code> (for example to <code>inline</code>).</p> <ul> <li>Press <code>F1</code> and search for <code>Preferences: Open Settings (UI)</code> or <code>File</code> > <code>Preferences</code> > <code>Settings</code></li> <li>Search for following term <code>@lang:quarto editor.snippetSuggestions</code>. <code>Editor: Snippet Suggestions</code> should show up.</li> <li>Change value to a not-<code>none</code> value.</li> </ul> <h5 id="document-navigation-1">Document Navigation</h5> <p>If you have a large document use the outline view for quick navigation between sections:</p> <p>You can also use the Go to Symbol in Editor command or keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+O for type-ahead navigation of the current document’s outline.</p> <p>Use the Go to File command Ctrl+P to navigate to other files and the Go to Symbol in Workspace command Ctrl+T for type-ahead navigation to all headings in the workspace:</p> <h5 id="learning-more-20">Learning More</h5> <p>Besides the traditional source editor described above, you can also use one of the following other editors depending on your preferences and task at hand:</p> <ul> <li>The Visual Editor for WYSIWYG editing of <code>.qmd</code> documents.</li> <li>The Notebook Editor for editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks.</li> </ul> <h3 id="positron-notebook-editor">Positron Notebook Editor</h3> <h4 id="positron-notebook-editor-1">Positron Notebook Editor</h4> <p>In addition to editing Quarto documents as plain-text <code>.qmd</code> files, you can also use the Positron Notebook Editor to author <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks that are rendered with Quarto. In this article we’ll review the basics of editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks for use with Quarto.</p> <h5 id="render-and-preview-5">Render and Preview</h5> <p>After you’ve done an initial Quarto: Preview, the preview will automatically update every time you save the notebook.</p> <h5 id="yaml-front-matter-1">YAML Front Matter</h5> <p>The first cell of your notebook should be a Raw cell that contains the document title, author, and any other options you need to specify. Note that you can switch the type of a cell to Raw using the cell type menu at the bottom right of the cell:</p> <p>In this example we specify that we want code to appear collapsed by default. There are YAML options to control many other aspects of document rendering. See the documentation on Authoring and Output Formats for additional details.</p> <h5 id="markdown-cells-1">Markdown Cells</h5> <p>Here’s the underlying code for the markdown cell:</p> <p>Note that a Quarto cross-reference (<code>@fig-polar</code>) is included in the markdown. Any valid Pandoc markdown syntax can be included in markdown cells.</p> <h5 id="output-options-3">Output Options</h5> <p>Quarto uses leading comments with a special prefix (<code>#|</code>) to denote cell options. Here we specify the <code>label</code> and <code>fig-cap</code> options so that the plot generated from the cell can be cross-referenced.</p> <p>Note that options must appear at the very beginning of the cell. As with document front-matter, option names/values use YAML syntax.</p> <p>There are many output options available, including options to optionally hide code, warnings, and/or output. See the documentation on Output Options for additional details.</p> <h5 id="cell-execution-3">Cell Execution</h5> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <p>There are many other execution options available (e.g. to control caching, optimizing kernel start-up time, etc.). Learn more about these options in Execution Options.</p> <h5 id="converting-notebooks-1">Converting Notebooks</h5> <p>You can convert between .ipynb and .qmd representations of a notebook using the <code>quarto convert</code> command. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto convert basics-jupyter.ipynb quarto convert basics-jupyter.qmd</code></pre> <p>See <code>quarto convert help</code> for additional details on converting notebooks.</p> <h3 id="rstudio-ide-2">RStudio IDE</h3> <h4 id="rstudio-ide-3">RStudio IDE</h4> <h5 id="overview-127">Overview</h5> <p>RStudio v2022.07 and later includes support for editing and preview of Quarto documents (the documentation below assumes you are using this build or a later version).</p> <p>If you are using Quarto within RStudio it is strongly recommended that you use the <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">latest release</a> of RStudio.</p> <p>You can download RStudio from <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">posit.co</a>.</p> <h6 id="creating-documents-1">Creating Documents</h6> <p>Use the File : New File : Quarto Document… command to create new Quarto documents:</p> <h6 id="render-and-preview-6">Render and Preview</h6> <p>Use the Render button to preview documents as you edit them:</p> <p>If you prefer to automatically render whenever you save you can check the Render on Save option on the editor toolbar.</p> <p>The preview will appear alongside the editor:</p> <p>The preview will update whenever you re-render the document. Side-by-side preview works for both HTML and PDF output.</p> <h6 id="projects-11">Projects</h6> <p>If you want to create a new project for a Quarto document or set of documents, use the File : New Project… command, specify New Directory, then choose Quarto Project:</p> <p>You can use this UI to create both vanilla projects as well as websites and books. Options are also provided for creating a <a href="https://git-scm.com/">git</a> repository and initializing an <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/renv/">renv</a> environment for the project.</p> <h5 id="visual-editor-1">Visual Editor</h5> <p>RStudio IDE includes a visual editor for Quarto markdown, including support for tables, citations, cross-references, footnotes, divs/spans, definition lists, attributes, raw HTML/TeX, and more:</p> <p>To learn more, see the documentation on Using the Visual Editor with RStudio.</p> <h5 id="knitr-engine-1">Knitr Engine</h5> <p>Quarto is designed to be highly compatible with existing <a href="https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/">R Markdown</a> documents. You should generally be able to use Quarto to render an existing Rmd document without changes.</p> <p>One important difference between R Markdown documents and Quarto documents is that in Quarto chunk options are typically included in special comments at the top of code chunks rather than within the line that begins the chunk. For example:</p> <pre><code>```{r} #| echo: false #| fig-cap: "Air Quality" library(ggplot2) ggplot(airquality, aes(Temp, Ozone)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) ```</code></pre> <p>Quarto uses this approach to both better accommodate longer options like <code>fig-cap</code>, <code>fig-subcap</code>, and <code>fig-alt</code> as well as to make it straightforward to edit chunk options within more structured editors that don’t have an easy way to edit chunk metadata (e.g. most traditional notebook UIs).</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Note that if you prefer it is still possible to include chunk options on the first line (e.g. ```<code>{r, echo = FALSE}</code>). That said, we recommend using the comment-based syntax to make documents more portable and consistent across execution engines.</p> <p>Chunk options included this way use YAML syntax rather than R syntax for consistency with options provided in YAML front matter. You can still however use R code for option values by prefacing them with <code>!expr</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste("Air", "Quality")'</code></pre> <p>Caution</p> <p>the <code>!expr</code> syntax is an example of a YAML “tag” literal, and it can be unintuitive. <code>!expr</code> needs to be followed by a single YAML “flow scalar”: see the <a href="https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#73-flow-scalar-styles">YAML spec</a> for details on how double-quoted, single-quoted, and unquoted strings work.</p> <h5 id="jupyter-engine">Jupyter Engine</h5> <p>You can also work with Quarto markdown documents that target the Jupyter engine within RStudio. These files will typically include a <code>jupyter</code> option in the YAML front matter indicating which kernel to use. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Matplotlib Demo" author: "Norah Smith" jupyter: python3 ---</code></pre> <p>If you want to work within a virtual environment (<a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment">venv</a>), use the File : New Project… command, specify the Jupyter engine with a venv, and specify which packages you’d like to seed the venv with:</p> <p>RStudio will automatically activate this virtual environment whenever you open the project. You can install additional Python packages into the environment using the RStudio Terminal tab. For example:</p> <h5 id="yaml-intelligence-1">YAML Intelligence</h5> <p>YAML code completion is available for project files, YAML front matter, and executable cell options:</p> <p>If you have incorrect YAML it will also be highlighted when documents are saved:</p> <h5 id="r-package">R Package</h5> <p>If you are not using RStudio and/or you prefer to render from the R console, you can do so using the quarto R package. To install the R package:</p> <pre><code>install.packages("quarto")</code></pre> <p>Then, to render a document:</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_render("document.qmd")</code></pre> <p>To render a website (ie; all qmd in a directory organized as a website):</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_render()</code></pre> <p>To live preview (automatically render & refresh the browser on save) for a document you are working on, use the <code>quarto_preview()</code> function:</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_preview("document.qmd")</code></pre> <p>If you are working on a website or book project, you can also use <code>quarto_preview()</code> on a project directory:</p> <pre><code>library(quarto) quarto_preview()</code></pre> <h3 id="text-editors">Text Editors</h3> <h4 id="text-editors-1">Text Editors</h4> <h5 id="overview-128">Overview</h5> <p>If you are editing plain markdown documents (with no embedded computations) you may want to use your favorite text editor (Vim, Emacs, Sublime, etc.) to author Quarto documents. This articles provides some guidance on the optimal workflow when using text editors with Quarto.</p> <p>Note that if you are using either the <a href="https://jupyter.org/">Jupyter</a> or <a href="https://yihui.org/knitr/">Knitr</a> computational engine you will likely be better off using JupyterLab or VS Code (for .ipynb notebooks) or Positron or RStudio (for .qmd documents) as these environments provide code-completion, incremental cell execution, and other useful tools for working with executable code.</p> <h5 id="workflow-8">Workflow</h5> <p>The ideal workflow for authoring Quarto markdown documents is to run the <code>quarto preview</code> command from within a terminal:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview document.qmd</code></pre> <p>The document will be rendered and a web browser with a “live preview” opened. Position this browser so that you can see it as you edit and save the document:</p> <p>Every time you save the preview will be automatically updated. You can use <code>quarto preview</code> for both HTML and PDF output.</p> <p>Preview uses the default format specified within the document—to use an alternate format pass the <code>--to</code> option to <code>quarto preview</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview notebook.qmd --to pdf</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are authoring a book or website you can also use <code>quarto preview</code> on the project directory, which will create a live preview for the entire project.</p> <h6 id="render-without-preview-1">Render without Preview</h6> <p>You can render a document (or group of documents) without previewing them using the <code>quarto render</code> command:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd</code></pre> <p>Use the <code>--to</code> argument to render to a specific format:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render document.qmd --to docx</code></pre> <h6 id="file-extension">File Extension</h6> <p>Most text editors have a syntax highlighting mode that applies to markdown files (typically with the <code>.md</code> extension). You will likely want to configure your editor to also recognize the <code>.qmd</code> extension as having markdown content.</p> <h3 id="visual-editing-in-positron">Visual Editing in Positron</h3> <h4 id="visual-editing-in-positron-1">Visual Editing in Positron</h4> <h5 id="overview-129">Overview</h5> <p>The <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Quarto VS Code Extension</a> includes a visual markdown editor that supports all of Quarto’s markdown syntax including tables, citations, cross-references, footnotes, divs/spans, definition lists, attributes, raw HTML/TeX, and more:</p> <p>You can switch between visual and source mode at any time and can even edit documents concurrently in both modes. To switch between visual and source mode:</p> <ul> <li>Use the ⇧⌘ F4 keyboard shortcut.</li> <li>Use the context menu from anywhere in a document:</li> <li>Use the Edit in Visual Mode and Edit in Source Mode commands:</li> <li>Use the editor menu: You can also right click a <code>.qmd</code> document in the file explorer and select the Open With… command, which will prompt you for the editor to open the file with:</li> </ul> <p>Note that this menu also provides an option to configure the default editor for <code>.qmd</code> files: use this if you want to primarily edit in visual mode and occasionally switch to source mode.</p> <h5 id="keyboard-shortcuts-1">Keyboard Shortcuts</h5> <p>Visual mode supports both traditional keyboard shortcuts (e.g. ⌘ B for bold) as well as markdown shortcuts (using markdown syntax directly). For example, enclose <code>**bold**</code> text in asterisks or type <code>##</code> and press space to create a second level heading.</p> <p>Here are the available keyboard and markdown shortcuts:</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Markdown Shortcut</p> <p>Bold</p> <p>⌘ B</p> <p><code>**bold**</code></p> <p>Italic</p> <p>⌘ I</p> <p><code>*italic*</code></p> <p>Code</p> <p>⌘ D</p> <p><code>code</code></p> <p>Strikeout</p> <p><code>~~strike~~</code></p> <p>Subscript</p> <p><code>~sub~</code></p> <p>Superscript</p> <p><code>^super^</code></p> <p>Heading 1</p> <p>⌥⌘ 1</p> <p><code>#</code></p> <p>Heading 2</p> <p>⌥⌘ 2</p> <p><code>##</code></p> <p>Heading 3</p> <p>⌥⌘ 3</p> <p><code>###</code></p> <p>Heading Attributes</p> <p><code>{#id .class}</code></p> <p>Link</p> <p>⌘ K</p> <p><code><href></code></p> <p>Blockquote</p> <p><code>></code></p> <p>Code Block</p> <p>⇧⌘<br /> </p> <p>`````</p> <p>Code Cell</p> <p>⌥⌘ I</p> <p>```<code>{python}</code></p> <p>Raw Block</p> <p>```<code>{=html}</code></p> <p>Div</p> <p><code>:::</code></p> <p>Bullet List</p> <p><code>-</code></p> <p>Ordered List</p> <p><code>1.</code></p> <p>Tight List</p> <p>⌥⌘ 9</p> <p>List Check</p> <p><code>[x]</code></p> <p>Emoji</p> <p><code>:smile:</code></p> <p>Definition</p> <p><code>:</code></p> <p>Non-Breaking Space</p> <p>⌃ Space</p> <p>Hard Line Break</p> <p>⇧ Enter</p> <p>Paragraph</p> <p>⌥⌘ 0</p> <p>Image</p> <p>⇧⌘ I</p> <p>Footnote</p> <p>⇧⌘ F7</p> <p>Citation</p> <p>⇧⌘ F8</p> <p><code>[@</code></p> <p>Table</p> <p>⌥⌘ T</p> <p>Editing Comment</p> <p>⇧⌘ C</p> <p>Select All</p> <p>⌘ A</p> <p>Clear Formatting</p> <p>⌘<br /> </p> <p>Edit Attributes</p> <p>F4</p> <p>For markdown shortcuts, if you didn’t intend to use a shortcut and want to reverse its effect, just press the backspace key.</p> <h5 id="insert-anything">Insert Anything</h5> <p>You can also use the catch-all ⌘ / shortcut to insert just about anything. Just execute the shortcut then type what you want to insert. For example:</p> <p>If you are at the beginning of a line (as displayed above), you can also enter plain <code>/</code> to invoke the shortcut.</p> <h5 id="editor-toolbar">Editor Toolbar</h5> <p>The editor toolbar includes buttons for the most commonly used formatting commands:</p> <p>Additional commands are available on the Format, Insert, and Table menus:</p> <p>Format</p> <p>Insert</p> <p>Table</p> <h5 id="editor-options">Editor Options</h5> <p>There are a variety of Positron options available to configure the behavior of the visual editor. You can locate these options by filtering on <code>quarto.visualEditor</code> in the settings pane:</p> <p>Options enable configuration of appearance (font size, content width, etc.), markdown output (e.g. column wrapping), spell checking, and default spacing for lists.</p> <h5 id="zotero-citations">Zotero Citations</h5> <p><a href="https://zotero.org">Zotero</a> is a popular free and open source reference manager. The Quarto visual editor integrates directly with Zotero, enabling you to use the Insert Citation command to use references from your Zotero libraries:</p> <p>Zotero references will also show up automatically in visual editor completions:</p> <p>Items from Zotero will appear alongside items from your bibliography with a small “Z” logo juxtaposed over them. If you insert a citation from Zotero that isn’t already in your bibliography then it will be automatically added to the bibliography.</p> <p>If you are running both Positron and Zotero on your desktop, then no additional configuration is required for connecting to your Zotero library. If however you want to access your Zotero library over the web, then a few more steps are required (see the Zotero Web API section for details).</p> <h6 id="group-libraries">Group Libraries</h6> <p><a href="https://www.zotero.org/support/groups">Zotero Groups</a> provide a powerful way to share collections with a class or work closely with colleagues on a project. By default, Zotero Group Libraries are not included in the Insert Citation dialog or citation completions. However, you can use the Quarto > Zotero: Group Libraries option to activate one or more group libraries (either globally, or per-workspace):</p> <p>After you’ve added a group library to the list, a sync will be performed and you should see the library in the Insert Citation dialog. If you don’t, double check the exact spelling of the group library name you are configuring (you may even want to copy and paste it from Zotero so you are certain to get it right).</p> <h6 id="zotero-web-api">Zotero Web API</h6> <p>If you don’t have Zotero installed locally, you can still access your Zotero library using the Zotero Web API (assuming you have a Zotero web account and have synced your libraries to your account).</p> <p>If you are running Positron on your desktop it’s generally easier to also run Zotero on your desktop and access your library locally. That said, it is possible to access Zotero web libraries from Positron on the desktop if you prefer that configuration.</p> <h6 id="api-access-key">API Access Key</h6> <p>Zotero integration uses the Zotero Web API, so the first step is to <a href="https://www.zotero.org/user/register">create a Zotero account</a> and then configure Zotero to sync its data to your account. You can do this using the Sync tab of the Zotero preferences:</p> <p>Once you’ve configured your library to sync, you need to <a href="https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys/new">create a Zotero API Key</a>:</p> <p>Follow the instructions to create a new access key. Note that if you want to use Group Libraries, you should change the default to provide read-only access to groups (as illustrated above).</p> <p>Be sure to record your key after generating it (i.e. copy it to the clipboard and/or save it somewhere more permanent) as you won’t be able to view it again after you navigate away.</p> <h6 id="library-configuration">Library Configuration</h6> <p>Finally, go to Zotero settings and specify that you’d like to use your <code>web</code> Zotero library rather than a local one:</p> <p>You’ll then be promoted to enter your Zotero Web API Key:</p> <p>After you provide your API key and it is validated, an initial sync of your Zotero libraries is performed. After this, you are ready to start inserting citations from Zotero.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>If you need to change your Zotero API key, you can always execute the Quarto: Zotero - Connect Web Library command. To force a sync of your web library, execute the Quarto: Zotero - Sync Web Library command (note that your web library is synced automatically so it is unlikely you’ll need to use this command explicitly).</p> <h5 id="markdown-output-1">Markdown Output</h5> <p>The Quarto visual editor generates markdown using Pandoc. This means that in some cases your markdown will be rewritten to conform to standard Pandoc idioms. For example, Pandoc inserts 3 spaces after list bullets and automatically escapes characters that might be used for markdown syntax.</p> <p>Here is a list of conventions for Pandoc generated markdown that might differ from your own markdown writing style:</p> <ul> <li><code>*text*</code> is used in preference to <code>_text_</code></li> <li>Backtick code blocks are written as ```<code>{.md}</code> rather than ```<code>md</code></li> <li>Backtick code blocks with no attributes are rendered as 4-space indented code blocks</li> <li>Horizontal rules are written as dashes spanning the full width of the document</li> <li>Plain links are written as <code><https://yihui.org></code> rather than <code>https://yihui.org</code></li> <li>Bullet and numbered lists use additional leading spaces before list item content</li> <li>The blockquote character (<code>></code>) is included on each new line of a blockquote</li> <li>Table captions are written below rather than above tables</li> <li>Multiline HTML and TeX blocks use the explicit raw attribute (e.g. ```<code>{=tex}</code>)</li> <li>Inline footnotes are replaced with footnotes immediately below the paragraph</li> <li>Nested divs use <code>:::</code> at all levels so long as their attributes are distinct</li> <li>Unnumbered sections are designated with <code>{.unnumbered}</code> rather than <code>{-}</code></li> <li>Characters used for markdown syntax (e.g. <code>*</code>, <code>_</code>, or <code>#</code>) are always escaped While some of this behavior might be bothersome at first, if you decide that visual editing mode is useful for your workflow it’s probably best to just adapt to writing your own markdown the same way that Pandoc does.</li> </ul> <h6 id="writer-options">Writer Options</h6> <p>Some aspects of markdown output can be customized via global, project, or file-level options, including:</p> <ul> <li><p>How to wrap / break lines (fixed column, sentence-per-line, etc.).</p></li> <li><p>Where to write footnotes (below the current paragraph or section, or at the end of the document).</p></li> <li><p>Whether to write inline or reference style links. You can specify these options in one of two ways:</p></li> <li><p>As a global or per-workspace Positron option (you can find the options that affect markdown output by filtering on <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdown</code>).</p></li> <li><p>Specifying them within document or project level YAML (described below).</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="line-wrapping">Line Wrapping</h6> <p>By default, the visual editor writes Markdown with no line wrapping (paragraphs all occupy a single line). However, if you prefer to insert line breaks at a particular column (e.g. 72 or 80), or to insert a line break after each sentence, you can use the <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownWrap</code> and <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownWrapColumn</code> options accessible from the settings editor in Positron.</p> <p>You can also set this behavior on a per-document or per-project basis via the <code>wrap</code> option. For example, to wrap lines after 72 characters you would use this:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: 72 ---</code></pre> <p>To insert a line break after each sentence, use <code>wrap: sentence</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: sentence ---</code></pre> <p>The algorithm used for sentence wrapping will handle English and Japanese text well, but may not detect the end of sentences accurately for other languages.</p> <p>If you have enabled a global line wrapping option and want to turn off wrapping for a given document, use <code>wrap: none</code>.</p> <h6 id="references-42">References</h6> <p>By default, references (footnotes and reference links) are written at the end of the block where their corresponding footnote appears. You can override this behavior using the <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferences</code> Positron setting or by using the <code>references</code> option within document or project YAML.</p> <p>For example, to write references at the end of sections rather than blocks you would use:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block ---</code></pre> <p>Valid values for the <code>references</code> option are <code>block</code>, <code>section</code>, and <code>document</code>.</p> <p>If you are aggregating a set of markdown documents into a larger work, you may want to make sure that reference identifiers are unique across all of your documents (e.g. you don’t want to have <code>[^1]</code> appear multiple times). You can ensure uniqueness via the <code>prefix</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block prefix: "mydoc" ---</code></pre> <p>This will result in footnotes in this document using the specified prefix (e.g. <code>[^mydoc-1]</code>), ensuring they are globally unique across the manuscript.</p> <p>Note that if you are within a Quarto book project then a references <code>prefix</code> is applied automatically so no changes to <code>editor</code> options are required.</p> <h6 id="links-4">Links</h6> <p>Links are written inline by default, however they can be written as reference links (below content as with footnotes) by adding the <code>links: true</code> option to the <code>references</code> section of document or project YAML. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block links: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can alternatively enable reference links using the Positron <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferenceLinks</code> option.</p> <h6 id="known-limitations-1">Known Limitations</h6> <p>There are a handful of Pandoc markdown extensions not currently supported by visual editing. These are infrequently used extensions, so in all likelihood they won’t affect documents you edit, but are still worth noting.</p> <p>Extension(s)</p> <p>Example</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p>Inline footnotes</p> <p><a href="#fn1" class="footnote-ref" id="fnref1" role="doc-noteref"><sup>1</sup></a></p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Footnote identifiers</p> <p>[^longnote]</p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Example lists</p> <ol start="3" class="example" type="1"> <li>First example</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Auto-list numbers</p> <ol> <li>First item</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Reference links</p> <p>This is a [link]</p> <p>Converted to ordinary links.</p> <p>MultiMarkdown attributes</p> <p># Heading [id]</p> <p>Converted to Pandoc attributes.</p> <p>The visual editor is unable to parse non-YAML title blocks (e.g. old-style % titles or MultiMarkdown titles) and also unable to parse non top-level YAML metadata blocks. If these forms of metadata are encountered, visual mode will fail to load with a warning.</p> <p>Note that support for reference links can be enabled via the <code>editor: markdown: references: links</code> option in document or project YAML, or the Positron <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferenceLinks</code> option. HTML and TeX blocks use the explicit raw attribute (e.g. ```<code>{=tex}</code>)</li> <li>Inline footnotes are replaced with footnotes immediately below the paragraph</li> <li>Nested divs use <code>:::</code> at all levels so long as their attributes are distinct</li> <li>Unnumbered sections are designated with <code>{.unnumbered}</code> rather than <code>{-}</code></li> <li>Characters used for markdown syntax (e.g. <code>*</code>, <code>_</code>, or <code>#</code>) are always escaped While some of this behavior might be bothersome at first, if you decide that visual editing mode is useful for your workflow it’s probably best to just adapt to writing your own markdown the same way that Pandoc does.</li> </ul> <h6 id="writer-options-1">Writer Options</h6> <p>Some aspects of markdown output can be customized via global, project, or file-level options, including:</p> <ul> <li><p>How to wrap / break lines (fixed column, sentence-per-line, etc.).</p></li> <li><p>Where to write footnotes (below the current paragraph or section, or at the end of the document).</p></li> <li><p>Whether to write inline or reference style links. You can specify these options in one of two ways:</p></li> <li><p>As a global or per-workspace VS Code option (you can find the options that affect markdown output by filtering on <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdown</code>).</p></li> <li><p>Specifying them within document or project level YAML (described below).</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="line-wrapping-1">Line Wrapping</h6> <p>By default, the visual editor writes Markdown with no line wrapping (paragraphs all occupy a single line). However, if you prefer to insert line breaks at a particular column (e.g. 72 or 80), or to insert a line break after each sentence, you can use the <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownWrap</code> and <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownWrapColumn</code> options accessible from the settings editor in VS Code.</p> <p>You can also set this behavior on a per-document or per-project basis via the <code>wrap</code> option. For example, to wrap lines after 72 characters you would use this:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: 72 ---</code></pre> <p>To insert a line break after each sentence, use <code>wrap: sentence</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: sentence ---</code></pre> <p>The algorithm used for sentence wrapping will handle English and Japanese text well, but may not detect the end of sentences accurately for other languages.</p> <p>If you have enabled a global line wrapping option and want to turn off wrapping for a given document, use <code>wrap: none</code>.</p> <h6 id="references-43">References</h6> <p>By default, references (footnotes and reference links) are written at the end of the block where their corresponding footnote appears. You can override this behavior using the <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferences</code> VS Code setting or by using the <code>references</code> option within document or project YAML.</p> <p>For example, to write references at the end of sections rather than blocks you would use:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block ---</code></pre> <p>Valid values for the <code>references</code> option are <code>block</code>, <code>section</code>, and <code>document</code>.</p> <p>If you are aggregating a set of markdown documents into a larger work, you may want to make sure that reference identifiers are unique across all of your documents (e.g. you don’t want to have <code>[^1]</code> appear multiple times). You can ensure uniqueness via the <code>prefix</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block prefix: "mydoc" ---</code></pre> <p>This will result in footnotes in this document using the specified prefix (e.g. <code>[^mydoc-1]</code>), ensuring they are globally unique across the manuscript.</p> <p>Note that if you are within a Quarto book project then a references <code>prefix</code> is applied automatically so no changes to <code>editor</code> options are required.</p> <h6 id="links-5">Links</h6> <p>Links are written inline by default, however they can be written as reference links (below content as with footnotes) by adding the <code>links: true</code> option to the <code>references</code> section of document or project YAML. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block links: true ---</code></pre> <p>You can alternatively enable reference links using the VS Code <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferenceLinks</code> option.</p> <h6 id="known-limitations-2">Known Limitations</h6> <p>There are a handful of Pandoc markdown extensions not currently supported by visual editing. These are infrequently used extensions, so in all likelihood they won’t affect documents you edit, but are still worth noting.</p> <p>Extension(s)</p> <p>Example</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p>Inline footnotes</p> <p><a href="#fn2" class="footnote-ref" id="fnref2" role="doc-noteref"><sup>2</sup></a></p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Footnote identifiers</p> <p>[^longnote]</p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Example lists</p> <ol start="4" class="example" type="1"> <li>First example</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Auto-list numbers</p> <ol> <li>First item</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Reference links</p> <p>This is a [link]</p> <p>Converted to ordinary links.</p> <p>MultiMarkdown attributes</p> <p># Heading [id]</p> <p>Converted to Pandoc attributes.</p> <p>The visual editor is unable to parse non-YAML title blocks (e.g. old-style % titles or MultiMarkdown titles) and also unable to parse non top-level YAML metadata blocks. If these forms of metadata are encountered, visual mode will fail to load with a warning.</p> <p>Note that support for reference links can be enabled via the <code>editor: markdown: references: links</code> option in document or project YAML, or the VS Code <code>quarto.visualEditor.markdownReferenceLinks</code> option. Reference links will be written according the reference location option (either the <code>block</code> or <code>section</code> in which they appear, or alternatively at the end of the <code>document</code>).</p> <h3 id="vs-code-4">VS Code</h3> <h4 id="vs-code-5">VS Code</h4> <h5 id="overview-131">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks represented as plain text (<code>.qmd</code>) or as a normal notebook file (<code>.ipynb</code>). The <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">Quarto VS Code Extension</a> includes many tools that enhance working these documents, including:</p> <ul> <li>Integrated render and preview for Quarto documents.</li> <li>Syntax highlighting for markdown and embedded languages</li> <li>Completion and diagnostics for YAML options</li> <li>Completion for embedded languages (e.g. Python, R, Julia, etc.)</li> <li>Commands and key-bindings for running cells and selected lines.</li> <li>Live preview for LaTeX math as well as Mermaid and Graphviz diagrams The Quarto extension integrates directly with the Jupyter, R, and Julia extensions.
