For example, here the Quarto extension runs a Python cell and shows contextual help for Python functions:</li> </ul> <p>You can install the Quarto extension from the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto">VS Code Extension Marketplace</a> or the <a href="https://open-vsx.org/extension/quarto/quarto">Open VSX Registry</a>.</p> <h5 id="vs-code-editors">VS Code Editors</h5> <p>Depending on your preference and the task at hand, you can author documents for rendering by Quarto using three different editors within VS Code:</p> <ul> <li>The source code editor for editing <code>.qmd</code> documents as text.</li> <li>The Visual Editor for WYSIWYG editing of <code>.qmd</code> documents.</li> <li>The Notebook Editor for editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks. We’ll cover the source code editor below, however you might also want to consult the documentation for the Visual Editor or Notebook Editor after you’ve become familiar with the basics.</li> </ul> <h5 id="render-and-preview-7">Render and Preview</h5> <p>The Quarto VS Code extension includes commands and keyboard shortcuts for rendering Quarto documents (both standalone and within websites or books). After rendering, <code>quarto preview</code> is used behind the scenes to provide a preview pane within VS Code alongside your document:</p> <p>To render and preview, execute the Quarto: Preview command. You can alternatively use the Ctrl+Shift+K keyboard shortcut, or the Preview button () at the top right of the editor:</p> <p>Note that on the Mac you should use <code>Cmd</code> rather than <code>Ctrl</code> as the prefix for all Quarto keyboard shortcuts.</p> <h6 id="other-formats-2">Other Formats</h6> <p>The Quarto: Preview command renders the default format of the currently active document. If you want to preview a different format, use the Quarto: Preview Format command:</p> <p>When you execute Preview Format, you’ll see a quick pick list of formats to choose from (any formats declared in the document as well as some standard formats like PDF and MS Word):</p> <p>After previewing a different format, the Quarto: Preview command and Ctrl+Shift+K keyboard shortcut will be automatically rebound to the newly selected format for the duration of the current preview. To switch back to previewing the original format, use Quarto: Preview Format command again.</p> <p>Embedded preview is currently supported for HTML and PDF based formats (including <code>revealjs</code> and <code>beamer</code> slideshows). However, for Word and other formats you need to use an appropriate external program to preview the output.</p> <h6 id="render-command-1">Render Command</h6> <p>The Quarto: Preview command is what you will most commonly use while authoring documents. If you have a single format (e.g. HTML or PDF) then previewing also renders your document so it’s ready for distribution once you are happy with the output. However, if you have multiple formats will need to explicitly render them (as preview only renders a single format at a time). You can do this with the Quarto: Render Document command:</p> <p>If you have multiple declared formats you can render all of them. You can also selectively render any of the declared formats or other standard formats like PDF and MS Word.</p> <h5 id="render-on-save-1">Render on Save</h5> <p>By default Quarto does not automatically render <code>.qmd</code> or <code>.ipynb</code> files when you save them. This is because rendering might be very time consuming (e.g. it could include long running computations) and it’s good to have the option to save periodically without doing a full render.</p> <p>However, you can configure the Quarto extension to automatically render whenever you save. You can do this either within VS Code settings or within the YAML options for your project or document. To configure the VS Code setting, search for <code>quarto.render</code> in settings and you’ll find the Render on Save option:</p> <p>You might also want to control this behavior on a per-document or per-project basis. If you include the <code>editor: render-on-save</code> option in your document or project YAML it will supersede whatever your VS Code setting is. For example:</p> <pre><code>editor: render-on-save: true</code></pre> <h5 id="external-preview-1">External Preview</h5> <p>If you prefer to use an external browser for preview (or have no preview triggered at all by rendering) you can use the Preview Type option to specify an alternate behavior:</p> <h5 id="code-cells-6">Code Cells</h5> <p>There are a variety of tools that make it easier to edit and execute code cells. Editing tools include syntax highlighting, code folding, code completion, and signature tips:</p> <p>For Python, R, and Julia cells, commands are available to execute the current cell, previous cells, or the currently selected line(s). Cell output is shown side by side in the Jupyter interactive console: R and Python cells are executed in the appropriate Console, and output is shown in the pane:</p> <p>Here are all of the commands and keyboard shortcuts available for executing cells:</p> <p>Quarto Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Run Current Cell</p> <p>⇧⌘ Enter</p> <p>Run Selected Line(s)</p> <p>⌘ Enter</p> <p>Run Next Cell</p> <p>⌥⌘ N</p> <p>Run Previous Cell</p> <p>⌥⌘ P</p> <p>Run All Cells</p> <p>⌥⌘ R</p> <p>Run Cells Above</p> <p>⇧⌥⌘ P</p> <p>Run Cells Below</p> <p>⇧⌥⌘ N</p> <p>You can quickly insert a new code cell using the Ctrl+Shift+I keyboard shortcut.</p> <p>Enhanced features for embedded languages (e.g. completion, code execution) can be enabled by installing the most recent version(s) of these extensions:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.python">Python Extension</a> and <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-toolsai.jupyter">Jupyter Extension</a></li> <li><a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=REditorSupport.r">R Extension</a></li> <li><a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=julialang.language-julia">Julia Extension</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="execution-directory-1">Execution Directory</h6> <p>Embedded language extensions handle the working directory for execution in distinct ways:</p> <ul> <li>The Python Extension runs code within the directory of the source file from which code is executed. You can customize this behavior using the <code>jupyter.notebookFileRoot</code> option.</li> <li>The R Extension runs code within the working directory of the R session running in the R Interactive terminal. You can change this directory manually using <code>setwd()</code>.</li> <li>The Julia Extension runs code within the working directory of the Julia session running in the Julia REPL terminal. You can change this directory manually using <code>cd()</code>.</li> </ul> <h5 id="contextual-assistance-2">Contextual Assistance</h5> <p>Execute the Quarto: Show Assist Panel command to show a panel in the sidebar that shows contextual assistance depending on the current cursor location:</p> <ul> <li>Help/documentation is shown when editing code</li> <li>A realtime preview of equations is shown when editing LaTeX math</li> <li>Thumbnail previews are shown when your cursor is located on a markdown image. For example, below help on the matplotlib <code>plot()</code> function is shown automatically when the cursor is located on the function:</li> </ul> <h5 id="live-preview-3">Live Preview</h5> <p>While editing LaTeX math or Mermaid and Graphviz diagrams, click the Preview button above the code (or use the Ctrl+Shift+L keyboard shortcut) to open a live preview which will update automatically as you edit.</p> <p>Here we see a preview of the currently edited LaTeX equation displayed in the Quarto assist panel:</p> <p>Here we see a Graphviz diagram preview automatically updated as we edit:</p> <h5 id="yaml-intelligence-2">YAML Intelligence</h5> <p>YAML code completion is available for project files, YAML front matter, and executable cell options:</p> <p>If you have incorrect YAML it will also be highlighted when documents are saved:</p> <h5 id="code-snippets-2">Code Snippets</h5> <p>Code snippets are templates that make it easier to enter repeating code patterns (e.g. code blocks, callouts, divs, etc.). Execute the Insert Snippet command within a Quarto document to insert a markdown snippet:</p> <h6 id="intellisense-1">IntelliSense</h6> <p>VS Code uses IntelliSense to suggest snippets or possible values for a specific function while typing. This is turned off by default for snippets, but not for values. To enable snippet suggestions in IntelliSense while typing or when selecting a text snippet and pressing <code>ctrl+space</code>, the setting <code>editor.snippetSuggestions</code> needs to be set to a value other than <code>none</code> (for example to <code>inline</code>).</p> <ul> <li>Press <code>F1</code> and search for <code>Preferences: Open Settings (UI)</code> or <code>File</code> > <code>Preferences</code> > <code>Settings</code></li> <li>Search for following term <code>@lang:quarto editor.snippetSuggestions</code>. <code>Editor: Snippet Suggestions</code> should show up.</li> <li>Change value to a not-<code>none</code> value.</li> </ul> <h5 id="document-navigation-2">Document Navigation</h5> <p>If you have a large document use the outline view for quick navigation between sections:</p> <p>You can also use the Go to Symbol in Editor command or keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+O for type-ahead navigation of the current document’s outline.</p> <p>Use the Go to File command Ctrl+P to navigate to other files and the Go to Symbol in Workspace command Ctrl+T for type-ahead navigation to all headings in the workspace:</p> <h5 id="learning-more-21">Learning More</h5> <p>Besides the traditional source editor described above, you can also use one of the following other editors depending on your preferences and task at hand:</p> <ul> <li>The Visual Editor for WYSIWYG editing of <code>.qmd</code> documents.</li> <li>The Notebook Editor for editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks.</li> </ul> <h3 id="vs-code-notebook-editor">VS Code Notebook Editor</h3> <h4 id="vs-code-notebook-editor-1">VS Code Notebook Editor</h4> <p>In addition to editing Quarto documents as plain-text <code>.qmd</code> files, you can also use the VS Code Notebook Editor to author <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks that are rendered with Quarto. In this article we’ll review the basics of editing <code>.ipynb</code> notebooks for use with Quarto.</p> <h5 id="render-and-preview-8">Render and Preview</h5> <p>After you’ve done an initial Quarto: Preview, the preview will automatically update every time you save the notebook.</p> <h5 id="yaml-front-matter-2">YAML Front Matter</h5> <p>The first cell of your notebook should be a Raw cell that contains the document title, author, and any other options you need to specify. Note that you can switch the type of a cell to Raw using the cell type menu at the bottom right of the cell:</p> <p>In this example we specify that we want code to appear collapsed by default. There are YAML options to control many other aspects of document rendering. See the documentation on Authoring and Output Formats for additional details.</p> <h5 id="markdown-cells-2">Markdown Cells</h5> <p>Here’s the underlying code for the markdown cell:</p> <p>Note that a Quarto cross-reference (<code>@fig-polar</code>) is included in the markdown. Any valid Pandoc markdown syntax can be included in markdown cells.</p> <h5 id="output-options-4">Output Options</h5> <p>Quarto uses leading comments with a special prefix (<code>#|</code>) to denote cell options. Here we specify the <code>label</code> and <code>fig-cap</code> options so that the plot generated from the cell can be cross-referenced.</p> <p>Note that options must appear at the very beginning of the cell. As with document front-matter, option names/values use YAML syntax.</p> <p>There are many output options available, including options to optionally hide code, warnings, and/or output. See the documentation on Output Options for additional details.</p> <h5 id="cell-execution-4">Cell Execution</h5> <p>Note that when rendering an <code>.ipynb</code> Quarto will not execute the cells within the notebook by default (the presumption being that you have already executed them while editing the notebook). If you want to execute the cells you can pass the <code>--execute</code> flag to render:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto render notebook.ipynb --execute</code></pre> <p>You can also specify this behavior within the notebook’s YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>notebook.ipynb --- title: "My Notebook" execute: enabled: true ---</code></pre> <p>There are many other execution options available (e.g. to control caching, optimizing kernel start-up time, etc.). Learn more about these options in Execution Options.</p> <h5 id="converting-notebooks-2">Converting Notebooks</h5> <p>You can convert between .ipynb and .qmd representations of a notebook using the <code>quarto convert</code> command. For example:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto convert basics-jupyter.ipynb quarto convert basics-jupyter.qmd</code></pre> <p>See <code>quarto convert help</code> for additional details on converting notebooks.</p> <h2 id="visual-editor-2">Visual editor</h2> <h3 id="content-editing">Content Editing</h3> <h4 id="content-editing-1">Content Editing</h4> <p>Visual mode supports editing all of Pandoc markdown. Standard formatting commands (headings, bold, italic, etc.) work just the way they do in a conventional word processor.</p> <p>See the Using the Editor section for more details on how to access core editing commands. Note also that you can access all editing commands via keyboard shortcuts.</p> <p>Editing of links, images, blockquotes, lists, tables, etc. is also available, as is the ability to specify Pandoc attributes and insert special characters and emojis.</p> <h5 id="editing-tables">Editing Tables</h5> <p>You can insert a table using the Table menu. You can then use either the main menu or a context menu to insert and delete table rows and columns:</p> <p>Note that if you select multiple rows or columns the insert or delete command will behave accordingly. For example, to insert 2 rows, first select 2 rows then use the insert command.</p> <p>When you make a selection of multiple rows and/or columns as illustrated above, you can also copy and paste groups of cells within the table.</p> <h5 id="editing-lists">Editing Lists</h5> <p>As described above, you can create a new list by just typing <code>-</code> or <code>1.</code> at the beginning of an empty paragraph. To add items to the list, just press Enter within a list item. To exit the list, press Enter within an empty list item.</p> <p>While this covers many simple list editing tasks, there is a variety of other actions you may want to take within lists, including creating nested lists and adding paragraphs or code blocks to an exiting list item. From an empty list item (pictured at left), the following keyboard gestures can be used to do this:</p> <p>Empty Item</p> <p>(enter to exit list)</p> <p>Tab</p> <p>(add sublist)</p> <p>Backspace</p> <p>(add block)</p> <p>You can also use Shift+Tab to lift a list item into the previous level.</p> <h6 id="tight-lists">Tight Lists</h6> <p>Markdown distinguishes between normal and tight lists, where tight lists have less vertical spacing between items. In markdown source code, you designate a tight list by having no empty lines between your list items.</p> <p>Visual mode creates normal lists by default (you can change this behavior via Editor Options). You can toggle between normal and tight lists using the keyboard shortcut. You can also change the list type using the Format -> Edit Attributes dialog (also accessible via the F4F4 shortcut). If you have existing tight lists in your markdown source files, they will remain so within the visual editor.</p> <h5 id="pandoc-attributes">Pandoc Attributes</h5> <p>Several of Pandoc’s block types (e.g. headings, code blocks, and divs) enable you to specify a set of <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#heading-identifiers">custom attributes</a>. Attributes include IDs and class names, as well as arbitrary key-value pairs that are passed through to output formats (e.g. as attributes for HTML tags). For these block types, an edit button will appear at the top right when your cursor is within the block:</p> <p>Note that any ID as well as the first class specified within the attributes are also displayed. Click the edit button or use the F4F4 keyboard shortcut to edit the attributes.</p> <h5 id="special-characters-1">Special Characters</h5> <h6 id="hard-line-breaks">Hard Line Breaks</h6> <p>You can insert a <a href="https://practicaltypography.com/hard-line-breaks.html">hard line break</a> using the Insert -> Special Characters -> Hard Line Break command or via the Shift-EnterShift-Enter keyboard shortcut.</p> <h6 id="non-breaking-spaces">Non-Breaking Spaces</h6> <p>You can insert a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-breaking_space">non-breaking space</a> using the Insert -> Special Characters -> Non-Breaking Space command or via the Ctrl-SpaceCtrl-Space keyboard shortcut. Non-breaking spaces are displayed with an alternate background color to distinguish them from normal spaces.</p> <p>A markdown non-breaking space will result in the <code>&nbsp;</code> character within HTML output and a <code>~</code> character within LaTeX output.</p> <h6 id="emojis">Emojis</h6> <p>To insert an emoji, you can use either the Insert menu or the requisite markdown shortcut plus auto-complete:</p> <p>Insert -> Special Characters -> Emoji…</p> <p>Markdown Shortcut</p> <p>For markdown formats that support text representations of emojis (e.g. <code>:grinning:</code>), the text version will be written. For other formats the literal emoji character will be written. Currently, the gfm and hugo (with <code>enableEmoji = true</code> in the site config) formats both support text representation of emojis.</p> <p>If you want to add support for markdown emoji output to another Quarto format, you can add the <code>emoji</code> extension to the <code>from</code> option in document metadata. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" from: markdown+emoji ---</code></pre> <h6 id="unicode-symbols">Unicode Symbols</h6> <p>To insert an arbitrary Unicode character, use Insert -> Special Characters -> Unicode…:</p> <p>You can search for characters either by name or by entering an explicit Unicode code point (e.g. “U+0420”).</p> <h6 id="smart-punctuation">Smart Punctuation</h6> <p>When the Pandoc <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#typography"><code>smart</code></a> extension is enabled (which it is by default), straight quotes are interpreted as curly quotes, <code>---</code> as em-dashes, <code>--</code> as en-dashes, and <code>...</code> as ellipses. In addition, non-breaking spaces are inserted after certain abbreviations, such as “Mr.”</p> <p>Visual mode supports these same transformations (so when you type <code>---</code> it becomes an em-dash). If you didn’t intend for this transformation to occur just hit backspace and it will be reverted.</p> <h5 id="spell-checking">Spell-Checking</h5> <p>When RStudio real time spell-checking is enabled (you can do this using Spelling preferences), misspelled words will be underlined as you type:</p> <p>To resolve a spelling error, right-click on the misspelled word, then either choose an alternate spelling, ignore the word (which applies to the current document only), or add the word to your user dictionary (which applies to all documents).</p> <p>If you ignore a word by mistake, right-click it again to unignore it. If you want to edit your personal dictionary, use the Edit User Dictionary… button located within Spelling preferences.</p> <h5 id="commenting-2">Commenting</h5> <p>When reviewing a document you often want to provide inline comments with suggested revisions. This is possible in Quarto using HTML comments (which are ignored by all output formats). Visual mode includes a command for inserting HTML comments as well as special highlighting treatment to easily parse out editing comments from surrounding text.</p> <p>Note that the <code>#</code> prefix used in the comment is what triggers the special background highlighting. If you remove the <code>#</code> it will still be a valid HTML comment, but just won’t be highlighted as shown above.</p> <p>You can insert an HTML comment using the Comment button on the toolbar or via the keyboard shortcut. Remember, HTML comments won’t show up in rendered output so they are ideal both for review but also for leaving yourself to-do notes within a document.</p> <h5 id="css-styles-1">CSS Styles</h5> <p>One of the benefits of authoring with markdown is that your content can be easily published to a wide variety of formats. This is possible in significant measure because of the limitations that markdown imposes: you author in terms of the structure and semantics of your content, rather than worrying about specifically how things will appear.</p> <p>Sometimes however you know that you’ll be publishing to HTML, and you want to exert more control over how things look. In this case, you can use <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS">CSS</a> (Cascading Style Sheets) along with markdown to do custom formatting. This section covers how to:</p> <ul> <li>Define CSS styles for your document; and</li> <li>Apply those styles to entities within your document. If you are new to CSS, you may want to <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/CSS">brush up on the basics</a> before proceeding.</li> </ul> <p>CSS styles apply only to HTML output, and will not have any impact on the formatting of other output types like PDF or MS Word.</p> <h6 id="defining-styles">Defining Styles</h6> <p>The best way to include CSS styles is to create an external stylesheet (e.g. <code>styles.css</code>), then include it within the output options of your document. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "CSS Demo" format: html: css: styles.css ---</code></pre> <p>The <code>styles.css</code> file might look something like this:</p> <pre><code>.important { color: maroon; } .illustration { border: 1px solid rgb(230, 230, 230); }</code></pre> <p>Note that it’s also possible to define styles inline with a <a href="https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/language-engines.html#javascript-and-css">CSS code chunk</a>, but we recommend using an external file for easier manageability.</p> <p>Within a markdown document you can apply one or more CSS classes to various document entities including headings, images, divs, and spans. CSS classes are applied using pandoc attributes. Once you’ve applied a class to an entity, it will derive its formatting from the CSS properties of the specified class.</p> <h6 id="headings-2">Headings</h6> <p>To add a CSS class to a heading, use the edit button at the top right of the heading that appears when your cursor is within it (or use the F4F4 keyboard shortcut):</p> <p>Note the presence of the <code>.important</code> class within the Edit Attributes dialog.</p> <p>CSS classes applied to headings affect all content beneath the heading (an HTML <code><section></code> tag is wrapped around the content by Pandoc), so heading classes are a great way to provide custom styles for entire sections of your document.</p> <p>Note that the visual editor doesn’t currently render content using styles applied through CSS classes so you won’t see the custom formatting while editing. You will however see it when rendering and previewing the HTML version of the document.</p> <h6 id="images">Images</h6> <p>You can apply CSS classes to images (for example, to give them a special border) using the standard Image dialog. To do this, double-click the image (or use the F4F4 shortcut with the image selected) and apply the desired classes:</p> <p>Note again that the visual editor won’t display your image with the applied CSS classes while editing, however when actually rendering the document to HTML you’ll see the styles reflected.</p> <h6 id="divs-1">Divs</h6> <p>Divs are special entities that allow you to apply identifiers and/or styles to a region of a document. Divs are block elements (like paragraphs).</p> <p>You can create divs using the Insert -> Div command, and you can apply attributes (including CSS classes) to divs the same way as you apply attributes to headings (clicking the edit button or using the F4F4 keyboard shortcut when you are within a div):</p> <p>Note the presence of the <code>.important</code> class within the Div Attributes dialog.</p> <h6 id="spans-1">Spans</h6> <p>Spans are special entities that allow you to apply identifiers and/or styles to a region of text. Spans are inline formatting marks (like bold or italic).</p> <p>Spans can be created by selecting text and using the Format -> Span command:</p> <p>Here we’ve applied a span to the text “customize PDF reports” and we’ve used the span to apply the <code>.important</code> CSS class. Note that as with headings and images the formatting is not displayed in the visual editor, but will be visible when the document is rendered.</p> <h3 id="markdown-output-3">Markdown Output</h3> <h4 id="markdown-output-4">Markdown Output</h4> <h5 id="overview-132">Overview</h5> <p>The Quarto visual editor generates markdown using Pandoc. This means that in some cases your markdown will be rewritten to conform to standard Pandoc idioms. For example, Pandoc inserts 3 spaces after list bullets and automatically escapes characters that might be used for markdown syntax.</p> <p>Here is a list of conventions for Pandoc generated markdown that might differ from your own markdown writing style:</p> <ul> <li><code>*text*</code> is used in preference to <code>_text_</code></li> <li>Backtick code blocks are written as ```<code>{.md}</code> rather than ```<code>md</code></li> <li>Backtick code blocks with no attributes are rendered as 4-space indented code blocks</li> <li>Horizontal rules are written as dashes spanning the full width of the document</li> <li>Plain links are written as <code><https://yihui.org></code> rather than <code>https://yihui.org</code></li> <li>Bullet and numbered lists use additional leading spaces before list item content</li> <li>The blockquote character (<code>></code>) is included on each new line of a blockquote</li> <li>Table captions are written below rather than above tables</li> <li>Multiline HTML and TeX blocks use the explicit raw attribute (e.g. ```<code>{=tex}</code>)</li> <li>Inline footnotes are replaced with footnotes immediately below the paragraph</li> <li>Nested divs use <code>:::</code> at all levels so long as their attributes are distinct</li> <li>Unnumbered sections are designated with <code>{.unnumbered}</code> rather than <code>{-}</code></li> <li>Characters used for markdown syntax (e.g. <code>*</code>, <code>_</code>, or <code>#</code>) are always escaped While some of this behavior might be bothersome at first, if you decide that visual editing mode is useful for your workflow it’s probably best to just adapt to writing your own markdown the same way that Pandoc does. Note that you can also configure source mode to write markdown using these conventions, ensuring that the same markdown is written no matter which mode edits originate from.</li> </ul> <h5 id="writer-options-2">Writer Options</h5> <p>Some aspects of markdown output can be customized via global, project, or file-level options, including:</p> <ul> <li>How to wrap / break lines (fixed column, sentence-per-line, etc.).</li> <li>Where to write footnotes (below the current paragraph or section, or at the end of the document).</li> <li>Whether to use the visual mode markdown writer when saving markdown from source mode (to ensure consistency between documents saved from either mode). You can set these options within the R Markdown Global Options or Project Options, or can alternatively set them on a per-file basis using YAML (as described below).</li> </ul> <h6 id="line-wrapping-2">Line Wrapping</h6> <p>By default, the visual editor writes Markdown with no line wrapping (paragraphs all occupy a single line). This matches the behavior of markdown source editing mode within RStudio.</p> <p>However, if you prefer to insert line breaks at a particular column (e.g. 72 or 80), or to insert a line break after each sentence, you can set a global or per-project editor option to this effect.</p> <p>You can also set this behavior on a per-document basis via the <code>wrap</code> option. For example, to wrap lines after 72 characters you would use this:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: 72 ---</code></pre> <p>To insert a line break after each sentence, use <code>wrap: sentence</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: sentence ---</code></pre> <p>The algorithm used for sentence wrapping will handle English and Japanese text well, but may not detect the end of sentences accurately for other languages.</p> <p>If you have enabled a global line wrapping option and want to turn off wrapping for a given document, use <code>wrap: none</code>.</p> <h6 id="references-44">References</h6> <p>By default, references are written at the end of the block where their corresponding footnote appears. You can override this behavior using the <code>references</code> option.</p> <p>For example, to write references at the end of sections rather than blocks you would use:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block ---</code></pre> <p>Valid values for the <code>references</code> option are <code>block</code>, <code>section</code>, and <code>document</code>.</p> <p>Note that you can also set a global or per-project editor option to control reference writing behavior.</p> <p>If you are aggregating a set of markdown documents into a larger work, you may want to make sure that reference identifiers are unique across all of your documents (e.g. you don’t want to have <code>[^1]</code> appear multiple times). You can ensure uniqueness via the <code>prefix</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: references: location: block prefix: "mydoc" ---</code></pre> <p>This will result in footnotes in this document using the specified prefix (e.g. <code>[^mydoc-1]</code>), ensuring they are globally unique across the manuscript.</p> <p>Note that if you are within a Quarto book project then a references <code>prefix</code> is applied automatically so no changes to <code>editor: markdown</code> are required.</p> <h6 id="canonical-mode">Canonical Mode</h6> <p>If you have a workflow that involves editing in both visual and source mode, you may want to ensure that the same markdown is written no matter which mode edits originate from. You can accomplish this using the <code>canonical</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" editor: markdown: wrap: 72 references: location: block canonical: true ---</code></pre> <p>With <code>canonical: true</code>, edits in visual mode and source mode will result in identical markdown output. This is especially useful if you have multiple authors collaborating using version control, with a mixture of source and visual mode editing among the authors.</p> <h5 id="known-limitations-3">Known Limitations</h5> <p>There are a handful of Pandoc markdown extensions not currently supported by visual editing. These are infrequently used extensions, so in all likelihood they won’t affect documents you edit, but are still worth noting.</p> <p>Extension(s)</p> <p>Example</p> <p>Behavior</p> <p>Inline footnotes</p> <p><a href="#fn3" class="footnote-ref" id="fnref3" role="doc-noteref"><sup>3</sup></a></p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Footnote identifiers</p> <p>[^longnote]</p> <p>Converted to numeric footnote.</p> <p>Example lists</p> <ol start="5" class="example" type="1"> <li>First example</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Auto-list numbers</p> <ol> <li>First item</li> </ol> <p>Read/written as ordinary numbered lists.</p> <p>Reference links</p> <p>This is a [link]</p> <p>Converted to ordinary links.</p> <p>MultiMarkdown attributes</p> <p># Heading [id]</p> <p>Converted to Pandoc attributes.</p> <p>The visual editor is unable to parse non-YAML title blocks (e.g. old-style % titles or MultiMarkdown titles) and also unable to parse non top-level YAML metadata blocks. If these forms of metadata are encountered, visual mode will fail to load with a warning.</p> <h3 id="shortcuts-options">Shortcuts & Options</h3> <h4 id="shortcuts-options-1">Shortcuts & Options</h4> <h5 id="shortcuts">Shortcuts</h5> <p>Visual mode supports both traditional keyboard shortcuts (e.g. for bold) as well as markdown shortcuts (using markdown syntax directly). For example, enclose <code>**bold**</code> text in asterisks or type <code>##</code> and press space to create a second level heading.</p> <p>Here are the available keyboard and markdown shortcuts:</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Markdown Shortcut</p> <p>Bold</p> <p><code>**bold**</code></p> <p>Italic</p> <p><code>*italic*</code></p> <p>Code</p> <p><code>code</code></p> <p>Strikeout</p> <p><code>~~strike~~</code></p> <p>Subscript</p> <p><code>~sub~</code></p> <p>Superscript</p> <p><code>^super^</code></p> <p>Heading 1</p> <p><code>#</code></p> <p>Heading 2</p> <p><code>##</code></p> <p>Heading 3</p> <p><code>###</code></p> <p>Heading Attributes</p> <p><code>{#id .class}</code></p> <p>Link</p> <p><code><href></code></p> <p>Blockquote</p> <p><code>></code></p> <p>Code Block</p> <p>`````</p> <p>R Code Chunk</p> <p>```<code>{r}</code></p> <p>Raw Block</p> <p>```<code>{=html}</code></p> <p>Div</p> <p><code>:::</code></p> <p>Bullet List</p> <p><code>-</code></p> <p>Ordered List</p> <p><code>1.</code></p> <p>Tight List</p> <p>List Check</p> <p><code>[x]</code></p> <p>Emoji</p> <p><code>:smile:</code></p> <p>Definition</p> <p><code>:</code></p> <p>Non-Breaking Space</p> <p>Ctrl-SpaceCtrl-Space</p> <p>Hard Line Break</p> <p>Shift-EnterShift-Enter</p> <p>Paragraph</p> <p>Image</p> <p>Footnote</p> <p>Citation</p> <p><code>[@</code></p> <p>Table</p> <p>Editing Comment</p> <p>Select All</p> <p>Clear Formatting</p> <p>Edit Attributes</p> <p>F4F4</p> <p>Run Code Chunk</p> <p>Run Previous Chunks</p> <p>For markdown shortcuts, if you didn’t intend to use a shortcut and want to reverse its effect, just press the backspace key.</p> <h5 id="insert-anything-2">Insert Anything</h5> <p>You can also use the catch-all shortcut to insert just about anything. Just execute the shortcut then type what you want to insert. For example:</p> <p>If you are at the beginning of a line (as displayed above) you can also enter plain <code>/</code> to invoke the shortcut.</p> <h5 id="global-options-1">Global Options</h5> <p>You can customize visual editing options within R Markdown -> Visual (note that the visual editor was originally created for use with R Markdown so its options are located there — these options are also applicable to usage with Quarto):</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Use visual editing by default</p> <p>Switch to visual mode immediately when creating new documents.</p> <p>Show document outline by default</p> <p>Show the navigational outline when opening documents in visual mode.</p> <p>Editor content width</p> <p>Maximum width for editing content. This is intended to keep editing similar to the width that users will see.</p> <p>Editor font size</p> <p>Base font size for editor content (default: inherit from IDE settings).</p> <p>Show margin column indicator in code blocks</p> <p>Show vertical line that indicates location of editing margin column (e.g. 80).</p> <p>Default spacing between list items</p> <p>Whether to use tight or normal spacing between list items by default. See Tight Lists for details.</p> <p>Automatic text wrapping (line breaks)</p> <p>When writing markdown, automatically insert line breaks after sentences or at a specified column (default: flow text; no auto-wrapping). See Line Wrapping for details.</p> <p>Write references at end of current</p> <p>Write references (footnotes) at the end of the block or section where they appear, or at the end of the document. See References for details.</p> <p>Write canonical visual mode markdown in source mode</p> <p>Use the visual mode markdown writer when saving markdown from source mode (ensure consistency between documents saved from either mode).</p> <h5 id="citation-options">Citation Options</h5> <p>You can customize visual editor citation options within R Markdown -> Citations:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Zotero Library</p> <p>Location of Zotero citation library (Local or Web).</p> <p>Zotero Data Directory</p> <p>Location of Zotero local data directory.</p> <p>Use libraries</p> <p>Zotero libraries to use as reference sources.</p> <p>Use Better BibTeX for citation keys and BibTeX export.</p> <p>Optionally use <a href="https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/">Better BibTeX</a> to generate citation keys and export BibTeX from Zotero (this option appears only if Better BibTeX is installed).</p> <h5 id="project-options-2">Project Options</h5> <p>Global options that affect the way markdown is written can also be customized on a per-project basis. You can do this using the R Markdown pane of the Project Options dialog:</p> <p>By default projects inherit the current global settings for markdown writing and Zotero libraries.</p> <h5 id="file-options">File Options</h5> <p>Global and project options that affect the way markdown is written can also be customized on a per-file basis . You can do this by including an <code>editor: markdown</code> key in the YAML front matter of your document. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" author: "Jane Doe" editor: markdown: wrap: 72 ---</code></pre> <p>You might want to do this to ensure that multiple authors on different workstations use the same markdown writing options.</p> <p>You can also instruct RStudio to use these same options when saving files from source mode. To do this add the <code>canonical</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- editor: markdown: wrap: 72 canonical: true ---</code></pre> <p>With <code>canonical: true</code>, edits in visual mode and source mode will result in identical markdown output. This is especially useful if you have multiple authors collaborating using version control, with a mixture of source and visual mode editing among the authors.</p> <p>See the documentation on Writer Options for additional details on markdown writing options.</p> <h3 id="technical-writing">Technical Writing</h3> <h4 id="technical-writing-1">Technical Writing</h4> <p>Visual mode includes extensive support for Quarto features frequently used in technical writing including equations, citations, cross-references, footnotes, embedded code, and LaTeX. This article describes using these features in more depth.</p> <h5 id="equations-4">Equations</h5> <p>LaTeX equations are authored using standard Pandoc markdown syntax (the editor will automatically recognize the syntax and treat the equation as math). When you aren’t directly editing an equation it will appear as rendered math:</p> <p>As shown above, when you select an equation with the keyboard or mouse you can edit the equation’s LaTeX. A preview of the equation will be shown below it as you type.</p> <h5 id="cross-references-46">Cross References</h5> <p>Cross References make it easier for readers to navigate your document by providing numbered references and hyperlinks to various entities like figures, tables, and equations.</p> <p>Every cross-referenceable entity requires a label (unique identifier) and caption (description). For example, this is a cross-referenceable figure:</p> <pre><code>![Elephant](elephant.png){#fig-elephant}</code></pre> <p>The presence of the caption (“Elephant”) and label (<code>#fig-elephant</code>) make this figure referenceable. This enables you to use the following syntax to refer to it elsewhere in the document:</p> <pre><code>See @fig-elephant for an illustration.</code></pre> <p>Here is what this would look like rendered to HTML:</p> <p>See the article on Cross References for full documentation on creating cross references and customizing their display.</p> <p>Use the Insert -> Cross Reference… command to insert a cross reference:</p> <p>You can also just type the prefix of a cross reference label (e.g. <code>@fig-env</code>) and select it via auto-complete:</p> <p>Similar to hyperlinks, you can also navigate to the location of a cross-reference by clicking the popup link that appears when it’s selected:</p> <p>You can also navigate directly to any cross-reference using IDE global search:</p> <h5 id="footnotes-22">Footnotes</h5> <p>You can include footnotes using the Insert -> Footnote command (or the keyboard shortcut). Footnote editing occurs in a pane immediately below the main document:</p> <p>By default footnotes will be written in markdown immediately below the block in which they appear. You can customize this behavior via editor options.</p> <h5 id="embedded-code">Embedded Code</h5> <p>Source code which you include in a Quarto document can either be for display only or can be executed by Jupyter or Knitr as part of rendering. Code can furthermore be either inline or block.</p> <h6 id="displaying-code">Displaying Code</h6> <p>To display but not execute code, either use the Insert -> Code Block menu item, or start a new line and type either:</p> <ul> <li>````` (for a plain code block); or</li> <li>```<code><lang></code> (where <code><lang></code> is a language) for a code block with syntax highlighting. Then press the Enter key. To display code inline, simply surround text with backticks (<code>code</code>), or use the Format -> Code menu item.</li> </ul> <h6 id="code-chunks">Code Chunks</h6> <p>To insert an executable code chunk, use the Insert -> Code Chunk menu item, or start a new line and type:</p> <p>```<code>{r}</code></p> <p>Then press the Enter key. Note that <code>r</code> could be another language supported by <code>knitr</code> (e.g., <code>python</code> or <code>sql</code>) and you can also include a chunk label and other chunk options.</p> <p>To include inline R code, create normal inline code (e.g., by using backticks or the shortcut) but preface it with <code>{r}</code> (or <code>r</code>). For example, to include the current date using the R function <code>Sys.Date()</code> you would use: <code>{r} Sys.Date()</code>.</p> <p>Note that when the code displays in visual mode it won’t have the backticks (but they will still appear in source mode).</p> <h6 id="running-chunks">Running Chunks</h6> <p>You can execute the currently selected R or Python code chunk using either the run button at the top right of the code chunk or using the keyboard shortcut:</p> <p>You can execute code chunks up to the current one using the toolbar button or using the keyboard shortcut.</p> <h5 id="latex-and-html">LaTeX and HTML</h5> <p>You can also include raw LaTeX commands or HTML tags when authoring in visual mode. The raw markup will be automatically recognized and syntax highlighted. For example:</p> <p>The above examples utilize inline LaTex and HTML. You can also include blocks of raw content using the commands on the Format -> Raw menu. For example, here is a document with a raw LaTeX block:</p> <p>Note that Pandoc ignores LaTeX commands when not producing LaTeX based output, and ignores HTML tags when not producing HTML based output.</p> <h5 id="citations-5">Citations</h5> <p>Visual mode uses the standard Pandoc markdown representation for citations (e.g. <code>[@citation]</code>). Citations can be inserted from a variety of sources:</p> <ul> <li>Your document bibliography.</li> <li>Zotero personal or group libraries.</li> <li>DOI (Document Object Identifier) references.</li> <li>Searches of <a href="https://www.crossref.org/">Crossref</a>, <a href="https://datacite.org/">DataCite</a>, or <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/">PubMed</a>. If you insert citations from Zotero, DOI look-up, or a search then they are automatically added to your document bibliography.</li> </ul> <h6 id="bibliographies">Bibliographies</h6> <p>Pandoc supports bibliographies in a wide variety of formats including BibTeX and CSL. Add a bibliography to your document using the <code>bibliography</code> YAML metadata field. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" bibliography: references.bib link-citations: true ---</code></pre> <p>Note that we’ve also specified the <code>link-citations</code> option, which will make your citations hyperlinks to the corresponding bibliography entries.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#citation-syntax">Pandoc Citations</a> documentation for additional information on bibliography formats.</p> <h6 id="inserting-citations">Inserting Citations</h6> <p>You insert citations by either using the Insert -> Citation command or by using markdown syntax directly (e.g. <code>[@cite]</code> or <code>@cite</code>) .</p> <p>Citations go inside square brackets and are separated by semicolons. Each citation must have a key, composed of ‘@’ + the citation identifier from the database, and may optionally have a prefix, a locator, and a suffix. The citation key must begin with a letter, digit, or <code>_</code>, and may contain alphanumerics, <code>_</code>, and internal punctuation characters (<code>:.#$%&-+?<>~/</code>). Here are some examples:</p> <p>Blah Blah <span class="citation" data-cites="doe99 smith04">[see @doe99, pp. 33-35; also @smith04, chap. 1]</span>.</p> <p>Blah Blah <span class="citation" data-cites="doe99">[@doe99, pp. 33-35, 38-39 and passim]</span>.</p> <p>Blah Blah <span class="citation" data-cites="smith04 doe99">[@smith04; @doe99]</span>.</p> <p>Smith says blah <span class="citation" data-cites="smith04">[-@smith04]</span>.</p> <p>You can also write in-text citations, as follows:</p> <p><span class="citation" data-cites="smith04">@smith04</span> says blah.</p> <p><span class="citation" data-cites="smith04">@smith04 [p. 33]</span> says blah.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#citations">Pandoc Citations</a> documentation for additional information on citation syntax.</p> <p>Use the toolbar button or the keyboard shortcut to show the Insert Citation dialog:</p> <p>Note that you can insert multiple citations by using the add button on the right side of the item display.</p> <h6 id="markdown-syntax-4">Markdown Syntax</h6> <p>You can also insert citations directly using markdown syntax (e.g. <code>[@cite]</code>). When you do this a completion interface is provided for searching available citations:</p> <h6 id="citation-ids">Citation IDs</h6> <p>Before inserting a citation from an external source you may wish to customize its ID. Within the Insert Citation dialog, click the edit button on the right side of citations to change their ID:</p> <p>If you insert a new citation via code completion, you will also be provided with the opportunity to change its default citation ID.</p> <p>For citations inserted from Zotero, you can also use the <a href="https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/">Better BibTeX</a> plugin to generate citation IDs (this can be enabled via Citation Options if you have Better BibTeX installed).</p> <h6 id="citation-preview">Citation Preview</h6> <p>Once you’ve inserted a citation, place the cursor over it to see a preview of it along with a link to the source if one is available:</p> <h6 id="citations-from-dois">Citations from DOIs</h6> <p>Use the From DOI pane of the Insert Citation dialog to insert a citation based on a DOI (e.g. that you have retrieved from a PubMed or other search):</p> <p>If you are using markdown syntax, you can also paste a <a href="https://www.doi.org/">DOI</a> after the <code>[@</code> and it will be looked up:</p> <p>Once you’ve confirmed that it’s the correct work (and possibly modified the suggested ID), the citation will be inserted into the document and an entry for the work added to your bibliography.</p> <h6 id="citations-from-search">Citations from Search</h6> <p>Use the Crossref, DataCite, and PubMed panes of the Insert Citation dialog to search one of those services for a citation:</p> <p>Items inserted from a search will automatically be added to your bibliography.</p> <p>Note that for PubMed queries you can use the full supported query syntax. For example, this query searches on the author and title fields: <code>Peterson[Author] AND Embolism[Title]</code>. You can learn more about building PubMed queries here: <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/advanced/">pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov</a>.</p> <h6 id="citations-from-zotero">Citations from Zotero</h6> <p><a href="https://zotero.org">Zotero</a> is a popular free and open source reference manager. If you use Zotero, you can also insert citations directly from your Zotero libraries. If you have Zotero installed locally its location will be detected automatically and citations from your main library (My Library) will be available:</p> <p>Zotero references will also show up automatically in completions:</p> <p>Items from Zotero will appear alongside items from your bibliography with a small “Z” logo juxtaposed over them. If you insert a citation from Zotero that isn’t already in your bibliography then it will be automatically added to the bibliography.</p> <p>If you are running both RStudio and Zotero on your desktop, then no additional configuration is required for connecting to your Zotero library. If however you using RStudio Server and/or want to access your Zotero library over the web, then a few more steps are required (see the Zotero Web API section for details).</p> <h6 id="group-libraries-2">Group Libraries</h6> <p><a href="https://www.zotero.org/support/groups">Zotero Groups</a> provide a powerful way to share collections with a class or work closely with colleagues on a project. By default, Zotero Group Libraries are not included in the Insert Citation dialog or citation completions. However, there are options available to use group libraries at a global, per-project, or per-document level.</p> <p>For example, here we specify a project-level option to use the Reproducible Research Series (Year 1) group library:</p> <p>You can also specify one or more libraries within YAML. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Reproducible Research" zotero: "Reproducible Research Series (Year 1)" ---</code></pre> <p>Note that you can also turn off Zotero entirely for a document using <code>zotero: false</code>:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Reproducible Research" zotero: false ---</code></pre> <h6 id="zotero-web-api-2">Zotero Web API</h6> <p>If you are using RStudio Server and/or don’t have Zotero installed locally, you can still access your Zotero library using the Zotero Web API (assuming you have a Zotero web account and have synced your libraries to your account).</p> <p>If you are running RStudio Desktop, it’s generally easier to also run Zotero on your desktop and access your library locally. That said, it is possible to access Zotero web libraries from RStudio Desktop if you prefer that configuration.</p> <h6 id="api-access-key-2">API Access Key</h6> <p>RStudio accesses Zotero web libraries using the Zotero Web API, so the first step is to <a href="https://www.zotero.org/user/register">create a Zotero account</a> and then configure Zotero to sync its data to your account. You can do this using the Sync tab of the Zotero preferences:</p> <p>Once you’ve configured your library to sync, you need to <a href="https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys/new">create a Zotero API Key</a> to use with RStudio:</p> <p>Follow the instructions to create a new access key. Note that if you want to use Group Libraries with RStudio that you should change the default to provide read-only access to groups (as illustrated above).</p> <p>Be sure to record your key after generating it (i.e. copy it to the clipboard and/or save it somewhere more permanent) as you won’t be able to view it again after you navigate away.</p> <p>Finally, go to the R Markdown -> Citations preferences to connect Zotero to RStudio using your key:</p> <p>Set the Zotero Library option to “Web”, then paste in your Zotero Web API Key. You can use Verify Key… button to confirm that your Zotero API key is working correctly.</p> <p>Once you’ve confirmed your connection you are ready to start inserting citations from Zotero.</p> <h3 id="visual-editing-in-rstudio">Visual Editing in RStudio</h3> <h4 id="visual-editing-in-rstudio-1">Visual Editing in RStudio</h4> <h5 id="overview-133">Overview</h5> <p>The Quarto visual editor provides a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WYSIWYM">WYSIWYM</a> editing interface for all of Pandoc markdown, including tables, citations, cross-references, footnotes, divs/spans, definition lists, attributes, raw HTML/TeX, and more. The visual editor also includes support for executing code cells and viewing their output inline:</p> <p>The visual editor doesn’t attempt to abstract away or obscure the underlying markdown document. Rather, it aims to provide a highly productive writing interface for people that love markdown. You can also still use most markdown constructs (e.g., ## or bold) directly for formatting.</p> <h6 id="switching-modes">Switching Modes</h6> <p>Markdown documents can be edited in either source or visual mode. To switch into visual mode for a given document, use the Source or Visual button at the top-left of the document toolbar (or alternatively the keyboard shortcut):</p> <p>Note that you can switch between source and visual mode at any time (editing location and undo/redo state will be preserved when you switch).</p> <h5 id="getting-started-4">Getting Started</h5> <p>The Quarto visual editor is currently available as a feature of the <a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">RStudio IDE</a>. The visual editor will eventually also be made available in standalone form.</p> <p>To get started with the visual editor, download the latest release of RStudio for your platform from:</p> <p><a href="https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/">posit.co</a></p> <h5 id="using-the-editor">Using the Editor</h5> <h6 id="keyboard-shortcuts-3">Keyboard Shortcuts</h6> <p>There are keyboard shortcuts for all basic editing tasks. Visual mode supports both traditional keyboard shortcuts (e.g. for bold) as well as markdown shortcuts (using markdown syntax directly). For example, enclose <code>**bold**</code> text in asterisks or type <code>##</code> and press space to create a second level heading. Here are some of the most commonly used shortcuts:</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Keyboard Shortcut</p> <p>Markdown Shortcut</p> <p>Bold</p> <p><code>**bold**</code></p> <p>Italic</p> <p><code>*italic*</code></p> <p>Code</p> <p><code>code</code></p> <p>Heading 1</p> <p><code>#</code></p> <p>Heading 2</p> <p><code>##</code></p> <p>Heading 3</p> <p><code>###</code></p> <p>Link</p> <p><code><href></code></p> <p>R Code Chunk</p> <p>```<code>{r}</code></p> <p>See the editing shortcuts article for a complete list of all shortcuts.</p> <h6 id="insert-anything-3">Insert Anything</h6> <p>You can also use the catch-all shortcut to insert just about anything. Just execute the shortcut then type what you want to insert. For example:</p> <p>If you are at the beginning of a line (as displayed above), you can also enter plain <code>/</code> to invoke the shortcut.</p> <h6 id="editor-toolbar-2">Editor Toolbar</h6> <p>The editor toolbar includes buttons for the most commonly used formatting commands:</p> <p>Additional commands are available on the Format, Insert, and Table menus:</p> <p>Format</p> <p>Insert</p> <p>Table</p> <h5 id="learning-more-22">Learning More</h5> <p>Check out the following articles to learn more about visual markdown editing:</p> <ul> <li>Technical Writing covers features commonly used in scientific and technical writing, including citations, cross-references, footnotes, equations, embedded code, and LaTeX.</li> <li>Content Editing provides more depth on visual editor support for tables, lists, pandoc attributes, CSS styles, comments, symbols/emojis, etc.</li> <li>Shortcuts & Options documents the two types of shortcuts you can use with the editor: standard keyboard shortcuts and markdown shortcuts and describes various options for configuring the editor.</li> <li>Markdown Output describes how the visual editor parses and writes markdown and describes various ways you can customize this.</li> </ul> <h2 id="websites-5">Websites</h2> <h3 id="about-pages-1">About Pages</h3> <h4 id="about-pages-2">About Pages</h4> <h5 id="overview-134">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto makes it easy to create a simple about page for an individual or organization. When the <code>about</code> option is provided for a document, a special template will be used to layout the content of the current page with a custom layout designed to present a person or organization.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Finley Malloc" about: template: jolla image: profile.jpg links: - icon: bluesky text: Bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app) - icon: github text: Github href: [github.com](https://github.com) --- Finley Malloc is the Chief Data Scientist at Wengo Analytics. When not innovating on data platforms, Finley enjoys spending time unicycling and playing with her pet iguana. ## Education University of California, San Diego | San Diego, CA PhD in Mathematics | Sept 2011 - June 2015 Macalester College | St. Paul, MN B.A in Economics | Sept 2007 - June 2011 ## Experience Wengo Analytics | Head Data Scientist | April 2018 - present GeoScynce | Chief Analyst | Spet 2012 - April 2018</code></pre> <p>The contents of this page will be laid out using the <code>jolla</code> template with the <code>profile.jpg</code> image, and generate a set of links for the items specified in <code>links</code>.</p> <p>You can write and format the content of the page however you’d like - when the page is rendered, Quarto will use the content and options provided in the <code>about</code> option to create the about page, arranging the content of the <code>about</code> option with the content in the page itself.</p> <h5 id="templates-1">Templates</h5> <p>Quarto includes 5 built in templates, drawing inspiration from the <a href="https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/postcards/readme/README.html">Postcards R Package</a>. Built-in templates include:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>jolla</code></p></li> <li><p><code>trestles</code></p></li> <li><p><code>solana</code></p></li> <li><p><code>marquee</code></p></li> <li><p><code>broadside</code> Each template will position the about elements with the content in a different layout. Select the template using the <code>template</code> option:</p> <p>about: template: trestles</p></li> </ul> <p>Here is a preview of each of the templates:</p> <ul> <li>jolla</li> <li>trestles</li> <li>solana</li> <li>marquee</li> <li>broadside</li> </ul> <h6 id="image">Image</h6> <p>The image for the about page will be read from the document-level <code>image</code> option:</p> <pre><code>title: Finley Malloc image: profile.jpg about: template: jolla</code></pre> <p>In addition, you can customize how the image is displayed in the page to better meet your needs by setting the following options.</p> <p>option</p> <p>description</p> <p>templates</p> <p><code>image-width</code></p> <p>A valid CSS width for your image.</p> <p>all</p> <p><code>image-shape</code></p> <p>The shape of the image on the about page. Choose from:<code>rectangle</code>, <code>round</code>, <code>rounded</code></p> <p><code>jolla</code>, <code>solana</code>, <code>trestles</code></p> <p><code>image-alt</code></p> <p>Alternative text for image</p> <p>all</p> <p><code>image-title</code></p> <p>Title for image</p> <p>all</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>title: Finley Malloc image: profile.png about: template: trestles image-width: 10em image-shape: round</code></pre> <h6 id="links-6">Links</h6> <p>Your about page also may contain a set of links to other resources about you or your organization. Each template will render these links in a slightly different way. Here are the options that you can specify for each link:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>href</code></p> <p>Link to file contained with the project or an external URL.</p> <p><code>text</code></p> <p>Text to display for navigation item (defaults to the document <code>title</code> if not provided).</p> <p><code>icon</code></p> <p>Name of one of the standard <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com/">Bootstrap 5 icons</a> (e.g. “github”, “twitter”, “share”, etc.).</p> <p><code>aria-label</code></p> <p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-label">Accessible label</a> for the navigation item.</p> <h5 id="partial-page-content">Partial Page Content</h5> <p>By default, the about page will be generated using the entire contents of the page. If you’d like, however, you may also choose to use only a portion of the page’s content to populate the about template. In this case, you can specify an <code>id</code> for the about page in the document front matter. When rendering the page, Quarto will find any <code>div</code> with that <code>id</code> and use the contents of that <code>div</code> to populate the about template. The <code>div</code> that provided the contents will be replaced with the formatted ‘about’ content. For example, you could write:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Finley Malloc" about: id: hero-heading template: jolla image: profile.jpg links: - icon: bluesky text: Bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app) - icon: github text: Github href: [github.com](https://github.com) --- ### This content appears above the formatted about page content. :::{#hero-heading} Finley Malloc is the Chief Data Scientist at Wengo Analytics. When not innovating on data platforms, Finley enjoys spending time unicycling and playing with her pet iguana. ## Education University of California, San Diego | San Diego, CA PhD in Mathematics | Sept 2011 - June 2015 Macalester College | St. Paul, MN B.A in Economics | Sept 2007 - June 2011 ## Experience Wengo Analytics | Head Data Scientist | April 2018 - present GeoScynce | Chief Analyst | Sept 2012 - April 2018 ::: ### This content appears below the formatted about page content.</code></pre> <h3 id="creating-a-blog">Creating a Blog</h3> <h4 id="creating-a-blog-1">Creating a Blog</h4> <h5 id="overview-135">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto websites include integrated support for blogging. Blogs consist of a collection of posts along with a navigational page that lists them in reverse chronological order. Blogs can include a custom about page, publish an RSS feed, and use a wide variety of themes.</p> <p>You can create websites that consist entirely of a single blog, websites that have multiple blogs, or you can add a blog to a website that contains other content.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-9">Quick Start</h5> <p>Follow the Quick Start for your tool of choice to get a simple blog up and running. After covering the basics, read on to learn about more advanced blog features.</p> <ul> <li>Positron</li> <li>VS Code</li> <li>RStudio</li> <li>Terminal To create a new blog project within Positron, execute the Quarto: Create Project command from the command-palette:</li> </ul> <p>Then, select Blog Project:</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to select a parent directory to create the project within. Then, you’ll be asked to name the directory for your blog project:</p> <p>The new blog project will be created and opened within Positron. Click the Preview button () to preview the blog:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new blog project within VS Code, execute the Quarto: Create Project command from the command-palette:</p> <p>Then, select Blog Project:</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to select a parent directory to create the project within. Then, you’ll be asked to name the directory for your blog project:</p> <p>The new blog project will be created and opened within VS Code. Click the Preview button () to preview the blog:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new blog project within RStudio, use the New Project command and select Quarto Blog:</p> <p>Then, provide a directory name and other relevant options for the blog:</p> <p>Click the Render button to preview the blog:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new blog project from the Terminal, use the <code>quarto create project</code> command with <code>blog</code>, specifying the directory that will hold the new project as first argument:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project blog myblog</code></pre> <p>This will create the scaffolding for a simple blog in the <code>myblog</code> sub-directory. Use the <code>quarto preview</code> command to render and preview the blog:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview myblog</code></pre> <p>The blog preview will open in a new web browser. As you edit and save <code>index.qmd</code> (or other files like <code>about.qmd</code>) the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>Here’s a summary of the key files created within the starter blog project:</p> <p>File</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>_quarto.yml</code></p> <p>Quarto project file.</p> <p><code>index.qmd</code></p> <p>Blog home page.</p> <p><code>about.qmd</code></p> <p>Blog about page.</p> <p><code>posts/</code></p> <p>Directory containing posts</p> <p><code>posts/_metadata.yml</code></p> <p>Shared options for <code>posts</code></p> <p><code>styles.css</code></p> <p>Custom CSS for website</p> <p>In the following sections we’ll take a closer look at the various components of the project.</p> <h5 id="home-page">Home Page</h5> <p>The home page is a listing page for all of the documents in the <code>posts</code> directory:</p> <p>Here’s the source code for the home page:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "myblog" listing: contents: posts sort: "date desc" type: default categories: true ---</code></pre> <p>When you render a new post, the listing page will automatically updated, adding the most recent post to the top of the list.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>It is not recommended that you use dynamic dates (for example <code>today</code> or <code>last-modified</code>) in your blog posts. This will cause the order of your blog and feed to be changed each time the document is rendered or modified.</p> <p>See the article on Listing Pages to learn more about customizing listings, including use a grid layout rather than the default shown above.</p> <h6 id="categories">Categories</h6> <p>The listing page is configured to enable categories, which display in the right margin of the page:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "myblog" listing: # (additional metadata excluded for brevity) categories: true ---</code></pre> <p>The categories are read from the front matter of documents included in the listing. For example, here is sample post metadata that includes categories:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Post With Code" description: "Post description" author: "Fizz McPhee" date: "5/22/2021" categories: - news - code - analysis ---</code></pre> <p>See the article on Categories to learn more.</p> <h5 id="about-page">About Page</h5> <p>The <code>about.qmd</code> document includes additional information on the blog and its author. For example:</p> <p>Here’s what the source code of an <code>about.qmd</code> might look like:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "About" image: profile.jpg about: template: jolla links: - icon: bluesky text: Bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app) # (additional links excluded for brevity) --- ## About this blog This is the contents of the about page for my blog.</code></pre> <p>See the article on About Pages to learn about the various options available for customizing page output.</p> <h5 id="posts-directory">Posts Directory</h5> <p>The posts that make up the contents of the blog are located in the <code>posts</code> directory.</p> <p>Add a new post to your blog by creating a sub-directory within <code>posts</code>, and adding an <code>index.qmd</code> file to the directory. That <code>qmd</code> file is the new blog post and when you render that, the blog home page will automatically update to include the newest post at the top of the listing.</p> <h6 id="drafts">Drafts</h6> <p>Add <code>draft: true</code> to the document options to indicate a post is a draft. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Post" description: "Post description" author: "Fizz McPhee" date: "5/22/2021" draft: true ---</code></pre> <p>Draft posts will appear when you preview the site, but will be blank when you render the site and will not appear in listings, navigation, the site map, or site search. You can read more about drafts in Website Drafts.</p> <p>To publish the post when it is complete, simply remove <code>draft: true</code> from the document options and then render it.</p> <h6 id="last-updated">Last Updated</h6> <p>To indicate the date of the last modification, but preserve the original publication date, you can add the <code>date-modified</code> field to the document options. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Post" description: "Post description" author: "Fizz McPhee" date: "5/22/2021" date-modified: "5/23/2021" ---</code></pre> <h6 id="freezing-posts">Freezing Posts</h6> <p>Blogs posts that contain executable code often have the problem that posts created last year can’t be rendered this year (for example, because the packages used by the post have changed). A similar problem can also arise when a blog has multiple contributors and not everyone has the right software (or the right versions) to render all of the posts. Finally, posts that include computations can often take a while to render, and you don’t want the cumulative time required to render the site to grow too large.</p> <p>The solution to these problems is to freeze the output of computational blog posts. When a post is rendered with <code>freeze: true</code>, the markdown output from the underlying engine (e.g. Jupyter or Knitr) is saved. When the entire site is rendered these computations are not re-run, but rather read from the previously frozen results.</p> <p>The only time an article with <code>freeze: true</code> is rendered is when you explicitly re-render it. By specifying this option for blog posts you can ensure that posts rendered now will always re-render well with the rest of the site, even if the software required to originally render them isn’t available.</p> <p>In the default blog we include a file (<code>_metadata.yml</code>) that establishes shared metadata for all documents within the <code>posts</code> directory. In this file, we specify that we want <code>freeze: true</code> set by default for all posts:</p> <pre><code># options apply to all posts in this folder # freeze computational output freeze: true</code></pre> <p>See the article on the <code>freeze</code> option to learn more about freezing computational output within websites.</p> <h5 id="themes-1">Themes</h5> <p>Blogs can use any of the 25 <a href="https://bootswatch.com/">Bootswatch</a> themes included with Quarto. You can also create your own themes. The default blog generated by <code>quarto create project</code> uses the <a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a> theme. Here are links to the available themes along with thumbnails of what the simple default blog looks like under a few of them:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/default/">default</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cerulean/">cerulean</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cosmo/">cosmo</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/cyborg/">cyborg</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/darkly/">darkly</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/flatly/">flatly</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/journal/">journal</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/litera/">litera</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lumen/">lumen</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/lux/">lux</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/materia/">materia</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/minty/">minty</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/morph/">morph</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/pulse/">pulse</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/quartz/">quartz</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sandstone/">sandstone</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/simplex/">simplex</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/sketchy/">sketchy</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/slate/">slate</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/solar/">solar</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/spacelab/">spacelab</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/superhero/">superhero</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/united/">united</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/vapor/">vapor</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/yeti/">yeti</a></li> <li><a href="https://bootswatch.com/zephyr/">zephyr</a> litera</li> </ul> <p>solar</p> <p>morph</p> <h5 id="rss-feed">RSS Feed</h5> <p>Blogs typically include an RSS feed that allows their content to be easily syndicated to feed readers and other websites. You can enable RSS for a blog by doing the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>In the <code>_quarto.yml</code> file, add a <code>site-url</code> and <code>description</code> to the <code>website</code> key (without these options being set in the project file, Quarto cannot generate a feed). For example:</p> <p>website: title: “myblog” site-url: <a href="https://www.myblogexample.io">myblogexample.io</a> description: “A great sample blog”</p></li> <li><p>In your blog home page <code>index.qmd</code> add the <code>feed: true</code> option to the listing. For example:</p> <table> <tbody> <tr class="odd"> <td>title: “myblog”</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>listing:</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>contents: posts</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>sort: “date desc”</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>type: default</td> </tr> <tr class="even"> <td>categories: true</td> </tr> <tr class="odd"> <td>feed: true</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></li> </ul> <p>Now, when your site is rendered, an RSS feed will also be generated. To learn more, see the article on RSS Feeds.</p> <p>TipIncluding an RSS Link on the Navbar</p> <p>You can add an RSS link to your navbar by including the following in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> project file. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: title: "myblog" site-url: [myblogexample.io](https://www.myblogexample.io) description: "A great sample blog" navbar: right: - icon: rss href: index.xml</code></pre> <h6 id="category-feeds">Category Feeds</h6> <p>You can also generate RSS feeds for specific categories in your blog. For example, to create feeds for the categories <code>news</code> and <code>posts</code> in a blog, you could write the following:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "myblog" listing: contents: posts sort: "date desc" type: default categories: true feed: categories: [news, posts] ---</code></pre> <p>This will create an <code>index.xml</code> file with the RSS feed for the listing, but also create an <code>index-news.xml</code> and <code>index-posts.xml</code> file with RSS feeds for the respective categories.</p> <h5 id="publishing-12">Publishing</h5> <p>There are a wide variety of ways to publish Quarto blogs. Blog content is by default written to the <code>_site</code> sub-directory. Publishing is simply a matter of copying this directory to a web server or web hosting service.</p> <p>The article on Publishing Websites describes in more detail how to publish to the following services:</p> <ul> <li>Quarto Pub</li> <li>GitHub Pages</li> <li>Netlify</li> <li>Posit Connect</li> <li>Firebase</li> <li>Site44</li> <li>Amazon S3</li> </ul> <h5 id="subscriptions">Subscriptions</h5> <p>You may want to allow readers of your blog to subscribe to updates via email. You can use a third party email service to manage and send these emails.</p> <p>Third party email services will typically take your RSS Feed as input (e.g. <code>https://www.myblogexample.io/index.xml</code>) and provide HTML for a subscription widget that you can place on your blog. A good place to locate that widget is often right margin of your blog.</p> <p>Here are the steps required to add a subscription widget:</p> <ul> <li><p>Use your email service features to generate the HTML for your subscription widget. MailChimp, for example, provides HTML like this for a minimal subscription widget.</p> <p><span style="font-weight: 600;">Subscribe</span></p> <p>Begin Mailchimp Signup Form <link href="[cdn-images.mailchimp.com](http://cdn-images.mailchimp.com/embedcode/slim-10_7_dtp.css)" rel="stylesheet" type="text/css"></p> <style type="text/css"> #mc_embed_signup{background:#fff; clear:left; font:14px Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif; width:170px;} /* Add your own Mailchimp form style overrides in your site stylesheet or in this style block. We recommend moving this block and the preceding CSS link to the HEAD of your HTML file. */ #mc-embedded-subscribe-form{margin-left:-5px;} </style> <div id="mc_embed_signup"> <form action="<site_url>" method="post" id="mc-embedded-subscribe-form" name="mc-embedded-subscribe-form" class="validate" target="_blank" novalidate> <div id="mc_embed_signup_scroll"> <pre><code> <input type="email" value="" name="EMAIL" class="email" id="mce-EMAIL" placeholder="email address" required> real people should not fill this in and expect good things - do not remove this or risk form bot signups <div style="position: absolute; left: -5000px;" aria-hidden="true"><input type="text" name="b_f718424fc5df77c22533bdaa6_a3c37fb57b" tabindex="-1" value=""></div> <div class="optionalParent"> <div class="clear foot" style="margin-top: 10px;"> <input type="submit" value="Subscribe" name="subscribe" id="mc-embedded-subscribe" class="button"> <p class="brandingLogo"></p> </div> </div> </div></code></pre> </form> </div> <p>End mc_embed_signup</p></li> <li><p>Warning</p></li> <li><p>The above widget HTML will not work in your blog as the subscription HTML needs to contain value specific to your blog. See your email service provider’s instructions for generating a subscription widget.</p></li> <li><p>Create the file <code>subscribe.html</code> in the root of your project.</p></li> <li><p>Paste the HTML for your subscription widget into <code>subscribe.html</code> and save the file.</p></li> <li><p>Add <code>subscribe.html</code> to the <code>margin-header</code> in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file:</p> <p>website: # (additional metadata excluded for brevity) margin-header: subscribe.html</p></li> </ul> <p>The result looks like this:</p> <h3 id="creating-a-website">Creating a Website</h3> <h4 id="creating-a-website-1">Creating a Website</h4> <h5 id="overview-136">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto Websites are a convenient way to publish groups of documents. Documents published as part of a website share navigational elements, rendering options, and visual style.</p> <p>Website navigation can be provided through a global navbar, a sidebar with links, or a combination of both for sites that have multiple levels of content.
