You can also enable full text search for websites.</p> <p>Quarto websites can be published to a wide variety of destinations including GitHub Pages, Netlify, Posit Connect, or any other static hosting service or intranet web server. See the documentation on Publishing Websites for additional details.</p> <h5 id="quick-start-10">Quick Start</h5> <p>Follow the Quick Start for your tool of choice to get a simple website up and running. After covering the basics, read on to learn about website navigation and other more advanced website features.</p> <ul> <li>Positron</li> <li>VS Code</li> <li>RStudio</li> <li>Terminal To create a new website project within Positron, execute the Quarto: Create Project command from the command-palette:</li> </ul> <p>Then, select Website Project:</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to select a parent directory to create the project within. Then, you’ll be asked to name the directory for your website project:</p> <p>The new website project will be created and opened within Positron. Click the Preview button () to preview the website:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new website project within VS Code, execute the Quarto: Create Project command from the command-palette:</p> <p>Then, select Website Project:</p> <p>You’ll be prompted to select a parent directory to create the project within. Then, you’ll be asked to name the directory for your website project:</p> <p>The new website project will be created and opened within VS Code. Click the Preview button ()to preview the website:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new website project within RStudio, use the New Project command and select Quarto Website:</p> <p>Then, provide a directory name and other relevant options for the website:</p> <p>Click the Render button to preview the website:</p> <p>The preview will show to the right of the source file. As you re-render <code>index.qmd</code> or render other files like <code>about.qmd</code>, the preview is automatically updated.</p> <p>To create a new website project from the Terminal, use the <code>quarto create project</code> command, following the prompt to select the type and to provide a name for the project (will be used as the directory name):</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto create project website mysite</code></pre> <p>This will create the scaffolding for a simple website in the <code>mysite</code> sub-directory. Use the <code>quarto preview</code> command to render and preview the website:</p> <pre><code>Terminal quarto preview mysite</code></pre> <p>The website preview will open in a new web browser. As you edit and save <code>index.qmd</code> (or other files like <code>about.qmd</code>) the preview is automatically updated.</p> <h5 id="workflow-9">Workflow</h5> <p>Above we have demonstrated how to create and edit a simple website. In this section we go into more depth on website workflow.</p> <h6 id="config-file-1">Config File</h6> <p>Every website has a <code>_quarto.yml</code> config file that provides website options as well as defaults for HTML documents created within the site. For example, here is the default config file for the simple site created above:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: website website: title: "today" navbar: left: - href: index.qmd text: Home - about.qmd format: html: theme: cosmo css: styles.css toc: true</code></pre> <p>See the documentation on Website Navigation and Website Tools for additional details on website configuration. See HTML Documents for details on customizing HTML format options.</p> <h6 id="website-preview">Website Preview</h6> <p>If you are using VS Code or RStudio, the Preview button (VS Code), or Render button (RStudio), automatically renders and runs <code>quarto preview</code> in an embedded window. You can also do the same thing from the Terminal if need be:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # preview the website in the current directory quarto preview</code></pre> <p>Note that when you preview a site (either using VS Code / RStudio integrated tools or from the terminal) changes to configuration files (e.g. <code>_quarto.yml</code>) as well as site resources (e.g. theme or CSS files) will cause an automatic refresh of the preview.</p> <p>You can customize the behavior of the preview server (port, whether it opens a browser, etc.) using command line options or the <code>_quarto.yml</code> config file. See <code>quarto preview help</code> or the project file reference for additional details.</p> <p>Important</p> <p>As you preview your site, pages will be rendered and updated. However, if you make changes to global options (e.g. <code>_quarto.yml</code> or included files) you need to fully re-render your site to have all of the changes reflected. Consequently, you should always fully <code>quarto render</code> your site before deploying it, even if you have already previewed changes to some pages with the preview server.</p> <h6 id="website-render">Website Render</h6> <p>To render (but not preview) a website, use the <code>quarto render</code> command, which will render the website into the <code>_site</code> directory by default:</p> <pre><code>Terminal # render the website in the current directory quarto render</code></pre> <p>See the Project Basics article to learn more about working with projects, including specifying an explicit list of files to render, as well as adding custom pre and post render scripts to your project.</p> <h5 id="render-targets-1">Render Targets</h5> <p>By default, all valid Quarto input files (.qmd, .ipynb, .md, .Rmd) in the project directory will be rendered, save for ones with:</p> <ul> <li><p>A file or directory prefix of <code>.</code> (hidden files)</p></li> <li><p>A file or directory prefix of <code>_</code> (typically used for non top-level files, e.g. ones included in other files)</p></li> <li><p>Files named <code>README.md</code> or <code>README.qmd</code> (which are typically not actual render targets but rather informational content about the source code to be viewed in the version control web UI).</p></li> <li><p>AI assistant configuration files (<code>CLAUDE.md</code>, <code>AGENTS.md</code>) which provide instructions for AI coding assistants and are not intended as rendered content. If you don’t want to render all of the target documents in a project, or you wish to control the order of rendering more precisely, you can add a <code>project: render: [files]</code> entry to your project metadata. For example:</p> <p>project: render: - section1.qmd - section2.qmd</p></li> </ul> <p>Note that you can use wildcards when defining the <code>render</code> list. For example:</p> <pre><code>project: render: - section*.qmd</code></pre> <p>You can also use the prefix <code>!</code> to ignore some files or directories in the <code>render</code> list. Note that in that case you need to start by specifying everything you do want to render. For example:</p> <pre><code>project: render: - "*.qmd" - "!ignored.qmd" - "!ignored-dir/"</code></pre> <p>Note</p> <p>If the name of your output file needs to start with <code>.</code> or <code>_</code> (for instance <code>_index.md</code> for Hugo users), you must name the Quarto input file without the prefix (for instance <code>index.qmd</code>) and add an explicit <code>output-file</code> parameter in the YAML such as</p> <pre><code>--- output-file: _index.md ---</code></pre> <h5 id="linking">Linking</h5> <p>When creating links between pages in your site, you can provide the source file as the link target (rather than the <code>.html</code> file). You can also add hash identifiers (<code>#)</code> to the source file if you want to link to a particular section in the document. For example:</p> <pre><code>[about](about.qmd) [about](about.qmd#section)</code></pre> <p>One benefit of using this style of link as opposed to targeting <code>.html</code> files directly is that if you at some point convert your site to a book the file-based links will automatically resolve to section links for formats that produce a single file (e.g. PDF or MS Word).</p> <h5 id="website-theme">Website Theme</h5> <p>The look of your website is controlled via HTML themes. These options are set under the <code>format</code> option in your website configuration file:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml format: html: theme: cosmo css: styles.css</code></pre> <p>See HTML Theming for details on the available options.</p> <h5 id="learning-more-23">Learning More</h5> <p>Once you’ve got a basic website up and running check out these articles for various ways to enhance your site:</p> <ul> <li>Website Navigation describes various ways to add navigation to a website, including top-level navigation bars, sidebars, or hybrid designs that uses both. This article also covers adding full-text search as well as a site-wide footer.</li> <li>Website Tools covers adding social metadata (e.g. for Twitter Cards) and Google Analytics to your site, as well as enabling users to toggle between dark and light color schemes.</li> <li>Website Options provides a comprehensive reference to all of the available website options.</li> <li>Code Execution provides tips for optimizing the rendering of sites with large numbers of documents or expensive computations.</li> <li>Publishing Websites enumerates the various options for publishing websites including GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Posit Connect.</li> </ul> <h3 id="custom-listings">Custom Listings</h3> <h4 id="custom-listings-1">Custom Listings</h4> <h5 id="overview-137">Overview</h5> <p>In addition to the three built-in types of listings, you can also build a completely custom display of the items. This custom display can generate any HTML and can optionally still take advantage of the sorting, filtering, and pagination provided by listings.</p> <h5 id="listing-templates">Listing Templates</h5> <p>To use a custom template, add the <code>template</code> option to your listing configuration:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: contents: posts template: gallery.ejs.md ---</code></pre> <p>Quarto passes the listing contents to the template as an array called <code>items</code>. Each item is populated with the fields described in Listing Fields, plus any custom metadata from the document.</p> <p>The template uses <a href="https://ejs.co">EJS</a> to combine HTML and JavaScript (inside <code><% %></code> tags) to process <code>items</code>. For example, this template constructs a list of links by looping through <code>items</code> and accessing the <code>path</code> and <code>title</code> fields:</p> <pre><code>gallery.ejs.md ```{=html} <ul> <% for (const item of items) { %> <li><a href="<%- item.path %>"><%= item.title %></a></li> <% } %> </ul> ```</code></pre> <p>The result is a simple bulleted list of links to the documents in the listing:</p> <p>Quarto processes EJS templates as Markdown, so we recommend using the <code>.ejs.md</code> extension for your template files. Since most templates output HTML, wrap your HTML in a raw block (```<code>{=html}</code>) to avoid performance issues and escaping problems.</p> <p>If you want a field like <code>title</code> to support Markdown formatting (e.g., <code>My **bold** title</code>), exit the raw HTML block to output the Markdown content, then re-enter it:</p> <pre><code>gallery.ejs.md ```{=html} <ul> <% for (const item of items) { %> <li><a href="<%- item.path %>"> ``` <%= item.title %> ```{=html} </a></li> <% } %> </ul> ```</code></pre> <p>NoteHTML Escaping</p> <p>Use <code><%- value %></code> to escape HTML characters in a value, or <code><%= value %></code> to output without escaping:</p> <pre><code>HTML escaped value: <%- value %> HTML unescaped value: <%= value %></code></pre> <p>This syntax comes from <code>lodash</code>, which Quarto uses to render EJS templates.</p> <h5 id="metadata-listings">Metadata Listings</h5> <p>The <code>contents</code> option for a listing most commonly contains a list of paths or globs, but it can also contain metadata. When contents are metadata, the metadata will be read into items and passed to the template. For example:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - name: First Item href: [quarto.org](https://www.quarto.org) custom-field: A custom value - name: Second Item href: [rstudio.org](https://www.rstudio.org) custom-field: A second custom value ---</code></pre> <p>could be rendered using:</p> <pre><code>custom.ejs.md ```{=html} <ul> <% for (const item of items) { %> <li> <a href="<%- item.href %>"><%= item.name %></a><br/> <%= item['custom-field'] %> </li> <% } %> </ul> ```</code></pre> <p>which produces a simple HTML display like:</p> <h5 id="metadata-file-listings">Metadata File Listings</h5> <p>The <code>contents</code> option for a listing can also point to one or more <code>yaml</code> files (which contain metadata). In that case, the metadata will be read from the files into items and passed to the template. For example:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - items.yml ---</code></pre> <p>where the contents of <code>items.yml</code> is:</p> <pre><code>items.yml - name: First Item href: [quarto.org](https://www.quarto.org) custom-field: A custom value - name: Second Item href: [rstudio.org](https://www.rstudio.org) custom-field: A second custom value</code></pre> <h6 id="template-examples">Template Examples</h6> <p>Portions of this website are built using custom listings. The best place to start is with our gallery, which is a listing built using a custom template and a metadata file. You can view the source code used to create the gallery page in our <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web">Github repository</a>.</p> <p>File</p> <p>Description</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/blob/main/docs/gallery/gallery.yml">gallery.yml</a></p> <p>The metadata that controls what items are displayed in the gallery listing.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/blob/main/docs/gallery/gallery.ejs">gallery.ejs</a></p> <p>The template used to display the items on the page.</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-web/blob/main/docs/gallery/index.qmd">index.qmd</a></p> <p>The Quarto document that configures and positions the listing in the <code>#gallery</code> div.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>The <code>gallery.ejs</code> template wraps all content in a raw HTML block, so Markdown formatting is not processed.</p> <h5 id="sorting-filtering-and-pagination">Sorting, Filtering, and Pagination</h5> <p>By default, sorting, filtering, and pagination are disabled for custom listing templates. To enable them, include the following in your template:</p> <ul> <li><p>Include a <code>list</code> class on the HTML tag that contains the list of items.</p></li> <li><p>For each item, include <code><%= metadataAttrs(item) %></code> in the HTML tag that contains the item. Quarto uses these attributes for sorting and filtering.</p></li> <li><p>Within each item, include a class that identifies the tag whose text represents the contents of an item’s field. The class must be the name of the field prefixed with <code>listing-</code>, for example the tag whose inner text is the <code>item.name</code> should include a class <code>listing-name</code>. For example, modify the above <code>custom.ejs.md</code> template as follows:</p> <p>custom.ejs.md</p> <ul class="list"> <% for (const item of items) { %> <li <%= metadataAttrs(item) %>> <a href="<%- item.href %>" class="listing-name"><%= item.name %></a><br/> <span class="listing-custom-field"><%= item['custom-field'] %><span> </li> <% } %> </ul></li> </ul> <p>Once you have included these items in your template, you can then enable the options in your listing:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: sort-ui: true filter-ui: true page-size: 10 ---</code></pre> <p>The UI elements will now appear on the page and should interact properly with your custom listing.</p> <h6 id="field-display-names">Field Display Names</h6> <p>You may want to provide a custom display name for your field to provide a better name than the field name. For example, the field name would appear in the sort UI. You can use <code>field-display-names</code> to create mapping from a field to a display name. For example:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - items.yml sort-ui: true filter-ui: true page-size: 10 field-display-names: name: "Name" custom-field: "Custom" ---</code></pre> <h6 id="date-sorting-and-formatting">Date Sorting and Formatting</h6> <p>To properly format and sort date values, you can specify type information for fields in your items. If you specify a field is a date, it will automatically be formatted using the specified date formatting (either default or specified using <code>date-format</code>) and will support date sorting in ascending or descending order. If you specify a field as a number, it will support ascending and descending numeric sorting.</p> <p>You can specify field types as follows:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - items.yml field-types: custom-date: date custom-number: number ---</code></pre> <h6 id="required-fields">Required Fields</h6> <p>Since listings are generated using fields that are specified in other documents or via metadata, it can be helpful to ensure that required fields are present. You can note required fields as following:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - items.yml field-required: [name, custom-field] ---</code></pre> <p>If the listing page is rendered and any of contents is missing a value for either of the required fields, an error will be thrown noting the field that is required and the file or metadata that has omitted it.</p> <h5 id="template-parameters">Template Parameters</h5> <p>You may also make your custom template more dynamic by using parameters to control its behavior. You can provide parameters for custom templates using the <code>template-params</code> option like:</p> <pre><code>index.qmd --- listing: template: custom.ejs.md contents: - items.yml template-params: param1: "param-value" ---</code></pre> <p>Template parameters can then be accessed in your template using <code><%= templateParams.param1 %></code>. For example, modify the above <code>custom.ejs.md</code> template as follows:</p> <pre><code>custom.ejs.md ### <%= templateParams.param1 %> ```{=html} <ul class="pub-list list"> <% for (const item of items) { %> <li <%= metadataAttrs(item) %>> <span class="listing-title"><%= item.title %>.</span> </li> <% } %> </ul> ```</code></pre> <h3 id="document-listings">Document Listings</h3> <h4 id="document-listings-1">Document Listings</h4> <h5 id="overview-138">Overview</h5> <p>Listings enable you to automatically generate the contents of a page (or region of a page) from a list of Quarto documents or other custom data.</p> <p>Listings are useful for creating blogs, providing navigation for large numbers of documents, or any other scenario where you’d like the contents of a page to be automatically updated as documents are added, updated, and removed.</p> <p>You can enable listings on a page using the <code>listing</code> option in the document front matter. This will instruct Quarto to generate additional content (the ‘listings’) when the page is rendered. For example, the following YAML in the front matter of a document:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Listing Example" listing: default ---</code></pre> <p>will result in a listing of all documents in the directory (with the exception of the current document). It might look something like this:</p> <h5 id="listing-contents">Listing Contents</h5> <p>You can control what documents are included in the listing by using the <code>contents</code> option, which allows you to provide a set of input files (or globs of input files) that should be included in the listing. For each of the inputs that matches the <code>contents</code> of a listing, an item will be included using the metadata in the front matter of the document.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>To have an item in the list, it must contain at least the “title” metadata.</p> <p>For example to include all the Quarto documents in the <code>posts</code> directory, you would write:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Listing Example" listing: contents: posts ---</code></pre> <p>You can write much more complex rules for including content by using globs and using a list of targets in the contents, such as:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Listing Example" listing: contents: - "reports/*.qmd" - "lab-notes/*reports.qmd"</code></pre> <p>Review the Quarto Glob Reference for more information about supported glob syntax.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>If you provide a path to a directory, it will be treated as <code><directory>/**</code> - the directory will be searched recursively for project inputs.</p> <p>It is important to note that when providing a list of targets, these will be identified relative to the location of the listings page, not the root of the project file. For example, if your listings page is located at <code>/pages/listings.qmd</code> specifying <code>contents: "reports/*.qmd"</code> will search in <code>/pages/reports/</code> not <code>/reports/</code> for the targeted files.</p> <p>In addition to specifying lists of files or globs, contents can contain lists of metadata as well. For more about this, see Custom Listings.</p> <h5 id="listing-types">Listing Types</h5> <p>There are three built-in types of listings that you can choose from. Use the <code>type</code> option to choose the appearance of the listing:</p> <pre><code>--- listing: contents: posts type: default ---</code></pre> <p>The type field accepts the following values:</p> <p>Type</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>default</code></p> <p>A blog style list of items.</p> <p><code>table</code></p> <p>A table of listings.</p> <p><code>grid</code></p> <p>A grid of listing cards.</p> <ul> <li>Default</li> <li>Grid</li> <li>Table By default, listings will appear in full width rows that display the item’s metadata (author and date), title, description, and image.</li> </ul> <p>Grid style listings display a card for each item.</p> <p>The table listing style provides a traditional tabular layout.</p> <h5 id="sorting-items">Sorting Items</h5> <p>By default, listings created from documents will be ordered by their title. Use the <code>sort</code> option to control the order of the listing. For example:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts sort: "date"</code></pre> <p>Each <code>sort</code> key can include a field name and optionally either <code>asc</code> or <code>desc</code> to control whether to sort in ascending or descending order. When only the name is specified, sorting by that field will be in ascending order.</p> <p>The sort key can also contain one or more fields to sort by. For example:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts sort: - "date" - "title desc"</code></pre> <p>This will sort the documents in the <code>posts</code> directory first by their date in ascending order, then by their title in descending order.</p> <p>If you’d like to disable sorting entirely and display the items in the order in which they are specified, you can pass <code>sort: false</code> (which will disable sorting and preserve the item’s original order).</p> <h5 id="listing-options">Listing Options</h5> <p>It is possible to customize the appearance of listings using the following options for each type of listing display.</p> <h6 id="default">Default</h6> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>max-items</code></p> <p>The maximum number of items to include in this listing.</p> <p><code>image-align</code></p> <p>Whether to place the image on the right or left side of the post content. Defaults to <code>right</code>.</p> <p><code>image-height</code></p> <p>The height of the image being displayed. The width is automatically determined and the image will fill the rectangle without scaling (i.e. cropped to fill).</p> <p><code>image-placeholder</code></p> <p>The default image for items if they have no image.</p> <h6 id="grids">Grids</h6> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>max-items</code></p> <p>The maximum number of items to include in this listing.</p> <p><code>image-height</code></p> <p>The height of the image being displayed. The width is automatically determined and the image will fill the rectangle without scaling (i.e. cropped to fill).</p> <p><code>image-placeholder</code></p> <p>The default image for items if they have no image.</p> <p><code>grid-columns</code></p> <p>The number of columns in the grid display. Defaults to 3.</p> <p><code>grid-item-border</code></p> <p>Whether to display a border around the item card. Defaults to <code>true</code>.</p> <p><code>grid-item-align</code></p> <p>Aligns the content within the card (<code>left</code>, <code>right</code>, or <code>center</code>). Defaults to <code>left</code>.</p> <h6 id="tables-49">Tables</h6> <p>Options</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>max-items</code></p> <p>The maximum number of items to include in this listing.</p> <p><code>image-height</code></p> <p>The height of the image being displayed. The width is automatically select and the image will fill the rectangle without scaling (i.e. cropped to fill).</p> <p><code>image-placeholder</code></p> <p>The default image for items if they have no image.</p> <p><code>table-striped</code></p> <p>Display the table rows with alternating background colors (<code>true</code> or <code>false</code>). Defaults to <code>false</code></p> <p><code>table-hover</code></p> <p>Highlight rows of the table when the user hovers the mouse over them (<code>true</code> or <code>false</code>). Defaults to <code>false</code>.</p> <p><code>field-links</code></p> <p>A list of fields that should link to the document in the table (defaults to <code>title</code>).</p> <h6 id="advanced-options">Advanced Options</h6> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>field-display-names</code></p> <p>A mapping that provides display name for specific fields. For example, to display the title column as ‘Report’ in a table listing you would write:</p> <pre><code>listing: field-display-names: title: "Report"</code></pre> <p><code>image-lazy-loading</code></p> <p>When <code>true</code>, listing images are loaded only as they come into view. When <code>false</code>, images are automatically loaded. Default: <code>true</code></p> <p><code>max-description-length</code></p> <p>The maximum length of the description displayed in the listing (in characters). Defaults to 175.</p> <p><code>date-format</code></p> <p>The date format to use when displaying dates (e.g. <code>d-M-yyyy</code>).</p> <p>You may either provide a date style (<code>full</code>, <code>long</code>, <code>medium</code>, <code>short</code> or <code>iso</code>) or a format string for formatting the date. The behavior of date styles varies depending upon locale, but examples in the <code>en</code> locale are as follows:</p> <p>full</p> <p>Saturday, February 5, 2022</p> <p>long</p> <p>February 5, 2022</p> <p>medium</p> <p>Feb 5, 2022</p> <p>short</p> <p>2/5/22</p> <p>iso</p> <p>2022-05-22</p> <p>Learn more about supported date formatting values here.</p> <p>In addition to the above listing-wide options, each listing type has a variety of options to customize its appearance.</p> <h5 id="categories-1">Categories</h5> <p>In addition to displaying the listing contents, listings can also automatically add a list of categories to the page that they appear on. To enable categories you can set the <code>categories</code> option like:</p> <pre><code>listing: categories: true</code></pre> <p>which results in categories appearing in the right sidebar:</p> <p>When users click a category, the page will be updated to show only the listing items that match the selected category.</p> <h6 id="category-appearance">Category Appearance</h6> <p>You can choose between a few different display styles for categories:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>numbered</code></p> <p>Displays a list of categories in alphabetical order with the number of items in that category displayed next to the category name.</p> <p><code>unnumbered</code></p> <p>Display a list of categories in alphabetical order.</p> <p><code>cloud</code></p> <p>Displays a ‘word cloud’ of categories.</p> <p>When multiple listings appear on the page, categories will be enabled based upon the option set in the first listing. If categories are enabled for the first listing, all listings on the page will contribute their item categories to the list of categories and all will be filtered when the user clicks a category.</p> <h5 id="feeds">Feeds</h5> <p>You can also have an RSS feed generated based upon the contents of a listing. This is great to allow your content to be syndicated or to be accessible via RSS Readers. Include a feed for your listing by including the <code>feed</code> option:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts feed: true</code></pre> <p>When a feed is enabled for a listing on a page, an RSS file will be automatically generated using the name of the file. For example, <code>index.qmd</code> will produce a feed at <code>index.xml</code>. A link to the feed will be included in the <code>head</code> of the page as well.</p> <p>Generating feeds requires that the <code>site-url</code> be set for the site in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file. For example:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: site-url: "[quarto.org](https://www.quarto.org)"</code></pre> <p>You can further customize your feed by passing options to the <code>feed</code> key:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts feed: items: 10</code></pre> <p>The following options are available:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>items</code></p> <p>The number of items to include in your feed. Defaults to 20.</p> <p><code>type</code></p> <p><code>full</code>, <code>partial</code> or <code>metadata</code>. <code>full</code>, the default, includes the full contents of each document in the feed. <code>partial</code> includes the description, if available, otherwise the first paragraph in the feed. <code>metadata</code> includes only the title, description, and other document metadata in the feed.</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The title for this feed. Defaults to the site title provided in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file.</p> <p><code>image</code></p> <p>The image for this feed. If not specified, the image for the page the listing appears on will be used, otherwise an image will be used if specified for the site in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file.</p> <p><code>description</code></p> <p>The description of this feed. If not specified, the description for the page the listing appears on will be used, otherwise the description of the site will be used if specified in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file.</p> <p><code>language</code></p> <p>The language of the feed. Omitted if not specified. See <a href="https://www.rssboard.org/rss-language-codes">rssboard.org</a> for a list of valid language codes.</p> <p><code>categories</code></p> <p>Generates a separate feed for each of the categories included in this list of category names.</p> <h5 id="listing-fields">Listing Fields</h5> <p>When reading the contents of a listing, Quarto uses the metadata read from the front matter of the document or the contents of the document itself to populate the following fields for each item:</p> <p>Field Name</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The title of the item, read from the <code>title</code> field of the front matter (or the first H1 of the document).</p> <p><code>subtitle</code></p> <p>The subtitle of the item, read from the <code>subtitle</code> field of the front matter.</p> <p><code>author</code></p> <p>The author of the item, read from the <code>author</code> field of the front matter.</p> <p><code>description</code></p> <p>The description of the item, read from the <code>description</code> or <code>abstract</code> field of the front matter or from the first paragraph of the document.</p> <p><code>date</code></p> <p>The date of the item, read from the <code>date</code> field of the front matter.</p> <p><code>image</code></p> <p>The image for this item, read from the <code>image</code> field of the front matter, or automatically discovered by taking the first of an image of class <code>preview-image</code>, an image with a file name starting with <code>feature</code>, <code>cover</code>, or <code>thumbnail</code>, or the first image to appear in the document.</p> <p><code>image-alt</code></p> <p>The alt text for the image for this item.</p> <p><code>word-count</code></p> <p>A word count for this item.</p> <p><code>reading-time</code></p> <p>An estimate of the reading time for this item, computed by counting the words in the item and assuming a reading speed of 200 words per minute.</p> <p><code>categories</code></p> <p>Categories for the item, read from the <code>categories</code> field of the front matter.</p> <p><code>filename</code></p> <p>The name of the input file.</p> <p><code>file-modified</code></p> <p>The last modified date of this input file.</p> <p>Depending upon the type of listing that you are using, different fields are displayed automatically:</p> <p>Field</p> <p>Type: Default</p> <p>Type: Table</p> <p>Type: Grid</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p><code>subtitle</code></p> <p>x</p> <p><code>author</code></p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p><code>description</code></p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p><code>date</code></p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <p><code>image</code></p> <p>x</p> <p>x</p> <h6 id="customizing-fields">Customizing Fields</h6> <p>Though specific columns are displayed by default, each of the types will allow you to display any of the above columns by using the <code>fields</code> options. For example, to display more fields in a table (as columns), you write:</p> <pre><code>listing: type: table contents: posts fields: [image, date, title, author, reading-time]</code></pre> <p>which produces:</p> <p>Each type of listing will handle the fields in different ways.</p> <p>Default</p> <p>For default type listings, the various fields will be placed logically, with the <code>image</code> in the right column, the <code>title</code>, <code>subtitle</code>, and <code>description</code> in the center column, and any other fields in the left column.</p> <p>Tables</p> <p>For table type listings, the list of fields will be displayed as columns in the order that the fields appear in the list.</p> <p>Grid</p> <p>For grid listings, the <code>image</code>, <code>title</code>, <code>subtitle</code>, <code>reading-time</code>, <code>categories</code>, <code>description</code>, <code>author</code>, and <code>date</code> fields will be arranged on the body of the card. The <code>filename</code> and <code>file-modified</code> fields will appear in the card footer. Any other fields will appear in a table at the bottom of the card body.</p> <h5 id="including-or-excluding-items">Including or Excluding Items</h5> <p>You can control what documents are included or excluding based upon the metadata of the items by using the <code>include</code> and <code>exclude</code> options. These options allow you to specify one or more field names and values that must be present or absent in order for the item to be included or excluded. For example, to include only items authored by <code>Harlow</code> or <code>Tristan</code>, you write:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts type: grid include: author: "{Harlow,Tristan}*"</code></pre> <p>To exclude any items authored by <code>Charles</code>, you write:</p> <pre><code>listing: contents: posts type: grid exclude: author: "Charles*"</code></pre> <p>When including or excluding items based upon a string field value, Quarto will use glob syntax when comparing values. Any other type of comparison will be done by testing for equality.</p> <h5 id="user-tools">User Tools</h5> <p>Listings support interactive tools to allow the viewer of the listing to sort, filter, or page through listings.</p> <h6 id="sorting">Sorting</h6> <p>Users can use the select box to choose how to sort the items in the listing (or in the case of tables, by clicking on the column headings). By default, the sorting control will allow the user to sort by <code>title</code>, <code>date</code>, or <code>author</code>. You can stop this UI from being displayed to the user with the option:</p> <pre><code>listing: sort-ui: false</code></pre> <p>You can control which fields are included in the sort list by providing a list of field names in the <code>sort-ui</code> key:</p> <pre><code>listing: sort-ui: [title, date]</code></pre> <h6 id="filtering">Filtering</h6> <p>Listings include a filter box positioned on the top right of the listing content. The filter box allows readers to perform a ‘typeahead’ search of the listing contents. You can disable the filtering control using the option:</p> <pre><code>listing: filter-ui: false</code></pre> <p>By default, if the filtering control is enabling, all fields that are being displayed in the listing will be searchable. If you’d like to limit searching / filtering to specific fields, you can do so by providing a field list in the <code>filter-ui</code> key:</p> <pre><code>listing: filter-ui: [title, date]</code></pre> <h6 id="pagination">Pagination</h6> <p>Listings also natively support pagination of the items. The default number of items displayed on a page depends up the listing type:</p> <p>Listing Type</p> <p>Items Per Page</p> <p><code>default</code></p> <p>25</p> <p><code>table</code></p> <p>30</p> <p><code>grid</code></p> <p>18</p> <p>You can control the number of items displayed per page using the option <code>page-size</code>:</p> <pre><code>listing: page-size: 36</code></pre> <h5 id="listing-location">Listing Location</h5> <p>By default, listings will simply be appended to the main content region of the page. If you’d like to control where a listing appears, set an <code>id</code> for that listing and use that <code>id</code> on a corresponding div in the page. For example, updating the page used in the previous example to this:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Listing Example" listing: id: sample-listings contents: posts sort: "date desc" type: table --- You can review the following documents for additional information: ::: {#sample-listings} ::: Learn more about Quarto [here](https://www.quarto.com).</code></pre> <p>Results in a listing page like:</p> <h5 id="multiple-listings">Multiple Listings</h5> <p>You can place any number of listings on a single page. The following would populate two listings on a single page:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Team Documents listing: - id: lab-reports contents: "lab-reports/*.qmd" type: table - id: meeting-notes contents: "meeting-notes/*.qmd" type: table --- ## Lab Reports :::{#lab-reports} ::: ## Meeting Notes :::{#meeting-notes} :::</code></pre> <h5 id="yaml-listing-content">YAML Listing Content</h5> <p>In addition to populating a listing with inputs that match one or more globs, you can also provide items explicitly via a YAML file. For example, the following listing:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "Listing Example" listing: id: sample-listings contents: - posts - archived-items.yaml sort: "date desc" type: table ---</code></pre> <p>will include all the documents in the <code>posts</code> directory, but will also merge in the contents of the <code>archived-items.yaml</code> file. The contents of the <code>archived-items.yaml</code> file should be a list of items, each of which is a map of field names to values. For example:</p> <pre><code>- title: "Archived Item 1" author: Norah Jones date: 2020-01-01 path: "archived/archived-item-.html" categories: [archived, technology]</code></pre> <p>This is useful for cases such as migrating existing content to Quarto - you can begin creating new content as Quarto documents, but still include existing content in your listings by providing their metadata via a yaml file.</p> <h3 id="output-for-llms">Output for LLMs</h3> <h4 id="output-for-llms-1">Output for LLMs</h4> <h5 id="overview-139">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto can generate <a href="https://llmstxt.org/">llms.txt</a> format output for your website, making your content more accessible to large language models and AI-powered tools. When enabled, Quarto creates an <code>llms.txt</code> index file and <code>.llms.md</code> markdown files for each page.</p> <h5 id="enabling-llms.txt">Enabling <code>llms.txt</code></h5> <p>To enable <code>llms.txt</code> output, add <code>llms-txt: true</code> to your website configuration:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: title: "My Documentation" llms-txt: true</code></pre> <h5 id="generated-output">Generated Output</h5> <p>When you render your site, Quarto creates files in the output directory (typically <code>_site/</code>).</p> <h6 id="llms.txt-index"><code>llms.txt</code> Index</h6> <p>An <code>llms.txt</code> file is created at the root of your site. This index lists all pages with their titles, using your site’s title and description from the website configuration in <code>_quarto.yml</code>.</p> <h6 id="markdown-files">Markdown Files</h6> <p>For each HTML page, a corresponding <code>.llms.md</code> file is created alongside it (e.g., <code>guide.html</code> gets <code>guide.llms.md</code>). These contain clean markdown versions of your content.</p> <h5 id="content-conversion">Content Conversion</h5> <p>HTML content is converted to markdown using Pandoc. Navigation elements, sidebars, breadcrumbs, footers, and scripts are removed. Tables, code blocks, callouts, tabsets, and images are converted to standard markdown formats. Internal links are automatically rewritten from <code>.html</code> to <code>.llms.md</code> extensions, including links with anchors.</p> <h5 id="conditional-content-4">Conditional Content</h5> <p>To include content only in the <code>.llms.md</code> output, use the <code>llms-txt</code> format with conditional content classes.</p> <p>For example, to include content only in <code>document.llms.md</code>:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd ::: {.content-visible when-format="llms-txt"} This content appears only in the `.llms.md` output. :::</code></pre> <p>To exclude content from <code>document.llms.md</code>:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd ::: {.content-hidden when-format="llms-txt"} This content appears in HTML but not in `.llms.md` output. :::</code></pre> <h5 id="draft-handling">Draft Handling</h5> <p>Draft pages are automatically excluded from both <code>.llms.md</code> generation and the <code>llms.txt</code> index. The 404 page is also excluded from the index.</p> <h5 id="build-behavior">Build Behavior</h5> <p>On full builds, all <code>.llms.md</code> files and the <code>llms.txt</code> index are regenerated. On incremental builds, individual <code>.llms.md</code> files are updated but <code>llms.txt</code> is preserved, matching the behavior of sitemap generation.</p> <h3 id="website-drafts">Website Drafts</h3> <h4 id="website-drafts-1">Website Drafts</h4> <h5 id="overview-140">Overview</h5> <p>Use drafts to preview and plan content before it is ready to publish. By default, draft pages will be blank in your rendered site, and will not appear in navigation, listings, search results, or the sitemap. On this page, learn how to specify pages as drafts, control how drafts appear in rendered sites and how drafts appear in site previews.</p> <h5 id="specifying-drafts">Specifying Drafts</h5> <p>To specify a page or post is a draft, you can add <code>draft: true</code> to the document YAML:</p> <pre><code>posts/post-with-code/index.qmd --- title: "Post with Code" draft: true ---</code></pre> <p>To specify all documents in directory are drafts set <code>draft: true</code> in the directory metadata:</p> <pre><code>posts/_metadata.yml draft: true</code></pre> <p>As an alternative to the <code>draft</code> document option, you can also specify the website option <code>drafts</code> in <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: title: "Cool Website." drafts: - posts/post-with-code/index.qmd</code></pre> <p>If you would like to specify a list of paths in a separate file, use a metadata include. For example, you could specify your drafts in <code>drafts.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>drafts.yml website: drafts: - posts/post-with-code/index.qmd</code></pre> <p>Then, provide this file to <code>metadata-files</code>:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: title: "Cool Website." metadata-files: - drafts.yml</code></pre> <p>You can also set the website <code>drafts</code> option using project profiles.</p> <h5 id="appearance-of-drafts">Appearance of Drafts</h5> <p>You can use the <code>draft-mode</code> option to control the content and linking of draft documents in the rendered website. The values for <code>draft-mode</code> are:</p> <ul> <li><code>gone</code>(default)—Empty and unlinked</li> <li><code>unlinked</code>—Rendered and unlinked</li> <li><code>visible</code>—Rendered and linked A URL will exist for an empty page but the page itself will be blank. Drafts that are rendered will additionally include a draft banner:</li> </ul> <p>A rendered draft document will include a “Draft” banner</p> <p>When a draft is unlinked it will not appear in search results, listings, the sitemap, or navigation (sidebars, navbars, and footers). If another page links to an unlinked draft document, the link will be omitted leaving the content of the link without the hyperlink itself.</p> <p>As a complete example, consider the following website configuration:</p> <p>Listing 1: A complete <code>_quarto.yml</code> example</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml project: type: website website: title: "Cool Website." navbar: left: - stuff/item1.qmd - stuff/item2.qmd 1 drafts: - stuff/item2.qmd 2 draft-mode: unlinked</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p>The project is providing a simple list of draft documents. The same thing could be specified using <code>draft: true</code> in <code>stuff/item2.qmd</code>’s front matter.</p> <p>2</p> <p>The draft mode is set to <code>unlinked</code>, so drafts are rendered but not linked to.</p> <p>When rendered the navbar in the above site will omit the item for <code>stuff/item2.qmd</code>:</p> <p>However, <code>stuff/item2.qmd</code> is still available at <code>stuff/item2.html</code> and shows the draft banner:</p> <h5 id="previewing-drafts">Previewing Drafts</h5> <p>Regardless of the <code>draft-mode</code> setting, when you preview a site with <code>quarto preview</code> drafts will be <code>visible</code>. Draft pages will be rendered and display a draft banner, and any links or navigation items pointing at the draft pages will be visible and active. For example, when the site described in Listing 1, is previewed a link to <code>stuff/item2.html</code> appears in the navigation:</p> <p>This preview behaviour includes previews generated with the Render button in RStudio, and the Preview button in Positron or VS Code.</p> <h3 id="website-navigation">Website Navigation</h3> <h4 id="website-navigation-1">Website Navigation</h4> <h5 id="overview-141">Overview</h5> <p>There are a variety of options available for providing website navigation, including:</p> <ul> <li>Using top navigation (a navbar) with optional sub-menus.</li> <li>Using side navigation with a hierarchy of pages.</li> <li>Combining top and side navigation (where top navigation links to different sections of the site with their own side navigation). In addition, you can add full text search to either the top or side navigation interface.</li> </ul> <h5 id="top-navigation">Top Navigation</h5> <p>To add top-navigation to a website, add a <code>navbar</code> entry to the <code>website</code> config in <code>_quarto.yml</code>. For example, the following YAML:</p> <pre><code>website: navbar: background: primary search: true left: - text: "Home" href: index.qmd - talks.qmd - about.qmd</code></pre> <p>Results in a navigation bar that looks something like this:</p> <p>Above we use the <code>left</code> option to specify items for the left side of the navigation bar. You can also use the <code>right</code> option to specify items for the right side.</p> <p>The text for navigation bar items will be taken from the underlying target document’s title. Note that in the above example we provide a custom <code>text: "Home"</code> value for <code>index.qmd</code>.</p> <p>You can also create a navigation bar menu by including a <code>menu</code> (which is a list of items much like <code>left</code> and <code>right</code>). For example:</p> <pre><code>left: - text: "More" menu: - talks.qmd - about.qmd</code></pre> <p>Here are all of the options available for top navigation:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>Navbar title (uses the <code>site: title</code> if none is specified). Use <code>title: false</code> to suppress the display of the title on the navbar.</p> <p><code>logo</code></p> <p>Logo image to be displayed left of the title. When using a <code>_brand.yml</code> with a logo, the brand logo is automatically displayed. Use <code>logo: false</code> to suppress the brand logo on the navbar.</p> <p><code>logo-alt</code></p> <p>Alternate text for the logo image.</p> <p><code>logo-href</code></p> <p>Target href from navbar logo / title. By default, the logo and title link to the root page of the site (<code>/index.html</code>).</p> <p><code>background</code></p> <p>Background color (“primary”, “secondary”, “success”, “danger”, “warning”, “info”, “light”, “dark”, or hex color).</p> <p><code>foreground</code></p> <p>Foreground color (“primary”, “secondary”, “success”, “danger”, “warning”, “info”, “light”, “dark”, or hex color). The foreground color will be used to color navigation elements, text and links that appear in the navbar.</p> <p><code>search</code></p> <p>Include a search box (true or false).</p> <p><code>tools</code></p> <p>List of navbar tools (e.g., link to github or bluesky, etc.). See Navbar Tools for details.</p> <p><code>left</code> / <code>right</code></p> <p>Lists of navigation items for left and right side of navbar.</p> <p><code>pinned</code></p> <p>Always show the navbar (true or false). Defaults to false, and uses <a href="https://wicky.nillia.ms/headroom.js/">headroom.js</a> to automatically show the navbar when the user scrolls up on the page.</p> <p><code>collapse</code></p> <p>Collapse the navbar items into a hamburger menu when the display gets narrow (defaults to true).</p> <p><code>collapse-below</code></p> <p>Responsive breakpoint at which to collapse navbar items to a hamburger menu (“sm”, “md”, “lg”, “xl”, or “xxl”, defaults to “lg”).</p> <p><code>toggle-position</code></p> <p>The position of the collapsed navbar hamburger menu when in responsive mode (“left” or “right”, defaults to “left”).</p> <p><code>tools-collapse</code></p> <p>Collapse tools into the navbar menu when the display becomes narrow.</p> <p>Here are the options available for individual navigation items:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>href</code></p> <p>Link to file contained with the project or external URL.</p> <p><code>text</code></p> <p>Text to display for navigation item (defaults to the document <code>title</code> if not provided).</p> <p><code>icon</code></p> <p>Name of one of the standard <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com/">Bootstrap 5 icons</a> (e.g., “github”, “bluesky”, “share”, etc.).</p> <p><code>aria-label</code></p> <p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-label">Accessible label</a> for the navigation item.</p> <p><code>rel</code></p> <p>Value for <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel">rel</a> attribute. Multiple space-separated values are permitted.</p> <p><code>target</code></p> <p>Value for <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/a#target">target</a> attribute. E.g., <code>_blank</code> to open in a new tab.</p> <p><code>menu</code></p> <p>List of navigation items to populate a drop-down menu.</p> <p>For more information on controlling the appearance of the navigation bar using HTML themes, see HTML Themes - Navigation.</p> <h6 id="navbar-tools-1">Navbar Tools</h6> <p>In addition to traditional navigation, the navbar can also display a set of tools (e.g., social actions, GitHub view or edit actions, etc.) A tool definition consists of an icon name and an href to follow when clicked. For icon, use the icon name of any of the 1,300+ Bootstrap Icons.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>website: navbar: tools: - icon: bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app) - icon: github menu: - text: Source Code href: [code.com](https://code.com) - text: Report a Bug href: [bugs.com](https://bugs.com)</code></pre> <p>Tools specified for a navigation bar will appear on the right side of the Navbar. If you specify a dark theme or reader mode for your website, the controls for those options will appear with any specified tools.</p> <p>When the navbar is collapsed into a menu on smaller screens, the tools will be placed at the bottom of the menu.</p> <h5 id="side-navigation">Side Navigation</h5> <p>If your site consists of more than a handful of documents, you might prefer to use side navigation, which enables you to display an arbitrarily deep hierarchy of articles.</p> <p>If you are reading this page on a desktop device then you will see the default side navigation display on the left (otherwise you’ll see a title bar at the top which you can click or touch to reveal the navigation).</p> <p>To add side navigation to a website, add a <code>sidebar</code> entry to the <code>website</code> section of <code>_quarto.yml</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: sidebar: style: "docked" search: true contents: - text: "Introduction" href: introduction.qmd - section: "Basics" href: basics-summary.qmd contents: - index.qmd - basics-knitr.qmd - basics-jupyter.qmd - section: "Layout" contents: - layout.qmd - layout-knitr.qmd - layout-jupyter.qmd - section: advanced.qmd contents: - raw-code.qmd - custom-theme.qmd - acknowledgment.qmd</code></pre> <p>There are two styles of side navigation available: “docked” which shows the navigation in a sidebar with a distinct background color, and “floating” which places it closer to the main body text. Here’s what the “docked” and “floating” styles look like (respectively):</p> <p>Here are all of the options available for side navigation:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>id</code></p> <p>Optional identifier (used only for hybrid navigation, described below).</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>Sidebar title (uses the project title if none is specified).</p> <p><code>logo</code></p> <p>Optional logo image. When using a <code>_brand.yml</code> with a logo, the brand logo is automatically displayed. Use <code>logo: false</code> to suppress the brand logo on the sidebar.</p> <p><code>logo-alt</code></p> <p>Alternate text for the logo image.</p> <p><code>logo-href</code></p> <p>Target href from sidebar logo. By default, the logo and title link to the root page of the site (<code>/index.html</code>).</p> <p><code>search</code></p> <p>Include a search box (true or false). Note that if there is already a search box on the top navigation bar it won’t be displayed on the sidebar.</p> <p><code>tools</code></p> <p>List of sidebar tools (e.g., link to github or bluesky, etc.). See the next section for details.</p> <p><code>contents</code></p> <p>List of navigation items to display (typically top level items will in turn have a list of sub-items).</p> <p><code>style</code></p> <p>“docked” or “floating”.</p> <p><code>type</code></p> <p>“dark” or “light” (hint to make sure the text color is the inverse of the background).</p> <p><code>background</code></p> <p>Background color (“none”, “primary”, “secondary”, “success”, “danger”, “warning”, “info”, “light”, “dark”, or “white”). Defaults to “light”.</p> <p><code>foreground</code></p> <p>Foreground color (“primary”, “secondary”, “success”, “danger”, “warning”, “info”, “light”, “dark”, or hex color). The foreground color will be used to color navigation elements, text and links that appear in the sidebar.</p> <p><code>border</code></p> <p>Whether to show a border on the sidebar. “true” or “false”.</p> <p><code>alignment</code></p> <p>Alignment (“left”, “right”, or “center”).</p> <p><code>collapse-level</code></p> <p>Whether to show sidebar navigation collapsed by default. The default is 2, which shows the top and next level fully expanded (but leaves the 3rd and subsequent levels collapsed).</p> <p><code>pinned</code></p> <p>Always show a title bar that expands to show the sidebar at narrower screen widths (true or false). Defaults to false, and uses <a href="https://wicky.nillia.ms/headroom.js/">headroom.js</a> to automatically show the navigation bar when the user scrolls up on the page.</p> <p>A single <code>sidebar</code> item without an <code>id</code> or <code>title</code> will result in a global sidebar applied to all pages. A sidebar with an <code>id</code> or <code>title</code> will only be applied to pages within the contents of the sidebar or pages that specify the sidebar id.</p> <p>To use a specific sidebar on a page or a group of pages, specify the <code>sidebar</code> ID in the front matter of the page or in the <code>_metadata.yml</code> file. For example, to include the sidebar with <code>id: tutorials</code> on a page, add the following to the page’s front matter:</p> <pre><code>sidebar: tutorials</code></pre> <p>For more information on controlling the appearance of the side navigation using HTML themes, see HTML Themes - Navigation. If you need to control the width of the sidebar, see Page Layout - Grid Customization.</p> <h6 id="auto-generation">Auto Generation</h6> <p>Above we describe how to explicitly populate the <code>contents</code> of your sidebar with navigation items. You can also automatically generate sidebar navigation from the filesystem. The most straightforward way to do this is to specify the <code>contents</code> option as follows:</p> <pre><code>sidebar: contents: auto</code></pre> <p>Using <code>contents: auto</code> at the root level will result in all documents in your website being included within the navigation (save for the home page which can be navigated to via the title link). Navigation is constructed using the following rules:</p> <ul> <li><p>Navigation item titles will be read from the <code>title</code> field of documents.</p></li> <li><p>Sub-directories will create sections and will be automatically titled based on the directory name (including adding capitalization and substituting spaces for dashes and underscores). Use an <code>index.qmd</code> in the directory to provide an explicit <code>title</code> if you don’t like the automatic one.</p></li> <li><p>Order is alphabetical (by filename) unless a numeric <code>order</code> field is provided in document metadata. Automatic navigation automatically includes items in sub-directories. If you prefer not to do this, use an explicit <code>/*</code> to indicate only the documents in the root directory:</p> <p>sidebar: contents: /*</p></li> </ul> <p>Rather than specifying that all documents should be included, you can also specify a directory name or a glob pattern. For example, the following values for <code>contents</code> are all valid (note that the second form for <code>reports</code> is non-recursive):</p> <pre><code>sidebar: contents: reports sidebar: contents: reports/* sidebar: contents: "*.ipynb"</code></pre> <p>Note that in YAML we need to quote any strings that begin with <code>*</code> (as we do above for <code>*.ipynb</code>).</p> <p>You can automatically build sidebar <code>contents</code> anywhere within a sidebar hierarchy. For example, here we add a section that is automatically generated from a directory:</p> <pre><code>sidebar: contents: - about.qmd - contributing.qmd - section: Reports contents: reports</code></pre> <p>You can also include automatically generated items in the middle of a list of normal items by including an item with an <code>auto</code> property. Here we add an <code>auto</code> entry in the middle of a list of items:</p> <pre><code>sidebar: contents: - about.qmd - contributing.qmd - auto: "*-report.qmd"</code></pre> <p>Note again that we quote the <code>auto</code> entry with a <code>*</code> in it so that it is correctly parsed.</p> <h6 id="sidebar-tools-3">Sidebar Tools</h6> <p>In addition to traditional navigation, the sidebar can also display a set of tools (e.g., social actions, GitHub view or edit actions, etc.) A tool definition consists of an icon name and an href to follow when clicked. For <code>icon</code>, use the icon name of any of the 1,300+ <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com">Bootstrap Icons</a>.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>website: sidebar: tools: - icon: bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app) - icon: github menu: - text: Source Code href: [code.com](https://code.com) - text: Report a Bug href: [bugs.com](https://bugs.com)</code></pre> <h5 id="hybrid-navigation">Hybrid Navigation</h5> <p>If you have a website with dozens or even hundreds of pages, you will likely want to use top and side navigation together, where the top navigation links to various sections, each with their own side navigation.</p> <p>To do this, provide a group of <code>sidebar</code> entries and link each group of <code>sidebar</code> entries with a <code>navbar</code> entry by matching their <code>title</code>s and listing the page linked from the <code>navbar</code> as the first content in the <code>sidebar</code> group. For example, if you are using the <a href="https://diataxis.fr/">Diátaxis Framework</a> for documentation, you might have separate sections for tutorials, how-to guides, explanations, and reference documents, your page might look like the following.</p> <p>With hybrid navigation, if then you click on, say, Tutorials, you might land in a page like the following.</p> <p>To achieve this layout, your site configuration needs to look something like this:</p> <pre><code>website: title: ProjectX navbar: background: primary search: true left: - text: "Home" href: index.qmd - text: "Tutorials" href: tutorials.qmd - text: "How-To" href: howto.qmd - text: "Fundamentals" href: fundamentals.qmd - text: "Reference" href: reference.qmd sidebar: - title: "Tutorials" style: "docked" background: light contents: - tutorials.qmd - tutorial-1.qmd - tutorial-2.qmd - title: "How-To" contents: - howto.qmd # navigation items - title: "Fundamentals" contents: - fundamentals.qmd # navigation items - title: "Reference" contents: - reference.qmd # navigation items</code></pre> <p>Note that the first sidebar definition contains a few options (e.g., <code>style</code> and <code>background</code>). These options are automatically inherited by the other sidebars.</p> <p>An alternative approach is to make the <code>sidebar</code> entries available from a drop down menu from the <code>navbar</code> items they’re grouped with. To do this, provide a list of <code>sidebar</code> entries and give them each an <code>id</code>, which you then use to reference them from the <code>navbar</code>.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>A page that doesn’t appear in any sidebar will inherit and display the first sidebar without an <code>id</code> or <code>title</code> - you can prevent the sidebar from showing on a page by setting <code>sidebar: false</code> in its front matter.</p> <p>To achieve this, your site configuration needs to look something like this:</p> <pre><code>website: title: ProjectX navbar: background: primary search: true left: - text: "Home" href: index.qmd - sidebar:tutorials - sidebar:howto - sidebar:fundamentals - sidebar:reference sidebar: - id: tutorials title: "Tutorials" style: "docked" background: light collapse-level: 2 contents: # navigation items - id: howto title: "How-To" contents: # navigation items - id: fundamentals title: "Fundamentals" contents: : # navigation items - id: reference title: "Reference" contents: # navigation items</code></pre> <h5 id="breadcrumbs">Breadcrumbs</h5> <p>By default, navigational breadcrumbs are displayed above the page title on each page that is nested deeper than one level in the sidebar navigation. For example, given this <code>sidebar</code> definition:</p> <pre><code>website: sidebar: - contents: - section: "Tutorials" contents: - text: "Tutorial Landing" href: tutorials.qmd</code></pre> <p>The page <code>tutorials.html</code> contains the following breadcrumb:</p> <p>You can disable breadcrumbs for a website using the <code>bread-crumbs</code> option:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: bread-crumbs: false</code></pre> <p>You can also disable breadcrumbs on individual pages:</p> <pre><code>document.qmd --- title: Page without breadcrumbs bread-crumbs: false ---</code></pre> <h5 id="page-navigation-1">Page Navigation</h5> <p>If you have a website with several pages in a section or subsection, it is often convenient to offer the user the ability to navigate to the next page (or previous page) at the bottom of the page that they’ve just finished reading. You can enable this using:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: page-navigation: true</code></pre> <p>When enabled, page navigation will be displayed at the bottom of the page whenever there is a next or previous page (including in the next or previous section). This option is enabled by default for books but not for websites.</p> <p>You can also enable or disable page navigation at the page level by specifying <code>page-navigation</code> in the YAML header, e.g.:</p> <pre><code>basics.qmd --- page-navigation: false ---</code></pre> <p>Or to control page navigation for all pages in a directory specify <code>page-navigation</code> in <code>_metadata.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>_metadata.yml page-navigation: false</code></pre> <h6 id="separators">Separators</h6> <p>If you include a page separator in the sidebar (either between sections or items), page navigation controls will not appear to continue pagination across the separator. For example, in the following sidebar:</p> <pre><code>website: sidebar: contents: - section: "First Section" contents: - href: document1.qmd - href: document2.qmd - href: document3.qmd - text: "---" - section: "Second Section" contents: - href: document4.qmd - href: document5.qmd - href: document6.qmd</code></pre> <p>When the user reaches the bottom of document3.qmd, they will see previous navigation to go back to document2.qmd, but they will not see next navigation to continue onto document 4. This behavior is useful when you have sections of contents that don’t naturally flow together in sequential order. Use the separator to denote this in the sidebar with a horizontal line and to break up pagination.</p> <h5 id="back-to-top">Back to Top</h5> <p>You can include a “Back to top” link at the bottom of documents in a website using the <code>back-to-top-navigation</code> option. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: back-to-top-navigation: true</code></pre> <p>Note that you can disable back to top navigation on a page by page basis by specifying <code>back-to-top-navigation: false</code>.</p> <h5 id="page-footer-1">Page Footer</h5> <p>Use the <code>page-footer</code> option to provide a common footer for all of the pages in a website. The simplest footer just provides text that will be centered and displayed in a lighter typeface:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: page-footer: "Copyright 2021, Norah Jones"</code></pre> <p>You can alternatively target the <code>left</code>, <code>right</code>, and <code>center</code> regions of the footer individually:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: page-footer: left: "Copyright 2021, Norah Jones" right: - icon: github href: [github.com](https://github.com/) - icon: bluesky href: [bsky.app](https://bsky.app/)</code></pre> <p>Note for the <code>right</code> region of the footer we included navigational items for GitHub and Bluesky rather than text. You can include navigational items in any region of the footer.</p> <p>You can use the <code>background</code>, <code>foreground</code>, and <code>border</code> options to further control the appearance of the footer. By default, the footer has no background color and a top border. To eliminate the border you would do this:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: page-footer: border: false</code></pre> <p>To use a light background (e.g. to match a navigation bar) you would do this:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: page-footer: background: light</code></pre> <p>Unless specified, the color (<code>foreground</code>) used for elements that appear in the footer will be automatically determined by using a color that contrasts with the footer background.</p> <h5 id="hiding-navigation">Hiding Navigation</h5> <p>For some pages (especially those with a completely custom layout) you can hide navigation altogether (<code>navbar</code>, <code>sidebar</code>, or both). In these case, add the following to the page front matter:</p> <pre><code># Hides the sidebar on this page sidebar: false # Hides the navbar on this page navbar: false</code></pre> <h5 id="reader-mode">Reader Mode</h5> <p>If you’d like users to be able to hide the side navigation and table of contents and have a more focused reading experience, you can enabled <code>reader-mode</code>. When enabled, a <code>reader-mode</code> toggle will appear on the navbar, if present, or on the sidebar. When pressed, the toggle will ‘roll up’ the sidebar and table of contents.</p> <p>To enable <code>reader-mode</code>, use the following in your project:</p> <pre><code>website: reader-mode: true</code></pre> <h5 id="site-search">Site Search</h5> <p>You can add site search by including <code>search: true</code> in either your <code>site-navbar</code> or <code>site-sidebar</code> configuration. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: sidebar: style: "docked" search: true contents: - section: "Basics" contents: - index.qmd - basics-jupyter.md # etc</code></pre> <h5 id="github-links">GitHub Links</h5> <p>You can add various links (e.g., to edit pages, report issues, etc.) to the GitHub repository where your site source code is hosted. To do this, add a <code>repo-url</code> along with one or more actions in <code>repo-actions</code>. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: repo-url: [github.com](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-demo) repo-actions: [edit, source, issue]</code></pre> <p>The links will be displayed immediately below the page’s table of contents:</p> <p>There are a couple of additional options that enable you to customize the behavior of repository links:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>repo-subdir</code></p> <p>Subdirectory of repository containing source files (defaults to root directory).</p> <p><code>repo-branch</code></p> <p>Repository branch containing the source files (defaults to <code>main</code>)</p> <p><code>issue-url</code></p> <p>Provide an explicit URL for the ‘Report an Issue’ action.</p> <p><code>repo-link-target</code></p> <p>The <code>target</code> attribute to use for repo action links. E.g., set to “_blank” to open in a new tab or window.</p> <p><code>repo-link-rel</code></p> <p>The <code>rel</code> attribute to use for repo action links.</p> <p>If you want to suppress the GitHub links on a specific page, you can set <code>repo-actions</code> to <code>false</code> in the document YAML:</p> <pre><code>page.qmd --- repo-actions: false ---</code></pre> <h5 id="redirects">Redirects</h5> <p>If you rename or move a page on your site, you may want to create redirects from the old URLs so that existing links don’t break. You can do this by adding <code>aliases</code> from old pages to renamed pages.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>Redirects are HTML files created directly at the path you specify in your <code>aliases</code>. You should use the extension <code>.html</code>, not the <code>.md</code> or <code>.qmd</code> extension of the original page source.</p> <p>For example, let’s say you renamed <code>page.qmd</code> to <code>renamed-page.qmd</code>. You would add the following <code>aliases</code> entry to <code>renamed-page.qmd</code> to create the redirect:</p> <pre><code>renamed-page.qmd --- title: "Renamed Page" aliases: - page.html ---</code></pre> <p>This can also be useful for situations where you re-organize content on your site into a different directory hierarchy or break one large article into smaller ones.</p> <p>For re-organizing content into a new directory hierarchy, you may need to specify an absolute path with a leading <code>/</code>. For example, if you moved <code>/old-directory/index.md</code> to <code>/new-directory/index.md</code>:</p> <pre><code>/new-directory/index.md --- title: "Reorganized page" aliases: - "/old-directory/index.html" ---</code></pre> <p>When breaking one large article into smaller ones, you may want to add the URL hash of the section that you have broken out into a new page. For example:</p> <pre><code>learning-more.qmd --- title: "Learning More" aliases: - overview.html#learning-more ---</code></pre> <p>Tip</p> <p>Depending on where you are deploying your site there may be more powerful tools available for defining redirects based on patterns. For example, Netlify <a href="https://docs.netlify.com/routing/redirects/"><code>_redirects</code></a> files or <a href="https://www.danielmorell.com/guides/htaccess-seo/redirects/introduction-to-redirects"><code>.htaccess</code></a> files. Search your web host’s documentation for “redirects” to see if any of these tools are available.</p> <h5 id="pages-2">404 Pages</h5> <p>When a browser can’t find a requested web page, it displays a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_404">404 error</a> indicating that the file can’t be found. Browser default 404 pages can be pretty stark, so you may want to create a custom page with a more friendly message and perhaps pointers on how users might find what they are looking for.</p> <p>Most web serving platforms (e.g., Netlify, GitHub Pages, etc.) will use a file named <code>404.html</code> in the root of your website as a custom error page if you provide it. You can include a custom 404 page in a Quarto website by creating a markdown file named <code>404.qmd</code> in the root of your project. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: Page Not Found --- The page you requested cannot be found (perhaps it was moved or renamed). You may want to try searching to find the page's new location.</code></pre> <p>Note that you can use HTML alongside markdown within your <code>404.qmd</code> file in order to get exactly the appearance and layout you want.</p> <p>Your 404 page will appear within the chrome of your site (e.g., fonts, css, layout, navigation, etc.). This is so that users don’t feel that they’ve irrecoverably “left” your site when they get a 404 error. If you don’t want this behavior, then provide a <code>404.html</code> rather than <code>404.qmd</code>.</p> <p>Here are some examples of how various popular websites handle custom 404 pages: <a href="https://blog.fluidui.com/top-404-error-page-examples/">blog.fluidui.com</a>.</p> <h6 id="non-root-site-paths">Non-Root Site Paths</h6> <p>If your website is served from the root of a domain (e.g., <code>https://example.com/</code>) then simply providing a <code>404.qmd</code> file as described above is all that’s required to create a custom 404 page.</p> <p>However, if your website is not served from the root of a domain then you need to provide one additional bit of configuration to make sure that resources (e.g., your site’s CSS) are resolved correctly within 404 pages.</p> <p>For example, if your site is served from <code>https://example.com/mysite/</code> then you’d add the following to your project <code>website</code> configuration within <code>_quarto.yml</code>:</p> <pre><code>website: title: "My Site" site-path: "/mysite/"</code></pre> <p>Note that if you are already providing a <code>site-url</code> (which is required for generation of sitemaps and social metadata preview images) then it’s enough to simply include the path within the <code>site-url</code>:</p> <pre><code>website: title: "My Site" site-url: "[example.com](https://example.com/mysite/)"</code></pre> <h3 id="website-search-1">Website Search</h3> <h4 id="website-search-2">Website Search</h4> <h5 id="overview-142">Overview</h5> <p>Quarto includes support for full text search of websites and books. By default, Quarto will automatically index the contents of your site and make it searchable using a locally built index. You can also configure Quarto search to use a hosted <a href="https://www.algolia.com/products/search-and-discovery/hosted-search-api/">Algolia</a> index.</p> <h5 id="search-appearance">Search Appearance</h5> <p>Search is enabled by default for websites and books. If the site has a navbar the search UI will appear on the navbar, otherwise it will appear on the sidebar. You can control the location of search with the following options:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>location</code></p> <p><code>navbar</code> or <code>sidebar</code> (defaults to <code>navbar</code> if one is present on the page).</p> <p><code>type</code></p> <p><code>overlay</code> or <code>textbox</code> (<code>overlay</code> provides a button that pops up a search UI, <code>textbox</code> does search inline).</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>website: search: location: navbar type: overlay</code></pre> <p>Note that the above example reflects the default behavior so need not be explicitly specified. Note also that search is enabled by default for websites (you can disable it with <code>search: false</code>).</p> <p>The <code>overlay</code> option displays the search UI as follows:</p> <p>The <code>textbox</code> option displays search like this:</p> <p>When the search is displayed as a textbox, by default, there is no placeholder text. You can specify placeholder text using the <code>search-text-placeholder</code> key of the <code>language</code> option (note that this is at the top-level, not inside the <code>website</code> option):</p> <pre><code>language: search-text-placeholder: Search</code></pre> <h5 id="keyboard-shortcut">Keyboard Shortcut</h5> <p>In addition to clicking on the search UI, users can activate search using the keyboard shortcuts ss, ff or //. You can override these shortcuts by specifying the <code>keyboard-shortcut</code> option. In this example, search will be activated with ?? or HH:</p> <pre><code>website: search: keyboard-shortcut: ["?", "H"]</code></pre> <h5 id="customizing-results">Customizing Results</h5> <p>You can use the following <code>search</code> options to customize how search results are displayed:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>limit</code></p> <p>The number of results to display in the search results. Defaults to 20.</p> <p><code>collapse-after</code></p> <p>The number of sections matching a document to show before hiding additional sections behind a ‘more matches’ link. Defaults to 2.</p> <p><code>copy-button</code></p> <p>If true, the search textbox will include a small icon that when clicked will copy a url to the search results to the clipboard (this is useful if users would like to share a particular search with results). Defaults to false.</p> <p><code>show-item-context</code></p> <p>Control whether page parents are displayed next to items in search results. Use <code>tree</code>, <code>parent</code>, <code>root</code>, or boolean (if true, <code>tree</code> is the default).
