E.g. <code>tree</code> results in “Guide > Authoring > Figures”:</p> <h5 id="search-result-highlighting">Search Result Highlighting</h5> <p>When you click a search result, Quarto navigates to the destination page and highlights the matching terms with <code><mark></code> elements. This works with both the built-in search and Algolia search.</p> <p>The highlighting is driven by a <code>?q=</code> URL parameter. You can manually add <code>?q=term</code> to any page URL to highlight occurrences of that term — useful for sharing links that draw attention to specific content.</p> <p>Highlights remain visible until you navigate away from the page. When a match is found inside a tabset, the correct tab is automatically activated to reveal the highlighted content, including nested and grouped tabsets. Multi-word search terms are highlighted correctly even when they span across formatting boundaries such as bold, italic, code spans, or syntax-highlighted code blocks.</p> <p>URLs that combine a search query with a section anchor (e.g., <code>page.html?q=term#section</code>) scroll to the specified section rather than jumping to the first match. For example, <a href="https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html?q=%22%23%23%20Heading%202%5Cn%22#raw-output">this link</a> searches for <code>"## Heading 2\n"</code> on the Execution Options page with a <code>#raw-output</code> anchor — the Knitr tab is activated (instead of the default Jupyter tab), matches are highlighted inside the code block, and the page scrolls to the Raw Output section:</p> <h5 id="using-algolia">Using Algolia</h5> <p>In addition to the built-in search capability, Quarto websites can also be configured to use an external Algolia search index. When rendering a website, Quarto will produce a JSON file (<code>search.json</code> in the site output directory) which can be used to update an Algolia index. For more on creating indexes with Algolia, see <a href="https://www.algolia.com/doc/guides/sending-and-managing-data/send-and-update-your-data/">Send and Update Your Data</a> using Algolia.</p> <h6 id="basic-configuration">Basic Configuration</h6> <p>In order for Quarto to connect to your Algolia index, you need to provide basic connection information in your Quarto project file. You can find this connection information for your Algolia index in the Dashboard in the <a href="https://www.algolia.com/doc/guides/security/api-keys/">API Keys</a> section. The following basic connection information is required:</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>index-name</code></p> <p>The name of the index to use when performing a search.</p> <p><code>application-id</code></p> <p>The unique ID used by Algolia to identify your application.</p> <p><code>search-only-api-key</code></p> <p>The Search-Only API key to use to connect to Algolia.</p> <p>Important</p> <p>Be sure to use the Search Only API key, which provides read only access to your index and is safe to include in project files. Never use your Admin API key in a Quarto document or project.</p> <p><code>show-logo</code></p> <p>Displays a ‘search by Algolia’ logo in the footer of search results.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>website: search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key></code></pre> <h6 id="custom-index-schema">Custom Index Schema</h6> <p>If you are simply using the <code>search.json</code> file generated by Quarto as your Algolia index, the above configuration information is all that is required to set up search using Algolia.</p> <p>However, if you are generating an index in some other fashion, you may need to provide additional information to specify which fields Quarto should use when searching. You do this by including an <code>index-fields</code> key under <code>algolia</code> which specifies the names of specific fields in your index.</p> <p>Option</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>href</code></p> <p>The field to use to read the URL to this index entry. The user will be navigated to this URL when they select the matching search result. Note that Quarto groups results by URL (not including the anchor when grouping).</p> <p>This field is required (either as an existing field in your index or with a mapped field name).</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The field to use to read the title of the index entry.</p> <p>This field is required (either as an existing field in your index or with a mapped field name).</p> <p><code>text</code></p> <p>The field to use to read the text of the index entry.</p> <p>This field is required (either as an existing field in your index or with a mapped field name).</p> <p><code>section</code></p> <p>The field to use to read the section of the index entry. Quarto groups results by URL and uses the section information (if present) to show matching subsections of the same document.</p> <p>This field is optional.</p> <p>Any or all of the above may be specified in your Quarto project file. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key> index-fields: href: url section: sec text: body</code></pre> <h6 id="algolia-insights">Algolia Insights</h6> <p>By default, Algolia provides a number of insights based upon the performance of your Algolia search. In addition, it may be helpful to understand more detailed tracking of the results that are viewed and clicked. You can enable click and conversion tracking using Algolia by setting the <code>analytics-events</code> to true:</p> <pre><code>website: search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key> analytics-events: true</code></pre> <p>You can confirm that events are being properly sent to Algolia using the <a href="https://www.algolia.com/events/debugger">Event Debugger</a>.</p> <h6 id="cookie-consent-and-user-tracking">Cookie Consent and User Tracking</h6> <p>Algolia Insights uses user tokens to track click and conversion events. Quarto uses a privacy-first approach for handling cookies:</p> <ul> <li><p>Without cookie consent enabled: A random session token is generated for each browser session. This allows tracking of search interactions during a single visit without storing persistent cookies. This privacy-first approach avoids persistent cookies entirely.</p></li> <li><p>With cookie consent enabled: When you enable cookie consent, cookies are blocked by default until the user expressly grants consent. After the user grants “tracking” consent, Algolia will use cookies to maintain an anonymous user identifier across sessions:</p> <p>website: cookie-consent: true search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key> analytics-events: true</p></li> </ul> <p>With this configuration, the Algolia Insights API will use cookies to maintain an anonymous user identifier across sessions, but only after the user has explicitly granted consent.</p> <p>ImportantPrivacy Regulations</p> <p>The default session-only tracking (without cookie consent) provides meaningful analytics about search usage patterns without using persistent cookies. When cookie consent is enabled, Quarto uses an opt-in approach (express consent) by default, blocking cookies until the user explicitly agrees.</p> <p>While these features are designed with privacy regulations in mind, website owners should consult with legal counsel to ensure their specific implementation meets applicable privacy laws and regulations in their jurisdiction.</p> <h6 id="advanced-configuration">Advanced Configuration</h6> <p>In addition to the above configuration, you may also pass Algolia specific parameters when executing a search. For example, you may want to limit results to a particular facet or set of tags. To specify parameters, add the <code>params</code> key to your <code>algolia</code> yaml and provide params. For information about available parameters, see Algolia’s <a href="https://www.algolia.com/doc/api-reference/search-api-parameters/">Search API Parameters</a>.</p> <p>For example:</p> <pre><code>website: search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key> index-fields: href: url section: sec text: body params: tagFilters: ['tag1','tag2']</code></pre> <h5 id="disablingforcing-search">Disabling/Forcing Search</h5> <p>You can disable search for an individual document by adding <code>search: false</code> to the document metadata. For example:</p> <pre><code>--- title: "My Document" search: false ---</code></pre> <p>If you’d like to disable search support for an entire website, you can do so by including the following in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file:</p> <pre><code>website: search: false</code></pre> <h6 id="forcing-the-inclusion-of-individual-elements">Forcing the inclusion of individual elements</h6> <p>If you need elements from the document to be included in the search that otherwise wouldn’t, add the <code>quarto-include-in-search-index</code> class to the element. To include only a portion of a paragraph, etc, wrap the text in a span or a div and add the class to the element.</p> <h3 id="website-tools-1">Website Tools</h3> <h4 id="website-tools-2">Website Tools</h4> <h5 id="headers-footers">Headers & Footers</h5> <p>You can provide standard headers and footers for pages on your site. These can apply to the main document body or to the sidebar. Available options include:</p> <p>Value</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>body-header</code></p> <p>Markdown to insert at the beginning of each page’s body (below the title and author block).</p> <p><code>body-footer</code></p> <p>Markdown to insert below each page’s body.</p> <p><code>margin-header</code></p> <p>Markdown to insert above right margin content (i.e. table of contents).</p> <p><code>margin-footer</code></p> <p>Markdown to insert below right margin content.</p> <p>For example (included in _quarto.yml) :</p> <pre><code>body-header: | This page brought to you by <[example.com](https://example.com)> margin-header: | ![Logo image](/img/logo.png)</code></pre> <p>Note that links to figures should start with a <code>/</code> to work on each level of the website.</p> <h5 id="announcement-bar">Announcement Bar</h5> <p>Captured view of the Quarto website, showcasing the dynamic announcement bar feature.</p> <p>Add an announcement to display a prominent, customizable bar at the top of your website that grabs visitors’ attention. It’s perfect for highlighting important information, such as alerts, promotions, or updates. You can set an icon, make it dismissable, and even include formatted content like bold text. The announcement bar can be positioned to fit seamlessly within your site’s layout (e.g., <code>below-navbar</code> or <code>above-navbar</code>), ensuring the message is both impactful and integrated.</p> <p>Here’s an example of how you might configure it:</p> <pre><code>_quarto.yml website: announcement: 1 icon: info-circle 2 dismissable: true 3 content: "**Alert** - this is some information that you should pay attention to" 4 type: primary 5 position: below-navbar</code></pre> <p>1</p> <p><code>icon</code> - The Bootstrap icon to display in the announcement bar. You can choose from any of the <a href="https://icons.getbootstrap.com/">Bootstrap icons</a>.</p> <p>2</p> <p><code>dismissable</code> - Whether the announcement bar can be dismissed by the user. It can be <code>true</code> or <code>false</code>.</p> <p>3</p> <p><code>content</code> - The content of the announcement bar. You can use markdown to format the content.</p> <p>4</p> <p><code>type</code> - The type of the announcement bar. It can be one of <code>primary</code>, <code>secondary</code>, <code>success</code>, <code>danger</code>, <code>warning</code>, <code>info</code>, <code>light</code>, <code>dark</code>.</p> <p>5</p> <p><code>position</code> - The position of the announcement bar. It can be one of <code>below-navbar</code> or <code>above-navbar</code>.</p> <h5 id="social-metadata">Social Metadata</h5> <p>You can enhance your website and the content that you publish to it by including additional types of metadata, including:</p> <ul> <li><p>Favicon</p></li> <li><p>Twitter Cards</p></li> <li><p>Open Graph One important thing to note about using website tools is that while these tools are added to websites within the <code>website</code> key, in a book you should include the same options in the <code>book</code> key. For example, in a website you would include a favicon and twitter card as follows:</p> <p>website: favicon: logo.png twitter-card: true site-url: <a href="https://example.com">example.com</a></p></li> </ul> <p>In a book you’d use the <code>book</code> key instead:</p> <pre><code>book: favicon: logo.png twitter-card: true site-url: [example.com](https://example.com)</code></pre> <p>As you read the documentation below, keep in mind to substitute <code>book</code> for <code>website</code> if you are authoring a book.</p> <h6 id="favicon">Favicon</h6> <p>The favicon for your site provides an icon for browser tabs and other sites that link to yours. Use the <code>favicon</code> option to provide the path to a favicon image. For example:</p> <pre><code>website: favicon: logo.png</code></pre> <h6 id="twitter-cards">Twitter Cards</h6> <p><a href="https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/twitter-for-websites/cards/overview/abouts-cards">Twitter Cards</a> provide an enhanced appearance when someone links to your site on Twitter. When a link to your site is included in a Tweet, Twitter automatically crawls your site and fetches any Twitter Card metadata. To enable the automatic generation of Twitter Card metadata for your site, you can add the following to your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file:</p> <pre><code>website: twitter-card: true</code></pre> <p>In this case, Quarto will automatically generate a title, description, and preview image for the content. For more information about how Quarto finds preview images, see Preview Images.</p> <p>You may also provide additional metadata to be used when generating the Twitter Card, including:</p> <p>Key</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The title of the page. Quarto will automatically use the <code>title</code> metadata from the page metadata. If you’d like you can override this just for the Twitter Card by including a <code>title</code> in the <code>twitter-card</code> metadata.</p> <p><code>description</code></p> <p>A short description of the content. Quarto will automatically use the <code>description</code> metadata from the page metadata. If you’d like you can override this just for the Twitter Card by including a <code>description</code> in the <code>twitter-card</code> metadata.</p> <p><code>image</code></p> <p>The path to a preview image for this content. By default, Quarto will use the <code>image</code> value from the document metadata, or if that isn’t specified, the <code>image</code> value from the <code>website:</code> metadata. If you provide an image, you may also optionally provide an <code>image-width</code> and <code>image-height</code> to improve the appearance of your Twitter Card.</p> <p>If <code>image</code> is not provided, Quarto will automatically attempt to locate a preview image. For more information, see Preview Images.</p> <p><code>card-style</code></p> <p>Either <code>summary</code> or <code>summary_large_image</code>. If this is not provided, the best style will automatically selected based upon other metadata. You can learn more about Twitter Card styles <a href="https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/twitter-for-websites/cards/overview/abouts-cards">here</a>.</p> <p><code>creator</code></p> <p><code>@username</code> of the content creator. Note that strings with special characters such as <code>@</code> must be quoted in yaml.</p> <p><code>site</code></p> <p><code>@username</code> of website. Note that strings with special characters such as <code>@</code> must be quoted in yaml.</p> <p>Here is a more comprehensive example of specifying Twitter Card metadata in a <code>quarto.yml</code> file:</p> <pre><code>website: twitter-card: creator: "@dragonstyle" site: "@rstudio"</code></pre> <p>Quarto will automatically merge global metadata found in the <code>website: twitter-card</code> key with any metadata provided in the document itself in the <code>twitter-card</code> key. This is useful when you need to specify a mix of global options (for example, <code>site</code>) with per document options such as <code>title</code> or <code>image</code>.</p> <h6 id="open-graph-2">Open Graph</h6> <p>The <a href="http://ogp.me/">Open Graph protocol</a> is a specification that enables richer sharing of links to articles on the web. It will improve the previews of your content when a link to it is pasted into applications like Slack, Discord, Facebook, Linkedin, and more. To enable the automatic generation of Open Graph metadata for your content, include the following in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file:</p> <pre><code>website: open-graph: true</code></pre> <p>In this case, Quarto will automatically generate a title, description, and preview image for the content. For more information about how Quarto finds preview images, see Preview Images.</p> <p>You may also provide additional metadata to be used when generating the Open Graph metadata, including:</p> <p>Key</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>title</code></p> <p>The title of the page. Quarto will automatically use the <code>title</code> metadata from the page metadata. If you’d like you can override this just for the Open Graph metadata by including a <code>title</code> in the <code>open-graph</code> metadata.</p> <p><code>description</code></p> <p>A short description of the content. Quarto will automatically use the <code>description</code> metadata from the page metadata. If you’d like you can override this just for the Open Graph metadata by including a <code>description</code> in the <code>open-graph</code> metadata.</p> <p><code>image</code></p> <p>The path to a preview image for this content. By default, Quarto will use the <code>image</code> value from the document metadata, or if that isn’t specified, the <code>image</code> value from the <code>website:</code> metadata. If you provide an image, you may also optionally provide an <code>image-width</code> and <code>image-height</code> to improve the appearance of your Twitter Card.</p> <p>If <code>image</code> is not provided, Quarto will automatically attempt to locate a preview image. For more information, see Preview Images.</p> <p><code>locale</code></p> <p>The locale that the Open Graph metadata is marked up in.</p> <p><code>site-name</code></p> <p>The name which should be displayed for the overall site. If not explicitly provided in the <code>open-graph</code> metadata, Quarto will use the <code>website:title</code> value.</p> <p>Here is a more comprehensive example of specifying Open Graph metadata in a <code>quarto.yml</code> file:</p> <pre><code>website: open-graph: locale: es_ES site-name: Quarto</code></pre> <p>Quarto will automatically merge global metadata found in the <code>website: open-graph</code> key with any metadata provided in the document itself in the <code>open-graph</code> key. This is useful when you need to specify a mix of global options (for example, <code>site</code>) with per document options such as <code>title</code> or <code>image</code>.</p> <h6 id="preview-images">Preview Images</h6> <p>You can specify a preview image for your article in several different ways:</p> <ul> <li><p>Full URL: You can explicitly provide a full url to the preview image using the <code>image</code> field in the appropriate metadata. For example:</p> <p>page.qmd</p> <p>title: “My Document” image: “<a href="https://quarto.org/docs/websites/images/tools.png">quarto.org</a>”</p></li> <li><p>Relative Path: You may provide a document relative path to an image (such as <code>images/preview-code.png</code>) or a project relative path to an image (such as <code>/images/preview-code.png</code>). If you provide a relative path such as this, you must also provide a <code>site-url</code> in your site’s metadata. For example in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file:</p> <p>_quarto.yml</p> <p>website: site-url: “<a href="https://www.quarto.org">quarto.org</a>”</p></li> <li><p>and in your document front matter:</p> <p>page.qmd</p> <p>title: “My Document” image: “/docs/websites/images/tools.png”</p></li> <li><p>Image Class: Any image that is being rendered in the page may also be used as a preview image by giving it the class name <code>preview-image</code>. Quarto will select the first image it finds with this class. For example, the following image will be used as the preview image when included on a page:</p> <p><img src="images/tools.png" class="preview-image" /></p></li> <li><p>If you label an image with this class, you must also provide a <code>site-url</code> in your site’s metadata.</p></li> <li><p>Image Filename: If none of the above ways of specifying a preview image have been used, Quarto will attempt to find a preview image by looking for an image included in the rendered document with one of the following names: <code>preview.png</code>, <code>feature.png</code>, <code>cover.png</code>, or <code>thumbnail.png</code>. If you’d like to provide a default that is used when pages specify a preview image in none of the above ways, specify it at the site level:</p> <p>_quarto.yml</p> <p>website: image: “<a href="https://quarto.org/quarto-dark-bg.jpeg">quarto.org</a>”</p></li> </ul> <p>If you would like to prevent preview image discovery on a page, set <code>image</code> to <code>false</code>:</p> <pre><code>page.qmd --- image: false ---</code></pre> <h5 id="analytics">Analytics</h5> <h6 id="plausible-analytics">Plausible Analytics</h6> <p><a href="https://plausible.io/">Plausible Analytics</a> is a lightweight, open-source, and privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics. Plausible is designed with privacy as a core principle: it doesn’t use cookies, is GDPR compliant by default, and all data is processed anonymously.</p> <p>To add Plausible Analytics to your Quarto website:</p> <ul> <li>Sign up at <a href="https://plausible.io/">plausible.io</a> and add your website to your account.</li> <li>In your Plausible dashboard, navigate to your site’s settings.</li> <li>Go to the “Site Installation” section and click “Review Installation” to get your unique tracking snippet.</li> <li>Copy the complete script snippet provided by Plausible from your dashboard.</li> <li>Add it to your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file. You can provide the Plausible snippet in two ways:</li> </ul> <p>Option 1: Inline snippet</p> <p>Paste the snippet directly in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration file under the <code>plausible-analytics</code> key. Use the <code>|</code> character after the key to preserve line breaks in the snippet:</p> <pre><code>website: plausible-analytics: | <script async src="[plausible.io](https://plausible.io/js/pa-XXXXXX.js)"></script> <script> window.plausible=window.plausible||function(){(plausible.q=plausible.q||[]).push(arguments)},plausible.init=plausible.init||function(i){plausible.o=i||{}}; plausible.init() </script></code></pre> <p>Option 2: File path</p> <p>Save the snippet to a file (e.g., <code>_plausible_snippet.html</code>) and provide the path:</p> <pre><code>website: plausible-analytics: path: _plausible_snippet.html</code></pre> <p>The script will automatically be included in the <code><head></code> of every page on your website. Important: Make sure to copy and paste the complete snippet exactly as provided by Plausible - the example above shows the typical structure, but your actual snippet will have a unique tracking code instead of <code>XXXXXX</code>.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>The snippet from your Plausible dashboard may include multiple <code><script></code> tags and initialization code. Copy the entire snippet as-is - don’t modify or simplify it. Using the file path option can be useful if you want to keep the snippet separate from your configuration or if you need to update it frequently.</p> <h6 id="optional-enhanced-measurements">Optional Enhanced Measurements</h6> <p>Plausible offers optional enhanced measurements that you can enable directly in your site settings dashboard (such as outbound link tracking, file downloads, etc.). When you enable these features in Plausible, your tracking snippet will be automatically updated in your dashboard. Simply copy the updated snippet and replace it in your <code>_quarto.yml</code> configuration.</p> <p>For more information about available enhanced measurements and configuration options, see the <a href="https://plausible.io/docs/plausible-script">Plausible script documentation</a>.</p> <h6 id="privacy-benefits">Privacy Benefits</h6> <p>Unlike traditional analytics solutions, Plausible Analytics:</p> <ul> <li>Uses no cookies: Plausible doesn’t use cookies or generate any persistent identifiers, so no cookie consent banners are needed</li> <li>Is GDPR compliant: All visitor data is anonymized and processed in the EU</li> <li>Is lightweight: The script is under 1 KB, significantly smaller than Google Analytics</li> <li>Has no cross-site tracking: Plausible doesn’t track users across different websites Because Plausible is privacy-friendly by default, you typically don’t need to implement Cookie Consent when using it (though you should verify this with your own privacy requirements).</li> </ul> <h6 id="google-analytics">Google Analytics</h6> <p>You can add <a href="https://analytics.google.com/">Google Analytics</a> to your website by adding a <code>google-analytics</code> key to your <code>_quarto.yml</code> file. In its simplest form, you can just pass your Google Analytics tracking Id (e.g. <code>UA-xxxxxxx</code>) or Google Tag measurement Id (e.g. <code>G-xxxxxxx</code>) like:</p> <pre><code>website: google-analytics: "UA-XXXXXXXX"</code></pre> <p>Quarto will use the key itself to determine whether to embed Google Analytics (analytics.js) or Google Tags (gtag) as appropriate.</p> <p>In addition to this basic configuration, you can exercise more fine grained control of your site analytics using the following keys.</p> <p>Key</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>tracking-id</code></p> <p>The Google tracking Id or measurement Id of this website.</p> <p><code>storage</code></p> <p>cookies - Use cookies to store unique user and session identification (default).</p> <p>none - Do not use cookies to store unique user and session identification.</p> <p>For more about choosing storage options see Storage.</p> <p><code>anonymize-ip</code></p> <p>Anonymize the user ip address. For more about this feature, see <a href="https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2763052?hl=en">IP Anonymization (or IP masking) in Google Analytics</a>.</p> <p><code>version</code></p> <p>The version number of Google Analytics to use. Currently supports either 3 (for analytics.js) or 4 (for gtag). This is automatically detected based upon the <code>tracking-id</code>, but you may specify it.</p> <h6 id="storage">Storage</h6> <p>Google Analytics uses cookies to distinguish unique users and sessions. If you choose to use cookies to store this user data, you should consider whether you need to enable Cookie Consent in order to permit the viewer to control any tracking that you enable.</p> <p>If you choose <code>none</code> for storage, this will have the following effects:</p> <ul> <li>For Google Analytics v3 (analytics.js)</li> <li>No tracking cookies will be used. Individual page hits will be properly tracked, enabling you to see which pages are viewed and how often they are viewed. Unique user and session tracking will not report data correctly since the tracking cookies they rely upon are not set.</li> <li>For Google Tags (gtag)</li> <li>User consent for ad and analytics tracking cookies will be withheld. In this mode, Google Analytics will still collect user data without the user identification, but that data is currently not displayed in the Google Analytics reports.</li> </ul> <h5 id="cookie-consent">Cookie Consent</h5> <p>Quarto includes the ability to request cookie consent before enabling scripts that set cookies, using <a href="https://www.cookieconsent.com">Cookie Consent</a>.</p> <p>The user’s cookie preferences will automatically control Google Analytics and Algolia search analytics (if enabled) and can be used to control custom scripts you add as well (see Custom Scripts and Cookie Consent). You can enable the default request for cookie consent using the following:</p> <pre><code>website: cookie-consent: true</code></pre> <p>You can further customize the appearance and behavior of the consent using the following:</p> <p>Key</p> <p>Description</p> <p><code>type</code></p> <p>The type of consent that should be requested, using one of these two values:</p> <p>express - (default) This will block cookies until the user expressly agrees to allow them (or continue blocking them if the user doesn’t agree).</p> <p>implied - This will notify the user that the site uses cookies and permit them to change preferences, but not block cookies unless the user changes their preferences.</p> <p><code>style</code></p> <p>The style of the consent banner that is displayed:</p> <p>simple - (default) A simple dialog in the lower right corner of the website.</p> <p>headline - A full width banner across the top of the website.</p> <p>interstitial - A semi-transparent overlay of the entire website.</p> <p>standalone - An opaque overlay of the entire website.</p> <p><code>palette</code></p> <p>Whether to use a dark or light appearance for the consent banner:</p> <p>light - A light colored banner.</p> <p>dark - A dark colored banner.</p> <p><code>language</code></p> <p>The language to be used when displaying the cookie consent prompt specified using an IETF language tag. If not specified, the document language will be used.</p> <p><code>policy-url</code></p> <p>The url to the website’s cookie or privacy policy.</p> <p><code>prefs-text</code></p> <p>The text to display for the cookie preferences link in the website footer.</p> <p>A custom example might look more like:</p> <pre><code>website: cookie-consent: type: express style: headline palette: dark google-analytics: tracking-id: "G-XXXXXXX" anonymize-ip: true search: algolia: index-name: <my-index-name> application-id: <my-application-id> search-only-api-key: <my-search-only-api-key> analytics-events: true</code></pre> <p>When cookie consent is enabled, Google Analytics and Algolia search analytics will use cookies based on user preference: for <code>type: express</code>, the default, they will not use cookies unless a user opts-in; for <code>type: implied</code>, they will use cookies unless a user opts-out. Without cookie consent enabled, Algolia will use session-only tracking without cookies. See Algolia Insights for more details.</p> <h6 id="cookie-preferences">Cookie Preferences</h6> <p>In addition to requesting consent when a new user visits your website, Cookie Consent will also add a cookie preferences link to the footer of the website. You can control the text of this link using <code>prefs-text</code>. If you would rather position this link yourself, just add a link with the id <code>#open_preferences_center</code> to the website and Cookie Consent will not add the preferences link to the footer. For example:</p> <pre><code>Change [cookie preferences]{#open_preferences_center}</code></pre> <h6 id="custom-scripts-and-cookie-consent">Custom Scripts and Cookie Consent</h6> <p>Cookie Consent works by preventing the execution of scripts unless the user has expressed their consent. To control your custom scripts using Cookie Consent:</p> <ul> <li><p>Insert script tags as <code>type='text/plain'</code> (when the user consents, the type will be switched to <code>text/javascript</code> and the script will be executed).</p></li> <li><p>Add a <code>cookie-consent</code> attribute to your script tag, setting it one of the following 4 levels:</p></li> <li><p>Level</p></li> <li><p>Description</p></li> <li><p><code>strictly-necessary</code></p></li> <li><p>Strictly scripts are loaded automatically and cannot be disabled by the user.</p></li> <li><p><code>functionality</code></p></li> <li><p>Scripts that are required for basic functionality of the website, for example, remembering a user language preference.</p></li> <li><p><code>tracking</code></p></li> <li><p>Scripts that are used to track users, for example Google Analytics.</p></li> <li><p><code>targeting</code></p></li> <li><p>Scripts that are used for the purpose of advertising to ad targeting, for example Google AdSense remarketing. An example script that is used for user tracking would look like:</p> <script type="text/plain" cookie-consent="tracking"> // My tracking JS code here </script></li> </ul> <h5 id="site-resources">Site Resources</h5> <p>Besides input and configuration files, your site likely also includes a variety of resources (e.g. images) that you will want to publish along with your site. Quarto will automatically detect any files that you reference within your site and copy them to the output directory (e.g. <code>_site</code>).</p> <p>Quarto also recognizes the following files and copies them to your output directory:</p> <ul> <li><p><code>404.html</code>, one option for providing a 404 Page</p></li> <li><p><code>robots.txt</code>, a file specified by the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309">Robots Exclusion Protocol</a> that tells search engine crawlers which pages or files on your website they can or cannot access</p></li> <li><p><code>_redirects</code>, a file used by some publishing providers to provide page redirects, e.g. <a href="https://docs.netlify.com/routing/redirects/#syntax-for-the-redirects-file">Netlify</a></p></li> <li><p><code>CNAME</code>, a file used by some publishing providers to specify a custom domain, e.g. GitHub Pages</p></li> <li><p><code>.nojekyll</code>, a file used by GitHub pages to bypass building with Jekyll, e.g. when publishing from <code>docs/</code> If this auto-detection fails for any reason, or if you want to publish a file not explicitly linked to from within your site, you can add a <code>resources</code> entry to your configuration. For example, here we specify that we want to include all Excel spreadsheets within the project directory as part of the website:</p> <p>project: type: website resources: - “*.xlsx”</p></li> </ul> <p>Note that the <code>*.xlsx</code> value is quoted: this is because YAML requires that strings that begin with non-alphanumeric characters be quoted.</p> <p>You can also add a <code>resources</code> metadata value to individual files. For example:</p> <pre><code>title: "My Page" resources: - "sheet.xlsx"</code></pre> <p>Images are the most commonly used type of resource file. If you have global images (e.g. a logo) that you want to reference from various pages within your site, you can use a site-absolute path to refer to the images, and it will be automatically converted to a relative path during publishing. For example:</p> <pre><code>![](/images/logo.png)</code></pre> <h5 id="dark-mode-4">Dark Mode</h5> <p>Quarto websites can support both a light and dark mode. For example, you may use the <code>flatly</code> and <code>darkly</code> themes (which are designed to be used in tandem as dark and light appearances) as:</p> <pre><code>theme: light: flatly dark: darkly</code></pre> <p>For more about selecting the dark and light themes for your website, see Dark Mode.</p> <p>Light</p> <p>Dark</p> <p>When enabled, a toggle that allows your reader to control the appearance of the website will appear. The toggle will automatically be added to the website navigation as follows:</p> <ul> <li>If a navbar has been specified, the toggle will appear in the top right corner of the nav bar.</li> <li>If there is no navbar present, but a sidebar has been specified, the toggle will appear in the same location that the sidebar tools appears (adjacent to the title or logo in the sidebar).</li> <li>If there is no navbar or sidebar present, the toggle will appear in the top right corner of the page.</li> </ul> <h2 id="miscellaneous-3">Miscellaneous</h2> <h3 id="gallery">Gallery</h3> <p>Quarto can produce a wide variety of output formats. Here are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>Articles & Reports</li> <li>Presentations</li> <li>Dashboards</li> <li>Websites</li> <li>Books</li> <li>Interactive Docs Articles and reports with Python and </ul> <h3 id="troubleshooting-1">Troubleshooting</h3> <h4 id="troubleshooting-2">Troubleshooting</h4> <p>This page documents a number of strategies you can employ in case you run into problems with Quarto. As always, we welcome feedback and bug reports on the <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues">Quarto issue tracker</a>, but this page might help you get up and running quickly.</p> <h5 id="basics-1">Basics</h5> <h6 id="check-the-version-of-quarto-and-its-dependencies">Check the version of quarto and its dependencies</h6> <p>You can check the version of Quarto and its dependencies by running <code>quarto check</code>. Here’s an example of the output it generates:</p> <pre><code>Quarto 1.10.2 [✓] Checking versions of quarto binary dependencies... Pandoc version 3.4.0: OK Dart Sass version 1.70.0: OK Deno version 1.46.3: OK Typst version 0.11.0: OK [✓] Checking versions of quarto dependencies......OK [✓] Checking Quarto installation......OK Version: 1.10.2 Path: /Applications/quarto/bin [✓] Checking tools....................OK TinyTeX: v2026.04 Chromium (deprecated): (not installed) Chrome Headless Shell: (not installed) VeraPDF: (not installed) [✓] Checking LaTeX....................OK Using: TinyTex Path: /Users/username/Library/TinyTeX/bin/universal-darwin Version: 2026 [✓] Checking basic markdown render....OK [✓] Checking Python 3 installation....OK Version: 3.12.1 Path: /.venv/bin/python3 Jupyter: 5.7.2 Kernels: python3 [✓] Checking Jupyter engine render....OK [✓] Checking R installation...........OK Version: 4.4.2 Path: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.4-arm64/Resources LibPaths: - /Users/username/Library/R/arm64/4.4/library - /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.4-arm64/Resources/library knitr: 1.49 rmarkdown: 2.29 [✓] Checking Knitr engine render......OK</code></pre> <h6 id="get-a-stack-trace">Get a stack trace</h6> <p>Setting <code>QUARTO_PRINT_STACK=true</code> in your environment will cause Quarto to print a stack trace when an error occurs.</p> <ul> <li><p>Windows</p></li> <li><p>Unix On PowerShell:</p> <p>$env:QUARTO_PRINT_STACK=“true”</p></li> </ul> <p>On bash-like shells:</p> <pre><code>export QUARTO_PRINT_STACK=true</code></pre> <h6 id="verbose-mode">Verbose mode</h6> <p>Quarto will print more information about its internal state if you set <code>QUARTO_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG</code> in your environment.</p> <ul> <li><p>Windows</p></li> <li><p>Unix On PowerShell:</p> <p>$env:QUARTO_LOG_LEVEL=“DEBUG”</p></li> </ul> <p>On bash-like shells:</p> <pre><code>export QUARTO_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG</code></pre> <p><code>--log-level debug</code> can also be passed at command line e.g. <code>quarto render index.qmd --log-level debug</code></p> <p>If you prefer to have the log be written to file, you can set <code>QUARTO_LOG</code> in your environment, or <code>--log</code> at command line.</p> <h6 id="inspect-log-files">Inspect log files</h6> <p>Quarto creates log files that can help you diagnose problems. These are stored in different locations depending on your operating system:</p> <ul> <li>Windows</li> <li>macOS</li> <li>Linux <code>%LOCALAPPDATA%\quarto\logs</code></li> </ul> <p><code>\${HOME}/Library/Application Support/quarto/logs</code></p> <p>If <code>\$XDG_DATA_HOME</code> is set, <code>\${XDG_DATA_HOME}/.local/share/quarto/logs</code>, otherwise <code>\${HOME}/.local/share/quarto/logs</code></p> <h6 id="out-of-memory-issues">Out-of-memory issues</h6> <p>When building a large project or website, you might run into memory limits. In that case, consider adjusting the <code>QUARTO_DENO_V8_OPTIONS</code> environment variable.</p> <p>In this example, we’re setting the maximum amount of memory to be allocated by Deno to be 8GB. Adjust this to your computer’s limits.</p> <ul> <li><p>Windows</p></li> <li><p>Unix On PowerShell:</p> <p>$env:QUARTO_DENO_V8_OPTIONS=“–max-old-space-size=8192”</p></li> </ul> <p>On bash-like shells:</p> <pre><code>export QUARTO_DENO_V8_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192</code></pre> <h6 id="installer-issues">Installer issues</h6> <ul> <li>macOS In macOS, installers write their output to <code>/var/log/install.log</code>. Inspecting this file might offer hints to what went wrong.</li> </ul> <p>Warning</p> <p>If you’re going to ask for help on public forums, be aware that every macOS installer writes to the same file <code>/var/log/install.log</code>. You should make sure you’re not accidentally disclosing installation information you would rather not.</p> <h6 id="pdflatex-issues">PDF/LaTeX issues</h6> <p>If quarto finds an existing installation of <code>texlive</code> in your system, it will use that. If you’re seeing issues with rendering to PDF, make sure you have an up-to-date installation of <code>texlive</code>. Alternatively, you can have quarto use its own version, by calling <code>quarto install tinytex</code>.</p> <h5 id="environment-libraries-and-dependencies">Environment, Libraries, and Dependencies</h5> <p>One common source of tricky problems is the presence of multiple installations of R and Python in a system. Quarto will attempt to find an R or Python installation, and sometimes your shell environment is pointing to a different one.</p> <h6 id="knitr-9"><code>knitr</code></h6> <p>If you suspect that quarto is finding the wrong version of an R installation, you can obtain information about the R installation that Quarto sees by running the following .qmd file:</p> <pre><code>--- engine: knitr --- ```{r} sessionInfo() Sys.getenv() .libPaths() # If the sessioninfo package is available, # it provides output that is easier to read, # and can write its results to a file sessioninfo:::session_info(to_file = "quarto-session-info-output.txt") ```</code></pre> <p>You can then also run those commands from your R environment, and compare the output. If <code>sessioninfo</code> is available, then you can ask for a difference between the outputs more directly:</p> <pre><code>sessioninfo:::session_diff(new = "quarto-session-info-output.txt")</code></pre> <h6 id="julia-5"><code>julia</code></h6> <p>One potential source of trouble in Julia execution and installationwith both the <code>jupyter</code> and <code>julia</code> engines are stale library versions in caches. In those situations, consider removing the contents of the directory described under <code>Quarto cache location</code> in <code>quarto check</code>.</p> <h5 id="advanced-2">Advanced</h5> <h6 id="debugging-jupyter-engine-issues">Debugging Jupyter engine issues</h6> <p>To enable Jupyter debugging, add the following to your YAML front matter:</p> <pre><code>execute: debug: true</code></pre> <p>Quarto creates a log of the execution of jupyter notebooks in its log directory under <code>jupyter-kernel.log</code>.</p> <p>If Jupyter execution is hanging instead of failing, you can force immediate flushing of the log by setting <code>QUARTO_JUPYTER_FLUSH_LOGS=true</code> in your environment before running Quarto.</p> <h6 id="jupyter-appears-to-find-wrong-ijulia-kernel">Jupyter appears to find wrong <code>IJulia</code> kernel</h6> <p>Jupyter maintains a global list of installed kernels, which Quarto searches with <code>jupyter kernelspec list</code>. Often, Julia installation upgrades will change their paths, and Jupyter’s list of kernelspec files becomes stale. In that case, you will need to explicitly reinstall the <code>IJulia</code> kernel.</p> <h6 id="debugging-lua-filters">Debugging Lua filters</h6> <h6 id="useful-lua-helper-functions">Useful Lua helper functions</h6> <p>Quarto includes a number of useful Lua helper functions that can be used to debug Lua filters. These are available in the <code>quarto</code> module, and can be used as follows:</p> <pre><code>quarto.log.output(obj) -- prints a potentially complex object to the console</code></pre> <h6 id="filter-tracing">Filter tracing</h6> <p>Setting <code>QUARTO_TRACE_FILTERS=<FILENAME>.json</code> in your environment will cause Quarto to produce a trace of the Lua filters it runs, and write it to disk. This will be a file written to same the directory of the rendered file. We include an interactive Quarto document that can be used to visualize this trace, which you can find in the <code>quarto-cli</code> repository at <a href="https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/tree/main/tools/trace-viewer/trace-viewer.qmd"><code>tools/trace-viewer/trace-viewer.qmd</code></a>. Run <code>quarto preview trace-viewer.qmd</code>, and you will be shown two text fields, “Trace 1” and “Trace 2”. Drag and drop the JSON file onto either of the fields and you will be shown the trace. If you wish to compare two traces, drag them onto the two fields.</p> <aside id="footnotes" class="footnotes footnotes-end-of-document" role="doc-endnotes"> <hr /> <ol> <li id="fn1"><p>inline<a href="#fnref1" class="footnote-back" role="doc-backlink">↩︎</a></p></li> <li id="fn2"><p>inline<a href="#fnref2" class="footnote-back" role="doc-backlink">↩︎</a></p></li> <li id="fn3"><p>inline<a href="#fnref3" class="footnote-back" role="doc-backlink">↩︎</a></p></li> </ol> </aside> </body> </html>
